en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The New Commentary on the Sīlakkhandha-vagga of the Dīgha Nikāya.
The Introduction to the Composition of the Book:
He who, having taught the sublime Dhamma—profound, difficult to see, and excellent—established the Dispensation for a long time throughout the distant future. 1.
Having paid homage to him— the expert who has subdued his own latent tendencies, the one of great wisdom and great compassion—
together with the True Dhamma and the Community, who are worthy recipients of reverence.
I shall now set forth that which has ascended into the three councils of the excellent Long Discourses (Dīgha Āgama).
And the commentary upon that [work], a well-expounded explanation, was composed by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla himself;
it is a perfect elucidation of the meaning, which is subtle, profound, and difficult to perceive. 3–4.
Granted that it is such, yet having been handed down through successive tradition,
it contains many errors in both reading and meaning due to numerous scribal mistakes. Furthermore,
because of its brevity, it is very difficult for listeners to understand correctly.
Therefore, recollecting the request of my fellow celibates—
[I am] that lord of many elephants, the king who rules over various realms,
whose mind always maintains firm resolve for the purification of the Teaching. (6–7)
Relying on that, he reflected: "May this too be a support for me in illuminating the Teacher’s dispensation.
Thus, I shall begin the commentary on the Great Path with its underlying purpose.
Relying upon that purpose, and others as well as appropriate,
for the wise who desire the increase of the Wheel and seek the delight of the mind—
listen with concentrated attention to this [work] named *Sādhuvilāsini*. 10.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Book:

Composing this commentary—which elucidates the profound and difficult-to-comprehend meaning of the excellent *Dīgha Āgama*, which encompasses the three trainings that are skillful in various methods, profound, and diverse;

which has been praised by those who followed the Buddha; and which is endowed with qualities that inspire faith—the author is one capable of plunging into the dense thickets of his own tradition and those of other traditions.

This teacher, a great expounder, while performing the rites such as the homage to the Triple Gem and the purpose [of the work] at the beginning of his commentary, first offers homage to the Triple Gem and says: “O you whose heart is cooled by compassion,” and so forth.
Regarding this, teachers elaborate in many ways on the purpose of offering homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of a commentary. For they explain it thus:
“At the beginning of the commentary, the act of paying homage to the Teacher is for the purpose of generating confidence in the Teacher by way of the Dhamma’s being well-expounded,
and for the purpose of generating confidence in the Dhamma by way of revealing the Teacher’s state of teaching that which is not otherwise.
For it is through confidence in both of these that the accomplishment of great benefit occurs.”
Alternatively: "The words of salutation to the Triple Gem are for the purpose of making known one's own faith in the Triple Gem;

that, in turn, is for the purpose of pleasing the minds of the wise; that is for the purpose of causing them to grasp the commentary; and that is for the purpose of bringing about all forms of excellence. Alternatively:
"At the commencement of the commentary, the homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of announcing the purity of the source and the basis of the Dhamma to be commented upon."

"Furthermore, it is for the purpose of generating great respect among the wise regarding the expositions of the Dhamma, and for the purpose of accomplishing all benefit and happiness through right practice—such as the correct learning and retention of that [Dhamma]—which must be acquired by them.
Alternatively: "Because it is auspicious; because it is the preliminary duty in all undertakings;
because it has been practiced by the wise; and because others will follow one's example in the future."

And this is the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem within this commentary. Alternatively: “For one who desires to comment upon the Dhamma and Vinaya endowed with the fourfold profundity—just as for one entering the great ocean—even though they possess analytical wisdom, a great fear may arise;
yet this performance of homage and worship, born from recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem, brings about the destruction of that fear.”
And therefore, in this commentary, there is an act of homage to the Triple Gem.

Alternatively, it is for the purpose of establishing the world’s recognition of the Teacher as such in the Perfectly Enlightened One—the Teacher who truly exists—despite the world’s adherence to one who is not the Teacher;
and for the purpose of causing the world to relinquish its recognition of one who is not the Teacher; [and] having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
Furthermore, the act of homage in the commentary is for the purpose of avoiding the faults mentioned [in the verse], namely, "it burns itself.

Alternatively, by performing homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One, it is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those practicing the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) for the attainment of the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One;
and by performing homage to the True Dharma (*saddhamma*), it is for the attainment of the state of a Pacceka-Buddha.
"The act of homage in this commentary is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those practicing the vehicle of the *paccekabuddhas* by means of paying homage to the *saṅgha*,

and for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those practicing the vehicle of the disciples (*sāvakayāna*) for the attainment of the state of the ultimate *saṅgha* through the performance of homage to the *saṅgha*.
Alternatively, [it is] because treatises beginning with those on auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) are free from obstacles, endure for a long time, and are highly esteemed."
"Furthermore, the act of homage in this commentary is for the purpose of gladdening the minds of those who hold such a view.
Alternatively, "The act of homage in this commentary is for the purpose of ensuring that hearers achieve mastery, retention, and so forth, without obstacle, by means of the aforementioned homage.
For it was with the primary aim of assisting hearers that the teachers undertook the composition of this commentary."
"Sentences expressing homage are placed [at the beginning] because, otherwise, even without such a placement, the intended purpose would be accomplished through physical and mental homage alone;
so what is the point of this inclusion which only serves to increase the bulk of the text? and so forth.
We, however, shall demonstrate here only the purpose intended in this context; therefore, at the commencement of the commentary, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is performed.
It should be understood that the purpose is the completion of the commentary exactly as promised, without obstacle.
And this alone is the purpose intended by the Teacher here. For he will say: "Thus, with a mind clear in faith...
[and so on]... by its power. Indeed, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the sake of completing the commentary exactly as promised without obstacle.
Because of the worship of the Triple Gem, wisdom becomes sharp; and because of that sharpness of wisdom, the stains of lust and so forth are destroyed. For this has been said:
"At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion."
“...the mind becomes straight; at that time his mind is indeed upright,” and so forth.

Therefore, through the worship of the Triple Gem, which washes away defilements, proficiency in wisdom (*paññā*) is established. Alternatively, because the worship of the Triple Gem is a cause for concentration (*samādhi*) that has wisdom as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), there is proficiency in wisdom. For it is said:
“Moreover, Mahānāma, a noble disciple with an upright mind gains knowledge of the meaning (*atthaveda*), gains knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammaveda*),” and so on.
“One gains joy connected with the Dhamma; for one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil;
one whose body is tranquil feels happiness; and the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
Furthermore, the fact that concentration is the foundation for wisdom is stated in the passage: “One who is concentrated understands things as they really are.”
Therefore, having overcome weariness with such mature wisdom, he will bring the commentary on what was promised to completion.
For this reason it was said: "The act of paying homage to the Triple Gem... [is for the sake of] the state of proficiency in wisdom.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the completion of the work without hindrance is due to the increase in lifespan, beauty, happiness, and strength resulting from worship of the Triple Gem. By means of this homage to the Triple Gem...
For indeed, longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength increase. For this has been said:
"For one who is habitually respectful and constantly honors the elders, four things increase: longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength."
Therefore, it is said that "the completion of the task occurs through the increase of life, beauty, happiness, and strength" by means of worshiping the Triple Gem;
or rather, because worshiping the Triple Gem brings about the non-decline of inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāna*), its completion should be understood as occurring without obstacle.
For worshiping the Triple Gem brings about non-decline. Indeed, this has been said:

“Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that prevent decline. What are the seven? Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, friendship with the virtuous, and being easy to correct.
Thus, because there is no decline in inspired speech, one completes what was promised; hence it is said: “The Triple Gem... [and so forth].”

"It should be understood. Alternatively, it should be understood that because worship toward the objects of confidence (pasādavatthu) constitutes a preeminent state of merit (puñña), it is brought to completion without obstacle.
For worship toward the objects of confidence is indeed a preeminent merit. For this has been said:
"For one who worships those worthy of worship—the Buddhas or their disciples..."
"To those who have transcended conceptual proliferation, who have crossed over sorrow and lamentation—
those such as these, who have attained Nibbāna and are fearless from any quarter,
it is not possible for anyone to calculate the merit of one who honors them, even by so much as this."
And it is an excellence of merit that serves as the means for completing one’s intended undertaking. As it is said:
“This is a treasure that grants all desires to gods and humans;
whatever they aspire to, all that is obtained by means of this.”
And for one who has entered upon the means, there is indeed the completion of what is to be done; thus it is said: “...should be understood among the grounds for serene confidence...
In this way, the worship of the Triple Gem is an unsurpassed field of merit; its power is immeasurable as a preeminent excellence of merit that brings about full awakening.
Even amidst a worldly existence with its manifold obstacles, it is capable of destroying all defilements that constitute the bond of those obstacles.
And it wards off dangers such as fear. Therefore, it is well said:

"At the commencement of a commentary, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem should be understood as being for the purpose of completing the commentary without obstacle, in accordance with one's promise.
Thus, wishing to perform this homage to the Triple Gem along with its specific purpose, [the author]—since the remaining Gems are rooted in the Buddha-Gem—[proceeds].
First, he spoke in order to pay homage to him: “With a heart cooled by compassion... [etc. ...liberated from rebirth.
For the jewels of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha have the jewel of the Buddha as their root; and among those, the jewel of the Saṅgha has the jewel of the Dhamma as its root.

Furthermore, this state of affairs is such that: “The Blessed One is like the full moon; the Dhamma taught by him is like the mass of moonbeams; and those gladdened by the moonbeams produced by it...”
The Saṅgha is like the world,” and so forth—thus it should be clarified by means of the similes found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Alternatively, having established that he is the foremost of all beings, the Buddha is mentioned first; because he is the source and because the Dhamma is taught by him, the Dhamma is mentioned immediately after him;
and because they share in that Dhamma and because of their cultivation of it, the Saṅgha is mentioned immediately after that Dhamma. “Of all beings... [and so on].
The sequential order should be understood according to the method found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: first the Buddha is mentioned because he is the one who enjoins others to what is beneficial;

immediately after him, the Dhamma, because it is for the welfare of all beings; and immediately after that, the Saṅgha, because they have practiced the path for the attainment of welfare and have attained that welfare.
When making an obeisance to the Jewel of the Buddha, because it is preceded by praise rather than being a mere prostration, it is characterized by an excellence of distinction;

thus, with the words "whose heart is cooled by compassion" and so forth, he demonstrates that it is preceded by praise. For through an obeisance preceded by praise, there is an association with the Teacher’s preeminent qualities;
from that, his state of being unsurpassedly worthy of veneration; and by that, the fact that one's own obeisance has reached its proper field. By that—
Thus, it has been shown that his bowing while having gone to the field [of the Buddha] was the cause for the accomplishment of his intended purpose.

And in order to show that this [act] was preceded by praise, he intends to provide a commentary on that which is primarily characterized by compassion and wisdom—namely, the teaching of the Suttas—rather than a teaching of the Vinaya, which is primarily characterized by compassion, nor a teaching of the Abhidhamma, which is primarily characterized by wisdom; rather, it is characterized by both.
He begins the praise. For this is the custom of the Master: namely, that the praise is commensurate with the undertaking.
And for this very reason, at the beginning of the commentary on the teaching of the Vinaya, he made it centered on compassion: “He who, even in ten million eons... [of] that Great Compassionate One”;
and at the beginning of the commentary on the teaching of the Abhidhamma: “Like compassion... according to one’s preference.”
And the praise begins with wisdom as the primary factor. For the teaching of the Vinaya is primarily characterized by compassion;

even though it was established by one who possesses ordinary human nature, he laid down the training rules while listening to what ought not to be heard, asking what ought not to be asked, and saying what ought not to be said, out of sheer compassion regardless of the [disciples'] underlying dispositions (*āsaya*) and so forth.
For even one whose moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) have reached the highest limit [acts thus].
With a mind impelled by great compassion, the Blessed One spoke in the midst of the great assembly words such as "Sikharaṇī" and "Sambhinnā"—
terms that even worldly virtuous people ought to avoid— as well as words of censure according to the offense;
and with regard to the necessity of establishing various rules of training, he personally experienced physical hardship in Verañjā and other places.

Therefore, although the wisdom that originates the formulation of the Vinaya—being unique to [the Buddha]—possesses a preeminent function, just like the discourses on different planes of existence, conditions, modes, and periods, the function of compassion is even greater than that;

thus, the predominance of compassion in the teaching of the Vinaya is stated. For it is due to the predominance of the activity of compassion that the teaching is said to have compassion as its primary basis.

The teaching of the Abhidhamma, however, is dominated exclusively by wisdom (*paññā*), because it functions with particular excellence therein for the sake of the wisdom capable of penetrating the ultimate phenomena (*paramattha-dhamma*) according to their true nature.

The teaching of the Suttanta, on the other hand, is dominated by compassion and wisdom, because it functions among sentient beings for the sake of the wisdom capable of discerning the various distinctions such as the inclinations, latent tendencies, dispositions, and temperaments of those respective beings.
And because great compassion (mahākaruṇā) functions with particular pre-eminence therein.

For, through his teaching of the Suttantas, the Blessed One—abounding in meditative attainments (samāpatti)—established profound meanings and phrases within the mental continuums of those to be trained, in accordance with their inclinations and by way of conformity to their dispositions.
Therefore, it should be understood that the praise was made primarily in terms of compassion and wisdom, corresponding to the undertaking [of the teaching]. This is the collective meaning here.
This, however, is the analysis of the components: it is called *karuṇā* because it scatters (*kirati*).

The meaning is that it scatters away—that is, it removes—the suffering of others by causing a deficiency in its conditions. Alternatively, it is called *karuṇā* because it is extended (*kiriyati*) toward those who are suffering. Or else, it is called *karuṇā* because it consumes (*kiṇāti*);
for when there is the suffering of others, it consumes or afflicts the one who possesses compassion, or it means that it destroys the suffering of others. Regarding the suffering of others...
Alternatively, it is called *karuṇā* because the trembling of the virtuous (*sādhu*) causes heart-weariness (*hadaya-kheda*). Or else, *ka* means happiness (*sukha*);

it is *karuṇā* because it obstructs (*rundhati*) that [happiness]. For this [compassion], characterized by the desire to remove the suffering of others, obstructs—that is, hinders—the happiness of compassionate ones due to their disregard for their own happiness. In all these cases, the derivation of the word follows the rules of grammar (*saddasattha*).

It should be understood thus: it is called *sīta* because it is resorted to by those afflicted by heat; it is the alleviation (*abhisamana*) of heat. It is called *sītala* because it takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gaṇhāti*) that [coolness].
In the passage, "I shall hurl your mind away, or I shall split your heart (*hadaya*) asunder," the chest (*uro*) is referred to as "heart.
In the passage, "the kidney is the heart," it refers to the physical heart-organ (*hadayavatthu*). In the passage, "as if knowing heart with heart, he cuts it through," it refers to—

"Mind": here too, it is mind itself that is called "heart" (*hadaya*) in the sense of being internal. Or, according to etymologists, it is "heart" because it carries (*harati*) its own intrinsic nature;
they change the letter *ra* to *da*. One whose heart is cooled by compassion is "one whose heart is cooled by compassion" (*karuṇāsītalahadayo*);
that [person] is "one whose heart is cooled by compassion."
In this context, although it is true that loving-kindness (*mettā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) are found to cause a cooling state of mind—

due to their nature as meditative absorptions that do not abandon the happiness and welfare brought about for others, and because they are direct opposites to ill-will (*byāpāda*) and so forth, thereby functioning to sever the torment within the mental continuum of sentient beings— nevertheless,
their essential flavor (*rasa*) consists in the inability to endure the suffering of others, as they function in the mode of removing that suffering from others.
Non-violence toward beings and compassion are specifically stated to be the cause of that very coolness of mind, just as the tranquility of the mind (*cittapassaddhi*) is a sign of its coolness;

thus, their status as causes for the mind’s state of coolness is explained. Alternatively, it should be understood that by way of compassion, loving-kindness (*mettā*) and gladness (*muditā*) are also stated to be causes for the heart’s coolness.
For not every meaning is taught in its entirety in all instances; [the teaching] may also proceed according to the principles of predominance, association, or inseparability.
Because it is grasped exactly as it is being obtained. Furthermore, in this context, it is specifically the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) that has attained a pre-eminent state not shared by others;

for, through its inclusion within the six uncommon knowledges associated with that [knowledge], it serves as the basis for the distinction of uncommon knowledge, and—like the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa)—it has reached the state of Great Compassion by pervading its entire object-domain completely and without remainder.

It is stated [as such] because it serves as the cause for the coolness of the heart. Alternatively, although both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) possess the nature of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) that brings about the welfare of others and does not abandon their happiness, and although they are preeminently dependent on the coolness of the heart, compassion (*karuṇā*) alone is stated to be the cause of that coolness of the heart because it is the cause of all the specific qualities of a Buddha.
Indeed, all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their root.
For the Blessed One—whose heat of suffering in *saṃsāra* was extinguished by the power of compassion;
who, out of a desire to remove the suffering of others, remained untiring even for many incalculable eons while delighting in the accumulation of all the qualities that constitute a Buddha;
and who had attained mastery over the Dhamma—even when confronted with the causes that inflame the heart within the assembly of beings—[remained so].

"Even in the slightest degree, there was no alteration in the cooling state of his mind. Here, among these three alternatives, it should be understood that in the first alternative, the compassion is that which has reached the stage of Buddhahood without distinction;
in the second, it is likewise that which has attained the state of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
and in the third, it is the compassion of the Blessed One as it occurred throughout all three stages, beginning from the initial resolution (*paṭhamābhinīhāra*).
It is called *paññā* because it understands; the meaning is that it penetrates according to the true nature of things by way of various modes.
Or, it is called *paññā* because it makes known (*paññapeti*); the meaning is that it makes those respective objects clear.

That very same [wisdom], because it abandons the veil over the knowable and illuminates the true nature of phenomena through its various modes, is the "light of wisdom" (*paññā-pajjota*). For when one possessed of wisdom sits even in a single cross-legged posture, the ten-thousandfold world system...
She becomes one who has a single lamp. For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, there are these four lamps. Which four?
The moon-lamp, the sun-lamp, the fire-lamp, and the wisdom-lamp. These, bhikkhus, are the four lamps.
Of these four lamps, bhikkhus, the foremost is this: the wisdom-lamp.”
It is "dispelled by the light of wisdom" (*paññāpajjotavihata*) because it has been specifically destroyed and eradicated; this specific nature will be made clear further below.
It is called "delusion" (*moha*) because beings are deluded by it, or because it itself is deluded, or because its essence is merely deluding; it is thus ignorance (*avijjā*).
That very same [ignorance] is "the darkness of delusion" (*mohatama*), as it is like darkness due to its concealment of the true nature of objects. Furthermore, even though...
Since the word *tama* (darkness) denotes ignorance (*avijjā*) without the need for a comparison, its qualification by the word *moha* (delusion) present here is appropriate;
thus, there is a comparison. "One whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom" is *paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo*;
[the compound] refers to that person whose darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.
But surely, for all those whose taints are destroyed, the state of having dispelled the darkness of ignorance by the lamp of wisdom is possible;

so why is the praise of the Blessed One expressed by means of a distinguished quality not shared by others? Because of the possibility of a distinction not shared by others due to the abandonment [of defilements] along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).

For although all those whose taints are destroyed possess the state of having dispelled the darkness of ignorance by the lamp of wisdom, [there remain those who are] devoted through faith (*saddhādhimutta*).

Just as there is a distinction in the abandonment of defilements among those who have attained vision—namely, between disciples, paccekabuddhas, and perfectly enlightened buddhas—due to the latter’s abandonment of them along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanappahāna*), so too is there a distinction here.

Alternatively, because [the state of being a *tathāgata*] has been accomplished (*nipphāditattā*) within one's own continuum through the complete removal of the darkness of ignorance (*avijjandhakāra*) without depending on the instruction of others—and because of mastery over omniscience and the [ten] powers (*bala*) therein—[it is so called]. (cf. Ma. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1)
Because he has attained it himself, and because it was correctly set in motion within the mental continuum of others through the power of his preeminent teaching of the Dhamma,
the Blessed One alone is especially worthy of praise by virtue of having dispelled the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom.

And in this interpretation of the meaning, by the phrase "lamp of wisdom," both the wisdom of penetration, which dispels the delusion residing in one's own continuum, and [the wisdom that dispels the delusion] residing in the continua of others are intended.

And the wisdom of teaching is included by way of the general description or by the method of "single remainder" (ekasesanaya). However, it should be understood that it is not [included] solely as the wisdom of penetration (paṭivedhapaññā) as in the first alternative regarding the meaning.

Another method: because the Blessed One’s knowledge has the limit of all that is knowable, it possesses the capacity to awaken to the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of all phenomena that are objects of knowledge.

The praise of the Blessed One should be understood as being due to his state of unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*), which consists in the lamp of wisdom (*paññāpajjota*) that has destroyed the darkness of delusion (*mohatama*) obscuring the true nature of all things to be known (*sakalañeyyadhamma-sabhāva*).

Furthermore, in this interpretation of the meaning, "unobstructed knowledge" refers to the fact that he has attained the destruction of the darkness of delusion through the lamp of wisdom that is not shared by others.
It should be understood that by way of metaphorical designation for the cause, it is the dispelling of the darkness of delusion within one's own continuum.

For the abandonment of the obscurations to the knowable (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*)—which is the abandonment of the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*)—is indeed the perfection of the resolution (*abhinīhāra*).

However, because it serves as the cause for the dispelling of the darkness of delusion in the continua of others, unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) itself is spoken of as the "dispelling of the darkness of delusion" by way of metaphorical designation for the fruit. Thus, it is called "unobstructed knowledge."

And it is indeed omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), by means of which one performs the reviewings of the teaching of the Dhamma. For these two types of knowledge are in fact one in meaning. Because its object consists of all conditioned and unconditioned conventional phenomena without exception, omniscient knowledge is called "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) by way of its unimpeded movement due to the absence of any obstruction therein;
this is from the perspective of the engagement with its objective domain.
However, it is stated as being divided into two for the purpose of showing that these are not shared by others, within the classification of the six kinds of unique knowledge (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*).

What, then, is the reason here that only the "eradication of ignorance" (*avijjāsamugghāta*) is taken as the praise of the Blessed One by way of the excellence of abandonment, and not the "supreme and complete abandonment of all defilements"? It is said: by the very mention of that abandonment...
Indeed, because it illuminates the total eradication of all defilements through its singleness of purpose, the abandonment of defilements without remainder is understood here.
For there is no such defilement that is not abandoned by the eradication of ignorance without remainder.

Alternatively, just as knowledge (*vijjā*) is the cause for the arising of all wholesome states and for the turning back from *saṃsāra*, [ignorance is the cause] for the arising of all unwholesome states without remainder.

Since ignorance alone is the primary cause for the occurrence of saṃsāra, and because the eradication of the entire mass of defilements is established by the very statement regarding its destruction, it is this [ignorance] alone that is grasped.
Alternatively, because ignorance is the summit of all defiled phenomena, its eradication alone is grasped. As it has been said:
“Know that ignorance is the seal, and true knowledge is that which destroys the seal;
it is joined with faith, mindfulness, concentration, desire, and energy.
Regarding the phrase “the protector of the world of humans and devas,” here, in the first sense, a being is called a “human” (nara) without distinction.
But here, by the second nature, he is indeed a human male (*manujapurisa*); otherwise, the word "world" (*loka*) would be inapplicable.

For just as a being who, by his first nature, lies (*seti*) or exists (*pavattati*) in a former high place (*pure uccaṭṭhāne*) in the sense of being superior to other natures is called a "male" (*purisa*), so too, because he leads others to the state of being eldest (*jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ neti*), he is a "man" (*nara*). This applies even when he has become a son or a brother.
For it is said in the *Nāvāvimānavannanā*: "A person stands in the place of a father even toward his mother’s elder sisters and younger sisters, let alone toward those who have become his wives.
By applying the grammatical principle of *ekasesa* (single remainder) or by forming a plural compound (*puthuvacananta-viggaha*), [the term] *narā* [is explained]:
*maraṇaṃ* is *maro*; those who do not possess that [death] are *amarā*. Together with humans (*narehi*) and with the immortals (*amarehi*), it is thus *sanarāmara*. *Garati*.
It is "heavy" (*garu*) because it rises up, becomes elevated, and becomes manifest; for the word *gara* signifies rising.
Furthermore, it is called "heavy" in the sense of being burdensome, like a stone parasol.
[This applies] toward mother, father, and teachers, and toward that which is difficult to digest and that which is insignificant.
The word *garu* occurs in reference to those who have risen high, to those who perform services such as nursing, and likewise to specific distinctions of excellence.

Here, however, it refers to the Tathāgata, the teacher of the entire world. Some, moreover, explain that by taking both *garu* and *gurū* as two forms, they denote the sense of being "heavy" (i.e., venerable).
Some say that the word *garu* refers to a teacher, whereas the word *guru* denotes a teacher; this should not be accepted.

For within the scope of the canonical texts (*pāḷi*), when all the aforementioned meanings are to be expressed, only the word *garu* is to be sought, because we see the form *gārava*—a derivative (*taddhita*) word ending in *-va* with the vowel lengthened—from the substitution of the letter *a* by the letter *ā*.
However, in the scope of the Sanskrit language, only the word *guru* is to be sought.
Because the word ending in a *taddhita* suffix is seen in a different form due to the increase (*vuddhi*) of the vowel *u*. "Together with men and gods, that world" is *sanarāmaraloka*;
"the teacher of that" is *tathā*; [thus] "the teacher of the world together with men and gods" (*sanarāmaralokagaru*).

They also read it as "the teacher of the world of men and gods" (*sanaramarūlokagaru*), which is likewise appropriate because it is an Ariya verse, both in terms of its grammatical function and its meaning. For, in terms of meaning:
Even though they possess long lifespans, because they are subject to death according to their allotted limit, these beings are called "immortals" (*amara*).
By this, he shows that the Blessed One is a benefactor even to those remaining beings—just as he is to gods and humans—by bringing about specific qualities appropriate to each.
But surely, in this context, gods and humans are the primary subjects; why then is it said that they are not the primary ones?

Why is it explained [in this way]? Because it must be grasped according to its primary significance in terms of meaning (*attha*). For the sequence of words (*saddakkama*) is one thing, and the sequence of meanings (*atthakkama*) is another;
therefore, one should not demand that the status of being primary or secondary follow the sequence of the words.

In such compound expressions, even that which is primary is explained as if it were secondary, as in the case of "the assembly together with the king" (*sarājikāya parisāya*); therefore, in all instances, it is from the meaning alone [that the primary sense is determined].
The intended meaning must be sought, not merely the literal expression. As the ancients have said:
"The Protector spoke of the meaning as the refuge, not the letter, O Great Sage, who benefits the world."
"Therefore, without taking delight in the objects of the senses,
a wise person should fix his mind upon the goal.
Herein, although the world is threefold— consisting of sentient beings, formations, and the receptacle world— it is the state of weightiness that is intended here.
The meaning should be understood in terms of the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*), for it is precisely that which is capable of showing respect that is appropriate [here].

For that is called "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, as well as their ripening, are "found" (*lokyanti*) therein; and those skilled in grammar maintain that the word *loka* has the sense of "seeing.

Furthermore, by the mention of "immortals" (*amara*) here, the deities born of rebirth (*upapattideva*) are intended. According to another method, the word *loka* here has the sense of a "collection" (*samūha*).
It is so called because it is perceived and designated as a whole. "Together with men" (*sanara*) means those very beings who are immortal (*amara*);

thus, "the world of men and immortals" (*sanarāmara*). It should be construed in the same manner as the previous method. Furthermore, by the term *amara*, both the deities of rebirth (*upapatti-deva*) and the deities of purity (*visuddhi-deva*) are included.
For they too, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), are immortal due to the absence of death. In this [context]...

However, in the eighth alternative, only "humans and gods" (narāmarā) are mentioned by way of an inclusive designation (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*), as in the expression “the Teacher of gods and humans. For indeed,

[he is so called] because he possesses immeasurable and incomparable power and qualities, because he is the ultimate benefactor to the generation including gods and humans through his unsurpassed perfection of application— which is intent upon providing for their welfare and happiness without exception and preceded by the removal of all that is harmful— and because of his being the supreme helper to the world of gods and humans.
And the Blessed One, the supreme among all beings, is the object of reverence for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems;

his status as an object of reverence is unsurpassed and not shared by others. Granted that the Blessed One is indeed venerable because he is likewise beneficial to women, it should be understood that he is described here in the masculine gender in order to indicate the preeminent state of the world.
As for the grammarians (Neruttikas), however, [they maintain this] in a context where no distinction is intended.
They desire it to be demonstrated in such a way that [it is said]: “Men, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having paid homage, departed.
And so they have said: “It should be understood that when there is no specific distinction made, a word may be expressed with either a neuter gender or a masculine gender.”
Regarding the word *vandeti* here: it occurs in the present tense and in the fifth and seventh case endings;
the word *vanda* functions in these three places.
But here, because no other [meaning] is possible while the word is being employed, the meaning must be taken according to the "supreme person" (*uttamapurisa*), namely:
"I pay homage. The teachers accept the word *vandati* in the senses of bowing and praising; therefore, one should connect it by supplying either the word *sugata* or the word *nātha*.
He whose going (*gata*) or movement (*gamana*) is beautiful (*sobhana*) is a *sugata*. And here, "going" refers to—
There are two kinds of bodily movement: the movement of knowledge and the movement of the body. The movement of the body is twofold: approaching those who are to be trained and ordinary movement.
For the Blessed One, approaching those who are to be trained is invariably beautiful because it accomplishes their welfare and happiness;

likewise, due to his physical body being adorned with the primary and secondary marks, it is free from defects such as haste, slowness, stumbling, dragging, pressing, contraction, crookedness, and confusion.
His gait is like that of a majestic swan, a bull, an elephant, or a lion, yet it is also his natural stride;

and his movement of wisdom, though endowed with the distinguished qualities of stainless, vast compassion, mindfulness, energy, and so forth, is truly beautiful in its faultlessness from the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*) until the attainment of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Alternatively, "by means of self-born wisdom (*sayambhūñāṇa*), fully understanding the entire world through the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*)," [he proceeds] rightly.

He who has gone and understood is the Sugata. For that which is the meaning of "going" (gati) is the meaning of "awakening" (buddhi); and that which is the meaning of "awakening" is the meaning of "going.
Likewise, by abandoning the origin of the world through the realization of abandonment and bringing it to the state of non-arising, he has rightly gone beyond; thus he is the Sugata.
By means of the realization of direct knowledge of the cessation of the world, he has rightly gone to and attained it.
The Sugata: he is called the Sugata because he has gone rightly and entered upon the path leading to the cessation of the world through the development and clear realization [of the truths].

This meaning is to be clarified by the method of exposition found in the *Niddesa*, such as: “He does not go back to, does not return to, and does not re-enter those defilements which have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry; thus he is the Sugata.”
Another method: He has gone to, or attained, the beautiful perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), or indeed Nibbāna; thus he is the *Sugata*.
Alternatively, he is the *Sugata* because he speaks (*gadati*) correctly (*sammā*) to those to be trained words that are real, true, conducive to welfare, and appropriate to the occasion and timely;
here, the letter *da* is changed to *ta*, hence "that Sugata. By way of rebirth through meritorious and demeritorious kamma...
"Gatis" means destinations, which are specific types of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). These are fivefold, distinguished as hell and so forth.

Because all karma leading to existence has been rendered incapable of ripening through the attainment of the Noble Path, one is "released from the destinations" (*gativimutta*) by being dissociated and liberated from all five of them.
For the gods who go to ever-higher existences [do so] in accordance with the time when the respective karmic results are due to be given.
Although they are freed from this or that existence, they are merely freed [from it], but not freed by way of dissociation;
and because they are included within the realms of existence (*gati*), the noble path has not turned back the karma leading to those various existences. The Blessed One is not like that.
Rather, the Blessed One, having become dissociated in the manner described above, is truly freed. Therefore, in this regard, there is no place where the Blessed One...
This shows that he is not included within the [mundane] destinies (gati). For this reason, the Blessed One is called "the God beyond gods. Thus he said:
"By what one might be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or as a bird;
by what one might go to the state of a yakkha, or attain human status—"
“Those taints of mine have been exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.

For since the kamma and defilements that lead to various states of existence were abandoned by the Supreme Path right at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, there is no inclusion of the Blessed One within any such state;
thus, the Blessed One is absolutely free from all realms of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings.
"Completely liberated. Alternatively, although he is indeed liberated from those states of existence even by means of the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining,

it should be understood that this verse praises him specifically by means of the phrase "one whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," which is included right here [in this context], thereby extolling him even by way of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.
In this context, however, the praise of the Blessed One is performed in two ways, by way of his own attainment of welfare and his practice for the welfare of others.

Among these, "attainment of one's own welfare" consists of the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge, the absolute abandonment of the defilements along with their latent tendencies, and the realization of *nibbāna* without residue;
whereas [the practice for the welfare of others] consists of the application of teaching the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering, by one whose mind is indifferent to gain, honor, and the like.

Even toward beings such as Devadatta who were hostile, his constant aspiration for their welfare and his arrival at the proper time for the ripening of the knowledge of those beings to be trained constitute what is called "practice for the benefit of others through intention.

This practice for the benefit of others is twofold—by way of intention and by way of application—and the attainment of one's own welfare is threefold; all these are appropriately revealed in this verse. "With a heart cooled by compassion" [is said].

For by this [term], through its sense of "dwelling" (āsayato), there is the practice for the welfare of others; and by the word *sugata* in the sense of "well-spoken" (sammā gadana-), there is the practice for the welfare of others through application (*payogato*).

By these phrases—"one whose darkness of delusion has been dispelled by the lamp of wisdom, liberated from the [six] destinies"—and by the word *sugata* in the sense of the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, there is the threefold accomplishment of one’s own welfare.
Furthermore, by that [word] in its remaining sense, and by the phrase "venerable to the world of humans and gods," [the welfare of others is shown].
By this, the entire accomplishment of one’s own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others have been elucidated.

Alternatively, the praise has been performed in three ways by way of cause, fruit, and assistance to beings. Therein, "cause" refers to the conjunction with great compassion and the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment;
both of these are expressed by the first phrase, both according to the literal meaning and by implication.
And this has been explained. The fruit, however, is fourfold by way of the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of power, and the perfection of the form-body.
Therein, the perfection of knowledge consists of the knowledge of the path which has omniscience as its proximate cause, and the ten powers and other knowledges rooted therein.
The perfection of abandonment is the bringing about of the state of absolute non-arising for all defilements along with their latent tendencies. Regarding the accomplishment of whatever is desired...

Sovereignty is the perfection of power; however, the perfection of the physical body is the excellence of the personal form adorned with the primary and secondary marks, which serves as the consecration for the eyes of the entire world.
Among these, the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment are indicated by the second word and by the term *sugata* in the sense of the penetration of the Truths;
the perfection of power is indicated by the third word; and the perfection of the physical body is indicated by the sense of "one who possesses a beautiful body and gait."
Because that [supreme welfare] is absent without the perfection of the primary and secondary marks (lakkhaṇa-anubyañjana), it is indicated by the word *sugata*.

Both types of practice for the benefit of others as previously described constitute the excellence of assistance to beings; furthermore, it should be understood that this is manifested by the word *sugata* in the sense of "one who has gone rightly" (*sammā gadana*).
Moreover, by means of this verse, the Teacher has [indicated] full enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), its root, the practice thereof, and many other qualities of a Buddha.
These things have been made manifest. For this is the nature of teachers: namely, to make known some further meaning by whatever means possible.
How so? By the phrase "whose heart is cooled by compassion," he shows the root of Perfect Enlightenment.
For the Blessed One, his mind impelled by Great Compassion, having made the resolution to lift sentient beings out from the mire of *saṃsāra*, gradually fulfilled the perfections (*pāramīs*).
Having fulfilled [the perfections], he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttara-sammāsambodhi); thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment.

By the phrase, “The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom,” he demonstrates perfect enlightenment. For the knowledge of the supreme path (aggamagga-ñāṇa) has the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), and the knowledge of omniscience has the knowledge of the supreme path as its proximate cause; this is what is called “perfect enlightenment. By the term *sugata*, in the sense of “one who has gone rightly,” [he shows] perfect enlightenment.
It demonstrates the practice by way of elucidating the Middle Way— free from the two extremes of attachment to sensual pleasure and self-mortification,
as well as the dogmatic adherence to eternalism and nihilism— which is supported by compassion and wisdom and serves as the basis for overcoming dullness and agitation.

By contrast, it shows through the others the purpose of Right Enlightenment, distinguished by its primary and secondary aspects, which consists here in the crossing over of sentient beings from the great flood of saṃsāra.

There is the primary [purpose] and the other, which is secondary. Among these, by means of the primary purpose he demonstrates the practice for the benefit of others; by the other, the attainment of his own welfare;

and by both together, he makes manifest that the Blessed One belongs to the fourth category among the four types of persons—namely, those who have entered upon the practice for their own welfare, and so forth.
And by that, he demonstrates his unsurpassed status as one worthy of offerings and his supreme [excellence].
It clarifies the state of being worthy of homage and one’s own status as a field for such homage.

Furthermore, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the perfection of all mundane qualities is shown through the illumination of extraordinary qualities that have attained a sublime state among worldly things;

and by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), the perfection of all supramundane qualities is shown through the illumination of the knowledge of the path, which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause.
For the meaning established by the inclusion of both [compassion and wisdom] is elaborated upon in such passages as, "He who is honored by the world of men and gods.

Furthermore, by the mention of compassion, he shows the Blessed One’s approach that is free from defilements; by the mention of wisdom, he shows his departure [from the world]. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, he shows the Blessed One’s activity in accordance with worldly convention, since compassion is the domain of worldly discourse; by the mention of wisdom, [he shows his transcendence of it].

Non-transgression beyond worldly convention. For, through a lack of understanding of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena, one transcends their intrinsic nature and clings to [the notions of] a "being" and so forth.
Likewise, by the mention of compassion, he shows the dwelling in the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*);
by the mention of wisdom, he shows the unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths, and the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*catu-paṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence; the remaining unique knowledges, since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is included by the mention of "compassion";
the six direct knowledges (abhiññā); the knowledges of being unshakable by the eight assemblies; the ten powers; the fourteen qualities of a Buddha; the sixteen modes of conduct of knowledge;
the eighteen attributes of a Buddha; the forty-four bases of knowledge; and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
By means of these and many other such classifications of wisdom, he demonstrates the range of his knowledge. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, he shows the perfection of his conduct;
by the mention of wisdom, the perfection of his true knowledge (*vijjā*). By the mention of compassion, there is self-mastery; by the mention of wisdom, mastery over the Dhamma.
By the mention of compassion, there is the state of being a protector of the world; by the mention of wisdom, the state of being one's own protector. Likewise...
By the mention of compassion, there is the quality of being a benefactor; by the mention of wisdom, there is gratitude. By the mention of compassion, there is the absence of self-torment;
by the mention of wisdom, there is the absence of tormenting others. Or else, by the mention of compassion, there is the accomplishment of the qualities that make one a Buddha;

by the mention of wisdom, there is the accomplishment of the state of Buddhahood. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, there is the saving of others; by the mention of wisdom, there is the saving of oneself.
Thus, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the state of having a mind that favors all beings is shown;

and by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), the state of having a mind detached from all phenomena is shown. Furthermore, among all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion is the beginning because it is the primary cause, and wisdom is the end because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing the beginning and the end, all the qualities of a Buddha [are indicated].
...are thus shown. Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*)—preceded by the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*)—is shown;
for virtue has compassion as its source, since it proceeds from the abstention from killing and so forth, and that [compassion] is associated with the three jhānas.

By the term "wisdom" (*paññā*), the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) is indicated. Furthermore, virtue is the beginning of all the qualities of a Buddha, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end.
"Conclusion": In this way, all the Buddha-qualities are shown to be excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, because they are shown by way of method (*nayato*).
For this indeed is the means for showing the Buddha-qualities without remainder, namely, grasping them by way of method;
otherwise, who indeed would be capable of showing the Blessed One’s qualities word-for-word without omission? Therefore he said:
“Even if a Buddha were to speak the praises of another Buddha for an entire eon,
without speaking of anything else,
that eon would come to an end after a very long time.”
"The praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

And for this very reason, when the Venerable Sāriputta Thera was questioned by the Blessed One regarding the delimitation of the Buddha's qualities, he rejected [the attempt to measure them] by saying, "Certainly not, Bhante," and then stated in the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*: "But, Bhante, the inference from the Dhamma is known to me."

Thus, having briefly performed an act of homage preceded by a praise of the Blessed One for his entirety of omniscient qualities, he now says “The Buddha too,” and so forth, while performing an act of homage preceded by a praise of the True Dhamma as well.
Herein, this is the summary meaning together with the connection of the words: the Buddha, who is endowed with the multitude of various aforementioned qualities...
Having developed that Dhamma known as the Noble Path, together with the Dhamma of the preliminary practice leading to it, and having realized that Dhamma known as the fruit and Nibbāna—
whether together with the Dhamma of the scriptures and the Dhamma of practice— he attained the state of Buddhahood known as Perfect Enlightenment.
He also pays homage to that Dhamma, which is stainless and unsurpassed.

Regarding this, the meaning of the word *buddha* should first be understood according to the method of exposition [found in the Niddesa], such as: "One who has awakened to the truths is a Buddha; one who awakens the generation is a Buddha," and so forth.
Alternatively, by means of attaining the knowledge of the supreme path, [one awakens from] the sleep of delusion together with its latent tendencies.

He is called "Buddha" in the sense of awakening (*jāgaraṇa*) and blossoming (*vikasana*), because of his absolute departure [from defilements] and because he has blossomed through the attainment of omniscient knowledge adorned by an immeasurable multitude of qualities.
Alternatively, because there is no knowable object whatsoever that remains unawakened to him,
and because he does not take up any specific knowable object as an object of action, there is an absence of the desire for verbal expression regarding such an object of action.
Only a designation of the agent is obtained by way of the sense of "understanding"; therefore, he may also be called "Buddha" because he has awakened (buddhavā).
For when there is no mention of a specific portion, the fact that what is to be grasped is without limitation is understood, just as in the expression, "one who has been initiated does not give.
And this being the case, it should be understood that the word *buddha* is established in its grammatical function as the agent alone, independent of any specific object, according to its meaning.

However, the Buddha is that continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) which has been thoroughly permeated by the perfections (pāramitā), wherein all defilements (kilesa) have been utterly destroyed and shattered along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā) by means of self-awakened knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa); it is the substratum for an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). As it is said:

"Buddha refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū), teacherless, who has personally awakened to the truths regarding phenomena never heard before, and who has therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers (bala)."

The word *api* (even) is used here in the sense of esteem (*sambhāvana*). By it, he demonstrates esteem for the Dhamma, showing: "If even that Blessed One, endowed with such distinguished qualities, having developed and realized this very Dhamma, attained the state of a Buddha—what need is there to mention others who have attained the status of disciples and so forth?
The term *buddhabhāva* refers to perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). For by means of that [Dhamma] as the instrumental cause...

The name "Buddha" is applied to the Blessed One by means of the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) which has the knowledge of the supreme path (aggamaggañāṇa) as its proximate cause, and by means of the knowledge of the supreme path which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause; and the knowledge that takes that [name] as its object also occurs. That very thing is what is called here "the state" (bhāva). For it is said:
"That by which the words 'intellect' (buddhi) and 'awakened one' (buddha) come into being is the state (bhāva). Indeed, they speak thus:
“By whatever sign cognition and sound proceed, that very sign is expressed by means of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapaccaya*).
*Bhāvetvā* means having produced or having increased.
*Sacchikatvā* means having made manifest before one’s eyes. The word *ca* (and) [is used] both as *ceva* and as *ca*.

And the word *ca* (and) signifies a conjunction of both [meanings]. By those two words, he conjoins that the Blessed One did not attain the state of a Buddha merely through the cultivation of the Dhamma, nor merely through its realization, but rather through both together.
"Attained" (*upagata*) means reached or achieved; this is to be connected with the phrase "the state of a Buddha. "Free from stain" (*vītamala*)...
Here, it is "vīta" because it comes (eti) or proceeds by way of being separated (viraha). It is "vītamala" because it is separated from impurity (mala), or that which has its impurity separated;

thus, it is "vītamala. The reading "gatamala" is also seen; in that case, even though the word *gata* is without a prefix, it should be understood as expressing the sense of separation (*viraha*), just like when it is with a prefix, because verbal roots have multiple meanings. It goes (*gacchati*), it departs (*apagacchati*).
It is the Dhamma because it has gone; or, the stain has gone—this is a compound according to the previous method. It is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) because it is devoid of anything superior.
It is called Dhamma because it holds (dhāreti) one who practices as instructed, preventing them from falling into the states of misery (apāya) or into saṃsāra;
thus, it refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. This is because it reveals that [Dhamma] and because the methods of realization and comprehension are applicable to it.
The Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyattidhamma) is also included here.

For it is stated in the Commentary: "He reached the ocean of the Abhidhamma method; he mastered the three Piṭakas. Likewise, because it is said, "having developed and realized that Dhamma," it includes, along with the perfections (pāramitā)—which constitute the qualities that make one a Buddha through their fitness for development and realization—the [other factors].
It should be understood that the preliminary training in higher virtue and the others are also included here.
For these too are "stainless" because they are free from opposing factors, and "unsurpassed" because they are not shared by anyone else.

But how is it that the Blessed One, having developed and realized these, attained the state of a Buddha? It is said: for the sake of beings' escape from the suffering of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
What is the Great Resolve? It is that disposition which is refined by the endurance of great compassion, and which, through the cultivation and realization of supreme qualities—
such as generosity, self-control, and restraint— which are purified by the excellence of wisdom, has been practiced with diligence, continuity,
and completeness regarding kamma and other factors for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons.
Having attained mastery, possessing wonderful and inconceivable great power, and having reached the supreme pinnacle of perfection in higher virtue (*adhisīla*) and higher mind (*adhicitta*),
the Blessed One dispatched the Great Vajra-knowledge through twenty-four million four hundred thousand aspects regarding the nature of conditions (*paccayākāra*),
thereby attaining the state of Buddhahood known as unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*).

With this verse, however, he praises the True Dhamma by means of numerous qualities such as the perfection of knowledge (*vijjā*) and liberation (*vimutti*), each according to its appropriateness. How so?

For here, by the word "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*), he praises it through the perfection of knowledge; by the word "having realized" (*sacchikatvā*), he praises it through the perfection of liberation.
Likewise, by the first [word] he praises it through the perfection of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), and by the second, through the perfection of deliverance (*vimokkha*). By the first...
Or, by the first, through the perfection of concentration, and by the second, through the perfection of attainment.

Or else, by the first, in the sense of the knowledge of destruction (*khaya-ñāṇa*), and by the second, in the sense of the knowledge of non-arising (*anuppāda-ñāṇa*). Or, by the first, through its similarity to lightning, and by the second, through its similarity to a thunderbolt.

Or, by the first, through the attainment of dispassion (*virāga*), and by the second, through the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). Likewise, by the first, in the sense of the state of deliverance (*niyyāna*),...
He praises the Dhamma by means of the second aspect as the state of escape. Or, he praises it by means of the first aspect as the state of cause, and the second as the state of the unconditioned.
Or, he praises it by means of the first aspect as the state of vision, and the second as the state of seclusion.

Or, he praises it by means of the first aspect as the state of sovereignty, and the second as the state of the Deathless. Alternatively: "Having developed that Dhamma, he attained the state of a Buddha."
By this [phrase], he praises the Dhamma for its being well-expounded; by the phrase "having realized it," he praises it for its being directly visible.

Likewise, by the first [phrase] he praises it for its being timeless, and by the second for its being inviting one to come and see. Or, by the first he praises it for its leading onward, and by the second for its being personally verifiable.
Or, by the first he praises it together with the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those in training, along with the preliminary virtues and so forth.
With the second [phrase], he praises the Dhamma together with the unconditioned element by means of the qualities of those beyond training (*asekkha*).
By the term “stainless” (*vītamala*), he praises the Dhamma for its purity through the indication of the absence of defilement;

by the term “unsurpassed” (*anuttara*), he praises it for its perfection through the indication of the absence of anything else more distinguished. Alternatively, the first [phrase] refers to the perfection of abandonment (*pahāna-sampadā*).
By the second [term], it is due to the perfection of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Or, by the first, it is due to its fitness for the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*).

For by the quality of cultivation, it is the eradicator of the stains of defilement; therefore, by this, he states the fruit of the act of cultivation. By the second, it is due to its fitness for the fruit of realization (*sacchikiriyāphala*).
For because there is nothing further to be done beyond that, and because it is not shared with others, its state of being unsurpassed (*anuttara*) arises from the production of realization.
Therefore, by this [verse], he expresses the fruit of realization.
Thus, having briefly paid homage preceded by praise for the True Dhamma through all its qualities of the True Dhamma,
he now speaks the words beginning with "of the legitimate sons of the Sugata" while paying homage preceded by praise for the Noble Saṅgha as well.
In this context, "of the Sugata" is a statement of relationship; it is to be connected with the word "of sons. Those who exist in, are born from, or have grown in the breast (*uras*) are *orasā*.
Among the four kinds of sons—the one born of oneself (*attaja*), the one born of the field (*khettaja*), the apprentice (*antevāsika*), and the one given (*dinnaka*)—the son born of oneself is meant.
However, because they resemble him, the noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) are called "sons of the breast. For just as among humans...
Just as biological sons, by virtue of being born from one’s own body, are special sharers in the inheritance belonging to their father,

so too these [disciples], at the conclusion of hearing the True Dhamma, by virtue of being born through noble birth, are special sharers in the inheritance of the bliss of liberation and the jewel of the Dhamma belonging to the Blessed One.
Alternatively, through the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, they [attain] the plane of the Noble Ones.

Entering and having entered [the path], the noble disciples—by virtue of being born from the effort generated by the Blessed One’s breast—are worthy, even without resorting to figurative designation, of being called "sons from the breast" (*orasā*) in the primary sense alone.
For it was by observing their disposition, latent tendencies, conduct, and inclination, and by reflecting upon their faults, that the Blessed One took them to heart;
he restrained them from what is blameworthy and established them in what is blameless, thereby nourishing the body of Dhamma consisting of virtue and the other factors.
They were brought up. As the Blessed One said in the *Itivuttaka*: “I, monks, am a brahmin...
you are my sons, born from my breast, born from my mouth,” and so forth. Is it not the case that even a teaching delivered by a disciple brings about the state of a Noble One?
True; however, because it is rooted in him and lacks the specific characteristics [of a Buddha’s own teaching], it is called “the Blessed One’s Dhamma-teaching.”
Thus they have come to be so designated; therefore, their status as the Blessed One’s own legitimate sons (*orasaputta*) alone should be asserted.
By this, he shows that among the four kinds of sons, the Noble Saṅgha possesses the status of being "sons born of oneself" (*attaja*).

They are called "sons" (*putta*) because they purify and cleanse their own family, or because they fill the hearts of their parents; these include those "born of oneself" and the others. However, the Noble Ones [purify] by means of cleansing the thread of the Dhamma.
They are called "sons of the Blessed One" because they please his mind through practice in accordance with the Dhamma and because they resemble him;
[the word] "of them" connects with the term "multitude.
He is Māra because he kills (māreti) and afflicts virtue by acting as a cause for defilement; he is Devaputtamāra. He binds others...

It is called an *senā* (army) because it binds (*bandhati*) and comes together (*eti*). Likewise, it is Māra’s army. They are called "crushers of Māra’s army" (*mārasenamathanā*) because they crush and scatter both Māra and his army.

Regarding the phrase "of those who crush Māra and Māra’s army," although one might expect it to be stated as "māramārasenamathanānaṃ," it is expressed in this way by means of the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpekaśeṣa* (retaining only one member of a group that is partially identical).
Alternatively, by the proximity of the word "Māra," the word "army" (*senā*) should be understood as "Māra’s army" due to the requirements of the metrical composition of the verse.

And here, the vowel is short. Although there is a reading in some places as “mārasenamaddanānaṃ,” that is indeed incorrect, because this verse belongs to the category of the Ariyavansa (Noble Lineage).
For surely, at the time of attaining the Path, neither a Devaputta-Māra nor Māra’s army discourages the Noble Disciples, just as they did not discourage the Blessed One;
so why has it been stated thus? [The answer lies in] the reason for their being discouraged...
Because they have been crushed. For when the defilement—the cause for which those [beings] are to be disparaged—is crushed, they too are said to be crushed.

Alternatively, because the host of the power of the defilements enters into the role of an ally for the Devaputta Māra in slaying the qualities—just as it does for the Māras of the aggregates, formative activities, and Death—the "army of Māra" is spoken of here in this way, as the Blessed One said:
“Sensual pleasures are your first army; the second is called discontent.
The third is hunger and thirst for you; the fourth is said to be craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor for you; the sixth is called fear.”
Doubt is your seventh, and flattery and obstinacy are your eighth.
Gain, fame, honor,
and that reputation acquired through wrong means— these are yours.
He who exalts himself and despises others— this,
Namuci, is your army, the assault of Kaṇha.
“No coward overcomes it, but having conquered it, one gains happiness.

And that river of defilements, which consists of one thousand five hundred divisions—or rather, infinite divisions—was specifically churned, shattered, and destroyed by those noble disciples with the weapons of the qualities such as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and serenity;
therefore, they are called “the destroyers of Māra’s army. In this context, “churning” (vilothana) means—

It means shattering or destroying. Furthermore, because it crushes the Māra of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*), the Māra of the formative forces (*abhisankhāramāra*), the Māra of death (*maccumāra*), and the Māra of the son of a deva (*devaputtamāra*), as well as the defilement-māra (*kilesamāra*) which is reckoned as an army by virtue of its association with those [others], the meaning “crusher of Māra’s army” (*mārasenamathana*) should also be understood.

And this being so, the meaning is complete through the state of crushing the five-fold Māra. For even noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), by way of the full understanding (*pariññā*) that abandons the origin (*samudaya*)...
They "crush" the Māra of the aggregates by making them cease altogether through the lack of any companions;
the Māra of volitional formations by making them cease altogether through the destruction of their power and the transcending of their domain; the Māra of Death by the same means;
and the Māra of the Devas' sons by the abandonment of utter eradication through making them cease altogether. By this, however, [it is shown] that they are his legitimate sons.

The word "cause" (kāraṇa) shows that they are born after [the Buddha] among his three sons; for they are the Blessed One’s legitimate sons because they crush Māra’s army, and they are "born after" him.
"Of eight" is a limitation by number;
by this, although there are many hundreds of thousands of different divisions among them according to their respective distinctions, [they are still counted as eight].

He shows that these do not exceed this numerical limit because they do not transcend the states of one standing on the path or one established in the fruit, through the classification of the Dhamma as the noble state, the path, and the fruit.
The word *pi* (or *api*), used in an inappropriate place due to reasons such as metrical play (*padalīḷā*), should be joined here with the term "the Noble Saṅgha" (*ariyasaṅgha*).
By doing so, it includes not only the Buddha and the Dhamma, but also the Noble Saṅgha.

Even though there is no such thing as a "collection" (samudāya) existing apart from its constituent parts—since a collection can only be spoken of in dependence upon its parts—a collection that is not currently being cognized ought to be distinguished by means of a collection that is being cognized; thus he said, "the aggregate of eight.
By this, it is shown that in the phrase "the Noble Saṅgha," [the distinction] is not made by any particular shape or the like, but rather by the completeness of the body (kāyasāmaggi).
It does not mean the state of being a collection (*samudāya*), but rather it specifies [the meaning] as the state of being on the path and the state of being in the fruit.

It is called *samūha* because it is to be gathered together (*sampiṇḍetvā*), inferred (*ūhitabbo*), reflected upon (*vitakketabbo*), or assembled (*saṃūhanitabbo*)—that is, joined together; and that very thing is *samoha* due to the smoothness of the expression and so forth.

For both readings are appropriate. [It is called *ariya*] because of being far removed (*āraka*) from defilements, because of not proceeding in what is not the right way (*anaya*), and because of proceeding in what is the right way (*aya*).

The noble ones (ariya) are so called according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*). Alternatively, they are "noble" because they are worthy of being approached (*araṇīya*) and approached (*upagantabba*) by the world including the devas, and because the goal is accomplished for those who have approached them;
they are united by a commonality of view and virtue. Or, the Saṅgha is so called because it is a unified assembly (*samagga*), having come together as a collective (*samupagata*).
Thus, it is the Saṅgha of the noble ones, and it is both noble and a Saṅgha according to the method already stated.

Or it is the Noble Saṅgha; that is the Noble Saṅgha. Because the attainment of even the jewels of the Buddha and the Dhamma after the Blessed One depended upon the jewel of the Saṅgha, the phrase "I revere with my head" was stated right here in order to show the great service rendered by the Noble Saṅgha.
And this meaning must certainly be accepted, because it has been stated thus in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā and other works.

Some, however, bring that same phrase forward and apply it even to the preceding verses; but that is indeed improper, because this [verse] is the place for proclaiming the unique qualities of the Triple Gem, and because the reasons already stated are intended to apply to all modes of commentary.
By this verse, however, many qualities of the Noble Saṅgha—such as the perfection of its origin and the perfection of its abandonments—are shown.
They exist. How so? By the phrase "the legitimate sons of the Sugata," he demonstrates the excellence of the Noble Saṅgha’s origin, as it indicates its derivation from the Perfectly Enlightened One.
By the phrase "the destroyers of Māra’s army," he demonstrates the excellence of their abandonment, as it indicates the abandonment of all defilements.
By the phrase "the assembly of the eight," he demonstrates the excellence of their knowledge, as it indicates the state of being established in the paths and fruits.
By the phrase “the Noble Saṅgha,” the excellence of its intrinsic nature is indicated, as it demonstrates the preeminence of all Saṅghas.

Alternatively, by the phrase “the legitimate sons of the Sugata,” the state of being a pure support for the Noble Saṅgha is demonstrated. By the phrase “the destroyers of Māra’s army,” the state of having entered upon the practice that is right, straight, and proper is demonstrated.
By the phrase “the assembly of the eight [types of noble ones],” the state of being worthy of offerings and so forth is demonstrated.

“Ariyasaṅgha” indicates that he is an unsurpassed field of merit. Likewise, by the phrase “the legitimate sons of the Sugata,” he shows the presence of supramundane taking of refuge within the Ariyasaṅgha;

for it is through the attainment of supramundane refuge that they have become the legitimate sons of the Blessed One. By the phrase “the destroyers of Māra’s army,” he shows [their] accomplishment through the perfection of their initial resolve.
This demonstrates the right practice in the prior stage. For those who have made the resolution and are practicing rightly conquer Māra or the host of Māra.

By the phrase “the assembly of the eight,” he shows the qualities of the trainees (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*)—who constitute the opposite side that has been shattered—by means of a reference to persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), since the qualities of the path and fruit are thereby shown. By the phrase “the Noble Saṅgha,”...
It demonstrates the state of being the foremost worthy of offerings because it shows the state of being the unsurpassed field of merit.
Furthermore, going for refuge is the beginning of all the qualities of the disciples; the training in the aggregates of virtue and so forth, together with their preliminary practice, is the middle;
and the aggregates of virtue and so forth of those beyond training (asekkha) is the conclusion. Thus, in brief, all [these qualities] are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
"The qualities of the Noble Saṅgha have been shown.

Thus, having performed a salutation to the Triple Gem by way of a brief recital of its entire range of virtues through these three verses, he now says "Thus for me," etc., dedicating that act of prostration toward the intended purpose. Therein:
The word *iti* is used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). By means of those three verses, he illustrates the method as it has been described.

With the word *me* (by me), he indicates himself by means of the instrumental case to express the state of being the agent. Its connection is with the elliptical phrase “the merit that has been obtained by me”;
