or else, this is an indication of the recipient (*sampadāna*), with the elliptical phrase “there is,” or an indication of the possessor (*sāmi*), as in “the merit consisting of my homage which belongs to me.”

One who has confidence is "clear-minded" (*pasannamati*). Since this compound word emphasizes the characteristic of the second member of the compound, it is stated as "of clear mind" (*pasannamatino*).
It is called a "jewel" (*ratana*) because it leads, generates, or carries delight;
thus, according to etymologists, these [faculties] are like the sevenfold or tenfold jewel. This is an application of similarity elsewhere.
However, the status of the Buddha and the other [jewels] as "treasures" is established precisely by the meaning of the words already stated.

For when one adverts to their qualities as they truly are, according to the passage beginning, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," a no small measure of rapture and gladness arises, which serves as the cause for attaining the Deathless.
As it has been said:
“Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred...
nor by delusion... At that time his mind is directed straightly toward the Tathāgata.
And when his mind is directed straightly, Mahānāma, the noble disciple attains...”
“He obtains knowledge of the meaning, he obtains knowledge of the Dhamma, he obtains joy connected with the Dhamma; in one who is joyful, rapture arises,” and so forth.
Alternatively, the meaning of “jewel” (ratana) is the state of being esteemed and so on. For this has been said in the commentaries:
“Esteemed and of great value, incomparable, and rare to behold;”
“Because it is enjoyed by beings who are peerless, it is therefore called a ‘jewel’ (ratana).

Furthermore, qualities such as being highly esteemed and so forth, which are not shared by others, are found in an eminent degree only in the Buddhas and others. A detailed explanation should be sought in the commentary on the *Ratana Sutta*.
Moreover, this meaning has not been stated here by way of etymological derivation; rather—
If one asks "by what [means]?"—the masters of grammar say it is by way of the object being worthy of veneration, as it is esteemed as a treasure in the world.

Furthermore, it is a "treasure" (*ratana*) because it delights the virtuous (*sādhu-ramana*), because it enables one to cross the ocean of *saṃsāra* (*saṃsāra-uttaraṇa*), and because it leads to happy rebirths and *nibbāna* (*sugati-nibbāna-nayana*).

This is according to a compound with identical referents (*tulyārtha-samāsa*). Enough of this prolixity. [The term is established] by applying the rule of single remainder (*ekasesa*) and by the etymological derivation of the plural form.
Or [it means] "jewels. A collection of three, or three combined together, or that which has three components is *tayaṃ*.

Since it is the *tayaṃ* of jewels alone and not of other things, it is called the *Ratnattaya* (Triple Gem). However, because there is no whole apart from its parts, it is the three jewels themselves that are so designated, and not merely the collection. Yet, with reference to the collection as a single unit, the singular number is used.

It is called *vandana*. It is that which is venerated, and thus it is "consisting of veneration" (*vandanāmaya*), just as there are things "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*) or "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamaya*).
Here, veneration consists of an inclination toward the qualities of the Three Jewels by means of body, speech, and mind, or else it is praise.

Furthermore, veneration is the state of being conditioned by that volition (*cetanā*) together with its co-nascent factors—such as faith, wisdom, mindfulness, and energy—which act as its support; it is by means of these that one is habitually disposed.
"Consisting of homage" (*vandanāmaya*) is, for example, "made of gold" or "made of silver"; in meaning, however, it is simply the aforementioned volition (*cetanā*).
"Consisting of homage to the Triple Gem" (*ratanattayavandanāmaya*) means homage to the Triple Gem, or that which consists of homage to the Triple Gem.

It is called "merit" (*puñña*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), because it produces the fruit of becoming venerable; or, merit is so called because it purifies (*punāti*) and cleanses one's own agent or continuum, as it possesses an object of action (*sakammakatā*).

Grammarians maintain that the explanation of the meaning of a root is obtained by way of its functional activity (*kāritava*), whereas the production of the word-form is achieved solely by way of its pure phonetic form (*suddhavasena*).
An obstacle (*antarāya*) is so called because it comes (*eti*) between (*antara*) and within (*majjhe*) the continuum of a being, acting as a hindrance to various attainments;
it refers to misfortune pertaining to the present life and so forth. It is "thoroughly destroyed" (*suṭṭhu vihata*)—that is, shattered—by the method described for the purpose of the salutation.

"May there be no obstacle" means having obstacles well-removed. Here, "removal" should be understood as the prevention of those obstacles from arising by way of avoiding the causes that produce them. "Having been" (*hutvā*) refers to an action in the prior time;
it is connected with the phrase "I shall explain the meaning. "Of that" (*tassa*) refers to the merit consisting of homage, which was indicated by the relative pronoun *yaṃ*.
“By *ānubhāvena* means by power (*balena*).

‘Radiance (*tejo*), energy (*ussāha*), will (*manta*), lordliness (*pabhū*), and potency (*sattī*)—these five are called ‘majesty’ (*ānubhāvo*), and you should call them ‘influence’ (*pabhāvo*) as well. — [Vibhaṅga 178]

For among the meanings stated [for the prefix *anu*], it is used here in the sense of "power" (*satti*). It is called "majesty" (*anubhāva*) because it repeatedly causes that which possesses it to develop and increase;

this very thing is thus "great majesty" (*ānubhāva*), according to the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā. In terms of meaning, however, it is simply the power of the merit consisting of the act of homage, characterized by the continuous reinforcement of strength from previous karma caused by the attainment of such success as has been obtained. And that [power] exists because obstacles have been well dispelled.
Either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the cause (*hetu*) is possible here.
Furthermore, by the phrase "of one with a clear mind," he demonstrates his own perfection of faith.

By the phrase "consisting of homage to the Triple Gem," he demonstrates the perfection of the Triple Gem as the field (*khetta*), and from that, the perfection of that merit through his own perfection of faith.
And by the perfection of the Three Jewels as a field, he demonstrates through these two factors the capacity to dispel obstacles and calamities that impair the exposition of the meaning.
For just as the volition of giving possesses four factors, so too the volition of salutation, by virtue of possessing these two factors,
pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) through its power to dispel hindrances.

Having thus shown the purpose for performing acts of homage toward the Triple Gem, [the author] now speaks the words beginning with "Dīghassa" in order to praise—by way of a specific eulogy of its qualities—that very Dhamma teaching whose meaning he intends to comment upon, after first showing it by way of its nature as the Dhamma to be commented upon.
For this is the custom of the Master: namely, in those various commentaries...
Praise (*thomanā*) consists of the extolling of the specific qualities of each respective phenomenon (*dhamma*) to be lauded from the very beginning.

For instance, in the *Papañcasūdanī*, *Sāratthappakāsinī*, *Manorathapūraṇī*, *Aṭṭhasālinī*, and so forth, there is, respectively: "of the crusher of opposing views," "of the generator of the differentiation of knowledge," and "of the producer of diverse eloquence for the preeminent preachers of the Dhamma."
"Of that Abhidhamma, which is profound in its insights, frequently plunged into, and variegated by manifold methods—from the beginning," and so forth—thus was the praise offered.
Therein, "of the long" means of that which is named "Long. "Woven with long discourses" means [woven] with those verbal compositions that are extended in length.
By the phrase "characterized by suttas," he shows that the designation "long" (dīgha) is a conventional term (samaññā) for this Āgama that conforms to its meaning.
But surely the suttas themselves are the Āgama; how then can it be marked by them? This is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha).

However, from the perspective of conceptual designation (paññatti), because the status of being an Āgama is designated based upon the suttas, the Āgama—which is the whole—is [designated] by means of its parts, the suttas.

It is marked (aṅkīyati). For just as the conventional designation "Sutta" applies to a collection of meaning and phrasing, so too the conventional designation "Āgama" applies to a collection of Suttas.

It is "subtle" (nipuṇa) because it possesses subtle meanings such as dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and so forth. It is called "Āgama" because one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so on, come (āgacchanti) therein, by means of it, or from it;
and it is "excellent" (vara) in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being desirable—thus it is the "Excellent Āgama" (āgamavara).

Furthermore, it is also called the "Excellent Scripture" (*āgamavara*) because it is proclaimed by those recognized as authorities among outsiders, such as the *Bhārata*, the *Purāṇa*, the *Kathā*, the *Narasīhapurāṇa*, and so forth.

Regarding that [scripture]: "Awakened after the Buddhas" (*buddhānubuddha*) refers to the Noble Ones, such as the Chief Disciples, who have realized the Truths by following the penetration of the Truths by the Buddhas.
By means of these [Noble Ones], there is a commentary on the meaning and a commentary on the qualities.

And it is "thus" (*tathā*) because it has been praised by them. Alternatively, it is "thus" because it was praised by the Buddhas and the *Anubuddhas* (those who have awakened after) according to the manner already described;

for the teachers say that the sequence for the commentary on the meaning of all three Piṭakas was spoken by the Fully Enlightened One himself, and thereafter it was [established] by the disciples through means such as the communal recitation (*saṅgāyana*). And it is said in the *Madhyamāgama-ṭīkā*:

In the commentary on the Upāli-sutta, after explaining the term "of the exposition" (*veyyākaraṇassa*), it says: "It is that which illuminates the meaning. For there is no passage in the scriptures (*tantipada*) left unexplained by the Blessed One;

the meaning of all of them has indeed been told. Regarding "the quality that brings about faith" (*saddhāvahaguṇassa*): this refers to the quality that brings about confidence (*pasāda*) in the Buddha and others.
But is it not the case that the entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) contained in the Three Baskets (*tepiṭaka*) possesses precisely the quality of bringing about faith? Indeed, it does. Yet...
Why is he praised by means of a quality that is not shared with others? Because he possesses that quality in an eminent degree.

For this Āgama [the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*] does so by way of the exhaustive exposition of virtue, views, and so forth in such texts as the *Brahmajāla Sutta*; by way of the exposition of the qualities of previous Buddhas as well in such texts as the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*;
and by way of crushing the non-Buddhist teachers and uttering the irreversible lion’s roar in such texts as the *Pāṭika Sutta*.
In particular, by elucidating the qualities of the Buddha in such discourses as the *Anuttariya Sutta*, it brings about an exceptional degree of faith in the Triple Gem.

Having thus offered praise for the Dhamma that is to be expounded, he now says, "For the purpose of explaining the meaning," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the purity of the lineage of the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) which is about to be described.
For, according to this verse, [the commentary] is derived specifically from the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* as it was included in the three councils (*saṅgīti*).
This commentary that is about to be explained has come down [to us] without even a trace of the Sinhalese language, and not from any other source;
by stating this very reason, he shows the purity of the provenance of his own commentary, implying that it is not otherwise. According to another method:

because it is impossible for others to speak of this excellent scripture—the domain of the Buddha, which is supremely subtle and profound—relying solely on his own power, he says: "I shall explain it."
In order to show the basis for his commentary, he says: "For the purpose of elucidating the meaning," and so forth. By this, he shows his own basis for the commentary, thinking:
"Relying indeed upon the power of the former teachers, I shall explain its meaning. Therein, "for the purpose of elucidating the meaning" (atthappakāsanatthaṃ) refers to:

the meaning of the text (pāṭhattha), the meaning of the intrinsic nature (sabhāvattha), the meaning of what is to be known (ñeyyattha), the meaning corresponding to the text (pāṭhānurūpattha), the meaning corresponding to that [nature] (tadanurūpattha), and the meaning with remainder (sāvasesattha).

It is for the purpose of, or for the sake of, elucidating the manifold meanings—such as "the meaning that hinders" (*nīvaraṇa-sattha*), "the explicit meaning" (*nīta-ttha*), and "the meaning that requires interpretation" (*neyya-ttha*).
It is divided into two parts due to the requirements of the metrical composition of the verses. It is called *aṭṭhakathā* because the meaning (*attha*) is explained (*kathīyati*) by means of it;
this very term becomes *aṭṭhakathā* by changing the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*, just as in the expression "the meaning of oppression is suffering" (*dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho*). And this...
This is the rule for *sa-saññoga* (conjoined) [compounds] because they possess the nature of an Aryan formation.

For even grammarians, having stated the rule "the *yuga* [pair] is likewise *anaṭṭha*," cite this very example: "That by which they praise the meaning, following the sequence of phonemes, meanings, and words."
This commentary is considered to be connected with the *Nidāna-vatthu*.

"From the beginning" means at the start, during the first council (*paṭhama-saṅgīti*). They are called "the masters" (*vasino*) because they were endowed with the supreme mastery of mind through the possession of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and because of the presence of the fivefold mastery over the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth;
these are the elders (*therā*) such as Mahākassapa and others, numbering five hundred.

"Recited" (*saṅgītā*) means that which was spoken by collecting [the material] together—stating "this is its meaning, this is its meaning"—in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) where it was appropriate to clarify the sense.
"And recited subsequently" (*anusaṅgītā ca pacchāpi*) means not only at the first council (*paṭhamasaṅgīti*), but also later at the second and third councils.
Nor was it recited from the beginning by the five hundred elders alone; [it was also recited by others].
Rather, the meaning should be understood as a conjunction: "and [it is] that which was recited by the Elder Yasas and others.
For each of these two conjunctions individually connects the time of the action.

Now, as for the objection regarding redundancy: "Since the ancient commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) already exists, what is the purpose of this new commentary composed now?"—this refers to the charge of tautology.
Recalling the fault of pointlessness and avoiding it, he said, "The Island of Sihaḷa," and so forth.

By that very avoidance, he shows the cause (nimitta) for this commentary. Therein, one who "takes" (*lāti*) or seizes a lion (*sīha*) is a *Sīhaḷa*—the letter *la* being changed to *ḷa*, just as in the word "Garula. The first person in that lineage was Prince Sīha.

Furthermore, the kṣatriyas born in that lineage on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, as well as all its people, are called Sīhaḷas either by way of a derivative suffix (*taddhita*) or through conventional usage.
Their island of residence should also be understood as "Sīhaḷa" either by way of a derivative suffix or by way of a metonymy (*ṭhānīnāma*).

It is called an "island" (*dīpa*) because it shines in the midst of water, or because water flows there in two directions; it is that very island which, when considered in relation to its divisions, [is designated thus].
"Of them, it is the island"—so it is said. The word *pana* indicates a lack of approval (*aruci*).
Thus, although it is true that she has been included in the three councils (*saṅgīti*), nevertheless, by saying "she is such [a person]," it indicates the absence of approval.

However, because of its connection with the meaning of the preceding verse, the construction "although she was recited and subsequently recited" can be understood as being employed for the sake of emphasis (*sānuggaha*). For it is also used in other instances in that way.
"It is seen" means: "brought" refers to having been brought from Jambudvīpa. "Then" (*atha*) means after the time of the Council; if this is the case, it connects with the word "brought.
Alternatively, "then" means after the time when it was brought by the Elder Mahāmahinda; if this is the case, it connects with the word "established.
For that [Pāḷi] was first recited as the Three Piṭakas by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, and then...
Because it was set down in the path of oral transmission precisely in accordance with the commentary on the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*), it was already included within the three councils; thereafter,
it was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Elder Mahāmahinda, and subsequently,

it was established in the Sinhalese language by the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi for the purpose of avoiding the confusion of tenets belonging to other schools (*nikāyantara*).— Thus says the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
However, he clarifies only the latter connection because it is difficult to perceive.

Likewise, the phrase "for the benefit of those dwelling on the island" (*dīpavāsīnamatthāya*) must also be construed with the words "was established" (*ṭhapitā*) and "removing [the old] and setting up [the new]" (*apanetvā āropento*).

For even a single word can come to be connected with multiple meanings through methods such as *āvutti* (repetition). And here, by the former connection, it is for the benefit of those dwelling on the island of Siṃhala.
By stating that [the text] was established in the Sinhalese language to avoid the confusion of tenets belonging to other schools,
he demonstrates the purpose for which the Theras of Tambapaṇṇi established it. Furthermore, by way of the final connection,

he indicates the purpose of removing the Sinhalese language and replacing it with a language appropriate to the system of the discourses (tantinaya) for the benefit of those dwelling in Jambudīpa and those dwelling on other islands through this commentary.
And it is for this purpose. Because of his great sovereignty, his name during his time as a prince was Mahinda; later, however, due to the greatness of his virtues, he is called Mahāmahinda.
As for the so-called Sinhala language, because it expresses even a single meaning through many syllables, it is extremely difficult for others to master;
it is like a bodice, the customary speech of the Sinhalese.

"Let it be so regarding the ancient commentary; but now, when there is the inquiry as to how this commentary being composed is to be made, he says 'Having removed,' etc., in order to show the manner of composing this commentary.
Therein, 'having removed' means having taken away the Sinhalese language from that original commentary (mūlaṭṭhakathā) by way of not including it in the manuscript, thus making it absent."

The connection [is as follows]: by this, it is shown that the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) about to be explained—which is merely the removal of the Sinhalese language from the original commentary (mūlaṭṭhakathā) established during the three councils—accords with and is consistent with that original commentary in meaning, just as "the water of the Yamunā" accords with "the water of the Gaṅgā.
The words beginning with "manorama" are indicators of the natural etymological nature of the word "bhāsa" (speech).
These are the qualifications. It is called *manoramā* because it delights the minds of the wise by way of its intrinsic nature and its etymological derivation.

It is called *tanti*—that is, the *pāḷi* (the sacred text)—because it extends the meaning (*tanoti atthaṃ*), or because it is extended (*tanīyati*) and explained according to the meaning, or because it carries beings across the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), or because they cross over doubt regarding various objects of meaning by means of it.
Of that [text], which is a "way" (*gati*) reckoned as a method (*naya*), [one should grasp] the skin and the luster...

"Anugata" means conforming to the method of the *tanti* (the original source). It is "free from defects" because it is devoid of faults such as being mixed with unrefined expressions, incorrect terminology, or foreign languages.
Such a work, consisting of refined expression, is said:
"That is the Māgadhī root-language, the one which men spoke in the first eon."

“Both the Brahmās and the Perfectly Enlightened Ones have spoken thus.”—The meaning is that he is recording in writing what has been set down in the text according to the flow of the canonical tradition (*pāḷigati*); by this, he indicates the absence of faults in the phrasing (*saddadosa*).

“Without violating the *samaya*” means without contradicting the established doctrine (*siddhanta*); by this, however, he indicates the absence of faults in the meaning (*atthadosa*). Because it is not contradictory...
For indeed, those Theravāda traditions will also be made clear here. To the question "Whose system? he says "of the Elders" (*therānaṃ*), and so forth;
by this, he excludes the systems of the schools of the Jetavanavāsins, the Abhayagirivāsins, and others, such as the teachers of Rāhula.
They are called "Elders" (*therā*) because they are endowed with stable qualities consisting of virtue, learning, meditation, and liberation. As it is said: "O monks, there are these four..."
The qualities that make one an elder (*therakaraṇā dhammā*). Which four? "In this case, monks, a monk is virtuous," and so forth.
Furthermore, they are elders because they are endowed with the qualities that make one firm, such as truth and the Dhamma. As the King of Dhamma said in the *Dhammapada*:
"In whom there is truth and the Dhamma, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control..."
“He indeed, having cast off impurities and being wise, is called an ‘Elder’ (thera).
Of these [teachings], the lineage of Elders (theravaṃsa) is the succession of teachers that has come down through such as the Elder Mahākassapa and others.

Being included within that [lineage] and being endowed with both scriptural learning and realization, they illuminate it in a particular manner by means of the light of wisdom, which blazes forth because of its perfection.

Or, "those who are like lamps in that [tradition]" refers to the lamps of the Elder lineage (*theravamsa*). It is called a "detailed exposition" (*vinicchaya*) because it is determined in various ways;
it is a discourse that cuts through doubt, proceeding like the removal of a splinter at knotty points.

Those for whom the detailed exposition is very skillful and subtle are "those of very skillful exposition" (*sunipuṇavinicchaya*). Alternatively, it is called a "detailed exposition" (*vinicchaya*) because it determines (*vinicchinoti*) the aforementioned subject matter.
"Sunipuṇavinicchayā" means those who possess very subtle and skillful discernment (*vinicchaya*).

"Mahāvihāra" refers to the monastery situated in the Mahāmeghavana forest, which shines with the Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) of the Teacher; those whose habit is to dwell there are the "Mahāvihāravāsins.

The meaning is that they do not violate the tradition of such [teachers]. By this, it is indicated that [the teaching] has come down through the succession of elders beginning with the Thera Mahākassapa, and for that very reason...
The phrase "the non-perverted, subtle, and refined exposition" shows that the system of the Mahāvihāravāsins is authoritative by way of its person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).

"Having abandoned the matter brought here and there again and again" means that having discarded—due to its state of being repetitive and its resulting heaviness of the text—the matter already stated in one place but brought again elsewhere, I shall clarify the meaning of that excellent Āgama.
Having thus shown the manner of composition, [he states] another purpose for the commentary than the stated purpose "for the benefit of the inhabitants of Dīpa."

In order to show the purpose (*payojana*), he said, "And for the sake of the virtuous person" (*sujanassa ca*), and so forth. Therein, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*);
by it, he conjoins that it is not only for the sake of those dwelling in Jambudīpa, but also for the sake of pleasing the noble people (*sādhujana*).
By this very [conjunction], the meaning that it is also for the sake of those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi is established, because [the work] is easy to master and so forth.
Because they too are of great benefit. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of long endurance," here too the word *ca* (and) indicates a cumulative sense;

it shows that it is not merely for the sake of those two purposes, but also for the sake of the long endurance—lasting for a period of five thousand years—of the threefold Dhamma of the Dispensation, or specifically the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). For, through the endurance of the Dhamma of the scriptures...
The Dhamma of practice and the Dhamma of penetration also endure because they have that very [Dhamma of the scriptures] as their root.
However, the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) remains well-established for a long time through its words and phrases being well-arranged and its meaning being correctly presented.
Furthermore, through commentary, the words and phrases become unerringly well-arranged, and the meaning also becomes unerringly well-presented.
Therefore, because it serves as the means for the unerring arrangement of words and phrases and for the correct determination of their meaning within the commentary, it is said:
"and for the long endurance of the Dhamma. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, these two things lead to the stability, the non-confusion, and the non-disappearance of the True Dhamma. Which two? Well-arranged words and phrases, and well-determined meaning. These, monks... [lead]... and so forth.

Having thus shown the purpose, he said, “The discourse on virtue,” and so forth, in order to avoid the burden of the text by relinquishing its magnitude through the commentary that is about to be explained.

For it has been said: “I shall not analyze that [in detail]. There is another method: when one desires to compose a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the *Visuddhimagga* must be taken as a portion of it; this is for the sake of those who expound it.
While giving this instruction, he said, "The discourse on virtue," and so forth, in order to show by way of enumeration the teachings discussed therein.

Therein, "the discourse on virtue" refers to an extensive discussion of virtue by way of what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided. "Ascetic qualities" (dhutadhammā) refers to the thirteen qualities that shake off the defilements, such as the practice of eating only almsfood.
"Meditation subjects" (kammaṭṭhānāni) are so called because they are the bases for the engagement in the work of yoga, which is termed "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
The various types of phenomena known as meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) should not be taken as only those thirty-eight that have come down in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
Rather, it is said "all of them" in order to indicate that there are also two [meditation subjects] that have come down in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

"Accompanied by the method for determining temperament" means it proceeds together with the determination of the nature and so forth of temperaments such as lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*). This, however, refers to the "Detailed Exposition of Jhāna Attainments."
This is its qualification. Herein, the fine-material-sphere jhānas are "jhāna," while the immaterial-sphere jhānas are "attainment" (samāpatti).
Alternatively, both of these, when merely acquired, are "jhāna," whereas when they have reached mastery in entering them, they are "attainment.
Furthermore, both of those are indeed "jhāna," but the fruition-attainments and the attainment of cessation are "attainments"; this is the meaning of their detailed explanation.
The phrase "and all the higher knowledges" is stated for the purpose of including all six higher knowledges (abhiññā), both mundane and supramundane.

"Discernment by way of synthesis" (paññā-saṅkalanavinicchaya) refers to the discernment that follows from reckoning, combining, or summing up wisdom according to its divisions—such as the singlefold division and so forth—as set forth in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* and other texts.
They are called "noble" (ariyāni) because they are to be penetrated by the noble ones (ariya), such as the Buddhas and others.
Alternatively, they are called "noble" (ariya) because they accomplish the state of a noble one (ariyabhāva), by dropping the final member of the compound.
Or, they are "noble" because they are to be sought after (araṇīya) or understood (avagantabba) as being non-false (avitatha);

this is a qualification for the term "truths" (saccāni). The mode of conditionality (paccayākāra) is the state of being helpful to the conditioned phenomena arising from conditions, by way of the status of being a root-condition, object-condition, and so forth, for those phenomena that serve as causes and so on.
The meaning is that his teaching is thus the discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

Furthermore, it is "perfectly pure" because it is free from the confusion of the tenets of other schools; it is "subtle" because the resolution of the compact mass [of phenomena] is extremely difficult;

and it is "investigated therein together with the methods of unity and so forth. Thus he said, "by means of perfectly pure and subtle methods. For these three terms also refer to the teaching on the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).
This is the qualification. Because it has been investigated without abandoning the method as it appears in the *Paṭisambhidā* and other texts, its path is "unreleased" (*avimutta*);

thus, it is "one whose path is unreleased" (*avimuttatantimaggā*). Here, "path" (*magga*) refers to the means (*upāya*) known as the scripture (*pāḷi*), because it serves as the means for the realization of those respective meanings or for the penetration of the Truths (*sacca*).
Alternatively, it is a "continuity" (*pabandha*) because, by virtue of its length, it resembles a natural path.
This, however, is a qualification for the two terms "insight" (*vipassanā*) and "development" (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding the phrase "thus all," here the word "thus" (*iti*) indicates completion, because the enumeration as it was set forth has been concluded;
the meaning is "all this much. The particle "pana" is merely an ornament of speech, as it has no separate meaning. [It applies] to that which is interspersed with the meanings of the words...
Because there is nothing remaining that ought to be said but has not been said, it is "perfectly pure" due to its being easy to understand;
this connects with the word "all" (*sabba*). Alternatively, this is a neuter noun, as it connects with the word "stated" (*vutta*).
"Bhiyyo" means "moreover" or "exceedingly extensive"; by this, he shows that he will investigate merely the meaning of the words.
I shall not examine all of this here in the commentary because it would involve redundancy and because it would result in excessive bulk—this is the intention.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the phrase "I shall examine" does not imply an increase in length due to the metrical form of the verses.
Even so, this *Visuddhimagga* might fail to clarify the meaning of the scriptures; therefore, it follows that all of this must indeed be examined here.
Having determined that non-investigation is the sole cause for such censure, and thus avoiding it, he says: "The Path of Purification in the midst," and so forth.
Therein, "in the midst" means within the interior of the other four Āgamas as well as the Khuddaka.
The word *hi* denotes a reason; by it, he illuminates the reason already stated. "Therein" refers to among those four Āgamas. "As it was spoken" means by the Blessed One.

"Whatever has been taught" means either in accordance with what was taught; furthermore, it also means whatever has been spoken by the commentators in the course of their commentary, in accordance with what they spoke.
"Thus indeed" (*icceva*): here, by the word *iti*, he points to the reason already stated;
the meaning is, "for this very reason," or "keeping this very reason in mind. Regarding the word "composed" (*kato*): [here too, the reference is to] the *Visuddhimagga*.
The phrase "this" (esā) should be understood as being connected with the state of being the action (kammabhāva) by way of repetition (*āvutti*) and so forth. "Having grasped that too" (*tampi...
gahetvāna*) means having grasped even that Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*) by means of knowledge. "By this" (*etāya*) refers to this commentary named *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*.
And here, by the expression "standing in the middle," which indicates a state of neutrality (*majjhattabhāva*), [it shows] specifically regarding all four Āgamas...
This indicates that the *Visuddhimagga* is a common commentary (*sādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), unlike the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and others, which are specific commentaries (*asādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
However, without distinction, there are indeed appropriate common commentaries for the Vinaya and Abhidhamma as well;

and because of their inclusion therein, even though they are likewise common to the remainder of the Minor Collection (*Khuddaka-āgama*) in particular, [the *Visuddhimagga*]— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the full logical structure of the argument as presented.)
It is stated that these [verses] are common only to the four Āgamas themselves.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixteen verses.
The commentary on the introductory discourse of the work is finished.
Commentary on the Nidānakathā:
Having thus performed the commencement of the treatise through the various methods such as the salutation as previously described,
it is now shown that for those possessing analytical discernment, the revelation of intrinsic nature is well-revealed and well-explained precisely by means of demonstrating its divisions.
Regarding the word "hoti" (it occurs), he first said, "In that regard, 'the long augment' (dīghāgamo)... and so forth, in order to show the classification by way of the *vaggasutta*.
Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) refers to the statement: "I shall explain the meaning of the excellent long augment.
That which was promised as "I shall explain the meaning of which," namely the "long augment," [is explained] by way of the *vaggasutta*.
The meaning is that it should be understood in this way, or that it should be analyzed in this way. Alternatively, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to the statement "dependent on a long arrival.
That which was called a "long arrival" is so named by way of the *vaggasutta*. It should be analyzed in this manner, or its nature is such.
For the distant expression stated by "of the long" (*dīghassa*) and so forth is [referred to] by the pronoun *taṃ*.
Just as one might point back to something previously mentioned, even a word denoting proximity— such as "dependent on a long journey"—
is pointed back by the pronoun *taṃ* (that), because it occurs as if revolving in one's own mind as though it were present before one.
For in such instances, whether revolving in one's mind as being face-to-face or out of sight, it may be pointed back in whatever manner is appropriate.
It is appropriate [to explain it] by way of a mere indication of the sound, because there is no contradiction with the meaning. The derivation of terms such as *vaggasutta* will be clarified later.

That which has three sections (*vagga*) is "three-sectioned" (*tivagga*). That in which thirty-four suttas are collected, or wherein the collection—that is, the enumeration—of those [suttas] occurs, is "the collection of thirty-four suttas" (*catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaha*).
In order to show that his own commentary proceeds according to the very sequence established in the First Council, it is said: "Of that...
the introduction is first. Here, the state of being "first" should be understood solely according to the sequence of the councils.
Why, however, was the Dīgha Nikāya recited first among the four Āgamas, and within that, why was the Sīlakkhandha-vagga recited first?
Is it not placed there, and within that [section] is the Brahmajāla Sutta, and within that too is the Nidāna?
This inquiry does not fail to proceed anywhere, for it must be pursued everywhere based merely on the sequence of the words.
Moreover, because it possesses qualities that inspire faith, the Dīgha Āgama was recited first at the council. For faith is the seed of wholesome states, as it is said: "Faith is the seed..."
"...and it is conducive to austerity. Furthermore, its quality of inspiring faith has already been demonstrated above.

Moreover, it was recited first because it is easy to learn and memorize due to its being a collection of only a few suttas and its limited extent. For it consists of a collection of thirty-four suttas and measures sixty-four bhāṇavāras.
Furthermore, because it contains a great abundance of discourse on virtue, it is called the Sīlakkhandhavagga (Virtue Section) and placed first.
It is deposited [in this section]. For virtue (*sīla*) is the beginning of the Dispensation, because it is the foundation for all wholesome qualities. Therefore it was said:
"Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify the beginning among wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is perfectly purified," and so forth.
Because of the great abundance of discourses on the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), it is called the "Sīlakkhandha-vagga" (The Chapter on the Aggregate of Virtue).

It has been said. However, because it provides a discourse for disentangling views, it should be understood that the *Brahmajāla Sutta* was placed first in the Suttanta Piṭaka as a complete analysis of all views.

Indeed, within the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, there is no other sutta like the *Brahmajāla* that analyzes the various types of views by making them clear and free from entanglement. As for the introduction (*nidāna*), at the First Council—

It was placed first by the Venerable Ānanda, who was questioned by the Elder Mahākassapa, for the purpose of indicating the place, time, and other such details. Therefore he said, "Of the Brahmajāla Sutta," and so forth.
In that context, the phrase "by the Venerable" and so on specifies the teacher, while "at the time of the First Council" specifies the time; this meaning will be made clear further below.
Commentary on the Account of the First Great Council:
Now, in connection with the mention of "at the time of the first great council," the author, desiring to show that first great council— or rather,
wishing to provide a commentary following the sequence established within that first great council— clarifies it as follows:
In order to show the reason for mentioning this here, even though it has already been included in that *tanti*, he said: "And this is called the First Great Council," and so forth.
Here, there is a slight objection: although... [the text continues] ...it has been included in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka* of the *Tanti*, why is it stated again here?
And if it were stated, would it not be purposeless and result in the bulkiness of the text? This is the essence of the objection.
[The author] shows this. However, by the statement, “The Nidāna... should be understood,” he resolves [the objection] by showing a distinguishing reason:
that because it serves the purpose of skill in the Nidāna, the aforementioned fault would not occur.

In the phrase, “And this is called the First Great Recital (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti),” the word “and” (ca) has the sense of including what ought to be mentioned in such contexts. For it was indeed spoken at the time of the First Great Recital:
This summarizes the meaning as follows: "The introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning, and this should be understood as what is called the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*).
Alternatively, the word *ca* has the sense of introducing a supplementary statement; for "introducing a supplementary statement" (*upaññāsa*) is said to be the commencement of a sentence.
Indeed, it is the custom of authors that when they have said something and then begin to say something else, they employ the word *ca*. As for that which...
The statement by Vajirabuddhi Thera, “And here the word *ca* has a cumulative sense (*atirekattha*);
by it, he indicates that there are others as well” (*Vajira-ṭīkā*, Commentary on the Introduction to the External [Nidāna]), is indeed incorrect.
For the meaning intended by him is not understood from the word *ca* here. If, moreover, the particle *ca* were intended here solely for the purpose of indicating that meaning, then—
Therefore, it need not even be performed [again], because by the very word "first," the existence of other councils—the second and so forth—is demonstrated.
For the application of the term "first" presupposes a second and so on, just as the application of the terms "short" and so forth presupposes a "long" and so forth.
Having collected the Dhamma and Vinaya that were taught and established here and there in a scattered manner according to circumstances, [the first council was held].

"Singing" (*gāyana*) means recitation (*kathana*) or chanting (*saṅgīti*). By this, the words of the compilers (*saṅgītikāraka*)—which are placed at the beginning and end of each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and discourse (*sutta*), as well as in between them according to their connection—are included.
Because it has a vast scope and because it is honored, it is a "great compilation," a *mahāsaṅgīti*. The first great compilation is the "first great compilation" (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*).
*Kiñcāpi* means "even though" for the purpose of showing favor; by this, he shows favor [to the text] by implying that it has indeed been included in the recitation of the Canon (*pāḷi*).

However, with the word *pana*, he indicates a sense of dissatisfaction, showing that merely because it is included there, the listeners here do not possess proficiency regarding the introduction (*nidāna*).
It is called *nidāna* because it lays down (*nidadāti*) the teaching—making known what was previously unknown—by way of the teacher, the time, and so forth, thereby pointing it out (*nidasseti*).
Skill in that [matter], for the sake of that—this is the meaning.
Now, in order to show this in detail, it was said: “For the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma,” and so forth.
In that context, although there exist other activities of the Blessed One which serve as causes for sentient beings to obtain the unsurpassed vision, the going for refuge, and so on;

Because it conforms to the promise, "May the Buddha awaken [others]," the very activity that serves as the cause for the arising of the paths and fruits in those to be trained is, in the primary sense, called the "work of a Buddha" (*buddhakicca*).
To show its specific nature, it is said: "For the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma... [and so forth]...
is the training. Furthermore, even for those who hear what was spoken by the Blessed One prior to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, [it is beneficial].

It has arisen as pertaining only to the stage of purification by means of serenity (*vāsanābhāgiya*), not as pertaining to the stage of the trainee (*sekkhabhāgiya*), nor as pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), like the giving of refuge by Tapussa and Bhallika.
For this is the natural law (*dhammatā*); therefore, it should be understood that this alone is stated in the sense of a boundary.

The factors such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) are themselves the "wheel" (*cakra*) in the sense of proceeding; thus, it is the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*). Alternatively, "wheel" (*cakra*)...

Because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is the Dhamma; and because it is that wheel, it is the "Wheel of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*). It is also the "Wheel of the Dhamma" because it is a wheel according to the Dhamma, according to the principle.
For it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "It sets the Dhamma in motion and it is a wheel, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.

It sets a wheel in motion and it is the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma. It sets [it] in motion by means of the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma. It sets [it] in motion through the practice of the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma," and so forth.
Its "turning" (*pavattana*) is likewise. As for "turning," there are two meanings according to the present and the past:
that which is turning and that which has been turned. It is with reference to this that it is stated in the commentaries:
"While teaching the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*, he is said to be 'turning the Wheel of Dhamma,' starting from the moment the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña attained the path and its fruition."
"...is called 'set in motion. However, in this context, the meaning is appropriate only in terms of the present. "Yāva" is a particle used in the sense of a limit;
the meaning should be understood in the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*) as "having made the conversion of the wanderer named Subhadda the final limit.
For the Blessed One converted him while still reclining upon the bed of his final Nibbāna. It was "done," meaning brought to completion.
"By which [means] the work of a Buddha was performed"—thus it is said; "when the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, had performed the work of a Buddha and attained final nibbāna" is the connection.
By this, he illuminates the fact that there remained nothing whatsoever of the duties to be performed by a Buddha.

For it is precisely for this reason that the Blessed One is said to have attained final nibbāna. But is it not the case that even those disciples who were trained by others were actually trained by the Blessed One himself?
Indeed, a discourse spoken by a disciple is called "spoken by the Buddha. Furthermore, those to be disciplined by disciples have not yet been disciplined;

therefore, should it not be said that "the work of a Buddha has been completed"? This is not a fault, because the means for disciplining them has been entrusted to the disciples. For this very reason, he said:
“Evil One, I shall not attain final nibbāna until my bhikkhu disciples have become accomplished,
disciplined, confident, learned, and bearers of the Dhamma... until they, having thoroughly refuted with the Dhamma the doctrines of others that have arisen,
shall teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles,” and so forth.

The statement beginning with “In Kusinārā,” which specifies the place and time of the Blessed One’s final passing away (*parinibbāna*), is intended to show that the notion “the Blessed One has not yet attained final nibbāna” is incorrect,
and also to demonstrate his having been born and raised within the world. For indeed, in order to make manifest his human nature,
even the Great Bodhisattvas, in their final existence, undertake the taking of wives and so forth.

“They were performing [the funeral rites]”: at Kusinārā, in the city of that name. For that city is called “Kusinārā” because it was built on a site where a man with a *kusa*-grass bundle could be seen;
here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*). “In the Mallans’ Sal-wood grove at Upavattana”:
in the *sāla* forest belonging to the Mallan kings, situated on the outskirts of that city. For that *sāla* grove was [located] such that those wishing to enter the city...
It is called *Upavattana* because people approach from the park and proceed along it.
Just as the Thūpārāma is situated in the south-western direction of Anurādhapura, so too that park is situated in the south-western direction of Kusinārā.
And just as the road leading from the Thūpārāma into the city through the southern gate proceeds facing eastward, [so does this road].
"It turns northward": thus, having gone from the park toward the east along the row of *sāla* trees, it turns northward;

therefore, it is called "Upavattana. Others, however, say: "It became well known as 'Upavattana' because, after entering that *sāla* grove and taking leave of his friends and kinsmen, he turned back. "Between the twin *sāla* trees" means...

Between the twin *sāla* trees. It is said that there was one row of *sāla* trees at the head-end of the Blessed One’s prepared bed for the final passing away (*parinibbāna*), and another at the foot-end.
There too, one young *sāla* tree was close to the head-end and one to the foot-end;
therefore, it is said, "between the twin *sāla* trees. Furthermore, as for what are called the "twin *sāla* trees," by their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves...

It is also stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*: "The halls stand interwoven with one another. Regarding the word *mā*, it refers to the moon (*canda*), because by its movement the day is measured; since it is then full with the completion of all its phases, it is called *puṇṇamā*.
However, grammarians, taking the Pali system as expressed in the Sanskrit tradition—"*mo* is Śiva and also the moon"—accept that it is also a vowel-ending term (*okārantampi*).
They maintain that the word *ma* denotes the moon. "The full moon day joined with Visākhā" is *visākhāpuṇṇamā*;
that very day is likewise [referred to as such], and [the phrase] means "on that. Regarding *paccūsa*: it is called *paccūsa* because it destroys (*vināseti*) the darkness (*timira*);
for etymologists say that the word *usa*, preceded by *pati*, means "to break. That very time is a specific period of time included within the final watch of the night.
It is said to be [present] therein. This means on such a day as the full moon of Visākhā, at the final stage of the night.
That which is grasped by karma and defilements is "upādi" (the substrate); it consists of the resultant aggregates and the matter produced by past karma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).

However, that *upādi* was not relinquished when the Mara of Defilements and the Mara of Volitional Formations were crushed; here, it is relinquished when the Mara of the Aggregates and the Mara of Death are crushed.

It is known; therefore, there is no "remainder" (sesa) consisting of the substrate (upādi) for this [state], or it is called "without remainder" (anupādisesa) by taking the sense that there is no remainder of the substrate.

Here, by "the element of Nibbāna" (nibbānadhātu), mere extinction (nibbuti) is intended; and because it is both Nibbāna and, by virtue of maintaining its own intrinsic nature, an "element" (dhātu), it is so designated.
For the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu) is spoken of in that way by way of being the cause of extinction. [The suffix -tā] is used here in the sense of a characteristic of such a state.

And this is a description of the instrument (karaṇaniddesa). It is said that the third [case ending] is used for the meaning designated as the element of Nibbāna (nibbānadhātu), which is the characteristic of the Blessed One who has become, attained, and reached final Nibbāna (parinibbuta), namely this mode known as "without residue" (anupādisesa).

But is it not the case that "anupādisesāya" is actually a qualification of the element of Nibbāna itself, and not of the Blessed One who has reached final Nibbāna? Why, then, did the Blessed One [use it in that way]?

Is it said that he has "attained"? Because of his co-existence with the element of Nibbāna (*nibbānadhātu*). For through co-existence with that, even the Blessed One is said to have "attained" the state of being without residue (*anupādisesa*).

Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say that the third case ending is used for the act of perceiving the characteristic of this element of Nibbāna, which is designated as the state of being without residue. [The phrase is: *anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā*.

And the meaning is: "having become the Nibbāna-element without residue. Regarding the phrase, "with a bowl having fewer than five repairs," they explain the meaning here as: "having [attained] a bowl having fewer than five repairs. Furthermore, it is also appropriate to understand it as:
"having become, having been, without residue in the Nibbāna-element without residue. For this is stated in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā, in the commentary on the Nanda-sutta:
Regarding the phrase “with hair half-shorn,” this is an instrumental expression used as a characteristic mark of a particular state;
the meaning is “characterized by having the hair half-shorn. This is the method to be applied in similar cases.

The phrase “on the day of the bowl-offering for the relics” refers specifically to the fifth day of the waxing moon in the month of Jeṭṭha; furthermore, that is not an adjective qualifying the word “assembled.”

Regarding the phrase “he inspired enthusiasm,” the qualification “on the day of the distribution of the relics, he inspired enthusiasm among the bhikkhus” is used because the act of inspiring enthusiasm and its time are distinct; that is, they constitute a distinction of different loci (bhinnādhikaraṇa).

For indeed, the bhikkhus had already assembled on days prior to the day of the distribution of the relics. Alternatively, the word “assembled” (*sannipatitānaṃ*) may refer to their physical gathering together.
This was said with reference specifically to the formal assembly (*sannipātana*), not merely to their coming together.
Therefore, the phrase "on the day of the distribution of bowls" can function as a qualification for the term "those who have assembled.

Furthermore, this [phrase] should also be connected with the word "of the monks" (*bhikkhūnaṃ*) in the passage "it arouses the enthusiasm of the monks. "The elder of the Saṅgha" means the senior monk of the Saṅgha. And he...
When asked, "What is the measure of the Saṅgha? he replied, "Of seven hundred thousand bhikkhus.
For this was stated again precisely for the purpose of making known the measure that was not understood by the word *saṅgha* alone. However, those learned in grammar say:
"Both compounds and derivatives serve as qualifiers regarding the meanings of sentences."
The commonality [of the terms] is established: "oil" and "the Sugata’s robe.
Therefore, this [term] was stated again specifically for the purpose of qualifying the Elder of the Saṅgha, who is merely a name;

and because of its constant requirement [for a complement], a compound is formed in such cases, as in the expression "Devadatta’s teacher's family. And here, the word *saṅgha* possesses this constant requirement.

Even when there is expectancy (*sāpekkhatta*), the sound of "one hundred thousand bhikkhus" functions as an indicator of the meaning to be expected within the sentence—just as in the case of other words—because no other word intervenes.

For the connection of the phrase "of seven hundred thousand bhikkhus" with the word "Saṅgha" is by way of being its constituent part (*avayavībhāva*), and the connection of that [phrase] with the word "Thera" is by way of being its possessor (*sāmibhāva*). Thus: "Of seven hundred thousand bhikkhus."
And this was said specifically with reference to the monks who were the leaders of the community. For at that time, the number of monks assembled there exceeded the range of calculation.

Indeed, when they heard in the village of Veḷuva that "the Blessed One will soon attain final Nibbāna," starting from the suppression of his pain, among the monks who had arrived from here and there, not even a single monk remained behind.
There was no [other] name [for him]. As it has been said:
"Of the seven hundred thousand monks, the Elder Mahākassapa alone was then the chief monk, the senior of the Saṅgha."
The Venerable Mahākassapa, having recollected, reflected, and pondered, generated an effort;
or rather, the connection is that the Venerable Mahākassapa, while recollecting, reflecting, and pondering, generated an effort.
Because he was endowed with the great aggregates of virtue and so forth, he was a "Great Kassapa," thus Mahākassapa. Furthermore, regarding the name "Mahākassapa":
Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, Gayākassapa, and Kumārakassapa—these are called the minor and lesser elders.
When the question arises as to why the Venerable Mahākassapa exerted himself, he spoke the words beginning with "seven days after the Parinibbāna" in order to explain the reason for it.
Seven days brought together constitute "seven days" (sattāhaṃ). Seven days...

"Of one who has attained final Nibbāna" (*parinibbutassa*) means "just as [one says] 'recently departed' or 'a month-old [infant]'"; this is a compound with the final member being a relative pronoun (*aññapadasamāsa*).
It refers to that [period]. What is meant is that seven days had elapsed starting from the day of the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna;
this connects with the phrase "the spoken words. Likewise, it also connects with the phrase "by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age."

In this context, "Subhadda" is merely his name; however, because he went forth in old age, he is referred to as "the one who went forth in old age" (*vuḍḍhapabbajita*), by which [the author] distinguishes him from the wanderer Subhadda and others.
With the words "Enough, friend," etc., he indicates the speech uttered by him.
For when the Blessed One had been completely extinguished for seven days, the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa—
While on the road from Pāvā toward Kusinārā with about five hundred bhikkhus, he saw some bhikkhus who had not yet overcome their passions.
Having seen them— having heard of the Blessed One’s final nibbāna from a Ājīvaka they encountered along the way,
casting aside their bowls and robes, and raising their arms while lamenting in various ways— he spoke as follows.

But why did he speak thus? It was out of resentment toward the Blessed One. It is said that this man, who had previously been a barber and had gone forth when old, was mentioned in the *Khandhaka* in the context of the story of Ātumā.

While the Blessed One was traveling from Kusinārā to Ātumā with one hundred and fifty monks, he heard, "The Blessed One is coming," and thought, "When he arrives, I shall offer him a gift of rice gruel."
To his two sons who were standing on the level of novices, he said this:
"Sirs, it seems the Blessed One is coming to Ātumā together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty.
Go, sirs, taking shaving kits, and wander from house to house with them in baskets or bags; [bring] salt, oil, and rice."
“Gather some solid food as well; when the Blessed One has arrived, we shall offer him a gift of rice-gruel.

They did so. Then, after the Blessed One had returned from his alms-round and entered the straw hut, Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening, addressed the people, and having requested their labor, saying, “Give me a little manual work,” he asked, “What?”
When they said, "Venerable sir, we shall do so," he had them take all the requisites, saying, "Take this and that.
Having had cooking hearths prepared in the monastery, he put on one black *kāṣāya* robe and draped himself in another of the same kind.
Wandering about all night long, directing them, "Do this, do that," he spent a hundred thousand [pieces of money] to provide rice gruel for eating and honey-balls.
He had it prepared. "Eating-gruel" (bhojjayāgu) refers to gruel that is to be drunk after having eaten;

therein everything that is called "hard food" (khādanīya)—such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flowers, fruits, juices, and so forth—is included. It was fragrant with sweet scents, suitable for anointing the heads of those wishing to play.
Then the Blessed One, having attended to his physical needs at the proper time, set out toward Ātumā for alms, surrounded by the community of monks.
Then they informed him: "The Blessed One is entering the village for alms;
for whom has the rice-gruel been prepared by you? He, wearing those very black robes as he had put them on, with one hand—
Taking both the ladle and the spoon, and placing his right knee upon the ground like Brahmā,
he paid homage and said, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my rice-gruel. Then,

according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka— that “Tathāgatas, though they already know, ask”— the Blessed One questioned him, and having heard [his response], [he accepted] that elder who had gone forth late in life.

Having rebuked him regarding that matter, and having laid down two training rules—the rule concerning the undertaking of what is improper and the rule concerning the carrying of razor equipment—he said: "Monks, for many millions of eons you have spent your time merely seeking food;
yet this food of yours is improper, obtained through unrighteous means. Having consumed this..."
"Many thousands of future existences will arise for you only in the states of misery; go away, do not take anything," he said, and then set out toward his alms-round.
Not even a single monk took anything. Subhadda, becoming displeased, thought, "This man wanders about saying 'I know everything';
if he had not wished to take anything, he should have sent someone to inform me."
"Even cooked food, when it lasts for the longest time, would last only for seven days; yet this [poison] would have been sufficient for me for as long as I live.
He has ruined everything! This man is a well-wisher of my harm.

Having thus harbored resentment toward the Blessed One, he was unable to say anything while the One of Ten Powers was still living. It is said that this thought occurred to him: "This [man] is high-born..."
“Having gone forth from a noble family, if I were to say anything while he is still living, he would surely rebuke me.
But today, traveling with the Elder Mahākassapa, upon hearing that “the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna,” he felt as if he had gained his breath;
joyful and elated, he spoke thus. However, when the Elder heard this, it was like a blow to his heart, or like a dry thunderbolt falling upon his head.
He thought, "It is as if [it were] a dry bone" (Dīghanikāya Aṭṭhakathā 3.232), and a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma arose in him:
"The Blessed One has been completely extinguished for only seven days, yet today his body still retains its golden color.

Such a great evil, a dregs-like thorn, has so quickly arisen against the Dispensation won by such hardship through the Blessed One. Indeed, it is enough that this evil one should not continue to grow."
“Having obtained other companions such as these, they will cause the Dispensation to decline.

Then the Elder thought: “If I were to have this old man brought out right here after making him dress in rags and covering him with ashes, people would say, ‘While the body of the ascetic Gotama was still living, his disciples—’”
Thinking, "They will dispute thus and show us fault," I shall endure it for now. For the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of flowers not yet gathered;
just as flowers struck by the wind go here and there, even so, as time passes under the influence of such people, one or two training rules (sikkhāpada) will be lost from the Vinaya.
"In the Sutta, one or two sections of questions will be lost; in the Abhidhamma, one or two sections of the planes will be lost.
Thus, by degrees, when the root is lost, we shall become like demons. Therefore, I shall compile the Dhamma and Vinaya;
for if this is done, this Dhamma and Vinaya will remain unshakable, like flowers gathered together on a strong thread."
For it was for this purpose that the Blessed One came out three *gāvutas* to meet me; he granted me full ordination with three exhortations;
he exchanged robes with me body-to-body; and while moving his hand in the air, as he spoke the "Moon-like Practice," he did so making me alone his witness;
he entrusted the entire jewel of the Dispensation to me three times—[all] for one such as me.
"While this monk remains, may this evil one not find growth in the Teaching, as long as non-Dhamma does not shine forth, Dhamma is not obstructed;
as long as non-discipline does not shine forth, discipline is not obstructed;
as long as those who speak non-Dhamma are not powerful, those who speak Dhamma are not weak; as long as those who speak non-discipline are not powerful..."
Those who speak according to the Vinaya will not be weak; for now, I shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together.
After that, the monks, each taking what they are capable of, will discuss what is allowable and what is not. Then this evil one will come to his own defeat by himself;
he will no longer be able to lift up his head, and the Teaching will become prosperous and flourishing.
Thinking, "It will be so," and not telling anyone that such a thought had arisen in his mind, he reassured the community of monks;
then, on the day of the enshrining of the relics, he inspired the monks to undertake the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
Thus it is said: "The Venerable Mahākassapa, seven days after the Parinibbāna... [etc.]"
"He roused the enthusiasm of the bhikkhus for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya.
In this context, *alaṃ* is a word of refusal, meaning "it is not fitting. He addresses the lamenting bhikkhus as "Āvuso" (friends).
"Mā socittha" means do not grieve with the powerful sorrow arisen in the mind; "mā paridevittha" means do not lament with speech.
"Do not utter lamentation. For it is said: "Lamentation is weeping. He states the reason for not grieving and so forth with the words beginning, "Well-released" (*sumuttā*).
In the phrase "by that Great Ascetic" (*tena mahāsamaṇena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the ablative; or else, it is a substitution for the locative case (*smā*-ending).

However, in the word "afflicted" (*upaddutā*), the connection is by way of the third case (instrumental) denoting the agent. This word depends on both [the preceding and the following]. Thus, [the meaning is]: "And we are afflicted."
The present tense used here refers to that time; the word "then" (*tadā*) is understood as the remainder.

Alternatively, it is a present tense used in the sense of the past, meaning "we were. He recollects solely by way of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) regarding the Dhamma, and not by way of anger or other such emotions.
For spiritual urgency is the knowledge of self-reproach (*sahottappa-ñāṇa*) that arises through reflection on the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*). Indeed, this has been said:
“Amidst all conditioned phenomena, it is established in the form of moral dread (*ottappa*);
for those whose burden is bewildered by ignorance, it is known as spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) regarding the Dhamma.
To show another reason for generating enthusiasm, he said, “of such a kind,” and so forth. Therein, “and of such a gathering of the Saṅgha” means:
He speaks with reference to the assembly of the Saṅgha, which exceeds the range of calculation and is headed by the Elder who is the leader of a group of seven hundred thousand.

By the words “It is possible that this may happen,” etc., he also shows another reason. It is called a *ṭhāna* (ground) because the fruit stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein, since its existence depends upon it;
thus, it is a cause. The word *kho* is used for emphasis. The word *pana* is a poetic ornament (*vacanālaṅkāra*).
The meaning is: "This possibility exists; it is not non-existent. But what is that? He says: "Those evil monks," and so forth.
*Yaṃ* is a mere particle, or it is a designation of the cause; by whatever means they might cause [the Dhamma] to disappear, that very possibility exists.
"Evil monks" (*pāpabhikkhū*) refers to monks who are possessed of evil, base, and ignoble conduct. Past...
*Satthā* here means "of this" (*etassa*), thus [it refers to] that which has passed away as its teacher (*atīta-satthuka*), just as in the expression *bahukattuko*.
*Pāvacanaṃ* is a word for "teaching" (*padhāna-vacana*). Here, the word *pā-* is a particle (*nipāta*), as in such examples as *pā eva vuttyassā*;
or it is a prefix (*upasagga-pada*), though it is stated with a long vowel in that way, as they also say *pāvadati*. *Pakkhaṃ* means the faction of the shameless (*alajjipakkhaṃ*).
By the passage beginning with “As long as,” etc., [the author] shows both the cause and the proof for the long endurance of the Dispensation through the communal recitation (saṅgīti).
Indeed, the word “therefore” (*tasmā*) should be supplied from the context and connected with the word “should recite” (*saṅgāyeyya*).
In that regard, “as long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure” means for as long a period as the Dhamma and the Vinaya remain among persons possessing a sense of shame (*lajjipuggala*).
[The Buddha] remains. He said, "For this has been said," and so forth, referring to what was spoken by the Blessed One while lying on his parinibbāna bed in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.
The particle *hi* serves to strengthen the point based on scriptural authority (*āgama*).
"Taught and laid down" means that the Dhamma is both taught and laid down; for the handing over and the awakening of the Dhamma comprised within the Suttas and the Abhidhamma [are intended].
Teaching (*desanā*) is the making known of that very [Dhamma] by way of its specific modes, and the establishing and setting forth within the mental continuum of those to be trained (*vineyya*).
Discipline (*vinaya*) is both taught and laid down. For "teaching" is the bestowing and awakening to the meaning comprised within the body of discipline (*vinayatanti*);

"laying down" is the making known of that very same thing by way of its specific modes and establishing it without confusion. Therefore, both pairs—of teaching and laying down, and of action and non-action—are likewise [to be understood].
It should be understood that "adherence" (sambajjhana) is appropriate.
"He" (so) refers to that Dhamma and Vinaya. "After my passing away" (mamaccayena): this is a locative construction used in the sense of the instrumental;
for thus say the grammarians. Or, it is an instrumental expression used in the sense of cause: "on account of my passing away, you [are] the Teacher."
The meaning is: "He will come to be [the teacher]. For it is said in the *Mahāparinibbāna-sutta-vaṇṇanā*: "When I have attained final Nibbāna, he will fulfill for you the task of a Teacher.
Here, the statement of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa-vacana*) establishes the sense of a causal relationship (*hetvattha*), just as in the expression "when the guide has gone straight.
This is what is meant: while I am still standing [among you], [he will say] "this is light, this is..."
"This is grave; this is curable; this is incurable; this is an offense against the world; this is an offense by rule;
this offense is cleared in the presence of an individual; this [is cleared] in the presence of a group;

this is cleared in the presence of the Saṅgha"—thus, with respect to the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses, the *Khandhaka-parivāra* deals with matters that have been brought forward.

The *Ubhatovibhaṅga* is taught as the *Mahāvinaya*; even this entire *Vinayapiṭaka*, once I have attained final Nibbāna, will fulfill for you the function of a Teacher by instructing through the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done, saying: "This is to be done by you; this is not to be done by you.
Furthermore, while I am still present, [I have taught]: "These are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts..."
"The four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path"—
having thus analyzed these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment again and again according to the specific inclinations of those to be trained,
the Sutta Piṭaka was taught; and that entire Sutta Piṭaka is [contained] within me.
When he has attained final Nibbāna, he will fulfill the Teacher’s task for you by instructing you in right practice according to each respective mode of conduct;

and while I am still present, [I shall teach: "These are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine causes, the four nutriments, the seven contacts, the seven..."
“Feelings, seven perceptions, seven volitions, and seven types of consciousness.
Therein, so many phenomena belong to the sense sphere, so many to the fine-material sphere, so many to the immaterial sphere; so many are included, so many are not included;
so many are mundane, so many are supramundane. Having analyzed these phenomena again and again, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka was taught.
"Even this entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, after I have attained final Nibbāna, will fulfill for you the work of a Teacher,
since it brings about the realization of the Four Truths when understood through the analysis of the aggregates and so forth.
Thus, all of this— from the time of my full enlightenment until my final Nibbāna— spoken and uttered over forty-five years, constitutes the Three Piṭakas and the Five Nikāyas."
"The ninefold division and the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma"—thus it is of such great variety. These eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma shall endure;
I alone shall attain final Nibbāna, and now I alone advise and instruct you.
But when I have attained final Nibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Buddhas will advise you.
“They will instruct” means because they accomplish the task of instruction and admonition.
“The Dispensation” (*sāsana*) refers to the threefold Dispensation by way of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and realization (*paṭivedha*);

but in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), it consists of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*). “Enduring” (*addhaniya*) means capable of traveling the path; it goes the distance and withstands the journey.
The meaning is as follows: "Ciraṭṭhitikaṃ" means that which has long duration.

This is what is intended: "If I were to recite together the Dhamma and the Vinaya in such a manner that this teaching would be enduring, and by that very means would have long duration—how excellent that would be!"
Now, recollecting the particular favor shown to him by the Perfectly Enlightened One and demonstrating even the manner of his reflection, he said: “And since I was by the Blessed One,” and so forth.
Therein, the word “yañca” (and since) is connected with the words “anuggahito” (favored) and “pasaṃsito” (praised).
“Yaṃ” means “because”; or it is a reference to the action, by which [it is understood] “I was favored and praised.”
Here, he refers to both the act of favoring and the act of praising. However, the words beginning with "Will you wear it?
were spoken by the Blessed One while seated upon a saṅghāṭi robe prepared by the Elder Mahākassapa at the foot of a certain tree;
as he sat there, he touched that saṅghāṭi with his hand, which was the color of a lotus flower, from end to end. For this has been stated in the *Kassapasaṃyutta*:
The Elder Mahākassapa himself, addressing the Elder Ānanda, spoke thus:
"Then, friend, the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, approached the foot of a certain tree;
then, friend, having spread out my outer robe made of patches of cloth folded fourfold, I said this to the Blessed One."
“‘Let the Blessed One sit here, venerable sir; it will be for my benefit and happiness for a long time.
Then, friends, the Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, friends, the Blessed One said this to me:
‘This outer robe made of patches of cloth is indeed soft for you, Kassapa. Let the Blessed One accept from me, venerable sir, this outer robe made of patches of cloth.’”
"Out of compassion for my outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," [the Blessed One said]. "But will you, Kassapa, wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes?
"I shall wear them, Bhante, those worn-out hempen rag-robes of the Blessed One.
Thus, friend, I gave the Blessed One my outer robe made of strips of cloth, while I myself took the Blessed One's hempen [robes].
“He has donned rag-robes that are worn out.
In this context, “They are soft for you; indeed, these are soft for you. But why did the Blessed One speak thus?
Because he wished to exchange robes with the Elder. Why did he wish to exchange them? Because he wanted to place the Elder in his own position.
It was because he wished to set them aside. [The question: "Are Sāriputta and Moggallāna not there? [The answer: "They are; however, it occurred to him:
'These two will not remain for long. Kassapa, however, has a lifespan of two hundred years;
after I have attained final Nibbāna, he will dwell in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, compile the Dhamma and Vinaya, and cause my dispensation to endure for a period of five thousand years.'"
He established him in his own position, thinking, "In this way, the monks will consider that they ought to listen to Kassapa.

Therefore, he spoke thus. But since it is the proper custom for one to say, "Take this," when the praises of a robe or a bowl have been spoken, the Elder said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept it from me."
"But will you wear these, Kassapa?"—Kassapa, he says this asking whether you will be able to put on these rag-robes worn out by use.
And that was not said with reference to physical strength; rather, he spoke thus with reference to the fulfillment of the practice.
This is the intended meaning here: "I [shall give] this robe to the slave girl named Puṇṇā..."
Having put it on, I entered the cemetery where it had been discarded in the raw charnel ground;
there, surrounded by insects the size of gourds, I shook off those insects and, standing in the Great Noble Lineage, I took it up.
On the day I took this robe, the great earth in ten thousand world-systems trembled with a great roar, and the sky resounded with a crashing sound.

The deities of the world-system gave their applause, saying: "It is fitting for the monk who accepts this robe to be one born into the lineage of those who wear rag-robes, those who dwell in the forest, those who sit at a single seat, and those who go on alms-round from house to house;
