will you be able to act in a manner worthy of this robe? The Elder, too, [possessed] the strength of five elephants himself...

He bore it; without conjecturing, with the resolve, "I shall fulfill this practice," and desiring to make [the robe] suitable for the Sugata’s robe, he said, "Venerable sir, I shall wear it. "I practiced" means: I have practiced.
But after they had thus exchanged robes, the Blessed One donned the robe worn by the Elder, and [donned] the Teacher's robe...
At that time, the great earth, bounded by the waters, thundered and shook. "Sāṇa rag-robes" refers to rags from dust-heaps wrapped around a corpse and discarded;
they are robes made of hemp-fiber (sāṇa-vāka) taken after shaking off the thumb-sized worms [found therein].
"Worn-out" means those whose function as clothing has been fulfilled; "worn out through use" means...
This is the meaning. And here, although that robe is indeed only one, the plural number is used because it consists of many parts;

this is stated in the *Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada*. Regarding the phrase "by means of common use with respect to the robe," since the sense "by means of common use together with oneself" is understood, and because there is freedom in the usage of a word whose meaning is already understood, the word "together with oneself" (*attanā*) [is supplied].
It was not stated [explicitly]. For because it was said, “Kassapa, will you accept my hempen rag-robes?
it is understood that [the robes] were for use in common with himself alone, and not with anyone else. Indeed, the determination of meaning is not always based on the word alone;
for in most cases, the meaning is established through the context of the matter and other such factors. However, regarding this point, by the Elder Master Dhammapāla...

Thus it has been said: regarding the phrase "by means of common use of the robe," the word "attanā" (by oneself) mentioned here—as in "by establishing equality with oneself"—should be brought forward and connected as "by means of common use of the robe with oneself.
For whatever has a connection with something, that [connection] belongs to it even if it stands far away.
"For proximity is not a cause for things that are dissimilar in meaning.

Alternatively, it should be construed as: 'He was favored by the Blessed One through the common use of robes,' because even a single instrumental case ending can indicate both the association with companions and the sense of the agent. That which has the same holding is its [commonality].
"Common" means such a shared enjoyment; thus, it is "common enjoyment," by which [he is assisted].
The connection is: "assisted by common enjoyment and by establishing equality. Now—
“Monks, as long as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought,

with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion; and Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought.”

By means of this passage from the Kassapa Saṃyutta, presented through the method of a series (*peyyāla*) and indicated by the phrase "beginning with" (*ādiggahaṇena*), the Blessed One spoke for the purpose of establishing himself as the equal of others in the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) distinguished by the nine successive dwellings (*navānupubbavihāra*) and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). This is stated as follows: “He enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is rapture and pleasure born of seclusion,” and so forth.
Showing it in brief, he said, “I, monks,” and so forth.
Therein, “yāvad eva” means “for as long as”; the sense is: for whatever length of time I desire, for that long I abide.
For this very reason, in both the *Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada* and the *Cūḷa-gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: “‘yāvad eva’ is what is meant by ‘yāvadeti’.”
It has been written. In the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā* as well, the meaning of "yāvade ākaṅkhāmī" is stated as "yāvadeva icchāmi" (as much as I desire).
For likewise, in that same work, in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla states:
"The word 'yāvade' has the same meaning as this [word] 'yāvadeva'. However, in some manuscripts, the reading is simply "yāvadevā."
It is seen. Furthermore, the meaning should be understood by supplying the ellipsis as follows:
"In the case of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), [the phrase] 'as far as I wish to dwell in a state of attainment, for that long I dwell in a state of attainment';
and in the case of the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), 'as far as I wish to employ the terminology of direct knowledge, for that long I employ the terminology of direct knowledge.'"
The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla also, in order to show that same meaning according to the method of his sources, stated:

"In as many dwellings of attainment (*samāpatti-vihāra*) or in as many modes of expression regarding direct knowledge (*abhiññā-vohāra*) as I desire to dwell in and express, in that same way did Kassapa [dwell]; such is the meaning.
Others, however, explain: "'As far as' (*yāvadā*) means: 'Whatever first jhāna I desire, having attained that first jhāna...'"

They say: "In the context of the attainments (*samāpatti*), such as in the passage beginning with 'I dwell,' and in the context of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), the word *ta-* (that) which has been drawn forward [from the previous clause] should be construed according to its object (*kamma*);

however, in the context of the remaining direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), it should be construed according to its instrument (*karaṇa*), as in: 'Whatever divine ear (*dibbasota*) I desire, by that divine ear I hear sounds.
Regarding the phrase "quite secluded from sensual desires" (*vivicceva kāmehi*), the word *eva* (quite/only) has the sense of restriction (*niyama*).
It should be applied in both places. What is to be said regarding this will be made clear further on.

Regarding the phrase "the classification of the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges": here, the "nine successive dwellings" are so designated because they are to be attained in successive order;
they consist of the eight attainments together with the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). The "six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiññā*)...
It is called the five higher knowledges (*pañcābhiññā*) together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*). In some manuscripts, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is seen here;
however, it is not intended, because there is no remainder of the meaning to be understood from the aforementioned canonical text.
It is the Dhamma of those among humans who have become superior to humans, or of superior humans—namely, the meditators and the noble ones (*ariya*).
"Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) means either "states beyond the human condition" or "states superior to the human condition.

Herein, the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*) are called "human states" because they can be accomplished by humans through their very nature even without cultivation or mental attention, and because they bring about a human existence.
However, it should be understood that the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth, which are superior to those, are "superhuman states."

"By establishing as equals" means by establishing [the Buddha] as equal [to Kassapa], thinking: "For as long a time, in as many meditative attainments, and to as great an extent as I employ the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), so too did Kassapa.

This refers either to establishing him in numerous respects, or to establishing him as absolutely equal because there is no human quality whatsoever that he does not possess in its entirety. Thus it is said: "by establishing as equals."
This should be understood as a mere praise on account of the commonality of possessing the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).

For the Venerable Mahākassapa does not, like the Blessed One, enter into meditative attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand million daily, nor does he exercise the direct knowledges by means of the Twin Miracle and so forth. Herein—
And this [statement], "by establishing oneself as equal to others in superhuman states," should be understood as merely an illustration.

For it is said: "Exhort the bhikkhus, Kassapa; deliver a Dhamma discourse to the bhikkhus, Kassapa. Either I, Kassapa, shall exhort the bhikkhus, or you. Either I, Kassapa, shall deliver a Dhamma discourse to the bhikkhus, or you.
In this way too, he indeed established himself as equal to others.
"In such a manner" means that the application of form was praised exactly as it was assisted.

"Having moved his hand in the air" refers to the Blessed One moving his own hand in the air; the connection is that he praised [the practice] by means of that very act, which served as the instrument for a mind unattached to families.

Alternatively, in the phrase "by means of an unattached mind," the locative case is used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*); thus, it means that after moving his hand in the air, [he praised] one who frequents families with an unattached mind.

The meaning is that he praised me by making me his witness, because it is appropriate for a bhikkhu to have a mind that is unattached among families, owing to his state of having an unattached mind. As it was said:
"Then the Blessed One waved his hand in the air; just as, bhikkhus, this hand does not cling to the air..."

"It is not grasped, it is not bound; even so, monks, when the mind of any monk who approaches families does not cling, is not grasped, and is not bound among those families—thinking, 'May those who desire gain obtain gain;
may those who desire merit perform meritorious deeds'—then, just as he is pleased and glad at his own gain, so too is he pleased and glad at the gain of others."
He is joyful. Such a monk, bhikkhus, is worthy to visit families.
When Kassapa visits families, bhikkhus, his mind does not cling, is not captivated, and is not bound among families, thinking, "May those who desire gain obtain it;
may those who desire merit perform meritorious deeds. Just as he is satisfied and joyful with his own gains, so too is he.
“Thus, one is glad and joyful at the gain of others.

In that context, “he moved his hand in the air” means that, as if moving twin flashes of lightning within the blue expanse of the sky, he moved his hand in the lower part, the upper part, and on both sides; and this [is found] in the Buddha-word of the Tipiṭaka.
“Unconfused words” means: “With a glad mind” (*attamano*) means with one’s own mind; it is not a mind seized by cutting it off through dejection (*domanassa*).
“With a happy mind” (*sumano*) means with a contented mind. Now, suppose someone of inferior disposition and wrong practice were to say:
“The Fully Enlightened One speaks out of place when he says, ‘Approach families like a bird moving in the sky due to the state of an unattached mind.’”
“[He] imposes an unbearable burden; make him do that which cannot be done.

Having thus cut off his line of argument, and showing that it is indeed possible to do so by taking the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera himself as witness—thinking, “There exists such a monk”—the Blessed One said, “Of Kassapa, monks,” and so forth.

He speaks of another praise as well: “And by the moon-like practice. This means he was praised because of the practice that resembles the moon acting as the instrument, or else he was praised by making that very practice his witness, with it serving as the basis. As it is said:
“Monks, approach families like the moon, keeping the body withdrawn, keeping the mind withdrawn, ever-new among families, free from arrogance.
Just as if, monks, a man were looking down into an old well or a mountain precipice...”
Or as one would approach a river-crossing or a difficult mountain pass by withdrawing both body and mind—
just so, monks, do you approach families like the moon, withdrawing both body and mind, always fresh among families and free from arrogance.
Kassapa, monks, approaches families like the moon, withdrawing both body and mind.
"Always new among families, free from arrogance.
In this context, "like the moon" means being similar to the moon. Is it similar by way of its roundness?
No; rather, just as the moon, when ascending into the vault of the sky, does not form intimacy, affection, or attachment with anyone...
or attachment, or longing, or obsession, yet he is dear and pleasing to the great multitude;

in the same way, by not engaging in intimacy with anyone, you too shall become dear and pleasing to many people like the moon, and thus approach the four classes of families, such as the kṣatriya clans—this is the meaning. Furthermore, just as...

The moon dispels darkness and spreads light; likewise, one should understand the meaning through such methods as "becoming like the moon by dispelling the darkness of the defilements and spreading the light of knowledge.
Regarding the phrases "having withdrawn the body" and "having withdrawn the mind," it means that by not engaging in intimacy and so forth, one withdraws both body and mind.
"Having drawn away," "having pulled," or "having removed"—this is the meaning. "Always new-comers" (*niccanavakā*) means always like newcomers;

that is, remaining exactly like guests. For when a guest enters a house reached in turn, if the masters of the house see him and, out of compassion, think, "Even our own sons and brothers, when away from home, used to wander about in this way," and they have him sit down...
They feed them, and as soon as they have finished eating, they rise and depart, saying,
"Take your bowls," neither forming intimacy with them nor arranging for their tasks or duties; in the same way, you too, having entered a house in due order,
should take whatever people give who are pleased with your deportment, and then depart, having severed all intimacy.
He indicates: "Depart, being unoccupied with their duties and obligations. "Without arrogance" means not being arrogant;
the meaning is: "approach families free from the eight grounds of bodily arrogance, the four grounds of verbal arrogance, and the many grounds of mental arrogance."
"Jarudapāna" means a ruined well. "Pabbatavisaṃsa" means a steep, precipitous place on a mountain.
"Nadīvidugga" means a difficult-to-cross place with broken banks in a river. Regarding the phrase "evameva kho":
here is the application of the simile—the four families are like the ruined well and so forth; the monk is like the man looking down; and just as one whose body and mind are not withdrawn...
Just as a man looking at those [pools] falls into them, so too a bhikkhu who approaches families with his body and other faculties unguarded becomes attached to those families;
from that, he encounters various kinds of misfortune, such as the breaking of the foundation of virtue (*sīla*).
But just as a man whose body and mind are withdrawn does not fall into them, so too [he should approach families] with his body guarded.

When a bhikkhu approaches families with speech guarded, mind guarded, and mindfulness well-established—having withdrawn both body and mind—he is not fettered by those families. Then his feet, hands, belly, and head—consisting of virtue, faith, concentration, and wisdom—are not broken;
he is not pierced by the thorns of lust and the like, and being happy, he goes wherever he desires.

He goes toward the direction of Nibbāna never before reached; thinking, "Such is this Mahākassapa," and in order to cut off the path of speech for those of inferior inclination or wrong practice, he spoke the words beginning with "Kassapa, monks," making the Elder Mahākassapa himself the witness.
Thus, one who desires the meaning here [should understand it] by means of the moon-like method of practice characterized by unflagging mental application.

If it were the case that [the Buddha] was praised by making me the instrument (*karaṇa*), or by making me the locus (*ādhāra*) for that [praise], then the word *eva* and the word *ca* would not be employed, because the two phrases would have the same grammatical core (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).
Indeed, this very meaning appears to be the more appropriate reading, as seen in the commentary on the *Parinibbāna Sutta*: "In the sky, the hand... [etc.]
For it was said: "Having set in motion the moon-like path of practice, he spoke to me, making me a witness with his own body.
What other freedom from debt could there be for him, other than the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya? This is the intended meaning.

In that context, "for him" (*tassa*)—having supplied the word "therefore" (*tasmā*) as a demonstrative indicating the reason for the relative pronoun *yam*—the meaning is "for him, [who is] me" (*tassa me*). [This refers to] the reference to the action.
...but rather for the sake of favoring him and praising him. In some manuscripts, the reading "tassa me" (of that mine) is seen;
if that were the case, then in reference to the action, the further word "tassā" (of her/that) would have to be supplied.
One who has no debt is "aṇaṇo"; the state of being such is "āṇaṇyaṃ. Apart from the communal recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, what else [is there]?
The meaning is that there will be for him a state of being free from debt, and it will not be otherwise.
By the passage beginning with "Did not the Blessed One," he clarifies the very same point by means of a simile. Regarding the phrase "by the granting of his own armor and sovereignty":

here, "armor" (*kavaca*) refers to a breastplate—that by which the chest is covered—and its inclusion is indicated by the mention of the robe (*cīvara*); as for "sovereignty" (*issariya*), [it refers to...]
But it should be understood as being by way of the demonstration of the higher knowledges and attainments (*abhiññā-samāpatti*).

"One who establishes the lineage" (*kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpaka*) means one who establishes the family lineage, the family tradition. Because the word "me" (*me*) has a constant requirement for a complement, the compound is "one who establishes the lineage of the True Dharma" (*saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpaka*). This is what is meant: for the purpose of establishing his own family lineage by crushing the host of enemies.
Just as a king, by bestowing the sovereignty of his armor, grants a son who will establish the lineage, so too the World-Honored One, the Far-Sighted One,
considering that I would become the one to establish the lineage of the True Dhamma, has bestowed upon me this extraordinary favor—
known as the gift of robes and the establishment of an equal status— in order to crush the hosts of adversaries to the Sasana and to establish the lineage of the True Dhamma.
"Did he not favor me? And did he not praise me with this sublime praise?"—thus he reflected.

Here, by the word *iti*, the three statements beginning with "It is possible that they might cause [the Dhamma] to disappear," "I shall recite it," and "What other freedom from debt will there be?"—which are preceded by the words "Would they cause it to disappear? and "I shall recite it"—are indicated.
Furthermore, the phrase "Indeed, it is possible" and so forth is pointed out by the word *iti*.

Now, in order to substantiate the aforementioned matter by means of the text of the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*, he says, "As it has been said," and so forth. Therein, as for "as it has been said" (*yathāha*): what has it been said?
It is meant to ask, "What has been said that serves to substantiate the meaning stated by me?

Or, the meaning is: "In whatever manner or by whatever method it was stated by me, in that very same manner it has also been stated in the canonical text (*pāḷi*). Or, as for "as": [it refers to] that which...

He stated this in the Pāḷi; thus, by that statement, my own words both coincide with and accord with it—just as one might say "the water of the Yamunā [is the same as] the water of the Gaṅgā"—because the fact that they serve as a proof for the Pāḷi is directly perceived, and because there is freedom in the application of a word whose meaning is already understood. This is for the purpose of clarifying the intended meaning.

This is the application of the meaning (*atthayojanā*). Or alternatively, the meaning is: "In whatever way, by whatever manner he generated the enthusiasm of the monks for the purpose of the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, in that same way it is stated even in the Pāḷi. Such is the case in similar instances.
Regarding the phrase *ekamidāhaṃ*, here *idaṃ* is merely a particle. And *ekaṃ samayaṃ* is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative.
"At one time" is the meaning. "From Pāvā" means from the city of Pāvā;
it is said that having wandered for alms there, he set out upon the highway with the intention, "I shall go to Kusinārā. "Highway" (addhānamagga) refers to a long road;
here, the word *addhāna* is a synonym for "long. "Great" means great both by way of greatness in virtue and greatness in number.
By the phrase “with about five,” etc., he shows the greatness of the number; and the word *matta* is a term for measure, as in such expressions as “moderation in eating,” and so forth.

The passage beginning with “Then indeed” (*atha kho*), which was cited to establish the meaning “he generated the effort for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya,” does not establish that stated meaning. For here—
He says, "The entire Subhadda Chapter should be understood in detail," in order to avoid the objection that [the method] has arrived merely as a way of generating enthusiasm.
Thus, this objection remains in its original state; therefore he says, "After that, he said," and so forth.

Furthermore, since the canonical text (pāḷi) that establishes the aforementioned meaning is very extensive, for the sake of avoiding the burden of the text, he employs the method of abbreviation (peyyāla) in the middle.
Showing the entire text from beginning to end, he said: "The entire Subhadda Chapter should be understood in detail.

By this, he shows the Subhadda Chapter starting from the passage, "Then indeed, friends, having stepped down from the path, I sat down at the foot of a certain tree," up to its conclusion with the passage, "Whatever we do not wish for, that we shall not do."

The passage beginning with “Tato paraṃ” (After that), however, shows the remaining portion of the text which demonstrates the manner of generating enthusiasm, namely the words “Handa mayaṃ āvuso” (Come, friends) and so forth.

Therefore, regarding the phrase “tato paraṃ āha” (after that he said), the meaning should be understood as: after the Subhadda-khaṇḍa, he spoke the words demonstrating the manner of generating enthusiasm.
Indeed, this very same meaning is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*. The Elder Master Sāriputta also [said the same].
It is intended exactly thus. However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has stated: "Beyond that" means "after generating enthusiasm among the bhikkhus.
This must be examined, because the manner of generating enthusiasm was not mentioned in the Canon (pāḷi) below this point.
For this very manner of generating enthusiasm is as follows: "Come, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together."

“Only unrighteousness shines,” and so forth. However, if one were to say that the Subhadda Chapter itself constitutes the “arousing of enthusiasm”—because it explains the words spoken by Subhadda which served as the cause for arousing enthusiasm—then there would be no need for further deliberation here.
Regarding the phrase “only unrighteousness shines”: here, “unrighteousness” (*adhamma*) refers to that which is the opposite of the ten courses of wholesome action.
Alternatively, because of the context of generating enthusiasm for the purpose of the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, there may also arise a multitude of faults caused by that non-recitation;

and because it is said, "those who speak what is not Dhamma become powerful, while those who speak the Dhamma become weak," they say that the multitude of faults such as evil desire (pāpicchatā), which have their cause in failures of virtue (sīlavipatti) and so forth, is also "non-Dhamma" (adhamma). It also shines before.

The word *nāma* signifies "doubt. For the word *pure* has the sense of doubt. Alternatively, the meaning is: "prior to the time when unrighteousness (*adhamma*) becomes capable of obstructing righteousness (*dhamma*).
This word *pure* is used here in the sense of "nearby" rather than in its intended sense [of "before"]. Regarding the word *dippati*: it means "it will shine" (*dippissati*).
For, due to its connection with the word *pure*, this present tense usage (*vattamāna-payoga*) is employed in the sense of the future, just as in the following example: [text omitted].
“‘The sky will rain soon’”— for it has been said:
“The word *pura* is employed by poets to refer to both the future,
when something is about to happen, and the past, when something occurred long ago.”
“Whether it be always or at some time, in the conjunction ‘pureyāva-purā,’ even when ‘laddha’ (obtained) is stated, why would the present tense become the future?
Some, however, explain it here as follows: *pure* means later or in the future, just as for one traveling along a path...
The path to be traversed is called "ahead" (*pure*); likewise here too, by way of proceeding along a path, the future time is called "ahead.
This being so, the use of the present tense is possible here with reference to that time.

Regarding the phrase "the Dhamma will be obstructed," the meaning should be understood by connecting it with the word *pure* according to the method already stated; likewise, "Dhamma" [is used] in the sense of being the opposite of "adhamma."

From this point onward, the same method applies. "Non-discipline" (*avinaya*) refers to that which is the opposite of the discipline of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*) and the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*).

Regarding the phrase "those who speak of discipline are weak," the reading includes the particle *iti*; this [particle] should be connected with the word *āha* ("said") in the expression "after that he said."
*Tena hi* is a particle used in the sense of exhortation. For, while exhorting [others] to select [monks], they said to the Elder Mahākassapa, "Let him select the monks," meaning:
"Having selected and scrutinized the monks suitable for the communal recitation (saṅgīti), let him take them.

By the phrase "He encompassed all... and so forth, [it refers to] those aforementioned individuals, ending with the dry-insight practitioners (sukkha-vipassaka) and those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).

Even though the possibility of scriptural learning (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*) exists [elsewhere], this [text] demonstrates its great utility for the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*), because it represents the pinnacle of the perfection of both scripture and realization for those endowed with qualities such as the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*) along with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
"The entire ninefold division" (*sakalanavaṅga*) means that the nine divisions, beginning with the discourses (*sutta*) and verses (*geyya*), are contained within this, or belong to this;
thus, it is the "Teacher’s Dispensation" (*satthusāsana*), the dispensation of the Blessed One, the Teacher, which is taught (*sāsīyati*).

"By this" means having made it so; "the very teaching of the Teacher" refers to the entire ninefold teaching of the Teacher (*navaṅga-satthusāsana*). Alternatively, it is "ninefold" (*navaṅga*) because the nine factors—discourse (*sutta*), verse (*geyya*), and so forth—are contained therein, or because it belongs to that [ninefold set]. That very teaching of the Teacher is thus "entire," not merely a partial portion.
It should be mastered and studied by one desiring welfare, or in order to accomplish the welfare of persons pertaining to the present life and so forth.
“Pariyatti” means that which is mastered or capable; it refers to the three Piṭakas, the entire teaching of the Teacher consisting of the ninefold division (navāṅga).
Those who bear this are so called; the meaning is "those who possess such [a mastery]. Regarding the passage beginning with "puthujjana... pe... sukkhavipassaka-khīṇāsava-bhikkhū," it is said here:
"Two kinds of worldlings (puthujjana) were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun."
“The blind worldling is one, and the noble worldling is another.”— Among those mentioned,
it is specifically the noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) who are intended, because even through the proximity of other words, a specific meaning must be understood.

They are called “dry-insight practitioners” (*sukkha-vipassaka*) because their insight is dry, coarse, and unsmeared due to the absence of the moisture of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*).
“Those very ones whose taints are destroyed” is likewise [to be understood]. However, the word “bhikkhus” should be applied in all instances.

For it has been said: “That which is heard from one possessing a meaning, or even by way of ellipsis, is connected individually with each [term], according to what is available, or sometimes [even] when not [explicitly] present.”
Regarding the phrase "one who bears all the various divisions of the *Tipiṭaka* learning": here, the collection of the three *piṭakas* is the *tipiṭaka*.
Those who bear all the various divisions of the learning (pariyatti) reckoned as that *tipiṭaka*, which is divided into many categories such as the ninefold division (*navanga*), are thus described;
[it refers to] such persons. That which brings about (*bhāveti*) and increases (*vaḍḍheti*) the possession of that [learning] for each individual is *anubhāva*; that very thing is *ānubhāva*.
Those who possess radiance (*pabhāva*) and great majesty (*mahanto ānubhāvo*) are called "those of great majesty" (*mahānubhāvā*).

Because it occurs based on the words spoken by the Blessed One, "This is the foremost, monks" (*etadaggaṃ bhikkhave*), the term *etadagga* is a name derived from imitation, just as in the case of the term *yevāpanaka*.

By virtue of that [designation], the phrase "this is the foremost" (*etadaggaṃ*) refers here to the state immediately following [the attainment]; the meaning is that this monk has been assigned to that [foremost rank]. This monk is the foremost.

The term *agga* (foremost) is appropriate even when [the status] has been formally conferred. To show that even those not so conferred are selected there because they are endowed with the remaining qualities, it is said "for the most part" (*yebhuyyena*).
*Tevijjā* means the three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*); those for whom the three knowledges are the beginning—such as the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and so forth—are the "tevijjādayo.
Those whose various divisions (*bhedā*) are of many kinds are "tevijjādibhedā. Alternatively, he who possesses the three knowledges...

“Of one whose taints are destroyed” (*khīṇāsavassa*) means one who possesses the threefold knowledge (*tevijjo*). Those for whom the sixfold direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and so forth are the beginning are called “those possessing the threefold knowledge and so forth” (*tevijjādayo*).

Those for whom these very things constitute their distinctions are “those distinguished by the categories of the threefold knowledge and so forth” (*tevijjādibhedā*). What is meant is that there are monks whose taints are destroyed, who are divided into many categories by way of the threefold knowledge, the sixfold direct knowledges, and so on.
“With reference to whom it was said” means with reference to those monks that this statement beginning with “Then indeed” (*atha kho*) and so forth was spoken.

This was stated in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*. Although it is stated there without distinction in the text, nevertheless, one should reconcile this with the text by understanding that it refers specifically to those bhikkhus whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), as previously described.

For are there not indeed many hundreds and many thousands of those whose taints are exhausted who uphold the entire scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*) of the Teacher’s dispensation consisting of the ninefold division?
Having raised the objection, "And why did the Elder omit one [verse]?", he spoke the passage beginning with "But for what purpose...

in order to resolve it by showing the specific reason. Therein, "kissa" means "for what reason. The particle *pana* indicates an alternative position. "Okāsakaraṇatthaṃ" means for the sake of making room, that is, for the purpose of making room, for the cause of making room.
For the word *attha* [is used here] in the sense of "purpose," as in: "Having gone out from the city for the purpose of a festival..."
In such instances as "Let him ascend Mount Missaka," it is a word expressing the cause (kāraṇa); and in such instances as "For what reason?

(kissa hetū), it is a nominative form used in the sense of a causal particle (hetvatthe). For they explain it thus: "'For the sake of the festival' (chaṇatthaṃ) means for the purpose of the festival, for the cause of the festival.
This being so, the answer shares the same nature as the question; this is the method to be applied in such cases.
But why did he grant him the opportunity? To this he said, “Therefore,” and so forth. The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used in the sense of a reason.
By the passage beginning with “That venerable one,” he shows the individual reasons for the statement, “It is not possible either together or apart.

Some, however, say that [this phrase] “explains that meaning”; that is incorrect, because of the appearance of the word expressing the reason, namely “therefore” (*tasmā*). For by the passage beginning with “therefore,”...
In the sense of indicating a cause, the word *hi* is indeed a causal indicator. However, in cases such as these, particles like *sākhābhaṅgopamā* and *hi* indicate a mere sign (*saññāṇamatta*).
One who trains is a *sekkha*; or, training (*sikkhā*) is the training itself, and that very thing is his virtue (*sīla*), thus he is a *sekkha*.
For, because his training is not yet completed and because he is intent upon it, he is exclusively one whose nature is to train, and not...
Like one beyond training (*asekkha*), he has completed his training and his exertion therein has subsided;

yet he is not like the ordinary person who has abandoned the training and lacks devotion to it. Furthermore, the meaning here is understood according to its essential nature through the benefit of that [training], just as in the term "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*).
Alternatively, he is "born" (*jāta*) into the three trainings by way of noble birth, or in them...
"One in training" (*sekkha*) means one who possesses insight (*ikkhā*). Furthermore, *ikkhā* is that by which one sees; it is right view of the path and its fruit.
One who possesses this insight is "one in training. Because the function of the three higher paths has not yet been completed, one is "with something still to be done" (*sakaraṇīya*).

The word "his" (*assa*) refers to "by him" (*anena*), and it is connected with the phrase "that which is called 'not directly perceived'. Alternatively, "his" (*assa*) is the recipient of the action in the sentence "there is not" (*natthi*).
Because it exists as a state of skillful activity, there is no such thing as "not being directly perceived. However, in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:

"There is nothing called 'received in the absence [of the Teacher]'" (asammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ nāma natthi). This was said by taking into account that even what is described as "two thousand [verses] from a monk" is indeed considered to have been received in the very presence of the Blessed One. For likewise, even a discourse spoken by a disciple is called "spoken by the Buddha."
With the words beginning “As it was said,” etc., [the author] shows that the very verse uttered by the Venerable Ānanda serves as the proof.
For this verse was spoken by Gopakamoggallāna, a certain brahmin, who asked: “You are renowned in the Buddha’s teaching as one of great learning;
how many teachings were spoken by your Teacher, and how many have been retained by you? It was given as his reply.
This was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda himself in the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta by way of showing his own virtues, and it is also stated in the Theragāthā.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: from the Buddha, the Teacher, I received and mastered eighty-two thousand divisions of the Dhamma;
two thousand divisions of the Dhamma [I received] from the monks, such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and others.

I received them from the presence of the bhikkhus. Those teachings which were on the tip of my tongue or in my heart, those that were familiar or mastered by recitation—having combined both of these, they constitute the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*).
However, some [commentators], making the word-division *ye ime* for the phrase *yeme*, [interpret it as] "those teachings which belong to the Buddha and the bhikkhus..."

They state the following connection: "I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha among those teachings that were set in motion by the Buddha; I received two thousand from the monks; thus there are eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma.
However, because this connection does not make it known with certainty that "there are only this many divisions of the Dhamma," it is designated as the "theory of some" (kecivāda).

Because the reason for saying “it cannot even with [them]” is more powerful than the reason for saying “it cannot without [them],” since it is more helpful for the communal recitation (saṅgīti), the passage beginning with “If indeed” was stated there to show the objection and resolve it. In that context, “If indeed” means:
if it cannot be done without [them] in this way, then such being the case; [this applies to] a trainee (sekkha) as well.

The person in training (sekkhapuggala) is also "equal" (samāno). Here, the word *māna* is used in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). "Because of being of great service" means because of being of great assistance.
For the word *kāra* expresses the idea of assistance, as in such passages as: "Even a small deed done, when it is a deed (*kāra*), becomes merit of great fruit.
*Assa* means "it would be. The word *atha* is used in the sense of a question. For in a question, one asks: "Now, in what way (*kena vaṇṇena*)..."
They cite the application [of the rule]. However, the meaning should be stated as "this being so.

"Because of avoiding the censure of others" means because of the desire to avoid the imputed censure from others who do not understand the aforementioned reason. He explains that with the words beginning, "For the elder...
"Exceedingly confident" means one who is highly trustworthy. To show by what this is known, he says, "For thus... and so forth. This is for the purpose of strengthening [the argument].
Or rather, this is the meaning of the word. For those skilled in grammar say: “*vuttaṃ* and *tathā hi* are used for the purpose of strengthening [an argument].
The word *naṃ* refers to the Elder Ānanda. It is connected with the verb *ovadati* (he exhorts).
When the Elder Ānanda’s assembly was for the most part departing because it consisted mostly of novices, the Elder Mahākassapa said: “This youth does not know his measure. Likewise...

Indeed, after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa sat in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assembled at the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna and, having selected five hundred bhikkhus for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya, said:
"Friends, dwelling for the rains retreat in Rājagaha, we shall recite the Dhamma and Vinaya; you [should] before the commencement of the rains..."
Having said, “Cut off your own impediments and assemble at Rājagaha,” he himself went to Rājagaha.

The Elder Ānanda also took the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, and after going to Sāvatthī while instructing the great multitude, he departed from there and traveled toward Rājagaha, wandering on alms-round in Dakkhiṇāgiri. At that time, regarding the Elder Ānanda...
About thirty co-residents, mostly young boys—both bhikkhus of one or two years' standing and those who were not yet fully ordained—left the Order.
Why did they go forth, and why did they leave? It is said that their parents thought:
"The Elder Ānanda is trusted by the Teacher; having requested eight boons, he attends upon him, and wherever he wishes to go..."
“If he is able to take the Teacher and go, we shall have our children ordained in his presence;
thus he will return taking the Teacher with him, and when he has arrived, we shall be able to perform a great honor for him.
For this reason, their relatives ordained them. But after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, their [desire]—
Their aspiration was cut off, and then they were expelled from the order on that very same day.
Later, when the Elder Ānanda returned to Rājagaha after wandering on tour in Dakkhiṇāgiri, the Elder Mahākassapa saw him and spoke thus. For this is said in the *Kassapasamyutta*:
“Now, friend Ānanda, why is it that you [have come] with these new bhikkhus who have not guarded the doors of their sense faculties?”
"You wander on tour with those who are immoderate in eating and not devoted to wakefulness;
it is as if you are wandering about destroying crops, as if you are wandering about destroying families. Your assembly, friend Ānanda, is falling apart;
your new recruits are falling away. This young man does not know moderation."
"Venerable Kassapa, gray hairs have grown upon my head, and yet even today we are not released from being called 'boys' by the Venerable Mahākassapa. "But, friend Ānanda,
it is because you are with these young bhikkhus who do not guard the doors of their sense faculties, who are immoderate in eating, and who are not devoted to wakefulness."
"You are wandering on a journey; I think you are wandering about destroying the crops, I think you are wandering about destroying families.
Indeed, friend Ānanda, your assembly is falling apart; indeed, friend, your new recruits are dissolving. This young man does not know his measure.
In this context, "I think you are wandering about destroying the crops" means you are roaming about as if you were destroying a harvest. "I think [you are] destroying families..."
"You wander about as if destroying families. "It crumbles" means it falls apart and breaks.

"Your novices, friend, are indeed crumbling away" means, friend Ānanda, these novices of yours—mostly new ones, those with one year of seniority, two years of seniority, and the young ones—are crumbling away.
"This boy does not know his measure" means this boy [does not know] himself...

"Indeed, he does not know the measure"—this was said by way of rebuking the elder. "We are not released from the charge of being like children" means we are not released from the accusation of being like children.
"For thus indeed you [speak]" is stated for the purpose of showing the reason why he should be addressed in this manner.
This is the intended meaning here: because you, with these new [monks] who lack restraint of the sense faculties and who are immoderate in food...
"You wander together with children; therefore, as you wander with children, you deserve to be called 'a child'.

In the phrase "Or perhaps this child did not know his measure," the word *vā* is used for the purpose of filling out the meter (*padapūraṇe*). Indeed, the word *vā* is seen in many senses, such as comparison, conjunction, doubt, exclusion, alternative, and metrical filler.
For instance, it is seen in the sense of comparison in passages such as "He is wise, or even so" (*paṇḍito vāpi tena so*).
The meaning is “similarity. In such passages as “The wise sages perceive that too,” it is used for conjunction (*samuccaya*).

In such passages as “Who are these, or whose are they? it is used for doubt (*saṃsaya*). In such passages as “Of all these ascetics and brahmins, this one is the most foolish and the most deluded,” it is used for exclusion (*vavassagga*).
In such passages as “Whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be, monks,” it is also used for option (*vikappa*). “Or not, I... [and so forth].

In such passages as "I eat leaves; this is not my food," it is used for the purpose of completing the meter (*padapūraṇa*). Here too, it should be understood as being for the purpose of completing the meter.
For this very reason, when the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla was enumerating the meanings of the word *vā*, he stated:
"In such cases as 'this boy did not know moderation,' it is used for the purpose of completing the meter. This same point is also stated in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*.
It is said: “‘Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī’—this youth, reproaching the elder, said: ‘Indeed, you do not know your own measure.
Here too, the word “vatā” is used for the sake of euphony (vacana-siliṭṭhatā).
Alternatively, by making the word-division “na ve ayaṃ” instead of “na vāyaṃ,” the word “vatā” is used to indicate the meaning of the particle “ve.”
For indeed, when the particle *ve* has the sense of "certainly" (*ekamsattha*), the etymologists (*neruttika*) cite that very passage from the Canon as an example.

However, the Elder Vajirabuddhi says: "In this context, 'they do not blow' (*na vāyanti*) means 'there is blowing' (*vāti vibhāsā*); [it means] 'he knew' (*aññāsi*) and also 'he did not know' (*na aññāsi*).
This is merely his own opinion, because it is not stated so in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*. This is one cause for the possibility of being censured by others.
The phrase “therein some” and so forth is to be connected [with the preceding].

He states another reason as well: “and the Venerable One was born into the Sakyan clan. This means that the Venerable Ānanda was born in the Sakyan clan, or was well-known by virtue of being of the Sakyan clan.
Therein... [the connection is] “they would criticize,” and so on. He states yet another reason.

“He is the Tathāgata’s brother, the son of his younger father. Here, he is called “brother” because he is the younger brother by virtue of being the son of the younger father, and not because he was born at the same time as [the Buddha] in terms of age.
“Suddhodana, Dhotodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, Amitodana;”
“Amitā, Pālitā, and so on—these five and these two.
For among those mentioned, the youngest of all was the Venerable Ānanda, the son of King Amitodana. Indeed, it is stated in the *Manorathapūraṇī*:
“But after giving gifts for a hundred thousand eons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta...”
Having passed away from there, he was reborn in the house of the Sakyan Amitodana;
because he was born making all his kinsmen joyful and delighted, they gave him the name ‘Ānanda.
It is stated exactly thus in the *Papañcasūdanī* as well:
“But others say: ‘The Venerable Ānanda was not born at the same time as the Blessed One;

rather, because he was younger in age and was the son of his father’s younger brother, he was indeed the Blessed One’s younger brother. For this reason, he is not included in the calculation of those born together [with the Buddha] in the commentary on the First Nipāta of the Manorathapūraṇī.

What is said there should be accepted. ‘Therein’ means when that state of being trusted and so forth exists. Because of his being the son of the Sakyan clan who was exceedingly trusted, and because of his being the brother of the Tathāgata.”
This has been stated. For in some instances, when characterizing a state by means of another state, the sense of a causal relationship (*hetu*) arises.
Thus, in the commentary on the *Netti*, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, in his explanation of the verse beginning "If cows are running away," says:

"‘All those go crookedly’ means all those cows go only in a curved manner; why? ‘When the leader has gone crookedly,’ that is, when the leader has gone in a curved way; the meaning is ‘because the leader has gone crookedly.’"
In the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*, too, in the commentary on the Sutta passage, "When this exists, that comes to be," it is said:
"It should be understood that by means of the state of the cause—the locative case having the sense of a reason—the state of the effect, which is inseparable from it, is indicated.

Alternatively, the meaning of "therein" (*tattha*) is "in the confidence [of the mind] and so forth, which have become the sign"; they also say it refers to "the selecting" (*uccinane*). This is the approach through desire (*chandāgamana*).
The word division here is *viyāti ettha chandā āgamanaṃ*. The term *chandā* is an ablative used in the sense of a cause (*hetumhi*);
the meaning is "as if the arrival [or occurrence] were due to desire. What is meant is that it is like performing what should not be done by means of desire.
Alternatively, *chandāgamanaṃ* refers to that which arrives [or arises] through association with desire; such a state leads to rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*).
An unwholesome arising of consciousness. Alternatively, "non-going" (*agamanam*) is going in an improper manner.
"Going through desire" (*chandāgamanam*) means going or proceeding in an improper way through desire—that is, through affection—which is like doing what should not be done;

this is what is meant. The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) are those of one beyond training (*asekkha*); "one who has attained them" means having reached that state. Furthermore, they are both "beyond training" and "those who have attained the analytical knowledges."
*Vā* means "or," [referring to] such [states]. Regarding the phrase *sekkhapaṭisambhidāppattaṃ*, the same principle applies here as well.

In the word *parivajjento*, the suffix *-anta* has the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe*); thus the meaning is "on account of avoiding. *Anumatiyā* means "by permission" (*anuññāya*); it is equivalent to saying "by request.

The statement "even though he is a learner" (*kiñcāpi sekkho*) is said because [this category] is selected specifically for those who are beyond training (*asekkha*), not because learners are capable of going to a bad destination (*agatigamana*).
For it is by the very first path that the four wrong courses (*agatigamana*) are abandoned;
therefore, although he is still a trainee (*sekkha*), the connection is that the Elder nevertheless selected the Venerable Ānanda.

It does not mean, however, that although he is a trainee, he is incapable of going on a wrong course. By the words "incapable" (*abhabbo*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates his worthiness (*arahabhāva*) for the recitation of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgīti*).

He speaks of qualities that actually exist; this shows that when the council for the determination of the Dhamma and Vinaya arrives, he will not speak otherwise out of favoritism or other such motives, but will speak exactly as it is.
"Agati" means a destination that should not be gone to, or an inappropriate course; that [he avoids]. "Pariyatti" means that which has been mastered and learned.

By the words beginning with “Evaṃ,” he shows the enumeration of the conclusion (*sanniṭṭhānagaṇana*). “Uccinitena” means that which was selected and taken up. Furthermore, they say that “Evaṃ... pe... uccinī” is the conclusion (*nigamana*), while “Tenāyasmatā” and so forth show the enumeration of the conclusion.
Having thus shown the manner of the compiler’s selection, he says “Atha kho” and so forth, showing other aspects such as the selection of the location for the purpose of compilation.
Therein, “etadahosi” means that this reflection occurred. By the word “nu,”...
This indeed shows the process of reflection. Regarding "Rājagaha," the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries state that it is spoken of by including the vicinity of Rājagaha.
It is called *gocara* because cattle (*go*) graze there; it is a place for cattle to roam. That which is like this is a *gocara*, meaning a place for monks to roam.
Because it is great, it is "Mahāgocara" (the Great Pasture), or because they roam therein, it is Mahāgocara. It is also [the site] of the eighteen great monasteries (*mahāvihāra*).
Because of its existence, there are abundant dwellings.
"Stable action" means long-lasting action. A "dissimilar person" is like Subhadda. "He would obstruct" means he would prevent [the Dhamma from spreading].
The word *iti* is used in the sense of "this"; the meaning is: "By means of this attention acting as a cause, this occurred. This is for the purpose of generating a sense of reverence.

He informed the Saṅgha by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*), not merely by a motion following a request (*apalokanañattikamma*); this is the intended meaning.
To the question "When was this performed?", he says "This, however," and so forth.

He shows that the fact of its having been performed is understood through this calculation with the words "For the Blessed One," and so on. The word *atha* is a particle used in the sense of immediate succession; the meaning is "immediately after the Parinibbāna."
"Seven days" is stated including even the day of the Parinibbāna. "Assa" refers to the Blessed One; it is connected with the word "body.

Because they celebrated by repeatedly praising the grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and singing songs connected with impermanence (*aniccatā*) as a form of worship, those beautiful days of celebration are called "days of excellent celebration" (*sādhukīḷanadivasa*), in the sense of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others.

It is also appropriate that they celebrated for several days by repeatedly praising the grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) of those true persons (*sappurisa*) who had been declared "Excellent" (*sādhu*).

And during these preceding seven days, they performed the "Excellent Celebration" (*sādhukīḷana*) only partially; however, it was done especially on the days of the relic-worship (*dhātupūjā*) and other such occasions.
For it is said thus in the *Mahāparinibbāna-sutta-aṭṭhakathā*:
“During the first two weeks, those bhikkhus, while preparing seating and space for the Saṅgha and providing hard and soft food, found no opportunity for fine entertainment. Then it occurred to them:
‘For this week we shall enjoy ourselves with fine entertainment; however, there is the possibility that we might become heedless.’”
“Having learned this, someone might come and seize the relics; therefore, let us establish a guard and play. Thus they acted.
Nevertheless, because they also performed worship of the relics, these days are called “Relic-Worship Days.

Furthermore, since there was nothing else specifically to be done for the Blessed One, even though it was only partially so, it is called “Sādhukīḷana Days” (Days of Exclamations of “Well Done! by way of that partial performance.
"They became manifest," he said, "in this way, there were seven days known as days of excellent sporting.

Regarding "on the funeral pyre": on a funeral pyre made of sandalwood logs twenty-one cubits high; and it is stated that by virtue of his primary purpose alone, he burned on the funeral pyre with fire for seven days.
For it was not by way of absolute conjunction that he remained continuously for exactly seven days.
He meditated by means of fire because he meditated on that very same day as the last of the seven days; therefore, the meaning should be understood as "during the seven days.
For if one meditates on any day whatsoever within the seven-day period between the first and the last seven days, it is appropriate to say, "one who meditates for seven days. As it has been said:

“Now at that time, four leading Mallas, having washed their heads and dressed in new clothes, thinking, ‘We shall set fire to the Blessed One’s funeral pyre,’ were unable to set it alight,” and so forth.

“Having made a cage of spears” means that he speaks by way of illustration of the Malla kings’ act of guarding the relics of the Blessed One with men holding spears, swords, and other weapons in their hands.
For those men with spears in their hands held the spears just as [one might say] “spears are moving about. By means of them...
It is called a "sword-cage" (*sattipaṃjara*) because it resembles a cage due to its function of providing protection on all sides. A "council hall" (*sandhāgāra*) is a great hall belonging to kings.
For at times such as when preparing for a military expedition, kings stand there and give orders:
"So many should go in front, so many behind, so many on both sides; so many should mount the elephants, so many the horses, so many..."
They make a compact and establish a boundary by saying, "The chariots [shall stop here]"; therefore, that place is called a "council hall" (*sandhāgāra*).

Furthermore, even when kings have arrived from the camp, they remain there for two or three days, resting and dispelling fatigue until they have applied fresh cow dung and plaster to their dwellings. Thus it is also called a council hall.
A *sandhāgāra* is a hall where kings deliberate on affairs of state together; it is called a *sandhāgāra* by changing the letter *ha* to *dha* and adding the suffix *anusāragama*.

Alternatively, because kings assemble there and deliberate upon the duties of household life according to such principles as "it is proper to plow at this time" and "it is proper to sow at this time," it is therefore [called] *chinnavicchinna*.
It is also called *sandhāgāra* because they maintain their household dwellings there.
From the full moon of the month of Visākha until the new moon of the month of Visākha, sixteen days are taken according to the Sinhalese reckoning;
adding five days from the waxing fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, he said, "Thus twenty-one days have passed. On that very last day, the relics...
They distributed [the robes], and on that very day this formal proclamation (kammavācā) was made. Therefore it is said: “On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Jeṭṭha-Mūla,” and so forth.
In that context, either the Jeṭṭha asterism or the Mūla asterism was conjoined with the moon on the full moon day of that month;
therefore, that month is called the “Jeṭṭha-Mūla month. “Improper conduct” refers to the improper conduct mentioned below.
If this is so, why is it stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* and in the *Maṅgala-sutta-aṭṭhakathā*:

“When the seven days of the joyful celebration and the seven days of the relic-worship have passed”? Because when the seven days of relic-worship are taken, the seven-day period of burning on the funeral pyre in between is also implicitly included due to its inseparable connection with them; thus, it was not mentioned separately.
It appears as if it were so. If this is the case, why was it said, "Half a month has passed;
one and a half months remain"? This is not a fault. For a very small deficiency or excess does not count toward the total;
therefore, considering that even a collection increased by a small amount is as if it were not increased, it is said, "Half a month has passed," even when five days have been added to the half-month.
Just as there is the expression "eighty khandhaka-vattas" in some places regarding what were stated as the eighty-two khandhaka-vattas,
so too, considering that even a collection deficient by a small amount is as if not deficient,

it is said in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* that when five days are lacking from one and a half months, "one and a half months remain," and similarly, when half a month is lacking from six months.
This is like the statement, “Recitation should be performed for two months”; otherwise, there would be mutual contradictions among the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Furthermore, according to the opinion of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas, it is stated here that “twenty-one days have passed” by way of three weeks.
However, in the commentaries on the *Vinaya*, the *Suttanipāta*, and the *Khuddakapāṭha*, according to the opinion of the Khuddaka-bhāṇakas...
Having treated the day of the Parinibbāna itself as a single [unit], it is stated that "half a month has passed and one and a half months remain" by way of the remaining two weeks.

One should understand that, as in the case of the first words of the Buddha and so forth, there are variations in the wording even within the commentaries according to the opinions of various reciters.
Regarding this, they say as follows: from the day of the Parinibbāna...
Starting from the beginning, there were four days of celebratory festivities; after that, three days of festivities and one day of cremating the funeral pyre;

after that, one day of cremating the funeral pyre alone; after that, three days of cremating the funeral pyre and one day of honoring the relics; and after that, four days of honoring the relics alone.
Thus, by counting according to each respective task performed, they complete three weeks; however, by including what was previously omitted, it amounts to exactly half a month.
Furthermore, the statement here that "twenty-one days have passed" is also according to that same counting based on each respective task.
One should accept this after considering how, in this way, the statements found in all four commentaries (aṭṭhakathās) are brought into harmony—thus [said] by the Elder Vajirabuddhi.
However, as for what was stated—"When it is said 'half a month has passed,' one day is lost;

that is the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), which is called the day of clamor, and therefore it is not included here"—that is not correct, because in the Pāli of the *Parinibbāna Suttanta*, the seven days are reckoned starting precisely from the first day of the fortnight, and in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), [the calculation] is made together with the day of the Parinibbāna... of the three [days].

Because of the counting of seven-day periods. For, by counting three seven-day periods together with the day of the Parinibbāna, the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha-Mūla becomes the twenty-first day.
"Forty days" refers to the period from the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Jeṭṭha-Mūla up until the full moon of Āsāḷhī.
This was stated after having calculated [the time]. "In the meantime" means within forty days. "The impediment of illness" (*roga-palibodha*) is simply illness itself.

"The impediment of teacher and preceptor" (*ācariya-upajjhāya-palibodha*) refers specifically to the duties that must be performed toward the teacher and the preceptor; likewise for the impediment of mother and father.
It is called an "impediment" (*palibodha*) because it hinders, obstructs, or prevents the intended purpose or task from proceeding; this is the derivation of the *ra*-sound.
"Having made the letter *la*. [This means: "Having severed that obstacle, let him perform that duty";
thus, having severed every such obstacle, let him perform that very duty known as the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Other great elders" refers to the Elder Anuruddha and others. "Afflicted by the arrow of sorrow" means by the arrow designated as sorrow.

It has entered into and been penetrated. Because ignorance (*avijjā*) and the latent tendency of craving (*taṇhānusaya*) have not been severed, one generates and brings forth a personal existence (*attabhāva*)—consisting of the five aggregates (*khandha*)—within the realms of becoming, birth, destiny, station, and the abodes of beings, by means of karma conditioned by ignorance and craving;

thus, it is called "the person" (*jana*). Alternatively, it is called "the person" because it generates, has generated, or will generate defilements (*kilesa*); likewise, it is "the great person" (*mahājana*).
"Taṃ. "Āgatāgataṃ" means each one as they arrived, just as in the expression "one by one. Here it might be asked:
"The Elder went to Rājagaha surrounded by his own retinue of five hundred;

other great elders also, taking their respective followers, departed for various directions, desiring to comfort the great multitude who were pierced by the arrow of grief"—is this not what is stated here?
Furthermore, the statement in the *Samantapāsādikā*— “The Elder Mahākassapa, saying ‘Friends,
let us go to Rājagaha,’ took half of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and set out on one path, while the Elder Anuruddha also took the other half and set out on another path”—
is mutually contradictory. For here [in that account], the Elder Mahākassapa and the others...
The meaning that follows is that [the elders] went to various directions together with their own retinues of monks.
But in that case, did the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Anuruddha each go along a separate path together with half of the Saṅgha? It is said:

both of these statements are indeed not contradictory, because they are consistent in their meaning. For here, there is simply a statement regarding the individual departure of the elders without exception.

In that [previous context], it was shown by way of method (*naya*); here, however, it is shown by the statement regarding going with one’s own respective retinue, whereas in that [context] it was stated by way of going together with half of the Saṅgha.

For "half of the Saṅgha" refers to a group of monks (*bhikkhu-gaṇa*) consisting of one's own respective retinue, because the word "half" (*upaḍḍha*) applies even when not referring to an equal division.
For if [it were meant] that while the Saṅgha is assembled, [one goes] with half of the Saṅgha...
If one were to take the meaning as "together with the Saṅgha," that would not be tenable because the Saṅgha is beyond the range of counting.
And if one were to take the meaning as "together with half of the Saṅgha" selected for the purpose of the recitation— namely, from among the five hundred bhikkhus—
this too would not be tenable, because those who were selected were specifically the leaders of their respective groups (*paccekagaṇino*).
Indeed, it is said: “Seven hundred thousand [monks], among whom were the preeminent bhikkhus. Since these two statements correspond in meaning, they do not contradict one another.
Some also say that this was spoken according to the specific tradition of various reciters (*bhāṇaka*).

It should be construed with the passage beginning, “While the Blessed One had not yet attained final Nibbāna,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “having taken up bowl and robe,” here [the bowl] refers to the stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings.
The meaning is: "and having taken up the robe of the Sugata. For that very bowl was always used by the Blessed One.

Indeed, it is stated in the commentary on the *Samacittapaṭipadāsutta*: "Desiring to demonstrate that even at a time of more than twenty years—according to the sequence of his rainy-season residence—it was still being used by him, [the Blessed One] performed his bodily grooming early in the morning and, having put on his well-fitting undergarment..."

“Having donned the robe of the Sugata and taking a stone bowl, surrounded by the community of monks, he entered the city through the southern gate and wandered for alms”—thus, because perfumes, garlands, and so forth were in their hands, they are described as “with perfumes, garlands, and so forth in hand.
“Therein” means in that Sāvatthī. “Sudam” is merely a particle. “Connected with impermanence and so forth” means: “All...”

Because it is connected with the nature of impermanence through such statements as "formations are impermanent. It is *dhammī* because it is joined with the Dhamma, or because it is worthy of the Dhamma;
[it refers to] such [a place]. *Saññāpetvā* means having made [her] well-understand, which is to say, having comforted her.
*Vasita-gandhakuṭiṃ* is a compound because of its constant dependence [on the word "dwelt"]. Because it is a shrine of use (*paribhoga-cetiya*), [it is called] "the Fragrant Chamber" (*gandhakuṭi*).
It is said, "having paid homage. Here, "having paid homage" and "having opened" refer to prior actions. For thus it was stated by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta:

"Regarding 'having opened the door of the Fragrant Chamber'—because the Fragrant Chamber is a *paribhoga-cetiya* (an object of use for the Buddha), it should be understood that he first paid homage to the Fragrant Chamber and then opened the door of the Fragrant Chamber. It is like a withered garland; that very [garland]...
"Garbage" refers to withered flowers, or that which is called "garbage" when it consists of withered garlands.

"Having brought [them] over" means having brought them toward the place where they were first placed. "Having placed them in their proper place" means having placed them exactly where they stood before, without exceeding the original location.
"He performed all the duties to be done at the time the Blessed One was present" refers to the duties to be performed regarding the dwelling-place (*senāsana*).

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "And performing" (*kurumāno ca*) means performing all that routine (*vatta*). This word *māna* is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇe*).
"The sweeping of the bathing shed and the placing of water therein, and those [activities] beginning with which the teaching of the Dhamma, the exhortation, and so forth [occur]"—that is how it is;
the meaning is "at the times for those. "The lion’s bed" (*sīhaseyyā*) is the bed of the lion, the king of beasts, by way of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
Or, by way of figurative usage, even the reclining of the Blessed One is called the "lion's reclining. Or it is the supreme reclining because of its preeminence in the postures of fire-like power;

with reference to this it was said: "Then the Blessed One lay down on his right side in the lion's reclining posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending. This refers to the time of reclining, which should be construed as the time of performing [the action]. "Is it not so? (nanu) is to be connected [with the preceding].
With the words “Just as he,” etc., the author clarifies the aforementioned matter by means of a simile. Therein, the construction is as follows:

just as another person—[omitting the intermediate text]—who possessed love for the Blessed One firmly established and whose taints were not yet exhausted, and who, through a heart softened by the sense of having rendered service on many occasions, acted [in such a way], so too did the Venerable Ānanda, being one whose love for the Blessed One was firmly established, whose taints were not yet exhausted, and whose heart was softened by the sense of having rendered service through his virtues [omitting the intermediate text], act [in that same way]. The word *taṃ* is a mere particle.
Furthermore, by this he shows the cause for acting in such a way:
just as others of the aforementioned nature acted, so too did the Venerable Ānanda [act] toward the Blessed One...

because of his established affection, because his taints were not yet exhausted, and because his mind was softened by the sense of having rendered service in many instances... since the sense of a causal reason (*hetu*) is thus applicable. For these [passages] contain the core of a reason.
These words [are so called] because they serve as the cause for making that very meaning real.
This should be illustrated by such Jātaka stories as the *Dhanapāladamana*, the *Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa*, and the *Cūḷahaṃsa* and *Mahāhaṃsa*. A "group" (*gaṇa*) of qualities;

that very group, because it is like a substance that produces the deathless (*amata*), is the "deathless flavor" (*amatarasa*). "Because of having the nature of knowing that" is the reason for the established term. "Benefit... softness" refers to the state of being preceded by benefit.
Having thoroughly cleansed his mind, he was gentle. Showing that for this reason he consented even thus, [the author] said, "Tamenam," and so forth.
Therein, "tamenam" means that venerable Ānanda. For the word *eta* is merely an ornament of the phrase;
such is the nature of words, namely that when two pronouns occur, only the preceding one carries the full meaning. "Saṃvejesī" means: "Did not the Blessed One..."
"It was spoken beforehand [to inspire urgency] with the words, 'There is separation and dissociation from all that is dear and beloved,' and so forth," as stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
This being the case, the construction would be joined with the elliptical remainder of the text: "Venerable sir...
please comfort me," having first said this. However, according to the literal sense, by means of the word *iti* in the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*), [the passage is understood].

The construction “he stirred him with these and other words” is indeed appropriate; for whatever word he used to generate a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), all of that constitutes the means for producing such urgency.

“Having steadied himself” means having restrained and established himself by refraining from lamentation and the like. “With aggravated humors” means having an accumulation of the bodily defects (*dosa*) such as bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*semha*).
For here, the three elements—bile, phlegm, and wind—are intended in their capacity as medicine;
these are what are called in the world "humors" (*dosa*) and "impurities" (*mala*). Furthermore, they are each fivefold when divided into earth, water, fire, air, and space. For it has been said:
“The humors (doṣa) are wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as the elements (dhātu) and the impurities (mala);
even therein, they are said to be fivefold, each sustaining the body individually.
The humors are so called because they corrupt the body, and the impurities are so called because they cause defilement.”
“Those elements are indeed called by names according to their respective functions.
“To comfort” means to satisfy. On the second day after the day the deity was moved to spiritual urgency, or the day he entered the Jeta Grove Monastery.
It is called a purgative (*virecana*) because one is purged by it; it is simply milk processed with medicinal herbs that serves as a purgative.
Likewise. "With reference to which" means with reference to which medicinal drink. He is beautiful in his limbs and members, thus he is *subha*;
the offspring of *manu* is *mānava*, but when the letter *na* is changed to *ṇa*, it becomes *māṇava*.
For *manu* was a person who stood in the place of a parent for human beings during the time of the first eon, who is called in the Teaching the "Mahāsammata King. He indeed...

One who knows for the welfare of the entire world with his mind is called a *manu*. Thus they say here: "The word *mānava*, when joined with the dental letter *na*, is a term common to all beings; however, the word *māṇava*, when joined with the palatal letter *ṇa*, is a term for one who is contemptible and deluded. The meaning of the word *māṇava* when combined with the letter *ṇa* as in *muddhaja-ṇa* has been described. Regarding this, the teachers state in the commentary (*Taṭṭīkā*) as well:
"In the world, the designation *māṇava* is applied to offspring that are contemptible or deluded;

and since beings for the most part possess deluded constituents during their youth, its meaning is explained as referring to that very [state]. And elsewhere, it refers to one under twenty years of age.
A young man (*māṇava*); here, however, by that same designation, even an elder is included. For it is said in the commentary on the *Cūḷakammavibhaṅgasutta*:

"They addressed him as 'young man' during his youth, and even in his old age he was still addressed by that same designation"—the meaning is: by the designation "young man" acquired through his beautiful name.
Furthermore, [he thought]: "The Teacher has attained final Nibbāna; the Elder Ānanda..."
Having heard that he had arrived bringing his bowl and robes and that a great crowd was approaching to see him, [the householder thought]:
"If I go to the monastery, it will not be possible for me to easily exchange greetings with the great crowd or hear a discourse on the Dhamma;
rather, having seen him when he has come to my very home, I shall easily exchange greetings. Furthermore, I have a certain doubt."
Thinking, "There is [something], and I shall ask him about it," he sent a young brahmin; with reference to that, he said, "The young brahmin was sent.
Here, the suffix *kap* is used in the sense of "small" (*khuddaka*). "He said this" means the Elder Ānanda spoke these words beginning with "It is not the right time.
"It is not the right time" means today is an unsuitable time to go. If one asks why, he replied, "I have... and so forth. "A mere medicine" means a small amount.
“Medicine. Here, the word *matta* has no specific meaning [other than "a little"], as in such expressions as “the sacrifice of even a small amount of pleasure” (*mattā sukhapariccāgā*).

“Drunk” means having drunk. Regarding the phrase “even though,” the Venerable Vajirabuddhi Thera stated: “In this context, the particle *api* implies permission (*anuññā*) even when [something] is doubted (*apekkha*).
His intention, however, is this: when a mere doubt is expressed with the words “perhaps,” the fact that [an action] is permitted is not established.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing that point, the word “even” (api) was spoken; by this he illuminates the following meaning:
“Perhaps we might approach tomorrow, and being capable of approaching, we shall indeed approach.
On the second day means on the day after the day the milk-purgative was drunk. By the Elder Cetakatthera means in the country of Cetiya.
By the Elder who had received the name Cetakaputta because he was born among the Cetakas. "By a monk following behind" means by a monk who followed after him;
here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the agent. "Questioned by the young man Subha" means:
"Regarding those teachings upon which the venerable Gotama established this world—have they perished since his passing, or do they still endure? If they endure..."
“Master Ānanda will know; let me ask him,” he thought, and said:
“Of those teachings for which Master Gotama was a proponent, and wherein he exhorted, settled, and established this generation—of which teachings, sir Ānanda, was Master Gotama a proponent?”

When asked, "Was Gotama one who spoke in praise [of these]? and so forth, the Elder, showing the three Piṭakas by subsuming them under the three aggregates beginning with the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), spoke here in this Sīlakkhandhavagga the tenth sutta, beginning with: "Of the three aggregates, O young man, that Blessed One was one who spoke in praise.
It is with reference to this that he said: "In this... he spoke," and so forth.
*Khaṇḍa* means broken. *Phulla* means split, or the spreading of moss, algae, mushrooms, and so forth;
their repair is making them properly as they were before, which is to say, restoring them anew. *Upakaṭṭhāya* means when it is near.
It is called *vassūpanāyikā* because they enter (*upanenti*) or approach (*upagacchanti*) the rains there; it refers to the time of entering the rains. [This is stated] in the *Saṅgītipāḷiyaṃ*.
