Although the statement was spoken in general terms, he said “For thus,” and so forth, in order to harmonize or establish that it was indeed spoken with reference to this very situation.
“Having surrounded Rājagaha” means by way of their standing outside the city. “Discarded, fallen, and filthy” means discarded, fallen, and filthy.
This is what is meant: by those going to the place of the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna...
"Abandoned and neglected by the bhikkhus, and because they were eaten by ants and other creatures right there, they fell here and there;
and due to the absence of sweeping, they became filthy because of the accumulation of refuse. This very meaning is clarified by the passage beginning with "Of the Blessed One," and so forth.
"Uklāpo" means that which has reached a state of putrefaction (*avakuthi*); the letter *tha* is changed to *la*. It also means "abandoned" (*ujjhiṭṭho*).

*Uklāpa* means a collection or an aggregate; it is stated thus by way of the gathering of colors, just as in the cases of "secondary defilement" (*upakleśa*) or "moisture" (*sneha*), and thus they are "furnished with that. *Pariveṇa* means those things which are seen as being enclosed or demarcated.

*Kurumānā* means those who desire to act. Because the rules for lodgings (*senāsana-vatta*) have been laid down, and because [the matters] connected to lodgings are treated in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
Because many words have been spoken, even the repairing of lodgings is indeed an act of worship toward him;
thus he said, "for the purpose of worshipping the word of the Blessed One. "The first month" means the first month of the rainy season (*vassa*).

This is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). To make clear the meaning already stated—"and for the purpose of avoiding the doctrines of the sectarians"—[he says]:
The passage beginning with “the sectarians” (*titthiyā*) and so forth has been stated.

The word *yaṃ* refers to the making of the formal agreement (*katikavatta*). For in such instances, the pronoun *yaṃ* does not require the correlative *taṃ*, because the meaning is complete by itself.
Alternatively, it is with reference to that very formal agreement that the passage beginning with “then indeed” (*atha kho*) was spoken; that same [agreement] is what I have also [referred to].
The meaning is "it was spoken. This same method applies to such cases as when [the Blessed One]... pe ...
"praised" it; that is, by one who was prescribing the rules for lodgings (*senāsanavatta*) in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* and speaking words connected with lodgings, he praised them.
Regarding the phrase "we shall recite," here the word *iti* connects with both "it was spoken" and [the following], or else there is the elision of one *iti*.
"On the second day" means on the day following the day he had thus reflected; and that was indeed the second day from the day of entering the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*).
For the elders, having assembled on the very first day of the month of Āsāḷha (the full moon) and entered the rains retreat, reflected in this way.
"At the king's gate" means at the gate of the royal palace. "Hand-work" (*hatthakamma*) means manual labor; of hand-work...
"Making" is what is meant [by *karoti*]. "They made known" means they caused others to know. "Confident" means having minds free from apprehension.

The "Wheel of Authority" (*āṇācakkam*) is the very authority itself, in the sense of proceeding with unimpeded activity. Likewise, the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkam*) is the Dhamma itself as a wheel;

however, in this context, it is appropriate in both ways—namely, by way of the knowledge of teaching and the knowledge of penetration—and it is through both of these that the recitation (*saṅgīti*) occurs.
Because it causes [the Dhamma] to proceed. For it is stated in the commentaries: “‘The Wheel of Dhamma’ (dhammacakka) is a name for both the knowledge of teaching and the knowledge of penetration.
“Place of assembly” means a place where people gather and sit together. “Sattapaṇṇī” means that which has seven leaves; the meaning is:
at the door of the cave situated on that [mountain] which is also called “Chattapaṇṇo” and “Visamacchado.”
“By Vissakamma”: this refers to the son of the gods who is the director of all tasks for Sakka, the lord of the devas.

Regarding the phrase “with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and staircases,” because the word *suvibhatta* (well-proportioned) is heard before the compound, it is connected with each member of the compound;
the same applies to the phrases beginning with “of various kinds... variegated. [The term] “the splendor of the royal palace.”
The splendor or the beauty of the royal palace. "As if laughing" means as if performing a derisive laugh.
"By glory" means by the fortune (lakkhī) designated as beauty. "Like a dwelling place" means like a residence;
there is also a reading, "as if burning. Like birds alighting at a single drinking pool, the eyes of all people [fell upon it].
It is said that they fall right upon the pavilion; thus it is stated: "A single flock... of birds.
"Of the eye-birds" means of those birds known as eyes. "As if the world's loveliness were gathered together" means:
if all the loveliness existing in the world were brought and gathered in one place, it would be like that; or rather, whatever in the world is worthy of being enjoyed for its beauty.

The meaning is that all of this is as if condensed together. "The essence-cream to be seen" means that among things worthy of being seen, it is like the core devoid of pith, and like the clear [liquid] free from dregs; it is the essential and the pure.

Furthermore, it is that which is to be seen (*daṭṭhabba*), which is visible (*dassanīya*), the essential (*sārabhūta*), the most distinguished, and whose *maṇḍa*—meaning cream, adornment, or ornament—is its very nature.
It is a *maṇḍapa* because it protects (*pāti*) the essence (*maṇḍa*) that is to be seen; or, it protects (*pāti*) the clear essence (*maṇḍa*) of all people;
or, it protects (*pāti*) the ornament (*maṇḍana*)—that is, it drinks (*pivati*) it in the sense of being fit for adornment—therefore it is a *maṇḍapa*.

And those flower-garlands (*kusumadāma*) which are hanging (*olambaka*) are "hanging flower-garlands" (*kusumadāmolambaka*). Here, the qualifying term is placed after [the qualified term] by way of poetic license (*paranipāta*).
As in the phrase “*agyāhita*. Likewise, it is so called because there are various hanging garlands of flowers;

and likewise, it is so called because there is a beautiful (*cāru*) canopy (*vitāna*) that is as if vomiting, or specifically ejecting, or emitting them. That which is taken by means of a wall (*kuṭṭa*) and made level is *kuṭṭima*;
or *koṭṭima*. A gem of such a kind is a *maṇi-koṭṭima*; a floor (*koṭṭima*) made of various gems is a *nānāratana-vicitra-maṇikoṭṭima*.

Its floor was likewise. Alternatively, because it is produced by the carving of jewels—having been fashioned from jewels that have been ground—it is called a "jewel-carved floor" (*maṇikoṭṭima-tala*);
such is the floor. Thus, the connection is: "its well-finished flooring was likewise variegated with various flowers and offerings. A flower-offering is a *puṣpūpahāra*.
For here, the inclusion of the phrase "variegated with various jewels" [is intended] to indicate that the floor itself was like that [carved floor].

The mention of the variegated nature of the offering of various flowers is to be understood as an illustration [of its beauty], while the mention of the floor surface made of jewels is to be understood as indicating that the work on the ground was perfectly finished.
"Naṃ" refers to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). "Like a Brahmā’s celestial mansion" (*brahmavimānasadisaṃ*) is a neuter adjective;

the meaning is: having adorned it so that it shines just as a Brahmā’s celestial mansion does. It is called a *vimāna* because it is to be especially honored (*vi-mānetabba*). However, those learned in grammar [explain it differently].

“They move and go through the atmosphere; therefore they are called *vimāna*,” so they say. Alternatively, it is a *vimāna* because it is measured (*mīyati*) or constructed (*nimmīyati*) specifically by means of well-performed kamma.
Or again, *vī* refers to a bird; it is a *vimāna* because it is measured or constructed in the shape of that [bird].
It may also be explained in such ways. However, in the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “Because they possess specific measurements, such as one or two *yojanas* in extent...”
It is called a "vimāna" because it possesses an excellence of beauty and, in particular, because it is worthy of honor.
"Priceless" (anagghāni) means that they have no value; the sense is that they are of immeasurable worth or incapable of being valued.

"Spreads" (paccattharaṇāni) means those things which are suitable or should be spread out individually; there were hundreds of such. "Facing north" (uttarābhimukhaṃ) means directed toward the northern direction.
The Dhamma is indeed the Teacher because it fulfills the function of a Teacher; thus it is said: "Having prepared a Dhamma-seat worthy of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

This was also stated to show that one who teaches the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata is worthy of sitting on such a seat, since they carry out the function of a Teacher, as expressed in the passage beginning: "Whoever... after my passing shall be the Teacher," and so forth.
“Worthy of a seat” means worthy of sitting upon. “A Dharma-seat” (dhammāsana) is a seat for one who teaches the Dharma, or a seat suitable for delivering a discourse on the Dharma.
“Inlaid with ivory” means inlaid with ivory; it is said to be made from elephant tusks. For it is stated:
“The word ‘danta’ refers to an elephant’s tusk. “Therein” means in this Dharma-seat. “My duty” (mama kiccaṃ).
"It is my work, or what must be done by me.
Now, showing the Venerable Ānanda’s attainment of the stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhūmi*), he said, "And on that very day," and so forth.
Therein, "on that very day" means on the day thus announced by the king, namely, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa.
This has been said. Because it produces harm and is like a source of poison, defilement (*kilesa*) is "poison" (*visa*);

its "sting" (*satti*) or "odor" (*gandha*) is the state of being otherwise [from its true nature] due to the presence of taints (*āsava*). For instance, it caused lamentation and the like during the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One and other such occasions.
Furthermore, because it resembles the odor of flowers and other things that produce poison, defilement alone is what generates the performance of various causes of suffering.
It is called “the stench of poison” (*visagandha*). For it has been stated: “It is called *visattikā* because it carries away poison; it is called *visattikā* because it is the root of poison;
it is called *visattikā* because it is the fruit of poison; it is called *visattikā* because it is the consumption of poison,” and so forth.

Furthermore, the “stench of poison” refers to the foul odor of flesh and such; the defilement is so named because it resembles that. For it is said in the *Abhidhammaṭīkā*: “The word *vissa* [is used] for what is foul.”
“Addhā” means certainly. “Saṃvegaṃ” means spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma. For the phrase “of those who have laid down the burden” is generally and primarily stated [in reference to Arahants].
However, in such instances, spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma is intended for others as well. Thus it is said in the commentary on the *Rajjumālā-vimāna*:
“Spiritual urgency (saṃvega) is knowledge accompanied by moral dread; that arose upon seeing the Blessed One.”

And at that time, she was one who had not yet understood the teaching and whose fruit was still to come. For otherwise, due to the agitation of the mind, it would follow that "distress" (*saṃvega*) is merely "fault" (*dosa*);
and this being the case, it could not be a single sufficient cause for his attainment of the stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhūmi*).

And since he was not such [a person], he certainly should not be mentioned here. Enough of this over-elaboration. "Therefore" means: because of that, at the assembly of the Saṅgha on the following day...

Because they are currently engaged [in training], or because they still have duties to perform as trainees (*sekkha*). "It is not fitting for them" means it is not fitting for you, or it is not appropriate for you to go to the assembly.
"This is mine" refers to this act of going of mine. "I who" (*yvāham*)—the word *yam* is a reference to the action; by that, [it is implied] "one should go."

Herein, he refers to the action of going; and as for the reference to the action, this is the natural gender of the pronoun *taṃ*, namely the neuter, and its number is the singular, because such suitability is seen in various instances.
For grammarians maintain that, by its very nature, action is neuter and singular. "He directed" (*āvajjesi*) means he brought it near.
"Released" means liberated. "And not yet reached" means not yet arrived; what is meant is that it has not yet been placed upon the bolster.
"In this interval" means in between these two points; what is meant is that it refers to the intermediate moment shown by these two words, or the gap between the two times thus indicated.
“It is used for cause, mind, moment, and opportunity;
and in meanings such as ‘in between’ and so forth—the word *antarā* has gone [into common usage].
Thus it is said. *Anupādāya* means without grasping at any phenomenon by way of craving or views, or without those defilements by which...

It is liberated without grasping even a mere trace of them. "From the taints" means from the defilements designated as *āsava*—so called because they flow (*āsavanti*) from existence up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), and because they flow toward the lineage (*gotrabhū*) in terms of the Dhamma—and because they proceed by way of hearing.
This is merely an illustrative expression; for, by virtue of being associated with those [taints], the mind is indeed liberated from all defilements and all evil states.

“Cittaṃ vimuccī” means that the mind, having been in the process of being liberated from the taints (āsava) at the moment of the path of Arahatship, was liberated at the moment of the fruit of Arahatship.

He explains this meaning with the words beginning “For this [person]...”. “By walking” means by the act of walking back and forth (caṅkamana). “A distinction” means a distinguished path and fruit superior to the path and fruit he had previously attained.
It refers to that which has been performed and accumulated as a necessary condition for turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya).
"By merit" means one who has performed merit; the meaning is that one has undertaken the necessary application for the attainment of arahantship.
"Exert yourself in striving" means apply yourself with energy; it is said: "Engage in the practice for the realization of arahantship.
"You will become" means you will be. "Fault in speech" means a defect in speech, its state of being false. "Over-exerted" means excessively exerted. "For agitation" means...
"To the state of agitation. *Handa* is a word of relinquishment; by it, he effects a relinquishment, thinking: "Therefore, I shall apply [myself] right now, yet I do not engage in prolixity.

"I shall apply myself to the evenness of energy" means that because the energy of walking meditation is excessive, by way of reducing it and bringing about evenness through concentration, I shall apply energy to its evenness—that is, to its state of balance.
Or, by means of energy, one may apply oneself to concentration known as *samatha*; this is also the meaning. For both readings are seen in the texts.
"I shall rest" means "I shall breathe. Now, in order to show specifically why he is worthy of praise, the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tenā*) was spoken.
"Therefore" refers to the reason of being free from the four postures. "Not lying down," and so forth, are all words referring to the present.

Even though he was already *parinibbūta*, he attained final *parinibbāna* in the sky itself. Therefore, the Elder’s *kilesa-parinibbāna* (extinction of defilements) and *khandha-parinibbāna* (extinction of the aggregates) are especially worthy of praise and are truly wonderful and marvelous.
"On the second day" means on the second day after the day the Elder attained *arahantship*. "On the fifth" refers to the observation of the lunar date (*tithi*).
It is stated [that this] is in grammatical apposition with the words "on the second day.
For even words of different genders are seen to have the same meaning, such as "virtue is the measure" (*guṇo pamāṇaṃ*) or "twenty minds" (*vīsati cittāni*), and so forth.

"Of the dark fortnight" refers to the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa. For they performed the repair of broken and dilapidated parts during the first month; and the status of being the "first month" is according to the usage of the Middle Country.
For in that context, they conventionally refer to the period from one full moon until the next full moon as a single month.
Then, for three days, the King had a pavilion constructed; on the second day, the Elder realized Arhatship; but on the third day, the Elders assembled and held the Council.
Therefore, [the calculation begins] from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha...
The fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa; thus, one month consists of [thirty] days plus five additional days. *Samāna* means arising.
*Haṭṭhatuṭṭhacitta* means having a mind of extreme gladness, or a mind gladdened by joy (*pāmojja*) and a mind satisfied by rapture (*pīti*).
*Ekaṃsaṃ* means on one shoulder; the meaning is "on the left shoulder. For it is said thus in the commentary on the Vaṅgīsa-sutta:
“Regarding the phrase ‘one shoulder bared’: this is stated here specifically in the sense of re-establishing [the robe’s position].

‘One shoulder’ is a designation for standing after having draped the robe over the left shoulder. Therefore, its meaning should be understood as: ‘having arranged the robe in such a way that it remains draped over the left shoulder.’”

“Like a bandha... pe ... it is like a well-ripened palm fruit that has fallen from its stalk. ‘Pale... pe ... it is like a noble gem placed upon a blanket of pale woolly fur endowed with white and yellow luster;
and here, by the word ‘noble’ (*jāti*), artificial gems are excluded. ‘Like the full moon risen...
it is like the moon risen on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, the Uposatha, complete with its sixteen digits. ‘Like a young... pe ...’”
It was as if a cluster of *satapatta* flowers had blossomed through contact with the radiance of the rising sun, its interior filled with pollen of a beautiful golden hue.
For it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that "the word *piñjara* is a synonym for the color of gold.
"Pariyodātena" means radiant. "Sappabhena" means endowed with the luster of physical beauty and the luster of virtue (*sīla*). "Sassirikena" means...

“Extremely glorious” means possessing great splendor, consisting of the excellence of physical beauty and so forth. “With his excellent face” means with a supreme countenance adorned with the aforementioned beauty.
Although he did not announce, “I have attained Arahatship,” all who saw him understood that fact because of his walking with such supreme grace;
therefore, it is said that he was as if announcing it himself: “Of himself...”
“He went as if announcing his attainment of Arahatship.
But for what purpose did he go as if announcing this? It is said:

He did so because he reflected, “The Blessed One has praised the ‘declaration by another’ (aññabyākaraṇa) rather than one that refers to oneself,” and [because] due to his status as a trainee (sekha), he was concerned regarding the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
He departed as if announcing this to the elder monks who were seated there, thinking, "Even though it is improper for us to take [the bowl],

we shall take it because of our great learning," in order to inspire joy by making them aware of the elder's attainment of Arahatship, and to demonstrate the fruitfulness of the exhortation given by the Blessed One,
"Be diligent. To the Venerable Mahākassapa, it occurred thus through the establishing of equality and so forth.
By the reason already stated, he has attained the status of a Teacher. "Dhareyya" means that he would exist [in this state].
He gave his approval with the words, "Truly, friend Ānanda, you shine forth through the attainment of Arahantship," and so on. This is the position of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas.
It is also appropriate as the position of the Sutta-nipāta and Khuddaka-pāṭha bhāṇakas among the Khuddaka-bhāṇakas, because it is stated as such in their respective commentaries.
Those who recite the *Majjhima Nikāya* by virtue of their proficiency are called the *Majjhimabhāṇakas*; these are the teachers possessing that specific quality.

"In order of seniority" (*yathāvuḍḍhaṃ*) means according to the sequence of age, or without overstepping it. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to within that community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*). The connection is: "This is the seat for Ānanda.
"At that time" (*tasmiṃ samaye*) means at the very moment of this conversation. The Elder thought: "Where has he gone?"
Because he would have become extremely well-known by showing himself to those who were questioning him, this is also the opinion of some among the Majjhima-bhāṇakas;
therefore, the connection is "thus some say. Some of that same group also say that he came through the air and showed himself on his own seat.
For when "some" (eke) is used in the masculine gender, it applies in all instances.

The meaning should be understood as "some. Furthermore, regarding these three accounts, apart from the mere fact that they have come down in various ways through their respective reciters (bhāṇakas), there is no other distinct reason for the different versions.
For when the Council of the Dhamma and Vinaya was held in the seventh month, it was sometimes done in the ordinary manner, sometimes by sinking into the earth, and sometimes...
Because he had come through the air, they spoke of his arrival in various ways accordingly. Furthermore, some say that on the very first day of the Council, he first arrived by his natural means;

thereafter, he rose up into the sky, and when it was time for him to join the assembly, he descended from there and, without disturbing the rows of monks, showed himself in his seat by sinking into the earth. Just as...
Whether he came in such a manner or that, the mere mode of arrival is not the criterion; rather, the criterion is the Venerable Mahākassapa’s giving of applause upon his departure.

This is because the attainment of Arahantship by others was made known precisely through the Teacher’s own granting of applause, and because the praise due to be received while the Blessed One was still living had already been received by the Elder.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that meaning, he said, "Or as," and so forth. "In all cases" means in all three of the aforementioned doctrines.
"He addressed the bhikkhus" means he called out to the bhikkhus; this is the meaning here. However, elsewhere it is seen in the sense of making known, as in "I address you, O bhikkhus;
I inform you, O bhikkhus"; and it is also seen in the sense of summoning.

Just as it is seen in the form of an address, such as "Come, bhikkhu, address Sāriputta with my words," and just as in "There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus!'," so too here [the term] is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* to mean "address.
However, because there is no mere address [here], it is distinguished by another meaning conveyed through the statement beginning with "What shall we recite first? and so forth.
And it is only appropriate that there be an indication through association; therefore, the meaning must be stated as "he addressed," which signifies "he informed" or "he made known.
For in such passages as, "There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus! and the bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir!
and so forth, only the mere act of addressing is seen, and no distinct further matter being communicated. That—
However, [the phrase] beginning with “In the past, monks” was introduced separately. Therefore, it is our opinion that such an address is appropriate only in those specific instances.
Grammarians, however, say: “In expressions such as ‘Having addressed Vissakamma of great psychic power,’ the word *āmantrita* refers to speech that is restrained;
thus, the meaning of ‘he addressed’ (*āmantesi*) is ‘he spoke with restraint’ (*sammantayi*). As for “Friend,” etc.:
This is an explanation of the manner of addressing. Regarding the phrase "either the Dhamma or the Vinaya," the word *vā* (or) is used here in the sense of an alternative (*vikappana*);
by this, he shows: "Which one among these should we recite first? He asks "Why [should it be recited] first? and answers with "Because the Vinaya stands firm," and so forth.
The words "because... therefore" (*yasmā... tasmā*) should be supplied and connected. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because of that similarity to life. "The burden" (*dhura*) means the foremost.
"No *nappahoti* means that it certainly does exist (*pahotiyeva*). For a double negation, when accompanied by an intensifier, indicates the original meaning.

*Etadaggaṃ* means ‘this is the foremost. This expression is used with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). *Yadidaṃ* should be construed as ‘which is this,’ or alternatively as ‘that which is called the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*).
For if it were so, then ‘the foremost’ would indeed have its grammatical gender according to the literal form. [And] ‘yadidaṃ’..."

And this is the inherent nature of the word *ya*: that it must be joined with whatever meaning is to be expressed according to the gender—either as "this which" (*yo ayaṃ*), or "this which" (*yā ayaṃ*), or "this which" (*yaṃ idaṃ*)—since it is shown to function exactly in that way in various contexts.
In the phrase "of the monks who are Vinaya-holders," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
“He approved himself by himself” means that he made himself approved by himself alone. For this word “by himself” (*attanā*) functions as an instrumental case qualification;
it excludes approval by others. Alternatively, *attanā* is an indeclinable (*abyaya*) word that resembles a case-ending. Some, however, say:
“The instrumental case is used here in the sense of gender (*liṅgatthe*), because the state of being the agent has already been expressed (*abhihitakattubhāvato*). That is indeed incorrect.
“Thera” (the elder) is used because the agent exists. It should be construed as: “he himself appointed himself for the purpose of answering.
Because the root *pucch* (to ask) takes two objects, the two objects are stated as “Upāli” and “the Vinaya.
Regarding the phrase “having taken a fan,” it should be understood that taking up a fan is the custom of those who preach the Dhamma. By means of that...
For indeed, among those who preach the Dhamma, the fidgeting of hands, facial distortions, and so forth are concealed by the assembly.
And the Blessed One takes up the variegated fan specifically for the purpose of demonstrating the true nature of things to those preachers of the Dhamma.
Otherwise, how could the moon-like orb of the Buddhas' faces—which is an ornament for the entire world and possesses the supreme excellence of training and self-restraint—be seen?
It should not be concealed. Why was it said, "Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* laid down?
Is it not the case that its status as "first" is inappropriate prior to the time of the Council (*saṅgīti*)? No, it is not inappropriate;
for its status as "first" is established by the sequence in which the Blessed One laid them down and by the sequence in which the *Pātimokkha* is recited. For the most part...
It should be understood that even during the Blessed One’s lifetime, the three Piṭakas were rehearsed in their established order, particularly the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.
Regarding the phrase "in what matter" (*kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), meaning "on account of sexual intercourse.

The statement beginning with "he asked about the matter" (*vatthumpi pucchi*) was said in order to include and show what remains after [the questions] such as "Where was it laid down? have been presented.
In order to dispel the doubt as to whether this is mixed with the words of the compilers of the Council or is the pure word of the Buddha,
and to demonstrate that it possesses authority exactly as it was compiled, he poses the question and provides the answer beginning with,
"What, then, in this regard? Here, "in the first *pārājika*" refers to the text of the first *pārājika* as thus compiled.
For this very reason he said: "Indeed, the Tathāgatas do not utter even a single syllable in vain.
That which is "to be removed" is speech that should be discarded because it is redundant, purposeless, or because it is improper due to its falsity.
That which is "to be added" is speech that should be supplied because it is incomplete. As to why [this is so], he said "for indeed," and so forth. But for the disciples and the deities...

"Or spoken"—this was said with reference to what was spoken by the Blessed One through such means as questioning and answering. "In all cases" means even in the speech of the Blessed One’s disciples and of deities.

By the words beginning with "But what is that," he shows that this inclusion is merely for the sake of connecting the discourse, and not because the meaning is logically consistent with its own intrinsic nature. "Merely for the sake of connecting the discourse" means...
It is merely a statement of the connection between what precedes and what follows.

Having defined it as "this is the first *pārājika*," they established it by means of this very recitation-path for the purpose of accomplishing the functions of learning, memorizing, and so forth; and for that same purpose, they performed communal recitation [beginning with the words] "thereby...
he dwells. They say that at the very moment the recitation began, the earth shook; and this—
However, it is said that "as if giving a cry of approval" in order to make it known that the earthquake was due to the power of the elders’ recitation of the Dhamma.
"Bounded by water" means bounded by the water that supports the earth; for when that [water] moves, the earth moves as well.
By this, he excludes the shaking of the earth in only a limited region.
Although there is no explicit enumeration in the text, the phrase "seventy-five training rules" is stated to demonstrate that exactly this many were included in the recitation;
the commentary explains the meaning as if giving its approval by saying "by the same method as before.
This is said to show that it is not only by way of the fixed arrangement of the *Sikkhāpada-kkhandha-vibhaṅga*, but also by way of a fixed measure.
It is said: “sixty-four recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*). And herein, a recitation section is defined as follows:
“Eight syllables make one word; four words make one verse-line (*gāthā*);
one verse-line is considered one verse; thirty-two syllables make one verse.”
"One recitation section (bhāṇavāra) is considered to consist of thirty-two thousand syllables, or five hundred and twenty [verses], totaling eight thousand syllables.
Thus, the text is said to measure eight thousand syllables. For it is called a "recitation section" (bhāṇavāra) because it is a section (vāra) that is to be recited (bhaṇitabba).
The meaning is that it is a section to be recited by way of a single method of study (*sajjhāyana*). "Khandhaka" refers to the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga;

for it is called "Khandhaka" because it is a collection of sections (*khandha*) or because it elucidates them. Here, "sections" (*khandha*) refers to the formal acts of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) such as going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*), as well as the formal rules (*paññatti*) consisting of the training precepts regarding conduct (*cāritta*) and prohibitions (*vāritta*). For these matters, such as going-forth, were [established] by the Blessed One...

They are called "designations" because they are designated. Furthermore, the word *khandha* is seen in the sense of a "designation," as in "a log of wood," "a mass of fire," "a body of water," and so forth.

Moreover, it is also appropriate to understand them as "divisions and collections" (*bhāga-rāsa*), because those designations are analyzed both by way of their parts and by way of their aggregates. That Vinaya Piṭaka, however, was protected by the reciters (*bhāṇakas*).

Thinking, "It will remain established for a long time without being lost, as if hidden by means of a basket," they entrusted it to the Venerable Elder Upāli, saying, "Friend, teach this to those who rely upon you.
Desiring to recite the Dhamma means desiring to perform the communal chanting of the Suttas and the Abhidhamma; [the phrase] "Dhamma and Vinaya" refers to both.
Because, as in passages such as "desito paññatto," the word *dhamma* occurs only in reference to the Suttanta and Abhidhamma by way of elimination (*pārisesanaya*).

This point will be made clear further on. Regarding the phrase "he informed the Saṅgha," the meaning should be understood according to the method explained below. "Which Piṭaka, friends? [is the question].

Between the two remaining Piṭakas of the Vinaya, which Piṭaka [is it]? Since the Vinaya and Abhidhamma are included within the Khuddaka Saṅgīti, it was stated [in the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*] that "there are four Saṅgītis in the Suttanta Piṭaka.

And the term "Saṅgītis" refers specifically to the Nikāyas, because they were compiled by being individually determined according to the Dīgha and other categories at the time of the recitations (saṅgāyana). Therefore, he said, "the Dīgha Saṅgīti," and so forth.

In order to show that there are no others, it is said: "Thirty-four suttas, three vaggas," by way of grouping the suttas together into three sections. Therefore, there are thirty-four suttas which constitute three vaggas;
or, there are thirty-four suttas, and by way of grouping them, they form three vaggas. This should be construed as: "in those three vaggas."
When it was said, "There is a discourse called the *Brahmajālasutta*; let us recite that first," the objection "Why? could arise;
therefore, he said, "Adorned with threefold virtue," and so forth. For these [phrases] contain the underlying reasons (*hetugabbha*).
Because they reveal the three types of virtue—namely, the minor, the intermediate, and the great—it is "adorned" or "embellished" by them. Likewise, regarding the various forms of wrong livelihood...
"Destroying various kinds of scheming, flattery, and so forth" means the destruction of the manifold forms of livelihood through scheming, flattery, and the like.

In this context, *kuhana* (scheming) means the act of deceiving (*kuhāyanā*), that is, the act of misleading by means of three bases known as the use of requisites, indirect hinting, and dependence on deportment.
*Lapanā* (flattery) refers to seeing people who have come to the monastery and [saying], "For what purpose..."
"Good sirs, you have come; why not invite the monks? If that is so, go ahead; I shall follow behind, taking the monks with me"—such is the manner of speaking.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the giving of flowers and so forth, as well as hinting (*nemittikatā*) and other such practices, are included.
Furthermore, here, by the term "wrong livelihood" (*micchājīva*), all other improper modes of seeking alms besides scheming (*kuhana*) and flattery (*lapanā*) are encompassed.
By the word "etc. (ādi), however, it should be understood that the remaining factors, such as great desire (mahicchatā) and so forth, constitute misconduct (dussīlya).

The sixty-two views themselves are a "net" (jāla) because they resemble a net in the sense of being an entanglement; the "unfurling" (viniveṭhana) of that [net] means making it no longer an entanglement.
In the phrase "between Rājagaha, O Bhante, and Nālandā," the word *antara* here signifies an interval (*vivara*). Furthermore, this...
...as in such passages as, "Monks, [the sound] comes from the interval between the Tapodā and the Mahāniraya.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "in the space between Rājagaha and Nāḷanda. However, because it is joined with the word *antarā*, the accusative case has been employed.
In such instances, grammarians say, "He goes between the village and the river," thus using only one [word for the interval].
They employ the word *antarā*; it must also be construed with the second word.

For if it were not so construed, the accusative case would not be reached, since the accusative is desired through its connection with the word *antarā* when there is the possibility of the genitive case.
In that context, they built a palace of variegated and wonderful designs for the king’s amusement; that is called "the king’s palace" (*rājāgāraka*).
In that [place]. Ambalaṭṭhikā was the king’s pleasure grove. It is said that near its gate there was a young mango tree (*amba-rukkha*), which they called "Ambalaṭṭhikā";
because it was situated near that [tree], the grove itself came to be designated as "Ambalaṭṭhikā," just as [the city] is called "Varuṇanagara.
Therefore, it means "in the royal palace within the pleasure grove named Ambalaṭṭhikā."
The meaning is as follows. This dual substratum is stated for the purpose of making known that which is not yet known:

either "it belongs to the king’s palace" (*rājāgāram etassa*), thus *rājāgārakaṃ*, or it is a pleasure grove (*uyyānaṃ*) [belonging to the king]. The meaning is: "in the pleasure grove named Ambalaṭṭhikā, which possesses a king’s palace. For some say:

"There are indeed qualifying words (*visesanapada*) even when they differ in gender. If this were so, however, the king’s palace would not function as the substratum. [Therefore, it is said: "*Rājāgārake*."
"In the garden named thus, there was also, it is said, a royal palace (rājāgāra) worthy of delight. Regarding this, the Venerable Vajirabuddhi says:

'In that case, by way of that [palace] by which it receives its name, the meaning follows that the garden itself is spoken of as "Rājāgāraka" by way of its name, having been distinguished from the nearby young mango tree by the term "Ambalaṭṭhikāye. And so it is."
The same fault as previously stated would apply. "Suppiya the wanderer" refers to Suppiya, the pupil of Sañjaya, and the wanderer Channa.
Regarding "the youth Brahmadatta," here the word *māṇava* is used for a young man, as in "Ambaṭṭha the youth," "Aṅgaka the youth," and so forth;
therefore, the meaning is "concerning the young man named Brahmadatta. "In praise and blame" means in terms of commendation...
And for both praise and blame. Alternatively, *guṇa* means praise (*vaṇṇa*) and *aguṇa* means blame (*avaṇṇa*);
the speaking of these is expressed in that way by the elision of the latter member of the compound, just as "the form-existence is form" (*rūpabhavo rūpan*).
Regarding the sequence of words beginning with "Thereafter," it is as follows: "But, friend Ānanda, where was the Fruit of the Ascetic Life spoken?"
“Venerable sir, at Rājagaha in Jīvakambavana. “With whom? “With Ajātasattu, the son of Vedehī.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda both for the occasion (*nidāna*) of the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* and for the person (*puggala*).
For in this context, instead of saying “with reference to whom,” one should say “with whom.”
Why is that? It is because this sutta was not spoken by the Blessed One alone; the King also spoke certain things, such as, "Now, as for these various fields of craft," and so forth.

Therefore, it must be stated exactly thus. By this same method, it should be understood that throughout all [the suttas], they made the recitation after stating, as appropriate, "with reference to whom" or "together with whom. Thus is the *tanti*.
The Pāḷi is established by way of the collection of the Sutta-vagga. And by doing so, the statement, "comprising three sections and adorned with thirty-four suttas," becomes appropriate.
"Maintain it" means: preserve it by means of learning, recitation, and so forth. "Thereafter, having chanted it together" is the connection [of the sentence].
“*Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and so forth” is a compound. The meaning is: “thus it was commented upon by the ancients.

By this, having rejected the position of the Vitaṇḍavādins who state that “the seven treatises together with the *Mahādhammahadaya* or the *Mahādhātukathā* constitute the Abhidhamma Piṭaka,” he shows the position of those who hold the same view as himself, who state that [the Abhidhamma Piṭaka] consists of [the seven treatises] “together with the *Kathāvatthu*” alone. For one of subtle knowledge...
Or, because it is the objective domain for those possessing subtle knowledge, it is the range of subtle wisdom.
The exposition is twofold, by way of the *Cūḷaniddesa* and the *Mahāniddesa*.

As for that which is included in the *Khuddakanikāya*, such as the *Jātaka*, and which for the most part consists of expositions of the Dhamma—such works are appropriately classified within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka itself, and not [elsewhere].

However, the Dīgha reciters (Dīghabhāṇakas) maintain that the Jātaka and other such works are included within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka— neither in the Sutta Piṭaka, such as the Dīgha Nikāya and its like, nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka,
which consists of the Paññatti and Niddesa sections. Furthermore, the Cariyāpiṭaka and Buddhavaṃsa are not included here because they belong to the category of the Jātaka,
while the Nettippakaraṇa, Peṭakopadesa, and others belong to the category of the Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, and Magga.

The Majjhimabhāṇakas, however, maintain that the inclusion of the Jātakas and other such discourses within the Sutta Piṭaka is appropriate because they were taught by way of specific occasions (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and thus constitute a teaching given according to circumstances;

it is not appropriate for them to be included in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which describes phenomena according to their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which describes designations (*paññatti*) according to offenses. Thus [they argue] regarding the Jātakas and the rest.
They say that it is included within the Sutta Piṭaka. Here, one should take what is appropriate after having investigated it.

Thus, having first shown the First Council by way of its sign, purpose, time, place, agent, instrument, and manner, [the author] now, for the sake of skill in the various classifications regarding the Dhamma and Vinaya established therein, shows the divisions beginning with the "singlefold."
He said, “It is just so,” and so forth. Therein, by the word “thus” (*evaṃ*), he points out the aforementioned manner of recitation which is to be referred to by the word “this” (*etaṃ*).

The detailed explanation begins with “For that which... and so on. “Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment” (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ*) refers to the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*), which has unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge, which has the knowledge of the path as its proximate cause. “In the interval between these” refers to the act of full awakening.
"And for the opening of final Nibbāna. This defines the duration by way of time as "these forty-five years.
The phrase "by one who reflects" refers to the phenomena occurring by way of the Udānas and so forth. The connection is that all the words spoken constitute the *tanti* (the sacred text).
To the question "But what is this?", he says: "It is the flavor of liberation itself," meaning it is not any other flavor.

It has been said. "It was liberated" (*vimuccittha*) means liberation (*vimutti*). That which is to be tasted and relished is "flavor" (*rasa*). That which has liberation as its designated flavor is "the flavor of liberation" (*vimuttirasa*);
the meaning is the relish of the fruit of arahantship. This is the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta.
However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, treating that as a certain interpretation, stated this meaning: "It is liberated; it was liberated."
“Liberation (*vimutti*) refers to the path and the fruit, as appropriate. ‘Taste’ (*rasa*) means a quality or a function of attainment; the compound is formed according to the method already stated.

‘The advantage of liberation’ (*vimuttānisamsa*) means that which possesses the attainment of liberation because it accomplishes the path and fruit, or it means the function of liberation because it brings about the absolute liberation from defilements—this is the meaning.
However, in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, regarding the enjoyment of the taste of the goal (*attharasa*), etc.:
It is said: "The 'taste of the goal' refers to the four fruits of asceticism; the 'taste of the Dhamma' refers to the four paths;
the 'taste of liberation' refers to the deathless Nibbāna.
Although, without distinction, the entire word of the Buddha is the Vinaya because it tames the defilements according to the instruction given...
Because it upholds one from falling into the states of misery when one is practicing, it is indeed "Dhamma";
nevertheless, in order to identify it specifically within this very Dhamma and Vinaya according to the desire for its formal definition, he said, "Therein, the Vinaya Piṭaka," and so forth.
The remainder of the Buddha’s word is "Dhamma," because it consists largely of teachings on the nature of phenomena (sabhāvadhamma) by way of the aggregates (khandha) and other categories. Now,
Or even if both the Vinaya and the Dhamma are indeed the same in terms of their status as the "teaching" (pariyatti) and so forth, nevertheless,

when the word *dhamma* is employed in the proximity of the word *vinaya* with a different grammatical referent (*bhinnādhikaraṇabhāvena*), it indicates that the "tradition" (*tanti*) of the Vinaya is distinct [from the tradition of the Suttanta],

just as in the expressions "the equipment of merit and knowledge" (*puññañāṇasambhārā*) or "the cow and the ox" (*gobalībadda*). By way of this application, he says, "Therefore it was said," and so forth.
It has been said. The meaning is that by means of the Vinaya... [and] the Dhamma, the Blessed One declared their true nature in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*.

This verse, "Through many a birth in saṃsāra," was spoken by the Blessed One immediately after the nineteenth reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), while he was reflecting upon his own attainment of Arahantship, which is the foundation for omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); therefore, it is called the "first word of the Buddha."
Thus it was said. This, they say, is the Udāna never abandoned by any Buddha. Its summary meaning is as follows:

"Seeking the builder of this house—which is to say, this personal existence—I, having made my aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara for the sake of that Bodhi-knowledge by which he can be seen, have wandered through the cycle of many births for so long a time."

Not finding, not attaining that knowledge, I wandered and transmigrated through the cycle of existence numbering many hundreds of thousands of births, without reaching its end. Since this thing called birth—
mixed as it is with aging, sickness, and death— is painful to undergo again and again, and since it does not cease while that [knowledge] remains unseen, I was searching for it.
They will run about for the sake of [rebirth]. Now, O builder of this house called the personality, you who are the carpenter of craving—you have been seen by me as I penetrate omniscient knowledge.
You shall not build this house called the personality again; you shall not make it. All your remaining rafters of defilement have been shattered and broken by me.
The pinnacle of this house, which is your own selfhood (*attabhāva*) built by you, namely the central dome of ignorance (*avijjā*), has been dismantled and destroyed.
Now my mind has gone to and entered into Nibbāna, which is beyond conditioned formations (*visaṅkhāra*), by way of making it its object.
And I have attained the path of Arahatship and the fruit of Arahatship, which is known as the destruction of craving (*taṇhā-khaya*).

"Or, 'I have attained, I have reached'—this is the meaning. In the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, however, the meaning stated is: "The mind itself, having gone beyond all conditioned things (*visaṅkhāra*), has attained or reached the path of Arahantship or the fruit of Arahantship, which is characterized by the destruction of craving (*taṇhā-kkhaya*).

Regarding the word "sandhāvissaṃ," the grammarians (*neruttika*) say: "In this verse, the suffix *-imassa* is used in the sense of the past. [And] "In this expression of desire for that time, even though it refers to the past..."
"Will there be [such]," some say. *Punappunaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of repetition. *Phāsu* means "to be drunk" or "to be protected";

the letter *pa* is changed to *pha*, or alternatively, it is *phāsu* because it is "to be touched. That itself is *phāsukā*. Regarding *ajjhagā*, they say that the suffixes *-taniya*, *-māta*, *-mi*, or *-aṃ* are added.
However, if the mind itself is the agent, then the verb form belongs to the remote past (*parokkhā*). This is by way of internal muttering.
It is said that the Blessed One spoke the two verses beginning with “Through many a birth in saṃsāra”; therefore, this [verse] is the beginning of those phenomena that proceed by way of the mind.
However, they say that the verse beginning with “When indeed phenomena become manifest” is the beginning of those phenomena that proceed by way of speech.
“Some” refers to the reciters of the Khandhaka; the view stated first, however, belongs to the reciters of the Dhammapada. “When... [and so forth].
In the phrase *dhammā*, the word *iti* is indicated as elided; it has both the sense of illustration (*nidassana*) and the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*).
For without the sense of illustration—which expresses a limit—the meaning would not be complete, as it would otherwise cause a distortion of the word-meaning.

Here, taking the word *iti* in the sense of "beginning," the word *iti* signifies the beginning, referring to the triad of verses starting with: "Therefore, being ardent... [and so on] ...the Dhamma together with its causes."
"He embraces [them]," so it was said by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta Thera. "In the Khandhaka" means in the Mahāvagga.

"Udānagāthā" (the verse of the Udāna) should be understood as a singular term for the genre; or else, it should be understood that this was stated specifically referring to the very first verse therein.
And here, the reciters of the Khandhaka say this: "Because the verses of the Dhammapada reciters were taught by means of the mind alone..."

"At that time, it was not for the benefit of the great multitude of people; however, because our verses were recited as vocal utterances, they were beneficial for the gods and Brahmās who heard them at that time.
Therefore, this alone is the first word of the Buddha. But the reciters of the *Dhammapada* say:
"The criterion for being 'first' is whether or not the teaching was beneficial to the people."
Some say: "Because it was first taught by the Blessed One with his mind, this alone is the very first word of the Buddha.
Therefore, it should be understood that both [explanations] are applicable in both ways.
But if the verse beginning "Through many births in saṃsāra" was indeed taught by the mind alone, then why does the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* state: "'Through many births in saṃsāra'—this..."?
Is it not said that the Teacher, while seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, uttered this as an *udāna* (inspired utterance), and later, when questioned by the Elder Ānanda, explained it?
It should be understood exactly so according to its meaning (*atthavasena*). For even there, the meaning must be taken simply as "having uttered [it] mentally.
For just like a formal teaching (*desanā*), an *udāna* is also an utterance made mentally, as well as an utterance made verbally.
It is understood in two ways. If this were an *udāna* expressed by speech, it would have been included in the *Udāna-pāḷi*;
therefore, the very fact that it is not included in the *Udāna-pāḷi* should be seen as the reason for its being an *udāna* in the mind rather than being uttered by speech.

The phrase "on the first day of the lunar fortnight" (*pāṭipadadivase*) should not be connected with the phrase "having attained omniscience" (*sabbaññubhāvappattassa*), but rather with "while reflecting" (*paccavekkhantassa*).
This, however, should be connected with the word "arisen. For it was on the full moon day of Visākha, at the time of dawn, that the Blessed One attained omniscience.
Although such a connection also occurs in worldly usage, it should not be understood here as referring to the terminology of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

Just as in the expressions "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*) or "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamaya*), so too *somanassamaya* means "consisting of joy," [referring] to the knowledge associated with that joy.
The meaning is as follows: it may also be understood as "performed by such knowledge" through its co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and other relations with joy (*somanassa*).
The particle *handā* is used in the sense of an exhortation; for it exhorts one to say, "Come now, accomplish this!
*Āmantayāmi* means "I inform" or "I awaken"—this is the sense. *Vo*, however, is the object (*kamma-pada*) of the verb "I inform. In the sense of addressing, the accusative case alone is used.
For after stating, "It is not the fourth [case]," the grammarians cite that very same example.

By the phrase "subject to decay" (*vaya-dhammā*), he clarifies the characteristics of suffering and non-self through the characteristic of impermanence, because of the statement: "What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is non-self.
And by means of this very method of clarifying the three characteristics, insight (*vipassanā*) which has those [characteristics] as its object—

It should be understood that he reveals the unerring path leading to Nibbāna, which is the exclusive domain of the Buddhas, consisting of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, and is inaccessible to all other sectarians. Now, he urges them toward right practice therein, saying:
"Accomplish this through diligence," by means of that unerring path leading to Nibbāna, which is based upon the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.

The meaning is: "Accomplish [your goal] through diligence. Furthermore, having inspired urgency by means of the brief statement, "All conditioned phenomena are subject to decay," he shows, by that same brief statement, the complete and exhaustive practice of right conduct with the words, "Accomplish [your goal] through diligence.
For the term "diligence" stands encompassing the entire, perfect teaching contained within the three trainings; it encompasses that which is included in the three trainings.
The meaning is: "Accomplish, through heedfulness, the right practice known as the teaching (sāsana), which is entirely complete.

Regarding the phrase "in between the two": it means within the interval or middle space between two statements. For here, although time is indicated by the word "time" (kāla), it should be understood that the time-period is also implied because of its inseparability from that [practice].
Regarding the term *Suttantapiṭaka*: here, *sutta* itself is *suttanta*, just as in the expressions "the edge of a field" (*kammanta*) or "the edge of a forest" (*vananta*).

The phrase "both what was recited and what was not recited" refers to all that possesses the same nature. "What was not recited" includes the *Saṅgītikhandhaka*, the *Kathāvatthu*, the *Pakaraṇa*, and so forth.
Some, however, claim that the *Subhasutta* was not recited at the First Council; that is incorrect. From the First Council...
"Indeed, it was at an earlier time that the Venerable Elder Ānanda, while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, spoke these words to the young brahmin Subha," so it was said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
As for the *Subhasutta*, however, it begins: "Thus have I heard:
at one time the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna," and so forth.
It has arrived. In that regard, the statement beginning with "Thus have I heard" would not be appropriate for the Venerable Ānanda Thera himself to utter at the First Council.
For the Venerable Ānanda Thera did not, having personally taught the Subha Sutta, then say "Thus have I heard" and so forth.
Rather, it should have been stated thus: "Once, Bhante, on one occasion, I was in Sāvatthī..."
“I dwell in Jeta’s Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery,” and so forth.
Therefore, it appears that the Subha Sutta was included in the recitation by the compilers of the second and third councils through the formula “Thus have I heard,” and so on.
Now, the Venerable Master Dhammapāla might hold this intention: “Even though the Subha Sutta was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda himself, after it had been included in the first council...”

"The Elder Mahākassapa and others, wishing to establish the tradition (*tanti*), established it with the words 'Thus have I heard' and so forth, according to the very method found in other discourses.

This being the case, it would be logical. Alternatively, even when the Venerable Ānanda himself taught the Subha Sutta, he taught it in the same manner as the Blessed One had taught it in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and elsewhere; thus, [he spoke] in the presence of the Blessed One.

Even if the intention is that [Ānanda] spoke the words beginning with “Thus have I heard” because he placed within himself the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One—teaching it while standing upon the method he had acquired—it is indeed appropriate.

There is also a reading, “And it was recited again. In terms of meaning, there is no difference whatsoever between this and the phrase “recited again” in the context of the second and third councils. Having brought them together, it is called the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The construction is as follows: it should be understood that there is the Sutta Piṭaka... [and so on] ...and it should be understood that there is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
There are two Pātimokkhas by way of the Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Pātimokkhas. There are two Vibhaṅgas by way of the Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅgas.
There are twenty-two Khandhakas found in the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga. Each [of these] consists of sixteen sections.
It is said that there are sixteen supplements (*parivāra*) because they are characterized as such.
For in the *Parivāra-pāḷi*, thirty-two sections are recorded: sixteen sections in the *Mahāvibhaṅga* and sixteen sections in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*.
However, in some manuscripts only the word "parivārā" is seen; yet in many manuscripts, as well as in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*, [the full title is given].
Because it is seen exactly thus as “sixteen groups,” this reading also cannot be rejected;

therefore, its meaning has been stated. By pointing out the Buddha’s word as spoken with the word “iti,” he refers back to it with the word “idaṃ. Alternatively, the word *iti* is used in the sense of “this”;
the word *idaṃ* is merely for the sake of euphony in the phrasing. Or else, the two synonyms *iti* and *idaṃ* both have the same meaning: “this.”
The term *vattati* is used in such contexts as “it exists now at this time,” and so forth; this same principle applies to similar cases.
The thirty-four discourses beginning with the *Brahmajāla* are collected herein, or by means of this, or their collection and enumeration is its [subject matter];

thus it is called the *Brahmajālādi-cattutiṃsa-suttasaṅgaha*. The same applies to the others. Among the accounts given previously regarding the Dīgha-bhāṇakas and the Majjhima-bhāṇakas, [the view] of the Majjhima-bhāṇakas alone...

Because it is more appropriate [to include them] within the discourse, he stated, "The *Khuddaka*... [etc. ...is called the Sutta Piṭaka," showing that even the *Khuddakapāṭha* and others are included in the Sutta Piṭaka itself.
In that context, since it is said, "Listen to the verses leading to the meaning for those of developed minds," the reading "Theragāthā and Therīgāthā" is appropriate.
Having thus defined the Three Piṭakas by way of their essential nature, the following passage beginning with “Tattha” is stated in order to show their etymological derivation (*nibbacana*).

“Tattha” means “among those three kinds of Piṭakas. “Vividhavisesanayattā” means “because of having manifold methods (*naya*) and because of having specific methods. “Vinayanatoti” means “because of the state of disciplining (*vinayana*);
this is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus, or else it is a case of eliding the abstract suffix (*bhāvalopa*); otherwise—

There might be the case where the substance (*dabba*) alone is the exertion; and if that were so, then because the substance of discipline (*vinaya-dabba*), which possesses the quality of disciplining, serves as the cause, it would be designated as "discipline" (*vinaya*)—but not by virtue of the quality of disciplining itself—and thus there would be the undesirable consequence (*anadhippetattha-pasaṅga*) of [the term] having an unintended meaning.

This same method applies to similar cases. Alternatively, it is that by which one is disciplined, or the act of disciplining; such is the meaning. This is the "Discipline" (*vinaya*) as a designation of meaning (*atthapaññatti*).

This *tanti* is designated as *saññā* (designation); it is called *vinaya*. By the statement "it is declared as *vinaya*," it is explained that what is known by the designation *vinaya* is that which has become a verbal designation (*saddapaññatti*).
For a "derivation" (*nibbacana*) consists in the elucidation of a name-designation (*nāmapaññatti*) through a meaning-designation (*atthapaññatti*).
Now, in order to clarify the meaning of this verse, he says: "For there are various methods here... and so forth. "Various methods (*nayā*) are found herein..."
Therefore, it should be connected with such passages as: “Because it possesses manifold methods, it is called *vinaya*. He demonstrates its manifold nature through the words “fivefold,” and so forth;
likewise, he shows its specific distinctions through the words “strengthening,” and so forth. In the training rules concerning worldly transgressions, the purpose is strengthening;
in those concerning conventional transgressions, the purpose is relaxation. Having overcome the limits of restraint...
Conduct that has proceeded [into excess] is transgression (*ajjhācāra*), a violation; it proceeds by way of body and speech. Its restraint is likewise [by way of body and speech].

By this method of showing that such restraint itself is called the "discipline of body and speech" (*kāyavācāvinayana*), he says "therefore" (*tasmā*) and then states its manifold examination with the words "because of its various methods" (*vividhanayattā*), and so forth. And the aforementioned verses [apply] to such [a discipline].
In order to show that [the definition] was stated for the purpose of clarifying the etymology, the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tenā*) was spoken.
They say that "therefore" (*tenā*) means by way of the instrument (*karaṇa*), on account of the reasons such as its possessing manifold methods (*vividhanayatta*).

Furthermore, they state the connection by saying that [the author] spoke the passage beginning with "Therefore" while demonstrating the excellence of the aforementioned sentence beginning with "For it is manifold" (*vividhā hi*). This being so, "therefore" (*tenā*) means by way of the reasons such as its possessing manifold methods.

The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, they say that the phrase beginning with "Therefore" (*tenā*) was spoken by the ancients in order to correlate this verse with the very words already mentioned;
thus, the meaning of the word "therefore" (*tenā*) is the same as in the second method. "This" (*etaṃ*) refers to the statement of the verse.
"Of this" (*etassa*) refers to the word *vinaya*, and it is connected with the phrase "the meaning of the expression. For [the compound] "the meaning of the expression" (*vacanassa attho*)...
Although the relationship has already been stated, it is mentioned again with the words "of this" (*etassa*) in order to show its specific distinction from other general statements.

Grammarians (*neruttikā*), however, maintain that since [the term] is established as a compound or a derivative (*taddhita*), and because of its status as a common noun and its nature as a nominal word (*nāmasadda*),
it must be specified by another word in such instances.
The term "atthānaṃ" (of the meaning) should be connected, as appropriate, with the terms "sūcanato... pe... suttāṇā" according to their respective grammatical relationships.
He explains that meaning with the words beginning with "tañhi" (for that). Regarding the "meaning" (attha) divided into one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth:
for one who recites, hears, causes to be recited, reflects upon, or teaches that Sutta, there is the meaning consisting of virtue and so on, which is comprised by the Sutta.
That [sutta] also exists for him, because it must be accomplished by another; thus, the word "another" indicates and illuminates both of those.
Likewise, the word "etc. includes meanings such as those pertaining to the present life and the future life, and mundane and supramundane meanings—these being the various types of meaning.
Furthermore, this word *attha* (meaning/purpose) is a synonym for "benefit," not a term denoting the literal sense of what was spoken.
If it were the case that a sutta indicates its own expressed meaning as well as that of another, then this would be stating an unintended meaning.

For whatever meaning is elucidated by a sutta belongs to that very sutta which elucidates it; therefore, the meaning of another is not indicated by it, because there is no other meaning to be indicated or to be excluded by it, and thus the inclusion of "one's own meaning" [is necessary].
It should not be so stated. Since there is no meaning of speech that is divorced from one's own welfare or the welfare of others, the inclusion of the word "beginning" (ādi) should also not be made.

Therefore, because the aforementioned meaning expressed by the term "welfare" is impossible within the Sutta itself, the welfare of oneself and others is spoken of here by way of the person who is the locus of the Sutta.
Alternatively, setting aside the specific sutta, those classifications of meaning such as one’s own welfare and so forth—
which were stated in the commentary on the phrase “there is no praise or gain for the sake of another”— are as follows: one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, the welfare of both,
welfare pertaining to the present life, welfare pertaining to future lives, manifest meaning, profound meaning, hidden meaning, and concealed meaning.

The meaning to be inferred (*neyyo attho*), the established meaning (*nīto attho*), the blameless meaning (*anavajjo attho*), the stainless meaning (*nikkileso attho*), the purified meaning (*vodāno attho*), and the ultimate meaning (*paramattho*)—

the sense is that [the commentary] indicates these various classifications of meaning. For although the "one's own welfare" and so forth are mentioned independently of the discourses (*sutta*), since they have not been specified as being the meaning of a discourse, even one of those classifications of meaning must be illustrated by means of a discourse.
"It does not overstep. And in this interpretation of the meaning, the word *attha* (meaning) also serves as a synonym for "that which has been spoken" (*bhāsita*).
For here, the first five divisions of meaning are synonyms for "benefit" (*hita*); those following them, the six divisions, are synonyms for "that which has been spoken";
and the final four possess the nature of both. Among these, because it is easily understood through its distinctness, it is "shallow" (*uttāna*), meaning its depth is unfathomable.
It is profound (*gambhīra*) because its state is unfathomable due to its difficulty of being mastered. It is unopened (*avivaṭa*) and hidden (*gūḷha*).

It is concealed (*paṭicchanna*), being covered over by letters, arrangements, and so forth, like roots, water, and the like [hidden] by soil. It is "to-be-guided" (*neyya*), meaning it must be brought out and made known.

It is "definitive" (*nīta*), meaning it is to be understood according to the literal expression. It is spoken by way of synonyms as faultless, the purification from defilements, and by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional states.
Or they should be applied according to their respective order. The ultimate meaning (*paramattha*) is Nibbāna, or else it is simply the non-perverted intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.

Alternatively, by saying "he himself is of few desires," he indicates his own welfare (*attattha*); and by saying "he is one who speaks to others about fewness of desires," he indicates the welfare of others (*parattha*).
Likewise, by saying "he himself abstains from taking life, and [encourages] another to abstain from taking life... [the same structure applies].
Suttas such as “he encourages [others] in abstinence” should be applied here. However, others say:
that which is spoken according to its true nature for one’s own benefit indicates the system of other sectarian teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, which pertains to the benefit of others;

or that which is included in the Sutta is for one’s own benefit, while that which conforms to the Sutta is for the benefit of others; or else, that which follows the method of the Suttanta is for one’s own benefit.

Some also say that it "clearly indicates the ultimate goal" as it constitutes the method of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma. Furthermore, the meaning of the word *sutta* must be explained in distinction from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma.

Therefore, because the teaching proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*), the welfare of oneself and others and so forth are manifested with particular excellence due to their being its primary focus;
however, this is not the case when the teaching proceeds by way of the nature of the law of commands (*āṇā-dhamma-sabhāva*).
This very [definition] is stated as: "Sutta is so called because it indicates the meaning (*atthasūcanato*). Furthermore, in this context, the vowel of the word *sūca* is shortened.

Regarding this, the Venerable Ācariya Sāriputtatthera has said: "And having established it thus, one should understand that in such passages as 'so much of the Blessed One's teaching has come down in the Suttas and is included in the Suttas,' and 'in our own tradition there are five hundred Suttas,' the word *sutta* is used figuratively (*upacāra*)."

Thus it has been said. Others, however, maintain by means of an etymology similar to that already stated that the word *sutta* denotes not only the discourses (*suttanta*) but also the Vinaya and the Abhidhamma.

Furthermore, in the case of the *sutta*, the nature of the authoritative teaching (*āṇādhammasabhāva*) conforms to the disposition of those to be trained (*veneyyajjhāsayamanuvattati*), whereas in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, the disposition of those to be trained does not conform to the nature of the authoritative teaching.
Therefore, the teaching of the *suttanta* leads exclusively to the attainment of welfare for those to be trained.

He said: “And here the meanings are well-spoken,” and so forth. The statement, “The teaching of the Suttanta conduces to the attainment of absolute welfare,” is also spoken with reference to the fact that the teaching of the Suttanta possesses the quality of being devoted (*tatparatva*) to the accomplishment of the welfare of those to be trained (*vineya*).

And this quality of being devoted should be understood as conforming to the inclinations of those to be trained. For this very reason, he said: “In conformity with the inclinations of those to be trained...”
“Because it has been so stated. By this reason, he addresses the inquiry: “Are not the Vinaya and Abhidhamma also well-stated?
Then why is only this [Sutta Piṭaka] stated in this way?
He answers by showing that the accomplishment of the goal occurs over time through the gradual training and so forth, using the phrase “like the fruit of a crop.”

It has been said. This is what is meant: just as a crop does not yield fruit at the very moment of sowing and planting, but yields it only after a period of time through successive stages such as cultivation and so forth, so too this [Dhamma] does not yield its meaning at the very moment of hearing and memorizing, but yields it only after a period of time through successive stages of training and so forth. And "it yields" (pasavati) means...
"It bears fruit" means "it brings about" (*abhinipphādeti*). For bringing about is indeed what constitutes bearing fruit.
Showing that the accomplishment of the goal occurs only for those who possess the proper means, he says, "like a cow [yielding] milk. This is the intended meaning here:
just as a cow—having given birth at the proper time and being milked by one who knows the method—causes her milk to flow only when she has taken up the udder, so too does it proceed.

It is not that those who have not yet given birth do so at the wrong time; nor does it flow for those who, even at the right time, lack the proper means when milking by grasping the horns and so forth.

Likewise, this [Dhamma] causes the virtues and other qualities to flow only for those who possess the means—namely, those who perform hearing, retention, and so on by way of renunciation and the like—but not for those who lack the means and perform hearing, retention, and so on according to the simile of the poisonous snake (*alagaddūpamā*). Even though it is said, "it flows" (*sūdatī*).

The meaning of *etassa gharati* is "it pours"; nevertheless, because it is a transitive verb (*sakammika-dhātu*), the meaning is stated in terms of its causal function (*kārita-vasena*) as "it causes to flow," just as the meaning of *tarati* is "he causes to cross.
He states the meaning of *suttāṇā* as "it protects them well" (*suṭṭhu ca ne tāyati*). *Ne* has the sense of "them."
“Suttasabhāgaṃ” means similar to a string. He shows that state with the words beginning, “Just as,” and so forth.
“A carpenter’s string” refers to the black string used by woodworkers. It serves as a measure because they cut according to it. This is what is meant:
just as, when a black string has been stretched out and marks have been made, what is to be taken up and what is to be let go becomes known; therefore—

That is the standard for the Takkhas; thus, when disputes arise, as soon as the Sutta is brought forward, the dispute is settled because it becomes clear that "this is to be accepted" and "this is to be rejected. Therefore, this is the authority for the wise.
Now, further clarifying the similarity to the Sutta in another way, he says "And just as," etc. "By the Sutta" means by the *pupphāvuta* (the flower-strewn).
"By whatever strong thread": "well-bound" means they are grasped evenly or fastened;
"not scattered" refers to the absence of being dispersed here and there; "not destroyed" refers to the absence of being cut or broken.
This is the intended meaning: just as flowers bound by a strong thread are not scattered by the wind.
They are not scattered; likewise, meanings gathered together by the Sutta are not dispersed nor destroyed by wrong doctrine.
Furthermore, because the teaching proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*), it exceptionally illuminates one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth;

thus, having distinguished it from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma—which consist of the rules of discipline (*āṇā*) and the nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*)—its commonality with the Sutta is stated. Regarding the phrase "Therefore" (*tenā*) and so on:
The connection and the meaning should be stated as appropriate according to the method already explained.

And here, although the word *anta* was mentioned below in the phrase "Suttantapiṭaka," its non-mention is for the purpose of showing that it has no separate meaning of its own, because its existence is expressed by that [compound].

For when a word used in conjunction is not explicitly mentioned, its remaining status indicates either its identity of substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) with the other term or its lack of independent meaning.
The particle *esa* is used here in the sense of cause; thus, the meaning is "by which. Here, in the context of the Abhidhamma, one should apply [the analysis] individually to each [term]:
"That by which the phenomena possessing growth (*vuḍḍhimanta*) are spoken of is called the Abhidhamma. This classification is according to the meaning of the prefix *abhi-*.
Demonstrating that it functions with that specific meaning, he says "For this... and so forth, thereby establishing that meaning.

The prefix *abhi-* indicates an excess of meaning characterized by the state of increase (*vuḍḍhibhāva*) in the sense of desiring action; thus it is said: "In such cases as ‘approaching’ (*abhikkamanti*), it occurs in the sense of increase.
"Well-known" (*abhiññātā*) means known by some sign such as the crescent moon; what is meant is that they are recognized or manifest.
Indeed, the state of being a crescent moon and so forth serves as a sign by way of characterizing the night, [as in the thought]: "Since..."
Because it is deficient, it is the eighth day; because it is full, it is the fifteenth day. Regarding the word *abhilakkhitā*, the same meaning should be understood here as well.
However, since the word *abhijñāta* (well-known) is a synonym for the word *abhilakkhita* in the *Bhayabherava Sutta* of the *Mūlapaṇṇāsaka*, he says:
“In such passages as ‘well-known’ (*abhiññātā*) and ‘distinguished’ (*abhilakkhitā*), [the suffix] has the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇe*).”
If this is so, since the prefix *abhi-* merely illuminates the meaning of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of the word it qualifies, would it not follow that *abhi-* is devoid of meaning?

It should not be viewed in this way, for even that [prefix] indicates that very meaning. For when placed in proximity to a denotative word, prefixes and particles serve merely to illuminate its meaning;
thus, while the word characterized is manifested by the denotative function, the prefix is manifested by the function of illuminating the meaning of that very characteristic.
It should be understood that it is stated that the word *abhi* also occurs in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).
