"King-abhirāja" means a king worthy of being honored by other kings. "Honored" means worthy of honor. This, however, is from the Sela Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta.

Regarding "Abhidhamma," it refers to such passages as: "Even in the case of an emission of semen during sleep, although there is no offense, unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*) is still found," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the Dhamma free from confusion concerning the formulation of the Vinaya":

because there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows, they say it is "in the Dhamma free from mutual confusion," since the aforementioned phenomena themselves are devoid of any mutual confusion.

Alternatively, in such passages as "Killing living beings is unwholesome," [it refers to] that which originates from the volitional effort of one intending death, which effects the cutting off of the life-faculty.
Volition is unwholesome, whereas the taking away—defined as the cutting off of the life-faculty known as a living being—is not.
Likewise, in such passages as "The intimation defined as the taking of what belongs to another, which is not given, is an indeterminate state;
the volition of theft that originates that intimation is an unwholesome state," the meaning should be understood as referring to states that are free from mutual confusion.
Regarding the term *abhivinaya*: here, one who says, "Gold and silver must not be accepted," is said to guide within the *vinaya*.

Furthermore, it is said that one who explains, "If one accepts in this way, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); but if in this way, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," is said to guide within the *abhivinaya*.
Therefore, for one who takes gold and silver belonging to another with a mind of theft—
According to the specific case, among the offenses of *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, or *dukkaṭa*, there is a *pācittiya* for one who takes [an object] under the pretext of being a storekeeper;
a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* for one who takes it for his own benefit; and a *dukkaṭa* of non-touching (*anāmāsa*) for one who takes it out of mere greed.
There is no offense for one appointed as a money-changer (*rūpiya-chaḍḍaka*). Thus, [the rules] are free from mutual confusion.
In the Vinaya as well, the meaning should be understood as "capable of training. Thus, showing the delimitation in its own form by way of a brief summary, he said: "mutually... [etc. ...occurs.
Regarding the word *abhikkantena*, it is stated that the prefix *abhi-* indicates the excellence (*adhikatā*) of the beauty (*kānti*); hence, "in the excellent" (*adhike*). Is it not so?
And regarding the word "abhikkamantī" (approaching), here the prefix *abhi-* indicates the state of increase or excess in the action of approaching;

in "abhiññātā abhilakkhitā" (well-known, distinguished), it indicates the excellence of the clarity of the actions of knowing and characterizing; and in "abhikkantena" (by the excellent), it indicates the superiority or distinguished nature of the beauty.
This much, first of all, is logical because of its function as a qualifier of the action.
Regarding the prefix (*upasagga*): for it is stated in the grammatical treatises (*saddasattha*) that "prefixes [occur] in connection with an action" (*pādayo kiriyāyoge upasaggā*).
But how could this be consistent [with examples like] *abhirājā* and *abhivinaye*, where the word *abhi* refers to a king or the Vinaya who are [respectively] honored or delimited?
For a word denoting a non-sentient thing cannot possibly denote a sentient being. There is no fault here, because even the actions of honoring and delimiting...
Because it illuminates [the meaning], and because it occurs even within royal legal codes (*rājavinaya*) associated with those actions.

For, in the sense of "the king is honored," the prefix *abhi-* primarily expresses the word *rāja* as an object (*kamma-sādhana*), taking the relationship between the action and its agent as the cause;
however, the action of honoring itself is secondary. Likewise, the Vinaya is thoroughly delimited.

Taking the relationship between the object, the action, and the agent as its cause, the prefix *abhi-* primarily expresses the Vinaya substance (*vinayadabba*) which functions as the object of the action, while it expresses the act of delimiting only secondarily.

Therefore, just as the prefix *ati-* is used in words such as *atimāla*, the prefix *abhi-* here expresses the action together with its instrument; thus, the terms *abhirāja* and *abhinaya* are indeed prepositional compounds (*sopasagga*).
It is established. Thus, it should be understood that even in the term *abhidhamma*, the prefix *abhi-* expresses an action such as growth (*vuḍḍhi*) together with its accomplishment;
this is the meaning shown.
Let the prefix *abhi-* have the meanings as previously stated, yet by its application, those qualities such as being possessed of growth and so forth are illuminated by the word *dhamma*.
When the question arises, "If these states were not mentioned here, how would this meaning be consistent? he says "And here" (*ettha ca*) and so forth, in order to resolve that objection.
In that context, "here" (*ettha*) means in this Abhidhamma. The particle *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of inclusion.
"Develops" (*bhāveti*) refers to the expansion of the mind; "pervading" (*pharitvā*) refers to the expansion of the object. Therefore, by means of those two—development and pervasion—there is growth.
The meaning is that even those states (dhammas) possessing growth have been spoken of. By "by way of object and so forth" is meant by way of object, association, kamma, door, path, and so on.
Because only supramundane states (lokuttara-dhammā) are exclusively worthy of honor, it is shown that they alone are honored by the phrase "states of the trainee" (sekkhā dhammā) and so on.
By the term "worthy of honor" (pūjārahā), one excludes the agent and other factors of action, as well as past time and so forth, or the sense of possibility.
The intended meaning shown here is that only those phenomena worthy of worship—which are free from restrictions regarding specific times—are stated to be "worthy of worship" in this context.
By the phrase "because they are delimited by their own intrinsic nature," it is meant that they are delimited by such natures as contact and so forth.

By the words "lofty" (*mahaggata*) and so on, he shows that the lofty phenomena are superior to those of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) due to their greatness, and that the unsurpassed phenomena (*anuttara*) are superior even to those, because they lack anything higher.
"By ten" means by the expression "possessing growth" and so forth, acting either as the instrument (*karaṇa*) or as the cause (*hetu*).
"But whatever is here" means that among these three—the Vinaya and the others—which are distinguished from one another, that which is undistinguished and common to them is the meaning of "Piṭaka.
For the three terms, Vinaya and the rest, are said to be "distinguished" because they do not share in one another's specific characteristics.
Furthermore, the word *piṭaka* is called "undifferentiated" because it is common to all three [collections].

The phrase "in the sense of the receptacle for the teaching" (*pariyatti-bhājana-attha*) means by way of the instrumental case endings (or as adjectives) signifying the sense of that which is to be mastered and the sense of the locus of establishment.

Moreover, the meaning should be understood as follows: "in the sense of the receptacle for the teaching" (*pariyatti-bhājana-attha*) is what is said [by the term *piṭaka*]. For the suffix *-to* here has the sense of the nominative, [as modified] by the word *iti*.

Because it is to be demonstrated. By means of this demonstration—just as etymologists (nairuktika) desire the word *piṭaka* [to mean] "that which is to be mastered" from the phrase "insightfully contemplating as impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and because it is a "receptacle" (*piṭaka*) for those respective meanings—it shows that it is called a "basket.
For this is a derivative word not [previously] established. However, grammarians [derive it] from the root *piṭ*, meaning "to collect" (*saṅghāṭe*).

Having stated this, they cite the very same application as explained here; therefore, according to their opinion, *piṭaka* is so called because it is stored (*piṭīyati*), gathered (*saddīyati*), or mastered (*pariyāpuṇīyati*).
Alternatively, the etymology should be made such that it is a *piṭaka* because it is stored (*piṭīyati*) or compiled (*saṅghāṭīyati*), meaning "that which contains various meanings herein.
With the words "By that," etc., he demonstrates the compound.
“Do not [accept it] by way of the collection of the Piṭakas”: this refers to the passage found in the Kālāma Sutta and the Sāḷha Sutta.
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on those suttas, the meaning is stated as: “Do not accept it thinking, ‘It accords with our own Piṭaka tradition. However, the Venerable Master Sāriputta Thera said:
“Do not accept it merely on the basis of the textual authority of the Piṭaka. “Taking a spade and a basket” means taking both a spade and a basket.
"Having taken. What is called "earth"? Because it is dug up and split open, a specific tool made of iron is called a "pickaxe" (*kudāla*).
Because they serve as containers for various things, a specific type of vessel made from palm leaves, bamboo, rattan, and so forth, is called a "basket" (*piṭaka*).
This, however, [is explained] in the *Kakacūpama-sutta* of the *Mūlapaññāsa*.
Having pointed out the verse-line “By that... [and] should be known,” he explains it with the words beginning “by that.

Whether the gender is taken from what has been expressed by all the pronouns (*sabbanāma*) such as *sabbā* and so forth, or from what is currently being expressed—here, however, considering that it is taken from what is expressed according to the speaker’s intention—it is stated:
“It is both the discipline (*vinaya*) and the basket (*piṭaka*). By the phrase “in the very manner already described,” [he refers to the passage]: “Thus, in two senses... [etc.]”

The phrase “having made [it so]” and the statement “because it is the state of the scriptures (pariyatti) and because it contains the meaning of this or that [teaching],” refer by extension to everything that has been said.
Regarding the expression “the three also” (*tayo pi*), the word *api*—or rather the particle *pi*—has the sense of aggregating the individual parts.
By saying “also” (*pi*) instead of saying “even” (*apī*), he shows that the particle *pi* exists as a separate indeclinable, just like the particle *api*.
*Desanā* (teaching) is the imparting and awakening [of others] through the method of instruction and so forth, dependent upon the teacher, regarding matters that ought to be spoken.
*Sāsana* (the dispensation) is the guiding and disciplining of the individuals to be trained, according to their respective faults and the manner in which they are to be trained.
*Kathā* (discourse) is the speaking of the matter to be explained—such as restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)—and the making of it dependent upon words.
This is what is meant: with regard to the Blessed One as the teacher, there is the "teaching" (*desanā*);

with regard to the person to be instructed, there is the "instruction" (*sāsana*); and with regard to the matter to be explained, there is the "exposition" (*kathā*). Thus, the distinction between these should be understood.
And here, although the teaching and the others are not independent of that which is to be taught and so forth, the commands (*āṇā*) and the rest are particularly [distinguished].
"Dependent on the teacher and so forth": the distinction between the teaching and other factors is stated according to their respective specific applications.

For just as the formulation of an injunction is specifically dependent on those worthy of giving commands due to the application of skill therein, so too the formulations of conventional and ultimate truth are dependent on the formulators;
thus, the dependence of the rules for injunctions and the like on the teacher is stated. And just as [the teaching] conforms to the offense and the disposition, it likewise conforms to the Dhamma.
The teaching is specifically [distinguished] by way of the individuals to be trained; thus, the teaching is described according to the persons who are to be instructed.

Furthermore, since the speaking of views that must be disentangled—just as with the analysis of restrained and unrestrained name-and-form—is dependent upon the presence of a basis for speech and not its absence, it is specifically dependent on that; therefore, [the classification] is according to the meaning to be expressed.
The discourse has been told. And there are these verses:
"By way of the teacher, this is called the 'Three Pitakas' (Piṭakattaya);
by way of those to be trained, it is called the 'Dispensation' (Sāsana)."
"By way of the meaning to be told, and also by way of 'telling';
thus one should clarify the distinction between the discourse on teaching (desanā) and the discourse on the instruction (sāsana).
Having combined these three terms and considering them as "the distinction between them," the word *bheda* (distinction) should be applied individually to each.

Because it is heard following the dual terms, [the phrase] "should appropriately elucidate the distinction in teaching, the distinction in the dispensation, and the distinction in discourse" is stated.

Furthermore, *bhedam* means diversity (*nānatta*) or distinction (*visesa*). Among those Pitakas, one should appropriately elucidate the training (*sikkhā*), the abandoning (*pahāna*), and the profound nature (*gambhīrabhāva*).
In the second verse, one should clarify the classification of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), the manner of mastering them, and their distinction.
The connection is as follows: "Whatever excellence and whatever failure a bhikkhu attains in whichever Piṭaka—such as the Vinaya—one should clarify all that therein.
Alternatively, [it refers to] whatever classification of scripture, excellence, and failure.
The connection should be made thus: "In whatever way a bhikkhu attains [anything], all that should be explained there in that same way.
And as for the word "in whatever way" (*yathā*), it means by those various modes such as the mastery of the causes for attack and so forth; specifically, it refers to these modes:

the mastery of the causes for attacking, escaping, and guarding the treasury of the Dhamma, as well as right practice and wrong practice—even though others also exist. Furthermore, in that same way...

They are called "bhikkhus" because they have attained a state of being constantly in close proximity to the eldest and most excellent [elders], and because, by practicing correctly according to the instructions, they are established in the Dhamma.
"Therein" means in those verses. "This" refers to the discourse that will now be spoken. "Elucidation" (paridīpanā) means a thorough, all-around manifestation.
The meaning is that one analyzes [the subject] without leaving even the slightest remainder.

Although it is described as "explanation" (*paridīpanā*) in this way, it is also "manifestation" (*āvibhāvanā*) in the sense of making it easily understood by listeners without leaving anything hidden or concealed.

Some also say that "explanation" refers to a concise description, while "manifestation" refers to a detailed exposition. Furthermore, these two terms are stated here in accordance with what was explained previously.

In terms of their meaning, however, they are one and the same. Therefore, it should be understood that the first verse provides the general indication (*paridīpanā*), while the second verse provides the detailed exposition (*vibhāvanā*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), the two meanings are mutually conjoined. As to why they are so called, he says: "For here... and so forth.

The particle *hi* is used in the sense of a reason (*kāraṇe*), as in expressions such as "in the case of a corruption of syllables" (*akkharavipattiyaṃ hi*) and the like; or it may mean "because" (*yasmā*), in which case [the question] is "why? (*kasmā*).
The meaning is as follows: one who is worthy of an *āṇā* (command) because he is capable of issuing (*paṇetuṃ*) or establishing it is called *āṇāraho*.

Because he is a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) and possesses great compassion (*mahākāruṇikatā*), his words are authoritative (*pamāṇavacana*) by virtue of being an unerring instructor of what is beneficial; thus, the meaning is "by the Blessed One, who is worthy of an *āṇā*.

Since both conventional and ultimate phenomena (*vohāra-paramattha-dhamma*) exist therein, it is said "because of the abundance of *āṇā*s"; by this, he indicates the method of majority (*yebhuyyanaya*). In the following passages as well...
The same method applies. It is called *vohāra* (convention) or *paññatti* (designation) because it specifically carries away the minds of beings; one who is skilled in that [is meant by] "by that.
Those for whom offenses, faults, and transgressions are frequent and numerous are "those of frequent offenses," such as the Elder Seyyasaka and others.

"According to the offense" means in accordance with the fault. Regarding the phrase "with various underlying tendencies" (*anekajjhāsayā*) and so forth: an underlying tendency (*āsaya*) itself is an underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*); in terms of its meaning...
In terms of its classification, it is fourfold: view, knowledge, and [the other two].
And it is said: “Eternalism and annihilationism as views, And conformity as acceptance, And that which is knowledge of things as they truly are— This is what is termed ‘disposition.’”
In this regard, because all views are subsumed under the views of eternalism and annihilationism, all beings who follow speculative views (diṭṭhigatika) rely upon these two very views.
As it is said: “For this world, Kaccāna, mostly relies on a duality: ‘it exists’ and ‘it does not exist.
For by “it exists,” the grasping for eternalism is intended; by “it does not exist,” the grasping for annihilationism is intended.
This, first of all, is the disposition (*āsaya*) of worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are dependent on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

However, for pure beings (*suddhasatta*) who are dependent on the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), the disposition is twofold: conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*) and knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*).

Among these, conformable acceptance is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*), while knowledge of things as they truly are is the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kamma-sakata-ñāṇa*). This disposition is fourfold; "disposition" (*āsaya*) means that beings dwell therein.
It is called an "abode" (*āsaya*) because one lies down there having come to the mind, like the abode of deer.

Just as a deer, even after going out for grazing, returns and lies down right there in the forest thicket, so that place is called its "abode"; likewise, wherever the mind, having functioned otherwise, returns and lies down, that is its "abode.
These are the seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), beginning with sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).

Just as rat poison manifests when it encounters its specific conditions, those who are Arahants in the future, past, and present are so called because they possess that same intrinsic nature (*tatsabhāva*).
For there is no difference in the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhamma*) due to a difference in time.

"Conduct" (*cariyā*) refers to the six root types of conduct, beginning with lustful conduct (*rāgacaritā*), which are manifold according to their internal subdivisions; however, by way of association (*saṃsagga*), they become sixty-three. Now...

"Or conduct (*cariyā*)" means that conduct is twofold by way of good conduct (*sucarita*) and bad conduct (*duccarita*). For that is explained in the *Vibhaṅga* in the section on the description of conduct.

Regarding "resoluteness (*adhimutti*)," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "'Resoluteness' is a firm determination proceeding with a tendency toward [a specific goal], such as 'I shall go forth this very day,' or 'I shall attain Arahantship this very day. However, by the Elder Master Dhammapāla...
“*Adhimutti* (inclination) is the preference of beings resulting from their past conduct; it is twofold, distinguished as inferior and superior,” so it is said.

For indeed, by means of which [inclination], beings of inferior inclination associate only with those of inferior inclination, and those of superior inclination [associate] only with those of superior inclination.
For if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous, the co-residents...
Those who possess virtue do not even approach their own teachers and preceptors; they approach only those bhikkhus of similar standing who are worthy.

If their teachers and preceptors are worthy while others are unworthy, they still do not approach their teachers and preceptors, but approach only those unworthy bhikkhus who are of similar standing. This is according to the *Dhātusaṃyutta*.

This meaning should be illustrated. Thus, this inclination (*abhiruci*) and disposition-element (*ajjhāsayadhātu*), which are restricted by mutual association and so forth among those of inferior inclination and the like, should be understood as "inclination" (*adhimuttī*).
[The compound] *anekājjhāsayādayo* means those who possess many inclinations and so forth, or those for whom there are many inclinations and so forth;
it is similar to the compounds *bahukattuko* (one who has many agents) and *bahunadiko* (one who has many rivers). *Yathānulomaṃ* means according to the sequence.

"According to their inclinations and so forth" means not overstepping what is concordant with their inclinations and so forth; or rather, the meaning is "by whichever inclinations and so forth are concordant.

They also say it means "in accordance with what is suitable for their latent tendencies (āsaya) and so forth. Because there is no analytical resolution of the compact mass [of aggregates], they possess perceptions that proceed in the manner of "I" and "what belongs to me," driven by views, conceit, and craving.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means: "There is no self here, nor anything belonging to a self..."
The meaning is: "in accordance with the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva)," as expressed in such passages as "or, this is merely the mere phenomenon (dhammamatta) itself.
Restraint (saṃvara) is the act of restraining; it is the non-transgression by means of body and speech. Non-restraint (asaṃvara) is a great restraint.

For here the vowel *a* has the sense of "increase" (*vuḍḍhi*), as in the term "states of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*). And because of its association with that [greatness], restraint is minor by way of elimination (*pārisesa*) and so forth.
“Restraint”: thus it is small, and there is also great restraint; this is the meaning. Therefore he said, “restraints and restraint,” and so forth.
“The unraveling of views” means liberation from views; in terms of its actual meaning, however, it refers to those states such as right view that are the direct opposites of those [wrong] views.
Thus it is said: “being the counteragent to the sixty-two views. [This applies to] name, form, and name-and-form.

And the delimitation [of objects] is the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpapariccheda*); furthermore, because of the statement that it "is the antidote to lust and so forth," it is simply knowledge occurring in such a manner.
With the words "In all three," etc., he explains the latter half [of the verse]. It is stated as "by way of distinction" because the possibility of those [terms] exists in all three.

This should be applied everywhere. In that regard, because of the statement, "That which is the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is the training intended here," he says, "In the Vinaya Piṭaka is the training in higher virtue.

Because of the abundance of teachings on concentration (samādhi) in the Suttanta Pāḷi, such as "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" and so forth, it is said, "In the Suttanta Piṭaka is the training in higher consciousness (adhicitta-sikkhā)."

Because the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the proximate cause for higher wisdom (adhipaññā), and because the remaining phenomena of name-and-form are taught for the sake of that higher wisdom, it is said: "In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, there is the training in higher wisdom.

Regarding "of the defilements" (kilesānaṃ): this refers to the phenomena of affliction (saṃkilesadhammā), or to both kamma and defilements; and this term [defilements] is used with reference to both. [This applies to] whoever, through the doors of body and speech...

“Transgression of the defilements, their abandonment, because it is their opposite”—in this [passage], the word “transgression” (*vītikkama*) is connected to the word “opposite” (*paṭipakkha*) by way of the abstract suffix (*bhāva-yoga*), whereas “of virtue” (*sīlassa*) is by way of the abstract suffix (*bhāva-paccaya*). This applies everywhere.

Defilements that persist in the continuum by way of latent tendencies (*anusaya*), even when they have become manifest (*pariyuṭṭhita*) upon obtaining their causes, [are abandoned] out of fear of the breaking of virtue.
"They do not obtain the opportunity to transgress" means he said, "because virtue is the opposite of transgression.
*Pariyuṭṭhāna* is the arising of defilements in the mind by way of providing them an occasion, which exhausts the occurrence of the wholesome;

its abandonment is what is meant by the abandonment of the manifestation (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of defilements through their non-arising within the continuum of consciousness. "Of defilements" (*kilesānaṃ*).
This is the governing principle; however, since that abandonment of the obsessions occurs by means of centering the mind, he said: "Because concentration is the antidote to the obsessions.

The seven defilements, such as sensual lust and the rest, which lie latent (anusaya) in the continuum by way of their unabandoned state—meaning they are prone to arise when they encounter suitable conditions and have become firmly established—are the "latent tendencies" (anusayas). Their abandonment, moreover, occurs entirely through the wisdom of the Noble Path.
"They are abandoned" means: "Because wisdom is the antidote to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

Just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp, the abandonment of each respective unwholesome state through each respective wholesome factor involved in the bases of meritorious action such as giving is "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).
However, in this context, because it is the section concerning the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*), [it refers to the restraint of the sense faculties].
The abandoning of each respective factor of immorality by means of its corresponding factor of virtue should be understood as "abandoning by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

The abandoning of those various states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) by way of suppression— through concentration distinguished as access and absorption, which prevents their occurrence just as the striking of a pot suppresses algae on the surface of water— is "abandoning by suppression" (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).

Abandonment by eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*) is the abandonment consisting in the absolute non-arising of the group of defilements belonging to the side of origination within the continuum of one who possesses each respective noble path, by way of its total severance through the cultivation of the four noble paths.
"Misconduct" (*duccarita*) is conduct that is badly performed, or conduct corrupted by defilements. That very [misconduct] is that which arises in whatever continuum.
"Defilement" (*saṃkileso*) refers to that which thoroughly defiles, afflicts, and torments; its abandonment is the goal.

The abandonment of defilement proceeding by way of misconduct of body and speech is stated here through the factor of "its constituent part" (*tadaṅgavasena*), because virtue is the direct opposite of misconduct.
Indeed, the meaning should be understood according to the three trainings. "Thirst" (*taṇhā*) means it torments; that very thirst is, in the manner already described, defilement.
Its abandonment is stated to be by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), because concentration (*samādhi*) is the direct opposite of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).

Defilement (*saṃkilesa*) is indeed [the nature of] views (*diṭṭhi*) according to the method already described; its abandonment is stated to be by way of eradication (*samuccheda*), because wisdom (*paññā*) reveals the nature of phenomena (*dhamma*) as being devoid of a self (*attā*) and so forth.
"In each one of these" means in each one of these three Piṭakas; the word *ca* (and) marks the commencement of the sentence.
Or [it means] "in another sense. The word *pi* or the word *api* is used here for the purpose of grouping together the parts;
by this, it indicates that the profundity does not belong to the fourfold [Dhamma] alone, but rather groups together each of its individual parts as well. This same method applies to such cases.

Now, in order to show those [parts] according to their own nature, the words beginning with "therein" (*tatthā*) were spoken. Therein, *tanti* refers to the Pāḷi, for it is the source of the exalted ones.

It is called "Pāḷi" because it is a row (*āḷi*) or series (*paṅkti*) of distinguished words, since they illuminate the meanings such as virtue (*sīla*), possess their own intrinsic nature and etymological derivation, and have been spoken by the Buddha and others. However, here,

according to the opinion of the grammarians (*saddavādī*) such as the author of the *Vinayagaṇṭhipada*, it refers to those compositions consisting of ultimate-true words (*paramattha-sadda*) that were previously established.
The *tanti* is what is called "Dhamma. For the word *iti* has the sense of "name," and thus it is called "Dhamma.

"Of that very" means of the *tanti* just as described; "established by the mind" means of that aforementioned *tanti*, which consists of a sequence of words regarding ultimate reality (*paramattha*), having been previously established by the mind through its engagement in learning, memorizing, and so forth.
"Teaching" (*desanā*) refers specifically to the *tanti*—the composition of words in their ultimate sense—which serves to awaken others at a later time.
Furthermore, "teaching" is the arising of consciousness that produces the aforementioned *tanti* known as "words.
Thus, it is the realization, in accordance with reality, of both the two kinds of *tanti* mentioned above and its meaning.

The meaning must be understood. For they say that the sound itself—which illuminates both the meaning and the conventional expression being spoken by the Blessed One—is what is called "Tanti" (the text).
But if, according to their view, even the Dhamma has the intrinsic nature of sound, what is the distinction between the Dhamma and the teachings of the Dhamma? [The answer is:
It is known as such by virtue of its capacity to make those various meanings known, and through its role in learning, memorizing, and so forth, as previously [stated].
The Dhamma is the collection of words concerning ultimate reality (paramattha) as it has been established;

the teaching (desanā), on the other hand, is the speech set forth subsequently for the purpose of making that known to others, which illuminates those respective meanings. This is the distinction between these two.

Alternatively, the "teaching" is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that produces the aforementioned speech—so called because the speech is "taught" or "produced" by it—just as in the case of [the offense of] false speech and so forth. Even in that case, [it is so designated].
For the volition that originates false speech and so forth is designated by the terms "false speech" and so on. Although it is the conventional term (*paññatti-sadda*),
which consists of a sequence of syllables, that makes the meaning known, nevertheless— because it is the fundamental cause—

it should be understood that the ultimate term (*paramattha-sadda*) alone is stated as the indicator of the meaning, just as in the case of expressions such as "known from the designation of syllables" (*akkharasaññāto*).
The phrase “the teaching of that series” is stated using a figurative expression (*sadisavohāra*), just as it is said:
“And the arisen wholesome states lead to further increase and abundance.

However, according to the opinion of those who maintain the conventional definition (*paṇṇattivādī*), such as the authors of the *Abhidhammagaṇṭhipada* and others, there is a distinction between the conventional (*sammuti*) and the ultimate (*paramattha*).

Dhamma is that which is called "Dhamma," consisting of a continuum (*tanti*) formed by the connection of name-designations (*nāmapaññatti*), which has been definitively established by the Blessed One through the mind among the terms of ultimate meaning (*paramattha-sadda*) due to its being a verbal expression corresponding to the meaning.
"Of that very [continuum]" means of that very continuum consisting of name-designation. "Established by the mind" refers to [the continuum] distinguished as conventional and ultimate.

The *tanti* is that which consists of a series of conventional designations (*nāmapaññatti*) established by the Blessed One through his mind among the words of ultimate meaning (*paramattha-sadda*), by virtue of their being expressive of corresponding meanings.

"Teaching" (*desanā*) is the communication of that *tanti*—which is defined as a series of words of ultimate meaning consisting of vocal utterance—through the act of manifesting it by means of speech for the sake of awakening others.
[The phrase] "of the *tanti* and of the meaning of the *tanti*" refers to the aforementioned [sequence].
The meaning is: the realization, in accordance with reality, of both types of *tanti* and their respective meanings. For they speak thus:

here, the designation (*paññatti*) established by the Blessed One through his mind, in accordance with both the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and the conventional expression (*vohāra*), is called "*tanti*.
And if, according to the opinion of those who maintain that it is sound (*sadda*), sound itself is what is meant here by "*tanti*," [then...]

There would have to be a difference between the *tanti* (the textual tradition) and the teaching (*desanā*). However, apart from the mere act of vocalizing it, there is no difference in the teaching from the *tanti* as established by the mind.
For when one demonstrates the teaching, the teaching is inseparable from the *tanti* as established by the mind, except for the mere vocalization of the *tanti*.

Non-difference has been stated. And likewise, because it is stated further on that "the teaching is the designation," the fact that the lineage (tanti) is also a designation is implied by its non-difference from the teaching.
Furthermore, if the teaching were something other than the lineage, [then regarding] "the lineage, the meaning of the lineage, and the teaching..."
One might have said, "the realization of things as they truly are" (*yathābhūtāvabodha*).

However, because it was stated instead, "the realization of the text (*tanti*) and the meaning of the text as they truly are," it is shown that there is no difference between the text and the teaching (*desanā*).
And by doing so, since he will later show that "teaching is indeed a designation (*paññatti*)," the status of the text as a designation follows from its non-difference from the teaching.
"It has been told. Now, both of these are, in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), nothing but sound, because there is no conventional designation (*sammuti*) that is divorced from the ultimate.
Adopting this very principle, some teachers state: "Both the Dhamma and the teaching are, in the ultimate sense, nothing but sound";
they too are indeed beyond reproach. Just as the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) resultants of the sense-sphere are called "having limited objects" (*parittārammaṇa*).

This should be understood in the same way. For it cannot be said that the rebirth-resultant consciousnesses of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) have as their objects only ultimate realities (*paramattha*), because they arise by taking as their objects both unwholesome states such as lust—which are preceded by conceptualization of the forms of "woman," "man," and so forth—and wholesome states such as loving-kindness (*mettā*).
However, this is merely a hypothetical assumption based on the fact that [the ultimate reality] is the root of all phenomena.
"It can be described as having the ultimate meaning (paramattha) as its object; it should be understood in this way here as well.

Let this be the opinion of those who maintain the doctrine of conventional designation (paṇṇattivādin). Even in the system of those who maintain the doctrine of words (saddavādin), the diversity of the teachings on phenomena (dhamma) has been explained by the teachers, such as the Elder Dhammapāla, according to the method already stated.
And herein there is this [verse]:
“Others, the venerable teachers, say: ‘The sound, the phenomenon (dhamma), and the teaching’; yet others say:
‘The phenomenon is the designation, while the sound is the teaching.

In all three of these views, the meaning of the ‘continuum’ (tantra) here is the penetration of the phenomenon, the meaning, and the teaching—namely, the continuum, the teaching, and the penetration of the meaning of the continuum.”

Since these three—[the Sutta, Vinaya, and Abhidhamma]—are the objects of the *tanti*, it is logical that they serve as the basis for the teaching and penetration of the meaning of the *Vinayapiṭaka* and so forth.
But how could the status of the *piṭakas* as the basis for the Dhamma be logical, given that the *piṭakas* are themselves merely *tantis*? [The answer is:

because the collection (*samudāya*) serves as the basis for the individual constituent *tanti*. For the collection possesses the status of a basis for its constituent part by virtue of a basis established through mere conceptual designation (*parikappanāmatta*).

It is said as in the expression “the branch on the tree. And here, because the Dhamma and so forth are difficult to fathom, the Vinaya and other teachings are profound by virtue of those [Dhamma] factors;

thus, the fourfold profundity of the Vinaya and the rest has indeed been stated. Therefore, one should not object that “only the Dhamma and so forth are profound because they are difficult to fathom, but not the Vinaya and the rest,” for this is not to be challenged directly, but rather from the perspective of the relationship between the object and the subject.
And because it is precisely the profundity of the Vinaya and so forth that has been stated [therein]. For the Dhamma is indeed the Vinaya and so forth, due to their non-difference.

Their object is the meaning (*attha*), because those very [words] which serve as the designators possess the state of being the designated; and the teaching and penetration of those [objects] constitute the state of having the Dhamma and the meaning as their objects.
In that regard, because penetration is difficult to achieve, [the profundity] of the Dhamma and the meaning [is established]; and because the knowledge of the teaching...
Its state of being difficult to penetrate should be understood from the fact that it is difficult to practice and that its teaching is difficult to fathom;

furthermore, its state of being difficult to penetrate should be understood from the impossibility of producing its penetration and from the difficulty of arising the knowledge that has it as its object.
Because the phenomena, their meanings, and their teachings are profound, the penetration of them is also profound, just as it is with the measurement of deep water.
"It must be by way of length; 'it is of such a nature,'" says the Elder Vajirabuddhi. [Objection:

The profound nature being stated of the *dhamma* and other categories that are constituent parts of the Piṭakas is already stated for the Piṭaka as their collection; therefore, some say one should not object in that manner.
[Response: This must be investigated, because those constituent parts of the Piṭakas do not exist for all [of them].

The connection is: "The great ocean is difficult to plunge into, as if it were impossible to find a footing. For there is a transformation of case, number, and gender according to the sense of the meaning (*atthavasā*).
They are plunged into with difficulty, or their plunging—the entry within—is difficult; thus they are "difficult to plunge into" (*dukkhogāhā*).

It is not to be obtained, hence *alabbhanīyo*; that very thing is *alabbhaneyyo*. Alternatively, *labbhanaṃ* is that which is obtained; it does not deserve that [to be obtained], hence *alabbhaneyyo*.
“Foundation” (*patiṭṭhā*) means that which is a place where one stands; or, standing itself is the foundation.
Those [teachings] in which no such foundation can be found are “those for which no foundation can be found” (*alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā*).
This was stated again to show that even by those of dull intellect who penetrate it only partially, it is simply impossible to find a foundation. “Thus,” etc., is the conclusion.
Now, demonstrating the profound nature [of the teaching] by way of cause, effect, and so forth, he says, "Another method," and so on.
Therein, "cause" (hetu) means a condition (paccaya). And because it "places" (dahati) or "establishes" (vidahati) its own fruit, it is a "dhamma"—the letter *da* being changed to *dha*.
To show how the word "dhamma" is understood here as a synonym for "cause," he says, "For this has been said," and so forth.

This is stated in the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga*. But one might ask: "By this statement, ‘Knowledge regarding the cause is the analysis of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*)’, how is it understood that the phenomenon itself possesses the state of being a cause?

It is because, when showing the meaning of the constituent members of the compound term *dhamma-paṭisambhidā*, it is stated as "knowledge regarding the cause. [Alternatively,] "The analysis with respect to phenomena is the analysis of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*)."
For here, by showing the meaning of "dhamma," it is said "in the cause" (hetumhi);
and by showing the meaning of "analytical knowledge" (paṭisambhidā), it is said "knowledge" (ñāṇa).

Therefore, by stating that the words *hetu* and *dhamma* are synonymous, as are the words *ñāṇa* and *paṭisambhidā*, the fact that *dhamma* has the nature of a cause is established. Likewise, [it is said]: "Knowledge regarding the cause and the fruit..."
By this statement, "the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)," it should be understood that the relationship between cause and fruit regarding the meaning (attha) is established.
The "fruit of the cause" (hetuphala) is the fruit resulting from a cause; and because that [fruit] is traversed or attained by following the cause, it is called "meaning" (attha).

Regarding the terms "teaching" (desanā) and "designation" (paññatti), according to the doctrine of those who maintain the reality of words, these consist of the unerring expression of the dharma and its linguistic formulation (nirutti) through both the meaning and the phrasing.
The *tanti*—consisting of a composition of words concerning the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*)—is called "teaching" (*desanā*), or rather, its meaning is "that which is called teaching.

It is a "teaching" (*desanā*) because the meaning is taught (*desīyati*) by means of it. It is a "conceptualization" (*paññatti*) because the meaning is made known by means of it in a specific manner, or because it makes [the meaning] known in a specific manner.

To show that very [conceptualization] according to its own nature, it is said: "The intended meaning is 'the verbal expression of phenomena in accordance with their true nature' (*yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpo*)."

Regarding the phrase *yathādhammaṃ*: here, the word *dhamma* encompasses both cause and all effects. This word *dhamma* denotes intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), not the teaching (*pariyatti*), the cause (*hetu*), and so forth;
therefore, the meaning is "in each respective case" regarding whatever phenomenon (*dhamma*) such as ignorance (*avijjā*), volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), and the rest.
Alternatively, it means "according to the nature" (*yathādhammaṃ*), that is, in accordance with those respective phenomena such as ignorance, volitional formations, and the rest.
For the teaching, like the penetration [of truth], proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma because it reveals its own object without error;

for that very reason, it is called "unerring expression. "Expression of the Dhamma" refers to that unerring expression which conveys both the meaning and the phrasing, which constitutes the terminology of the Dhamma, and which is known as the "Tanti"—a continuous string of words concerning the ultimate sense. For it is so called because it is expressed and uttered.
Expression (*abhilāpa*) is the unerring phenomenon that constitutes its own nature; such expression is called "expression of phenomena" (*dhammābhilāpa*).

By this, he demonstrates the "expression of phenomena" mentioned in the passage: "Knowledge regarding that expression of the language of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*)," because the teaching has the nature of sound. For it is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga-pāḷi* that the analytical knowledge of language has limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*), and so forth.

It has been stated. Furthermore, in the commentary on that [text], its status as having sound as its object is shown by the passage beginning, "having made that sound, which is the natural linguistic expression, the object.

For, after determining the relationship between a word and its meaning as "this sound is the designator of this meaning," the sound that proceeds by way of elucidating each respective meaning is called "teaching" (*desanā*).

By the word “intention” (*adhippāyo*), it is shown that the statement “teaching is a designation” (*paññatti*) was spoken with reference to the verbal expression of the Dhamma’s terminology (*dhammaniruttābhilāpa*), and not with reference to a designation abstracted from that [terminology]; for when multiple meanings are possible, one speaks only of the meaning intended by oneself.
This is the determination of the doctrine according to the proponents of words (*saddavādino*).

In the doctrine of those who maintain that things are mere designations (*paññattivādī*), however, "teaching" (*desanā*) refers to the designation by name (*nāmapaññatti*)— which is termed a "string" (*tantī*)—

determined by the Blessed One through his mind among words for ultimate realities (*paramattha-sadda*), by virtue of their being expressive of meanings corresponding to the distinction between conventional and ultimate reality. Or rather,
it is called "teaching" in the sense of showing that very [designation] by means of the word which serves as its fundamental cause, using the term for the cause figuratively (*kāraṇūpacārena*).
To demonstrate this, it is said: "The intention is that 'expression of the Dhamma' means [the expression] in accordance with the Dhamma.

For although in the phrase "expression of the Dhamma" (*dhammābhilāpo*), the word *abhilāpo* refers to sound—since it is called "expression" because it is expressed or uttered—and not to a designation (*paññatti*), nevertheless, when sound is spoken, one grasps the conventional usage corresponding to it;
and because one understands the meaning illuminated by that conventional usage, [the meaning is understood] through the sound.
When that [intention] has been stated, the corresponding designation (*paññatti*) is also stated merely by way of a metaphorical application of the cause.

Furthermore, because it was said, "The meaning is 'expression of the Dhamma'," rather than saying "the meaning is 'designation of the Dhamma'," it is clearly shown that what is called "teaching" (*desanā*) is not the sound itself.
Therefore, only the intention (*adhippāya*) is expressed by means of the word for the primary cause; it should not be taken here [as the literal teaching].
“The meaning of ‘desanā’ (teaching) is this”: such is the determination according to the doctrine of those who maintain the position of conventional designation (*paññattivādin*).
He states another meaning: “conformable... speaking,” by which he shows the arising of consciousness that originates the teaching mentioned above.

For it is called “kathana” because the meaning is spoken (*kathīyati*) by means of it. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), the modes of the textual tradition (*pāḷigati*) such as the definitive (*nīta*) and the interpretable (*neyya*), as well as the Nandiāvatta and so forth—beginning with the singlefold—are included.
And the methods based on the Pāli have been included.
It is "penetration" (paṭivedha) because one penetrates by oneself, or because one penetrates by means of this; it is knowledge (ñāṇa).

That very same thing is called "clear realization" (abhisamaya) because it realizes directly, or because one realizes directly by means of this. Now, that penetration, according to its classification as clear realization—

In order to make it clear by way of its mode of realization (*abhisamaya*), its object (*ārammaṇa*), and its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the passage beginning with "And that" (*so ca*) was stated. For therein, it is explained:

by way of its classification as mundane and supramundane; by way of its mode (*ākāra*) as non-delusion regarding the objective field (*visaya*); by way of its object (*ārammaṇa*) as [knowledge] regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), meanings (*attha*), and designations (*paññatti*);
and by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) as conforming to the meaning, conforming to the phenomenon, and conforming to the path of designation.

And it makes [the truth] manifest. In that context, "understanding" (avabodha) regarding phenomena (dhamma) and so forth, in accordance with their meaning (attha) and so on, according to their object (visaya), refers to mundane clear realization (abhisamaya) which has as its objects such phenomena as ignorance (avijjā), such meanings as volitional formations (saṅkhāra), and the designation (paññatti) of both of these.

"Understanding" regarding phenomena and so forth, in accordance with their meaning and so on, according to their lack of confusion (asammoha), refers to that which has Nibbāna as its object and is associated with the Path (magga) with respect to the aforementioned phenomena, meanings, and designations.
The supramundane realization is the destruction of delusion. For in this way,
mundane knowledge penetrates its object by way of taking it as a mental datum— thinking, "This is the cause, this is its fruit, and this is the conventional expression corresponding to both"—
whereas supramundane knowledge does so through non-delusion, because delusion regarding those causes, fruits, and so forth has been utterly eradicated by knowledge.
He penetrates [it]. Some, however, say that supramundane penetration is [penetration] of Nibbāna by way of its object, and of the other [the mundane] by way of non-delusion.

"In accordance with the meaning among the phenomena" means: "Ignorance is the cause; formations are cause-born; ignorance produces formations"—thus, in accordance with the effect among the causes. Alternatively, [it refers to] "among the meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations."
"In three [unwholesome courses of action], ignorance is the associated condition for the formation of demerit;

for the others, it is according to what is appropriate"—thus, there is also the sense of penetration into causes in accordance with their effects. "In meanings, according to the phenomena" refers to [the understanding] of effects in accordance with their causes, such as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise].
The "path of designation" (*paññattipatha*) is the path of the sixfold designation.
"Corresponding to that" means understanding within the designations (paññatti) in accordance with the dhammas being designated; such is the meaning.
To show another sense of "penetration" (paṭivedha) other than "clear realization" (abhisamaya), he said "of those," and so forth.

For it is said that "penetration" (paṭivedha) is that which is penetrated, namely, the non-erroneous intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of each respective dhamma, such as form and so on. In that context, "in each case" (tattha tattha) refers to in this or that [dhamma].

In the Piṭaka, or in the portion of the Pāḷi. "Designated by its own characteristic" means designated by its respective individual characteristic, such as being subject to transformation (ruppana), being named (namana), or touching (phusana).
He said "now," etc., in order to show the profundity of the Piṭakas through the aforementioned categories of phenomena (dhamma) and so forth.

"A class of phenomena" (dhammajāta) refers to a classification of causes, or the cause itself. "A class of meanings" (atthajāta) refers to a classification of effects, or the effect itself. And this which...
The connection is with "teaching" (*desanā*). One becomes "facing toward" it by way of understanding its meaning. "And that which is herein" means:

that penetration (*paṭivedha*) regarding each respective teaching and meaning found within these Piṭakas, and that unerring intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of those respective teachings within these Piṭakas—this is the meaning.
Because it is to be accumulated, the wholesome itself is the "requisite" (*sambhāra*); it has been correctly accumulated.
Those by whom the equipment of wholesome qualities has not been accumulated are, for that very reason, "of poor wisdom" (*duppañña*); the meaning is "devoid of wisdom" (*nippañña*).

For it is impossible for one who possesses wisdom, or for wisdom itself, to be "corrupt" or "defiled"; thus, they are "of poor wisdom" precisely because they lack wisdom, just as one is called "immoral" (*dussīla*) because of a lack of morality.
And herein, the state of phenomena such as ignorance and volitional formations is difficult to penetrate and hard to fathom.
Because it is difficult to establish them, because it is impossible to produce or make the object of penetration—
which is termed "clear realization"— and because penetration, which consists of the non-perverted intrinsic nature, is difficult to discern,
it should be understood as being difficult to fathom. In the phrase "even so" (*evampi*), the particle *pi* indicates another aspect mentioned previously.
He summarizes. Thus, showing that the meaning of the first verse has been explained in its entirety and without deficiency, he says, "To this extent," and so forth.

By this statement of renewed commencement—according to the principle that "once something is established, a new undertaking is for the purpose of indicating a different point or for the sake of restriction"—he demonstrates that the meaning has been explained fully and without deficiency.
"Ettāvatā" (to this extent) is a particle used in the sense of limitation.
The meaning is: "by this much sequence of words. Alternatively, *ettāvaṃ* means that which has this much as its measure; thus, the meaning is:
"by that [sequence] possessing such a measure, namely, by the sequence of the meanings of the words. For they say: "When the word is spoken, its meaning is indeed spoken as well.
That whose meaning (*attha*) has been stated—that is, expounded—is called *vuttatthā*.
“In this” (*ettha*) means “in this verse. The remainder [of the phrase] is either “thus is the meaning” (*attho*) or “thus is the exposition” (*vinicchayo*).

Regarding the expression “in the three Piṭakas,” it should be understood here as referring to “each one” (*ekekasmiṃ*) by virtue of the governing topic (*adhikāra*) or the context (*pakaraṇa*). For it was stated below: “And herein, in each one.
Alternatively, because the application of words follows the speaker’s intention, if one does not wish to state a specific selection (*niddhāraṇa*) here, the locative base alone [is used].

It has been said. And here it should not be objected that "the threefold division of the scriptures (pariyatti) should be seen as existing only within the three Piṭakas," because even for a statement made with reference to a whole, the intended meaning of its individual parts can still exist.
For the formation of sentences referring to individual parts is observed in such cases as "Let the Brahmins and others eat," and so forth;
therefore, enough of this excessive elaboration. [The meaning] is such that it does not contradict the purpose.
"It should be grasped in exactly that way. This applies in all instances. Regarding "the classification of the teachings" (*pariyattibheda*): *pariyatti* refers to mastery (*pariyāpuṇana*).
Here, the word *pariyatti* denotes the act of mastering, and not the sense of the canonical texts (*pāḷi*) themselves; therefore, the meaning is "the modes of mastery.
Alternatively, the very texts which are to be mastered in three ways are called "the teachings" (*pariyatti*). Likewise...

And they say that this is stated in the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā* and in the *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipada*. For in this way, because of the application of the method of mastering the *Alagaddūpama-sutta*, one can also say of the text itself:

"The mastery of the Alagaddūpama-pariyatti. And by taking it thus, the subsequent statement in the commentary, "The Alagaddūpama was mastered for the sake of finding fault and so forth, having been wrongly grasped," becomes appropriate. For in that context, it is the text itself...
It is appropriate to say that [the teaching] was "misapprehended" and "repeatedly studied.
*Alagaddūpamā* means that which has the seizing of a water-snake (*alagadda*) as its simile;
thus, it is the seizing of a water-snake that is expressed here by the word *alagadda*. In the term *āpūpika*, the word *āpūpa* refers to the eating of cakes.
And it is like the word *veṇikā*, where by the word *vīṇā* the playing of the lute is understood.
For by the "seizing of the water-snake" (*alagaddaggahaṇa*), the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) is illustrated, not the water-snake itself.

Or rather, although one should say "the simile of seizing the water-snake," the middle term has been elided—just as in the case of "lip-mouth" (*oṭṭhamukha*) and so on—and thus it is called "the water-snake simile. Furthermore, "water-snake" (*alagadda*) refers to a venomous serpent.
For "gada" is the name for poison, and that [poison] is sufficient and complete for it;

therefore, because its poison (*gada*) is sufficient (*alaṃ*), ready, and complete, it is called *alagadda*—having elided the nasal vowel and added the letter *d* according to the stated method—or else, because its poison is sufficient (*alaṃ*) to take away life, it is called *alagadda* by the same method.
Its purpose (*attha*) or utility (*payojana*) is the escape from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
They are for the purpose of escape. One appointed to the storehouse is a "storekeeper" (*bhaṇḍāgārika*); he is like one who protects the king’s treasures.

In the same way, one who protects the treasure of the Dhamma and is an arahant with taints exhausted is such [a protector]. The "learning of the storekeeper" (*bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti*) is the learning belonging to one who is a storekeeper alone, regardless of any other purpose.
“Misapprehended” means wrongly grasped. To define that very term by its specific nature, he said, “memorized for the sake of criticism and so forth”;
the meaning is that they were learned for the purpose of finding fault, engaging in contentious debate, or seeking self-justification.
It should be understood that memorizing them for the sake of gain, honor, and so on is also included herein. For this has been stated in the *Alagaddasutta-aṭṭhakathā*:
“Whoever, having mastered the word of the Buddha, masters it for the sake of gain and honor— thinking,
‘In this way I shall obtain robes and other requisites,’ or ‘The four assemblies will recognize me’— his mastery is called the ‘mastering of a venomous snake.
Indeed, it is better to fall asleep than to master the word of the Buddha by mastering it in such a manner.”
But surely, the study of the Dhamma is called "the simile of the water-snake" because it is compared to the seizing of a water-snake;
and if that is so, then even well-mastered study ought to be called "the simile of the water-snake," since in the Canon it is stated as a simile for the seizing of a water-snake.
For this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, suppose a man needing a viper, seeking a viper, wandering in search of a viper,
were to see a large viper; he would seize it well with a forked stick,
and having seized it well with the forked stick, he would grasp it firmly by the neck.
"Monks, even though that water-snake might wrap its coils around that man’s hand, or his arm, or any other limb, he would not on that account meet death or suffering amounting to death. Why is that?
Because, monks, the snake was grasped correctly. Even so, monks..."
"Here, certain sons of good family master the Dhamma—the discourses (sutta), the mixed prose and verse (geyya)," and so forth.
Therefore, how is this distinction understood here—that it is specifically the wrongly grasped scripture that is like the *alagadda* (water-snake) simile;
by what means is it known that the wrongly grasped [teaching], when mastered for the sake of criticism and the like, is called "like the *alagadda*"? This is true. This...
However, it should be understood that this is stated by way of elimination (*pārisesa*).

For, since the learning for the purpose of liberation, the learning of the storekeeper, and the learning of the scriptures have been mentioned separately, it is by way of elimination that the learning which is like seizing a water-snake incorrectly is known as "the simile of the water-snake" (*alagaddūpamā*).
Indeed, the learning that is like seizing a water-snake correctly is either the learning for the purpose of liberation or the learning of the storekeeper.
Therefore, this is well said: "The study... [is] wrongly grasped," and so forth. Now, establishing that meaning by means of the canonical text (pāḷi), he says:

"With reference to which... and so on. Therein, "which" refers to that wrong grasping of the study. This was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Alagaddasutta* of the *Mūlapaññāsa* in the *Majjhimanikāya*.
"Alagaddatthiko" means one who desires a venomous snake; "alagaddagavesī" means one who by his very nature seeks and searches for a water-snake (*alagadda*).
"Alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno" means wandering for the purpose of searching for a venomous snake.
Here, the word ending in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) or the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) refers to him, or it means wandering in the place where the water-snake is sought.
"Alagaddapariyesanaṃ" means "the search for a water-snake," because one searches for a water-snake therein. "Tamenam" refers to that very water-snake. "Bhoge" means in its body;
for it is said, "The body (bhoga) of a hooded serpent. It is called "bhoga" because it is bent (bhujīyati) or made crooked.
"Tassa" refers to that person. The connection is with "in the hand or in the arm," from the wrist up to the tips of the nails.

*Hattha*: Together with the upper arm (*aggabāhā*), the remainder of the arm is called "hand" (*hattha*); however, in some instances, it is stated that from the elbow (*kappara*) down to the tips of the nails is the "hand," because the arm is mentioned separately there.

With the exception of the hand and the arm as defined above, the remainder of the body is the "limbs and minor parts" (*aṅgapaccaṅga*). *Tatonidānaṃ* means "having that as its cause" (*tannidānaṃ*), which signifies "for that reason. That...
Regarding the phrase "tatonidānaṃ": since it means "that which has its source, cause, or reason in the hand, etc.," it should strictly be called "tannidānaṃ.

However, by treating the first member of the compound as an ablative (*nissakkavacana*) in the sense of the nominative (*paccattatthe*), and by not eliding the suffix *-to*, this designation is formed;

furthermore, the case ending of the nominative is used here in the sense of the instrumental (*hetvatthe*). Some also say that this is an indeclinable particle (*nipātapada*) used in the sense of a causal reason. Moreover, [it is explained as] "tatonidānaṃ."
This is a qualification according to the method stated here: "death or what amounts to death is suffering.

As for the question, "For what reason?"—if it is asked why the biting on the hand and so forth, and the resulting encounter with death and the like, occur, it is because that person has grasped the snake incorrectly.
*Idha* means in this teaching (*sāsana*). *Moghapurisa* means empty persons because they are devoid of the essence of virtue. *Dhamma* refers to the textual Dhamma (*pāḷidhamma*).
*Pariyāpuṇanti* means they learn; that is to say, they recite, master by word, and retain it.
By the words "Sutta" and so forth, he shows in detail what was stated generally as "Dhamma," for [the Dhamma] does not consist merely of the ninefold division beginning with the Suttas.
There is indeed another meaning for the word *dhamma*. For it has been stated: "of those *dhammas*. Here, the term "meaning" (*attha*) is a designation of the related object;
and by a general designation, or by the method of "single remainder," it refers both to the meaning as it was actually spoken and to the purposeful meaning.
For a word that illuminates multiple meanings through its commonality of sound is expressed by a general designation.
The phrase "or" (*vā*) should be understood everywhere according to the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*). "They do not examine" (*na upaparikkhanti*) means they do not grasp or investigate.

For regarding the word *ikkha*, among its meanings of "seeing" and "mark," the meaning here is simply "seeing"; and for that [seeing], among its meanings of "grasping," "eye," and "looking," it is simply "grasping";
and for that [grasping], among its two kinds—investigation and inclusion—it is simply "investigation"; and that [investigation]...

It is investigation itself, not sustained examination; and this "investigation" is intended here as being twofold: investigation into the meaning of what has been spoken and investigation into the purpose.
Of these, "investigation into the meaning of what has been spoken" is as follows: "In this place virtue was taught, in this concentration, and in this wisdom;
we shall fulfill them. And [the investigation into the purpose is]: "Virtue is for the sake of concentration..."
The meaning is that they do not investigate the purpose and the benefit, as expressed in such passages as, "What is the cause? It is concentration for the sake of insight.
"Anupaparikkhataṃ" means of those foolish persons who are not investigating.
"Na nijjhānakkhamantī" means they do not tolerate wisdom, which is thorough (niḥśeṣena) observation. For here the root *jhi* refers only to observing, not to thinking or burning.

And that is indeed contemplation by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), not contemplation by means of the eye; or rather, it is contemplation by means of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*), not contemplation by means of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).
Therefore, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: they are not to be grasped after having been seen and approved by wisdom (*paññā*).

For *nijjhāna* means "that by which one contemplates thoroughly" (*ni-sesena jhāyate pekkhati*). In the case of *nijjhānakkhamanti*, the *anusvāra* is elided due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*); thus, "contemplation" (*nijjhāna*)...
There is also a reading "khamantī," by which he illustrates this meaning: "Because they do not examine the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not become manifest to them;
they are unable to know that 'in this place, virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the round of existence, or the turning away from the round has been taught.'"

"And having the advantage of finding fault" means having the advantage of attributing defects to the doctrines of others. For "upārambha" (finding fault) is the intense attacking that consists in attributing defects to the doctrines of others;
what is meant is that it is the reviling of others by relying on one's own mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
Indeed, this is described as "having the characteristic of not bringing forward the faults of others. Thus, [it is] "and having the advantage of escaping from debate," and so forth.

Thus, by means of this mastery (*pariyatti*), it serves both as the benefit of gaining victory in debate and as the purpose of liberation from the censure and defeat imposed upon oneself by others, or from one's own position in debate. The word *iti* has the sense of "this";
by it, it refers back to "mastery" (*pariyāpuṇana*) in the phrase "they master. They say: "It is by means of this that they debate and they refute."

*Vādopamokkhānisanso*: that which has as its benefit the release from a charge, the act of releasing, or the one who causes the release; specifically, the release from a charge brought against oneself.
For a charge brought [against someone] is called "vāda" (the charge), just as one given by a god is called "Datta.
Alternatively, "vāda" refers to an accusation or censure, and the compound is formed according to the method already stated. This is what is meant: when others [accuse] one's own doctrine...
When a fault has been attributed, or when blame has been attributed, they master [the texts] for this reason: "We shall release that fault, or the blame, in such and such a manner.

Alternatively, "that particular argument" (*itivāda*): because the word *iti* occurs here with distributive repetition (*vicchā*) in the sense of the pronoun *ta*, it refers to each respective argument.
The "release from such arguments" (*itivādappamokkha*) is, according to the method already stated, that benefit (*ānisansa*).
The meaning is: for those [who possess it], this becomes the benefit of being released from various [wrong] views.

"For whose sake" means for the sake of the fulfillment of virtue and so forth, or for the sake of the liberation without clinging which consists of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Although there is no actual difference, this is a figurative expression of distinction, just as one says "the body of the statue";
or else, it is a relationship between the whole and its parts, just as in the phrase "for the sake of the kathina-cloth."
“Cloth has been brought,” he says. For it is said: “And that is for his benefit. The word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of restriction;
by this, he determines that the mastery of the teaching (*pariyāpuṇana*) occurs only for that purpose and not for any other.

“They master the Dhamma” means that both types of sons of good family—those following their birth-status and those following their conduct—master the Dhamma according to the proper method. And that is for his...

“They do not experience the goal” means that those who grasp this Dhamma incorrectly do not experience or find its goal—namely, the fulfillment of virtue and so forth, or the state of the path, fruit, and Nibbāna, which is known as liberation through non-clinging.
According to another method: for the sake of whatever censure or defense against such talk those foolish men [might employ], they [do not experience the goal]... the Dhamma...
When they have mastered [the texts], if others tell them, "This is not the meaning," because their grasp was faulty,

they are unable to establish that it is indeed that meaning; thus, being unable both to level a criticism against another's doctrine and to defend their own position, they neither experience nor realize that meaning— such is the case here.
The meaning should be understood as follows. Here too, the word *ca* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). In the phrases beginning with “of those,” the meaning is:
“Because those states were wrongly grasped, they lead for a long time to harm and suffering by way of being the cause for censure, conceit, detraction, and hypocrisy.
For the term “wrongly grasped” is a statement containing a reason. Therefore he said: “Because they were wrongly grasped, monks...”

Regarding the phrase "of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*): here, by way of figurative expression where the cause is treated as the effect, it is said, "those phenomena lead to harm and suffering," just as one says, "ghee is life" or "curds are strength.

For although those phenomena themselves do not actually lead to harm or suffering, nevertheless, for those who master them according to the stated method, at the time of recitation and at the time of debate, [suffering arises] rooted in those [phenomena].
Because there is the possibility for the arising of many unwholesome states, such as finding fault and so forth, it is said:
“They... lead to... (te... pe... saṃvattanti). Regarding the phrase “For what reason? (*taṃ kissa hetu*):

here, *taṃ* refers to the non-experience of the aforementioned meaning, and it points to the fact that those phenomena lead to harm and suffering. *Kissa* is a genitive case used in the sense of a reason; likewise, *hetu* is a nominative case.
Regarding the phrase "yā pana" (but which): here, the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the text as referring to an action (*kiriyā*).

In that context, within the category of action, the expression "which is well-grasped" (*suggahitā*) is used as a designation for a distinction even where there is no actual distinction, as in such cases as "he sets out on a journey" (*cārikaṃ pakkamati*) or "while wandering on a journey" (*cārikaṃ caramāno*).

He explains that very meaning with the words "the aggregate of virtue, etc. (*sīlakkhandhādī*); and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the aggregates of concentration, insight, and so forth are included here.
Inclusion. For one who, having mastered the word of the Buddha, fulfills virtue wherever virtue is required;
develops concentration wherever concentration is required; establishes insight wherever insight is required;
and masters [the teachings] wherever the path and fruit are required, thinking, "I shall develop the path and realize the fruit"—that is inclusion.
That very mastery of the scriptures (pariyatti) is called "for the sake of escape" (nissaraṇatthā). "Yaṃ" means that which is the thorough grasping of the scriptures.
As stated in the *Alagaddasutta*: "It leads to welfare and happiness for a long time.

This refers to those who, while fulfilling the virtues (sīla) and other qualities in the places where they are taught, attain Arahantship and teach the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly; and by those who have gained confidence through that teaching of the Dhamma...

The meaning is that these [qualities] lead to welfare and happiness for a long time, both for those who enjoy the four requisites when they have been offered, for those who raise objections against the doctrines of others in accordance with the Dhamma, and for those who ward off the faults attributed to their own position by others.
For it is not only by relying on the well-mastered scriptures that one attains the development of the path, the realization of the fruits, and so forth; [but also through these other qualities].
Moreover, the suppression of the doctrines of others and the establishment of one’s own doctrine are also accomplished. Thus it is said in the *Parinibbāna Sutta* and other texts:
“Having thoroughly suppressed with reasoned argument any arisen doctrine of another, they will teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles,” and so forth.
As for the phrase “but that which...”, here too the meaning is twofold according to the method already stated: one who has fully understood the aggregates through the full understanding of suffering.
One whose defilements have been abandoned through the abandoning of their origin is "one who has penetrated the unshakable" (*paṭividdhā-akuppa*).

"Unshakable" (*akuppa*) is a name for the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala*). For although there is no state of non-destruction common to the four paths and the four fruits, because the seven trainees (*sekkha*) attain successive higher names by relinquishing their own individual names, they are designated as "paths and fruits."
They are not called "unshakable" (akuppa). However, since an Arahant is always indeed an Arahant, the fruit of that very state is described as "unshakable" by way of the person's name.
And by this, he shows this meaning: "Only for one whose taints are destroyed is the mastery of the scriptures called 'the mastery of the storekeeper'.
For in him, there is nothing unknown, unabandoned, uncultivated, or unrealized; therefore—
Thus, even while mastering the word of the Buddha, he masters it by being a bearer of the thread, a protector of the lineage, and a guardian of the tradition;
for this very reason, it says, "for the sake of protecting the lineage," and so forth. And here, "lineage" (paveṇī) refers to the continuity of the Dhamma—the uninterrupted occurrence of the Dhamma.
And the "tradition" (vaṃsa) of the Blessed Buddha is precisely that aforementioned lineage.

But surely, if the mastery of the Buddha’s word for the sake of preserving the lineage is the "storehouse-learning" (bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti), then why was it stated specifically as "one whose taints are exhausted" (khīṇāsava)? For this same method applies even to some worldlings (puthujjana).
Indeed, a certain worldling bhikkhu, out of fear of hunger and so forth, might [apply himself] to one of those dedicated to the study of the scriptures...

When others were unable to remain in their positions and he himself was becoming exhausted by wandering for alms, he mastered the teachings, thinking: "May the exceedingly sweet word of the Buddha not perish;
I shall uphold the tradition, establish the lineage, and preserve the succession.
Therefore, why should his mastery of the texts not also be called the "storehouse mastery" (bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti)? It is said in reply: it is thus...
For even though a worldling possesses learning, it is not what is called the "learning of a storekeeper.

Indeed, although a worldling masters the texts with the intention, "I shall preserve the tradition," because he has not yet crossed over the wilderness of his own existence, that learning of his serves only for the purpose of escape; therefore, the learning of a worldling—
It is either like the *alagadda* (water-snake) simile or for the purpose of escape (*nissaraṇatthā*). For the seven types of trainees (*sekkhā*), it is solely for the purpose of escape.
