It should be understood that for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), it is merely the mastery of the storehouse-keeper. For one whose taints are destroyed is called a "storehouse-keeper" because of his similarity to a storehouse-keeper.
Just as a storehouse-keeper, having put away the ornaments, [brings them forth] at the time of adornment, [providing what is suitable for that occasion]...
Just as one presents a collection of ornaments to a king and adorns him, so too the one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava),
having received the treasure of the Dharma-jewel, perceives beings who are capable of attaining liberation and possess the necessary causes; seeing them,
he expands his teaching of the Dharma accordingly and adorns them with the supramundane ornament known as the factors of the path (maggaṅga) and the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).

Having thus analyzed the three types of mastery (*pariyatti*), he now speaks the passage beginning with “But as for the Vinaya,” etc., analyzing and determining the success and failure (*sampatti-vipatti*) appropriate to each of the three Piṭakas.
For in such passages as “By depending on the perfection of virtue (*sīla-sampadā*), one attains the three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*)”, it is because virtue, when being purified,
[is purified] by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajañña-bala*) and by the power of the knowledge of one’s own actions as one’s own property (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa-bala*).

And it is purified from the stain of defilement and reaches full perfection; therefore, when the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) is being accomplished, it establishes the power of mindfulness (*satibala*) and the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*) by way of being a supporting condition (*upanissaya*).

Thus, its status as a supporting condition for the three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) should be understood through its fulfillment of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*). For by the power of mindfulness, the accomplishment of the clear knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-vijjā*) is achieved;
and by the power of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), [the accomplishment of the clear knowledge of passing away and rebirth is achieved].

The accomplishment of the second clear knowledge (*vijjā*) follows from the practice of performing all duties with thorough insight, which is conjoined with the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*).

The accomplishment of the third clear knowledge results from the purity of aspiration (*ajjhāsayasuddhi*) by way of being a necessary condition for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), due to the presence of the abandonment of defilements through the absence of transgression.

Without the fulfillment of concentration and wisdom already accomplished previously, virtue cannot serve as a necessary condition for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*).

This should be illustrated by those whose taints are destroyed through dry insight (sukkha-vipassaka-khīṇāsava). From the statement, "One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are," the perfection of concentration is the proximate cause for the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā).

From the statement, "Indeed, wisdom is born from yoga," the perfection of wisdom—cultivated through prior application, living with a teacher, proficiency in the local dialect, study, interrogation, and so forth—is the basis for the analytical knowledge of the fourfold discrimination (paṭisambhidā-ppabheda).

The decisive support (*upanissaya*). And here, because it is stated, "by depending on the perfection of virtue" (*sīlasampadaṃ nissāya*), for one in whom the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*)—which are the manifestations of concentration—do not succeed in their entirety, there is no perfection of concentration (*samādhisampadā*) according to the highest limit;
thus, although the true knowledges (*vijjā*) are a part of the higher knowledges, the three true knowledges are those that have arisen from the perfection of virtue alone.
Just as the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), which arise from the perfection of wisdom,
are accomplished by the path alone for one endowed with the necessary supporting conditions— because they are acquired at the very moment of the path— so too,

the three types of higher knowledge (vijjā) arising from the perfection of virtue, and the six direct knowledges (abhiññā) arising from the perfection of concentration, [are accomplished] by the path alone for one endowed with the necessary supporting conditions.

"They succeed" means that their attainment should be understood as occurring precisely through the attainment of the path. For these specific attainments of these noble ones are similar to the attainment of the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha or a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha).
And regarding the phrase "and the statement of their classification therein," the restriction "of those very [attainments]" must be applied to those things to be attained.
This was stated with reference to the absence of detailed explanations for the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and the four analytical insights (*catupaṭisambhidā*) in the Vinaya;
for in the Verañjakaṇḍa, only the three true knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) are analyzed.

Furthermore, the inclusion by means of the word "and" (*ca*) is stated with reference to the fact that only a portion of these [six direct knowledges] is mentioned there, since only portions of the direct knowledges and the analytical insights are spoken of therein. In the second [case], it says: "of those very same."
This restriction is made with reference to the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), not to the three true insights (*vijjā*);

for since those [three] are included within the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), they have already been analyzed in the Sutta. Furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*), he includes the statement that the analytical knowledges represent only a portion [of the qualities].
In the third [case], by the word "and" in the phrase "and of those," he indicates the presence of the remaining [qualities] there as well; for in the Abhidhamma...
The three types of clear knowledge (tisso vijjā), the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā), and the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā) have already been mentioned.

However, wishing to show that there is no detailed explanation of the analytical insights elsewhere and that they are properly analyzed only in this very place, [the author], instead of using the restrictive particle in the manner stated above, reverses it by saying "only there" (tattheva) and thus establishes the restriction. "In the Abhidhamma..."

However, the three true knowledges (tisso vijjā), the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā), the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā), and other specific qualities such as the right efforts (sammappadhāna) and so forth have been analyzed. Although they have been analyzed, the Elder Vajirabuddhi says:

"The reversal of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) was made in the phrase ‘and of those very [qualities] there’ in order to show that, because he is by nature wise, he specifically attains only the four analytical insights."
“Thus,” and so forth, is the conclusion.
Those things which have a pleasant touch are called “pleasant-touching”; such items as rugs and coverlets are indeed permitted.
Because they share the common quality of touch, they are likewise “pleasant-touching. Those things which possess such a permitted pleasant touch are called “having permitted pleasant touch.”

Such things as rugs and coverlets [are so called] because they are identical in their tactile quality (*phassa*) with those [sexual organs]. "Clinging contact" (*upādinnaka-phassa*) is feminine contact;
it is precisely the act of sexual intercourse. This was stated by the monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-keeper.

For he was a learned preacher of the Dhamma who, among the five kinds of obstacles—namely, those consisting of karmic defilement, the ripening of karma, slander, and transgression of the Teacher’s command—[was hindered by the first two].
He did not recognize the obstacle of transgressing the commandments, but recognized only the other obstacles; therefore, having gone into seclusion, he thought thus:
"These householders, while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, are stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners;
even the bhikkhus see agreeable forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on] ...tangible objects cognizable by the body."
“They touch them and enjoy soft rugs and coverlets—all of this is permissible.
Why then are only the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles of women impermissible? These too are certainly permissible.

Thus, by conflating the blameless flavor of enjoying the requisites with the blameworthy flavor of enjoying the strands of sensual pleasure, and [conflating] the enjoyment characterized by desire and lust—
Treating the enjoyment of things free from desire and lust as one and the same, he produced a wicked view—
like one attempting to join extremely fine thread with thick hemp fibers, or like one asserting the similarity of Mount Sineru to a mustard seed— and thought:
"What was the purpose of the Blessed One’s great effort in establishing the first *pārājika* rule, as if he were trying to bind the great ocean?"

By asserting, "It has been so prescribed; there is no fault here," he contradicts the knowledge of omniscience, obstructs the knowledge of fearlessness (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*), and casts stumps and thorns into the Noble Path.
Thus, by claiming "there is no fault in sexual intercourse," he dealt a blow to the Wheel of the Conqueror (*jinacakra*).
Therefore, he said, "Thus have I [spoken]," and so forth.

They are called *antarāyika* (obstructive) because they are connected with obstacles in the sense of being impossible to bypass; or because they deserve the fruit of an obstacle; or because they have the habit of creating obstacles.
What is meant is that they create obstacles to heaven and liberation. And these are fivefold, by way of: action, defilement, result, slander, and transgression of a rule.
The detailed explanation should be taken from the commentary on the Ariṭṭha training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and other sources. This, however, is the connection between the words here:
— Those things which have been spoken of, taught, and prescribed by the Blessed One as "obstructive states"—
in whatever manner and by whatever means those states, for one who indulges in them, are not capable of being obstacles,
nor are they able to act as hindrances to heaven and liberation— in that very manner and by that very means, I [have understood] what was taught by the Blessed One.
"I understand the Dhamma. Thereby he reaches a state of immorality; that is, from that cause of perceiving [an act] as blameless, having transgressed, he reaches a state of immorality.
Regarding the phrase "the four... etc.," here the word "etc. includes—
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four? One who is practicing for his own welfare but not for the welfare of others;
one who is practicing for the welfare of others but not for his own welfare; one who is practicing neither for his own welfare nor for the welfare of others;
and one who is practicing both for his own welfare and for the welfare of others… [as before] …these, bhikkhus, are the four persons found existing in the world.”

By such means as this, he points to the Sutta-pāḷi associated with the teaching on persons (*puggala*). As for "the intention": he shows the Blessed One’s intention thus, "This is by way of the conventional expression (*vohāra*) of the teaching on persons, not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
For it is said: "The Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers, proclaimed two truths:
the conventional (*sammuti*) and the ultimate (*paramattha*); a third is not found."
Conventional speech is true because it accords with worldly consensus;
ultimate speech is true because it accords with the actual nature of phenomena.
Therefore, [one should honor] the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in conventional expression.
“For one who employs conventional designation, no false speech arises.
Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not abandon worldly convention; they teach the Dhamma while remaining established in worldly common usage, worldly terminology, and worldly expression.
Furthermore, [this is] for the purpose of illustrating moral shame and dread of blame, and for the purpose of illustrating that one is the owner of one’s own kamma.
"Thus, through these eight reasons, the Blessed One speaks on the matter of the person"—this is said by one who does not understand the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
This meaning will be clarified further below. "He grasps it wrongly" means that he grasps it incorrectly with such statements as:
"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the cycle of existence, and nothing other than it."

"Having made [a wrong grasp], he grasps"—this means he grasps erroneously. For "duggahitaṃ" (wrongly grasped) is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka-niddesa*), because it must be designated by the neuter gender as being a qualification of the action (*kiriyāvisesanabhāvena*).

Indeed, this is the nature of a neuter abstract noun, namely, that it must be designated by the neuter gender, that it stands for a state (*bhāvappatṭhānatā*), and that it is connected with an action that may or may not have an object (*sakammākammakiriyānuyogaṃ*).
And it is a word in the singular number of the personal pronoun. Therefore it is said: "having grasped it wrongly. The word *yaṃ* refers to the act of grasping wrongly.
This was spoken by the Blessed One concerning the monk Sāḷha, the son of Kevaṭṭa—who held such views—in the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa in the Majjhima Nikāya.
The ellipsis of the text is "by means of the Dhamma wrongly grasped by himself," that is, by means of its false nature.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, *duggahaṇaṃ* means "bad grasping. In the phrase *attanā*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī-atthe*), or it is an indeclinable particle resembling a case-ending.
Therefore, the meaning is: "by one's own bad grasping," that is, by a perverted apprehension. *Abbhācikkhati* means "he makes a false accusation.
One who digs up his own roots of merit is said to "dig up himself. *Tato* means "from that," namely, from the cause of having grasped [the teaching] wrongly.

“Reflection on the Dhamma” (dhammacintā) means an investigation into the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva). “Running too far” means proceeding by overstepping the proper boundary that ought to be maintained, thinking such things as:

“A gift is accomplished even by a mere thought,” “The mind itself becomes its own object,” or “Every state of consciousness has only phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) as its object.
These [objects] are impossible to contemplate and are of a nature unfit for such reflection.
Showing that these things are indeed "inconceivable," he said, "For it has been said," and so forth. In this context, "inconceivable" is a description of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"They are not to be thought about" is a description of the function to be performed therein. The phrase beginning with "which" is a demonstration of the reason for that.
One who thinks about them becomes a partaker of madness, mental derangement, distress, and affliction.
For him, these four are inconceivable and should not be thought about; or rather, these four are called "inconceivable" and should not be thought about;

or whatever [else]... for him, therefore they should not be thought about because they have become inconceivable—this is the construction of the phrase "these four are called the inconceivable. Furthermore, by the word *iti*—
“What are the four? Monks, the domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable;
it is not to be thought about. One who thinks about it would partake of madness and distress.

Monks, the domain of those in meditative absorption is inconceivable… [as before]… Monks, the ripening of kamma is inconceivable… [as before]… Monks, worldly speculation is inconceivable… [as before]… These, monks, are the four…”
Beginning with the *Acinteyya-sutta* (The Discourse on the Inconceivable) spoken in the *Caturaṅguttara*, it compiles all the canonical texts that illuminate the nature of what is inconceivable.

While the six inconceivable things—the uncommon knowledges and so forth—should indeed be reflected upon because they serve as causes for the arising of wholesome states in one who recollects them, these [other things] are not like that;
because they are fruitless, they must not be reflected upon. “Immorality… [etc.]”
By the phrase "the classification," he shows the failure (vipatti) in its specific form. By connecting it with the words "How?

By way of the Piṭakas," etc., he states "Thus in various ways" and so forth, demonstrating the connection between what precedes and what follows. For speech devoid of a connection between what precedes and what follows is confused;
it does not convey meaning to listeners, and such carefully considered speech is the domain only of those who understand the sequence of what comes before and after. As it has been said:
“One who knows what precedes and what follows, who knows the meaning, and is skilled in language and phrasing;
he grasps what has been well-grasped and thoroughly examines the meaning.
“Of those” refers to the Piṭakas. “This” refers to the word of the Buddha.
"Those which are comprised by three groups (vaggas)—namely, the Sīlakkhandha-vagga, the Mahā-vagga, and the Pāṭika-vagga—are called 'comprised of three groups' (tivaggasaṅgahāni).
According to the count of suttas in this Nikāya, there are exactly thirty-four suttas.

As for the term 'three-group compilation' (tivaggo saṅgaho), it refers to a compilation that has three groups by way of its grouping of chapters (vaggasaṅgaha). This first Nikāya is the Dīghanikāya; thus [the name] is in accordance with the facts."
"Not contrary" (*apaccanīka*), or "named after its conformity with the meaning" (*atthānulomanāmika*) because it conforms to the meaning; this is the sense of the term *anvatthanāma*.

In this context, the phrase "the compendium in three sections" (*tivaggo saṅgaho*) should be understood as a compound even when placed within the middle of a sentence—such as "of which"—and not as a separate syntactical clause, just like the expression "with the acquisition of a new robe" (*navaṃ cīvaralābhenā*) in the passage "But with the acquisition of a new robe by a bhikkhu. For it is so: [text continues]
The commentators on the *Aṭṭhakathā* explain: "That which is obtained is a 'gain' (*lābha*); a gain itself is 'acquisition' (*lābha*). What was obtained? A robe. Of what kind? New.

Thus, where one should say 'by the acquisition of a new robe' (*navacīvaralābhena*), the nasal vowel has not been elided, and it is stated as 'by the acquisition of a new robe' (*navaṃcīvaralābhena*);
the meaning is 'by means of a newly acquired robe. As for the particle *pana*, it is used between the two middle words. By a bhikkhunī..."

"By which it was obtained, that is the illustration. Here too, because there is an absence of logical connection (*yutti*) in the sentence either from the perspective of the word-form (*saddato*) or the meaning (*atthato*), only a compound (*samāsa*) is possible.
For if the word "threefold group" (*tivaggo*) were the instrument (*karaṇa*) in relation to "the collection" (*saṅgaho*), then it would necessarily have the instrumental case-ending.
And if these two words were in apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), then [the compound] would likewise necessarily be in the neuter gender.

It might be [understood] like the phrase "the three worlds" (*tiloka*). Likewise, for the term "threefold group" (*tivagga*), no connection to any other meaning is possible without the word "collection" (*saṅgaha*); furthermore, it is not appropriate to connect it with such a sentence there.
Therefore, even when there is an interval between words, the mere absence of contradiction regarding the meaning of the sounds is the cause of compounding; thus, it is a compound (*samāsa*).

Thus it is properly joined. For the phrase *tivaggasaṅgaho*—meaning "the collection consisting of three sections"—is formed by either substituting *o* for the vowel *a* or adding the augment *o* to the word *assa saṅgahassa*.
This is as in examples such as *sattāhaparinibbuto*, *acirapakkanto*, and *māsajāto*.

Furthermore, the phrase *assa saṅgahassa* means "of this collection," that is, "of this Nikāya which has been compiled. Others, however, take it as "that which has three sections" (*tayo vaggā yassa*) and thus [call it] "Saṅgaha."
It is only a case of grammatical coreferentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) that is possible with the word *pada*, and *saṅgaha* is a number. However, some say:
“The two words ‘three’ (*tayo*) and ‘sections’ (*vaggā*) in the phrase ‘this compendium has three sections’ (*tayo vaggā assa saṅgahassā*) were shown by the Commentator to be coreferential.
This is indeed incorrect, because the number and the numbered object are mixed together and because [the meaning] is not clearly evident.

In order to clarify the conformity with the purpose (*atthānulomikatta*), he says “Why? and so forth. By means of a metaphorical application of a quality (*guṇopacāra*) or through the use of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), it is shown by the word “long” (*dīgha*) that only those suttas of long measure are intended;
furthermore, he shows that the word *nikāya* functions, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhivasena*), in the senses of a collection and an abode, by saying “of those of long measure,” and so on.
This is because the relationship between the signifier and the signified is established by convention (*saṅketasiddhattā*) through actual usage.
Demonstrating that the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) for those things is established, he said, "Not I," and so forth. "Even a single group" (*ekanikāyam-pi*) means even a single collection.
"Thus-minded" (*evaṃ-cittam*) means thus variegated. "Just as these" (*yathā-idaṃ*) refers to these animals;
the Poṇikas and Cikkhallikas are Kṣatriyas, and their dwelling place is called the "Poṇika-group" and the "Cikkhallika-group."
“*Ettha*” (here) refers to the fact that the word *nikāya* denotes both a collection (*samūha*) and an abode (*nivāsa*).
“*Sādhakāni*” (proving factors) are called examples because they establish the intended meaning; this term is connected with the elliptical phrase “*samānītāni*” (brought together).

Alternatively, they are witnesses (*sakkhī*), acting as proving factors according to the method already stated. For that which, having been extracted, establishes the intended meaning, is called a “witness.”
They say this. For it is stated in the *Manorathapūraṇī*: “The *Pañcagarujātaka*, however, should be brought forward and told for the sake of providing testimony.
“From the Dispensation” (*sāsanato*) means from the application within the Dispensation, or within the Dispensation itself.

“From the world” (*lokatoti*) means from worldly application, or in the world. They say that this [specific method] is not found in the Three Piṭakas; therefore, they say it was spoken in this way. And here:
The first example should be understood as a statement proving [the point] from the Sāsana (the Dispensation), while the second is from the world (*loka*).
[The texts] are comprised of fifteen chapters (*vagga*), such as the *Mūlapariyāya-vagga* and others. "A half more than the second" means one and a half;
that itself is a hundred, that is, one hundred and fifty suttas—this is what is meant. "In which" refers to whichever Nikāya. "Comprised of fifteen chapters" means...
It is comprised and collected into fifteen chapters (*vagga*).
It is called *saṃyutta* because things are joined together (*saṃyujjanti*) therein. Of what are they joined? Of the groups of suttas (*suttavagga*).

For just as the designation "word" (*pada*) applies to a collection of phonemes (*byañjana*), "sentence" (*vākya*) to a collection of words, "sutta" to a collection of sentences, and "chapter" (*vagga*) to a collection of suttas, so too is this the conventional usage.

Thus, the designation "Saṃyutta" (Connected) applies to a collection of chapters. Because the chapters and so forth—such as those spoken by a deity when questioned—are connected (*saṃyutta*), they possess the status of being the "Devatāsaṃyutta" (Connected with Deities) and so on;
therefore, he said, "by way of the Devatāsaṃyutta and the rest," and so forth.
Regarding the reading, "seven thousand and seven hundred suttas," it means seven thousand suttas and seven hundred suttas.
It should be joined [to the previous]. There is also a reading: “seven thousand suttas and seven hundred suttas.
*Saṃyuttasaṅgaha* means the compilation or enumeration of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.

Regarding the term *Aṅguttara*, it is so called because in this [collection], there is an increasing or superior addition by each successive factor (*aṅga*). Thus he said, “by way of the increase of each single factor,” and so forth. For therein, starting from one, the factors are taught up to eleven. And the word *aṅga* refers to a portion of the Dhamma.

"Formerly" refers to the description in the Suttanta Piṭaka. The phrase beginning with "excepting" is stated in order to show, by way of a different formulation, what has already been said in brief and without distinction.
Indeed, by this different formulation, he shows what was already stated by the passage beginning with "the entire Vinaya Piṭaka," having condensed it.
Furthermore, whatever remains from what has been mentioned above, according to the method given by the Blessed One...

It should also be understood that this was said in order to show, by way of exhaustive inclusion, that everything taught by the Blessed One and approved by him—such as the *Nettippakaraṇa*, the *Peṭakopadesa*, and so forth—is entirely contained within this very [Abhidhamma Piṭaka].

For even when something is already established, a new undertaking is made either to indicate a different meaning or for the sake of restriction. And here, just as in the phrase "of those of long measure," and so forth...

Thus, it should be understood that after stating "of those of small measure" (*khuddakappamāṇānaṃ*) and so forth, the specific mention [of the *Khuddaka Nikāya*] is intended to include even those of long measure, such as the *Vinaya* and *Abhidhamma*, because they are contained within that category.
And by this, it is made known that its designation as "conforming to the meaning" (*anvatthasamaññatā*) does not apply everywhere to those included in the *Khuddaka*;
rather, it applies by virtue of the commonality of being contrary to the nature of the *Dīgha Nikāya* and the others.
"But in some places, it is designated by that [name]. "Other than those" means other than those four Nikāyas; this is the meaning. Regarding "ninefold division":
how, then, does this become ninefold? For it must be established by nine factors that are free from mutual confusion;
and if that were so, the Geyya-factor and the others would lack the essential nature of Sutta.

If, on the other hand, the *geyya* and other factors were of the very nature of *sutta*, then in that case, *sutta* would not exist as a distinct *sutta-aṅga*. This being so, it would follow that the Dispensation consists of only eight factors.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Commentary: "A *sutta* with verses is *geyya*; a *sutta* without verses is *veyyākaraṇa*. And indeed, what is called *sutta* is that which possesses verses.

It may be either with verses (*sagāthaka*) or without verses (*niggāthaka*); therefore, since both are included by these two factors alone, there is no discourse (*sutta*) apart from those two that lacks the specific designations such as *udāna* and so forth which could constitute a "discourse factor" (*suttaṅga*).

Even if, somehow, there were a separate discourse factor, the inclusion of the *Maṅgalasutta* and others within the discourse factor would not be possible, because they consist of verses (*gāthā*), like the *Dhammapada* and other such works.
Or could it be included under the *geyya* category because it contains verses, like the *Sagāthāvagga*?
Likewise, there are sections containing verses within the two *Vibhaṅgas* and so forth. It is replied:
"Sutta" is a general designation, while the others are specific designations.
Because they possess signs and are well-established, they are distinct from one another and not otherwise.
There is no room for the aforementioned fault here;
therefore, the ninefold teaching of the Teacher is indeed free from confusion.
For indeed, "Sutta" is the general designation for the entire word of the Buddha.
Thus, from such statements as, "So much of that Blessed One’s teaching has come down as Sutta, included in the Sutta;
in the Sutta-vibhaṅga at Sāvatthī, there are five hundred suttas in our own tradition," the term "Sutta" is seen to be applied even to specific portions of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.
And for that very reason, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana stated in the *Nettippakaraṇa*: "The ninefold investigation of the discourses" (*navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhī*).

For therein, the investigation, seeking, and examination of the meaning of the ninefold teaching by way of the discourses (*sutta*) and so forth is called "the ninefold investigation of the discourses.
However, among those [nine], the others—namely the *geyya* and so on—are specific types accompanied by their defining characteristics.
They are established by their respective characteristics (*nimitta*). For instance, the fact that the *Geyya* contains verses (*sagāthaka*) is its characteristic.
Indeed, even in the world, they call a collection of prose mixed with verse (*cuṇṇiyagantha*) "Geyya" when it possesses verses;

however, when it is devoid of verses, the state of answering after having posed a question is the characteristic of the *Veyyākaraṇa*. For the posing of a question and its answering— *...* (The text ends here)

It is called "byākaraṇa" (exposition); byākaraṇa itself is veyyākaraṇa (analytical exposition). This being the case, would it not follow that even those [texts] beginning with the Sagāthaka, which proceed by way of questions and answers, would possess the status of veyyākaraṇa?
It does not so follow, because there is no room for the designations of Geyya and the rest.
For a rule that provides an occasion is stronger than a rule that does not provide an occasion. Furthermore, [it applies only] "when there is an absence of verses."
Because it is specified. For a specification (*visesana*) is that which distinguishes the intended meaning from what is not intended.
Thus, in the *Dhammapada* and other works consisting solely of verse compositions; in those containing verses (*sagāthaka*) that are associated with verses composed of joy and knowledge;

in specific discourses (*suttavisesa*) connected with marvelous qualities (*abbhutadhamma*), and in connections with statements such as "For it has been said" (*vuttaṃ hetan*); [the distinction is made].
The designations "Gāthā," "Udāna," "Itivuttaka," and "Abbhutadhamma" are established according to their respective order.

For here, even though there is a connection with other types of designations, the designations "Gāthā" and so forth are established precisely because of the predominance of the designation "Aṅguttara-nikāya.

Likewise, even though they possess the nature of being composed in verse, the designation "Jātaka" is established for those [texts] that reveal the power of the Blessed One’s conduct in past births; and even though...

Because the designation *vedalla* is established for certain discourses (*suttanta*) on account of their being in the form of question-and-answer and containing verses, so too the designations such as *geyya* are established for those specific discourses by means of various characteristics such as containing verses;
thus, the *geyya* and other factors beyond the *sutta* division are specific types. However, that which here lacks the characteristics of the *geyya* division and so forth—
That is indeed a separate division of the Sutta Piṭaka, because it proceeds by means of general designations while avoiding specific designations. But even if that were so, one might object:
"In that case, a sutta containing verses would be Geyya, and a sutta without verses would be Veyyākaraṇa;
since there is no sutta apart from these two, there should be no separate division called Sutta at all. This objection remains in force. It is not so.

Because it has been clarified. For it was previously clarified that when there is an absence of verse, the state of being a question-and-answer constitutes the defining characteristic (*nimitta*) of an exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, as for what was said—that "because they lack the form of verse, the *Maṅgalasutta* and others would not be included within the category of *sutta*"—that too is not correct, because the status of being a *sutta* is conventional (*nirūḷha*) for the *Maṅgalasutta* and so forth.
Indeed, the status of being a *sutta* is conventionally established for the *Maṅgalasutta* and others; for they are not like the *Dhammapada*, the *Buddhavaṃsa*, and so on.
They are designated as such not by way of being verses (*gāthā*), but rather precisely by way of being discourses (*sutta*).

For that very reason, in this discourse (*akathā*), the name is taken as "named Sutta. Furthermore, as for what was said—that "because it contains verses, it might be included in the *geyya* division"—that too is not the case.
Why? Because it is accompanied by something else; for co-existence (*sahabhāva*) indeed occurs with something other than itself.

Regarding the phrase *sagāthakaṃ* (with verses): it means "together with verses. Now, there is no portion of a sutta within the *Maṅgala-sutta* and others that is devoid of verses such that it could be called "together with verses.

Furthermore, is it not the case that a collection of verses is something other than its individual constituent verses, by virtue of which one could say it is "together with verses"? That is not so; for [the whole] is not separate from its parts.

There is no such thing as a "whole" (*samudāya*) that could exist together with its own parts. However, in certain instances—such as in the phrase “of that which is marked by a long thread” (*dīghasuttaṅkitassa*) and so forth—the expression of the distinction between the whole and its parts is merely a conventional usage (*vohāramatta*) and is thus a figurative statement (*pariyāyavacana*).
This present discourse, however, is a discussion that demonstrates distinctions through non-figurative analysis (*nippariyāyena pabhedavibhāga*).
As for what was said regarding “the portions containing verses (*sagāthakappadesa*) in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and other texts,” [it refers to those portions].

If it is argued that there might be an inclusion of the *geyya* factor [in the *Udāna*], that too is not so, because they are distinct. For those verses are indeed different, as they are included within the *Jātaka* and other such categories.
They were taught therein for specific reasons appropriate to those contexts; therefore, the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and other texts do not possess the status of the *geyya* factor by virtue of those verses.
In this way, the absence of mutual confusion among the nine factors, beginning with the *sutta*, should be understood.
Now, showing these nine divisions by way of analysis, he says, beginning with “Therein,” and so forth. What is called the *Niddesa* is found in the *Sutta Nipāta* as follows:
“If, for one who desires sensual pleasures, those very pleasures are accomplished, then that mortal surely becomes joyful in mind, having obtained what he wished for. And so on.
The *Aṭṭhakavagga* having been recited:
“By what is the world enveloped? (Thus spoke the Venerable Ajita);
By what does it not shine forth?”
"Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsi,
kiṃsu tassa mahabbhayan? and so forth—
this refers to the Pārāyana-vagga that has been recited.
“Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
and not harming even one among them,
one should desire neither a son, much less a companion.”
"Let one wander alone like the rhinoceros horn," and so forth.
The detailed exposition (*niddesa*) of the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta* thus transmitted was composed by the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, who is like the Teacher himself;
this is what is called the *Mahāniddesa* and the *Cūḷaniddesa*. In this way, the *Niddesa* is included within the division of the Sutta Piṭaka.

This was shown by the teacher Bhadanta Buddhadhosa, as well as elsewhere in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* and other works, and also by the elder teacher Dhammapāla in his commentary on the *Nettippakaraṇa*.
Others, however, maintain that it is included within two of the factors for the exposition of verses (*gāthā-veyyākaraṇaṅga*) in the *Niddesa*.
For this was stated by the elder Upasena in the *Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā*:
“Thus, among the three Piṭakas—namely, the Vinaya Piṭaka, [the Sutta Piṭaka,] and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—it is included in the Sutta Piṭaka;
among the five Nikāyas—namely, the Dīgha Nikāya, [the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya,] and the Khuddaka Nikāya—it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya;

and among the nine factors of the Teacher’s Dispensation—namely, the Sutta, [the Geyya, the Veyyākaraṇa, the Gāthā, the Udāna, the Itivuttaka, the Jātaka, the Abbhutadhamma,] and the Vedalla—it is comprised within two factors as appropriate: the Gāthā and the Veyyākaraṇa.”
In this regard, since there is the presence of both questions and answers in some places, it may be appropriate to include a portion of the Niddesa within the *Veyyākaraṇaṅga*.
However, one must investigate how its inclusion in the *Gāthaṅga* could be justified, given the absence of verses (*agāthābhāvato*).

For the sole reason for something being included in the *Gāthaṅga*—as in the case of the *Dhammapada* and other such works—is its state of being composed entirely in verse. Indeed, in the *Dhammapada* and similar texts...
The designation "verse" (*gāthā*) is established only for those composed in metrical form; in the *Niddesa*, no portion whatsoever exists that is exclusively in verse.
Indeed, the Dhammasenāpati merely provided a commentary (*niddesa*) on those verses spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One that were included in the *Aṭṭhakavagga* and so forth.
For even though they were brought forward for the purpose of analyzing the meaning, they remain included within the *Aṭṭhakavagga* and other such collections.
The root verses (*mūlagāthā*) should not be counted as part of the *Niddesa* because, being included within the *Sutta Nipāta*, they are distinct from it;
even though they appear in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and other texts, they do not receive that designation, just like the verses included in the *Jātaka* and so forth.
Therefore, another reason must be sought here, or a more appropriate interpretation should be adopted.

The *Nālakasutta* is the discourse spoken by the Blessed One on the seventh day after the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, beginning with the words, “I shall teach you the sagehood (*moneyya*), O Nālaka,” which elucidates the practice of sagehood.

The *Tuvaṭṭakasutta* is the discourse addressed to the devas who had assembled for the teaching of the *Mahāsamaya Suttanta*, [beginning with] “Who indeed has attained arahantship?”... [and so forth].

The *Mūlapapañcasāṅkhāya-sutta*—spoken by the Blessed One after having a manifested Buddha (nimmitabuddha) pose questions to himself in order to explain that matter to certain deities whose minds had arisen [with such thoughts] regarding "practice"—is the discourse [in question].

Thus, the inclusion of the discourses within the Sutta-aṅga has been shown for the *Maṅgalasutta* and others that appear here in the *Suttanipāta*; likewise for those appearing in that very same collection:
He will also demonstrate the inclusion of the verse-components for the pure verses whose names are not mentioned in the suttas.
This being so, [it may be asked] at the beginning of the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*:
"If it is crowded with hundreds of verses and marked by *geyya* and *byākaraṇa*, why has it come to be designated by the name 'Suttanipāta'?"—thus [it is asked].
Why is it objected that the entire *Suttanipāta* is included within the *Geyya* and *Veyyākaraṇa* divisions [of the ninefold classification]? This is not a contradiction.
For in that objection, the objector merely raised a challenge by taking into account the presence of verses (*sagāthaka*) and, in some instances, the nature of questions and answers;
otherwise, since there would be no prose sutta (*niggāthaka*) at all in the *Suttanipāta*, its inclusion within the *Veyyākaraṇa* division would be impossible.
One should not raise an objection; therefore, the word of the accuser is not authoritative here.

Thus, according to the method explained in this and other Vinaya commentaries (*vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*) and so forth, the inclusion of that [text] under the categories of *sutta* and *gāthā* is demonstrated. "Sutta" refers to the *cuṇṇiya-sutta*.
By the phrase "specifically," he speaks with reference to that which exists as a collection (*rāsibhāva*). The connection is: "The Sagāthāvagga is *geyya*."
“It is said in all three *gaṇṭhipadas* that ‘the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, etc., is not included among the eight [canonical] factors.
However, others maintain that the *Paṭisambhidāmaggassa* is included within the two factors of *geyya* and *veyyākaraṇa*. For this is stated in its own commentary:
‘Among the nine factors of the Teacher’s dispensation, it is included as appropriate within the two factors of *geyya* and *veyyākaraṇa*.’”
Here too, the fact that it is included within the *geyya* factor should be investigated according to the method already stated.
"Not having the name of a *sutta*" means not having the name of a *sutta*, being unknown by the designation of *sutta* at the time of the recitation.

"The so-called 'pure verses' are the narrative verses (*vatthugāthā*)"—this is stated, it is said, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries; and "narrative verses" refers to those added by the Venerable [Mahākassapa] while establishing the introduction to the Pārāyana Chapter.

The fifty-six verses spoken by the Elder Ānanda at the time of the Council (saṅgīti), as well as approximately twenty verses spoken by him at that same time while introducing the introductory narrative (nidāna) of the Nālakasutta, are also cited. However, in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"When the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, who was performing the Council, was questioned regarding that very practice of the noble way (moneyyapaṭipadā)."
Because it is stated that the Venerable Ānanda, wishing to make clear everything from when he was exhorted until the time the Elder Nālaka questioned the Blessed One,
spoke twenty introductory verses beginning with “Ānandajāte” and then provided the answer—
all of which is called the “Nālaka Sutta”— the introductory verses of the Nālaka Sutta are included by the very mention of the Nālaka Sutta itself.
"Taken" means that here the introductory verses (*vatthugāthā*) of the *Pārāyanavagga* should be understood as the "pure verses" (*suddhikagāthā*). Furthermore, within that same *Pārāyanavagga*,
the question-verses of the sixteen brahmins beginning with the young brahmin Ajita, and the Buddha’s response-verses,
are not referred to by the name of a sutta in the text, but rather as "The Question of the Young Brahmin Ajita," "The Question of the Young Brahmin Tissa Metteyya," and so forth.

Because they have come down [in this way] and because they are not mixed with the *Cūḷa-nikāya* texts, it is appropriate to say that these are "pure verses" (*suddhika-gāthā*) not named after a specific Sutta.
By the phrase "connected with verses consisting of joy and knowledge," he shows that it is called an *udāna* in the sense of an *udāna* (an exclamation), according to its literal meaning.
What is this thing called an *udāna*? It is an utterance brought forth by the force of rapture (*pīti*). For just as when a substance to be measured, such as oil, is poured into a measure...
That which cannot be contained within the vessel and flows over is called "overflowing" (*avasesaka*).
And that water which cannot be contained within the pond and flows over it is called "a great flood" (*mahogha*);
in the same way, when the expansion of thought (*vitakkavipphāra*) generated by the surge of joy cannot be sustained within the heart, [it is called "overflowing"].
Having become excessive and not remaining within, it issues forth through the door of speech;
independent of a recipient, this particular utterance is called an "udāna. For the etymologists say, "The root *ud* is used in the sense of 'to rejoice' (*mode*) and 'in play' (*kīḷāya*");

and this [definition] is stated as a general rule, since even an utterance such as "If you fear suffering" (*Sace bhāyatha dukkhassa*) is called an udāna because it has arisen out of a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*).
Because it has come down in the Udāna-pāḷi, and likewise because the phrase "connected with verses" (*gāthāpaṭisaṃyuttā*) refers to the fact that even such passages as "There is,
monks, that sphere where there is neither earth nor water," which were spoken in the form of prose fragments (*cuṇṇiyavākya*),
have also been included therein. But is it not the case that what is called an *udāna* is something produced by joy and gladness, or produced by a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*)?

Or, why is the address "Bhikkhus" spoken here, when everywhere else [the Buddha's teaching] has occurred as an utterance proceeding either by way of composing verses or by way of prose sentences, independent of any recipient of the Dhamma?
It is solely for the purpose of making those bhikkhus aware, not for the purpose of making them recipients.
For the Blessed One [taught] the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna...

Having taught [the Dharma], and while uttering an inspired exclamation (*udāna*) born of the joy and gladness arising from recollecting the qualities of Nibbāna— thinking, "How is this phenomenon of Nibbāna attained without conditions?"—
[the Buddha] spoke the words "That sphere" (*tadāyatana*), desiring to make that matter known by discerning the mental reflection of those monks. However,
it should be understood that he did not do so by making them exclusively the recipients [of the teaching].
That [Dhamma] is threefold: spoken by an omniscient Buddha, spoken by a Paccekabuddha, and spoken by a disciple. Among these, that spoken by a Paccekabuddha is as follows:
"Having laid aside the rod toward all beings, not harming even one of them," and so forth.
It is found in the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta*. It is also spoken by a disciple:
“All passion has been abandoned by me;
all hatred has been uprooted.”
“All delusion has been dispelled by me;
I have become cool and attained Nibbāna. Thus it is said in the *Theragāthā*.
“I was restrained in body, and likewise in speech and mind;
having uprooted craving by its very root, I have become cooled and attained Nibbāna.
Thus it is recorded in the *Therīgāthā*. There are also other verses spoken by deities such as Sakka: “O, what a gift! A supreme gift!”

There are indeed *udānas* such as "Well-established upon Kassapa," spoken by people including the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, and those beginning with "Homage to that Blessed One" which were included in the three councils;
however, none of those are intended here. Rather, it is that which was spoken directly by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself, constituting the word of the Conqueror (*jinavacana*).

That very [text] was compiled by the Dhammasaṅgāhakas as the "Udāna," and it was with reference to that very [work] that the Blessed One, when dividing the Dhamma of the scriptures into nine categories and reciting them, spoke of the "Udāna. Furthermore, those verses beginning with "Through many births in saṃsāra...
were uttered by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree in the manner of an Udāna, [and they pertain to] the many hundreds of thousands of Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas.

And those [verses] which had become *udānas* were, because they were later taught by the Blessed One to the Dharma-treasurer (Ānanda), not included in the *Udāna-pāḷi* by the compilers of the Dhamma, but were instead included in the *Dhammapada*. Furthermore, there was the utterance of the *udāna*:
"Koṇḍañña has indeed understood! Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!", which spread as a resounding proclamation capable of being heard by gods and humans throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.
That which was spoken by the Blessed One at the time of his first enlightenment— such as the statement, "The bhikkhus have indeed pleased me on one occasion," and so forth,
which arose from reflecting upon the right practice of all those bhikkhus— was likewise, at the conclusion of the teaching of the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*,
[spoken] for the sake of his disciples regarding that portion of the Dhamma he himself had attained, namely, the Noble Path exactly as it was taught, for the very first time among his followers.
It should be understood that because the Elder had attained [the goal], this was merely an utterance produced by joy and gladness arising from reflecting on the fruitfulness of his own exertion;

it was not included in the Udāna collection by the compilers of the Dhamma, as it does not— like the words beginning "When indeed phenomena become manifest"— explain either the process of occurrence or the process of cessation.
In the Udāna-pāḷi, however, only eighty suttas are recited, ten being grouped together within each of the eight chapters (vagga).
For it is said in its commentary:
"In brief, there are exactly eighty suttas and eight chapters."
Furthermore, as for the statement here that there are “eighty-two suttantas,” this does not agree with the text of the *Udāna*; therefore, the reading should be “eighty suttantas.

Moreover, because it is stated exactly in that way not only here, but also in other commentaries on the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, [the discrepancy] is explained by the principle: “A small deficiency or excess, however, does not affect the count.”
It may be said that this is not stated with absolute certainty. For in various instances, the counting by means of inference results in a number that is either deficient or excessive;
otherwise, they say that [the count] would simply not exist. Or else, this is a statement regarding a careless scribal error.
Regarding the phrase "for this was said by the Blessed One," etc., the word "etc. (*ādi*) here includes such passages as: "For this was said by the Blessed One..."
"Thus have I heard from the Venerable Arahant: 'Monks, abandon one thing; I guarantee you non-returning. What is that one thing?
Monks, abandon greed, that one thing; I guarantee you non-returning.
By such passages, it comprises a collection of one hundred and twelve discourses, arranged according to the groups of ones, twos, threes, and fours.
For indeed, in the Itivuttaka-pāḷi itself, one hundred and twelve suttas have been compiled by counting them through the Udāna verses;

this is stated exactly so in its commentary (aṭṭhakathā) as well. Therefore, the reading must be "one hundred and twelve suttantas," or alternatively, it may be said that they were spoken in various ways according to the method already described. Nevertheless, in such a case...

They say that since the measure must be shown by one who demonstrates the correct standard, having determined it exactly as it is, this phrase "one hundred and ten suttas" should be understood as merely a later scribal error.
Thus, what was spoken by the Blessed One is *itivutta* (so-spoken). That which is so-spoken and compiled is the *Itivuttaka*.
Or rather, this is a conventional name (*ruḷhi-nāma*), just like [the names] "miscellaneous" (*yevāpanaka*) or "the section not belonging to you" (*natumhākavagga*).
This collection of suttas as previously described was chanted together by means of the introductory formula: "For this was said by the Blessed One; 'It was said,' so I have heard.

It is called a *jātaka* because it "tells" (*kāyati*), "speaks," or "proclaims" the Blessed One’s former lives (*pubbacarita*)—that which is born, that which has come to be, and that which occurred in the past.
To show that these are [the specific ones], he says: "The *Apaṇṇaka-jātaka* and the rest," and therein: "Five hundred and fifty *jātakas*."
However, this [number] was stated not as a definitive conclusion, because it is neither slightly less nor slightly more than what is required for calculation;
it was stated merely for the sake of convenience in common usage. For, according to the aforementioned calculation, there are actually forty-seven [nikāyas] when reduced by three.
Thus, there are fifty in the Ekanipāta, one hundred in the Dukanipāta, fifty in the Tikanipāta, and likewise in the Catukkanipāta.
In the Pañcaka-nipāta there are twenty-five; in the Chakka-nipāta, twenty; in the Sattaka-nipāta, twenty-one;
in the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta, ten; in the Navaka-nipāta, twelve; in the Dasaka-nipāta, sixteen; in the Ekādasaka-nipāta, nine; in the Dvādasaka-nipāta, ten;
likewise in the Terasa-nipāta; in the Pakiṇṇaka-nipāta, thirteen; in the Vīsati-nipāta, fourteen; in the Tiṃsa-nipāta, ten; and in the Cattālīsa-nipāta.

Five in the Paṇṇāsa-nipāta, three in the Saṭṭhi-nipāta, likewise two in the Sattati-nipāta, five in the Asīti-nipāta, and ten in the Mahā-nipāta; thus, exactly five hundred and forty-seven Jātakas have been chanted.

That wherein the wonderful quality (abbhuta-dhamma)—meaning the extraordinary nature—is spoken of is called an "abbhutadhamma. Regarding that, he said, "These four," and so forth. By the word "etc. (ādi) here—
“Monks, there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda. What are the four?
Monks, if a company of monks approaches Ānanda to see him, they are pleased even by the sight of him.
And if Ānanda speaks the Dhamma there, they are pleased by what he has spoken; indeed, monks, that company of monks remains insatiable.”
[If] there is [a question], then Ānanda remains silent. Monks, if there is an assembly of bhikkhunīs...
[and so on] ...an assembly of laymen... [and so on] ...an assembly of laywomen... [and so on] ...it remains silent.

Monks, all these discourses spoken here and there in such a manner—as beginning with "Monks, [these are the four assemblies]... [and so on] ...in the presence of Ānanda"—comprise the collection of suttas associated with marvelous and wonderful qualities.
The discourse spoken by the bhikkhunī named Dhammadinnā when questioned by the lay follower named Visākha is called the Cūḷavedalla.

That spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta when questioned by the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika is called the Mahāvedalla. The Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta was also spoken by that same [Venerable Sāriputta] when questioned by the bhikkhus.
These [suttas] are included in the Majjhima Nikāya. However, the Sakkapañha was spoken by the Blessed One when questioned by Sakka;

it is included in the Dīgha Nikāya. The Mahāpuṇṇamasutta, moreover, was spoken by the Blessed One when questioned by a certain bhikkhu on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, during the full moon night; it is included in the Majjhima Nikāya.

All such discourses as these, which have been approached here and there by the Blessed One and asked about after he had repeatedly attained both knowledge (*veda*) and joy (*tuṭṭhi*), are to be understood as "Vedalla.

*Veda* means knowledge. *Tuṭṭhi* means the joy and gladness that proceeds from the act of exultant appreciation (*abbhanumodanā*), such as saying "Excellent, noble lady! Excellent, friend! upon having understood the Dhamma teaching exactly as it was spoken. *Laddhā laddhā* means...
"Having obtained, having obtained," means "having obtained again and again.

By this, it is shown that the word *veda* occurs through the method of single-remainder (*ekasesa-naya*) as referring both to knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and to mental joy (*somanassa*), or by way of a general designation; and it shows that it is called *vedalla* because it is dependent upon knowledge in the sense of causing its attainment.
Having thus analyzed the entire word of the Buddha according to its constituent parts (*aṅga*), he now says “How?
and so forth, desiring to analyze it by way of the aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*). Therein, “by way of the aggregates of the Dhamma” means by way of the heaps of the Dhamma.
The meaning of this verse beginning with “Two hundred and eighty” has already been explained. “By way of the aggregates of the Dhamma thus elucidated” refers to [the teaching] by Gopaka Moggallāna.
When questioned by the brahmin in the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta, [the Buddha] spoke for the purpose of proclaiming his own qualities;

or, in the Theragāthā, through the mass of Dhamma revealed on all sides by the Venerable Ānanda Thera, he demonstrates that there are indeed other masses of Dhamma not yet fully revealed by him. Therefore, [this is seen] in the Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa, the Mādhuriya Sutta, and so forth, as well as in the Vimānavatthu and others.
It should be understood that, by way of certain verses, the number of Dhamma-categories (dhammakkhandha) exceeds even eighty-four thousand.

In this regard, as for the Subha Sutta and the Gopaka-Moggallāna Sutta—since they were spoken by the Elder Ānanda after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna—are they included among the eighty-four thousand Dhamma-categories or not? [This is discussed] in the *Paṭisambhidāgaṇṭhipada*.

To this extent it was said: "It should be understood that even though these aggregates of Dhamma were spoken by himself, he spoke thus having included them as if they had been received from a bhikkhu.
However, since these two suttas were spoken while standing within the method given by the Blessed One, it is even more appropriate to say:
"And although these two suttas were spoken by himself, they were spoken having been included as if they had been received from the Blessed One."
It appears as such because the disciples teach the Dhamma by standing upon the method given by the Blessed One;
for that very reason, even the words spoken by disciples—such as the *Kathāvatthu* and other texts—become known as "spoken by the Buddha.

And for this same reason, when the Venerable Ānanda Thera was arranging the recitation (saṅgīti), he spoke of even those things he himself had uttered, such as the *Subha Sutta*, saying, "Thus have I heard."
A discourse with a single connection (*ekānusandhika*) is one such as the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta].

For the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, beginning with the words, “This, monks, is the one-way path for the purification of beings,” proceeds by way of demonstrating the analysis of those very four foundations of mindfulness;
therefore, it is called “with a single connection. A discourse with multiple connections (*anekānusandhika*) is one such as the *Parinibbāna Sutta*. For the *Parinibbāna Sutta*...
Because it proceeds by way of various teachings on the Dhamma in diverse locations, it is called "having many connections" (*anekānusandhika*).
"How many should one cut off? How many should one abandon? How many should one cultivate further?
How many bonds has the bhikkhu transcended that he is called 'one who has crossed the flood'?"
The posing of questions in this manner through verses constitutes one division of the Dhamma.
“Cut off five, abandon five, develop five further;
the bhikkhu who has transcended five fetters is called ‘one who has crossed the flood.’”
An answer such as this constitutes one *dhammakkhandha*.

The analysis of the triplets (*tika*) and couplets (*duka*) should be understood according to the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* and the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. Therefore, that which was stated in the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* by way of analyzing the first term of the wholesome-triplet matrix (*mātikā*)—namely:
“Which states are wholesome? The three wholesome roots... [etc. ...these states are wholesome. Which states are unwholesome?”—[is to be understood in this manner].
“The three unwholesome roots... [as above] ...these states are unwholesome. Which states are indeterminate? The results of wholesome and unwholesome states...
[as above] ...these states are indeterminate. This is one category of the Dhamma.
This same method applies to the analysis of the remaining triads and dyads as well. Furthermore, that which was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*—
“What phenomena are wholesome? The wholesome in the four planes. These phenomena are wholesome. What phenomena are unwholesome?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. These phenomena are unwholesome. What phenomena are indeterminate?
The resultants in the four planes, the functional-indeterminate in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna. These phenomena are indeterminate.”
This is one section of the Dhamma that proceeds by way of analyzing the matrix of the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*). This same method applies to the remaining [sections] as well.
However, the classification of the sections on consciousness (*cittavāra*) should be understood according to the "Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness" (*Cittuppādakaṇḍa*).
For therein, what is stated for the purpose of classifying wholesome consciousness—
“What states are wholesome? At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, having a visible form as its object...
[and so on] ...at that time there is contact... [and so on] ...there is non-distraction. This is one aggregate of Dhamma.
Thus it is in each of the remaining consciousness-sets. “One aggregate of Dhamma” means (each individual).
The meaning is that each category of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha)—the six and the eight—is a single "category of the Dhamma.

For, according to the statement, "Each one is a container for triads and dyads; each one is a container for the mental cycles," this meaning is understood by implication even when the word "each one" is not explicitly stated.

The "subject matter" (vatthu) refers to the Sudinna-section and so forth. The "matrix" (mātikā) refers to such passages as, "Whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus... and so on.
The training rule (sikkhāpada) laid down for each specific transgression is the *uddesa*.

The "word-by-word analysis" (*padabhājaniya*) refers to the analytical explanation of each respective training rule, proceeding according to the method beginning with "‘But whoever’ means whoever of such a kind," and so forth.

An "intermediate offense" (*antarāpatti*) is an offense prescribed within the intervals between training rules, such as: "If he throws up what has been lowered, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so on.

*Āpatti* (offense) refers to the section on offenses (*āpattivāra*), which is stated according to each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and is free from the "cutting of the triads" (*tikaccheda*). *Anāpatti* (non-offense) refers to the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), which proceeds according to the method beginning with:
"There is no offense for one who does not know, for one who does not consent, for one whose mind is deranged, for one overwhelmed by pain, and for a first offender.
*Tikaccheda* (the cutting of the triads) refers to: "If ten days have passed and he perceives that they have passed, it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense."

The section on the triads (*tīkapariccheda*), which proceeds according to such methods as: "If ten days have elapsed and one is in doubt... [and so forth] ...if ten days have elapsed and one perceives they have not elapsed, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*)," is divided into categories such as the triad of *pācittiya* offenses and the triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in those sections concerning the matrices of the subject matter (*vatthu-mātikā*) and so forth.
Having thus shown the manner of the recitation adorned with many methods, [it continues]: "This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya... and so forth.
Having established the word of the Buddha through its divisions such as the Dhamma and Vinaya, the community of masters headed by Mahākassapa—
while chanting the "eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma"— determined, through a council adorned by the manifestation of many wonders,
that this Dīgha Āgama possesses the nature of Dhamma and the status of being the word of the Buddha and so forth.
Showing this, he said, "It is thus," and so forth. For although it was shown by means of a general statement, the teachers have stated this connection:
"That for the sake of which this [work] is begun to be praised—that alone is shown by way of its primary importance.
Another method: among the modes divided into the singlefold and other classifications mentioned above, the compilers of the Council [considered] the nature of the Dhamma and Vinaya, etc.

It may also be said that he spoke the words beginning with "Thus it is" (evam etan) in order to show that this was established at the time of the recitation (*saṅgīti*), and not subsequently established by mere mental construction (*kappana*).
Furthermore, by the phrase "and not only," he shows that the recitation was performed not only by establishing [the text] in the manner already described, but also in another way.
"The compendium of Uddānas" (*udānasaṅgaha*) refers to the introductory summaries of the introductory narratives (*vinītavatthu*) and so forth found in the first *pārājika* and other sections.
In brief, they were established by the compilers of the Dhamma by way of showing their inclusion as follows:
“The female monkey and the Vajjiputta, the householder and the naked one, the heretics;
the girl and Uppalavaṇṇā, and two others by way of the phonemes. And so forth.

Verses (*gāthāyo*). For "utterance" (*udāna*) means the giving of an upward [gift], that is, protection, of a meaning—whether being spoken or already spoken—by not allowing it to remain scattered; the sense is "a collected statement. There is a grouping by chapters (*vagga-saṅgaha*) such as the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* and the *Mūlapariyāyavagga*.

For "chapter" (*vagga*) is a conventional designation for a collection of discourses (*sutta*) established by the compilers of the Dhamma themselves. There is also a grouping by sections (*peyyāla*), such as the *Uttarimanussapeyyāla* and the *Nīlapeyyāla*.
The *Peyyālasaṅgaha* (Collection of Repetitions): "Peyyāla" refers to that which is not possible to recite, protect, or expand upon; it is a term used for showing [the text] by way of abbreviation.

The *Nipātasaṅgaha* (Collection of Nipātas) in the *Aṅguttaranikāya* and other collections refers to the grouping [of suttas] according to the number of factors (*aṅga*), such as single factors and so forth; for a "nipāta" is a collective formation.

The *Saṃyuttasaṅgaha* (Collection of Saṃyuttas) refers to the grouping according to the *Devatāsaṃyutta* and others; for the compilers of the Dhamma grouped them precisely within these sections (*vagga*).
The designation "Saṃyutta" has been established. By way of the *Mūlapaṇṇāsaka* and so forth, there is a grouping into fifties;
what is meant is that it is a collection formed by counting fifty suttas each. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the statements of the compilers found in various parts of the Canon are included.
It is likewise manifold through the *Udānasaṅgaha*, the *Paṇṇāsasaṅgaha*, and others. "In seven months."
In the section on action (*kiriyāpavagga*), the third [case] is as in such passages as: “He set out for Bārāṇasī in a single day; he completed the monastery in nine months,” and so forth.
For the swift completion of an action is indeed the conclusion of action (*kiriyāpavagga*).
Then, in order to generate faith in the virtuous by showing the manifestation of many wonders, he said: “At the conclusion of the recitation... (*saṅgītipariyosāne*)... [and so on].
"Cassā" and so forth. The connection is: at the conclusion of the recitation of that word of the Buddha, as if joy had arisen, and as if giving a cry of "Well done!", [the earth] shook...
[pe] ...and appeared. For the word "as if" (*viya*) should be applied in both instances.
"Capable of proceeding" means capable of continuing its course, or capable of being set in motion. "Bounded by water" means having the water that sustains the earth as its limit.
"Having struck it together with that water"—this is what is meant; by this, a mere partial shaking is excluded.
"It shook" (*saṅkampi*) means it shook thoroughly, moving upwards and upwards. "It trembled" (*sampakampi*) means it shook properly, moving both upwards and downwards.
"It quaked" (*sampavedhi*) means it shook even more thoroughly, moving in all four directions.
It quaked. Thus, by these three terms, he shows the sixfold shaking of the earth. Alternatively, it trembled by way of rising and falling from the east and the west;
it shook violently by way of rising and falling from the north and the south;
and it quaked intensely by way of rising and falling from the center and the periphery. In this way too, it was sixfold.
It shows the shaking of the earth, with reference to which it is said in the commentaries:
"The east rises and the west sinks; the west rises and the east sinks;
the north rises and the south sinks; the south rises and the north sinks; the center [rises and the edge sinks]..."
"It rose at the edges and sank in the middle; it sank at the edges and rose in the middle"—thus, in these six ways... [as before] ...it shook.

To show that the term "marvels" (*acchariya*)—which is appropriate for things like the clapping of hands—is well-known through other designations such as the rain of flowers and the tossing of garments, he said, "Those which in the world...
and so forth. By the first Great Council, presided over by the compilers of the Dhamma, Mahākassapa and others...
Because it was compiled and chanted by five hundred [monks], she (the collection) has five hundred [compilers]; thus she is called "Pañcasatā" (The Five Hundred).
And because it was made by elders, such as Mahākassapa and others, or because it was made by elders, she is called "Therikā" (The Elders' Collection) in the world.
This is the connection: that this is known as the First Great Council.
Having thus shown the first Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti), for which purpose it was presented here, he now says "of this" and so forth, showing that introduction by way of conclusion.
"Of the first Nikāya" means of the Dīgha Nikāya, which is the first among the five Nikāyas included within the Suttanta Piṭaka;
for the Vinaya, which is included in the Khuddaka [Piṭaka], was recited first. Likewise...

For it has been stated: "In the Suttanta Piṭaka. By the word "therefore" (*tena*), because it was spoken in such a manner, [the author] shows the connection between what precedes and what follows—that "it was spoken by me just as it was stated below with reference to that very statement at the first Great Council (Mahāsaṅgīti)"—or else, he demonstrates the excellence of the detailed explanation as it was just stated.
Thus ends the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, which elucidates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend.

By the Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati—the preceptor of the Great King of Kings; one who possesses the qualities of uprightness, gentleness, heroism, faith, mindfulness, fortitude, intelligence, patience, and energy;
who generates clarity in vast and stainless wisdom; who moves with unimpeded, unshakable, and confident knowledge regarding the Three Pitakas along with their commentaries;
who has plunged into the dense thickets of his own and other systems in their many varieties; a great leader of assemblies and a great expounder.
The explanation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the external introduction, titled *Sādhuvilāsinī*, has been completed.
The commentary on the *Nidānakathā* is finished.
1. The *Brahmajālasutta*.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Wanderers (Paribbājakakathāvaṇṇanā):
Having thus far shown, in general terms, the external introduction to the Brahmajāla Sutta— which is adorned with many kinds of methods that are supremely subtle,
delicate, profound, and difficult to see— [the author] now, while commenting on the internal introduction for the sake of attaining the meaning, [proceeds].

Because the state of having well-placed words is to be established through the analysis of words by means of revealing their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) as "this indeed is [it]," he first states "therein, thus," etc., in order to show the analysis of the words. For,
by means of the analysis of words, through the understanding that "this word is such-and-such," one [determines] the gender and case-ending appropriate to each respective word.
The well-arranged nature of the aforementioned phrase arises from the correct establishment of the speech, its timing, its application, and so forth;
and by that, the attainment of the meaning is achieved. As it has been said: "Monks, when the phrasing and syllables are well-arranged, the meaning is also well-guided," and so on.
Furthermore, [this is to be understood] through the connection, the words, the analysis of the words, the meaning of the words, and the inquiry.

And "by way of exclusion" means that the commentary on the meaning should be made in six ways. Therein, "connection" (*sambandha*) refers to the connection of the teaching, which worldly people also call "the uprooting.
That, moreover, is to be understood by way of the introductory narrative (*nidāna-pāḷi*) of the text, and the introductory narrative by way of the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*).
For, by demonstrating the first Great Recitation, the connection of the introductory narrative [is shown].
Since this has been shown, he says "Evaṃ" and so forth, providing a commentary by way of the words and so on.

Herein, he provides a commentary from the standpoint of the word and the analysis of the word by means of the passage beginning "Evaṃ is a particle-word," because the words and their specific qualifications have been demonstrated.
For by "analysis of the word" (padavibhāga), only the specific qualification of the words is intended, not the grammatical compounding of words. The words...

And there is the analysis of words (*padavibhāga*) and the compounding of words (*padaviggaha*). Alternatively, it should be understood that by means of the *ekasesa* (single-remainder) method, both words and word-compounds are also expressed by the term "analysis of words" (*padavibhāga*).

As for the compounding of words, he will provide a detailed commentary later on in the passage beginning with “the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,” and likewise through the application and resolution of the meanings of the words.
Thus, in this context, the word *iti*, which is indicated by elision, has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*), because words such as *ca* and *sadda* are included [in that category];
or alternatively, they are included by the mention of the term *naya*. Therefore he says: "‘Me’ and so forth are noun-words (*nāmapada*).

Otherwise, one would have to state that the particle *ca* and words such as *sadda* also possess the status of particles (*nipāta*). In the phrase “‘Me’ and so forth,” however, by the word *ādi*, [the list continues] as far as...
By the term *paṭisaddo* (echo), all remaining sounds are included. *Paṭi* is a prefix because it functions as the causal basis for the word *sadda*.

Now, explaining the meaning according to the sequence of the extraction of meanings (*atthuddhārakkama*), he says, "But as to the meaning," and so forth. At this point, however, the various modes of commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanāppakāra*) should be stated for the sake of the listeners' proficiency in the method of commentary. How so?
There is the "single-stalk" commentary (*ekanāḷikā kathā*), and likewise the "square" commentary (*caturassā*).
I shall now state the threefold commentary on the "Mode of Abiding" (Nisinnavatta).
Therein, the explanation of the meaning of each individual word after reciting the text is so called because it resembles measuring with a *nāḷi* measure;
or alternatively, each single word is the *nāḷa* (the stalk or root), or it is so called because each single word is the *nāḷikā* (the tube), as it is the path by which the meaning issues forth.

It is called *ekanāḷikā*. Because it is spoken by way of four sections—showing the opposing side and showing a simile for that opposing side, and showing one's own side and showing a simile for that one's own side—it is called *caturassā*, either because it is stated in four parts, or because it has four short [sections] as its means of observation (*sallakkhaṇūpāya*).
Its conclusion is reached solely by way of dissimilar phenomena.

Furthermore, because it reaches its conclusion by way of the common nature of the assembly (*sabhāgadhamma*), having caused [the listener] to sit and having established [them], it is called "the rule for those who have sat" (*nisinnavattikā*) due to its suitability for turning back;

or, considering that the conduct (*vatta*) of one who has sat down and begun [the discourse] necessarily turns back [to the beginning], it is said that even the individual conclusions of the matter as it was begun are connected [to the start]. This is stated along with examples.
Furthermore, the discussion on [the types of] discourse should be taken from the commentary on the *Gopālaka-sutta* in the eleventh nipāta of the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*.
"The discourse on analysis, the discourse on reality, and also the discourse by way of synonyms— thus,
a wise person should state the threefold exposition according to the sequence of meanings."
In this context, the investigation of the etymology and so forth is an analytical discourse (*bhedakathā*), such as: “He awakens, thus he is the Buddha,” and so on.

The investigation of the essential nature is a discourse on reality (*tatvakathā*), such as: “The Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-become and without a teacher,” and so on. The investigation of synonyms is a figurative discourse (*pariyāyakathā*), such as:
“The Buddha, the Blessed One, is the omniscient leader of the world,” and so on.

I shall explain the commentary in five ways: the purpose (*payojana*), the summary of the meaning (*piṇḍattha*), the connection (*anusandhi*), the objection (*codanā*), and the resolution (*parihāra*) in all cases.

Therein, "purpose" refers to the fruit of the teaching, which consists of knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth. "Summary of the meaning" refers to that which is [otherwise] scattered...
