Summarizing and explaining for the sake of easy comprehension of the meaning. *Anusandhi* (connection) refers to the connection of questions and so forth.
*Codanā* (objection) refers to stating a contradiction to the aforementioned statement. *Parihāra* (resolution) refers to stating a non-contradiction to that.
*Ummugghāta* (extraction) consists of the word itself, the meaning of the word, and the analysis of the word.
"Movement is the manifestation; speak the sixfold exposition.
Therein, "uprooting" refers to the removal of internal and other origins. "Word" (*pada*) is the statement of various specific word-differences, such as "it is thus";

the meaning of the word (*padattha*) consists of the literal meaning, the intended meaning, and so forth. "Word-analysis" (*padaviggaha*) is the etymological derivation in many ways. Movement (*cālanā*).
It is eightfold: the name, the enunciation, the manifestation,
the resolution, the origin, the meaning of the words,
the statement of existence, the method, the contradiction, the resolution, and the conclusion.
In this context, "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) refers to the internal and other causal conditions.

"Word-meaning" (*padattha*) is the manifold meaning of a word according to whether it is intended or unintended, and so forth. "State" (*bhāva*) refers to the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). "Modes of restatement" (*anuvādavidhiyo*):

the first statement is the injunction (*vidhi*), while the subsequent statement is the restatement (*anuvāda*) by way of revealing that [injunction]; alternatively, the terms "injunction" and "restatement" are designations for the qualifier and the qualified.

"Objection" (*virodha*) means an inquiry for the purpose of determining the meaning. "Refutation" (*parihāra*) means its resolution. "Conclusion" (*nigamana*) means a synthesis (*appanā*) that is appropriate to the connection.

At the beginning, its source, its purpose, the summary meaning (*piṇḍattha*), the word-by-word meaning (*padattha*), the relationship (*sambandha*), and the underlying intention (*adhippāyaka*) must be stated.
"I shall state the commentary in eight ways: as *codanā* (the challenge) and *sodhanā* (the resolution).

Herein, "connection" (*sambandha*) refers to the connection between what precedes and what follows, which is called the "link" (*anusandhi*). The remaining [terms] have already been explained; having understood these various modes of commentary encountered here and there through such [explanations], one should discern them appropriately in all instances.

Since this manifold variety of meanings is to be known from the very application [of the method], the passage beginning with "For it is thus" (*tathā hesā*) is stated in order to establish that point.

It has been stated. Alternatively, it should be understood that this was said in order to show that words—defined by convention as "this word is the designator of this meaning"—are indeed the designators of their respective meanings, and that convention itself is established through usage.
This applies to such cases as these. But is it not the case that—?
“Just as one might make many garlands from a heap of flowers, so too, by a mortal who has been born, much wholesome merit should be performed.
Here, since the word *evaṃ* expresses only the manner of the simile, might it not be that the word *evaṃ* has the sense of “manner”? No, because there is a specific distinction [in its usage].

In passages such as “It is indeed thus,” the term *ākāra* is intended to signify merely the general mode [of being], and not a specific mode. For here, although human rebirth— due to the convergence of causes such as reliance on true persons (*sappurisa*),
hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), and the performance of meritorious deeds like giving which result in the acquisition of wealth—
is like a heap of flowers by virtue of its association with qualities such as beauty and fragrance, [the term *ākāra* refers only to that general state].

Because it illuminates the meaning that many meritorious deeds, which resemble garlands of flowers, must be performed by a mortal being whose nature is subject to death, the "garland of flower-clusters" is indeed called a simile (*upamā*), since one is compared by means of it.
Furthermore, the manner of those similes is indicated without restriction by the word *yathā*; therefore, the word *evaṃ* has the sense of concluding the manner of the simile with certainty.
Although it is appropriate to speak thus, nevertheless, that mode of comparison, when being defined, is in fact a simile (*upamā*) in its meaning;
for, with the intention that without that which serves as the basis (*nissaya*), the mode of comparison which depends upon it cannot be obtained, he said, "it has come down in the form of a simile.
Alternatively, taking the act of comparing (*upamīyana*) to mean making something similar, it refers to the state of similarity characterized by the clusters of flowers and strings of garlands.
The term *upamā* (simile) refers precisely to the mode (*ākāra*). For it has been said: "The state of being the true Dhamma may serve as a simile.

Therefore, the word *evaṃ* signifies the meaning of the mode itself, denoting merely that mode. However, when it denotes a specific mode reckoned as a simile, it signifies the meaning of a simile; thus it is said, "it occurs in the sense of a simile.
Likewise, [it is used] in such passages as "In this manner (*evaṃ*), by this mode (*iminā ākārena*), one should advance," referring to conduct befitting a recluse.
Since even the manner of pointing out [the teaching] through the perfection of formal conduct is in fact nothing other than instruction itself, he said:

"Thus... [etc. ...in the instruction. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "thus indeed": for those who understand the meaning exactly as it was spoken by the Blessed One without error, the act of gladdening them by means of various modes of proclaiming the qualities existing therein, and making them joyful, is "encouragement" (*sampahaṃsana*). Within that, there is also the manner of encouragement.
In terms of meaning, it is simply "encouragement," as stated: "In 'encouragement' (sampahaṃsane). Here, "reproach" (garahaṇa) refers to words of censure through the manifestation of faults;
in terms of meaning, that very mode [of speech] is also called reproach. Therefore, it is said "in reproach.
And here, this mode of reproach is indicated by the word "thus" (evaṃ), due to the proximity of abusive terms such as "outcaste" (vasalī).

It is understood that just as it is here, so too the forms of similes and the like are to be seen as being mentioned by way of similes and so forth due to the proximity of words such as "heaps of flowers" (puppharāsi) which have been stated [in the preceding verses]. For particles (*nipāta*) are merely indicators. And "evameva" (just so) refers precisely to the manner just described.
The connection is: "This *vasalī*—so called because of her association with the qualities of an outcaste (*vasala*), or because she is ill-omened (*kāḷakaṇṇī*)—speaks in whatever place."
“‘So it is, venerable sir’ means ‘Excellent, venerable sir; well said, venerable sir.

In this context, however, for those bhikkhus who have applied themselves to the careful hearing and attention of the Dhamma, the very acknowledgment of their own established state therein is the acceptance of the words;
even that manner of expression is, in its actual meaning, simply called the acceptance of the words. Therefore he says: ‘in the acceptance of the words.’”
*Evaṃ byā kho* means "just like this. Regarding these words, grammarians say that the word *byā* is a substitute (*byāpadeso*) for the word *viya* within the phrase *evaṃ khoti*.
They further state that the word is established as long (dīgha) by changing the letter *va* to *ba*, adding the conjunct *ya*, and applying the long vowel.
*Ākāre* means "in mere appearance. *Appābādhaṃ* refers to the absence of discordant sensations. *Appātaṅkaṃ* refers to the absence of diseases that cause a difficult life.
“Quick rising” means rising endowed with lightness due to freedom from sloth. “Strength” means bodily strength.
“Comfortable living” means dwelling in happiness within the four postures. The detailed explanation will be made clear in the commentary on the *Dasama-subhasutta* itself.
“And speak thus” means: speak to the ascetic Ānanda in the same way that I am speaking. “Excellent!”... [text continues]
The words beginning with "It is said, sir" refer to the speech that is now to be spoken;
and since this manner of speaking is indicated here by the word *evaṃ*, it is stated as "in the sense of indication. "O Kālāmas" is an address to people belonging to the Kālāma clan.
"What do you think of this... or that? is the meaning: "regarding what has been spoken by me. "Accepted" (*samattā*) means fulfilled. "Adopted" (*samādinnā*) means undertaken.
Regarding the two statements, "they lead [to suffering]" or "they do not lead [to suffering]," one should connect them thus:
"What is your opinion on this? "Evaṃ no" means "our opinion on this is exactly so," or alternatively, "our opinion on this is indeed so.
And here, it is for the purpose of generating certainty regarding the fact that those aforementioned phenomena bring about harm and suffering.
When the question, "Do they lead [to such results] or not? What is your view in this regard? is asked, the answer given is, "In our view, it is thus.
By the word *evaṃ* (thus), the determination of that specific mode is revealed;
and since that mode—namely, the manner in which those phenomena lead to harm and suffering—is being restricted, it is in fact a definitive limitation (*avadhāraṇa*) in its actual meaning.

It is stated: "In the sense of restriction. In all other instances, the purpose of the *ākāra* [particle] should be understood through the method already explained, namely as a challenge (*codanā*) and a resolution (*sodhanā*).
Furthermore, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of meanings such as "this" (*idam-attha*), "questioning" (*pucchā*), and "measure" (*parimāṇa*) should be seen here.

For instance, in expressions such as "gone thus" (*evaṃ-gata*), "of such a kind" (*evaṃ-vidha*), and "of such a form" (*evam-ākāra*), it has the sense of "this"; however, the words *gata*, *vidha*, and *ākāra* are synonyms for *pakāra* (manner or mode).
For worldly people use the words *gata*, *vidha*, *yutta*, and *ākāra* in the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*). This is seen in such passages as:

“Do they amuse themselves, well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, adorned with jeweled earrings and ornaments, dressed in white garments, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, just as you do now together with your teacher?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama. And so forth.

In the case of a question; and in such instances as “thus rapidly revolving,” “thus having such a limit to its lifespan,” and so forth, it denotes measure. Here too, the statement beginning with “well-bathed, well-anointed” is a question; “rapidly revolving” and “the measure of the lifespan” are measures.
Since even their mode of appearance is, in meaning, both a question and a measure, therefore, in these cases, the word *evaṃ* (thus) carries the sense of both question and measure.

"It should be understood": here, however, in response to the objection—"In what cases does this occur? Is it everywhere, or is it indefinite, occurring only in a specific location?"—it is said, "But here...
and so forth. [Objection: "Could it not apply to only one meaning? Why then to all three? [Response: Let it be that there are three kinds of meanings; by which [meaning] is for what purpose?
And in order to avoid the objection that [the text] "illuminates," he said "In that regard" (*tattha*) and so forth. "In that regard" (*tattha*) means among those three meanings.

The various methods (*naya*)—whether they be classified as unity, diversity, non-exertion, and the nature of things (*evamdhammatā*), or as the "turning of the hook" (*nandiyāvatta*), the "lion's play" (*sīhavikkīḷita*), and the "elephant-goad" (*aṅkusasadi-saṇṭhāna*)—are manifold according to the distinctions of the basis (*ādhāra*) and so on;

or alternatively, the "methods" (*naya*) are the courses of the scriptures (*pāḷigatiyo*), and these are further divided into the "formal teaching" (*paññatti*), the "subsequent teaching" (*anupaññatti*), and so forth.

There are various methods (nānā-nayā) consisting of manifold modes according to the Tripiṭaka: by way of concise and detailed [expositions], by way of those pertaining to defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and so forth, worldly (lokiya) and so forth, and their mixture;

by way of the wholesome (kusala) and so forth; by way of the aggregates (khandha) and so forth; by way of inclusion (saṅgaha) and so forth; by way of those liberated at times (samayavimutta) and so forth;

by way of setting aside (ṭhapanā) and so forth; by way of the roots of the wholesome (kusalamūla) and so forth; and by way of the Tikapaṭṭhāna and so forth. By means of these, it is subtle and refined.

And likewise subtle. *Āsayo* (the underlying tendency) is the same as *ajjhāsaya* (inclination); these are manifold through their divisions such as eternalism and so forth, and therein they are diverse according to the presence of little dust in the eyes and so on.
Or rather, it is "likewise" because its source (*samuṭṭhāna*)—that is, its cause of arising—is precisely self-inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and the rest.

It is "perfect" and "complete" because it is endowed with both meaning and phrasing, owing to the absence of anything that needs to be added. Furthermore, [it is perfect] by way of making known, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and defining.
It is likewise endowed with six factors of meaning—by way of letters, phrases, phonemes, forms, etymologies, and explanations—and with six factors of phrasing.
Alternatively, it is so because it reaches the hearts of the wise;

because it generates insatiability upon hearing, due to its state of supreme profundity through the flavor of the phrasing; and because it generates insatiability upon investigation, due to the flavor of the meaning.
And likewise, it was perfect and sweet in flavor.
Regarding the meaning of the term *pāṭihāriya*: they say that it is "a miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes opposing factors, that is, because it eliminates defilements such as lust.
However, for the Blessed One, the opposing factors such as lust do not exist, which would need to be removed even at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Because all defilements together with their latent tendencies have been abandoned.

Furthermore, even in the case of worldlings (*puthujjana*), the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) occur only when the mind is free from secondary defilements, endowed with the eight qualities, and has destroyed its opposites;

therefore, even by the conventional usage current among worldlings, it cannot be called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) here. However, if [these powers] belong specifically to those to be trained (*veneyya*) by the Blessed One, who is Greatly Compassionate...
Because they desire to lift up the multitude of beings submerged in the mire of saṃsāra, the defilements are their adversaries;
therefore, it is said that they are "miracles" (pāṭihāriya) because they carry away (haraṇa) those adversaries consisting of the defilements residing in those to be trained.
This being so, this [etymology] is appropriate.

Alternatively, it is also appropriate to call it a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) because of the removal (*haraṇa*) of those who are adversaries of the Blessed One’s teaching—the heretics (*titthiya*)—who, being such adversaries, are removed.
Granted, in this context there would be no heretics actually to be removed;

however, by way of removing the views existing within their mental continuities, and because of the inability [of those views] to manifest [further] views, [the Buddha acts] through what are known as the miracles of psychic power (*iddhi*), instruction (*ādesanā*), and guidance (*anusāsanī*).
By all three wonders, they are indeed said to have been "carried away" or "removed.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "after," as in such expressions as "when he had entered [the water], another brahmin arrived.
Therefore, it means that after the mind has been concentrated, free from defilements, and the task accomplished, [the teaching] must be carried away—that is, set in motion—subsequently.
It is a marvel (*pāṭihāriya*); that very same thing is a marvel by way of its duration or by way of the grammatical suffix *paccaya* denoting "one's own purpose.

Alternatively, it is called a marvel because, once one’s own secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*) have been removed by means of the fourth jhāna and the path, others are subsequently removed for them in the manner already described.

For indeed, the miracles of psychic power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsani*) are performed for the benefit of beings by one who is free from secondary defilements and has accomplished his task.
Furthermore, because they must be performed again, and because they remove the secondary defilements (upakkilesa) of other beings while one’s own secondary defilements have been destroyed,
both of these etymologies are appropriate. Moreover,
by means of the aforementioned etymologies, the aggregate consisting of success (iddhi), manifestation (ādesanā), and instruction (anusāsanī) is termed a "wonder" (paṭihāriya).

[This is] the name. However, each individual instance within that existence is called a "pāṭihāriya" (miracle) because a specific verbal formation arises through the addition of a suffix that indicates a particular meaning;
or, *paṭihāriya* refers to the fourth jhāna and the Path because they remove opposing factors (*paṭipakkha*).

That which is born therein, or that which has that [Path] as its sign, or that which comes from it, is a *pāṭihāriya*. For the application of secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*) is indeed manifold.

However, because the teaching of the Blessed One is found to be manifold—divided into the categories of miracles of psychic power (*iddhi*), of mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and of instruction (*anusāsani*), as well as by way of its various objects—it is called "the manifold miracle.
For the Blessed One sometimes gives a teaching by means of psychic power, such as in the posing and answering of questions together with a manifested Buddha;
and sometimes he does so by means of mind-reading, as in the case of the Brahmin Āmagandha.

In the case of the teaching of the Dhamma and so forth, it is for the most part through instruction (*anusāsani*). For the constant teaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas is the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).
Thus, the quality of being a manifold miracle is attributed to the teaching by way of its various modes of instruction.
This meaning will be made clear later in the commentary on the eleventh sutta, the *Kevaṭṭa-sutta*. Alternatively, of that [teaching], even though it is of many kinds...
It is called "various miracles" because the Blessed One’s teaching indicates a miracle; the meaning is "the display of many kinds of miracles.

Because the teaching comes within the range of hearing for all who listen—each according to their own respective language—even while the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma through the very terminology of the Dhamma itself, he said:
"coming within the range of hearing for all... Here, "range of hearing" (*sotapatha*) means simply the ear.
"Listening" (*savana*) means hearing; its path is likewise [called] the "door of hearing" (*sotadvāra*). "In every way" (*sabbākārena*) means according to the manner in which it was taught.
"Who is capable of understanding?"—he is indeed incapable; therefore, there is an ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*) [to be supplied]. "But" (*pana*) has the sense of emphasis (*ekamsatthe*);

by this, he shows that one must generate the wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*) characterized by the wish to hear, using all one's strength—that is, by means of the powers consisting of faith, mindfulness, fortitude, energy, and so forth. "Even having generated [it]" (*janetvāpi*)...
Here, the word *pi* or the word *api* has the sense of esteem (*sambhāvanattha*), as in such expressions as “even the Buddha, having developed the state of Buddhahood.

By this, he expresses esteem for the Dhamma thus heard: “Even though one has generated a desire to hear with all one’s might and with absolute resolve, and has heard it in only one way, how much more so if it were otherwise? Some, however, [say] regarding such cases...
Some say that [the prefix *anu-*] has the sense of censure (*garahattha*), but that is indeed incorrect because the sense of censure is not present here;

for prefixes and particles indicate only those meanings that actually exist. Indeed, by the phrase "skilled in various methods" (*nānānayanipuṇa*) and so forth, he merely expresses the excellence of the Dhamma through its being impossible to hear in every respect.
Therefore, it is only in such passages as "even in celestial pleasures, he finds no delight" (*api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati*) and so on...
Among the meanings of *garaha* (reproach) and *sambhava* (possibility), the meaning of reproach is to be understood here.
Furthermore, in such instances, the word *api* is merely a particle (*nipāta*) and not a prefix (*upasagga*). For thus say the grammarians:
"The word *api* should be classified among the particles where it does not precede a verbal expression. As for the phrase *mayāpi*: here it means not only "by me alone," but rather—
The sense of "and by others who were likewise" (*aññehi pi tathārūpehi*) should be understood as a collective inclusion.
"He exists by himself" (*sāmaṃ bhavati*) means he is self-become (*sayambhū*), one without a teacher.

Regarding the phrase "we have not realized this ourselves," the meaning is understood from the context to be: "it was not realized by oneself through one's own knowledge alone. This applies even to the term "selfhood" (*sāmañña*).

For indeed, the apprehension of specific meanings is possible by way of association, dissociation, coexistence, contradiction, proximity, presence, signs, fitness, time, place, instruments, and so forth. This applies everywhere. Regarding the word "liberating":
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, conceals it from himself."

This is for the purpose of liberating [others] from the faults already mentioned; for the word *anta* is used in the sense of "cause" (hetu), as in such expressions as “*asambudhaṃ buddhanisevitam*” and so forth.

Having in mind that his own knowledge has been directly realized through this investigation of the methods of commentary on this Sutta, he says, “Now it shall be explained. For this is the natural way of commentators: namely, regarding the dhamma to be commented upon...

In all instances, there is first of all an investigation into the modes of commentary, thinking, "This is its meaning; I shall comment upon it here in this way. The meaning of the term *etadagga* has already been stated.

Regarding the phrase "of those who are learned" (*bahussutānaṃ*) and so forth, however, there are other elders who are learned, mindful, possessed of intelligence, possessed of fortitude, and attendants; yet this venerable one, while grasping the word of the Buddha...
Having stood in the learning of the storehouse-keeper (Bhaṇḍāgārika) within the teaching of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, he mastered it;

therefore, he became known as the foremost among those of great learning (*bahussuta*). Furthermore, having learned the word of the Buddha, this elder’s power of retention (*dhāraṇa-sati*) was stronger than that of other elders;
therefore, he became known as the foremost among those possessed of mindfulness (*satimant*). This very venerable one, standing upon a single word...
Memorizing sixty thousand phrases, he understood every word according to the method taught by the Teacher;

therefore, he became known as the foremost of those possessed of intelligence (*gatimanta*). Furthermore, that venerable one’s diligence in learning the Buddha’s word and his diligence in its recitation were peerless among others;
therefore, he became known as the foremost of those possessed of steadfastness (*dhitimanta*). While attending upon the Tathāgata...
He does not attend upon the Tathāgata in the same manner as other attendant bhikkhus.
For others indeed have attended upon the Tathāgata, yet they were unable to attend upon him by grasping the Buddha’s mind;
but this Elder, from the very day he obtained the position of attendant, having exerted himself with diligence, [attends] to the Tathāgata’s mind.
Having received [him], he attended upon him; therefore, he became known as the foremost of attendants (*upaṭṭhāka*).

"Skilled in meaning" (*atthakusala*) means one who is proficient in the meaning of what has been spoken and in the purpose (*payojana*). "Dhamma" refers to the *pāḷi*-dhamma, or various types of causes (*hetu*).

"Phrasing" (*byañjana*) refers to the syllable (*akkhara*), because it manifests the meaning; for even though the meaning is manifested by the word (*pada*), since the word is rooted in the syllable, it is said to be "by the syllable."
It is called "byañjita" (manifested). Alternatively, because it manifests the meaning (*attha*), even a sentence is here termed "byañjana" (the manifestor).
For it is by means of a sentence that the meaning is fully manifested; hence the Venerable Elder Mahākaccāyana said: "He reveals [it] by means of the manifestors (*byañjanehi*).
*Nirutti* means derivation (*nibbacana*), or else there are five methods of derivation (*niruttinaya*). For these also, by way of specific arrangements of words...

The inclusion [of this term] here is appropriate because it is the cause for attaining the goal. "Connection between what precedes and what follows" (*pubbāpara*) refers to the sequence of preceding and following sections, or the linking of the latter part of a discourse with its former part.

The connection is that this is in accordance with the state of being praised by the Blessed One through his fivefold status as the foremost (*etadagga*) and by the General of the Dhamma through his fivefold skill (*kosalla*). "Power of retention" (*dhāraṇabala*)...
"Strength reckoned as retention" (*dhāraṇa-saṅkhātaṃ balaṃ*) or "strength in retention" (*dhāraṇe balaṃ*); in both cases, what is meant is the capacity to retain.

"Being one who sees" (*dassento hutvā*), or "for the sake of seeing" (*dassana-hetu*), is also the meaning. Furthermore, by stating that it is "neither deficient nor redundant" in either its sense (*attha*) or its phrasing (*byañjana*), he expresses the result of the restriction.
The phrase "it should not be viewed otherwise" (*na aññathā daṭṭhabbaṃ*) serves to exclude other possibilities. As for "not otherwise" (*na aññathā*):
And this was heard from the presence of the Blessed One exactly as it occurred, and not otherwise; yet it was not according to the manner in which the Blessed One taught.

For the teaching of the Blessed One possesses inconceivable power. It is by taking it in this way that the statement previously mentioned—"Who is capable of understanding it in every aspect?"—is justified;
for otherwise, since one would be capable of hearing it precisely according to the manner in which the Blessed One taught it, [that statement] would be undermined.

Therefore, this should not be said. However, there is no contradiction with the demonstration of the power of retention (dhāraṇa-bala) in the sense already stated, because what is intended by "retention" is its non-contradiction with the manner in which it was heard;

otherwise, since one would be capable of retaining it only in the very form taught by the Blessed One, it would contradict the statement made previously. For here there is no [conflict] between two meanings.
The avoidance of the charge of being a different meaning is appropriate, because both of those meanings are shown to be of a single scope by way of their being heard [by the Elder];
otherwise, it would follow that the Elder was capable of receiving the Blessed One’s teaching in its entirety in terms of the latter meaning,
yet incapable in terms of the former meaning.

The word *me*— which is threefold and functions as that which causes the continuity known as one’s own internal self (*niyakajjhatta*) to proceed, as stated in the phrase “That which is not another is the self”—
is seen in the singular sense according to the continuity of one’s own internal self; nevertheless,
it is with reference to the existing diversity of case-endings by way of the instrumental, dative, and genitive designations.
It is said, “it is seen in three senses”; the meaning is that it is seen in the sense of the third case-ending (vibhatti) because it is connected with the word *attanā* (by oneself).
*Gāthābhigītaṃ* means sung to by a verse; that is, sung in the presence [of the verse].
*Abhojaneyyaṃ* means that which is not fit to be made into food. Because the word *abhigīta* requires an agent (*kattā*), the meaning is “by me. The same applies to the remaining cases.

Accordingly. Because the word *suta* (heard) functions as both an object (*kamma*) and an abstract state (*bhāva*), it appropriately fits two meanings—“I have heard” and “what was heard by me”—since it is a term whose intended sense depends on context.
Although a prefix (*upasagga*) qualifies the action, because its nature is merely indicative, the word *suta* alone [retains its meaning] even when that prefix is present.

Because it is said that "it expresses this or that meaning," there is no contradiction in including the verb root with its prefix when extracting the meaning of the word *suta* (heard) without its prefix;
thus he says: "both with prefix and without prefix. "Of it" (*assa*) refers to the word *suta*.

Even by means of a prefix, a verbal root expresses a specific meaning, as in the cases where it is said, "he experiences" (*anubhavati*) or "he perishes" (*parābhavati*), or as in "going" (*gacchanto*).

“Meaning. Likewise, even though the word *dhātu* (root) is without a prefix, it expresses a specific meaning just as if it were with a prefix; thus he says, “the meaning is ‘of the renowned Dhamma. It is the same in such cases.
“To be cognized by the ear” means to be known by consciousness dependent on the ear-door;
or this is a figurative expression (*sasambhārakathā*), meaning “to be cognized by means of the ear-door. “One who has cognized the Dhamma following the ear-door.”
"One who retains the phenomena cognized by the mind-consciousness following the ear-door. For a phenomenon is not cognized by the mere consciousness dependent on the ear-door;
rather, it is cognized precisely by the mind-consciousness that follows it. Thus, "one who retains what is heard" (*suta-dhara*) is said to be one who retains the phenomena thus cognized;
therefore, it is stated in this way because that very meaning is possible. The words *suta* (heard) and *dhamma* (phenomena) function as the instrument (*kamma-bhāva-sādhana*).

In order to show that [these things] arise, he said, "But here," and so forth. The logical consistency or inconsistency of the meaning is understood through the connection between preceding and subsequent words;
therefore, this meaning—namely, "consistent" (*upapanna*) or "inconsistent" (*anupapanna*)—should not be understood by means of the word *suta* alone.
Thus, in response to the objection, [the author explains] this meaning by way of the connection between preceding and subsequent words.
In order to demonstrate its applicability, the passage beginning with “of the word *me* (*me-saddassa hi*)” was stated. Regarding the phrase “when there is the sense of ‘by me’ (*mayāti atthe sati*):

this means when it is necessary to express the sense of “by me” (*mayāti*) by way of a designation of the instrument (*karaṇa-niddesa*) in the sense of the agent (*kattuttha*); that is to say, when the word *me* is designated as the instrument by way of the agent.
Regarding the phrase “when there is the sense of ‘mine’ (*mamāti atthe sati*): this refers to the sense of possession (*sambandhittha*) by way of a designation of the owner (*sāminiddesa*).
Since this meaning must be stated, it is implied that "when there is a designation of the possessor (*sāmin*) by way of connection.
Having thus made known the meaning to be understood from the word itself, he now says, "In these [cases] thus," etc., demonstrating the meaning that should be shown by them.
When the word *evaṃ* (thus) is employed in proximity to the word *suta* (heard), it must necessarily be indicative of the act of hearing, as its meaning exists [in that context].
It is said, "Because they are mere particles," that "the word *evaṃ* is an indication of the function of consciousnesses such as ear-consciousness.
For the form *evaṃ* indeed indicates hearing, it is an indication, and it is also a restriction;

therefore, all three meanings of the word *evaṃ* mentioned above are intended here by virtue of its being an indicator of the act of hearing. And by the word *ādi* (etc. here, [the functions of] receiving-consciousness and so forth are included.
It should be understood that this includes both the consciousnesses belonging to the ear-door and their respective impingements, as well as the consciousnesses belonging to the mind-door;
for it is in the sense of being cognized by following upon the ear-door that the word "heard" (*suta*) is used here.
Because the employment of the word "only" (*eva*) results in restriction, every sentence contains an implicit restriction; therefore, the meaning of the term "heard" is "heard only."
"It is obtained," he says, "by way of the negation of the state of not having heard. By this statement, he shows that which was refuted by means of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*).
Just as that which is heard must be defined as "heard indeed," so too, in order to show the fruit of the restriction—that such hearing is "properly heard"—it is stated:
"the demonstration of grasping [the teaching] without deficiency, without excess, and without error."

Alternatively, a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words; therefore, with reference to the fact that the meaning "it is not the case that it has not been heard" is obtained for the term "heard," it is said: "by way of negating the state of not having been heard.
By this, he excludes [the categories of] what is seen and so forth, because things such as what is seen must be excluded from being the meaning of other words in the sense of being "not heard."
This is what is meant: "This was not seen by me through my own knowledge, nor realized through the knowledge of a self-enlightened one (sayambhu-ñāṇa);
rather, it was heard, and that indeed was heard correctly. It is with reference to this very state of being correctly heard that he said:
"Without deficiency... [and so on] ...vision. And here there is this [verse]:
“Thus, by means of such restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and by the exclusion of other meanings (*aññatthāpohana*),
the word ‘thus’ (*evaṃ*) in two ways excludes another meaning as appropriate.
Furthermore, since this construction of the meaning is made with the word ‘thus’ (*evaṃ*) in the sense of restriction, it refers back to that [word] for the word ‘heard’ (*suta*).
The phrase "because of the negation of the state of not hearing" is stated with a restrictive sense; by the words "without deficiency...

[down to] seeing," he demonstrates the fruit of that restriction. Furthermore, because it is joined with the word for "state" (*bhāva*), the word *savana* here should be understood as having the object-denoting (*kamma-sādhana*) function, meaning "that which is heard.

It is "unmistaken" due to its being heard directly from the Blessed One in its entirety—neither deficient nor excessive—and because it is not contrary to what has been heard. Of that which is unmistakable...
Or the grasping of the sutta, and likewise its demonstration; thus this construction has been made by way of the cause for hearing, the person who hears, and the distinction of the hearing.
Having thus shown the construction of the meaning of the three terms in one manner, now, in order to show it by another manner as well, the words beginning with "tathā" (likewise) were spoken.
Therein, "of that" refers to the manner of hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.
The cognitive process (viññāṇavīthi) occurring at the mind-door (manodvārika) proceeds;

for that [process] is capable of proceeding toward an object in various ways, whereas the cognitive process occurring at the ear-door does not, because it proceeds only toward a single object. Thus it has been said: "by way of the ear-door.
By this, the cognitive process occurring at the ear-door is excluded. "In various ways" means in many different manners, as will be explained below.
By the phrase "in various modes reckoned as the ways of grasping the meaning of the phrasing," he shows that in this construction the word *evaṃ* (thus) is taken in the sense of "mode.
"The manifestation of the state of occurrence" means the manifestation of the existence of the occurrence.
Referring to that very object, in whatever mode the aforementioned stream of consciousness has occurred in various ways—
It is said to be “the proclamation of the Dhamma,” but this is not the meaning of the word *suta* (heard) as *dhamma*; therefore it is said, “this Dhamma was heard.
For in that cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*), only the object is called “this Dhamma was heard.

And when that is being defined, it is specifically the Sutta which serves as the object for the aforementioned cognitive process. This is what is meant by the passage beginning with “This here,” and so forth.

This is the clarification of the very meaning already stated. Here, the word *hi* (for/indeed) has the sense of making that [meaning] clear. By me, acting as the agent through the process (*vīthi*) of consciousness, nothing else was done;
rather, this object was made [the focus]. If it is asked, "What then was it?"—it is: "This Dhamma was heard.
However, the intended meaning here is as follows: when the word *evaṃ* (thus) is used in the sense of a mode (*ākāra*), [it means] "by one mode."

The mode (*ākāra*) that has been stated means, in terms of its actual meaning, nothing other than the state of the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) proceeding toward an object in various ways by following the ear-door;
and by that, hearing is performed only with respect to the phenomenon (*dhamma*) that constitutes its object, and not anything else.
Thus, the distinction between the instrument, the agent, and the object of the act of hearing is demonstrated in this interpretation.

He states another application [of the term] with the words "likewise" (*tathā*) and so forth. Having taken the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) for the purpose of illustration, and because that which is illustrated is inseparable from the illustration, it is said: "'Thus' is the elucidation of that which is to be illustrated.

For by this, he shows that because of that very inseparability, the entire sutta is referred back by means of the word "thus," [and thus] the word "heard" (*suta*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]

Because it consists of activity, and because it is bound to a common continuum of consciousness through the act of hearing, and because the conventional designation "person" (puggala) applies to that very continuum of consciousness, it is said: "the elucidation of the function of the person.

For here, the "person" is the conventional designation for the common continuum of consciousness, while the act of hearing is its function. Indeed, [this does not apply] where the conventional designation "person" is absent.

It should be understood that the act of hearing (*savanakiriyā*) occurs with respect to a continuity of phenomena (*dhammappabandha*), because that act falls within the domain of conventional designation (*vohāravisaya*).

The phrase "by me" (*mayā*) and so forth is a demonstration of the collective meaning (*piṇḍattha*); it refers to "me" as a person (*puggala*) consisting of the aforementioned continuity of consciousness (*viññāṇappabandha*).
"Hearing" (*suta*) is connected to the function of a person (*puggalakicca*) characterized by the act of hearing; however, regarding this connection:
It should be understood that this is an illustration of both the person who is the object of the person’s activity and of the person’s activity itself.

Having taken the word *evaṃ* (thus) in the sense of manner (*ākāra*), the phrase beginning with “*tathā*” (likewise) was stated to show another way of construing the meaning for the previous application.
“Of the mental continuum” (*cittasantānassa*) means of the aforementioned stream of consciousness (*viññāṇappabandha*). “Due to the occurrence in various modes” (*nānākārappavattiya*).

Because it occurs with respect to objects in various ways; or because it is the grasping of meaning and phrasing in various ways, or the grasping of various meanings and phrases—it is for that very reason called "description by way of aspect" (*ākārapaññatti*).
He confirms this meaning with the words beginning "For thus... and so forth.
Furthermore, "description by way of aspect" is indeed a dependent description (*upādāpaññatti*), but as for phenomena (*dhammā*),...

Because it is designated by way of its mode of occurrence (*pavatti-ākāra*), and in order to distinguish it from other types of derivative designation (*upādā-paññatti*), it is called "designation as mode" (*ākāra-paññatti*).

This is a description of the object; it is a description of the locus of arising. For the Dhamma, which has become the object of hearing, is the locus of occurrence for the person who has become the agent of the act of hearing, by way of that act of hearing; this is because the object of the action is the basis for the agent of the action.

And because that [receptacle] is also intended as the state of being a receptacle for the substance (*dabba*), whereas here the state of being the locus where the agent’s activity occurs is intended, the object (*kamma*) itself is stated by way of being the receptacle; therefore he said: "the completion of the agent’s grasping of the object.
Or, the object (*visaya*) is simply the objective support (*ārammaṇa*). For the objective support is the locus of occurrence for that which has it as its objective support. Thus also is the meaning.
It becomes easier to understand. To show the summarized meaning (*piṇḍattha*) of the aforementioned statement, the words beginning with "by this much" (*ettāvatā*) were spoken.
The connection is: "By this much—namely, by the three terms in the sense already stated—it is accomplished.

"By the occurrence in various modes" means by the occurrence in manifold ways upon the object. "By the mental continuum" means by that which is reckoned as the aforementioned series of consciousness (*viññāṇavīthi*).
By means of the continuity of consciousness (*cittappabandhena*). Here, this [continuity] is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of grasping.

Although, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), there is no agent whatsoever apart from the continuum of consciousness, by means of verbal usage (*saddavohāra*), and with the desire to express a distinction imagined by the intellect (*buddhiparikappita-bheda-vacanicchāya*), one treats the possessor of that [continuity] as if it were distinct from the continuum of consciousness;
thus, even though there is no actual difference, by way of a figurative expression of difference, it is said: "of the possessor of that [continuity] by means of the continuum of consciousness."

It has been stated: "For a word whose domain is conventional usage (*vohāra*) is not exclusively ultimate reality (*paramattha*). (In the *Kārakarūpasiddhi*, the *Sahetūsutta* which explains that which causes [an action] should be consulted.

Furthermore, although the phenomenon to be heard (*sotabbadhamma*) is the object of the act of hearing, it is said here that it is indeed the object of the agent, because for the continuum of consciousness proceeding by way of the act of hearing, it possesses the status of an agent in an ultimate sense.
Thus it is stated: "The conclusion regarding the grasping of the agent’s object."

Furthermore, because the act of hearing exists only through the occurrence of consciousness by way of the process of hearing, and because it is considered that the object belongs to the agent of that act—which is a collection of other mental and physical phenomena (nāma-rūpa) occurring by way of that [consciousness]—it was stated thus. This is what is meant:

in the former method, the act of hearing and its agent are, in the ultimate sense, nothing but the stream of consciousness proceeding in such a manner; therefore, even the object of the act [is likewise].

It is said to be "the domain of the agent. However, in the latter method, the continuum of consciousness proceeding in such a manner is the action (*kiriyā*), while the collection of other phenomena is the agent (*kattā*).
Therefore, although this phenomenon is exclusively the domain of action, it is nevertheless stated as "the domain of the agent who possesses that [action].
"Possessing that" means possessing that continuum of consciousness. "The agent" means...
Of the agent. "Object" (*visaya*) means the locus of occurrence by way of an objective support (*ārammaṇa*), or simply the objective support itself.
And because the Elder Suttācāra had reached a correct determination, it is called "the conclusion of the apprehension.
Another method: having made a connection with the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "aspect" (*ākāra*)—in the phrase "for whom... [etc. ...the designation of aspect"—that very same [term]...

It should be understood that even by taking the word *eva* (thus) in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), it was stated as "the determination of the apprehension was made" rather than simply "the apprehension was made," in order to apply it to this very method. For here, by means of restriction, what is intended is precisely this determination;
therefore, having taken the word *eva* in the sense of restriction in the phrase "up to this point" (*ettāvatā*) and so forth, this specific construction was employed.

It should be understood that [the word] "shows" (*dasseti*) is used; however, it should be seen that by this construction, the specific manner of grasping, the grasper, the act of grasping, and the distinction of the object are demonstrated.
He states another construction with the words "Or else" (*atha vā*), and so forth.

Its essential nature is the manifestation, determination, or indication of the form of the various kinds of meanings and phrasing—designated as "suttas"—which were previously heard and retained by oneself.

Regarding the word *evaṃ*: because it functions as a series of phenomena (*dhamma-pabandha*) that serves as the basis for the conceptual designation of a person (*puggala-paññatti*), which in turn constitutes the act of retention (*upadhāraṇa*)—consisting of the three aspects such as form (*ākāra*) and so forth—it is called "the description of the function of the person.
For the retention of the meanings and the phrasing of what has been heard by oneself is the triad of aspects and so forth;
and that is the meaning of the word *evaṃ*. Furthermore, that [retention] is dependent upon a certain series of phenomena for the conceptual designation of a person.
The agent is merely the function that constitutes his activity; therefore, the word *evaṃ* (thus) indicates the function of the person.
Granted that the act of hearing is the activity of the person without distinction, nevertheless, it is specifically the activity of consciousness;

thus it is called "the description of the function of consciousness. For even according to those who maintain the existence of a person (*puggalavādin*), the act of hearing does not exist independently of consciousness.
There is no [separate category] for hearing and so forth, because they are intended specifically as functions of consciousness (*viññāṇa*).

Since the occurrence of the word "self" (*meti*) refers exclusively to sentient beings (*satta*), and since the function of consciousness must be subsumed under that very same [category] by way of making no distinction between the six types of consciousness, it is said:
"This is a designation for a person endowed with both functions. The phrase beginning with "this" (*ayaṃ*) and so forth is the clarification of that point.
For here, the phrase "by one possessing the consciousness whose function is hearing" is stated with reference to the personal function indicated by the word "thus" (evaṃ).

However, in order to show that this is called a "personal function" precisely because it is the state of possessing the consciousness whose function is hearing on the part of the person, he did not say "by one possessing a personal function," but rather said "by one possessing the consciousness whose function is hearing. Therefore...
The meaning is: "one endowed with consciousness that possesses the function of hearing" as specified by the term *puggalakicca*.

This was stated with reference to the function of consciousness indicated by the word "heard" (*suta*) through the conventional designation of having acquired the function of hearing; that is, it is so called because its function is precisely hearing.
The phrase "the conventional designation of the function of hearing" (*savanakiccavohāro*) refers to the usage of the term "function of hearing," which has been acquired.
"So" (*so*) means "thus" (*tathā*). The meaning is: by way of the designation for the function of hearing, which is termed consciousness (*viññāṇa*), that is, by way of its functional capacity.

This, however, is the connection: "It was heard by me"—that is, by a person possessing the consciousness whose function is hearing—by means of that consciousness, which serves as the instrument, designated by the function of hearing.

Furthermore, the meaning of the word “thus” (*evaṃ*) is a designation for what does not exist (*avijjamāna-paññatti*), while the meaning of the word “heard” (*sutaṃ*) is a designation for what exists (*vijjamāna-paññatti*).

Therefore, showing those two as such designations by way of the activity of a person (*puggala-byāpāra*) who has become the basis for appropriation (*upādāna*), he said: “‘Thus’ is a description of the function of the person;
‘heard’ is a description of the function of consciousness. For if [the matter] were being determined solely from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), [it would not be so].
This distinction is obtained by way of the function of the person (*puggala*) and the function of consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that in this application, the designation of the agent’s activity, the instrument’s activity, and the agent itself has been made.
This is because every meaning attainable through words must be approached solely by means of its conceptual description (*paññatti*), and because of all...
Because these designations are included within the sixfold classification of designations— beginning with "existent" and so forth— he says, "And 'thus' (*evaṃ*)," etc.,
demonstrating the specific nature of the designations "thus" and so on among them. Therein,

because the meaning being expressed by "thus" and "to me" (*me*) consists of the mode (*ākāra*) and so forth of phenomena, and because it lacks the state of being clearly perceived (*sallakkhaṇa*), it is a designation of what does not exist (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).
He said: "It is a designation of what does not exist by way of the true and ultimate sense.
And "by way of the true and ultimate sense" means by way of the meaning that is real and the meaning that is supreme. This is what is meant:

that which, like an illusion or a mirage, is not a real entity, and which, unlike things grasped through hearsay and the like, is not a non-supreme object—that is the intrinsic nature of form, sound, and so forth.

Alternatively, the meaning that has the intrinsic nature of being afflicted (*ruppana*), experiencing (*anubhavana*), and so forth, is called the "actual reality" (*saccikaṭṭha*) and the "ultimate reality" (*paramattha*).
However, because the meaning of the words "Thus have I [heard]" (*evaṃ me*) is not real and is not supreme, it is not described in that way.

Therefore, by means of the "actual reality" and "ultimate reality"—which are designated as the "real meaning" and "supreme meaning" and function as qualifiers—it is precisely a designation of what does not exist (*avijjamāna-paññatti*). And by this qualifier...
It negates the mere conceptual designation imagined by foolish people as "it exists. It makes that very meaning clear, or establishes it through a reason with the words "What is there in this?

and so forth. Whatever collection of phenomena or collection of objects might receive the designation "thus" or "mine," that [is what is meant] here in this aggregate of phenomena such as form, contact, and so on, by the phrase "thus mine."

Or, regarding the meaning of the words: the construction is "it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramatthato*). The intention is that while it exists here from the perspective of ultimate reality as indicated by its nature as form, contact, and so forth, it does not exist as indicated by the phrase "thus to me.
However, he says "heard" with reference to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*), calling it a "designation of what exists" (*vijjamānapaññatti*).
And here, the governing topic is "by way of the true, factual, and ultimate reality" (*saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena*).

“*Yaṃ hī*,” etc., is an elucidation of that [term] or a demonstration of the reason. The meaning is: that sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*) which is apprehended by the ear—that is, by the ear-door or by the consciousness dependent upon it—and is thus to be attained.
By this, he shows that the sense-sphere of sound is taken here in the sense of the object (the *kamma-sādhana*).

Having thus determined the nature of the designations according to the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he now states "tathā" and so forth, determining the nature of the designations such as "evaṃ" among the six types of designation mentioned even by a method independent of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For the designations beginning with "upādāpaññatti" were stated by the Master, the compiler himself, independently of the ancient *Aṭṭhakathās*. [The] detailed exposition...
This should be understood from the *Abhidhamma-ṭṭhakathā*. The meaning is as follows: "That" (*taṃ*) refers to those various classes of phenomena (*dhammajātaṃ*).
Based on the phenomena that have come within the range of hearing, it is used in the sense of referring back to the determination of their mode of apprehension; thus it is said "this" (*evaṃ*).

And based on the aggregates included within one's own continuity, it is said "mine" (*me*). [The phrase] "based on and depending upon phenomena distinguished as form, feeling, and so forth" means having taken them as a support.
Taking [the parts] as the cause, it is a designation based on a substrate (*upādāpaññatti*), such as: “A chariot or a house by depending on this or that component;
a jar or a cloth by depending on this or that color, taste, and so forth; time or direction by depending on the revolution of the moon and sun,” and so on.
And this is called a “designation” (*paññatti*) in the sense of being that which is designated, not in the sense of the act of designating. As for that meaning...
This is a designation of what does not exist. It is said to be "expressible in relation to what has been seen, etc.

because it is expressible by taking what has been seen, heard, and cognized as a basis, a support, and a point of reference. For even when the conventional usage of "heard" occurs in regard to the sense-sphere of sound—which lacks the intrinsic nature of what has been seen and so forth—it refers back to what has been seen, heard, and cognized, just as the terms "second" and "third" refer back to the "first" and so on.
That which proceeds by depending [on something else] is called "comparative designation" (*upanidhāpaññatti*). This, moreover, is of many kinds:

comparative designation by depending on something other than that (*tadaññapekkhūpanidhā*), comparative designation by what is in hand (*hatthagatūpanidhā*), comparative designation by association (*sampayuttūpanidhā*), comparative designation by superimposition (*samāropitūpanidhā*), comparative designation by proximity (*avidūragatūpanidhā*), comparative designation by resemblance (*paṭibhāgūpanidhā*), comparative designation by abundance (*tabbahulūpanidhā*), comparative designation by excellence (*tabbisiṭṭhūpanidhā*), and so forth.
Among these, this [present case] is like [the expression] "the second, the third," and so on.
Because the first [terms] and so forth are stated in mutual dependence upon the seen and so forth, they are called "descriptions by way of relative reference" (*tadaññapekkhūpanidhāpaññatti*).

Having thus shown the meaning that must be demonstrated—namely, that even through such description there is the attainment of the referent (*atthādhigamanīyatā*)—he now speaks the passage beginning with "And here...
while determining and illustrating the meaning that is to be clarified by the inherent power of the words (*saddasāmatthiya*). "Herein" (*ettha*) means in these three statements.

The word *ca* is an introductory particle (*upanyāsa*), because it is employed by one desiring to begin a new subject matter. When "heard" (*suta*) is stated, the sense that "what was not heard is excluded" is thereby made manifest;

therefore, the specific modes of the Sutta personally realized by himself, which were manifested by the word "heard," are restated by the Elder with the word "thus" (*evaṃ*). Thus, by means of this word *evaṃ*, non-confusion is indeed indicated.
Therefore he says: "By the word 'thus,' he illuminates non-delusion. And "non-delusion" means non-delusion regarding the Sutta exactly as it was heard.
He establishes that very point through reasoning and by way of contrast (vyatireka) with the Sutta to be cited below, beginning with "For not," which is manifold and difficult to penetrate.
Thus, when the Sutta is manifold and difficult to penetrate, how could one who is deluded be capable of its manifold penetration?
"It will be so. By means of this reasoning and this contrast, it is meant that the meaning characterized by the Elder’s state of being undeluded in that regard is made known.

This applies accordingly to such cases. Because the Elder demonstrates above, exactly as it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One, the manner [of the teaching], it is said: "It demonstrates the non-forgetfulness of the Sutta."
It has been stated. "At another time" means at a time subsequent to the time of hearing [the teaching]. Regarding the phrase "he acknowledges...":
it is said that he acknowledges this because for him—unlike the lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel for the Elder—it remains undiminished and unobscured.
By the meaning thus illustrated, what is being made manifest? To this he says: "Thus for him," and so forth.

In this context, *iccassa* means *iti assa* (thus for him). Because it illustrates both non-delusion (*asammoha*) and non-confusion (*asammosa*), it is connected with the phrase "the accomplishment of wisdom for that elder" (*assa therassa paññāsiddhi*), and so forth.

By "non-delusion" (*asammohena*) is meant the absence of delusion. The accomplishment of wisdom (*paññāsiddhi*) occurs through the collection of qualities such as concentration (*samādhi*) and the rest, which are free from wisdom-deficiency;

for it is accomplished by the power of co-nascence (*sahajātādi-satti*) inherent in the wisdom associated with those qualities. Alternatively, it refers to that which is reckoned as wisdom (*paññāsaṅkhāta*) because it is the direct opposite of delusion (*sammoha*).

"By that which is born of the Dhamma. For the perfection of wisdom at a later time is established by means of the wisdom produced at the time of hearing, since it is accomplished through the primary condition (*upanissaya*) and other such factors.
In the other cases as well, the method should be applied accordingly.
To the question, "What is clarified by the meaning thus explained? he says: "Therein," and so forth. "Therein" refers to those two kinds [of persons].
Regarding phenomena (*dhammesu*): the aspect of the phrasing to be penetrated is not very deep;

there, one must simply perform the task of retaining what has been heard as it was taught. Therefore, the function of mindfulness (*sati*) is predominant there, while wisdom (*paññā*) is subordinate. Thus it is said, "preceded by wisdom," and so forth. For the etymology is:
that which is preceded by wisdom is "wisdom-preceded. And here, "being preceded" means being the primary factor.

As in such passages as “mental phenomena are preceded by mind,” and furthermore, just as in the case of eye-consciousness and so forth, although advertence and the like are preceding factors, they are subordinate because they do not cognize that object;

so too, since it is subordinate despite being a preceding factor, the etymological derivation “wisdom is its precursor” (paññāpubbaṅgamā etissā) is also appropriate. And here, “preceding-ness” (pubbaṅgamatā) means the state of going before.
Thus, two kinds of "preceding" (pubbaṅgama)—namely, that which precedes by way of co-arising (sahajāta) and that which precedes by way of pre-existence (purejāta)—are possible here.
Just as it is in this case, so too in the expression “preceded by” (pubbaṅgamāya), this method should be understood according to what is applicable.
Having thus explained the statement regarding "capability," he asks, "What is implied by that? and replies with the words, "By means of the conjunction of the capability of both," and so forth.
In this context, "endowed with meaning and phrasing" means being complete in both meaning and phrasing;
or, being possessed of the six factors of meaning beginning with "manifestation" (*saṅkāsanā*) and the six factors of phrasing beginning with "syllables" (*akkhara*);
or, being full of flavor through the essence known as meaning and phrasing. The Dhamma of the scriptures alone is sevenfold because it is a repository for the nine supramundane jewels.
The "Dhamma-treasury" (dhammakosa) is like a storehouse (*kosa*) containing a collection of the ten kinds of jewels; likewise, it is the "Dhamma-storehouse" (*dhammabhaṇḍāgāra*).

One who is appointed to that is a "keeper of the Dhamma-storehouse" (*dhammabhaṇḍāgārika*). Alternatively, one is a "storehouse-keeper" (*bhaṇḍāgārika*) because he is like a keeper of various royal goods;
thus, he is a "storehouse-keeper of the Dhamma," which is shown by pointing out the similarity between them.
Having been distinguished [from others], he was called "the Treasurer of the Dhamma. As it is said:
"O Sage, you are Ānanda by name, one who has heard much, who upholds the Dhamma, and who has mastered all the teachings in the Dispensation—the guardian of the Dhamma."
Furthermore, he illustrates the meaning that is to be shown by the phrase “another method,” and so forth.

Since the meanings of the words denoted by the term “thus” (evaṃ)—namely, the indication of mode, the demonstration of aspect, and the determination of limit—have as their object the unerring true nature of phenomena (saddhamma), it is appropriate to illustrate wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) toward those objects through those meanings;
thus it is said: “He illustrates... [wise attention]... ‘Thus. By the phrase “unwisely,” and so forth...
This is a demonstration of the probative reason (*ñāpakahetu*) by way of negative concomitance (*byatireka*). In this context, the word "hi" is seen in some instances;

it signifies a cause, meaning "because. By this very statement, since the realization of various aspects arises for one who attends wisely (*yoniso manasikaroti*), that [cause] is understood through its effect—just as fire is known through smoke—and thus he demonstrates the positive concomitance (*tadanvaya*) by means of presumptive testimony (*atthāpatti*). This...
The method is to be applied everywhere as appropriate. Regarding the question, "Friend, where was the *Brahmajāla* spoken?

and so forth, it is said that "it illuminates non-distraction" because, with respect to the discourse about to be presented—which has now reached its formal introduction by means of the word "heard" (*suta*)—such hearing in the presence of the Blessed One is not possible without concentration.

By means of the negative reason (vyatireka-hetu) beginning with “of one whose mind is distracted,” he shows the indicative cause and then supports that very point with the words “for thus,” and so forth.
“Of all perfections” means of the perfection consisting of all aspects, such as the meaning, the phrasing, the teacher, and the purpose.
To the question, “What is revealed by this? he says: “And herein, by means of wise attention,” and so forth. “Herein” refers to these two factors.

By the phrase beginning with “For one whose mind is distracted,” it is stated that non-distraction, acting as the cause, and reliance upon a true person (sappurisūpanissaya) are capable of accomplishing the hearing of the True Dhamma (saddhammassavana), which is the result;
however, it is not stated that non-distraction is capable of accomplishing reliance upon a true person. Why is this? Because for those whose minds are distracted...

Because the state of attending upon true persons (*sappurisa*) is established by its very nature. For it is precisely because it is evident through its own meaning that it was not explicitly mentioned. Here it is said:

just as the establishment of the causes—namely, one’s own right aspiration and previously performed merit—which result in the fruit of wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), was stated because they are inseparable from it;
likewise, [the establishment of] hearing the True Dharma and relying upon true persons, which result in the fruit of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), [is understood].
The accomplishment of the causes— namely, being unlearned and lacking reliance upon true persons— might be expected; yet, even though that is so,
by means of the words "for one whose mind is not distracted," etc., which establish the capacity [of the practice],
there is the accomplishment of the very result, which is the hearing of the True Dhamma, through the cause consisting of non-distraction and reliance upon true persons.
It has been stated [thus]; but why was it stated in this way? It is said: for such an establishment was stated because of the possibility of another underlying intention (*adhippāya*).

This, however, is the intention here: hearing the True Dhamma and relying upon a person of integrity (*sappurisa*) are not exclusively the causes of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), because they are external conditions;
whereas non-distraction, like reliance upon a person of integrity, is [itself] a condition for hearing the True Dhamma.

Because it is an internal cause, it is an absolute cause; therefore, since there exists an absolute cause, what is the purpose of postulating the existence of an effect with respect to a non-absolute cause?

Thus, its establishment is stated in that very way. And here, the first demonstration of the cause’s establishment by means of the effect is like [inferring] the presence of rain upstream from the swelling of a river; the second is by means of the cause.
The demonstration of the accomplishment of the fruit is like the occurrence of rain through the rising of clouds that rain unconditionally.
With the words "Another method," etc., he states the meaning to be explained in another way; the connection is "because it does not exist. "In this way...
[omission] ...is the exposition of various modes" was stated below; and that mode is the consciousness-process reckoned as following the ear-door.

The manner in which the entire excellence of the Dispensation is mastered— by way of discerning the distinctions between the meaning and the phrasing of the Blessed One’s word through the mind-stream’s engagement with the object in various ways, which is termed the grasping of diverse meanings and expressions—

is what is meant by "thus auspicious. It is "thus auspicious" because it is the cause for bringing about the complete fulfillment of the welfare of others through the aforementioned grasping of diverse meanings and expressions.
"Sundara-seṭṭho" is either a compound word (*samāsapada*) or it means "one for whom such a good [person] exists.
"Appaṇihito" means not directed; "one for whom the self is rightly not directed" is thus [the meaning], and [the text refers to] him.

"The attainment of the final pair of wheels" refers to the attainment of the two qualities consisting of right self-direction and previously performed merit. For it is precisely through the successive occurrence of these qualities that...

The state of being a wheel (*cakka*) is in the sense of causing to proceed. Alternatively, beings move by means of it toward a fortunate existence (*sampattibhava*), or they move within fortunate existences;
thus it is a wheel. It is with reference to this that it was said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels;
endowed with which the fourfold wheel of gods and humans rolls on," and so forth. Furthermore, the order of the last [two] here follows the sequence of the teaching.
"The attainment of the first two wheels" refers to the attainment of the two qualities consisting of dwelling in a suitable locality and reliance upon a virtuous person.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. Therefore, by the words "for it is not," etc., he states the reason here—that the preceding cause belongs to the preceding [wheel] alone.
To show what is revealed by that, he says "thus for her," etc. Thus, by means of this attainment of the four wheels which serves as the cause.
Of that elder. "By the accomplishment of the final pair of wheels" means by the accomplishment through the existence of the final pair of wheels.
"Purity of disposition" (*āsayasuddhi*) refers to the removal from afar of those defilements which are the causes of impurity for the two kinds of disposition:

namely, the conformable patience known as insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-ñāṇa*) known as the knowledge of one's own karma (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*) and path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
Purity. For that same dyad is the resort for pure beings who rely on the turning away from the round of existence.
One whose self is rightly directed and who has performed merit in the past is one whose disposition is pure. Thus it is said:
"A mind rightly directed makes him better than before," and, "You have performed merit, Ānanda; apply yourself to striving, and soon you will be free from the taints."
However, some say that "the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) is the disposition (āsaya)," but that is indeed incorrect because it contradicts the statement:

"And by that purity of disposition, there is the accomplishment of proficiency in realization. [Objection: Even so, is it not improper for the purity of the disposition—which is reckoned as path-knowledge—to be [said to result] from that accomplishment of proficiency in realization? [Reply: It is not improper, because of the preceding [context].
Because it is the causal condition for the path, the subsequent paths, and the fruits.

"Purity of application" (*payoga-suddhi*) means purity through the clarity of the application of hearing the Dhamma preceded by wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), or purity through the faultless nature of all bodily and vocal applications.
For one who dwells in a suitable location and associates with virtuous persons possesses the aforementioned purified application. By such purified [application]...

With a mind undistracted, through the practice of hearing the Dhamma preceded by wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), and through bodily and vocal conduct that brings about the absence of remorse, one becomes confident in the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
Since the Elder was such a person, it is understood from this that the Elder’s purity of practice was established by means of the accomplishment of the two preceding wheels.
To the question, "What is clarified by that? he says, "And by that," etc. [This refers to] the accomplishment of proficiency in realization (*adhigama*).
The accomplishment of skillfulness occurs in the attainment known as penetration (*paṭivedha*).

For in the Commentaries, "penetration" is explained as "attainment" because it is that which is to be attained and that which is to be penetrated; and it is called "scripture" (*āgama*) because by means of it one arrives at one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth, or because it is to be thoroughly understood and known.

To the question, "What was manifested by that? he says, "Thus" (iti), and so forth. "Thus" means in the manner already stated; alternatively, it is a designation of the reason, meaning "because it is established.

"Statement" refers to the introductory statement from the world and from the Dhamma. In order to make that meaning known through a simile established both from the worldly perspective and from the perspective of the Dhamma, he says, "Like the break of dawn," and so on.
For it is said: "In this world, some wise people understand the meaning through a simile."
For it has been said: "Aruṇa" refers to the ray that arises prior to the rising of the sun;
its "rising" (*uggamana*) is such that it ought to be the precursor and forerunner of the sun as it rises, as it is about to rise, or as it ascends from its place of rising.
This is what is meant: for a Thera of such a kind, distinguished by his mastery of the scriptures and his realization of the Dhamma...
The statement regarding the introductory cause (*nidāna*) ought to serve as the precursor to the Blessed One’s speech;
since it has attained the status of a cause, this collection of meanings is thus manifested.
Now, furthermore, by means of those things that illuminate the meaning which was previously stated—namely, that which is characterized by non-delusion and non-confusion—it is further explained:
Explaining the meaning that is to be made manifest by the words *evaṃ* and *suta*, he says, “Another method,” and so forth.

Therein, by the phrases “by that which illustrates penetration in its various modes” and “by that which illustrates penetration into the distinctions of what is to be heard,” he states the meaning to be illustrated—namely, non-delusion and non-confusion—which were previously indicated by those words; for through non-delusion, there is penetration in its various modes.

And because the penetration of the various categories of what is to be heard is accomplished through non-confusion. However, the words "of himself" (*attano*) and so forth serve to clarify the meaning that is to be made manifest.

Therefore, it was said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla: "By means of the words *evaṃ* and *suta*, which indicate the penetration of various aspects, and because they demonstrate the elder’s lack of delusion and non-confusion regarding both the meaning and the phrasing, [it is shown] by way of the four analytical knowledges (*catupaṭisambhidā*)."
“It shows eight yojanas. These two phrases contain the core of the reason;

what is meant is that they illuminate the meaning to be explained, namely, the penetration consisting of various modes [of understanding] and the penetration consisting of the distinctions of what is to be heard.

*Sabbhāva* is the state of being present (*santassa vijjamānassa bhāvo*); it is the presence of the attainment through the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of meaning (*attha*) and of inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).

Likewise, there is also the reading "sambhavam. "Sambhava" means arising; thus, it refers to the arising of the attainments of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) regarding meaning and inspired eloquence.

The same applies to the other cases as well. Regarding the phrase "by that which illuminates the penetration into the various divisions of what is to be heard," although this word *suta* (heard) is stated in a general sense—either because of its proximity to the word *evam* (thus), or with reference to what is yet to be explained—[it is specified here].
This shows that it "touches upon the specific qualities of the Dhamma to be heard.

Furthermore, since the meanings of the speech and the purposes of the Pāḷi—comprising the Dhamma to be heard—are to be demonstrated here, and because the knowledge occurring within the three types of knowledge possesses manifold aspects, it is appropriate to indicate the presence of the analytical knowledges of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*) and of expression (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*) by means of the word *evaṃ*, which illuminates the penetration of those very aspects. Regarding the Dhamma to be heard...

However, it should be understood that the word *suta* (heard), which indicates the various kinds of what is to be heard, appropriately demonstrates the presence of the analytical knowledge of the language of the Dhamma (*dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidā*), because it serves as the cause for attaining the goal, because by means of it the remaining varieties of causes are included, and because it possesses the nature of a linguistic derivation (*nirutti*).
Indeed, in order to make this very meaning known, [the commentary] says: "by way of indicating non-delusion, by way of indicating non-confusion," and so forth.
And having stated "it was spoken thus," he has now,
by means of the words *evaṃ* (thus) and *sutaṃ* (heard)— which illuminate the meaning to be illustrated consisting of non-delusion and non-confusion—
having first explained the meaning to be expressed, [proceeds] to explain the meaning to be illustrated consisting of wise attention and non-distraction.
Illuminating the meaning that must be revealed by those very lamps, he said, “And thus,” and so forth. For therein, by the phrases “‘Thus’...
[etc.]... speaking” and “‘Suta’ (heard)... [etc.]... speaking,” he states the meaning to be illuminated—namely, wise attention and non-distraction—which was previously indicated by those sounds.
Furthermore, by the words “These were by me,” and so forth, he indicates the meaning to be revealed as that which characterizes the application of hearing.
Because the application of hearing is accomplished by way of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), it was said with reference to that very point. For thus it was stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla:
"The hearing, retention, and verbal service regarding the teachings of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) are specifically dependent upon the fixing of the ear;
