therefore, having connected them with the word 'heard' (*suta*), which illustrates non-distraction... [and] the thorough investigation and penetration of the teachings of the scriptures by means of mental vision (*manoviññāṇa*).
In particular, these [teachings] are dependent upon mental attention (*manasikāra*); therefore, by means of words that illuminate them, he makes known this meaning:
"These teachings have been examined by me with the mind and well-penetrated through vision. Thus it is said: "And thus... he illuminates.

In this context, "teachings" (*dhammā*) refers to the teachings of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). "Examined by the mind" means: "Herein, virtue (*sīla*) is taught; herein, concentration (*samādhi*)."
"Herein is wisdom; herein are just so many connections"—thus it has been examined by the mind according to such classifications.

"Well-penetrated by view" means that the aforementioned material and immaterial phenomena have been thoroughly defined and penetrated by means of the view known as "acceptance through reflection" (nijjhānakkhanti) or the "full understanding of the known" (ñātapariññā), [understanding them] thus: "This is material form; this is the extent of material form," and so forth.
The service of hearing and retaining through speech is specifically dependent upon the attentive listening to the teachings of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma);
therefore, by means of the very words that illustrate this, it reveals the sense: "Many teachings have been heard, retained, and mastered by me through speech.
Thus it is said: "'Suta' (heard) ... [etc. ... illustrates this. In this context, "suta" means cognized by way of the ear-door.
“Dhātā” means it has been firmly established in the mind, like lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel, by means of achieving a state of well-settled mindfulness.
“Vacasā paricitā” means it has been mastered through speech, having been familiarized and recited by means of attaining proficiency.
Now, explaining the meaning that is to be clarified by the two aforementioned words which illustrate the two points to be manifested:

He says, “By both of these,” and so forth. Therein, “by both of these” means by that twofold sound which, according to the aforementioned method, makes manifest the meaning to be manifested, whether in the former or the latter mode.
“Illuminating the perfection of the meaning and the phrasing” is a statement of the reason for generating reverence.
He clarifies that very reason through a negative formulation (*vyatireka*) by way of logical reasoning (*yutti*).
Or he makes it firm by means of the passage beginning with, “For it is complete in both meaning and phrasing.

Here, in the word *asuṇanto*, the suffix *-anta* denotes either a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*). From “great benefit” means from a great benefit. “Excluded on all sides” means excluded in every respect.
By means of these two words, which illuminate the meaning that is to be manifested, he manifests the meaning that is to be emphasized: “Thus...”

He said, "‘Me sutan’ti,” and so forth. Although these words were previously applied to their respective individual meanings, the phrase "by the whole" is stated here to make it known that they are taken as having the status of expressing the power of a single meaning alone.
And although the word *me* has been joined with what precedes it in this place, because the words *evaṃ* and *suta* accompany it and are inseparable from it, [they must be understood here].
And it should be understood that it was spoken in such a manner. "Proclaimed by the Tathāgata" means known in its various aspects or spoken by the Tathāgata.
"Not attributing to oneself" means not placing [the thought] "this is mine" within oneself; here, this genitive case is used in the sense of a locative.
"The domain of the bad person" means the sphere of the bad person; and in terms of meaning, this refers to the state of being ungrateful, as in: "In this case, someone..."

“A wicked bhikkhu, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, burns himself”—thus were the modes of ignoble speech spoken by the Blessed One as an illustration of a great thief. And so it was said: “The Tathāgata... not burning [himself]. The word *hutvā* (“having been”) is to be supplied here.
Likewise, the phrase “professing discipleship” is a statement describing the manner of entering the stage of a true person (*sappurisa*).

But would it not be the case that the statement regarding the transcendence of the plane of the unworthy and so forth is purposeless, since the Elder Ānanda lacked the overweening pride of thinking "this is my word," and the Elder Mahākassapa and others likewise lacked any such suspicion? This is not so;
for by one who says "Thus have I heard," this meaning also is made manifest, since the very purpose is being shown. By that—

For he demonstrates only the matter that is to be experienced in that manner; it should be understood that this does not arise from the elder Ānanda’s overestimation (*adhimāna*), nor from the suspicion of the elder Mahākassapa and others at that time.
However, some say: "That statement was made with regard to the reflections of the deities;
therefore, such an objection has no place. At that time, it is said, for certain...
Then a reflection arose in the minds of the deities: "The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, and this Venerable Ānanda is skilled in teaching;
he is now teaching the Dhamma. He is born of the Sakyan clan, the brother of the Tathāgata, and the son of his father’s younger brother.
Does he teach the Dhamma that he has realized for himself, or does he merely repeat the words of the Blessed One exactly as he heard them?"
Having understood their very reflections in the mind, for the sake of protecting them and for the purpose of transcending the plane of the unworthy person (asappurisa), this power was manifested.
That aforementioned state of ignoble speech is the "untrue Dhamma" (asaddhamma);

and the profession of discipleship, which consists in rising above that state, is the "true Dhamma" (saddhamma). This being so, he shows the same original meaning through a different method of exposition.

It should be understood thus. Furthermore, the mass of unwholesome states proceeding by way of hypocrisy, flattery, and so forth, is the non-Dhamma (asaddhamma), while the state of being free from those is the True Dhamma (saddhamma).
The passage beginning with “entirely” (kevalaṃ) is a restatement of this same meaning by means of a different formulation;
it liberates one from the aforementioned state of ignoble speech. The meaning is that by professing discipleship, one refers back to the Teacher.
Furthermore, one liberates oneself from the act of [claiming] the Teacher’s appearance, because the suspicion of such an act might arise.
By referring to the Teacher, saying, "I have heard this very word of the Blessed One, the Teacher," there is the manifestation of another meaning.
Expressions such as "the Victor’s word" also show an alternative formulation, or they are simply manifestations of another meaning. It causes [one] to attain.
It demonstrates. It is a "guide" (*netti*) because it leads beings, as appropriate, toward the benefits pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal;
thus, the Dhamma itself is the guide. And here, according to the method already stated, the intended meaning should be understood in both ways.
Furthermore, by means of the phrase beginning with "Moreover," it emphasizes another matter that is to be emphasized. In that context, the state of having been produced...

The state of having proceeded by way of a teaching. "Expounding the previous statement" means making clear the very words of the Blessed One that were previously found to exist by way of being taught by the Blessed One; the connection is "this statement.

[He is] one who is confident through the four grounds of self-confidence, or one endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence which serve as the cause for confidence. [He is] the possessor of the ten powers of knowledge.

Of one who stands in the supreme position known as that of a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*); or, in the sense of "this belongs to the bull" (*usabha*), of one who stands in the state known as "bull-like," which is characterized by an unshakable nature.

Of one who roars the lion’s roar through many methods as described in such discourses as the *Sīhapuppha Sutta*, beginning with: "In this very way, monks, when a Tathāgata arises in the world... he teaches the Dhamma."

"Among all beings," or "of the supreme among all beings. And here, the compound is not formed by way of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), because there is an absence of the defining characteristic of selection.
For in all cases, it is stated exactly thus in the honored texts and in the texts of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
"Of the Lord of beings through the Dhamma"; they also say this means "of the Lord of the Dhamma itself" by way of its production. The remaining two phrases...
This is an exposition of another aspect of this same meaning: [the Buddha] who, like a lamp for the world, is possessed of the lamp called the Dhamma by virtue of being its originator;

for it is said: “‘The Dhamma-body,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata. Or, he is possessed of the Dhamma which has become the refuge of the world, or possessed of the refuge known as the Dhamma.
“For what reason? ‘What if I... [as before] ...were to dwell depending upon that very Dhamma, honoring it, revering it, respecting it, and worshipping it’—thus it was said.

This is the word of that Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who sets in motion the excellent wheel consisting of the true Dhamma such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), or who sets in motion the sovereign wheel of command of the true Dhamma; it was spoken in his very presence.
It should be construed as "received by me. Regarding the word *byañjana*: it refers to a sentence consisting of a collection of words.
"Doubt (*kaṅkhā*) or uncertainty (*vimati*)"—here, *kaṅkhā* is doubt firmly established [in the mind], while *vimati* is a mere state of mental wavering that does not involve excessive preoccupation.
"This was received by me in person" is the statement of the reason why it should not be done otherwise. By oneself...

By stating that he was "explaining the previous statement" rather than "admitting the state [of having] produced [faith]," this is a statement of the cause for the destruction of lack of faith and the production of the perfection of faith.
With the words beginning "Therefore by this," he shows the aforementioned meaning by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*).
By saying, “Thus have I heard,” the Venerable Ānanda— being a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One of the Gotama clan,
or a disciple connected to the Gotama clan— indicates that he has received [this teaching] directly from the Blessed One and that it was spoken by the Blessed One;
and by that very indication, the absence of faults such as slips of the tongue or incorrect terminology is established within the Dispensation.

The meaning is that it destroys lack of faith and increases faith. Herein, the three subsequent applications of meaning beginning with the fifth are shown by taking the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "manner" (*ākāra*) and so forth, without grasping any specific distinction;

the three following those are elucidated by taking the word *evaṃ* specifically in the sense of "manner"; but the final three, in their respective order, [take it] in the sense of manner, in the sense of illustration, and...
It should be understood that the word *evaṃ* is employed here by taking it in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
And in this regard, there are these verses: “Showing, illuminating, manifesting, analyzing, and experiencing—this is the fivefold meaning [of ‘thus’] through its connection with action.”
"By tradition it is received; by its occurrence in various meanings it is established;
thus have I heard—thus, in these three words, the one who knows the method [should apply it].
Now, the word *eka* is seen in the senses of "other," "best," "without companion," "number," and so forth. For instance, it is used in such passages as: "The self and the world are eternal..."
In such passages as "And some assert: 'This alone is true, all else is false,'" it is seen in the sense of "other";
in "one-pointedness of mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*), in the sense of "foremost"; in "alone, withdrawn," in the sense of "without companion";
and in "Monks, there is indeed one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," in the sense of "number. Here too, it is used in the sense of "number" alone.

Showing this, he said: “‘One’ is a designation for the delimitation of counting. The meaning is that the word ‘one’ is a designation for the delimitation of counting by way of its being neither less nor more—namely, that this occasion is indeed one, not two or three.
Thus, when there is the inquiry as to what it delimits, he said “occasion,” showing that it is so stated. Therefore he said: “‘Occasion’...”

“...the description of the delimited. By this phrase—“one... [etc. ...the illumination”—he shows that even though it is stated by way of being delimited by a boundary, because it is not specifically determined in its own form as “this is the time,” it is indeed an indefinite statement.
Now, having shown the multiplicity of meanings of the word *samaya* by way of extracting the meanings, [he states] the meaning intended here:
Restricting [the meaning], he says "therein" (*tattha*), and so forth. "Therein" means in those two phrases, "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*);
the connection is that the word *samaya* is applied equally [to both]. But it is not seen [to be used] because it occurs here only in one of those meanings.
In "conjunction" (*samavāye*) means in the assembly of conditions; the meaning is the conjunction of causes. In "moment" (*khaṇe*) means in an occasion. In "causes and views" (*hetudiṭṭhisu*).
Regarding both the cause and the conviction. "Assa" refers to the word *samaya*.

In the phrase "having taken into account the time (*kāla*) and the occasion (*samaya*)," here "time" means the appropriate time for approaching [the Teacher]. "Occasion" means the convergence of conditions for that very [approach];

in terms of meaning, however, it is the bodily strength corresponding to that [occasion] as well as the absence of obstacles or dangers related to it. "Taking into account" (*upādāna*) means by means of knowledge.
The grasping of these; therefore, the meaning is: having grasped and reflected upon the time and the occasion as they have been described by means of wisdom.

This is what is meant: "If tomorrow will be the appropriate time for our departure, if there will be sufficient strength in the body, and if no other discomfort resulting from the journey will arise, then [this] time and..."
And having considered the time, which is defined as the concurrence of the causes for going, [he thought]: "Perhaps we might even come tomorrow.
"Khaṇa" means opportunity. For the appearance of a Tathāgata and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the path, because it is the cause for obtaining its requisite conditions.
And "khaṇa" is indeed "samaya. The intention is that what is called both "khaṇa" and "samaya" is one and the same.
"One and a half months of the summer remain; it is the season of heat. The first month of the rains is the season of feverish intensity. "A great assembly" (*mahāsamaya*) means a great multitude.

Or this may be a compound or an analysis [of the same term]. "A forest that has grown" is *pavana*; in that [place], meaning in a grove known as the Great Forest (*Mahāvana*) on the outskirts of Kapilavatthu.
"And at that time" (*samayopi kho*): here, "time" (*samaya*) refers to the fulfillment of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
*Hetu*. "Bhaddāli" is the name of that bhikkhu. This is what is meant:
"Bhaddāli, there is one reason that ought to have been penetrated by you, yet it has not been penetrated or observed by you. To the question "What is that reason?
he says: "The Blessed One too," and so forth.
In the passage beginning with “Uggahamāno,” *māna* is the personal name of that wanderer;
however, because he was capable of learning various crafts, people knew him as “Uggahamāno” (the Learner), and thus he is called “Uggahamāno.
He was the son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, hence he is called Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta. It is said that he was an attendant of Devadatta. At a time...
One who speaks forth their doctrine (samayappavādaka) is so called because they speak their view (diṭṭhi) clearly there; the meaning is "one who proclaims a doctrine" (diṭṭhippavādaka).

It is said that at that place, brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, as well as renunciants such as the Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and Paribbājakas, having assembled together, spoke forth, discussed, and explained their respective doctrines in detail.
Therefore, that monastery is called "Samayappavādaka" (The Proclaimer of Doctrines).
It is called "Tindukācīra" because it was surrounded by a row of *timbarūsaka* trees known as *tindukācīra*. It is called "Ekasālaka" because there was a single hall (*sālā*) there.
Furthermore, although there was originally only one hall, later on, due to the presence of the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, who possessed great merit, many...
A *sālā* was built; therefore, because it was first constructed as that single *sālā*, it is called "Ekasālaka" (The Single-Hall) according to the name it previously received.
That park, covered with flowers and fruits, was a pleasure garden belonging to Queen Mallikā, the consort of King Pasenadi;
hence it is said, "in Mallikā’s park. "He dwells there" means he lives there in comfort.

"In the present life" (*diṭṭhe dhamme*) means in one's own directly perceived personal existence. "Welfare" (*attha*) means progress. Because one must go to (*samparetabba*) or properly reach (*sammā pāpuṇitabba*) it due to karma and defilements, it is called the "future state" (*samparāya*);
that is, the other world. That which pertains to this is "pertaining to the future state" (*samparāyika*), meaning welfare pertaining to the other world.
"The realization of welfare" (*atthābhisamaya*) refers to the attainment of the benefit comprised by both types of welfare as previously described. For even welfare pertaining to the future state—
Because the cause has been brought to fruition, it is said to be "attained"; thus, having combined these two meanings into one, it is called "the realization of the goal" (*atthābhisamaya*).
One "reaches" or grasps various objects by means of *dhī*, which is wisdom (*paññā*); or, one who possesses this *dhī*—wisdom—is a *dhīra*.
*Paṇḍā* is said to be wisdom. For that [wisdom] penetrates and proceeds even into subtle matters, or [it perceives] the mode of oppression and so forth of suffering and the rest.
"Paṇḍā" means wisdom (*paññā*). One who has gone by means of that is "wise" (*paṇḍita*). Alternatively, one for whom wisdom has arisen (*itā*) is wise;
or, one who goes by way of the course of knowledge (*ñāṇagati*) is wise. "Through the complete realization of conceit" means through the complete abandonment of conceit.

Here, "complete" refers to abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*) via the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamaggañāṇa*). "End" means the final limit. "Affliction" refers to the oppression of one who possesses it.
*Hiṃsanaṃ* means non-expansion; that same meaning is expressed by changing the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*.

The sense of being conditioned (*saṅkhataṭṭho*) is the state of having been produced through conditions after coming together. The sense of burning (*santāpaṭṭho*) is the tormenting and scorching by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth.

The sense of change (*vipariṇāmaṭṭho*) is that which must undergo transformation in two ways: through aging and through death. It is to be fully understood (*abhisametabbo*) and penetrated (*paṭivijjhitabbo*).
The meaning of *abhisamaya* (clear comprehension) refers to oppression (*pīḷana*) and so forth themselves.

For these are spoken of as "the meaning of clear comprehension" by being brought into a state of unity through their quality of being what must be clearly comprehended. Alternatively, the meaning of *abhisamaya*—that is, the object (*gocara*) of penetration (*paṭivedha*)—is called "the meaning of clear comprehension.

Thus, they are spoken of as a single entity based on the commonality of their entering into the state of being the objects of that [penetration]. And here, because prefixes are merely indicators, [the term] denotes the respective meaning.
The term *samaya* alone—thus, even when extracting the meaning of the word *samaya*, the form *abhisamaya* (with its prefix) is stated.

Regarding those meanings, this is the etymological analysis (*vacanattha*): it is called *samaya* because it comes together (*sameti*) or assembles (*samaveti*) in proximity by way of being a cooperative cause;
it is a collection (*samavāya*). It is so called because the noble path and the holy life come together (*sameti*) or meet (*samāgacchati*) here, by way of the person who is the locus of that [path].

*Samaya* means time (*khaṇa*). It is called *samaya* because phenomena or beings come together (*samenti*) therein, or because they meet (*saṅgacchanti*) with co-nascent factors and so forth, or with [the characteristics of] arising and so on;

thus it is time. For, although time does not exist as a substantial entity apart from the mere occurrence of phenomena, it is nevertheless designated as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the occurrence of phenomena, and it is spoken of by means of a form established through mere conceptualization, as if it were an instrument (*karaṇa*). *Samaṃ*, *sammā*...

Or, *samaya* is the coming together, the occurrence, or the persistence of parts; it is a collection (*samūha*), as in the term "aggregate" (*samudāya*). For a collection is simply the co-existence of parts;
there is no such thing as a "collection" existing as a separate ultimate reality apart from its constituent parts.
It is called *samaya* because the fruit comes (*eti*) into being through the meeting of other conditions, or because it occurs (*eti*) from this [meeting]; thus, it is a cause (*hetu*).
As in the term “origination” (*samudaya*). For it brings about the state of its own fruit’s arising and persistence precisely through the convergence of other conditions.
It “comes together” (*sameti*) because, being a fetter (*saṃyojana*), it exists as a bond;

or, because it is a firm grasping, beings connected with it “go” (*ayanti*) by means of it, proceeding according to their respective inclinations—thus it is “origination” (*samaya*), namely, view. By means of the fetter of views...
For beings are indeed exceedingly bound [by them]. *Samaya* means meeting, conjunction, coincidence, or acquisition.
It is the going toward or reaching of cessation (*nirodha*); or, it is the correct going away, the non-occurrence, the abandoning—this is *samaya*.

That which is to be correctly approached and reached by means of knowledge is *abhisamaya*; it is the unerring intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena. By way of its being directed toward [that nature]...

"Abhisamaya" means that one correctly approaches, goes toward, and awakens to each respective intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); it is the awakening to the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhamma*) as they truly are.

Now, since words do not adhere to a mere meaning as intended, such that multiple meanings are expressed by a single word—then why has the word *samaya* been stated here with multiple meanings? This is true.
When specific words are taken into account—indeed, when specific words are taken into account—it is not possible for a single word to denote multiple meanings.
For that which is the meaning "time" (*kāla*) etc. denoted by the word *samaya* is not the same as that which expresses the meaning "collection" (*samūha*) etc.
However, in this context, the multiplicity of meanings of the word *samaya* is established by taking into account the commonality of those various meanings being expressible by the word *samaya*.

"Thus it is said. This applies everywhere in the extraction of the meaning. And there is this verse on the matter: "By resorting to the state of being expressible through common terms, one may state the meaning in many ways;
for a single word cannot be restricted to only one meaning."

Because categories such as *samavāya* (inherence) are impossible here, and because time must be referred to from the very outset, it is said: "But here, its meaning is time. For, since time is intended here as a causal condition (*nidāna*)—just like place, teacher, and so forth—it too is referred to in this context.
To the question, "By what kind of time does this [word] indicate? he says: "By that," etc. "By that" means by the meaning of time.
By the word *samaya*. "Half a month" is stated by way of fortnights; "forenoon," etc., by way of divisions of the day; "the first watch," etc., by way of watches.
By the word "etc.," moments (*khaṇa*), instants (*laya*), and so forth are included. The meaning is that it indicates a single time in an unrestricted manner.
But why is time specified here in an unrestricted manner, rather than in a restricted manner by way of seasons, years, and so on?
He said, “In that regard, although... and so forth. The connection is: “although it has been understood through wisdom and well-established, nevertheless.

It is not possible to retain it by speech, to recite it oneself, or to have it recited by another, because of its manifold nature and because much must be said, extending as far as the divisions of time. When it is said, “at one time,” [the meaning follows].
However, he shows by the phrase "having combined that meaning with a single word" that there is no such distinction of time as could be included within this [category].
Having thus shown the meaning of *samaya* (time/occasion) by way of time as commonly accepted in the world, he now says "Or these...
and so forth, in order to show the meaning of *samaya* by way of time as well-known in the Dispensation (*sāsana*). Furthermore:
Showing that this merit is indeed obtained when the word *samaya* is used without restricting it to seasons, years, and so forth, he says, "Or these which are *samayas*," and so on.
For a general designation settles upon a particular, since its scope is the exclusion of other particulars.
Therein, the connection is: "these which are *samayas*. And here, the Blessed One’s time of entering his mother’s womb is the *gabbhokkantī-samaya* (the occasion of descent into the womb).
The period of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) is the time when, having seen the four signs, one experiences a sense of urgency.

The period of ascetic practice (*dukkarakārika*) is the time of wandering for six years in order to attain full enlightenment. The period of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) is the time spent each day entering the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and their fruits;
specifically, it is the time of engaging in the attainment of absorption for seven weeks. The period of forty-five years is the time of teaching various doctrines.

“An occasion for teaching. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), occasions such as the Twin Miracle are included. “Manifested” means made evident by the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system, the appearance of radiance, and so forth.

When it is said, “at one time,” the intention is to indicate that since there are other times besides that, the specific occasion designated here as an “occasion for teaching” is what is meant by “at one time,” as established by the implication of the statement.
In order to show that certain portions of the aforementioned classifications are subsumed under other categories, the passage beginning with "And that which...

was stated. For therein, the occasion for the function of knowledge (*ñāṇakicca-samaya*) and the occasion for the practice for one's own benefit (*attahita-paṭipatti-samaya*) are included within the occasion of full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi-samaya*) alone.

The occasion of noble silence (*ariya-tuṇhībhāva-samaya*) is the occasion for dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra-samaya*). The occasion for the function of compassion (*karuṇākicca*), the practice for the benefit of others (*parahita-paṭipatti*), and the discourse on the Dhamma (*dhammakathā-samaya*) [are likewise subsumed].
This is the time for instruction; therefore, it should be understood that only a portion of those aforementioned types of occasions is shown here by way of another method.

With reference to the occasion stated in the passage, “Bhikkhus, when you have assembled, two things are to be done: either a discourse on the Dhamma or noble silence,” the phrase “on the occasions of the two things to be done when assembled” was spoken.
“On those occasions as well” means on the occasions of the practice of compassionate activity for the benefit of others, of discourse on the Dhamma, and of teaching.
Because there is no difference in meaning, it is stated as “on one occasion” with reference to a particular occasion.
Furthermore, instead of making the designation here by means of the locative case—as is done elsewhere—or by means of the instrumental case, it is expressed here by means of the accusative case.
Desiring to determine the purpose of the exposition (*niddesa*), he raises an objection by way of a question: “But why here? and so forth.
“Here” (*ettha*) refers to this phrase “at one time” (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*); the connection is that the exposition is made by means of the locative case.
It is called the locative because [the meaning] exists there; it is the location, and the grammatical form occurring therein is the locative case ending.
*Karaṇaṃ* (instrument) is that by which one performs or accomplishes an action; it is the cause for the production of an action. *Upayoga* (object) is that which is to be employed for an action;
it is the *kamma* (object). Regarding that, the word is likewise [used]. With the words "In those" (*tatthā*) and so forth, he addresses the aforementioned objection.
"In those" (*tattha*) refers to those three: the Abhidhamma, the Sutta-padas other than that, and the Vinaya. "Likewise" (*tathā*) refers to the locative case and the instrumental case.

"And because of the possibility of meaning" (*atthasambhavato*) should be construed [with the preceding]. The meaning is: "because of the possibility of [the meanings of] the locative case, the state, and the characteristic of a state;

and of the meanings of the cause and the instrument. "Here" (*idha*) means in this sutta-passage. "Otherwise" (*aññathā*) means by way of the accusative case. "Because of the possibility of meaning" (*atthasambhavato*) means because of the possibility of the sense of absolute conjunction (*accantasaṃyoga*).
“*Tattha hi*,” etc., is the explanation of that [term]. *Ita* means from the sutta passage “at one time.

*Adhikaraṇattha* means the sense of location (the locus). *Bhāva* is being; it is an action (*kiriyā*). The definition of one action by another action is “characterization by state” (*bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa*).

That itself is the meaning; thus [it is so]. When the question arises as to by which sense of “time” these two meanings are possible, [the answer is given] in accordance with the possibility of those two meanings:

Strengthening that [meaning] in the sense of "occasion" (*samaya*), he said, "For an issue... and so forth. Indeed, the two aforementioned meanings are established from the very meaning of the word itself;

the grammatical case ending (*vibhatti*) is merely an indicator. In this context, "having the meaning of time" (*kālattha*) means that which has the meaning of the word *kāla*, or that which is reckoned as time.
"Having the meaning of a collection" (*samūhattha*) means that which has the meaning of the word *samūha*, or that which is reckoned as a collection. What is it? It is the "occasion" (*samaya*).

This is what is meant: *samaya* has the sense of time and the sense of a collection. In this context of the Abhidhamma, it is the locus or support for the phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) that are discussed there.

The meaning here is this: at whatever time, or within whatever collection of phenomena, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises, at that very same time, or within that very same collection of phenomena, contact and the other factors also exist. Is this not so?
Furthermore, this time is merely a designation based on grasping (*upādāpaññatti-matta*), and the collection is merely a conventional expression (*vohāra-matta*);

how then could it be the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the phenomena stated therein? This is not a fault. For just as time, although itself non-existent in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), is known as a substratum because it is delimited by phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*), and because it is delimited by phenomena possessing intrinsic nature, [it serves as the basis] for those things occurring at that very moment.
Because it does not exist prior to or after [its parts], as in the cases of "born in the forenoon, he comes in the evening," and so forth; and because a collection,
although not existing separately apart from its constituent parts, is designated as the locus of those parts— due to being established by mere conceptual construction—

as in "a branch on a tree" or "leaves produced in a heap of grain," so too here, because it is delimited by phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*), [the collection is designated as such].
And because it is established by mere convention, both of those are designated there as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the phenomena taught therein.

The phrase beginning with “of that which is reckoned as the moment, the collocation, and the cause” is a demonstration of the possibility of the meaning of a characteristic of state-by-state (*bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa*).

Therein, a “moment” (*khaṇa*) refers to the ninth moment of the arising of a Buddha, which is distinct from the eight [inauspicious] moments; or else, these [moments] which are... “four indeed... [and so forth].
“Monks, there are wheels, possessed of which the fourfold wheel of the deva-chiefs revolves.
Herein, dwelling in a suitable locality, reliance on superior persons, right self-exertion, and merit performed in the past—these four wheels have been mentioned;
taken together as a single unit in the sense of being an opportunity, they should be understood as the “occasion. For these [four] are for the arising of the wholesome.

They are the conditions that have become the occasion. "Conjunction" (samavāya) refers to the assemblage of conditions such as the eye and visible forms, established by way of producing a common fruit—eye-consciousness and so forth—as indicated in such passages as, "Dependent on the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises.
For the common fruit of eye-consciousness and so forth belongs to the eye, visible forms, and the rest. "Cause" (hetu) refers to the cause that generates appropriate attention and so forth.

The meaning is that by means of the state (bhāva) designated as "existence" (sattā), the state designated as "existence" of those phenomena such as contact (phassa) is characterized—that is, made known—by way of the occasion (samaya) designated as a moment (khaṇa), designated as a coincidence (samavāya), and designated as a cause (hetu).
This is what is meant: just as in the expression, "He went while the cows were being milked; he returned when they had been milked."
In this case, the act of going is indicated by the act of milking;
likewise here too, the act of arising of consciousness and the act of becoming of contact and so forth are indicated by the act of existence (sattā) of the aforementioned time. [Objection:
But surely, in this context, the act of existence is non-existent; how then can it indicate anything? [Reply: True; nevertheless, in that which—

When "at the time" (*samaye*) is stated, the meaning "when [it] exists" (*sati*) is understood in this way because, in the absence of a connection to any other action, there is no lack of existence for the word-meaning.
Therefore, it is characterized by that action of existence (*sattā-kiriyā*), which is understood through its sense.
For this is the meaning therein: when, at the aforementioned moment, in the concurrence of conditions, or when the cause exists, the sense-sphere [consciousness arises].
When a wholesome consciousness has arisen, at that very moment, when conditions coincide or when the cause is present, contact and the other factors also exist.
This point, however, is stated by way of illustration specifically in the Abhidhamma; this same method applies accordingly to other passages in the Suttas as well.
Therefore, [the word "tasmā"] has the sense of a locus (adhikaraṇa), or it has the sense of characterizing a state by another state (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa).

"And because it is possible. "For the purpose of illuminating that meaning" means for the purpose of demonstrating, by means of the locative case, that very meaning of both [the word *samaya*] which exists as the referent of the term *samaya*.
For case endings, like a lamp, illuminate only meanings that exist in the object; this point is well known in the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*).

Both the sense of cause (*hetuattha*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇattha*) are possible. Just as in expressions such as “he dwells by means of food” (*annena vasati*) or “he dwells by means of knowledge” (*vijjāya vasati*), the sense of cause is possible;
and just as in expressions such as “he cuts with an axe” (*pharasunā chindati*) or “he digs with a spade” (*kudālena khaṇati*), the sense of instrument is possible.
To explain how these are possible, he says, “For that which... and so forth, by way of the basis for requesting the formulation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*) as they appear in the Vinaya.
It is said that [the meaning] is difficult to understand even for Sāriputta and others, having established the Elder as the limit.

Regarding the phrase "by that occasion acting as the cause and acting as the instrument," in this context, the very transgression of the respective objects is both the cause and the instrument for the proclamation of the training rule (sikkhāpada).
For instance, when the Blessed One was first about to proclaim a training rule for those respective individuals in those respective instances...
In this context, he dwells observing each respective transgression as the cause for the formulation of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*);
since he dwells for that purpose by observing each respective transgression, it is established that the transgression of the object (*vatthu*) is the cause for the formulation of the training rule—
just as, in expressions such as "he dwells depending on food," the reason is stated as "he dwells for the sake of that [food]" by depending on food and so forth.

It is like the state of being a cause. However, at the time of the promulgation of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), one proclaims that rule by means of that very transgression which was already established;

therefore, because it is the most effective instrument for the promulgation of the training rule, the status of the transgression as an instrument (*karaṇa-bhāva*) is also established, just as in expressions such as "he cuts with a sword," where the sword and so forth are established as the instruments by reason of accomplishing the act of cutting.

It is like the state of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*). Even so, with regard to transgression, one dwells together with that [transgression] while also taking into account the time dependent upon it; thus, the status of "time" as a cause is also stated here.

Furthermore, when prescribing a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), one does not prescribe that rule by overstepping the specific time of that particular transgression, but rather prescribes it by means of that very time; therefore, [time is the cause] for the basis of transgression.
The status of time as an instrument (*karaṇa*) has also been stated; therefore, by this method, the status of time as both a cause (*hetu*) and an instrument is obtained, which is why it was said:

"by that occasion acting as a cause and acting as an instrument. However, in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*), the transgression itself is the cause and the instrument. For that [transgression], having been the cause at the moment of the transgression, subsequently...
At the moment of laying down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), there is also the act of making it so. "Laying down the training rules" means:

having asked about the transgression, having convened the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), having questioned that individual regarding the matter involved, and having rebuked him, [the Buddha]—without exceeding the time when that particular matter occurred—by means of that very time which serves as the instrument of action...
While laying down the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

"And considering the cause for the laying down of the training rules" means that, as in the case of the third *pārājika* and others, the Blessed One dwelt here and there at those various times which served as the causes for the laying down of the training rules, considering each specific occasion of transgression against the rule; this is the meaning.
“‘Laying down the training rules, and considering the reason for laying down the training rules’—
this is an explanatory statement regarding the state of being the instrument and the state of being the cause, respectively. Therefore,
although it should have been stated accordingly as ‘by that [time] which was the instrument and the cause,’ the phrase ‘which was the cause’ is stated first in reverse order.”
In this context, it should be understood that [the Blessed One] is said to have "dwelt" because the state of being the cause is intended in its preeminent sense.

For it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "While residing at Verañjā, the Blessed One dwelt at that time by means of that causal occasion, having regard for the moment of reflection which became the cause for the Elder Dhammasenāpati’s request for the formulation of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*)."
“What need is there for logical analysis here? One should accept this simply because the Master has no desire for a specific sequence of words in this context.
For this same sequence is stated in other commentaries as well;

nor is the phrase ‘At that time he was staying at Verañjā’ mentioned in those [commentaries] merely to indicate that the causal sense (*hetu-attha*) is especially intended in the Vinaya-pāḷi passage.”
Some say that because it is not the subject matter [of the rule], he lived according to the occasion as the cause and as the instrument while laying down the training rules;

and because he looked toward the cause for the laying down of the training rules, he lived according to the occasion as the cause—it is for this reason, due to the existence of a connection as far as possible, that it is stated thus.
"Therefore" refers to both kinds of meaning as they have been explained.

"From the possibility. "For the purpose of illuminating that meaning": according to the method already stated, this means for the purpose of illuminating the meaning of both [the training rules and their transgression] by means of the instrumental case.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in that Vinaya. And here, since the laying down of the training rule itself is the most effective factor (*sādhakatama*) for establishing the occasion for transgression, it is connected—by way of supplying the missing words—to the sense of its being the instrument (*karaṇabhāve*) as "laying down the training rules," or to the sense of its being the cause (*hetubhāve*).
However, because it is merely a reference to that [time], it should be understood as being expressed by the word "dwells" (*viharati*) alone. For it has been stated accordingly:

"By means of that time, which serves as both the cause and the instrument, the Blessed One dwelt here and there, prescribing the training rules and taking into account the reasons for the prescription of those training rules.
Indeed, the instrumental case signifies the act itself, not the cause as it does in the previous instance.

The instrumental case (*karaṇa*) signifies the instrument of action. However, the causal factor (*hetu*) is the instrument of action, yet its purpose is not action in the same way as the [ordinary] instrument is.
With the words "But here," etc., there is a demonstration of the possibility of the locative case (*upayoga-vacana*) having the sense of absolute conjunction (*accanta-samyoga*).
Absolute conjunction is the constant conjunction with substance, quality, and action; it is stated to be the state of being conjoined with those [factors] without any interval whatsoever.
It exists. That is the meaning of "thus" (*tathā*). "Of such a kind" (*evaṃjātiko*) means of such a nature (*evaṃsabhāvo*). To explain how this is possible, he says, "For that which... and so forth.
"Entirely" (*accantameva*) means from the beginning until the conclusion of the teaching, it is consistently and continuously so;

this is the meaning. "By the abiding in compassion" (*karuṇāvihārena*) refers to the abiding in compassion characterized by the practice for the welfare of others. For it is thus, because [the teaching] has compassion as its source.

In this context, the practice for the benefit of others through teaching is called the "abiding in compassion" (*karuṇāvihāra*), but it is not the abiding in the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of compassion.

For it is not possible for the knowledge of teaching—the object of which is the dhamma to be taught—to arise simultaneously with the great compassion whose object is sentient beings, because their objects are distinct.
Therefore, taking it as an abiding that proceeds by means of compassion, it is the abiding in the practice for the benefit of others.
Here, it should be understood as "dwelling in compassion. Therefore: because the sense of absolute conjunction is possible. "For the purpose of illustrating that meaning":

according to the method already stated, the accusative designation is made for the purpose of illustrating that meaning by means of the accusative case, as in "he studies for a month" or "he eats for a day.
"By that": by which reason [it is mentioned] in the Abhidhamma and in other scriptural passages.
The locative case has the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the sense of characterizing a state by means of another state (*bhāvena bhāva-lakkhaṇa*).

In the Vinaya, the instrumental case has the sense of a cause (*hetu*) and the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*); here, the sense of absolute connection (*accanta-saṃyoga*) is possible for the accusative case. Thus is the meaning.
"This" refers to the verse-line summarizing the aforementioned meaning. "Elsewhere" means in the Abhidhamma and in other [texts] besides this.

In the passages of the Suttas and in the Vinaya, the word *samaya* is used. For the word *samaya* occurs only with a case ending (*vibhatti*) when referring to sound, since it is impossible for it to have that meaning [of "time"] here.
The pronoun *so* refers to that very word *samaya*.
Having thus shown his own opinion, he now states, "But the ancients... and so forth, in order to show the opinion of the ancient teachers.
"Porāṇā" refers to the ancient masters of the Aṭṭhakathā. The connection is that "tasmiṃ samaye" (at that time) or "ekaṃ samayaṃ" (at one time) constitutes this distinction.
"Abhilāpamattabheda" means a distinction or difference merely in terms of expression, but not in terms of meaning;
therefore he said, "In all cases, the meaning is simply the locative," meaning that in all instances, the meaning is indeed the locus (ādhāra).

[The word] *hoti*. By this statement, he shows that a change of case-ending has been made in the Suttas and Vinaya, or that the accusative and instrumental case-endings are established in the sense of the locative.
With the words beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmā*), he states the benefit in demonstrating their understanding.
It is "heavy" (*garu*) in the sense of being burdensome. He establishes that very meaning through convention by means of the conventional usage [expressed as] "for it is heavy," and so forth.
The word *hi* (for/indeed) is established as that very [particle], and it serves to clarify the meaning. *Garū* means a person worthy of being honored (*garukātabba*).

By the word “in the world” (*loke*), he shows that the conventional designation *Bhagavā* is established not only within the Dispensation (*sāsana*) but also in the world, in the sense of being one who is to be honored.
If he is called *Bhagavā* in the sense of being worthy of honor, then showing that this very person is pre-eminently so-called *Bhagavā*, he says: “And this,” and so forth.
For thus the Lord of the World, by virtue of his possession of the distinguished qualities of immeasurable and incomparable splendor, virtue, and so forth;
by his unsurpassed perfection of application, which is preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful and intent upon the provision of every benefit and happiness without exception;
and by his state of being an ultimate benefactor to the generation of gods and humans—[is the supreme] for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems.
"An object of reverence": by the words "by the ancients," etc., he shows that this is not only in the world but also in the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

And "by the ancients" means by the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*). Even a word that denotes the best is itself called "best" because it is associated with the qualities of the best;
thus it is said, "the word 'Bhagavā' is the best. For "word" (*vacana*) is so called because meaning (*attha*) is expressed (*vuccati*) by it.
*Saddo* means sound. Alternatively, it is called *vacana* (speech) because it is spoken;

thus, the meaning is that the referent (*attha*) which is to be expressed by the word "Bhagavā" is the most excellent (*seṭṭha*). The same principle applies here to the phrase "the word 'Bhagavā' is supreme.

*Gāravayutto* means connected with the state of being venerable, due to being endowed with venerable qualities; or, it means connected with being worthy of being highly honored, which is to say, he is one who deserves reverence.
The connection is as follows: by virtue of those three reasons, the Tathāgata is "heavy" in the sense of being weighty;

therefore, he is called "Bhagavā. For these three terms show the manner of his heaviness. [The commentary explains: "Even teachers of crafts and the like are indeed called 'heavy,' yet they are not worthy of reverence;
however, this one is not like them. Therefore, having established him as 'heavy,' it is said that he is 'worthy of reverence.'"
Some [say]: "If this were so, then this would be a mere qualifying word, and only the first two words would constitute the demonstration of the cause.
Furthermore, *api ca* is a particle used in the sense of an alternative or a different point; the meaning is "another method. In that regard:
"Addition of a phoneme (*vaṇṇagama*), substitution of a phoneme (*vaṇṇavipariyāya*),..."
And there are two others: alteration of phonemes and elision;
the connection [of words] through the excellence of meaning of the bases—this is called the fivefold *nirutti*.

Having taken the characteristic of etymology as it has been stated, or having taken the characteristic of inclusion within the class-group beginning with *pisodara* according to the method of the word "as taught" (*yathopadiṭṭha*),
he is called "Bhagavā" because he possesses fortune (*bhāgya*)— that is, the perfection of virtue and so forth which produces mundane and supramundane happiness—
wherein, instead of saying "one who possesses fortune" (*bhāgyavā*), it is said "Bhagavā."

He said, "The Fortunate One" (*bhāgyavā*). By the term "the Fortunate One" (*bhaggavā*), he shows that although one should say "the Destroyer" (*bhaggavā*) because he has destroyed hundreds of thousands of defilements divided into many categories—or, in brief, the five Māras—it is instead called "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*).
Furthermore, in the world, the word *bhaga* occurs with reference to six qualities: sovereignty, virtue, fame, glory, beauty, and exertion.
To show the meaning that he possesses those qualities reckoned as *bhaga*, it is said: "and endowed with *bhagas*.

Since he should be called "Vibhattavā" (the Divider) because he has analyzed, divided, and revealed all phenomena through their many divisions such as the wholesome and so forth, it is said "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One);
thus he says, "Vibhattavā. [He dwells in] the divine, brahma, and noble abodes...
By the term "possessor of fortune" (*bhattavā*), it is shown that he is called "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*) because he "cultivated, frequented, and practiced extensively" seclusion of body and mind,
the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and other mundane and supramundane superhuman qualities— terms for which the word *bhattavā* should properly be used.

By the phrase "one who has vomited out wandering in the three realms of existence" (*bhavesu vantagamano*), it is meant that he has "vomited out" (*vantaṃ vamitaṃ*) the wandering (*gamana*) known as craving within the three realms of existence.

It should be said that by taking the letter *bha* from the word *bhava*, the letter *ga* from the word *gamana*, and the letter *va* from the word *vanta*, and making that [final vowel] long through the transposition of phonemes, it is shown that he is called “Bhagavā.
Thus, it is stated: “He who has vomited out (*vanta*) [defilements] and gone away (*gamana*) from existences (*bhavesu*).
This should be applied individually according to such passages as: “Because he possesses fortune (*bhāgyavā*), therefore he is Bhagavā,” and so forth. Of him...
“Of the word” means of the word “Bhagavā. “The meaning in detail” means the meaning that constitutes the detailed exposition.

By the words “And that,” etc., he avoids the excessive bulk of the text. The intention is that it has already been stated and need not be repeated here, because this commentary on the *Visuddhimagga* is but a single part of it.

Furthermore, he is called Bhagavā because he has sought (vaṇi) or vomited out (vamī) the "blessings" (bhaga). For he sought, cultivated, and frequented the blessings consisting of virtues such as morality;

or else, he sought and prayed, thinking, "How indeed might these virtues known as blessings arise within the mental continuums of those to be trained?"—thus he is Bhagavā because he sought the blessings.
Or alternatively, he vomited out like a globule of spittle the glory, sovereignty, and fame that constitute the blessings.

He abandoned them as if they were mere trash. For thus the Blessed One, without regard for the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) already in his hands, the lordship over the four continents, the glory based on the excellence of a wheel-turning monarch, and the fame resplendent with the seven treasures, abandoned them all.
Alternatively, "bhā" refers to the lunar mansions (nakkhattāni);
those which go with or proceed together with them are called "bhagā"—the vowel "ā" having been shortened—and these are located on Mount Sineru, Mount Yugandhara, and so forth.

The splendor of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). He vomited those [splendors] by abandoning the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound to them; thus, he is called "Bhagavā" because he "vomited the bhagas.
His meaning should be explained there and there according to the methods transmitted by the tradition, as seen in such passages;
however, we have overlooked it here for the sake of favoring those who fear voluminous texts and to avoid the burden of excessive wordiness.
Having thus shown the meaning of these individual parts (*avayava*), he now says "to this extent" (*ettāvatā*) and so forth, in order to show the meaning of the whole (*samudāya*).
By means of the remaining portion of the meaning expressed by the first three phrases, and because they are counterparts to those meanings, he shows them together with that as well.
"To this extent" (*ettāvatā*) refers to [the meaning] by the statement "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ me sutaṃ*) and by the statement "At one time the Blessed One" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā*).

The connection is with these [words]. "In this" means in this introductory statement (*nidāna*). Regarding the phrase "teaching the Dhamma as it was heard," here the word *anta* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
For it is because it has been taught in such a way that one is said to "make it manifest. This same method applies to the other instances as well.
From the statement, "Ānanda, the Dhamma... [etc. ...is the Teacher," there is a figurative expression (*pariyāya*) for the Dhamma as being the Teacher.
Having established that [the Dhamma] indeed exists, it is said: "He makes the body of the Dhamma manifest.
For the meaning of "Dhammakāya" is the body consisting of the Dhamma, which belongs to the Blessed One.
And thus it has been said: "O monks, 'Dhammakāya' is a designation for the Tathāgata. To the question, "For what purpose is that? he says: "By that," and so forth. And as for "by that":
The meaning is: "by such a means of making [the teaching] manifest.

This discourse, which is about to be spoken, is the "Pāvacana"—the distinguished, supreme word of the Blessed Buddha. Therefore, the meaning is that for you there is no state of having passed away from the Teacher (*atītasatthuka*);
that is, the Teacher has not passed away. For this designation emphasizes the state (*bhāva*), or else it is an elision of the state; otherwise, it would simply be "the word" (*pāvacana*).

They say that if it were "one whose Teacher has not passed away," then for people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher, the meaning would result in "the state of having a Teacher who has passed away"; and if that were so, there would be a contradiction with the statement:
"He comforts the people distressed by not seeing the Teacher, saying, 'This is your Teacher. This teaching [is established] by the fulfillment of the Teacher's function.

The meaning of "na atītasatthuka" (not having the Teacher passed away) is as follows: "Satthu" is a genitive case used in the sense of the object; alternatively, this is a compound word meaning "satthu-adassanena" (due to not seeing the Teacher).
"Ukkaṇṭhana" means "ukkaṇṭho," which refers to a life of hardship. For they say, "the root *kaṭha* is used in the sense of living in hardship. One who has reached that [state] is "ukkaṇṭhito";
or, being oppressed by dissatisfaction (*anabhirati*) and having a distracted mind, one lifts up the head and raises the throat.
Having done so, he wanders about and dwells looking here and there; thus, by way of etymology (*niruttinaya*), he is "distressed" (*ukkaṇṭhita*).

That is what is meant by "distressed. This [term] is obtained merely through the conventional power of words (*saddasāmatthiya*); however, in common usage (*vohāra*), the meaning is that he is "oppressed by discontent" (*anabhirati*).
This same method applies in all cases. "He consoles" means he generates consolation (*assāsa*).

"At that time" means at the time of the recitation of this Sutta. Although it would be appropriate to speak thus while the Blessed One was still present, here he speaks thus even though he is no longer present;

therefore, he says "showing his non-existence" to demonstrate the meaning by way of what was spoken with intentional reference (*sandhāya-bhāsita*). "Parinibbāna" is by way of the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

The final nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*). "By that" means by such a means of accomplishment. "Of one of such a kind" means of such a sort, or of such a nature; this is also the sense.
The word *nāma* is a particle used in censure, as in passages such as, "There is indeed, Ānanda, the elder monk who will look on with indifference while being harassed.
By this [word], it is meant: "Even the Blessed One, though he was of such a character, has attained final nibbāna; what more need be said?"

The word *aññesaṃ* indicates the sense of censure. *Ariyadhammassa* means either "of the Dhamma of the Noble Ones" (*ariyānaṃ dhammassa*) or "of the Dhamma that has become noble" (*ariyabhūtassa dhammassa*).
He is the "Bearer of the Ten Powers" (*dasabaladharo*) by virtue of the tenfold bodily power and the power of knowledge.

"Vajirasaṅghātakāyo" refers to one whose body is like a mass (*saṅghāto*), a collection (*samūho*), or a single solid block (*ekagghano*) of a particular kind of jewel named *vajira* (diamond/thunderbolt); thus it is so called. This...
It is said: just as that which is called the "diamond-impact" cannot be broken by any other gem or stone, but rather it itself breaks other gems or stones;

for this very reason it is said, "There is no gem or stone whatsoever that is unbreakable by the diamond," so too the Blessed One has a body that cannot be broken by anyone. For indeed, of the Blessed One—
"It is possible for someone to create an obstacle to the physical body (rūpakāya). Because the word *nāma* indicates censure, the particle *pi* indicates inclusion, meaning:

"Not only the Blessed One, but others as well. And here, although it would have been appropriate for him to exist with an unextinguished nature because he was endowed with such qualities, the words beginning with "thus" (*evaṃ*) are used to show the meaning that accords with the context: that he has indeed attained final nibbāna (*parinibbuto*).
It should be understood as "it is said. The meaning is that hope—that is, aspiration—should not be generated;

it simply should not be generated. "I have lived long, I am living long, I shall live long; I have lived happily, I am living happily, I shall live happily"—this conceit (māna) arising through such self-inflation is called the intoxication of life (jīvitamada).
One who is thus intoxicated and heedless is "so [intoxicated]. "He causes agitation" means:

It generates a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and from that very urgency, it generates enthusiasm for the True Dhamma in those people; for spiritual urgency is the cause of enthusiasm, according to the statement:
"One who is stirred up applies himself with wise effort.

It demonstrates the excellence of the teaching by means of the demonstrative particle "thus" (*evaṃ*) at the beginning of the entire sutta to be explained hereafter. [And it demonstrates] the excellence of the disciples...

He points out the excellence of the person who hears: "It was heard by me, a great disciple, who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and who was placed by the Blessed One in the foremost position among five points, and who was praised by the Venerable Dhammasenāpati for his five kinds of skill;
and that indeed was heard by me personally, not heard from others, nor brought down through tradition."

Because it illuminates the meaning. The Blessed One demonstrates the perfection of time (*kālasampatti*) by means of the word *samaya*, which is employed here in the sense of being in the presence of the Three Jewels, because it illuminates the state of being a time adorned by the arising of a Buddha. For the perfection of time has the arising of a Buddha as its supreme excellence. Therefore, this is said:
"In the degenerate age of the *kappa*-dust and strife, the arising of a Buddha—oh, what a great marvel!"
"Born amidst the fire, like a lotus with fully risen nectar.

This is its meaning: the collection of days known as the moment of the Buddha’s appearance—born within the aggregate of years and so forth recognized by the Sakya kings during the period called the Kali Yuga, which proceeds by way of recording the accumulation of time known as an eon—is, for the blind man, like the climbing of a mountain.
It is marvelous in the sense of its occurrence at such a time, and it is marvelous in the sense that it is worthy of being struck with wonder. If one asks, "In what way was it born?
It was born like a lotus flower (*vārija*) known as an *aravinda*—possessing honey and perfectly arisen—in the midst of the fire known as the consumer of oblations (*hutavaha*).
He points out the excellence of the teacher by means of the honorific term for the Supreme Being who is distinguished by his virtues.
Having thus provided a commentary on the meaning of the six terms according to their sequence,
he now states "And between" (*antarā ca*) and so forth, while giving a commentary on the meaning of the terms beginning with "And between Rājagaha and Nāḷanda.
In this context, the word *antarā* is seen used in the sense of being situated between, depending upon its reference to a general location.
The meaning is: "without the meaning contained within the power [of the context] of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*) and so forth.

By the phrase "that interval" (*tadantara*) and so on, he shows that its state of having different meanings is understood through usage (*payoga*). In that context, "that interval" (*tadantara*) means that cause (*kāraṇa*).

"Mañca tañca mantenti" means "they consider it as 'what' and 'that'"; the sense is: "what is the interval? what is the cause? "In the interval of lightning" (*vijjantarikāya*) means at the moment of a flash of lightning.

The connection is with the words "A woman washing [her feet] saw. "Internally" means in the heart. "Angers" refers to passion and the like, which are mental agitations because they cause turbidity of the mind.
"An intermediate end" means she reached a conclusion midway between the commencement and the completion.
"Nevertheless" means even so; that is to say, even though she was thus endowed with power. "Of the two great hells" refers to the Lohakumbhī hell.

He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "By way of the intermediate space" (*antarikāya*) means "within. It is said that the world of the great hungry ghosts (*petaloka*) pierces through the city of Rājagaha.
There, between two great hell-pots of molten iron (*mahālohakumbhīniraya*), this river Tapodā flows;
therefore, it flows boiling hot. Now, this [river] occurs here in the fissure because it cannot exist elsewhere. And herein—
In such passages as, “Who could know that interval—the eons between these [aeons] are incalculable by number;

how does one determine the intervals between them?”—only those instances of the word *antara* occurring in the sense of a causal interval (*kāraṇavemajjha*) should be cited, and not the words *antarika* or *antara* occurring in the sense of gaps between moments of consciousness (*cittakkhaṇa*). For this is the specific extraction of the meaning of the word *antara*.

However, the intended meaning here may be as follows: since the words *antarika*, *antara*, and *antara* have the same meaning—namely, that the word *antara* also occurs in those senses where the words *antarika* and *antara* occur—the word *antarika* and the word *antara* are cited as being used in the sense of *antara*.
Alternatively, it is the word *antara* itself that is used in the phrase "yassantarato" for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.
Having made it brief, it was said:
"He within whom there are no internal agitations,
who has transcended both 'thus' and 'becoming' and 'not-becoming';"
“Even the gods do not attain the sight of him who is free from fear, happy, and sorrowless.
This is the verse from the Bhaddiya Sutta in the Udāna. By adding the word *eka* used in its own sense, the phrase is thus expanded.
It is said, “of the intermediate space” (*antarikāya*); therefore, one should understand that there is no contradiction here between the example and that which is to be exemplified.

To the question, “For what purpose was this restriction of specific meanings made? he says, “Therefore,” and so forth. But is it not the case here that only the accusative case (*upayoga-vacana*) [is appropriate]?
Then why is the genitive meaning (*sambandhiyattha*) stated? Or, if the genitive meaning is intended, why is the accusative case used?
In order to avoid that [objection] based on the possibility of a grammatical connection (*anuyoga*), the passage beginning with “But by the word ‘antarā’” was stated.
By this, he shows that although there is the contingency of a genitive case in the sense of relationship, this accusative case is obtained through its connection with another word;
and showing that this is obtained not only in the Dispensation but also in common worldly usage, he says “And in such cases as... and so forth, by way of demonstrating the specific connection.
For this meaning is also demonstrated here. Because it is joined with even a single instance of the word *antara*, two accusative cases (*upayoga-vacana*) must be employed.

But what need is there to speak of when joined with two? This is because the meaning is established [even so]. Those who contemplate syllables (*akkhara*) by means of gender, case endings, and so forth, are called *akkharacintaka*—that is, grammarians (*saddavidū*).
And here, by the word "syllable" (*akkhara*), the words (*pada*) and other units derived from them should also be understood.

Even if [the words] are appropriate as a single unit in terms of their sound (*sadda*), he shows by means of the phrase "by the second word also" (*dutiyapadenapi*) and so forth that they must nevertheless be construed twice in terms of their meaning (*attha*), since even a single word can be realized in many ways through methods such as repetition (*āvutti*).

He asks, "But what is the fault if they are not so construed? and replies, "When not so construed, the accusative case ending (*upayogavacana*) does not reach [its proper application]. That is to say, the second word does not reach it.
Because of its connection with another word, the meaning [of *addhāna*] refers specifically to sound; for when there is the possibility of a genitive case, the accusative case is intended here.
Indeed, the application of cases occurs within the governing context of "sound.
Since the word *addhāna* is a synonym for "long," he says "a long road" (*dīghamagga*). But to what extent is that [road] called "long" in its actual sense?
He removes the objection with the words, “At the time of traveling on a journey,” and so forth.

“In the Vibhaṅga of the time of traveling on a journey” refers to the Vibhaṅga—the word-analysis (padabhājanīya)—of terms such as “time of traveling on a journey” found in the training rule (sikkhāpada) concerning eating in a group, and others.
Even half a *yojana* is considered a journey; how much more so that which exceeds it. Half of a *yojana* is simply “half-a-yojana” (*aḍḍhayojana*).
“Two *gāvutas* is the measure. However, here it is simply a *yojana* measuring four *gāvutas*; therefore, the intention is that he says, “one who has set out on a journey.

The word *mahanta* (great) here is intended in the sense of “supreme” and “numerous”; thus he says, “by the great,” and so forth. “By greatness of quality” means by the state of being great in qualities such as fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*).
“By greatness of number” means by the state of being great in enumeration. This is the meaning of that very point.
He explains this with the words beginning, "So hi" (for he). "That community of monks" refers to the community of monks who had arrived here and were present as his retinue at that time.
"Great" means supreme. For even in a sentence, they accept such usage according to the requirements of the application (*payoga*). "Fewness of wishes" (*appicchatā*) means freedom from greed;

here the word is used elliptically (*sāvasesa*), but the meaning is exhaustive (*niravasesa*). For it is not said in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "one should praise [him] for being 'of little greed'."
It has been stated [thus]. However, the commentator on the *Majjhima Āgama*, the Venerable Ācariya Dhammapāla, said this:
"In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that 'the phrasing is as if incomplete' by taking into account the limited scope of the term *appasadda*.

Yet, here it can also be understood in the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*), as in such expressions as 'I perceive freedom from illness' (*appābādhataṃ*) and so forth. [This applies] also by way of number.

Even when counted as a great number, it was vast; however, because it would have been like cutting off the word "bhikkhusaṅgho" (the community of monks) which is intended to be explained as a nominative singular form, that [word] is not referred to.
Instead, by making it concordant with the word intended to be explained as a nominative singular form in the subsequent phrase "tena bhikkhusaṅghena" (by that community of monks), this is done.
For such is the nature of those who provide commentaries: namely, by disregarding the case endings.

Having explained the meaning of the terms that are to be praised according to their appropriateness, and having again rearranged them according to the grammatical case-endings found therein, there is the "laying down" (nikkhepa).
To clarify the meaning of "Saṅgha" as being a collection due to the commonality of view and virtue, he said:
"by the group of recluses comprised by the commonality of view and virtue. In this context, however, "this noble view... [and so forth].
"By such a view as has been described— 'it leads out, leading the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering'—
he dwells having attained conformity in view. And as for those virtues which are unbroken,
untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration— in such virtues..."
And because it is said, “he dwells having attained equality in virtue regarding the precepts,” the Sangha is that which is assembled, gathered, and united by way of this commonality of virtue;
thus it is called the "assembly of recluses" (*samaṇagaṇa*), meaning it is joined together through the commonality of view and virtue.
There is also a reading: “by that which is designated as the assembly of the commonality of view and virtue. Likewise, it means "by that which is so designated and made."

This is the meaning. For indeed, because their views, moral conduct, and so forth possess a fixed nature, even stream-enterers are united with one another through the commonality of view and virtue, let alone once-returners and those beyond.
Thus it is said: "He is fixed, having enlightenment as his destination"; and:
"It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should intentionally deprive a living being of life."
“Such a thing is impossible,” and so forth. For an Ariyan person, even when standing at some distance from others, remains united precisely through the harmony of his own virtues;

for it is said: “He dwells having attained conformity of view with such a view, and he dwells having attained conformity of virtue with such virtues. Furthermore, by means of this conformity of view and virtue, [he is distinguished] even from worldlings (puthujjana).
The state of being combined (*saṃhatabhāva*) is indeed obtained. The word *saddhiṃ* is a particle used in the sense of "together" (*ekato*). In the phrase "five... measures" (*pañca...
mattāni*), a compound with an external referent (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) is expressed by contracting the word *matta* with the word *pañca*. "Of these" (*etesam*) refers to the hundreds of monks.
Furthermore, "five measures" (*pañca mattā*) means "five quantities"; here, the suffix *-ka* (*nika*) is elided because of the neuter gender.

"Suppiya" is merely his name, not a description of his qualities or other attributes. Not only was the Blessed One together with the community of bhikkhus, but Suppiya the wanderer was also together with the young Brahmin Brahmadatta; thus, he groups them as individuals.

And this is solely because they share the commonality of being set out upon the path, not because they share the same virtue, conduct, or other such traits—this is what is meant by the phrase "the word 'pi' (also)" and so forth.

The term "connector of words" (*padasandhikaro*) is stated with reference to the mere state of connecting preceding and following words for the sake of easy pronunciation; it does not, however, refer to a phonetic junction (*sandhi*) such as between vowels and consonants.
Therefore, he says, "it is stated by way of the smoothness of the syllables," which shows that it is merely for the purpose of completing the phrase.
Furthermore, the particle *kho* is also appropriate in the sense of emphasis, as in: "He heard... (*assosi kho*).
In passages such as "the Brahmin of Verañjā," it is indicated that he had indeed set out on the journey,
and that there was no obstacle whatsoever to his proceeding along the road. "Of Sañjaya" refers to the wanderer named Sañjaya,
a resident of Rājagaha, in whose presence Upatissa and Kolita also first went forth [into homelessness], just like Channa the wanderer.
He was not a naked wanderer (*acelaka-paribbājaka*). By the phrase "whenever that [time]," he shows that they were traveling on the road at that very same time.
In the Pāli text, the word *hoti* has the sense of the past tense through a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*), or it is stated thus in view of that specific time; the meaning is "he was then.
*Ante* means "nearby. *Vasati* (dwells) is a term applicable to all postures, referring to the performance of duties such as major and minor services (*vatta-paṭivatta*).
"It moves about" is what is meant; therefore it is said: "A 'near-moving' disciple is one who dwells in close proximity.

"Charged by the messengers of the gods" means that even though they have been charged, admonished, and stirred to a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) by these five messengers of the gods—namely, a young child, an aged person, a sick person, a person under judicial execution, or a corpse executed as a punishment—they remain so. For these are like messengers because they are like gods.
“Messengers of the gods” (*devadūtā*) means messengers of the pure deities. “Those who have gone to a lowly body” means those who have entered a body of the states of loss (*apāya*).
The connection is: “those youths reckoned as men. Here, a being is called a “youth” (*māṇava*) in a general sense, while the others [the gods] are mentioned in a specific sense;
for this is an extraction of the meaning established by the context. “By those who have performed deeds” means by those who have performed cruel deeds. “Taruṇo” means from sixteen years of age.
Starting from that point, one who has reached twenty years of age; for in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* it is said:
"From the day of birth until they reach fifteen years of age, beings are called 'children' (*kumāraka*) and 'fools' (*bāla*). Beyond that, for twenty years, they are called 'youths' (*yuvāno*).
In meaning, *taruṇa*, *māṇava*, and *yuvā* are one and the same; however, worldly people [reckon] from twelve years of age...
