Some say, "He is young as long as he has not reached old age.
Or, in the phrase "among those two persons," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

Alternatively, it is a reference back to the time previously established by the words "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*); thus, "there" (*tatra*) refers to that specific occasion when the Blessed One was between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā.
At that very time, Suppiya was traveling along that same highway and spoke dispraise, while Brahmadatta spoke praise.
"Nipātamattan" (merely a particle): here, by the word *matta*, it is shown that because there is no specific meaning [to be conveyed], it serves merely to complete the phrase.
"Madhupiṇḍikapariyāyo": this indicates that the sutta is known as the "Discourse on the Honeyball."
"Maintain it, O Rājanya"—this addresses the king named Pāyāsi-rājanya. "Pariyāya" means that which proceeds or revolves; thus it is a turn (vāra).
It is a "pariyāya" because it sets forth the meaning to be taught; thus it is a teaching (desanā).
It is a "pariyāya" because it proceeds by receiving its own fruit; thus it is a cause (kāraṇa). By the word "aneka" itself, [the sense of] "in many ways" (anekavidhena) is conveyed.
The meaning is understood by means of the mere intention; thus he said, "in many ways.

And here, the reason is merely a semblance of a reason, not a single-sided reason, because there is no actual ground for dispraise; therefore, "by way of a reason" means "by way of a semblance of a reason.
For he will say later: "having stated what is not a reason as 'a reason. This [term] has a plural sense by way of its genus.
By the words beginning with “by many,” he shows that it is in the singular number.

It is stated for the purpose of showing that the reasons which will be explained later—namely, “of one devoid of blemish” and “even of one endowed with incomparable qualities”—are not the actual causes [for the lack of praise].
The meaning is: even of one who is free from faults and even of one who is endowed with peerless virtues. Of the Buddha, the Blessed One...

The connection is with the disparagement, the fault, and the censure. By the words beginning with “In the world,” he shows the semblance of reasons for being tasteless, formless, devoid of enjoyment, a proponent of non-action, an annihilationist, loathsome, a follower of fatalism, an ascetic, and one lacking in noble birth.
Therefore, this [phrase] must be connected with these words: “tasteless... pe ... lacking in noble birth.
This is what is meant: that which is recognized by the world as consisting of salutation, rising from one’s seat, joining of palms, respectful conduct, and invitation to a seat.
The ascetic Gotama has no taste for concord; therefore, his nature is not endowed with that flavor known as concord, and he is devoid of that enjoyment known as concord.

His doctrine of what should not be done and his doctrine of what should be destroyed—all that is as loathsome to a person of refined character as excrement. He himself is its destroyer, because he does not practice it.
He is to be disciplined. By failing to perform that [salutation], he torments those who are old in years; or, by being devoid of such conduct, he is a wretched man.
By failing to perform that, he has departed from the womb of the deva-world; or, because of his failure to perform it, he is one of inferior birth.

Thus, this very failure to perform salutation and so forth should be seen as a semblance of a cause for qualities such as lack of flavor and ugliness. As for the passage, “There is no... no distinction,” however—

“Sundarikā the female wanderer’s lack of awareness of her own death, the admission that the beginning of *saṃsāra* is not known, and the answering of a question that should be set aside by means of an undeclared matter”—such reasons resembling [logical] arguments should be scrutinized. Likewise, regarding the passage: “The ascetic...
[speaks] what is struck down by reasoning... [and] his own inspired speech,” this refers to [knowledge] that is independent and self-evident.
"Teaching the Dhamma here and there in such and such a way through direct realization; in some instances, engaging in discussion by questioning others;

and providing explanations in the manner reported by Mahāmoggallāna and others"—these [are the reasons]. However, regarding the statements "The ascetic... is not the foremost person," [the reasons are]:
"the lack of sequential comprehension of all phenomena, the failure to know the end of the world, and the absence of the ascetic practices desired by himself."
And so forth. The jhānas, liberations, and so on, are superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) according to the method explained below.
Noble, pure, or supreme vision—consisting of knowledge—that is sufficient, capable of destroying the defilements, is "noble knowledge and vision" (*ariyañāṇadassana*);

one who possesses this, or for whom this exists, is "one possessed of noble knowledge and vision" (*alamariyañāṇadassano*). That very distinction is likewise [the same]. It is simply noble knowledge and vision.

Or, it is that which possesses a distinction (*visesa*) sufficient (*alaṃ*) and adequate (*pariyattaṃ*) according to the method already stated; or, it is one in whom there exists a distinction of noble knowledge and vision (*ariyañāṇadassana*), namely, a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
"Brought about by reasoning" (*takkapariyāhataṃ*) means brought forth from all sides by mere conceptualization (*kappa*), or constructed by initial application of thought (*vitakka*).
"Followed by investigation" (*vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ*) means repeatedly polished by means of inquiry (*vīmaṃsanā*). "One's own inspired flash" (*sayampaṭibhānaṃ*)...
The connection is: "He himself [declared] such a Dhamma as being manifest to himself. "Without reason" (*akāraṇa*) means what is improper or untenable;

this is an adjective qualifying the word "reason. For faults such as lack of flavor or ugliness do not exist in the Blessed One, nor do such things as being poorly taught or wrongly practiced exist in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.
Or, "without reason" may mean that which is devoid of logical grounds—merely his own personal assertion.
This is also a *pakatika-kamma-pada* (a compound where the case endings are retained).

Regarding the phrase "having stated the reason for this meaning," the word *iva* (like) should be construed here according to the method of metaphor (*rūpaka-naya*), because a corresponding reason is intended. The phrase "in such and such ways" refers to various modes, such as not saluting those who are senior by birth.
Since the word *vaṇṇa* (color/appearance) functions in the senses of quality and praise, it is stated in successive order as "disparagement (*avaṇṇa*)," "fault (*dosa*)," and "blame (*nindā*)."
“Badly expounded” (*durakkhāta*) means expounded badly; likewise for “badly penetrated” (*duppaṭivedita*). It leads out from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), thus it is “leading out” (*niyyāna*);
that very thing is “leading out” (*niyyānika*). Alternatively, it is “leading out” because its departure or escape is from there;

it is “leading out” because it is intent upon that. Or, it is “leading out” because it leads out from the round of existence; here, the letter *y* is changed to *k*, and the vowel *ī* is shortened. For the suffix *-anīya* is used extensively...

"Expressive of the agent," so say the experts in grammar; it is not, however, conducive to liberation in that way, as it does not lead to the subsiding of the suffering of saṃsāra according to the method already stated.
"A contrary practice" means a practice opposed to right practice. "A non-conforming practice" means a practice that does not conform to the practice of true persons (sappurisa).
"A practice conforming to what is not Dhamma" means a practice that does not conform to the supramundane Dhamma.

But why, in this context, is the present tense used in the expressions "he speaks dispraise" and "he speaks praise," when the time of that speaking of dispraise and praise is indeed past relative to the time of the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*)? This is true;
however, it is stated thus because the word *bhāsati* (speaks) has a past sense, just as the word *hoti* (is) does in the phrase "he was traveling on a journey."
It should be understood thus. Alternatively, this was said with reference to the time when they were speaking both dispraise and praise;
and by doing so, the interpretation of the word *tattha* as a reference to time (*kālapaṭiniddesa*), although not explicitly stated in the Commentary, becomes well-founded.
The statement beginning with “But his pupil... spoke,” serves to show the connection with the canonical text (Pāḷi): “But of Suppiya... and so forth.
The act of reviling the Noble Ones is not to be touched; likewise, it is not to be stepped upon. "He" refers to that teacher.
"The edge of a sword" means the sharpened portion of a blade. "In a row of saw-teeth" means in the uneven row of teeth belonging to a coarse saw.
It is as if one were playing, striking with the hand, the foot, or any other limb whatsoever. [This is said] by way of the locations known as the eye-sockets and the ear-cavities.

One whose intoxication (*mada*) has been shattered in three ways is "one with shattered intoxication" (*pabhinnamada*); [the text refers to] him. "Speaking dispraise" (*avaṇṇaṃ bhāsamāno*) means for the purpose of speaking dispraise;
for this word *māna* here has the sense of a cause. "Misfortune" (*anaya*) is that which is not prosperity (*aya*);

that itself is calamity (*byasana*), meaning excessive calamity—the sense being that one will encounter it because reviling the Triple Gem is exclusively and extremely blameworthy. For this very reason, he said:
“He who praises one who deserves blame,
or blames one who deserves praise,
gathers misfortune with his own mouth.”
“Because of that [evil] time, one finds no happiness.
By saying, “He was our teacher,” and so forth, [the text] shows the arising of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in Brahmadatta and the manifestation of compassion toward his own teacher.
Although a pupil ought to be in conformity with his teacher, this [pupil], because of his wise nature, [acted otherwise].
Thinking, "In such circumstances, one does not follow after that [defilement]," he now spoke the passage beginning with "But regarding the teacher...
in order to demonstrate the arising of his knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*). "Halāhala" is the poison that kills at that very moment.

It is called *halo* because it "strikes" (*hanati*); by changing the letter *na* to *la*, it becomes *halo*. A specific type of *halo* is *halāhalo*, where the vowel is long in the middle. By this, the other eight kinds [of poison] are also implied.
He turns back from the poison.
And it is said: “In the case of a male eunuch, a crow, *kālakūṭa* and *halāhala* poisons, the *sarotthika*, the *kosuṅkika*, the son of Brahmā, and the lamp-bearer;”
“Dārada and vacchanābha—these are the nine types of poison.
*Kharodaka* means water with a fierce current. There is also a reading *khārodaka*; the meaning is “bitter water” due to its excessive salinity.
*Narakapapāta* refers to a precipice for thieves. With the word “young men,” he addresses himself in order to exhort himself: “Even this time...”
As in such passages as, "Bhaddāli, you were one who had not penetrated [the truth]," and so forth.

By saying "owners of their own karma" (*kammassakā*), he states that karma itself is the property of the self, and he explains this very point by saying, "They go to a destination exactly according to their own karma," and so on. "By way of method" (*yoniso*) means by means of a skillful means or the right principle.

"Having emerged" (*ummujjitvā*): like a teacher, one who does not sink through improper speech toward the Noble Ones (*ayoniso ariyūpavāda*), but rather emerges from such improper speech toward the Noble Ones through proper method (*yoniso*).
"Having emerged" means having risen up. "Crushing" means crushing and breaking.
The word "properly" (*sammā*) is stated with the intention of showing that here the very cause of being one-shouldered is the [relevant] cause.
By the phrase "just as that," etc., he shows its commencement; the particle *ti* is merely an expletive. This is what is meant: just as another person of wise nature, by way of birth and conduct...
The son of good family began to speak in many ways on the praise of the Three Jewels;
this [discourse] was undertaken for that same purpose, thinking: "Perhaps this teacher might desist even from this much speaking of the praise of the Triple Gem.
"The beauty of the king of snakes" means the beauty of the king of serpents. "By the excellence of his color" means by the loveliness of his color, that is, by his beautiful body.
"Or: 'I do not strike nor break the water-born lotus; I smell it from afar,' is the meaning. 'Now' (atha) means even though this is so.
'A thief of fragrance' (gandhattheno) means a stealer of scent. 'Tied together' (saññūḷhā) means knotted or bound.
'Householder' (gahapati) is an address to the householder Upāli by Nāṭaputta. And here, he is to be described and made known as being 'of such a kind.'"
Color (vaṇṇa) and shape (saṇṭhāna). It is called "color" because it is described—that is, defined—without confusion; thus, it refers to genus (jāti).

It is called "color" because it describes—that is, makes manifest—the state of having entered the heart when undergoing transformation; thus, it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana). It is called "color" because by means of it the fruit is described—that is, discerned according to its true nature;
thus, it refers to the cause (kāraṇa). It is called "color" because it is measured—that is, determined—by way of smallness, largeness, and so forth; thus, it refers to measure (pamāṇa).

It is called *vaṇṇa* because it is described (*vaṇṇīyati*) or praised (*pasaṃsīyati*); thus, *vaṇṇa* means a quality (*guṇa*). Alternatively, *vaṇṇa* is the description (*vaṇṇanaṃ*), the recounting of qualities, or praise (*pasaṃsā*).

In this way, the various occurrences of the word *vaṇṇa* should be understood according to their respective contexts. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the author] includes gold, sand, letters, and so forth.

With the phrase "it is said that here both the quality and the praise [are intended]," he supports what was previously stated by the passage beginning with "this, it is said" (*ayaṃ kirā*). The particle *kira* [indicates hearsay or tradition].
And here [the particle *ca*] is used either for the purpose of recitation or merely as a word-filler. "Endowed with qualities" (*guṇūpasañhita*) means accompanied by qualities (*guṇopasaññuta*).
However, one who says "praise is endowed with qualities" shows that the expression of qualities is established through praise itself, because the two are inseparable;
therefore, he demonstrates that both of these meanings are appropriate.
To explain how he speaks, he says “Therein,” and so forth. He is one person, thus he is the “One Person” (*ekapuggala*). In what sense is he the One Person?
In the sense of being peerless, in the sense of having distinguished qualities, and in the sense of being unequaled by any equal.

For at the time of his first resolution, beginning with the mental advertence to the ten perfections in their proper sequence, [he was endowed] with the qualities of accumulating the requisites for enlightenment.

He is indeed peerless among the rest of the great multitude both by virtue of his Buddha-qualities and by virtue of his person. Even those qualities of his are superior to the qualities of other beings;
and while the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were unequal to all beings, this one alone is equal to them in both the physical body (rūpakāya) and the mental body (nāmakāya).
"In the world" means in the world of beings (*sattaloka*). Furthermore, the two phrases "arising" and "he arises" are both expressions used for an action still in progress.
Because the action of arising belongs to the present time. Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood thus: "Arising, he arises for the welfare of many beings, not for any other reason.

For this word *māna* (arising) denotes a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), and such a characteristic cannot be set aside by any other grammatical rule (*saddalakkhaṇa*). Moreover, that which is called "arising" simply arises.
In this context, the distinction should be understood as follows: "arising" (*uppajjamāna*) and "arisen" (*uppanna*).

Indeed, from the time he was at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), it is called "arising"; at the moment of the path of arahantship (*arahattamagga*), it is called "arising"; and at the moment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala*), it is called "arisen.
For in the case of Buddhas, the various powers such as the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*) do not arise sequentially, as they do for disciples (*sāvaka*).

However, along with the path to arahantship itself, the entire mass of qualities of omniscience is indeed said to have arrived; therefore, because all its functions have been accomplished, it is said to have "arisen" at the moment of the fruit of arahantship.
Because they have not yet been accomplished, at other moments it is appropriately called "arising as it arises.
In this sutta as well, the phrase "it arises" refers specifically to the moment of the fruit of arahantship.
It has been stated. Since even that which belongs to the past is seen in some instances to have a present application, the meaning here is "has arisen.

This being so, the word *māna* in the phrase "arising" (*uppajjamāno*) has the sense of capability (*sāmatthiya*). To the extent that the arising of Great Bodhisattvas in their final existence is intended by way of capability, to that same extent it is [intended] by way of capability as consisting of the requisites for enlightenment.
The meaning is: "having become endowed with [it] in its fullness. For it is called "arising" by virtue of being joined with such capability.
He is unequaled among all beings; he is equal only to the former Buddhas who were likewise unequaled, standing out preeminent like a piece of refined gold from amidst broken gold.
"The one person" is an epithet for him. He utterly eradicates craving, which is designated as *ālaya*.
"It completely cuts off" means the eradication of the underlying tendency (*ālayasamugghāta*). "It severs the cycle of existence" means the cutting off of the round of rebirth (*vaṭṭupaccheda*).

"By one who is capable" means by one who is able. Although it was said "the five collections" (*pañcanikāya*), because they consist of many constituent parts, they are not entirely exhausted by that alone; therefore, it is further stated:
"The Teacher’s dispensation has nine branches and eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma" (*navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassāni*).
It has been said. "By one who has not crossed over" means by one who has not reached the place of crossing.

It should not be said that [the commentary] is unnecessary because the Buddha and others possess immeasurable qualities, for it is accomplished through the very explanation of the Pāḷi by way of an exhaustive exposition of them here; and it is fruitful by way of accomplishing the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that gladdens the mind.
Its strength (thāma) should be understood as being due to its having been expounded with all its power. But what happens when one has thus plunged in?
He says, "It is said. Regarding the passage beginning with "But Brahmadatta," etc.: *Anussava* (tradition) is hearing repeatedly or in succession; it is hearing from one to another.
By the word "etc.," he includes reflection on modes (*ākāraparivitakka*), speculative views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*), and so forth.
Among these, *ākāraparivitakka* is the personal reflection on reasons, such as thinking, "This reason is excellent."
"Reflection on one's own view and the acceptance and approval [of it] is called 'acceptance through reflection on views' (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*) in the Commentaries;
the meaning is: 'connected with those very [views]. Here, the word *matta* has the sense of excluding other qualifiers;
by this, it excludes the aforementioned causes. 'By one's own power' means by the power of one's own knowledge alone, and not by that of the Buddhas and others."
The intended meaning is "in accordance with their qualities. For the qualities of the Buddhas and others are indeed incalculable and immeasurable in their divisions.
For this has been said: "Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon, without speaking of anything else..."
“An eon might pass away in the course of such a long time, yet the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.
Here too, he will say: “But this is indeed a trifling matter,” and so forth.
The word *iti* has the sense of illustration; it illustrates the aforementioned manner. He says “*evaṃ te*” (thus they), [adding] that the syllable *ha* is merely a particle.
Showing that “*aññamaññassā”* is a conventional form (*ruḷhipada*) like the expression “*eko ekāyā*,” he explains it by means of that very conventional form as “*aññoaññassā*.
Having stated that “*ujumevā*” is a restrictive compound (*avadhāraṇasamāsa*), he [explains] the meaning to be excluded by it.
He said, "Without avoiding even slightly," which means without deviating even a little. How so? He said, "By the teacher," and so forth.
Although it was previously stated that they speak both dispraise and praise as if it were only once, it should be understood that they speak in this manner many times;
to show this, [the text says] "again the other spoke dispraise..."
The other [term] is stated as "vaṇṇa" (color/appearance). By this, the multivalence of the prefix *vi-* is established.
"Sāraphalake" means on a plank of heartwood, or on an excellent plank. "Visarukkhaāṇiṃ" means a covering made of *visa*-wood.
They are followed by way of following the postures (*iriyāpatha*), not by way of following right practice (*sammāpaṭipatti*).
"Looking back over the shoulder" (*sīsānulokino*) means those who look back over the shoulder; the meaning is that they look while having raised their heads and following the sequence of the path.
"At that time" (*tasmiṃ kāle*) refers to whichever year, season, month, or fortnight the Blessed One had set out upon that journey;
it is by this [phrase] that the year, season, month, and fortnight are indicated without specific restriction.
“On that day”: because the day is specified separately, and because the moments (muhutta) and so forth are included within the day.

And here, “set out on that journey” is a locative expression (ādhāra-vacana). For it is precisely for this reason that, by way of showing the interruption of the action, the present tense description is made together with the prior actions, as in “he walks for alms in Rājagaha”; otherwise, [it would not be so].
At that time, [the Blessed One] was walking for alms in Rājagaha and had set out upon that road; thus, an unintended meaning would result.
For actions with dissimilar objects cannot have a single substratum. Furthermore, the action of setting out upon a journey intended here is not appropriate if it remains unspecified.
"In the vicinity of Rājagaha" means situated around the perimeter of Rājagaha.
By the phrase “in a certain place,” he shows that the Blessed One’s residence among them was not fixed. The word “he” refers to the Blessed One while dwelling thus in Rājagaha.
For even by the expression “wandering for alms there,” it indicates precisely his state of settled residence, since it speaks of a state of being bound to that location.
However, if one were to construe it as “the Blessed One, while wandering for alms,” the intended meaning would be exactly the same as what has already been stated.
"Should incur": "on that day" means on the very day one has set out on a journey; "set out on that journey" here expresses continuous connection (*accantasamyoga*).
"After the meal" (*pacchābhatta*) means after eating the meal, at that time following the meal.
"Having returned from alms-round" refers to where they eat after having wandered for the sake of alms-food.

Then he departed. Having set out on that journey, [the Blessed One thought]: "Desiring the accomplishment of various benefits and happiness for those to be trained in Nāḷandā, through this occasion I shall teach the Brahmajāla Sutta—adorned with the threefold morality, destroying various kinds of wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and boasting, unraveling the net of the sixty-two views, and shaking the ten-thousandfold world system."
He set out upon that aforementioned long journey; however, this reason is evident from the context itself, so it was not explicitly stated.
To this extent, the objection—"But why did the Blessed One set out on that journey?"—has been cleared away.
Now, in order to clear away the other objection as well, it is said: "Suppiya too. At that time, on that day...

“Following” (*anubandha*) means connection in the manner already described. “Morning-food” (*pātarāsa*) is that which is to be eaten in the morning; one by whom that has been eaten is “one who has eaten his morning meal” (*bhuttapātarāsa*).

“In this very way” (*icceva*) means having kept this very thing in mind, but not with the thought, “I will follow behind, right behind the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Therefore it was said: “the Blessed One’s state of having set out upon that path...”
“Or not knowing,” means that he followed while remaining in that state of not knowing. For he did not desire merely to see the Blessed One;
therefore it was said, “But if he had known, he would not have followed. To this extent, the objection, “And why did Suppiya follow? has been cleared away.
With the words beginning “He,” etc., he clears away another objection as well. At times...
However, the Blessed One sometimes travels in a particular disguise, as in the cases of the subduing of Aṅgulimāla, the departure for Pakkusāti, and so forth;
at other times, he does so with the splendor of a Buddha. To show that here too it was with such splendor of a Buddha, it is said: "shining with the splendor of a Buddha," and so on.

Here, "splendor" (sirī) refers to the excellence of the physical beauty of the body and other such perfections; this very point is illustrated by way of a simile in the passage beginning, "as if enveloped in red woolen cloth," and so forth.
"Moving" means *jaṅgama*, as in the word "caṅkama" (a walking-place). It means like the peak of a mountain that moves, such as the Golden Mountain (*kanakagiri*). "In that [place], it is said...
and so forth is an explanation of that; because it was not shown in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) and because it did not appear in the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
They say that the word "kila" (it is said) was used to show that this story is established by hearsay;

whether it be so or otherwise, it should be understood that what has not been seen, heard, or sensed by oneself is merely hearsay. It is six-colored by way of blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, and brilliant.
"All around" means from all sides, from the ten directions. "Measuring eighty cubits" refers to those rays.

This was stated by way of their natural mode of occurrence; therefore, it should be understood that rays of light, naturally dense, abide in a space measuring eighty cubits on each side and above. However, in the *Vinaya-ṭīkā*, it says:
"That indeed is called the fathom-wide radiance (*byāmappabhā*). From that, the six-colored rays stream out in the ten directions like water-channels from a reservoir."
“Because she appears to be only a fathom in height, she is therefore called ‘Byāmappabhā’ (Fathom-Bright),” it is said;
however, in the *Saṅgītisuttavaṇṇanā*, he will say: “A golden-colored ray rises from the front part of her body and extends to a distance of eighty cubits.
From the back part of her body... from her right hand... from her left hand, a golden-colored ray rises...”
It occupies a space of eighty cubits. From the top of the hairline upwards, rays the color of a peacock’s neck, arising from all the curls of the hair, occupy a space of eighty cubits in the sky.
From below, rays the color of coral, arising from the soles of the feet, occupy a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth. Thus, for a distance of about eighty cubits all around—
"the six-colored rays of the Buddha shine forth, quiver, and stream out"—some, however, speak otherwise by mere conjecture;
that should not be accepted, because it has not been mentioned elsewhere and is illogical.
But in order to show that those rays of the Buddha were not concealed at that time, [it says]: "In that..."
It is said, "at that time. For in that instance, as in the case of Pakkusāti’s departure and so forth, there was no reason for them to conceal themselves.
*Ādhāvanti* means they ran toward the direction [in front]. *Vidhāvantī* means they ran in various directions, having scattered in different ways.
Because the splendor of those rays was perceived by the way they appeared within that forest, he said, "like a jeweled braid," and so forth.
*Ratanāveḷā* means a crest-ornament made of jewels; it is called *aveḷā* or *āveḷā* because it stays upon and protects the head, that is, a head-garland.
*Ukkā* refers to those things that are set ablaze; a hundred of them is a "hundred," and their falling is a "falling" (*nipāto*).
It is thus "confused by that falling. *Piṭṭhaṃ* is so called because it is to be ground (*pisitabba*); *cīnapiṭṭhaṃ* is powder produced in the country of Cīna, that is, red powder.
That which is also called "sindūra" is simply powdered Chinese lac (cīnapiṭṭha). A cord (tanti) is likewise [so called] because it is cast here and there by the force of the wind.
An "Indra’s bow" (indadhanu) is so named by way of worldly convention; it is a particular appearance manifested in the sky through the rays of the sun.
It is called "lightning" (vijju) because it moves—that is, it flashes—crookedly and in an unsightly manner, not remaining for long.
“Tathā” means “just like that creeper,” because it possesses a nature similar to it; it is a ray produced by the force of the wind, as if by the impact with a cloud.
It is called a “tārā” (star) because it protects (tārayati) and guards the sky by way of not abandoning it. The word “gaṇa” (group) should be applied to each [term].
Its radiance is likewise. “As if expanded and scattered” means pervading in various ways through its luster, shining brightly.
And "vanantara" means the interior or opening of a forest; it is said that [the Blessed One] went from forest region to forest region.
It was likewise adorned with the eighty secondary marks, such as copper-colored nails and so forth.

"Kamala" refers to lotuses—*paduma*, *puṇḍarīka*, and the rest—which are blue, red, and white varieties of water-born flowers (*saroruha*) and lilies (*uppala*); thus, the fivefold class of lotuses is encompassed.
It exists. That stream whose blossoms are both fully opened and in full bloom is thus described.

Because it blooms and opens in every way, all around and on every side, it is called *sabbapāliphulla*—the vowel *a* being changed to *ā* and the consonant *ra* to *la*, just as in the word "pālibhaddo.
It is likewise blossomed and radiant with the rays of light, which are the shimmering glow of the stars.
The circumference of the halo of light is perfectly circular; thus, she is radiant and beautiful.
Because the marks of a Great Man are interconnected with one another, they are said to stand in the form of a garland; hence the phrase “the garland of the thirty-two excellent marks.
It should not be said that a garland of thirty-two moons and so forth has been strung together by someone and arranged in sequence, if—
For this was said—“having tied and placed a garland of thirty-two moons”—merely as a hypothetical assumption (*parikappanāmatta*).
This is indeed a simile of hypothesis (*parikappopamā*), and it is seen even in the world:
“The splendor of your face is mine alone; enough with your boasting of the moon.”
"Even though there was a lotus, it was purposeful"—this is a *parikappa-upamā* (a hypothetical simile).
The connection is: "as if surpassing with her own splendor the glory of the garland of thirty-two moons. This same method applies to the remaining [similes] as well.
Having thus shown the splendor of the Blessed One at that time, he now, showing the splendor of the Saṅgha of monks, says: "And that..."
He spoke thus, beginning with the words, "And furthermore": they are few in desire through the fourfold fewness of desire;
contented through the twelve kinds of contentment; secluded through the threefold seclusion; unassociated with kings, royal ministers, and the like;
reprovers of those who practice wrongly; censurers of evil and unwholesome states; exhorters of others toward beneficial practice; and patient with the speech of others.

The "knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimuttiñāṇadassana) refers to the knowledge of reviewing. By the phrase beginning with "of them," he demonstrates the splendor of the Blessed One through that connection.
A "thicket" (saṇḍa), "multitude" (samūha), or "grove" (vana) of red lotuses—having gone into the midst of that, [the Buddha] is described as such.
It is stated thus without a restriction on the leaves, for it is said, "The red lotus, the white pundarīka"; however, according to the restriction on the leaves, [it is otherwise].
The *paduma* has a hundred petals; the *puṇḍarīka* has fewer than a hundred petals. It is as if surrounded by a railing made of coral and lapis lazuli.
In the phrase "even of beasts and birds," the word *pi* (even) or the word *api* (also) expresses possibility;
hence he says, "how much more so for gods and humans. "Great elders" refers to the great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*). By virtue of being well-anointed, slightly...
"Cloud-colored" refers to its black color. "Having placed it on one shoulder" means having placed it on the left shoulder by way of draping it over one shoulder.
A "staff for support" (*kattaradaṇḍa*) is a staff used as a support for one who is old and infirm; this is a designation based on common usage.
"Well-armored" (*suvammavammitā*) means those who are covered and equipped with a beautiful covering; this is an illustration of their wearing of rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*).

Those whose entire contents of the womb—even grass, leaves, and so forth—become only various kinds of fragrance are called "scent-elephants" (*gandhahatthino*), who are also referred to as "Hemavatas.
These elders are similar to them by virtue of possessing the fragrance of qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*).

They are "those whose tangles are disentangled" (*vijaṭitajaṭā*) because they have disentangled the tangle of craving (*taṇhājaṭā*), which is comprised of internal and external entanglements. They are "those whose bonds are severed" (*chinnabandhanā*) because the fetter of craving has been cut.
The words beginning with “So” demonstrate the excellence of the speech as previously described. “Anubuddhehi” means by those who have awakened after the Buddhas;
for they too awaken to the Four Truths through a portion of the realization penetrated by the Blessed One.
“Pattaparivāritaṃ” means surrounded by flower petals. “Kaṃ” refers to the lotus and such; that which remembers (or shines) within it is called “kesaraṃ” (the filament).
*Kiñjakkha*: it is called *kaṇṇikā* because it is made for the ear; it is an ear ornament, and because its shape resembles that, it is a *kaṇṇikā*, namely the seed-capsule.
Just as Dhataraṭṭha, the king of swans, is the best among the six swan clans, so too is the Great Brahmā named Hārita.
The connection is that, having seen the Blessed One and the monks proceeding in this manner, he looked toward his own assembly.
*Kājadaṇḍaka* refers to a carrying-pole known as a *kāja*, or to a staff fixed upon a load on a *kāja*. A small seat is a *pīṭhaka*.
A triple-staff (*tidaṇḍa*) is a staff divided into three parts at the base and the tip.
A peacock-feather fan (*morahatthaka*) is a peacock’s tail-feather. A small bag is a *pasibbaka*. A water-pot is a *kuṇḍikā*; for it brings forth (*udeti*) or produces water (*kaṃ*).

Or, by way of etymology (*niruttinaya*), it is called *kuṇḍikā* because it protects. "Gahita... [and so on]... refers to the burden consisting of various requisites such as a seat, a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), and so forth—namely, that which is taken up from a lowly state, that which is worn out, and that which is variously decayed;

she bears and carries this burden, thus she is "one who has taken up... [and so on]... "one who is burdened. The word "iti" has the sense of illustration. The word "evaṃ" has the sense of "this. That is to say, this speech is the beginning of the speech [that follows].
Likewise, "one who has such useless speech" refers to those who possess useless words and so forth. One who has a mouth (*mukha*) is called *mukharo*;
while all beings indeed possess a mouth, this term is used specifically for one who possesses a mouth characterized by harsh speech; therefore it is stated thus.
For here, the suffix *-ra* is used in a derogatory sense. Alternatively, he is *mukharo* because he takes (*rāti*) or seizes (*gaṇhāti*) unpleasant actions with his mouth.
*Mukharā*: one whose speech is scattered, meaning one whose words are variously dispersed; *tassa*: of that wanderer Suppiya; *taṃ*:
that assembly of the kind already described; *idāni*:
at the moment of seeing such an assembly; *pana*: a particle used to indicate lack of approval, meaning "nevertheless."
The meaning [is as follows]. It is the cause for both gain... and loss. How is it a cause for loss? He says: "For among those of other sects," and so forth.

"Deprived of glory" means deprived of splendor; this point may also be illustrated by the *Morajātakam* and others. The detailed explanation regarding the loss of their following is given by the passage beginning, "Of Upatissa and Kolita," and so on.
[This occurred] in the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna.
With reference to their going forth (*pabbajjā*), it is said: "When they had departed.
This indicates that at the very moment they went forth, two hundred and fifty members of the wanderers' assembly (*paribbājakaparisā*) also went forth;

furthermore, the wanderers' assembly that followed them in succession was immeasurable. This is shown by the phrase: "That assembly of theirs also broke apart. For when any wanderers' assembly has gone forth...
His assembly is indeed called "divided" because they belong to the same faction; thus it was said. With the words "By these," etc., he shows the loss of the side of gain by way of conclusion.
"Vomiting of the poison of envy" (*usūyavisuggāro*) means the spitting out or disgorging of the poison known as envy; that [is what is meant].
And here, with the words "But since this," etc., [it is explained] why he speaks dispraise of the Triple Gem.
It purifies the exhortation; furthermore, since the entire passage beginning with "If" is merely supplementary speech to that, it is indeed purified by those [words] as well.

Some say that these people speak dispraise or praise for the purpose of testing whether the Blessed One is free from aversion or attachment, and that they speak thus because they are possessed by Māra; however, that is quite incorrect according to the Aṭṭhakathā.
Because it is directly opposed [to the truth]. This meaning is indeed evident. 2.
"Since the sun has set, therefore it is now the wrong time to go"—this is the connection.
"Ambalaṭṭhikā" is a designation used by way of proximity, as in "Varuṇanagara" or "Godāgāma. He says, "It is said that of him," and so forth.
The word *laṭṭhikā* in the sense of a tree refers to a young tree, as shown by the phrase "a young mango tree" (*taruṇambara-rukkho*) in such passages as:
"Having entered deep into the great forest, he sat for his midday rest at the foot of a *velu-laṭṭhikā* (bamboo-tree).
However, some say that "Ambalaṭṭhikā" is the name of a certain village according to the manner previously described; in their opinion, the locative case in *Ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ* expresses proximity.
“Endowed with shade and water” means possessed of both shade and water. “Mañjusā” means a chest.
“Variegated with fanciful designs” means variegated with fanciful paintings such as depictions of men and women in union;
by this, he shows that it is the king’s residence, and thus calls it the “Rājāgāraka. Some say that the “Rājāgāraka” is the celestial abode of the Great King Vessavaṇa.
“Full of perils” (*bahuparissaya*) means full of calamities. As for the question “By whom?”, it is said: “Even by thieves,” and so forth.
*Handā* is a particle used in the sense of a verbal exhortation; the intention is: “On account of its power, having approached now for the sake of being free from peril, we shall depart tomorrow.
In the Sinhalese Aṭṭhakathā, it is stated specifically: “Together with his pupil, the young Brahmin Brahmadatta”; and that...
It was included in the Canon precisely because it had been recited, and not because Suppiya’s assembly did not exist at that time;
it is stated here as "together with his own assembly" in order to show this point.

Why, then, is Brahmadatta alone included in the Canon and not the rest of Suppiya’s assembly? Because they were not dependent on the teaching and there was no purpose [for their inclusion]. Just as...
Thus, it should be understood that other similar [passages] were not included in the recitation by the compilers because they lacked a specific purpose.

However, some say: "Having stated the locus as 'it is spoken in the Pāḷi,' [the phrase] 'this is not a presentation of the method of the Sinhalese commentary, but rather a presentation of the fact that it is spoken in the Pāḷi'—that is not tenable.
For [the passage] is indeed [included] in the Pāḷi by virtue of its having been entered into the Pāḷi.
“‘Stated’ means because it arrives at the intended meaning. Therefore, the meaning should be understood precisely according to the manner already explained.
Alternatively, they say: “‘Stated’ means that it may also be stated by us here. For it was stated in this way at that time specifically to show that other members of the assembly were also present;
however, since it has been included in the Canon (Pāḷi), the intention that it may be stated here in another way is appropriate.”
Now, in order to show the connection with the Pāḷi passage beginning with “*Tatrāpi sudan*,” the words beginning with “*Evaṃ vāsaṃ upagato panā*” were spoken.
The connection is: “he sat surrounding [him]. *Kukataṃ* means that which is to be done in a contemptible way;
its state (*bhāva*) is *kukkuccaṃ*, meaning a contemptible action or a flickering to and fro here and there; thus, it is the “fidgeting of the hand.”
Likewise. By the words beginning with “For she,” he shows the cause for her being such as she is.
In a windless place means in a location devoid of wind. She is motionless due to the absence of the aforementioned defects. That splendor means such a kind of beauty.
“Chattering” means speaking variously due to the lapse of mindfulness. “With tongues lolling out” means with tongues protruding here and there. “Cawing” means [like] crows...
“Making a sound like the word *sadda*. “Gharugharupassāsino” means those who, having produced a sound like “gharugharu,” are watching.

“By way of envy” means by way of the resentment arising from the two aforementioned reasons. By the phrase “everything should be stated,” he indicates that “the method of reciting from the beginning [is intended].”
3. "They are capable of performing this or that legal act" means they are numerous; because there are many, it says "of the many.
Since a legal act of the Vinaya must be performed by a Saṅgha consisting of at least a quorum of four, the phrase "by way of the Vinaya," and so forth, is stated.
The expression "three persons" is an indicative description (upalakkhaṇaniddesa), as even two persons constitute a majority. In various places...

Because it has come down in that very way, he says, "according to the method of the Suttantas," and so forth. For this distinction is made according to the terminology found in various passages of the Canon (Pāḷi).
"Three people" means exactly three; from that point onward, they are "numerous," meaning four, five, and so on.
Furthermore, the word "from" (tato) here indicates a limit or boundary. "Maṇḍalamāḷa" is a conventional designation (samaññā) that functions with many meanings, but in this context—

Restricting it to such cases alone, he said, “In some instances,” and so forth. *Kaṇṇikā* refers to the pinnacle (*kūṭa*). “With a haṃsavaṭṭaka roof-covering” means with a roof-covering in the shape of a circle of swans.
That same roof-covering is described elsewhere as a “garuḍa-curved roof-covering.
A house joined with a pinnacle is itself a hall; thus, it is a gabled hall (*kūṭāgāra-sālā*). “Having surrounded the row of pillars” means the garland of pillars.
"Having surrounded [it]," means having made a row of pillars in a circular form. "Upaṭṭhānasālā" (attendance hall) is a hall for paying respects;
it is where they merely perform attendance, not where they sit for one or two nights and so forth.
However, by the words "But here," etc., he shows that this is indeed a sitting hall constructed in that manner. For that very reason, in the Pāḷi...
Rather than saying simply "of those who have gathered" (*sannipatitānaṃ*), it is also stated as "of those who are seated" (*sannisinnānaṃ*).

It is called a *māḷa* because it is to be honored (*mānitabbo*), or because it is measured (*mīyati*) or measured out (*pamīyati*). A *maṇḍalamāḷa* is a *māḷa* that is covered in the shape of a circle;

it is a specific type of dwelling with many corners. The term "seated" (*sannisinnānaṃ*) is stated by way of sitting, or alternatively, they are "seated" (*sannisinnānaṃ*) by virtue of having sat down.

The connection [between the terms] is established by bringing forward the words that are to be praised. By this, he shows that these two terms were spoken with reference to the posture of sitting (*nisīdana-iriyāpatha*) and their convergence (*samodhāna*) by way of bodily harmony (*kāyasāmaggī*).
"Discourse" (*saṅkhīyā*) is so called because it is spoken from the perspective of speaking correctly (*sammā khiyanato kathanato*).

Some say that "the nature of discourse" (*kathādhamma*) refers to the intrinsic character of discourse (*kathāsabhāva*), while others say it refers to the method of investigation (*upaparikkhā-vidhi*).
“‘Wondrous’ (acchariya), etc., refers to the seeing of his form; thus he said, ‘But what is that?’, and so forth. ‘That’ refers to the Dhamma of the discourse.
‘It leads [to understanding], thus it is a method (naya); a method that follows the science of grammar is a grammatical method (saddanaya),’ as stated by the Venerable Teacher Dhammapāla.

Alternatively, a method (naya) is a means (upāya) because the meaning is led [to comprehension] by it; it is a method arrived at in the science of grammar, serving as the means for grasping the meaning.”
The method of words (*saddanaya*). For in this context, the word *acchariya* is intended in the sense of that which does not occur frequently, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhivasena*).
Therefore he said: "It is like a blind man’s climbing a mountain," and so forth. Indeed, his climbing that [mountain] is not constant;

it might only happen at some time. So too is this [the marvelous]. By the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), *acchariya* means "suitable for a finger-snap" (*accharāyogga*), due to the elision of the word *yogga* through the application of secondary derivation (*taddhitavasena*).
Or, because the occurrence of the *niya*-condition is manifold, it is called the "method of the Aṭṭhakathā" since it is found only in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).

"Never before occurred" (*abhūtapubba*) means that which was not previously been; by this, he shows the etymology as "that which has not become" (*na bhūtaṃ abhūtaṃ*), and indicates that the word *bhūta* has the sense of the past.
Regarding "yāvañcidaṃ," he says "yāva ca idaṃ" because the nasal stop (*niggahita*) is inserted by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
And this [phrase] is connected with the word “well-penetrated” (*suppaṭividitā*). The sense of the passage, including the ellipsis, is as follows:
however much this diversity of inclinations (*nānādhimuttikatā*) is well-penetrated, it is not possible for us to penetrate it as being "only this much," nor can it be fully described.
For this very reason, he said: "By that state of being well-penetrated, he shows its immeasurability."
Because it is expressed in grammatical apposition with the words beginning with "by the Blessed One" (*bhagavatā*), the pronoun *ta-* in the phrase "by that" (*tena*) refers back to its own referent.

Therefore, showing that state of full enlightenment (*abhisambuddhabhāva*)—by virtue of which the Blessed One, being thus characterized, is well-known—as being the very essence of the Teaching, together with the path of approach (*āgamanapaṭipadā*), he says "He who... and so forth. For here [it is not the case that... [End of excerpt]

Thus, that meaning previously mentioned exists, which could have been referred to by those elders using the word "that" (ta-). Therefore, it should be understood that this [word] refers primarily to its own meaning, namely the aggregate of qualities as previously described.

"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ) refers to the unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa) which has the knowledge of the supreme path as its proximate cause (padatthāna), and [the knowledge of the supreme path] which has the unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause.
The knowledge of the supreme path. For both of these he perfectly and unerringly awakens by himself, or else that which is perfectly praised is beautifully awakened;

thus it is "perfect self-awakening" (sammāsambodhi). Furthermore, it bestows upon the Buddhas the perfection of all qualities, just as an anointing confers upon a king the status of sovereignty over the entire world;
therefore, it is called "the unsurpassed perfect self-awakening. He is "one who has fully awakened" (abhisambuddha).
"He directly knew and penetrated"—the meaning is: by such a Blessed One.

Although *ñāṇa* (knowledge) and *dassana* (vision) are here synonyms for *paññā* (wisdom), he spoke the words beginning with "of those various beings" in order to show how they function with respect to their respective specific objects according to their particular distinctions.
For here, he first shows the matter by way of uncommon knowledge (*asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa*). By means of the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*)...
The meaning is: "He sees by means of the knowledge of omniscience and the unobstructed knowledge.

The second [knowledge] is by way of the threefold clear vision (*vijjā*). "By means of the recollection of past lives, etc. refers to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

The third is by way of the unobstructed knowledge included within the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). Even though they are included among the higher knowledges, the phrase "by the three clear visions" is used for the purpose of showing the classification of those [knowledges] into groups.

It has been said. The meaning is: "He sees with the universal eye (samantacakkhu), which is designated as unobstructed knowledge. The fourth [knowledge] is the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) by way of the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu). "By means of wisdom" (paññāya) means by the knowledge of omniscience.
"Beyond a wall" (tirokuṭṭaṃ): beyond or on the other side of a wall (bhitti); or "inside," etc., regarding those and so forth.
"With the exceedingly purified" (ativisuddhena) means with that which is extremely pure, endowed with five colors, and adorned with eyelashes and eyebrows that are beautifully blue and pleasing.

By means of the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), which sees for a league (*yojana*) all around, both by night and by day. The fifth [knowledge] is by way of the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha*) and teaching (*desanā*).
It is stated categorically that it "accomplishes one's own welfare" (*attahitasādhikā*); however, figuratively (*pariyāyato*), it also accomplishes the welfare of others.

For through it, there arises the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) and so forth, for the purpose of uprooting the defilements (*kilesa*) that obscure the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*). By means of penetrative wisdom (*paṭivedhapaññā*)...

By means of the wisdom of the noble path (*ariyamaggapaññā*). Concentration accompanied by insight (*vipassanāsahagata-samādhi*) is its proximate cause and foundation; thus it is "having concentration as its foundation" (*samādhipadaṭṭhānā*), by means of that.
By means of the wisdom of teaching (*desanāpaññā*)—that is, by the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) which accomplishes the task of teaching.

Of "enemies" (*arīnaṃ*): of the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*), or the five Māras, or the heretics who are adversaries of the Dispensation. Their "slaying" is by means of the miracles (*pāṭihāriya*).

"Overpowering" (*abhibhavana*) means causing one to be speechless; "looking on with equanimity" (*ajjhupekkhana*) is chanted in the fifth chapter of the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsaka*, and the *Caṅkī Sutta* serves as the illustration here.
By this, he states the derivation of the word according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*): "He by whom enemies (*arayo*) are slain (*hanati*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the suffix *-ta* is applied to the root *han* because its scope is broad. Furthermore, [the term *arahant*] may also be explained by the word *anta* as "he who slays enemies."

The grammatical derivation (*padasiddhi*) involves the substitution of *a* for the vowel *i*. By the phrase "and because of being worthy of requisites, etc.," he demonstrates that the word "worthy ones" (*arahant*) refers either to those who are the recipients of the requisites and so forth, or to those who are worthy of receiving them. "Correctly" (*sammā*) means without error.
"By himself" (*sāmañca*) means by his own accord; it is implied that he has become one who is not led by others. But how is it that the term "of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammānaṃ*) is used here?

Is this distinction obtained? Because a general designation is restricted to a specific instance, and because a distinction must not be applied where it does not belong—if that were so, and the distinction "of phenomena" (*dhammānam*) were not applied, why would the meaning "of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammānam*) be applied?
[The answer is: because a mere portion is not grasped. For if there were no grasping of a partial portion, then of that which is to be grasped...
The state of being exhaustive is understood, as in the expression, “one who has been ordained does not give”; this is the method to be applied in such cases.

Now, in order to show the sixth meaning—which is his own most intended purpose—by means of four terms corresponding to the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), he says, “or regarding the obstructive states,” and so forth.
For he provides the conclusion with the words beginning with “thus.”

In this context, the terms should be applied respectively as follows: "by one who knows through the knowledge of obstructive states," "by one who sees through the knowledge of the states leading to liberation," "by an Arahant through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavas)," and "by a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) through the knowledge of omniscience.

Because they act for what is harmful, the defilements (kilesas) themselves are the enemies; thus, they are the "enemies that are defilements" (kilesārayo). Here it may be asked: by virtue of which knowledge...
Because he has perfectly and personally awakened to all phenomena, the Blessed One became known as the Sammasambuddha.
Now, regarding this knowledge that functions by way of awakening to all phenomena: does it function toward its entire object simultaneously, or rather successively?
What of it? If, first of all, it functions toward its entire object simultaneously, then...

If there were a simultaneous appearance of all conditioned phenomena— distinguished by such divisions as past, future, present, internal, and external— as well as unconditioned and conventional phenomena,
then there would be no clear comprehension through their individual manifestations, like one looking at a cloth-painting from a distance. And that being the case,
for those practicing insight into "all phenomena are non-self," all phenomena would not appear in the aspect of non-self [as they do].
One falls into the position that things become objects of the Blessed One’s knowledge in an undetermined form. Furthermore, those who maintain:
"The Buddha's knowledge operates at all times regarding the characteristic of stability (*ṭhitilakkhaṇa*) of all knowable phenomena, free from conceptual construction;
it is for this reason that he is called 'All-Knowing' (*sabbavidū*)," and having established it thus—
“The Naga is concentrated while walking; the Naga is concentrated while standing;
the Naga is concentrated while lying down; the Naga is concentrated even while sitting.
This statement from the *Nāgopama-sutta* in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, which illustrates the continuous flow of knowledge at all times, is indeed well-spoken.
If they say, “It does,” then the faults stated against their position do not cease to apply.

Furthermore, because the characteristic of stability is its object, and because that [stability] is absent in past and future phenomena, the Blessed One’s knowledge would have only a partial range as its domain;
therefore, it is not tenable that his knowledge operates upon the entire domain all at once. If, on the other hand, his knowledge operates upon the entire domain successively, even so—

This is not tenable. For when the objects of knowledge—which are divided into many categories by way of birth, land, nature, and so forth, as well as by way of direction, location, time, and so forth—are apprehended sequentially, their exhaustive penetration is impossible due to the limitless nature of the objects of knowledge.

However, those who say, "Because it does not deceive regarding the meaning, having made one portion of the objects of knowledge directly perceived, [one knows] 'it is likewise' regarding the remainder..."
Having resolved [upon the truth] through analytical determination, the Blessed One became known as the Omniscient One;

and that knowledge is not called "inferential" because it is devoid of doubt. For they say, "In the world, knowledge accompanied by doubt is inferential," yet even for them, that is indeed not logical.
For when everything is not directly perceived, [knowledge] is established by the non-deception regarding the object through a portion of the knowable.

This is because, after having made [the object] manifest to oneself, it is impossible to define it by resolving that "it is thus" with respect to the remainder, and because such a thing is incapable of being done.
For whatever remains is indeed not manifest; yet if even that were manifest, its status as a "remainder" would cease to exist.
Since the knowable is infinite, it is impossible to define it in that way. All of this is without reason.
Why? Because it is not an object of investigation. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, the domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable; it is not to be thought about. One who thinks about it would partake of madness and frustration.
But here is the definitive conclusion: whatever the Blessed One desired to know—whether in its entirety or in part—in each respective case...
Because its mode of operation is unimpeded, knowledge proceeds directly and there is constant concentration due to the absence of distraction.
Furthermore, if everything desired to be known were not within its range, its mode of operation would not be dependent on desire;
yet that dependence must certainly be admitted. All phenomena are dependent upon the advertence and the desire of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Because of the statement that "arising of consciousness is dependent upon attention," even the Blessed One’s knowledge regarding past and future objects is indeed direct perception (*paccakkha*),
since it is devoid of inference, scripture, reasoning, or conceptual grasping.

But would this not also entail that when one wishes to know everything, then at that very moment, because the entire range of objects is present, [the Buddha would have to know all things simultaneously]?
[Objection: "Would it not still fall into the aforementioned fault that the Blessed One’s knowledge would proceed in an unascertained form?
[Response: No, because that has been cleared away. For that domain of the Buddha is inconceivable.

Otherwise, if the knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas functioned identically to the knowledge of ordinary people, the inconceivability of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas would not exist; therefore, even though it has all phenomena as its object...
Having well-defined those phenomena as if they were a single object of focus, consciousness proceeds;
this is what is inconceivable here: "As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge. As far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable.
Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable."
There is no path of the knowable that transcends knowledge.

Those phenomena stand in mutual limitation, just as when two caskets are joined together, the lower casket does not overstep the upper one, and the upper casket does not overstep the lower one; they stand in mutual limitation. Even so.
Because the Buddha, the Blessed One, has perfectly and directly awakened to all phenomena— whether they abide as the object of knowledge (*neyya*) or as knowledge itself (*ñāṇa*),

each standing in mutual relation to the other... [as previously described]— those phenomena, through the power of that knowledge which proceeds either collectively, individually, simultaneously, or sequentially according to his wish,
he is therefore called the "Blessed One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One" (*sammāsambuddho*).
Here, however, is the method not found in the commentaries: one who knows the six objects, such as the possible and the impossible, by means of the six kinds of knowledge;
who sees beings passing away and being reborn according to their deeds by means of the knowledge of the divine eye regarding death and rebirth;

who is an Arahant because of the destruction of the taints along with their underlying tendencies by means of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints; and who possesses an unerring realization of phenomena such as the jhānas for himself alone, by way of their defilement and purification.

By the Fully Enlightened One, who is thus praised in four ways by way of the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*); furthermore, as one who knows through the state of unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times;
as one who sees through the practice of acting with circumspection due to the revolving of knowledge around all three types of karma;

as one who is worthy (*arahat*) through the perfection of abandonment which establishes the absence of the six [defilements] such as negligence; and as one who possesses the six great causes for non-arising, such as zeal (*chanda*).
The application should be made by way of the Buddha-qualities— which are comprised within the various purposes of knowledge,
vision, and abandonment— as they have been praised in these four ways by the Perfectly Enlightened One through his omniscience, which possesses inexhaustible eloquence, and so forth,
specifically by means of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (aṭṭhārasa-aveṇika-buddhadhamma).

With reference to the four kinds of intrepidity (*vesārajja*), it is said, “in four ways. By the phrase “by him who was praised,” he shows that this is an epithet for the word “Blessed One” (*bhagavatā*).
Although in the Canon only two types of inclination (*adhimutti*)—inferior and superior—are mentioned, they are nonetheless divided into many varieties according to the manner of their manifestation;
thus he says, “diversity of inclinations” (*nānādhimuttikatā*). That...
However, *adhimutti* (resoluteness), *ajjhāsaya* (inclination), and *dhātu* (disposition) themselves signify seeing, enduring, and finding pleasure in various ways;

this is made known by the term “diversity of inclinations” (*nānajjhāsayatā*). For it will be said later: “Diversity of resoluteness, diversity of inclination, diversity of view, diversity of endurance, and diversity of taste.
Regarding the phrase “to such an extent indeed,” [the word] “well-penetrated” (*suppaṭividitā*) [is to be supplied].

This is the connection. In that context, the word "this" (*idaṃ*) is merely for the purpose of completing the meter, or it is in grammatical apposition with the phrase "diversity of inclinations" (*nānādhimuttikatā*);
however, since its meaning is already evident, he said, "as far as they have been thoroughly understood. By the words "And this which...
and so forth, he shows the *Dhātusaṃyutta* scripture; having brought that very Saṃyutta to mind, [he explains] their...
This shows that this summarized teaching of the Elders arose by being combined with the speaking of dispraise and praise.

Therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows: he said "For this... and so forth in order to demonstrate, by way of the method of teaching the *Dhātusaṃyutta* (Connected Discourses on Elements), the Elder’s capacity for having thoroughly penetrated those [teachings]. For the demonstration of thorough penetration is... "this... [and so on].
The phrase beginning with "hī" (low) and so forth. Therein, the connection is: "this diversity of inclinations... [omission] ...is called 'liking'.
"By way of element" means by way of the element of disposition (*ajjhāsayadhātu*). "They harmonize" means they connect or inspire confidence. "They coincide" means they exist rightly or together.
The passage beginning with "those of low inclination" and so forth is an elucidation of that state of being. "Even in the past time" means in the past.

This is the accusative case used either for time or for continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). "Diversity of inclinations" (*nānādhimuttikatā*) is a synonym for "diversity of underlying tendencies" (*nānajjhāsayatā*).
"Diversity of views" (*nānādiṭṭhi*)... [etc] ... "likings" (*rucitā*): this is a demonstration of its specific nature. Diversity of views arises by way of such tenets as eternalism and so forth.

Diversity of tolerance (*nānakkhantitā*) arises by way of the dispositions toward evil conduct, virtuous conduct, and so forth. [It also arises] by way of having evil desires, having few desires, and so forth.
"Various inclinations" means [knowing] by the *nāḷi*, the *tumba*, or the *āḷhaka*. "By the scale" means by the measure (*māna*).
Here, by "knowledge of various dispositions," only the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is intended, not the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabalañāṇa*);
thus he says, "by the knowledge of omniscience. This is what was stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, and it appears thus in the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā* and the commentaries on the *Dasabalasutta*.
But the opponent says: "There is no such thing as the 'knowledge of the ten powers' (dasabalañāṇa) existing separately;

it is merely a classification of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa). That should not be viewed in that way. For the knowledge of the ten powers is indeed one thing, and omniscient knowledge is another.
The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own specific functions, whereas omniscient knowledge knows those as well as everything remaining beyond them. Regarding the knowledge of the ten powers:
For indeed, the first [knowledge] knows precisely what is the cause and what is not the cause; the second, precisely the difference in kamma and the difference in its ripening;
the third, precisely the delimitation of kamma; the fourth, precisely the cause for the diversity of elements; the fifth, precisely the underlying tendencies and inclinations of beings;
the sixth, precisely the state of sharpness or dullness of the faculties; and the seventh, precisely their defilement and so forth together with the jhānas and other states.

The eighth [knowledge] knows only the continuity of the aggregates (khandha-santati) as they existed in past lives; the ninth, only the death and rebirth-linking (cuti-patisandhi) of beings; and the tenth, only the analysis of the Truths (sacca-pariccheda).
However, the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) knows both what is to be known by these and what lies beyond them;

yet it does not perform all the functions of these others. For that [omniscient knowledge], having become meditative absorption (jhāna), is unable to enter [the attainment]; it is not supernormal power (iddhi).
Having become the path, it is not able to burn away the defilements; having become the fire, it is not able to consume the fuel. Furthermore, the opponent should be asked:

"Is this so-called knowledge of the Ten Powers with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought alone, or without applied thought and without sustained thought?
Is it of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere? Is it mundane or supramundane? One who knows [the answer]...
He will state that the seven knowledges in sequence are "with applied thought and sustained thought";

those following them, two, he will state are "without applied thought and without sustained thought"; and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints he will state "may be with applied thought and sustained thought, may be without applied thought and with sustained thought only, or may be without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Likewise, in sequence, there are seven belonging to the sense sphere, and after those, two.

The [knowledges] belonging to the fine-material sphere will be mentioned at the end as "supramundane" (*lokuttara*), but omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is indeed with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*), belongs only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and is mundane (*lokiya*) alone.
Thus, the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) is one thing, and omniscient knowledge is another;
therefore, they are known by means of both the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations—designated as the fifth power—and by omniscient knowledge.
The meaning is to be understood. For the letter *ca* is also seen in the manuscripts. The word *sā* refers to the aforementioned diversity of inclinations (*nānādhimuttikatā*).
Having briefly shown the meaning of the sutta spoken as "Two indeed...

and so forth, [the author] makes manifest the connection of that summarized teaching with those [inclinations] by means of the passage beginning with "And in these too. In the phrase "Thus indeed to me," the word *iti* has the sense of the word *evaṃ* (thus).

The word *iti* and the syllable *ha* are mere particles (*nipāta*), or else [the latter] is an augment (*āgama*). By means of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), it shows that there is either the elision of the vowel *i* or the substitution of the vowel *a*, as indicated by the phrase "thus these.
4. Regarding the term "having known" (*viditvā*): although the act of cognizing, which constitutes the primary meaning here, is common to all and thus undifferentiated in its general nature, it is—
The passage beginning with “The Blessed One indeed... was stated in order to show that there are many different classifications of the capacity for performing various [deeds].
“Dwellings” (*vatthūni*) refers to house-sites. The expression “having seen with the knowledge of omniscience, he knew” is merely a conventional way of speaking.
For there is no act of knowing distinct from the act of seeing by that [knowledge]. This knowledge is bound to adverting (*āvajjana*) and bound to desire (*ākaṅkhā*).
It proceeds bound to attention and bound to the arising of consciousness. By means of that knowledge, which is bound to adverting and so forth, what was the Blessed One doing when he knew?

To make the meaning easily understood by the listeners, he raises a challenge as if speaking to one face-to-face with the words, "What was he doing when he knew?"—namely, that he was performing the duties of the final watch of the night.
That knowledge, being bound up with adverting and the other [mental factors], knows it in that way; this is what is meant.
Since a specific term is meaningful when a general term exists, he says "this is merely a function," etc., by way of further inquiry.
Its eradication is accomplished by the path of Arahantship through the eradication of the defilements that give rise to it; hence, "there is no mind not engaged [in its task]."
This is stated among the eighteen qualities of a Buddha (*aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā*). Here, the meaning is that there is no purposeless activity of the mind.
He removes the objection that even if this is said, the application [of the term] remains in the same state, by means of the passage beginning with “that is fivefold.

In that context, the first two duties should be understood as pertaining to the divisions of the day, and the other three as pertaining to the divisions of the night, because they will be explained in exactly that way.

By the phrase, “For the sake of favoring his attendants and for the sake of the body’s comfort,” it is shown that the Blessed One’s excellent face—produced by the accumulation of merit gathered over many eons—is free from defects such as foul odors; nevertheless, he performs acts such as rinsing his mouth for both of those reasons.
For the entire body of all Buddhas is undefiled by external or internal impurities.
It is like a well-polished gem. "In a secluded seat" means in a seat conducive to the development of seclusion suitable for the attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"Spending time" refers to spending time through the attainments of fruition; yet even that is not for the sake of inclining toward seclusion, nor for the purpose of following the example of others.
[He wears] the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) with its double-layered border dyed a beautiful red, by way of changing it from his dwelling-robe (*vihāra-nivāsana*).
Having dressed himself and fastened his girdle, which resembled a flash of lightning, and having donned the cloud-colored robe of the Sugata, he took a stone bowl;
such is the intended meaning. For it is stated in various places that he acted in exactly this manner.
The passage beginning with “Sometimes alone” is a description of the Blessed One’s approach to suit the training of various disciples. [He would go] to a village or a town...
In this context, the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative (*vikappana*); by it, he also includes the city. The connection is:
"He enters by means of many miracles being performed according to his wish.
With the words beginning "namely" (*seyyathidaṃ*), he elaborates upon the latter alternative. And as for *seyyathidaṃ*, its meaning is "what is that? (*taṃ katamaṃ*).
The word *nipāto* may also mean "this entry accompanied by a miracle" (*sappāṭihīra-pavisana*).

"Gentle winds" (*mudugata-vātā*) means winds that have become gentle, or winds that have gone [there] by virtue of being gentle. "Sprays of water" (*udaka-phusitāni*) means drops of water. "Releasing" (*muñcantā*) means sprinkling.
"Having stilled the dust" (*reṇuṃ vūpasametvā*) means having caused the dust to settle; they remain as a canopy above, removing fierce winds, heat, falling snow, and so forth.

Because it performs the function of a canopy, and because the meaning—that flowers are brought from various places such as the Himalayas—is understood [from the context], it was not stated explicitly in that way. They incline and rise merely by being made level;

for that very reason, the ground becomes even at the time of setting down the foot. And this is merely an illustration, as it also includes the removal of pebbles, gravel, thorns, stumps, mud, and so forth.
This occurs according to possibility; it is the natural outflow (*nissanda-phala*) of the characteristic of having well-planted feet, not a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi-nimmāna*).
Regarding the phrase "lotus flowers come," the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative; thus, it means:
"If the ground is level in the manner already described, then those [beings] do not accept them; but if it is not so, they do accept them."

This shows that the Blessed One’s movement proceeds according to his own inclination. He says, "as soon as the right foot was placed," because the Blessed One’s every step is always adorned with the secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*) known as the lifting of the right foot first.
The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla and the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta state that this is said because the Buddhas are supreme in all respects;
the meaning is that it is spoken thus because they are the highest of all beings. This being so:
[The phrase] "because of the nature of the Supreme Beings" implies that [the light] reaches them. The connection is: "As soon as it was established, they emerged and ran forth.
And this was said with reference to the place where they were seen, for the Teacher’s miracle was solely for the purpose of training those to be trained.
Although he said "six-colored rays," the statement "as if yellowed by liquid gold" [is used].
It should be understood that the Blessed One’s body was for the most part of a golden luster (*pītābhā*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"In this context, the word *rasa* is a synonym for water, and the word *piñjara* is a synonym for the color of gold; thus the meaning is that they were golden-colored like a stream of molten gold.
As for the palaces, gabled chambers, and so forth, these were found in various villages, market towns, and other such places.
“Being adorned.

By the words “In that manner,” etc., he shows that the sounds were produced by them spontaneously through the very nature of things (*dhammatā*). “Approaching the body” means they approached the body;
they were not situated anywhere else. By the word “street,” [he indicates] for the Blessed One’s almsround...
He shows the path corresponding to his movement. For the Blessed One does not go anywhere at random like one who wanders for alms with restless intent.
It should be understood that those who had gone before, or those capable of giving alms appropriate to the occasion, would take up the Blessed One’s bowl as well.
"They honor" means they pay homage with mindfulness, or [they honor] the Blessed One.
