"Paṭimānāpenti" means they make a comparison. This is merely a conventional expression (*vohāramatta*); for the Blessed One, there is indeed no such thing as "comparison.
"Cittasantānāni" refers to the continuums of consciousness that have occurred in the past and those occurring at present.
The connection is: "He teaches the Dhamma so that some may become established in Arahatship. And the phrase "some having gone forth" refers to those who have attained Arahatship.
This is for the purpose of showing that they have reached the summary of going forth (*pabbajjā*), and not for the purpose of denying that householders can attain *arahantship*.
For this is the nature of householders who have attained *arahantship*: that on that very day they either go forth or pass away.
Thus it was said by the Venerable Elder Nāgasena: "The mark of a householder, Great King, is uneven; in an uneven mark..."

"O Great King, it is not the fault of Arahantship that a householder who has attained Arahantship due to the weakness of his physical marks either goes forth on that very day or passes into Parinibbāna; rather, this is the fault of the householder's mark itself, namely, its weakness.
All of this should be stated. And here, by means of the connection with the entry into the presence of the wonders, the benefit to the great multitude is demonstrated.

Furthermore, by way of entering without a formal invitation, the statement beginning with “well-robed and well-clad” should be connected as appropriate, and the benefit to the great multitude must be explained according to its meaning.
For that too is indeed a duty to be performed before the meal. And here, the "attendance hall" (upaṭṭhānasālā) refers to the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāḷa).
Having gone there, the reading written here is "in the circular pavilion" (maṇḍalamāḷe); it is also [referred to] as the "scented circular pavilion" (gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe).
It is seen in the *Manorathapūraṇī*, and in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) it is stated: "In the circular hall (*maṇḍalamāḷa*) on the veranda, with four kinds of fragrant scents.
Regarding the phrase "he enters the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*)," this is stated because of the connection with the action of entering and because of its proximity;
therefore, the meaning should be understood as "he goes to enter," and not that he remains inside. For thus [it says]: "Then..."
The statement beginning with "Then the Blessed One... is well-founded.
"Then" (*atha kho*) refers to the time of going to enter the Gandhakuṭī. "In attendance" (*upaṭṭhāne*) means in the vicinity.
Regarding the phrase "having washed his feet and standing on the footstool, he exhorted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," it means that while still washing his feet, [he stood] upon the footstool.
It should be understood that he exhorts while standing. For it was for this very purpose that he remained seated, awaiting the conclusion of the monks' meal.

"Rare is the attainment" means that even when human birth has been obtained, qualities reckoned as attainments—such as dwelling in a suitable locality, the integrity of the sense faculties, and the acquisition of faith—are rare. In the manuscripts, however, it reads: "Rare is the attainment of faith."
The reading [found there] is seen, but it is indeed inappropriate. *Tattha* means: at the time of giving exhortation while standing on that footstool;

or, among those monks, a place for dwelling at night is a "night-dwelling" (*rattiṭṭhāna*), and likewise a "day-dwelling" (*divāṭṭhāna*). The phrase beginning with "Some" (*keci*) and so forth is its explanation.
"The abode of the Four Great Kings" (*cātumahārājikabhavana*) is said with reference to the empty celestial mansions (*suññavimānāni*) in the world of the gods of the Four Great Kings. This...
This method applies to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and other realms as well. Then, having entered the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi), the Blessed One divides the afternoon into three parts;

if he so desires during the first part, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture (sīhaseyyā), and if he does not desire it, he enters the fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti) as practiced by the Buddhas. Then, according to the time limit, from there...

Having emerged from that state, during the second watch, in the third division of the final watch, he surveys the world as if looking over it, in order to see the ripening of the wisdom of those to be trained;
therefore he says, "If he so desires," and so forth. The meaning of "the lion’s posture" and so on has already been explained above.
We shall now comment only upon those words that are new and not yet fully elucidated. He should be properly comforted.
“Supported by means of grasping” means comforted. One whose body is such is “one who is thus. He assembles for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Referring to the fact that he has performed [the teaching] after knowing the mental disposition of that assembly, he says: “by a miracle appropriate to the assembled company.
That place where they speak the Dhamma together is called a *dhammasabhā*. “Timely” means—
“At this time, this should be said for him”—this refers to what is appropriate to each specific occasion.

“Appropriate to the occasion” (*samayayutta*) is a synonym for that very term; or, it means appropriate to the context of the origin of the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*). Alternatively, “appropriate to the occasion” means endowed with reasons and examples.
For the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma with its specific details at the proper time; having discerned the right time, he dismisses the assembly.

The intention is that he does not teach the Dhamma as long as it is dark. In some places, a variant reading is seen stating, “Having recognized the time, he dismissed the assembly,” but this was written later through negligence.

“Limbs” refers to the body itself, mentioned because it consists of many parts. By the phrase “he causes [the body] to take on the temperature,” it is meant specifically for the purpose of causing the temperature to be taken up.
This shows that it was for the purpose of sprinkling and not for the purpose of washing away dirt; for no dust or mud ever adhered to the Blessed One’s body.
A *gandhakuṭī* is a cell perfumed with four kinds of fragrant scents. Its courtyard is likewise called a *gandhakuṭī*.

He withdrew into seclusion for a moment by means of the attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "From there to there" means from his respective place for staying at night and his place for staying during the day.
*Upagantvā* means approaching, or standing near, attending upon, associating with, or serving; such is the meaning.
*Tattha* means in that place of sitting, or during the first watch of the night, or among those bhikkhus.
Accomplishing his purpose by means of answering questions and so forth, he did not say "the ten-thousandfold world-system," but rather of that...
The phrase "the entire ten-thousandfold world system" is stated for the purpose of including many constituent parts.

The intention is that because they could not find space due to the great crowds of people during the morning, afternoon, and first watch of the day, they are now finding space only during the middle watch;
or else, it means they are finding space because the Blessed One has granted them the opportunity. But what kind of question are they asking?
He said: "As it was formulated, even down to four syllables. "As it was formulated" means in accordance with what was formulated, or not exceeding that;
by this he shows that she asked in whatever way accorded to her own inspiration.
Regarding the time after the meal, in its three parts, the adoption of the lion’s posture in the first part is not absolutely required.
He said: "Of the body oppressed by sitting from before the morning meal onwards.
For it was by that very [statement] previously—"if he so desires"—that the non-binding nature of assuming the lion’s posture was clarified. "Fatigue" (*kilāsubhāvo*) means weariness.
The connection is: "In order to release the body from its state of fatigue, he passes the time by walking and assumes the lion’s posture."

"By the Buddha-eye" means by the Buddha-eye, which consists of the knowledge of the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the degrees of the faculties of others, and which constitutes the fifth and sixth powers.

For it is because of the frequency with which he surveys the world that this is called the "Buddha-eye," and this is stated here with reference to what was most commonly practiced by the Blessed One during the final watch of the night. Occasionally, however, it is performed by means of the remaining powers and knowledges as well.
And the Blessed One establishes that matter by means of his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
In order to support the point previously stated—that "he knew while performing the duties of the last watch of the night"—he said, beginning with "On that day," and so forth.
For the Blessed Buddhas, wherever they may dwell, this fivefold [knowledge]...
The duty remains unabandoned at all times because of the constant presence of well-established mindfulness and clear comprehension;
therefore, it should be understood that the "purpose of the fivefold duty" is mentioned here in order to demonstrate that state of non-abandonment even on that particular day.
"They walk there" means they walk in a place suitable for walking. "While walking, he knew"—thus it should be construed. Regarding the two meanings previously stated:

Taking only the latter meaning, it is said: “referring to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); for the former meaning is easily understood because it has already been established by the context of the treatise.
The passage, “Then the Blessed One, having understood this summarized teaching (*saṅkhiyadhamma*) of those bhikkhus, approached the Maṇḍalamāḷa,” is a reading that leaves something unsaid;
therefore, it means that he approached after having understood this and having reflected thus.
In order to show that the meaning should be understood, the passage beginning with “But having known this” was spoken.
Therein, “it occurred to him” means that this reflection arose in the Blessed One, or that this mental deliberation occurred;

this is a grammatical shift of gender (liṅgavipallāsa), as seen in expressions such as “this is the foremost” (*etadagga*). The function of omniscient knowledge is not manifest in every respect. “Uninterruptedly” means...
It is "without distinction" (*nibbivara*) by way of being announced in successive order, or "without difference" (*nibbisesa*) by way of announcing exactly what was spoken.
This is a gerundive neuter form. "Making that the occasion for the arising" (*aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā*) means making that speech as it was announced the cause for the arising of this sutta;
or alternatively, the meaning is "making the cause for the arising of the teaching of this sutta. The word *attha*—
And here, because it is the cause, he shows the introduction (*nikkhepa*) of this sutta as being based on an occasion (*aṭṭhuppattika*).
"In sixty-two positions" means in the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*).
"Irrefutable" means not to be overturned by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. "Roaring the lion's roar."
He roared an unafraid roar, known as the "supreme roar. Regarding this, worldly people say:
"In the masculine gender, the words *byaggha*, *puṅgava*, *usabha*, *kuñjara*, *sīha*, *saddūla*, *nāga*, and so forth, have the sense of excellence as their domain (*gocara*)."
This should be understood as being according to the majority of cases. Or, it is like one who utters a roar similar to a lion’s roar; this meaning is to be illustrated by the *Sīhanāda-sutta*.

Just as the maned king of beasts is called a "lion" (sīha) because of his endurance (*sahana*) and his slaying (*hana*), so too the Tathāgata is called a "lion" because of his endurance of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and his slaying of the doctrines of others (*parappavāda*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning is "roaring the roar of the Tathāgata-lion. For just as a lion, endowed with lion-strength,
confident in every respect and free from timidity, roars his lion's roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata,
confident in the eight assemblies and free from timidity, [utters the roar] beginning with, "These are the standpoints of views," and so forth.
By means of this method, he roars the lion’s roar, endowed with the elegance of various kinds of teaching. With reference to this it was said:
“Monks, ‘the lion’ is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Whatever Dhamma the Tathāgata teaches to the assembly, monks, that is his lion’s roar. [The passage beginning] “These are the bases of views,” etc., [is also spoken with reference to this].

For here, the "lion's roar" refers precisely to the teaching that is about to be expounded. It should also be understood that the convergence of the mode of conditionality occurs through the method to be explained in the passage beginning with, "With feeling as condition, craving arises.

By means of the two similes—beginning with "like Mount Sineru" and so forth—he demonstrates the extreme difficulty [of this teaching], owing to its being unique and not shared by others in the *Brahmajāla* exposition.
"With a golden peak" (*suvaṇṇakūṭena*) means by means of a particular tool or implement made of gold.
Just as a house is brought to completion by a pinnacle (*nikūṭa*), so too does he bring the *Brahmajāla Sutta* to its conclusion with the pinnacle of *arahantship*.

The meaning of "with the pinnacle" (*nikūṭena*) is "with that which has reached its completion," namely, the highest peak. And because this [sutta] culminates in the fruit of *arahantship*, which is the summit of all virtues, it is said to be "the most excellent of all.
Furthermore, the preceding word *me* (by me) refers to the teaching; thus, even for one who has attained final *parinibbāna*...
The meaning that this teaching [will last] for five thousand years in the future is appropriate.

The intention is that it will lead to the attainment of Nibbāna for those who cultivate familiarity through hearing, grasping, retaining, reciting, and so forth, and who likewise practice accordingly.

Just as the instrumental description "by which" (*yena*) applies to a certain extent, so too should "by that" (*tena*) be understood in that same sense. "This" (*etam*) refers to the phrase "by which... by that."

These are two words. "Therein" (*tattha*) means "in that maṇḍalamāḷa. Alternatively, *yena* is used in the sense of the locative case (*bhumm-atthe*), while *tena* is used in the sense of the accusative (*upayoga-atthe*).
Therefore, they also say that "therein" (*tattha*) refers to "that maṇḍalamāḷa.
Regarding "he approached" (*upasaṅkami*), the meaning is "approaching" (*upasaṅkamanto*), because the present tense is intended; however, as for that act of approaching—
Because it indicates a past state, the expression "he approached" (*upasaṅkami*) is stated in the past tense by way of reference to that time;
for in this way, the word "having approached" (*upasaṅkamitvā*) becomes well-founded. Otherwise, since both words would belong to the past tense, such a construction could not have been used.
Furthermore, the meaning of "approaching" (*upasaṅkamana*) is twofold: going (*gamana*) and drawing near (*upagamana*).

In this context, however, there is only the act of going. For when one goes to any place out of a desire to reach it, by virtue of passing through each successive location, one may be said to "approach that place" or "while approaching.
Therefore, he says "gone there," which excludes the sense of merely approaching.
For when one goes desiring to reach a certain place, it is precisely by reaching it [that the action is completed].
It is called "approaching" (*upagamana*). That word "having approached" (*upasaṅkamitvā*), which has not been commented upon here, indicates the conclusion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, one who has gone (*gata*) is one who has approached (*upagata*).

For even a term without a prefix can express a different meaning as if it had a prefix, and a term with a prefix can likewise express a meaning as if it were without a prefix. Therefore, by the word "having approached," one who has thus approached is indicated as being closer than that [mere going].
The meaning should be understood as: having approached a place capable of allowing him to either answer questions or teach the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus.

Furthermore, *yena* is used in the instrumental case to express cause; the meaning is: "for whatever reason the Blessed One should approach that pavilion, for that reason he approached. As for that reason: "These... [and so on].
“Bhikkhus,” and so forth, is exactly as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

Regarding the phrase “he sat down on a seat prepared,” when the inquiry arises as to by whom this was prepared, he said “it is said that during the time of the Buddha” and so forth, in order to show that it was by the bhikkhus.
Therein, “during the time of the Buddha” means during the period when the Blessed One was living. “Distinction” (visesa) [refers to...]
"Higher than what was obtained" refers to the fruit of the path of jhāna. "Atha" (then) is a particle used in the sense of doubt;
the meaning is "if he sees. The connection is "that bhikkhunī, while reflecting. Likewise, having shown the cause for seeing from that [state], and having "instructed," [he said].
"Anamatagge" means beginningless. "Upapatitvā ākāsaṃ" means having ascended into the sky. In such cases...
For it is stated in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* that only the meaning of "ground" (*bhummattha*) is appropriate here.

"A burden" (*bhāra*) refers to the heavy task resulting from the difficulty of obtaining a seat suitable for the Blessed One at that very moment. "A plank" (*phalaka*) is a board made for the purpose of sitting.
"A wooden slab" (*kaṭṭhaka*) is a block of wood other than a plank, fit for sitting. "Having gathered together" (*saṅkaḍḍhitvā*) means having brought together.
"Among those" (*tattha*) means on old leaves; it is stated thus because sitting on them alone would be inappropriate. Alternatively, "among those" refers to the benches and so forth.
This being the case, the connection is made by changing the grammatical case according to the sense: "having gathered [the leaves] together, they arrange them.
"Having shaken off" (*papphoṭetvā*) means that what was previously covered with dust, dirt, and the like is no longer suitable as it stands.
Having moved [the seat] for the purpose of purifying the magic spell (*tabbi*), they thought, "A conversation such as this of ours is likely to be the cause for a certain teaching;
the Blessed One will certainly come," and it was said with reference to the sitting mat itself.
And herein, it was placed by the king with the thought: "Let whatever ascetic or brahmin comes here take it for the time being and use it."
Furthermore, it should be understood that the seat used by him at the time of his arrival was the king’s own sitting seat.
Indeed, it is not proper for monks to use a seat left there in such a manner, nor is it proper for them to prepare one for the Blessed One.

Therefore, in order to show that such a seat as the king’s sitting seat is what is mentioned in the text, the words beginning with “referring to that” (*taṃ sandhāyā*) were spoken. [The term] *adhimutti-ñāṇa* means...

And the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) has as its object the various inclinations and mental supports of beings; this same point has already been stated regarding the "knowledge of the powers" (*balañāṇa*).
By the words "Thus," etc., he shows that the phrase "seated" indicates the conclusion of the act of sitting.
Since it was said, "Having understood these summarized teachings of those bhikkhus," the meaning is established that he asked [the question] while already knowing [the answer]; thus he said.
“Knowing indeed”: when there is no basis for the discussion, the successive specialized discourse appropriate to it does not flourish;
therefore, the question should be understood as being for the purpose of initiating the discussion. *Nu* is used in the sense of questioning.
The word *asa* is said to have the sense of proceeding; thus it is said: “By which [means]... do you exist? *Ettha* means in this place.

By means of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), there is simply the substitution of *okāra* for *ukāra*; he shows that there is no difference in meaning from the first passage with the words, "the meaning of that is also the same as before.
"The meaning is the same as before" refers to the meaning expressed as, "In what state do you exist?
Furthermore, in the phrase "And who," the word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of contrast (*byatireka*), as in: "But whoever [goes for refuge] to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha..."

[The particle *pana* is used] as in [the phrase] “gone,” and so forth. Furthermore, what is called *byatireka* (contrast) refers to a meaning that exceeds a distinction in relation to a previously stated sense;
and it illuminates that sense of contrast, which consists in the fact that the discourse—having been asked as before—is yet to be completed. The word *pana* is an ornament of speech.
Moreover, such a meaning is easily understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*) alone.
Having done so, in order to show the meaning of other [terms] as well, he said: “‘Antarākathā’ means talk concerning the meditation subject...

talk,” and so forth. Since attention to the meditation subject, instruction, inquiry, and so on, constitute the duties of a recluse (*samaṇakaraṇīya*), they should be expressed as being in a state of relation to the specific duties implied by the word *antara*;
however, because those very things are what ought to be expressed, it is said: “of attention to the meditation subject, instruction, inquiry, and so on.”
It has been said. For that very conversation by which those bhikkhus were seated together is the "intermediate conversation" (*antarākathā*) that is specifically asked about again when unfinished;
it is not some other topic such as attention to a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), recitation (*uddesa*), or interrogation (*paripucchā*).
He states another meaning for the word *antara* with the words "another, one. For these two terms are synonyms. Since this [word] is used in the sense of "another,"...
The word *antarā* is used here as in expressions such as "another place" (*bhūmantara*) or "another time" (*samayantara*).

Therefore, in the phrase "of the attention to the meditation subject, the recitation, the questioning, and so forth," the genitive case should be understood in the sense of an ablative (indicating separation). Alternatively, the word *antarā* means "in between";

however, since that [state] is distinct because it constitutes the interval between them, and because it is unmixed with them, it is "another, a single [state]"—this is the intended meaning shown by the words "another, a single."

And it has been said: *pakato* means "made in a particular way" (*pakārena karaṇaṃ*); that from which one is removed, or that in which what was made has departed, is *vippakata*, meaning "unfinished" or "incomplete.
*Sikha* means "conclusion. This, however, is a question expressing a desire to speak further by way of connecting with that [preceding point];

with reference to this, he says "I do not," and so forth. "For the purpose of breaking off the discussion" (*kathābhaṅgatthaṃ*) means for the sake of interrupting the discourse. Because it follows logically from the sense (*atthato*).
He performs the invitation of the Omniscient One. Because they do not lead to heaven or the path to liberation, worldly talk is called *tiracchānakathā*.
The term *tiracchānabhūtā* means "that which acts as a barrier" or "that which constitutes an obstruction.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), various kinds of useless talk are included here, such as talk about thieves, high officials, armies, and dangers.
This statement, "this very discourse," was spoken with reference to an inclusionary restriction (*antogadhāvadhāraṇa*) or the exclusion of other possibilities (*aññatthāpohana*).

The word "then" (*atha*) refers to the time when that [discourse] had not yet been completed. By the phrase "that to us," etc., he states what is implied by the sense. This same method applies to similar cases.
But is it not the case that those bhikkhus already brought that discourse to its intended conclusion with the words "Thus indeed to me," and so forth?
They were not brought to completion because they were interrupted by the Blessed One’s arrival.
For had the Blessed One not arrived at that moment, they would have continued in that same manner, still bound to that very thing; but through the Blessed One’s arrival, they did not proceed.
Therefore he said: "This [opportunity] for us... has arrived."

Now, demonstrating that the introduction (nidāna) or the commentary on the introduction has been concluded, and in order to establish that it is also in conformity with the words of the Blessed One, he says "to this extent" (*ettāvatā*), and so forth.
For "to this extent" means either: by this much, the introduction was spoken through the sequence of words beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam me sutam*);
or, by this much, [the introduction was spoken] through the sequence of words beginning with "In this context, *evaṃ* is a particle," and so on.
The commentary on the meaning is finished; thus, the meaning should be understood in two ways. Furthermore, by the passage beginning with “*kamala... pe ...
salilāya*,” he illustrates how that introductory narrative conforms to the words of the Blessed One. In that context, “*kamalakuvalayujjalavimalasādhurasasalilāya*” means:

by means of the waters which are pure, sweet, and radiant with *kamala* flowers—namely, the *paduma*, *puṇḍarīka*, *setuppala*, and *rattuppala*—and with the *kuvalaya*, namely the blue lotus (*nīluppalaka*).
And [it was] possessed of water that was bright, pure, and sweet-tasting.

"Adorned with jewel-stairways, beautiful through the grace of the arrangement of stainless stone slabs" means possessing jewel-stairways beautified by the grace—the playful charm—of the arrangement of stainless stone slabs;
or, possessing jewel-stairways beautified by the grace of the arrangement of stainless stone slabs, and by the beauty of well-constructed workmanship; [and] by the sounds beautified by grace.
Or rather, its state of being exceedingly beautiful is described.

"With ground parts white with powder of sand resembling the surface of scattered pearls" means possessing ground parts that are white in color due to the powder of variously scattered pearls and sand similar to their surface.
"Of that which is surrounded by well-proportioned walls and variegated railings" means of that which is beautiful with well-divided walls.
And of that which was surrounded by railings. With its sound of yawning, it was as if desiring to touch the sky, the path of the constellations, by rising higher;
such is the connection with the mind. "Of the mass of yawning" means possessing a multitude of playful movements.
"Resplendent with a collection of light from clusters of jewels entwined with golden creepers upon smooth, soft ivory slabs" refers to those made of ivory.
It was exceedingly beautiful, endowed with a radiant splendor from the mass of light emanating from clusters of gems entwined by golden creepers upon very smooth surfaces;
it was filled with the sweet sounds of the household folk talking and laughing,
intermingled with the clinking of golden bracelets, anklets, and other ornaments striking one another.
It was a place frequented by men and women living in houses who were endowed with sweet voices characterized by a mixture of sounds produced by laughter and talk;
it was adorned with the splendor of great majesty and wealth— meaning [adorned] by people possessed of high status,
people possessed of sovereignty, and people possessed of riches— or rather, by the men and women dwelling therein.

Of one adorned with supreme sovereignty and enjoyments. "With wide doorposts well-established, radiant and resplendent with the luster of gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth" means having wide doorposts that are well-established and shining, illuminated by the brilliance of gold, silver, various gems, pearls, coral, and the like.

It is called "indicative of the power of the Buddha’s qualities" because it correctly proclaims the majesty of the Buddha’s virtues by way of demonstrating his threefold morality and other attributes.
Of that [Dhamma]. It is thus adorned by way of the time, the place, the teacher, the subject matter, and the assembly—by means of these references and illustrations.

But for what purpose is the introductory statement (nidāna) uttered here when the compendium of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being made? Is it not the case that only the words spoken by the Blessed One should be compiled?
It is said: for the sake of ensuring the stability, non-confusion, and credibility of the teaching.
For a teaching established by being bound together through the factors of time, place, teacher, subject matter, and audience becomes long-enduring and possesses the quality of being non-forgettable;
it is like a legal decision that is made credible when bound by the specific details of the speaker, time, place, cause, and motive.
It was for this very reason that the Venerable Mahākassapa asked, "Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla spoken? and so forth.
When questions concerning the location and other details were posed, the Elder Ānanda, the Dhamma-treasurer, provided their answers by stating the *nidāna*.
Therefore, it is said here as well: "The *nidāna* is adorned with the time, place, teacher, subject matter, assembly, and specific reference.

Furthermore, the statement of the *nidāna* is for the purpose of manifesting the perfection of the Teacher; for in the case of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, there is an absence of prior composition, inference, scripture, or logic.

The establishment of his state as a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddhatta*). For, because of his status as a Perfectly Enlightened One, there was previously no room for conjecture—thinking, "It might perhaps be thus"—regarding his compositions, nor for deliberation based on other scriptures, with respect to all things knowable (*ñeyyadhamma*), due to the unimpeded range of his knowledge which is the sole authority.
Likewise, [he was free from] the state of being a teacher’s fist, stinginess regarding the Dhamma, or compliance with the expectations of disciples regarding the Dispensation.

The accomplishment of the state of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). For through the destruction of the taints, there is an absence of the "teacher’s fist" and the like, and the activity of benefiting others is purified.

Thus, by means of the qualities of the Fully Enlightened One’s purity—which indicate the absence of ignorance and craving (the defilements of the teacher that corrupt the perfection of view and conduct) and which manifest the excellence of knowledge and abandonment—the first two grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) are established.

And precisely because the absence of delusion regarding what constitutes obstacles and what leads to liberation is established thereby, the latter two forms of self-confidence (vesārajja) are established;
thus, the Blessed One’s possession of the four forms of self-confidence, as well as his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others, is revealed by the introductory statement,
since it is shown that he teaches the Dhamma through spontaneous eloquence appropriate to the inclinations of the assembled audience.
And because of such statements as “by one who knows and sees,” it is said: “The introductory statement (nidāna) is for the purpose of demonstrating the perfection of the Teacher.
Furthermore, the introductory statement is for the purpose of demonstrating the perfection of the Dispensation (sāsana).

For there is no purposeless activity on the part of the Blessed One, whose every action is encompassed by wisdom and compassion; nor does he act for his own benefit. Therefore, [his activity] is solely for the benefit of others.

The entire bodily, verbal, and mental action of the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has set all activities in motion, as it occurs and is being described, is called the "Sāsana" (Teaching) in the sense that it instructs beings appropriately according to the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal; it is not a mere poetic composition.
This conduct of the Teacher [is to be understood] by way of the time, the place, the teacher, the subject matter, and the assembly.
It is explained there and there, as appropriate, along with the introductory statements (*nidāna*).
Alternatively, the introductory statement is for the purpose of demonstrating the authoritative nature of the Teaching by way of demonstrating the authoritative nature of the Teacher;
and that demonstration of its authoritative nature is effected by the term "Bhagavā," which indicates that the Tathāgata is distinguished by qualities and is the supreme among all beings.
This is also elucidated by such passages as "by one who knows and sees," which illustrate the application of the knowledge of underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth.
This is merely an indication of the primary purpose of the introductory statement (*nidāna-vacana*) here.

For who is capable of fully elucidating, without remainder, the purposes of the introduction spoken by the Steward of the Dhamma (*dhammabhaṇḍāgārika*), who followed after the Buddha? And there are these verses on this point: [The verses follow]
“For the sake of the long endurance of the teaching, for the purpose of non-forgetfulness,
and as a source of faith, this was spoken by the illustrious one of clear vision.
It is for the sake of the perfection of the Teacher and for the excellence of the Dispensation.”
"...was spoken for the purpose of showing that state of being immeasurable.
Thus [ends the section] from the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which elucidates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend;

which generates an extremely pure and vast analytical wisdom; and which was composed by one endowed with the qualities of integrity, gentleness, modesty, faith, mindfulness, fortitude, intelligence, patience, energy, and so forth.
This is the elucidation of the hidden meaning of the internal introduction to the *Sādhuvilāsinī*, a commentary on the *Līnatthapakāsinī* composed by the Elder Ñāṇābhivamsa Dhammasenāpati—
the Great Preceptor, a great teacher of grammar, a leader of a large community, one whose conduct was characterized by unimpeded, unshakeable, and confident knowledge,
and who had plunged into the depths of the manifold divisions of his own tradition and those of other traditions, and who was the venerable teacher of the Great King of Dharma.
The commentary on the introduction (*nidāna*) is finished.
Having thus completed the commentary on the internal introduction, he now proceeds to comment upon the Sutta as it has been set forth.
A commentary that follows the proper sequence avoids the fault of confusion and is beneficial for the wise.

“Delighting the mind” (*cittārādhinī*) means that one who has received the burden must necessarily carry it; thus, by carrying the burden already received, this [verse] demonstrates the absence of any transgression of wise conduct on the part of the commentator.
Therefore, in order to establish the disclosure of that [fact], he says “Now,” etc., to investigate the occasion for the commentary.
“Of what has been set forth” (*nikkhittassa*) means “of what has been taught,” for “setting forth” (*nikkhepa*) is synonymous with “teaching” (*desanā*) in meaning.

Even though they are distinct, they are one in their essential nature; for "exposition" (*nikkhepa*) is so called because the teaching is placed within the mental continuums of those to be trained, consisting of the meaning of virtue and so forth that is to be taught.
To the question, "Is it not the Sutta itself that is being commented upon? he says, "But this [exposition]," and so on. This is what is meant:
the commentary being spoken after having investigated the exposition of the Sutta is [described as] "this teaching arises in such a manner."

Because the commentary on the Sutta becomes easy to understand through a thorough investigation of its introduction (*nidāna*), we shall first examine that very part in a general manner. For whatever discourse makes the explanation of the Sutta’s meaning clear must be stated by the commentator;
and since it is a means for understanding that meaning, it is, in a figurative sense, itself a commentary.
Furthermore, when that has been investigated, the commentary on the passages of the Sutta spoken as "Bhikkhus,
[regarding] me," "But this is indeed a trifle," and "There is, bhikkhus,"— which were set forth by way of analyzing the occasion for which this Sutta was delivered—
is easy to understand because it provides the pleasure of seeing the respective connections between them.

It should be understood. In this regard, just as the discourses (suttantas), though divided into many hundreds and thousands, do not exceed sixteenfold nature according to the method of the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*—beginning with those dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth—so too, by way of the four modes of presentation of discourses (*suttanikkhepa*) such as those arising from one’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), they possess a fourfold nature.
Thus he said, "the four modes of presentation of discourses. But is it not possible that there is also a division by way of association (*saṃsagga*)? Why, then, [does he say] "four"?
Is it said that there are "modes of presentation" (*suttanikkhepa*)? Because no distinction in association (*saṃsaggabheda*) is found everywhere.

For a distinction in association is possible with those [discourses] based on one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), those arising from a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), and those based on the inclination of another (*parajjhāsaya*) or on a question (*pucchāvasika*). [The fourfold classification is:
"Based on one's own inclination and based on the inclination of another; based on one's own inclination and based on a question; based on one's own inclination and..."

[The suttas are classified as] those based on another’s inclination (*parajjhāsaya*), those dependent on a question (*pucchāvasika*), and those arising from a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppattika*); [also] those based on another’s inclination and arising from a specific occasion;

those arising from a specific occasion and based on another’s inclination; and those arising from a specific occasion, based on another’s inclination, and dependent on a question—because of the existence of these transitions through inclination, questioning, and specific occasions.

However, there is no mutual conjunction between one’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and what arises from a specific occasion; therefore, [the classification] is exhaustive according to the method of expansion (*patthānanaya*).
It should be understood that this was said precisely because a separation from association is not possible.
Alternatively, there might be a separation through association even by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) or by one's own inclination;

however, since the other types of placement (*nikkhepa*) mentioned by way of association are included within it, the statement "there are four types of placement of the Suttas" refers specifically to the placement of the root [the *nidāna*].

However, it should be understood that in this interpretation of the meaning, he demonstrates the mere method [of exposition] by showing that the "laying down of the suttas" (suttanikkhepa) must be explained according to the system of the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*—namely, by way of single, pairs, triads, and tetrads as appropriate. Herein, this is the etymological explanation:
laying down (*nikkhipana*) means speaking; the laying down of a sutta is "suttanikkhepa," which means the teaching of a sutta. It is so called because it is laid down (*nikkhipīyati*).
Or, "suttanikkhepa" is the placement of the sutta itself; thus, it is the "placement of the sutta. "Attajjhāsaya" means one's own inclination (*ajjhāsaya*);
it is called "attajjhāsaya" because that [inclination] exists in him by way of being its cause, or because his own inclination follows the manner already described.
The same method applies to "parajjhāsaya" (the inclination of another). "Pucchāvaso" means the influence of a question (*pucchā*); he possesses that, hence it is "pucchāvaso."
"By the method already stated" means it is dependent on a question. That which is to be sought after and understood is called the "meaning" (*attha*), namely the subject matter of the discourse;
its arising is the "arising of meaning" (*atthuppatti*). By changing the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*, that same term becomes *aṭṭhuppatti*.

Since this [discourse] possesses such an arising according to the stated method, it is called "dependent on an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattika*). Furthermore, it is called a "laying down" (*nikkhepa*) because the discourse is laid down by means of it.
This is precisely the reason for the teaching of suttas such as the *Attajjhāsaya*. In this interpretation of the meaning, however, "one's own inclination" is *attajjhāsaya*;
"the inclination of others" is *parajjhāsaya*. That which is asked is "questioning" (*pucchā*), referring to the matter to be questioned.

The speech of those receiving the Dhamma that proceeds by way of that questioning is "dependent on questioning" (*pucchāvasika*). This very term, in view of the word used for its formal presentation (*nikkhepa*), [is so designated].

It is stated in the masculine gender as "dependent on a question" (*pucchāvasika*). Following the method already explained, the meaning should be understood as "dependent on an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattika*), because it arises from a specific occasion.
And herein, without depending on external causes such as the ripening of the faculties of others, [the Buddha] establishes the system of the Dhamma solely by his own inclination.
Because it is a teaching set in motion by his own inclination, its status as a separate category is appropriate. For this very reason, he will say:

"He speaks solely according to his own inclination. However, since those [teachings] that arise on account of questions prompted by the inclinations of others—questions posed by others that serve as the occasion for the teaching—are set in motion [by him], how could they not be included within the category of "arising from an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattika*)?

This should not be challenged by asking how there could be no restriction regarding the inclinations of others, given that the teachings were delivered in accordance with the inclinations of others, whether arising from questions or from the occurrence of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

For the reason for the delivery of a discourse is understood through the "occurrence of a specific occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattivasena*) even when it arises independently of the formal requests or detailed inquiries of others.
Thus, [the teaching] pertains to those instances where the questions arise from the inclinations of others.

The separate mention is for this reason: for instance, in the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* and others, that which is taught as a result of the acquisition of material gifts and so forth is called "occasioned by an incident" (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
That which is taught by taking the inclination of others as the motive, even without their having asked a question, is "occasioned by another's inclination" (*parajjhāsaya*).
That which is taught by means of a question is "occasioned by a question" (*pucchāvasika*); this meaning is well known.

"Unsolicited" (*anajjhiṭṭho*) means not requested or asked by means of questioning and so forth; the intention is that he speaks of his own accord for the purpose of establishing the framework of the Dhamma.
"Hārā" means a series (*āvaḷi*), as in "a pearl necklace" (*muttāhāro*); it is the "bearer" (*hārako*).
He is likewise the bearer of the *Sammappadhāna-suttantas*. For, in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, those discourses connected with the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are presented in successive order.

The series of discourses is called the "Bearer of the Discourses on the Right Exertions" (*sammappadhāna-suttanta-hāraka*), and likewise the "Bearer of the Discourses on the Bases of Psychic Power" (*iddhipāda-hāraka*), and so forth.

In the preceding terms, such as "Bearer of the Discourses on the Bases of Psychic Power, the Faculties, the Powers, the Factors of Enlightenment, and the Path," there is either elision of the subsequent word, or this is a compound containing a copulative (dvanda) within it, or it is an elliptical expression (*peyyāla-niddesa*).
"Of them" refers to the aforementioned discourses.

“Fully matured” (*paripakkā*) means ripened. “Conducive to the maturation of liberation” (*vimuttiparipācanīyā*) refers to the mental factors such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) that bring the fruit of arahantship to maturity.
“For the sake of destruction” (*khaye*) means for the purpose of destruction, or for the teaching of the Dhamma which is the cause of destruction.

“Inclination” (*ajjhāsaya*) means resolve (*adhimutti*). “Tolerance” (*khanti*) means the tolerance regarding the contemplation of views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*). “Mind” (*mana*) means consciousness (*citta*). “Application” (*abhinīhāra*) means aspiration (*paṇidhāna*).
"Bujjhanabhāvaṃ" means the nature of awakening, or the mode of awakening. "Avekkhitvā" means having reflected upon, or having looked toward.

"Cattāro vaṇṇā" means the four castes (kulas), or the four types of beings measured by form and so forth. "Mahārājāno" refers to the four Great Kings, the deities. What is being spoken of? The meaning is: "What are the five aggregates of clinging? He asks "Why?
and replies with "In the context of the origin of the discourse," and so on. In the phrase "vaṇṇāvaṇṇe," the locative case is used to denote the occasion; by the word "vaṇṇa,"...
And here, the praise uttered by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus beginning with “It is wonderful, friends! is also included.
For, taking that as the occasion for the teaching, he will begin the subsequent instruction with the words, “There are, bhikkhus, other qualities,” and so forth.
He explains that very point with the passage beginning “A teacher,” etc., regarding this [statement]: “Or, bhikkhus, others might speak praise of me.”
Because this was taught by making the praise spoken by Brahmadatta the occasion for the teaching (*aṭṭhuppatti*), he said, "The disciple’s praise.
Now, in order to show the connection with the text (*pāḷi*), he said "Thus," and so forth.

"Skilled in teaching" means one who is skilled in teaching, [thinking] "this teaching arises from this occasion"; by this, he offered a praise of the Blessed One that is consistent with the context of the work.
For this is the nature of those who offer praise: namely, the extolling of the Blessed One by means of the qualities acquired through various treatises in this or that context.
And here, the particle *vā* is seen in many senses, such as comparison, conjunction, doubt, speech, release, word-filling, similarity, option, and so forth.
For instance, it is seen in the sense of comparison in passages such as, "He is indeed wise," where it denotes similarity.

The meaning [of *vā*] is as follows: in passages such as “The wise proclaim that very [person] to be a sage,” it signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*). In passages such as “Who are these, or whose [are they],” it signifies doubt (*saṃsaya*).
In passages such as “Among these ascetics and brahmins, this one is the most foolish and the most deluded,” it signifies the dropping of a word (*vacanavossagga*).
In passages such as “This boy did not know his measure,” it serves as a mere filler for the line (*padapūraṇa*). [And in the phrase] “He thinks it is honey... [it signifies comparison].

In such passages as "The fool [remains so] as long as the evil does not ripen," the word *vā* has the sense of similarity. In such passages as "Whosoever, monks, they may be, whether recluses or brahmins," it has the sense of option (*vikappa*).
Here too, it is precisely in the sense of option. Because it indicates a variety of separate options—such as "of me, or of the Dhamma, or of the Saṅgha"—it is said:
"The word *vā* has the sense of option. As for the word *para*, however, it certainly exists [in this context].
The word *para* has the sense of "other," as in "If I were to teach the Dhamma, others might not understand me";
it has the sense of "additional," as in "the mastery of the higher and lower faculties" (*indriyaparopariyatta*); it has the sense of "subsequent," as in "he will come later" (*parato āgamissati*);
and it has the sense of "adversary," as in "having thoroughly refuted with reasoned argument any arisen opposing doctrine."
Here too, he shows that "paccanīka" means "hostile" by means of the phrase "beings who are opposed.
The meaning is: beings who have become adversaries and opponents of the Teaching (sāsana).
The word *ta* refers back to the aforementioned subject as qualified by the act of speaking dispraise; thus it is said: "among those who speak dispraise."
One might raise the objection: "But surely they have no resentment, because of the greatness of their virtues; so why was it said thus?
To show the mere hint of this objection, he removes it with the words beginning "Kiñcāpi" (Even though...). The meaning is: "Even though [resentment] does not exist, nevertheless...

Here, in the phrase "īdisesu pi," the particle *pi* has the sense of possibility (*sambhāvana*); by this, he indicates that even toward such [beings], an unwholesome thought should not be produced, even on account of the Triple Gem.
How much less would one imagine it to be the sign of the world’s bait of worldly goods?
The Dhamma of the scriptures itself is the "guide" (nettī) in the sense of leading to the True Dhamma; thus, it is the "Dhamma-guide" (dhammanetti).

"Strikes" (āhanati) means it strikes thoroughly, or it injures, afflicts, and torments—this is the meaning. In some places the reading "etthā" is seen; that was written later, following the ancient reading.

Because it contradicts the commentary and lacks logical consistency regarding the meaning. Even though [the term] strikes down dejection (*domanassa*) and so forth, he shows that it is established specifically for anger by saying, "This is a designation (*adhivacana*) for anger.

For, having shown the primary sense (*avayavattha*), he spoke thus while indicating its figurative sense (*pariyāyena attha*) therein. And a "designation" (*adhivacana*) is a word that functions with reference to something specific (*adhikicca*).
Or, the word *nāma* means "well-known" (*pasiddha*). The same applies to the others as well.

And here, in order to show that there is no agent other than the phenomenon of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), the word *āghāta* is presented in the sense of an agent with the phrase "it strikes" (*āhanati*). Furthermore, the meanings of instrument and state are also possible:
"that by which one strikes" (*āhanati etena*) or "mere striking" (*āhananamattaṃ*) is *āghāta*. The meaning of the term "unpleasant" (*appatītā*) is as follows:
When it is said, “discontented and unhappy,” this is a demonstration of the derivation of the word *appaṭicca* by way of its common usage;
however, by that same approach, it should be understood as *appaṭicca*, meaning “that which does not depend. *Abhirādhayati* means “to accomplish.
*Ettha* means “in these three terms. *Dvīhi* means “by two,” namely the terms *āghāta* and *anabhiraddhi*. *Ekena* means “by one,” namely the term *appaṭicca*.

To clear away the objection that "if only those [factors] are taken, their associated factors would not be included, yet it is impossible not to include them as well because they share the same nature of arising simultaneously," the passage beginning with "of these" (*tesaṃ*) was stated.
"Of these" refers to the aforementioned portions of the formations aggregate (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) and the feeling aggregate (*vedanākkhandha*).

"The rest" refers to the remaining portions of the formations aggregate, excluding perception (*saññā*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). "Producing" (*karaṇa*) means causing to arise. For, of hatred and so forth...
Here, the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is said to be the concurrence of conditions for the process [of consciousness]; however, in actual fact, it is simply its production.
For it is with reference to the non-production of that [consciousness] that it is stated in the Pāḷi: "it is not to be made.
It is indeed rejected, as appropriate, because of its state of having a single arising, cessation, object, and basis.
*Tattha* means "in that mental corruption. By the phrase "in those who speak dispraise," he shows the locative case (*bhummavibhatti*) in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*).
Alternatively, he says "or in that dispraise" to indicate that this locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*) or as a characteristic of a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇa*).
For neither a lack of virtue nor blame can possibly be the locus of anger and dejection, since those [emotions] depend upon the person who utters them. *Assatha* is the seventh case (*sattamī*).
By the phrase "if form" (*rūpaṃ ce*), he shows that it is the object of conceptualization through its connection with the word "if" (*ce*).
By the word "you might be" (*bhaveyyātha*), they say: "When one says 'if you might be' (*yadi bhaveyyātha'), these words are connected respectively as preceding and following terms.
By the phrase "angered by anger, displeased by dejection," [he indicates] "thus, according to the first method," and so forth.
The stated word is validated by demonstrating that there is no difference in meaning.

Just as the single term *tumha* has the same meaning as *tumhākaṃ*, and the term *amha* has the same meaning as *amhākaṃ*—as in the expression, "Therefore, our children do not die"—it is said, "It belongs to you alone" (*tumhākaṃyeva*). This is because the gender is changed according to the requirement of the sense; thus, by means of that...

And it is said: "and for the sake of dissatisfaction. When "an obstacle" (*antarāya*) is stated, since the meaning "of the specific qualities of the ascetic life" (*samaṇadhamma-viśeṣānam*) is understood from the context of the treatise, and because there is freedom to employ a word whose meaning is already understood, it is stated as "an obstacle to the first jhāna and so forth.
And here, this term "obstacle" is a statement of the reason for the non-performance of mental corruption.

Since that anger and so forth would create an obstacle to the first jhāna and the others for you yourselves, the intention is that those acts of malice and the like, described by way of anger and so on, must not be committed. By this he shows:
"I do not forbid you from that out of a sense of lordship, saying 'I am omniscient,' but rather for this very reason. And as for that statement of the reason, since...
There is the discernment of danger; therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "showing the danger" was stated previously.

Furthermore, that corruption of mind is not only an obstacle to welfare and happiness occurring at another time, but it is also an obstacle to welfare and happiness that ought to arise at that very moment; thus, the danger in the corruption of mind is even more severe.
In order to demonstrate this, the connection may also be stated as beginning with “api nu. Regarding the phrase “of others,” the meaning is “those who are other than oneself”;
it does not mean “of hostile beings” as in such passages as “one should speak dispraise of others,” but rather he says “of whoever they may be.
He supports that very point with the words “for when angry,” and so forth. In the Pāli text, there is also the knowing of well-spoken and ill-spoken words.
He says, "the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken," because that [meaning] is established by the very knowledge of its purpose.

"Blinding darkness" (*andhaṃtamaṃ*) means the darkness that causes blindness, or an exceedingly great darkness. The connection is: "the blinding darkness of that man whom it overcomes (*sahate*), that is, subdues.
Alternatively, *yaṃ* is a nominative form used in the sense of a locative; thus, "at which time it overcomes."
The meaning is that "then it becomes utter darkness"; or it is a description of the cause: by whatever cause one endures [the anger], by that [cause] it becomes utter darkness.
This being so, because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are always connected, the word *yadā* ("when") must be supplied.
Or rather, this is a reference to the action: that which was stated as the overcoming of anger—namely, "anger endures"—that is what is meant by "utter darkness."

And thus it should be connected: "An angry person does not know the meaning; an angry person does not see the Dhamma. "The meaning and the Dhamma" refers to the meaning of the Pāḷi and the Dhamma of the Pāḷi.
"Agitation of the mind" means that which corrupts the mind by causing it to abandon its natural state.
"From within" means from the interior, or fear has arisen from the mind due to anger. "That" refers to anger, which possesses such a nature.
Or the manner in which anger produces harm and so forth.
"In all cases" means in all three methods—the first, second, and third. The governing topic is "the manner in which one should proceed regarding dispraise.
Because those who speak dispraise are not the objects [of the teaching], the meaning of the word "therein" (tatra) is shown as "in that dispraise."
“*Abhūtan*” is a word functioning as the agent; the meaning is that it is a word which has come into being (*abhūta*).

By the phrase “*abhūtabhāveneva*,” he shows that *abhūtatā* refers to the very act of having come into being, because the state (*bhāva*) is predominant and because of the elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvalopa*).
To show that the passage beginning with “*itipetaṃ*” is an indication of the manner of unraveling, the words beginning with “*kathaṃ*” were stated.
*Tatra* means "in that statement. *Yojanā* refers to the application of the intended meaning. *Tuṇhī* is a particle used in the sense of silence; it is a neuter noun.
Having stated, "Thus this is unreal," he explains its meaning with the words, "That which by you...
and so forth. By the word *api* in the phrase "by this too," he combines many kinds of reasons. He states the nature of those reasons with the words, "Only the Omniscient One... and so forth.
The word *eva* should be applied to all three positions; it means that because [the Buddha] possesses omniscience, he is not non-omniscient;

because his teaching is well-expounded, it is not ill-expounded; and because he has practiced the path correctly, he is not one who has practiced wrongly—it is stated that for this reason, too, the objection must be resolved.
Furthermore, even regarding the counter-objection beginning with "But why is he omniscient?", it must indeed be resolved by showing those very reasons.
He said: "In this regard, there is this and that reason. "In this regard" means among those qualities such as omniscience (*sabbaññutā*).
Having shown various kinds of reasons and counter-reasons, the meaning is that the statement beginning with "he is not omniscient" must be refuted.
Herein, this is the reason: our Teacher is indeed omniscient because he teaches the Dhamma without error. It is well-expounded...
The Dhamma is thus because it leads exclusively to liberation; the Saṅgha is well-practiced because it is free from defilement.

Here, the demonstration of the cause and the subsequent cause should be understood as the very resolution of the statement regarding non-omniscience and so forth, since even those [latter] serve as causes for that demonstration.
For even the cause of a cause is called simply a "cause," and even the support of a support is called simply a "support."
For example: “The food is moistened with oil; he meditates on the Dhamma in the palace. The second phrase is the phrase “untrue” (*ataccha*).
“Of the first phrase” refers to the phrase “unreal” (*abhūta*). The fourth [phrase] is the phrase “but this is not found among us.
“Of the third” refers to the phrase “this does not exist among us. Various [synonyms] have the same meaning.

*Vevacanaṃ* means synonymous expression (*vivacana*). That very thing is a synonym (*vevacana*). Alternatively, the meaning is "expression" (*vacana*), because it is to be expressed by means of a word, as in such passages as:
"The word *Bhagavā* is the best; the word *Bhagavā* is the supreme.

It is called a synonym (*vevacana*)—in the manner already stated—because its expression has departed from a single nature due to its various aspects; the meaning is "a term used as a synonym" (*pariyāyavacana*).
Here it is asked: Why, however, is a figurative expression used here?

Is not the intended meaning established by each individual term alone? Since that is already established, what is the use of this figurative expression? For such a thing causes numerous faults, such as prolixity;
if it were necessary to state it, then only that [direct statement] would have been said, and nothing else. It is replied: At the time of the teaching, ...
Indeed, figurative expressions (*pariyāyavacana*) have been spoken for the sake of some person’s understanding of that meaning at a later time.

For among those who receive the teaching, whoever previously establishes a convention regarding those figurative expressions—thinking, "This is the word for this meaning"—for him, the understanding of that meaning occurs by means of that very convention.
Furthermore, [this applies] to those whose minds are distracted or preoccupied at that moment.
The statement using a different method has also been spoken for the purpose of making the meaning understood through that alternative approach.
For if those who do not hear it were to fail to understand the fully complete meaning as previously stated due to its omission,
then when the statement is given by way of an alternative method, through that means the understanding of the full meaning occurs.
It exists. Alternatively, this synonymous expression was stated so that those of dull intellect might not be confused by the characteristics of that meaning again and again.
For those of dull intellect become confused when they perceive a single meaning through only a single word;
however, such confusion does not arise when perceiving a single meaning through multiple synonymous expressions, owing to the presence of numerous modes of presentation.
Because the intended meaning is determined by the word occurring in that very same context.

Another method: it should be understood that the synonymous term is stated also for the purpose of avoiding any conceptualization of a different meaning that might arise from the thought, "Even multiple meanings may have identical phonemes. For indeed, among many meanings...
By virtue of having identical phonemes through the state of being expressible by a single word,
it avoids synonyms— which are the conceptualizations of alternative meanings occurring in listeners as to whether "this is the intended meaning" or "is this indeed the meaning"—
by way of mutual differentiation. And it has been said:
“The word used for a single meaning does not indicate a specific meaning;
however, when joined with a synonym, that synonym is what creates the distinction. Another method:
even when a synonymous expression is used for something else, by means of various individual names and designations...
Furthermore, a figurative expression (*pariyāya-vacana*) must be stated for the purpose of designating various meanings.
For when a figurative expression is uttered, listeners come to understand the designation of names in manifold ways, thinking, "This is also the name for this particular meaning.
From that, there arises skill in those respective designations, just as one gains proficiency through familiarity with a glossary (*nighaṇṭu*). Moreover—
It is also a figurative expression for the easy accomplishment of the Dhamma-preachers’ binding of the meaning of the texts within their own minds and their making that understood by others.

For by means of that speech, the making understood of the meaning of the texts by other listeners is easily accomplished through the Dhamma-preachers’ fixing and establishing that meaning in their own minds.
Alternatively, it refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One’s own attainment of the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*) regarding the Dhamma.
The Blessed One teaches this figurative expression for the purpose of analytical discernment and for the purpose of sowing the seed within those to be trained therein.
For such a figurative expression is not possible for one who has not attained that [analytical knowledge].

And by means of that figurative expression, when heard as it was taught, through the cultivation of that very attainment of the analytical knowledge of the language of Dhamma, and through the further development of other wholesome conduct, [one attains it].
And the sowing of the seed known as merit becomes possible. For who, indeed, when such an excellence is perceived, would not aspire to it?

Or rather, what need is there for much? Because of his thorough penetration of that *dhammadhātu*, just as the Perfectly Enlightened One possesses unimpeded range of knowledge regarding every meaning, so too does he possess it regarding every verbal expression; thus, even a single meaning—
He awakens them by means of many methods; therein there is no sluggishness or prolixity, nor is there any deficiency in the teaching of the Dhamma, for this is a unique quality of a Buddha.

Indeed, because of the well-penetrated nature of his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), through that knowledge—just as through the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidāñāṇa*)—there is unimpeded functioning regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, and the language; thus, even a single [word] of the Buddha’s grace...
He awakens [the listener] to the meaning through numerous methods, yet there is no deficiency in that verbal expression or in such awakening;
for this is a means for achieving correct awakening. Nor does the meaning become prolix thereby, because it is the cause for easily understanding the very same meaning that is to be taught.
Furthermore, there is no loss of the teaching of the Dhamma through those words, because they constitute a perfection of the teaching itself.

Therefore, it should be understood that a figurative expression (pariyāyavacana) possesses a specific purpose, and that it does not give rise to various faults such as the burden of excessive wordiness.
Furthermore, the statement, "If that were what was intended to be said, then only that would have been said, and nothing else," is also incorrect, because other purposes are possible.
For by speaking something other than that very point at the time of the teaching, [the Buddha] achieves a different objective.

Even for those whose minds are concentrated, the realization of that meaning occurs by taking as their object the sign of occurrence contained within each respective word, provided they receive [the teaching] correctly;
otherwise, even if that same word were repeated again and again, there would be no realization of that meaning for them.
And on this point, there are these verses:
“By whatever means, for the sake of awakening to the meaning from another sound,
even for those whose minds are distracted, a figurative exposition has been made.
And for the sake of the non-delusion of the dull-witted, there is the negation of other meanings.”
The figurative discourse was employed so that the meaning established by each respective name might be understood;

it was employed for the sake of making the meaning easy for those who teach, for the sake of awakening to the meaning of the thread [of the teaching], and for the sake of awakening to the linguistic expression of the Dhamma.
For the sake of sowing the seed within those capable of being trained,
and for his own sake, he employed figurative discourse through the playful power of the Dhamma-element.
Yet, without stating that very thing directly, he awakened them by means of other methods.
"Offered by those who receive it rightly, for the attainment of the goal.
Showing that this kind of justification (*nibbeṭhana*) should be made only in such cases and not in all instances, he said "And this," and so forth.
In that context, "only in dispraise" means either by stating a reason that appears plausible, or by way of censure through the establishment of a fault, whether such a reason is stated or not.
"Thus. "Not in all cases" means that one should not make an evasion in every instance, such as in cases of abuse, reviling, or contempt.
He makes this meaning clear with the words "If indeed," and so forth.
He refers back to the reason for the necessity of making such an evasion—stated as "he becomes suspicious"—with the word "therefore. "You are a lip-man," and so on.
“Not in all cases” is the explanation for this. [The insults consist of] ten bases of abuse, namely: birth, name, clan, occupation, craft, disease, gender, defilement, offense, and verbal abuse.
Patience as endurance (*adhivāsana-khanti*) means simply the act of enduring; it does not refer to the contemplation of views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhamanā*) and so forth.
Having thus provided an exposition of the grounds for dispraise, he now speaks in order to provide an exposition of the grounds for praise.
“‘Thus,’ and so forth. Therein, ‘in a place of dispraise’ means in a place where dispraise is proclaimed.

Regarding ‘the characteristic of one who is such (tādī),’ here, according to the method of exposition in the *Niddesa*: ‘One is such by five modes: one is such toward the desirable and undesirable; one is such because he has transcended;

one is such because he has crossed over; one is such because he is liberated; one is such because of that designation. Among these five meanings, here it is ‘such’ in the sense of the first. Herein, this is the exposition:”
How is it that the Arahant is the same toward the desirable and the undesirable? The Arahant is the same in gain and the same in loss;
the same in fame and the same in disrepute; the same in praise and the same in blame; the same in pleasure and the same in pain.

Even if they were to smear one arm with perfume and carve the other arm with an axe, he would have no lust for the one and no aversion for the other; having abandoned both attraction and repulsion, he remains the same.
Having transcended opening and closing, having surmounted attraction and aversion, thus the Arahant is "equanimous toward the desirable and undesirable" (*tādī*).
As for the etymology of the word: he sees that as it were (*tam iva dissati*), thus he is *tādī*; the meaning is that he views even the undesirable just like the desirable.

Its characteristic is the characteristic of equanimity (*tādilakkhaṇaṇa*); its nature is the state of looking upon the desirable and undesirable with equal regard. Alternatively, he sees that as it were...
“Tādī” means that very same nature; “tādilakkhaṇaṃ” means that very same characteristic. The connection [of the sentence] is:
“to show the characteristic of suchness (tādilakkhaṇa) in the section on color. Regarding the word *para* meaning “other,” he says “whosoever” and so forth.
He shows the instrumental sense of the word *ānanda* by stating that beings who possess it “rejoice intensely” (*ānandanti*) by means of it. *Sobhanamana*...
*Sumana* means one whose mind (*mano*) is bright (*sumana*), or one who possesses such a mind; it refers to the person endowed with that state.
Now, if the word denotes the mind, it is appropriate that its referent is mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*).

However, if it denotes the person, then the mind itself would be the referent, not mental pleasure, because the word *sumana* functions by way of a signifier for a physical object (*dabba-nimitta*), just as in the case of the term "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍitta*).
Regarding the phrase "well-considered" (*sikhitta*) and so forth: this is true when referring to a physical object (*dabba*).

However, here, without regard for that object, the word *sumana* is employed with reference solely to the mental happiness (*cetasika-sukha*) which is associated with that object and serves as its primary cause.
Therefore, even in this context, mental happiness alone is the intended meaning; thus he said, "This is a designation (*adhivacana*) for mental happiness."

By this statement, one does not incur the objection that the state of joy (*somanassa*) would consequently apply to other mental factors as well—since they too are bound to the mind and are mental activities—as the case may allow;
for it is a conventional term (*ruḷhisadda*), and thus [the author] resolves it by way of the example "mud-born" (*paṅkaja*).
"Ubbilayati" means "it bubbles up"; the sense is that it breaks through its previous state and attains a distinction.
That very same [state] is "ubbilāvita" (agitated) by way of the arrival of other conditions and so forth. Or, it is "ubbilāvita" because it "floats upwards" (*uddhaṃ palavati*);
this is formed by changing the *a*-vowels to *i* and *ā*. Since it is stated as "of the mind" (*cetaso*), it refers to the mind itself.

When the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is established, that [mind] is not distinct from it, because of the general nature of what is to be expressed in that word, or because that word is a nominal form (*nāmapada*). Therefore, [the question arises: "Of what? (*kassa*)?
In response to the inquiry regarding the specific relation [of the term], it was stated "of the mind" (*cetaso*); this is shown by the statement beginning with "of what?

(*kassā*). This same method applies to similar cases. By the phrase beginning with "conducive to restlessness" (*uddhaccāvahāyā*), he shows the actual nature of that worldly joy and elation (*odagyapīti*) which, when arisen, causes the body and mind to become distended like a bellows filled with air.
"Leading to agitation" (*uddhaccāvahāya*) means leading to a state of restlessness. "It makes the mind elated" (*uppilāpeti*) means it causes the mind to become elated;

thus it is "elation" (*ubbilāpanā*), which is itself rapture (*pīti*). By the phrase "here too" (*idhāpi*) and so forth, he indicates that there is a distinction in the phenomena (*dhamma*) by way of the aggregates (*khandha*).
The word "too" (*api*) is used in consideration of the preceding section, as in "this one too is defeated" (*ayampi pārājiko*); and here, although those monks were indeed elated...

It is not that [the unwholesome] does not exist; rather, by establishing the guide to the Dhamma (*dhammanetti*), he prevents the arising of unwholesome states in clansmen in such situations hereafter.

Regarding the statement that the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is expressed by two phrases and the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) by one, the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) states here as well:
"By means of those [two aggregates], the performance of the remaining associated phenomena is indeed excluded."

It was not stated that it can be understood according to the method already described. Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood as far as possible according to the method stated in the passage beginning with, “The word *pi* has the sense of esteem (*sambhāvana*).

Regarding the phrase, “For you alone there is an obstacle (*antarāya*) by means of that,” here too, the term “obstacle” is a statement of the reason why one should not cause agitation (*ubbilāvitatta*), and so forth.
The meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated by us in the section on dispraise below.

Furthermore, in this context, having taken "joyful and exultant" (*ānandino ubbilāvitā*) as referring specifically to *pīti* (rapture), the statement "by that state of being exultant" (*tena ubbilāvitattena*) implies that since there is no rapture devoid of *somanassa* (mental joy), the term *somanassa*—which was indicated by the word "well-minded" (*sumanā*)—is also established by that very expression. Thus it is done.
It has been stated. Alternatively, it should be understood that this was said because the fact of [somanassa] being an obstacle to [pīti] is manifest, whereas that is not the case for *pīti* itself.
But why is this so? This is a challenge posed by reflecting on the aforementioned meaning without making distinctions.
The Teacher, acknowledging that point as true with the words "That is so," addresses it by means of an analytical explanation starting with "But that... and so forth.
In this context, "that" refers to the statement regarding what Ānanda and others ought not to have done; the connection is: "Was it not indeed praised by the Blessed One?
Regarding "of those praising [him] as 'Buddha,'" this refers to virtuous people speaking the word "Buddha" by way of recollecting his qualities.
"Entirely" means by way of totality or in its fullness. "Of Jambudīpa" is a genitive of relation used in the sense of being a constituent part of that [totality].
Others, however, say that in the phrase "of Jambudīpa" (*jambudīpassa*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental;

according to their view, the words *kasiṇa* and *Jambudīpa* should be understood as being in grammatical apposition, and the instrumental case is used in the sense of the ablative. The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "how much more so even from one part" (*pageva ekadesato pana*) expresses possibility. And here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*),—
“Do not grieve, Udāyin; Ānanda might pass away while still possessing lust.
By that clarity of mind, he would exercise divine sovereignty seven times, and seven times he would exercise great sovereignty right here in Jambudīpa.
Furthermore, Udāyin, Ānanda will attain final nibbāna in this very life,” and so forth—this is the sutta.

“Included” (*saṅgahitaṃ*) refers to the joy and mental happiness mentioned in other discourses (*suttanta*). “Based on renunciation” (*nekkhammassitaṃ*) means based on wholesome states that have emerged from sense-desire.

“Here” (*idha*) means in this discourse. “Based on the household” (*gehassitaṃ*) means based on the strands of sensual pleasure known as the “household,” because they are the habitual practice of those living in a house.
To the question, “Why is that alone intended here? he says: “For this...”, etc. [The passage continues: “Of the Venerable...”
In order to make clear or to establish the meaning already stated—that it was "as if arising for Channa"—the words beginning with "teneva" (by that very [reason]) were spoken.
