He was unable to produce a distinction regarding the Blessed One because of his affection rooted in the household life toward the Dhamma.
At the time of the Parinibbāna means at the time close to the Parinibbāna; or the connection is to be understood as "shaken by what was proclaimed by the Blessed One."

The connection is as follows: either at the time of the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, or at the time when the Blessed One had already attained final Nibbāna, he was reborn having been urged by the Saṅgha.
By the "Brahma-punishment" (brahmadaṇḍa) means by that Brahma-punishment enacted [by the Saṅgha] such that: "The monks must neither speak to, nor exhort, nor instruct so-and-so.
Urged (tajjita) means moved to a sense of urgency (saṃvejita). "Therefore" (tasmā) means because of the joy and gladness associated with the household life.
Because it creates an obstacle to the jhānas and so forth; for this was said by the Blessed One in the *Sakkapañha Sutta*:
"O Lord of the Devas, I declare that joy is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
With the words "For this," etc., he supports that very point with a reason: because it is accompanied by lust, it creates an obstacle.
In this context, however, it might have been said: "This is joy and mental pleasure associated with lust.

Nevertheless, by the inclusion of "joy" (pīti), "mental pleasure" (somanassa) is also already included, because there is no joy devoid of mental pleasure; thus, according to the method explained below, only joy is taken.
Furthermore, because of the statement in the Sutta regarding the distinction between what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, mental pleasure is clearly [indicated].
The state of being an obstacle is not the same as joy; therefore, that [joy] alone is spoken of by distinguishing it as being accompanied by lust.
To make it clear by connecting it with the ground of dispraise, "And greed," etc., was said. "Similar to anger" means exactly similar to the anger mentioned in the ground of dispraise.
The meaning of the verses beginning with "The greedy person" should be understood according to the method stated in the verses beginning with "The angry person."

“Bhikkhus, if others were to speak in praise of me, or speak in praise of the Dhamma, or speak in praise of the Saṅgha, and if you were thereupon to become joyful, glad, and elated, would you then be able to discern what was well-spoken and what was ill-spoken by those others?
“Certainly not, Bhante. This is called the third section.

Because it must be brought forth in the third section according to the method stated in the "Grounds of Censure" (*avaṇṇabhūmi*), yet it did not appear in the teaching at that time due to the absence of any person to be enlightened by that particular section, it is nonetheless "present in meaning" because its purpose exists;
this is shown by the passage beginning with "But the third section... and so forth, in order to demonstrate how it appears in the *Kathāvatthu* treatise in detail.
This has been stated; by this, he shows that at the time of commentary, that section should be brought forward and commented upon according to those beings who would understand it in such a way.
With the words "Just as," and so forth, he clarifies the very possibility of that meaning. The connection is: "Just as one who is angry does not know the meaning."
In the section showing the manner in which one should practice, following the third section already mentioned, this is to be stated in the fourth section.
The construction extends from the words “Your Teacher” up until the words “it is true for this reason as well. The passage beginning with “For that Blessed One...
is its detailed explanation. In that context, *itipī* means “for this reason as well. This is the detailed exposition.

In the *Visuddhimagga*, although it is stated that “there is no offense for one who reports what is true to one who is fully ordained,” it is said that “it should be confessed only to fellow monks,” because reporting to those who are like-minded is appropriate. For they alone desire his welfare and consider his words trustworthy;
and thus, as it is said, “the fruitfulness of the Dispensation is demonstrated. This constitutes the corroboration of the stated meaning.
It may be so. “*Evañhi*” and so forth is a statement of the reason. The connection is: “both *pāpicchatā* (evil desire) itself has been avoided, or it [the avoidance] becomes the agent.
*Amoghatā* is non-futility due to its nature of leading to liberation (*niyyānika*).

“In the manner stated” refers to both the passage beginning with “*Tatra tumhehi*—in that praise, by you,” and the second word [of the first line] being [the cause] of the first word, and the fourth...
And by the method stated in such passages as, "the synonym for the third," and so forth.
Regarding the *Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā*: 7.

What is the connection (*anusandhi*)? This question [is raised because one might think]: "Is not the purpose of the teaching already fulfilled by this much, through the aforementioned dispraise and praise?"
It is "made" because of the possibility of inquiry as to whether [the meaning] has been "attained. "By means of praise and blame" refers to both those terms.

For phoneticians hold that the description of words is like the description of meanings. Alternatively, it is stated as "by means of phrases" (*padehi*) because they are the causes for such appearance and because they constitute constituent parts.
Furthermore, "by means of blame and praise" is said by way of demerit and merit, or by way of censure and commendation.

And there is the observation of similarity. Regarding this, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated: "The [discourse] was withdrawn because it lacked a foundation and because there was no person to be answered.
Having explained that, he continued: "Because there was no person to be enlightened by the teaching, the Blessed One’s intention was simply that it was not suitable for so much;
thus, it was withdrawn due to the absence of a teaching, just as occurred during the third round at Vaṇṇabhūmi."
It must be seen. Likewise, because it has attained the state of being answerable due to the existence of persons who are to be awakened, it indeed follows along.
Regarding the phrase "thus this is real," the word *iti* here has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*), because it continues even further beyond that; therefore he will say, "But here... and so forth.
Having thus shown that this is the connection of the commentary (*vaṇṇānusandhi*) up to this point, [he now addresses] those two kinds of commentaries.
Showing the connection of the praise for Brahmadatta, he said, "But he... and so forth. He will show the connection in the subsequent exposition of emptiness with the words, "There is, monks...
and so forth. Having thus stated the meaning of the whole by way of question and answer, he now shows the meaning of the parts with the words, "In that regard... and so forth.
Because it is broken (*khaṇḍita*) on all sides and in every way, it is called "limited" (*paritta*); thus he said: "‘A little’ (*appamattaka*) is a name for the limited.

*Mattā* is said to mean measure (*pamāṇa*), because it is measured or fully measured. By means of the suffix *-ka* at the end of the compound, it becomes *appamattaka*, just as in the case of *bahuputtaka*;
likewise, it applies to what is merely small (*oramattaka*). By this very [derivation], *appa* is the measure (*mattā*), and that which has this [measure] is *appamattā*.
By the phrase beginning with “*appamattakan*,” he also demonstrates that the *ka*-suffix has a specific meaning (*sātthaka*), because it is not different in meaning [from the base word].
Since the word *mattaka* does not have a separate meaning, "virtue alone" is "mere virtue" (*sīlamattaka*).

And its lack of a separate meaning is due to its expressing the same sense as the preceding word, for grammarians maintain that words do not become meaningless in isolation. But is it not the case that... [of the Blessed One]?

It has been stated that by the power of the perfections (*pāramitā*), not even a single meaningless syllable enters the excellent mouth, and that the entire teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*) reveals the Four Noble Truths at every step;

how, then, could its meaninglessness possibly occur? True, yet even that [meaningless word] expresses the very meaning conveyed by the other words, by way of qualifying the meaning expressed by those words.
However, since that meaning can be understood even without those other words, it was stated simply as "anatthakam. Did we not say: "The state of being meaningless...

because of its occurrence"? Furthermore, the Blessed One’s teaching proceeds in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained; and those to be trained have had their minds conditioned by worldly sounds alone throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, in common usage, even when there is no difference in meaning, the employment of words is observed by way of verbal elegance and so forth, such as:
"labbhati palabbhati," "khañjati nikhañjati," "āgacchati paccāgacchati," and so on.

Since the comprehension of meaning is easy for those who are accustomed to such linguistic usage through that very kind of word-employment, the employment of words that serve no [other] purpose was stated.
This applies everywhere. And in this regard, it is said:
“One should employ a word expressing a non-existent thing for the purpose of qualifying a meaning that must be expressed by another word, and likewise for the sake of awakening those to be trained.”

Alternatively, in the phrase "merely virtue" (*sīlamattaka*), the word *matta* has the sense of excluding other qualifiers, as in such expressions as "states consisting of applied thought and sustained thought only," "the mind-only element," and "the mind-element.
For the meaning already stated generally by the two phrases "slight" (*appamattaka*) and "trifling" (*oramattaka*) is here stated specifically by the phrase "merely virtue"; and by that, virtue—
To show that the grammatical derivation (*nibbacana*) should be made as "merely virtue" (*sīlamattaka*), it is stated: "Virtue itself is 'merely virtue'.

This, however, is the method according to the *Aṭṭhakathāmuttaka*: regarding the term *oramattaka*, here *ora* means the near side (*apārabhāga*), as in such expressions as "wealth on this side" (*oraṃ bhogaṃ*) or "this shore" (*oraṃ pāraṃ*).
Alternatively, the word *ora* has the sense of "below" (*heṭṭhā*); thus, *ora-āgamanāya* refers to those conditions [that lead downward].
It is as in such passages as "those lower fetters" (*orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni*). For virtue (*sīla*), in relation to concentration and wisdom, exists on the far side and on the lower side;
in both cases, the analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that which has its measure (*matta*) functioning in what is lower.

In the phrase "merely virtue" (*sīlamattaka*), the word *matta* also signifies "not great," as in "a mere dose of medicine" (*bhesajjamattā*) and so forth. Alternatively, even regarding virtue, it refers only to one part thereof.

In this context, the word *matta* is used to denote "only" for the purpose of inclusion; it does not signify "great. For indeed, the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) and the virtue dependent on requisites (*paccayasannissita-sīla*) have not been included here in the teaching.

Why is that? Because, unlike the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint and the virtue of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla*), those two are not manifest among all ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*).
Furthermore, in this instance, the neuter gender of *matta* is used in the sense of excluding any qualification.
In the case of words used as measures (*pamāṇappakatthesu*), however, *matta* or *mattā* are neuter and feminine genders respectively.
By the phrase "this is what is meant" (*idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti*) and so forth, he shows the summarized meaning (*piṇḍattha*) through its connection [with the context].

The syntactical connection is: "That virtue by which one might speak—this is merely a matter of virtue (*sīlamattaka*). Regarding the phrase "even after making an effort, thinking 'I am speaking praise' (*vaṇṇaṃ vadāmīti ussāhaṃ katvāpī*)," this refers to "praise" (*vaṇṇaṃ*).

This is the explanation of the term "vadamāno. For by this, he shows that the word *māna* possesses a sense of potentiality (*sāmatthiya*), as in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, one person, appearing in the world, appears," and so forth.

Furthermore, the use of the word "having made" (*katvā*) instead of saying "making effort" (*ussāhaṃ kurumāno*) indicates that, just like words ending in suffixes such as *-tvā*, words ending in the gerundive suffix *-māna* also necessarily depend upon the action of another.
"For the purpose of seeing. He shows that such an objection might arise from someone who, not understanding the intended meaning expressed by the words "In this regard, it might be...
and so forth, takes them as being of explicit meaning (*nītattha*) and thus perceives a contradiction with other suttas.

"In this regard" (*tattha*) means in that statement beginning with "But this is indeed trifling. A *yogī* is one who habitually applies himself to the cultivation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); [the word refers] to him.

*Alaṅkaraṇaṃ*, *vibhūsanaṃ*, and *alaṅkāro* refer to the act of adorning; it is called *alaṅkāro* because one makes oneself beautiful (*alaṃ karoti*) by means of it, namely, ornaments such as earrings.

*Maṇḍanaṃ* is that which is used for beautifying (*maṇḍīyate*), meaning the filling of deficiencies. Or, *maṇḍanaṃ* is that by which one is beautified (*maṇḍīyati*), namely, the requisites for filling deficiencies such as face powder.
However, in this context, through figurative usage or by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it is virtue itself (*sīla*) that is intended.
Thus it has been said. *Maṇḍane* means for the sake of adornment; the meaning is that he went for the purpose of the act of adorning.
Alternatively, one who adorns by nature is an *maṇḍana*, a person of an ornamental disposition. This singular number is used here with reference to the genus (*jāti*) even when there is a plurality.
For some maintain that the singular is also used in the sense of lifting up (*ubbāhana*), but that is indeed incorrect, as it has not been recorded in the grammatical treatises (*saddasattha*).
And because of the absence of logical consistency (*yutti*). For how could the use of a pluralizing particle (*ubbāhana-karaṇa*) be appropriate when [the word] is indicated in the singular?

This is because, in a single meaning, there is no other meaning to be pluralized. Therefore, this singular number should be understood as being used for a plural sense by way of a grammatical shift (*vipallāsa*); the meaning is "in the ornaments and virtues. For it was also said by the Elder Master Dhammapāla:
This very analysis has been stated here. "The foremost" means the state of being supreme (*agga*).

"He might wish: 'May I be'"—this is the connection; "might be" (*assa*) means "would exist. Here, in the word *paripūrakārī*, the particle *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or the sense of "manner," by which it indicates the entire *Sīla-thomanasutta*.
In the phrase "like a hen her egg," the particle *iti* is used here in the sense of "that" (*tad-attha*).
“Just as a hen guards her eggs, or as a yak guards its tail,
or as one guards a beloved son, or as one guards a single eye—
so too, guarding their virtue, they remain.”
"Be exceedingly joyful and always full of reverence"—thus he concludes the verse.
Having said "the fragrance of flowers," he spoke "not sandalwood" and so forth in order to show that [fragrance] by way of a single part of it.
For "sandalwood, tagara, and jasmine" are mentioned there as their fragrance because of their association with those [flowers]. Thus, "the fragrance of flowers."
The meaning is: the flower and whatever remains of it is the fragrance. Or, the remaining scent after the *tagara* and jasmine has been removed is called "the fragrance of the flower.
Regarding the phrase "the fragrance of the virtuous" (*sataṃ gandho*), here "fragrance" refers to virtue itself through figurative usage or by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
Alternatively, the sound of praise, which is bound to virtue, is intended as "fragrance" according to the method already stated. For virtue is the cause of renown.
As it is said: “The good reputation of the virtuous person spreads abroad.
A true person “blows forth” (pavāyati) because he scents in various ways, being comparable to a fragrant tree.

“Vassikī” refers to the jasmine flower (*sumana*); the reading “vassika” also has the same meaning. “Gandhajāta” means simply scents, or types of scents. The connection is: “that which blows,” namely, the supreme scent blows forth.

“Of those liberated through perfect knowledge” means: having known correctly through understanding, or of those liberated by the supreme path (*aggamagga*). “He finds no path” means he does not obtain the cause, or he does not know it.

Regarding the verse beginning with “Established in virtue”: a wise person endowed with the wisdom of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhipaññā*), ardent and energetic, a man known as a monk possessed of the wisdom of maintenance (*pārihārikapaññā*), being established in virtue, develops concentration—which is said to be the mind’s primary application—while cultivating his heart.

The brief meaning is as follows: by cultivating the cause of development—namely, wisdom and insight—one would "untangle," that is, disentangle and be capable of disentangling, this "tangle" known as the inner tangle and the outer tangle.
"Depending on the earth" means depending on the earth by way of perceiving its taste; however, in the case of virtue, one's establishment should be understood as being by way of fulfilling it.

Because it exists as a designation by way of comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*) due to its smallness or greatness—just like "this shore" and "the far shore"—it is stated, "in comparison to the higher qualities," in order to answer the question of how it is designated in relation to one another. In the phrase "for virtue indeed" (*sīlañhi*), the particle *hi* has the sense of a reason;
by this, he shows the following reason: "because virtue, although it is of great assistance to concentration by way of being its foundation..."
"But compared to his specific qualities such as majesty (pabhāva), it does not approach even a fraction [of them], nor do concentration and wisdom.
For this very reason he said "therefore," and so forth. "Does not reach" means it does not attain equality in terms of its qualities;
it is said that it does not equal them. "The higher" refers to concentration and wisdom. "Comparing" means making them a point of comparison.
For that serves as a support for such a presentation. "The lower" refers to the dyad of virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*).

The passage beginning with "How" is an explanatory statement. And here, the mention of the miracle at the root of the *kaṇḍamba* tree is intended by way of illustration, because it is more manifestly a miracle, establishing in some way or other the attainment of concentration by virtue.
This is how it should be understood. Furthermore, the passage beginning with “Abhi... pe...

titthiyamaddanaṃ” was stated for the purpose of showing the extreme clarity of that Twin Miracle, and to demonstrate its distinction from the other miracles performed by him at the foot of the Bodhi tree, during his meeting with his kinsmen, and so forth.
For even on the eighth day after his full enlightenment, the deities [proclaimed]: “The Buddha...”
In order to dispel the doubts that had arisen, he performed a miracle while walking back and forth upon a jeweled walkway fashioned in the sky.

Then, in the second year, having gone to his native city, he performed the Twin Miracle at the Nigrodha Monastery in the city of Kapilavatthu during a gathering of his kinsmen, for the purpose of causing them to abandon pride and intoxication. Therein, "from the time of the full enlightenment" means:
From the time of his full enlightenment. At the gate of the city of Sāvatthī means at the southern gate of the city of Sāvatthī.
At the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree means at the base of the tree named Kaṇḍamba, which was planted by Pasenadi the King’s park-keeper named Kaṇḍa.
When the thought arose in the Blessed One’s mind to perform the Twin Miracle, [he reflected: "A location suitable for that must be sought."
Some say that the Jewel Pavilion and so forth were made by Vissakamma at the command of Sakka, the king of the gods; others say they were created by the Blessed One.

However, in numerous commentaries it is stated: "The pavilion was made by the divine son Vissakamma, who was commanded by Sakka, the lord of the devas, while the walking path (caṅkama) was created by the Blessed One. [Likewise,] the divine white parasol was [offered] by the devas.
The meaning "being maintained" is understood, because it is impossible for others [to do so].
Regarding the phrase "of an assembly twelve yojanas [in extent]," this is said with reference to a human assembly extending twelve yojanas in each of the four directions.

At that time, it is said, even the devas and brahmās gathered together, filling the interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) from the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*). Anyone [who witnesses] such a miracle...
Because it is like an exhortation—“If he is capable of doing it, let him come”—it is called “the indication of a formal undertaking” (*attādānaparidīpana*).
For “formal undertaking” (*attādāna*) is understood as the application of oneself, that is, the taking up or grasping of a position opposed [to the opponent].
“The crushing of the sectarians” (*titthiyamaddana*) refers to the crushing of those sectarians who previously rose up with deceitful intent, thinking, “We shall perform a miracle. And that...

It is precisely the production of an inability to act in such a manner. These two phrases should be connected with the expression “the Twin Miracle. Everything here should be stated starting from the appearance of the sandalwood bowl of the Rājagaha merchant. The passage beginning with “from the upper part of his body,” etc., shows the method as it appears in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*; therefore it is said, “occurring in such a manner as this,” and “all should be expanded in detail. Herein, this is the remainder of the text: [The text continues with the description of the Twin Miracle. ... [The Buddha] performed the Twin Miracle. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Twin Miracle in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Twin Miracle in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Twin Miracle, he performed the Great Miracle. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Great Miracle in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Great Miracle in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Great Miracle, he performed the Miracle of the Universal Manifestation. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Miracle of the Universal Manifestation in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Miracle of the Universal Manifestation in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Miracle of the Universal Manifestation, he performed the Miracle of the Descent of the Gods. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Miracle of the Descent of the Gods in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Miracle of the Descent of the Gods in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Miracle of the Descent of the Gods, he performed the Miracle of the Lion’s Roar. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Miracle of the Lion’s Roar in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Miracle of the Lion’s Roar in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Miracle of the Lion’s Roar, he performed the Miracle of the Turning of the Wheel. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Miracle of the Turning of the Wheel in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Miracle of the Turning of the Wheel in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Miracle of the Turning of the Wheel, he performed the Miracle of the Great Compassion. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Miracle of the Great Compassion in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Miracle of the Great Compassion in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Miracle of the Great Compassion, he performed the Miracle of the Finality. From the upper part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the lower part of his body there issued a stream of water. From the lower part of his body there issued a stream of fire, and from the upper part of his body there issued a stream of water. He performed the Miracle of the Finality in various ways: sometimes he made the streams issue from one pore, sometimes from all his pores; sometimes he made them issue from the upper part of his body and rain down on the lower part, and from the lower part rain down on the upper part; sometimes he made them issue from the front of his body and rain down on the back, and from the back rain down on the front; sometimes he made them issue from the right side and rain down on the left, and from the left side rain down on the right; sometimes he made them issue from the left side and rain down on the right, and from the right side rain down on the left. He performed the Miracle of the Finality in these and other ways. Then, having performed the Miracle of the Finality, he performed the Miracle of the Descent from the Sky. From the upper part
“A mass of fire issues from his lower body, and a stream of water issues from his upper body.
Fire issues from his front body, and water from his back body; water issues from his back body, and fire from his front body.
Fire issues from his right eye, and water from his left eye; water issues from his left eye, and fire from his right eye. From his right ear canal...”
Fire from the left ear canal, water from the left ear canal; fire from the left ear canal, water from the right ear canal.
Fire from the right nostril, water from the left nostril; fire from the left nostril, water from the right nostril.
Fire from the right shoulder, water from the left shoulder; fire from the left shoulder, [water] from the right shoulder.
Water. Fire from the right hand, water from the left hand. Fire from the left hand, water from the right hand.
Fire from the right side, water from the left side. Fire from the left side, water from the right side.
Fire from the right foot, water from the left foot. Fire from the left foot, water from the right foot.
“From his fingers comes fire; from the spaces between his fingers comes water. From the spaces between his fingers comes fire;

from his fingers comes water. From each single hair comes fire; from each single hair comes water. From every single pore a mass of fire issues forth, and from every single pore a stream of water issues forth.”
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it appears simply as "from each single pore.

Regarding the phrase "of the six colors," here too the entire canonical remainder—namely, "blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, and brilliant"—is indicated by the method of abbreviation (*peyyāla*) and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). And herein, of the six colors...
The connection is with the elliptical phrase "pairs of colors proceed as if being pushed forward";
by this he will say, "the second rays, the second rays," and so forth.
For there, the separate occurrence of the adverting, the preliminary work, and the resolution, together with the manner of their proceeding in pairs, is shown. However, some [read] "of six colors."

They explain the connection of this [phrase] with the preceding words as "a mass of fire, a stream of water," but that is indeed incorrect, because it will be stated later that the fire-kasiṇa and air-kasiṇa are entered into for the purpose of the mass of fire and the stream of water.
Alternatively, the connection is made in terms of the agent, as in "the six colors proceed" (*chabbaṇṇā pavattanti*), just as in the case of "even for one... (*ekassa cepi*).

"A monk should not feel inclined to disparage that nun. For grammarians (neruttika) maintain that when there is a frequent occurrence of the agentive case (*sāmivacana*) in the sense of the subject, it may also be employed in the construction of a verb.
Having thus demonstrated the Twin Miracle according to the method of the Pāḷi, he now explains it according to the method of the Aṭṭhakathā by way of reverse order (*paccāsatti-naya*).
In order to explain first the phrase “of the six colors,” he said “of that,” and so forth.
Therein, “of that” means of the Blessed One. The expression “rays of golden color” is stated because of the predominance of their yellow luster;
the meaning is that it is as if they were adorned with rays of six colors. For those rays, having risen from within the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), reach as far as the Brahma-world.
Turning back, they seized the very rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

The interior of that single world-system became like a Bodhi-house with a curved rafter-beam, filled with a single light. Regarding the phrase "each successive ray," it refers to the rays that issued forth later and later from those that had issued forth before.
As for why the word "like" (*viya*) was used on account of their similar appearance, he said: "And of the two," and so forth.
There is no such thing as the simultaneous occurrence of two consciousnesses by which those [two] might exist;

nevertheless, the intention is that for these two reasons, they appear exactly so. "Dwelling in the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga-parivāsa*) means dwelling by way of the life-continuum, or dwelling designated as the life-continuum;
what is meant is "falling into the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga-patana*).
"By way of habitual mastery" means by way of the five modes, such as adverting and entering [jhāna], through having cultivated familiarity.
To dispel the objection—"But would not even two rays be possible during the occurrence of a single consciousness?"—he says, "But of each respective ray," and so forth.
Due to the diversity of the mental doors, there are the adverting and preparatory consciousnesses; due to the diversity of the kasiṇas...

The mental applications of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-citta*) also proceed individually. Here, the impulsions (*javana*) that occur three times at the conclusion of the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) are described by the name "preliminary work" (*parikamma*).
How so? He says: "For the sake of blue rays," and so forth. "For the sake of madder-colored rays, the red kasiṇa; for the sake of brilliant rays..."
Regarding the phrase "yellow kasiṇa," this is established by the very mention of the red and yellow rays;

it is not stated [separately] because the madder-colored and clear rays are merely specific subdivisions of those same [rays]. The passage beginning with "for the purpose of a mass of fire" is an explanation of the phrases beginning with "from the upper part of the body.
Furthermore, the masses of fire and water, remaining unmixed with one another, rise up as far as the Brahma-world.

They fell upon the rim of the world-system. On that day, however, the Teacher taught whatever Dhamma and performed whatever miracle suited the disposition of each person who was inspired with faith toward a particular teaching or miracle;
and while the Dhamma was being spoken and the miracles were being performed in this way, the great multitude—
There was a realization of the Dhamma. And in that assembly, seeing no one capable of grasping his own mind and asking a question, he manifested a created Buddha (nimmita-buddha).
The Teacher answered the question asked by him. He [the created Buddha] answered the question asked by the Teacher.
While the Teacher was walking up and down, the created one occupied one of the other positions, such as standing.
In order to show the meaning that while he [the disciple] was assuming one posture, such as walking, the Teacher assumed one of the others, such as standing,
the passage beginning with "The Teacher walks" was stated. By the phrase "all should be expanded in detail," it is indicated that for each of the four postures—
such as "the Teacher stands, while the emanation walks, sits, or lies down"— there are variations based on each individual posture.
This shows that all eight sections should be explained in detail: four on the side of the Teacher and four on the side of the created form.

Since virtue merely serves as a foundation for concentration and then ceases its function, while concentration alone—having established itself therein—carries out all the aforementioned miraculous tasks, therefore this is indeed the function of concentration alone.
It was said: “In this regard, even a single...
and so forth. By the words “But that which...,” the failure of concentration to reach wisdom is clarified;

the meaning is that what he penetrated—that act of penetration—is the function of wisdom (*paññākicca*). He shows this in sequence with the words “The Blessed One... and so forth. “For more than a hundred thousand aeons...”
The phrase "four incalculable eons" is stated starting from the first initial resolution made at the feet of Dīpaṅkara;

however, it should be understood that even prior to that, he accumulated as much of the equipment of merit as would have been required to attain the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi) had he so desired in that existence.
For this very reason, [it is said]: "Human birth, the possession of male gender, the cause..."
Among the eight qualities mentioned in the passage beginning with "seeing the Teacher," he possessed the perfection of the cause (*hetusampannatā*).

Some, however, speak of the prior equipment (*pubbasambhāra*) by dividing it into many ways according to mental aspiration and verbal aspiration, defining its limits as being for incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*);

but that is indeed incorrect, because it is not so stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) included in the *Saṅgaha*. For in those [commentaries], according to the method already described, there is only the perfection of the cause prior to the first resolution (*paṭhamābhinīhāra*).
It has been shown. The connection is: "having gone forth after renouncing the world at the age of twenty-nine.
Because he possessed the merit required for the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*), the Bodhisatta was endowed with the glory of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakravartin*);

therefore, his dwelling place is described as "the abode of the glory of a Wheel-turning Monarch. "Dwellings" (*bhavana*) refers to the residences known as Ramma, Suramma, and Subha. "Application to striving" (*padhānayoga*) refers to the practice of difficult austerities.
The application of supreme energy.
It is said that in Uruvelā, at Senānigama, a daughter of a householder named Sujātā, having reached marriageable age, made a vow at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River:
"If, having gone to a family of equal status, I give birth to my first child..."
"I shall obtain a son; I will perform a sacrificial offering with milk-rice," she thought, and her aspiration was fulfilled.
She had seven cows graze in the Laṭṭhivana forest, and having obtained their daughters as cows, she had them graze there in the same way;
then again their daughters likewise—thus, by means of cows descended through a lineage of seven generations of sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, she [obtained] milk.
Having taken it, she began to cook the milk-rice porridge. At that moment, Mahābrahmā held a three-league white parasol over her;
Sakka, the king of the gods, kindled the fire; and the deities cast into it every flavor existing in the entire world.
The porridge cooked turning to the right, and she [served] it together with a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand pieces.

Having given it to the Bodhisatta, she departed. Then the Bodhisatta, taking it, ate it at the bathing place named Suppatiṭṭhita on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, dividing it into forty-nine lumps each the size of a single palm tree trunk.
With reference to this, it is said: "On the full moon day of Visākha, in the village of Uruvelā, Sujātā offered him milk-rice mixed with divine honey."

"Having consumed [it]. In this context, "by Sujātā" refers to the wife of the merchant (seṭṭhi) named Sujātā, who was the mother of the Venerable Elder Yasa and who attained the foremost position among those who took refuge later on.

*Ojā* is a specific quality, a refined essence of the nutrient fluid that follows through every limb, which provides support and strength and is dependent upon the primary elements (*bhūta*). That which has divine (*dibba*) [nutrient] placed within it is called *pakkhittadibboja*.
That [is what is meant by] *pāyāsa*: it is a particular kind of food fit to be drunk after being made into a liquid (*rasa*) and fit to be eaten after being made into morsels (*ālopa*).
*Madhupāyāsa* is *pāyāsa* sprinkled with honey; that [is what is meant].

Then, because he had spent the day’s rest (*divāvihāra*) in the Great Sāla Grove on the bank of the Nerañjarā River by means of various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), [the text says] "at the time of evening," and so forth.

It has been stated. The details should be understood from their respective sources. By the words "to the north-east," he refers to the path leading from the daytime rest to the entrance of the Bodhi tree;
the meaning is: by way of a straight path extending to the north-east, adorned by deities.
They also say this: "To the north-east" means to the north-west (the beginning and end being included).
"Because the middle [direction] is also included, and because we see the use of elided expressions; for if this were so, it would accord with the statement in the *Jātaka-nidāna*:
'Having entered the seat of enlightenment by way of the south-western direction, he stands there. Others say:
'The north-eastern direction from the southern direction is the "south-north" (dakkhiṇuttara); having entered by way of that. However, some [hold that] the word 'north'..."
And here, it signifies a path. For if it were to signify a direction, one would have said, "to the south or north.

This is not so, because we see the use of the suffix *-ena* even with words signifying direction, as in "the Sīdā river flows to the north, deep and difficult to cross," and because the word *uttara* has not yet been used here to signify a path. Furthermore, this refers to a portion of the direction.
Thus it was said. For even a portion of a direction is called a "direction.

Then, having taken eight handfuls of *kuśa* grass given by a brahmin named Sotthiya while on the way, he approached the Bodhimanda—the ornament of the Bodhi tree, grown at the place that provides consolation to all Bodhisattvas and resembling a mountain of blue collyrium—and having circumambulated it three times clockwise, he sat down.
He stood in the southern direction, and that region trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf;
then, as the Great Being proceeded to and stood in the western and northern directions, those [regions] likewise trembled.
Thereupon, thinking, "Not even this entire region is capable of sustaining my virtue," he went toward the eastern direction.
There, a space the size of a cross-legged seat became perfectly still; that very spot is, in its primary sense, designated as the "seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Having resolved, "This is the place for the destruction of the defilements," the Great Man stood facing the northeast direction and, at that immovable spot, grasped those blades of grass by their tips and shook them; immediately, [the seat] became fourteen cubits in length.
There was a couch, and those blades of grass appeared as if they had been fashioned into the patterns of a quilted mattress.

There, having folded his legs into the three-jointed cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), and making the meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*) endowed with four factors his forerunner, he sat down, resolved upon the fourfold energy. To show this matter in brief: "At the seat of enlightenment..."
Having entered, he spoke the words beginning with “...”.

In this context, *bodhi* refers to the knowledge of the path to Arahatship and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). That which is adorned (*maṇḍati*)—meaning it becomes firm and gains confidence therein—is called the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
In the absolute sense (*nippariyāyena*), it is the aforementioned location; however, in a figurative sense (*pariyāyena*), it is here [at this place].
The King of Trees (*dumārāja*). For thus it was said by the Elder Ācariya Ānanda:
"The term *bodhimaṇḍa* is to be understood as referring specifically to the place of the first full awakening, and not to any place whatsoever where a Bodhi tree is established.
It is called *assattha* because it reassures the Blessed One through the victory over Māra, the attainment of omniscience, and so forth. For the prefix *ā-* [is used here].

They maintain that the word *sāsa* refers to instructions (*anusitthi*) and dwellings (*osana*), though in the world it is also called "caladala" (the trembling-leaved) and "kuñjarāsana" (the elephant-seated).

Because of its state of being loftily risen, because of its state of having reached the summit of the invincible ground, and because of its state of growing at the place where all the qualities of omniscience are acquired, it is the "king of trees" (*dumārāja*).
It is both the *assattha* tree and the king of trees; thus, it is the "Assattha-king-of-trees. Of these two...
By way of the joints of the thighs and knees, and the joint of the root of the thigh and the waist, there are three joints;
or, that which has three corners by way of its shape is "three-jointed" (*tisandhi*). That very *pallaṅka* is the "thigh-bound posture" (*ūrubaddhāsana*).

Regarding the term *parisamantato aṅkanaṃ āsanaṃ*, the letter *r* is changed to *l*, and the doubling of the consonant is applied, thus it is called *pallaṅka*. Alternatively, it is a *pallaṅka* characterized by three joints.
The "three-jointed cross-legged posture" (tisandhipallaṅka) refers to that. "Having folded [the legs]" means having bound them; it is said that both feet are placed together.
A detailed explanation will follow in the commentary on the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.

Regarding the meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*) endowed with four factors by way of its equal application toward the four—oneself, a friend, a neutral person, and an enemy—it is called "endowed with four factors."
This, moreover, should also be connected with the phrase “the foundation of energy.
For that too [is said]: “Let only skin, sinew, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood dry up in this body.
But as for that which is to be attained by human strength, human energy, and human exertion—that not being reached, there shall be no ceasing of my energy.”
"It will have a shape"—thus, it possesses exactly the four factors mentioned in the stated method.
That which has a measurement of fourteen cubits in its width is "fourteen-cubit. It is marked (aṅkīyate) all around by the assembly.
It is called *pallaṅka* because it is marked out (*lakkhīyate*) by way of delimitation; here, the letter *ra* becomes *la*, and that [letter] is doubled.

Furthermore, according to the statement in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "this is the place for the destruction of defilements (*kilesa*)," it is *pallaṅka* because one effects the destruction of defilements (*pallaṃ*) there;
this is formed either by the addition of the nasal *niggahita* or by a compound (*samāsa*) without elision (*alutta*). It measures fourteen cubits.
And that couch (*pallaṅka*)—being excellent in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being desirable—is the "excellent fourteen-cubit couch" (*cuddasahatthapallaṅkavara*).
He who has gone there, proceeded there, or sat there is likewise [described as such]. Furthermore, the measurement of fourteen cubits here should be understood by way of its width;
for those very grasses, through the power of immeasurable merit, came to exist in the form of a couch fourteen cubits wide.
Furthermore, those [seats] measuring eight handfuls cannot possibly reach fourteen cubits in height.
For this very reason, it is said here: "having spread out a grass mat," and in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and other works:
"having spread out grass... sitting down facing the east. And elsewhere: "on a grass seat considered to be fourteen cubits [in length]. Some [hold this view].

However, when they state, “It was fourteen cubits high precisely because of its towering nature,” this should not be accepted as such, for the reasons already stated and because it contradicts the evidence. Indeed, in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, it says:
“Having circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times and ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) which was fourteen cubits high...”

Although the reading "having spread out a grass mat in that place and sitting down, having resolved upon fourfold energy" is seen, nevertheless, it should be understood that in that context the word *ubbēdha* signifies breadth, just as in the Mahāpanāda Jātaka:
"In width sixteen [yojanas], they say it is a thousandfold in height. For thus it is stated in its commentary: "In width..."
"Sixteen-fingerbreadths high" means that its width was sixteen spans of a joint; [this is stated] in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (vol. 2, p.

302). Otherwise, the meaning would result in the implication that the grass-strewing was done in mid-air itself, rather than on a fixed spot, because that [space] would be the locus for the action of strewing; however, that meaning is not intended, as it is not found elsewhere.
The connection is: "as if having placed a silver mountain behind him. "Attha" means the western mountain.
"Mārabala" refers to Māra, the army of Māra, or the power of Māra. "Pubbenivāsa" means the aggregates (khandhas) in which one previously dwelt.
"Dibbacakkhu" means the knowledge of the divine eye. By way of aging and death, starting with the words, "Alas, this world has fallen into hardship," and so forth...

Having introduced knowledge into the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). Regarding the phrase "the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānacatutthajjhāna*), here too one should apply it by changing the grammatical case, thinking:
"This is the practice of all Buddhas. For they say that this too is indeed the habitual practice of the Buddhas.
"Making it the basis" means making it the cause or the foundation. "Having increased insight" means by way of the 360 million methods.
Having developed insight by way of causing one to grasp the womb of the Great Vajira-knowledge known as the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa),
and while comprehending formations in their manifold aspects and locations through the method of insight into phenomena according to their sequence for the attainment of omniscient knowledge,
even the insight-knowledge that proceeds by way of three hundred and sixty million modes is called "Great Vajira-knowledge."
It is said that this refers even to the knowledge that precedes and follows the meditative attainments (samāpatti) occurring daily in a number of twenty-four hundred thousand crores.

However, here it is specifically the knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa), and particularly the knowledge of the supreme path (aggamaggañāṇa); therefore, it should be understood that only this possesses the nature of the "womb" of insight (vipassanā).
Regarding "all the qualities of a Buddha," this refers to the entire range of a Buddha’s qualities, such as omniscience (sabbaññutā) and so forth. Having made that the foundation...
"Concentration is the turning back," it is said; "this is his work of wisdom. "His" (assa) refers to the Blessed One.
The clarification by means of a simile begins with "Just as in the case of the hand," and so forth. "In the hand" (hatthe) means in a handful or in the hollowed palms.
"In the bowl" (pātiyam) means in a saucer. "In the jar" (ghaṭe) means in a water-carrying jar. A *kuṇḍa* is a vessel with a capacity of holding thirty-two *doṇas*.
Kolamba; greater than that is cāṭi; greater still is mahākumbhī; soṇḍī; kusobbha; nadībhāga; kandara;
and at the base of the world-sphere mountains, the ocean is the Cakkavāḷa-mahāsamudda. By the phrase "the great ocean at the foot of Sineru," he refers to the Sītāntara ocean.
With the words "pāti" and so forth, he further elucidates that same meaning by means of another method.

The connection is: “It is brief, as follows. In order to show that very commentary—which was spoken for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the text—as being subordinate to it, the words beginning with “Therefore he said” were spoken; this is the case everywhere.
The passage beginning with “Two kinds of worldlings” was spoken solely for the purpose of showing the divisions found among worldlings, and not otherwise.

Because, as in the *Mūlapariyāya-saṃvaṇṇanā* and other works, the term "ordinary person" (*puthujjana*) here is intended specifically for the ordinary person without exception, in order to distinguish them from specific types of ordinary persons. For no ordinary person whatsoever is able to manifest the superior qualities of the Blessed One;
let alone the ordinary person, even for noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) and paccekabuddhas, the Buddha-qualities are simply beyond their range. Likewise...
For he will say, “stream-enterer,” and so forth. Because of his connection with the lineage of the Ādicca (Sun), he is a kinsman of the Sun-god Sūriya;
thus he is called *Ādiccabandhu*. This is stated in the Niddesa: “*Ādicca* is said to be the Sun (*Sūriya*).
Sūriya is of the Gotama clan, and the Blessed One is also of the Gotama clan. The Blessed One is a kinsman by clan and a relative by clan of Sūriya; therefore, the Buddha is *Ādiccabandhu*.”
The experts on words, however, prefer the reading “buddhassādiccabandhunā. This is because he has a kinsman in the form of a clan (bandhu) that is identical to the clan of the Sun (Ādicca);
thus, having analyzed it as "the Buddha who is the kinsman of the Sun," he is called Ādiccabandhu.

Furthermore, even through skill in the exposition of the aggregates and so forth, there exists great learning (bāhusacca) which serves as the cause for knowing the defilements and non-defilements, as it has been said:

“Venerable sir, to what extent is one called ‘learned’ (bahussuta)? To the extent that a bhikkhu is skilled in the aggregates (khandha); skilled in the elements (dhātu) ... [as before] ... skilled in the sense bases (āyatana) ... [as before] ... skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). To this extent, bhikkhu, one is learned. Therefore, it was said:

“For one who [is skilled] in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth,” etc. Here, by the word “and so forth” (ādi), everything up to dependent origination is included. In this context, “learning” (uggaha) is the act of committing to memory;
“interrogation” (paripucchā) is the thorough questioning of the meaning. According to the commentary...

"Listening" (*savana*) is the act of making the meaning dependent upon the door of the ear. "Retention" (*dhāraṇā*) is the upholding of the Dhamma by means of the correct placement and correct interpretation of both the phrasing (*byañjana*) and the meaning (*attha*).
"Reflection" (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is the pondering, mental examination, and reviewing of those [teachings] that have thus been heard, retained, and mastered.
Having shown this classification, he also shows the etymological definition (*vacanattha*) with the words "twofold," and so forth. "Of many kinds" (*puthūnaṃ*) means of various types.

[This refers to] the defilements and so forth. "Because they are included among the multitude of people" (*puthujjanantogadhattā*) means that because they are contained within the midst of many people, they are called *puthujjana*;
this is the connection. "A *puthu-jana*" means that this person has reached the reckoning as one who is distinct (*puthu*) and indeed separate.
"Thus" (*iti*) means therefore; this is the connection with the term *puthujjana*. This is the meaning shown briefly by way of the composition of the verse.
He explains [the passage] beginning with “so hi. By the phrase “of various kinds,” he shows that the word *puthu* here has the sense of “many.

By the word “etc.,” he indicates the meaning included therein; and demonstrating the proof for that meaning through the method of the *Ambasecanaka-jātaka* and the *Garuḷa-jātaka*, he says “as it is said,” etc., presenting the text of the *Niddesa*.
[The phrase] “unshaken views of self-existence” (*avihatā sakkāyadiṭṭhiyo*) means many and diverse.
These [beings] possess various unshaken views of self-existence (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*);

the meaning is that because they are not shaken by this [teaching], they produce various views of self-existence, or that they are produced by various views of self-existence. Alternatively, the word *jana* expresses the sense of "unshaken";
therefore, they produce—that is, do not shake—various views of self-existence, or they are people who are unshaken [from] various views of self-existence.

It is also appropriate to explain it as "they show this meaning. Furthermore, here the secondary placement of the qualifier (*visesanaparanipātana*) should be understood, as in the expression "one who has kindled the fire" (*agyāhito*).

By the phrase "looking toward the faces of various teachers" (*puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikā*), the derivation is shown: "various" (*puthu*) means many people, and "teachers" (*satthārānaṃ*) refers to those for whom they [look].
However, in the phrase "not emerged from all various destinies" (*puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitā*), [it refers to] by means of karma and defilements (*kammakilesehi*).

*Janā* (beings) are so called because beings are to be produced (*janetabbā*) or are born (*jāyanti*) therein; thus, the meaning of the word is "those for whom all various (*puthu*) destinations (*gatiyo*) are their *jana*.
Furthermore, by the phrase "they perform various (*puthu*) diverse volitional formations (*nānābhisaṅkhāre abhisaṅkharonti*)," it is shown that beings are produced (*janā*) by means of these;

namely, meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhārādayo*). These beings possess various (*puthu*) and manifold (*nānāvidhā*) volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*), hence they are "various" (*puthu*).

Or it expresses the meaning: "they produce various volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) and they perform volitional formations. Following that, however, regarding the three meanings beginning with "they are carried away by various floods (ogha)":

beings are called *janā* because they are born (*jāyanti*) by means of these; [the floods] are the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) and so forth, the torments of passion (*rāga-santāpa*) and so forth, the fevers of passion (*rāga-pariḷāha*) and so forth, or indeed all the fevers of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*).
These exist in various ways for them; thus they are "various" (*puthu*).
This is stated to show the etymological derivation [of "passion"]: they cause one to be born, they carry one away, they cause one to burn, and they cause one to be consumed.
The phrase "infatuated and greedy" (*rattā giddhā*) and so forth is a synonymous expression.
Furthermore, "infatuated" (*rattā*) means colored by the lust of desire (*chandarāga*), which causes a transformation of the mind just as cloth is colored by dye.

They are *giddhā* (greedy) because they are greedy through the nature of longing and intense coveting. They are *gathitā* (bound) because they are tied to that [object] as if knotted, being difficult to release.
They are *mucchitā* (infatuated) because, through the penetration of the defilements, they have become as if unconscious, having fallen into a delusion that has no other purpose.
They are *ajjhosannā* (clinging) because they remain having swallowed and finalized [the object], as if making it their own exclusive possession.
"They stick" (*lagganti*) means they are attached like cows to thorns, or they are submerged in a great quagmire such that they cannot be pulled out, like a man whose nose-tip has become stuck.
"They are stuck" (*laggitā*) means they are clung to by the five sense-faculties, as a monkey is by monkey-glue.
"Entangled" (*palibuddhā*) means bound; or "afflicted"—this is the meaning according to the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*.
It is said. By this [root *jan*], that which is born is called "people" (*jano*), such as lust, greed, and so forth.
The meaning shown is that these people—lust and the rest—are manifold and diverse; or alternatively, that among the fivefold sense-pleasures, these people are attached, greedy, and...
[omitted] ...obstructed. "Entangled" (*āvutā*) and so forth are merely synonymous expressions. Furthermore, "entangled" means covered; "shrouded" (*nivutā*) means hindered; "enveloped" (*ophutā*)...
"Enveloped" means covered over; "shrouded" means concealed; "overturned" means turned face-downward—thus it is stated right there [in the text].
And here, they are called "people" (*janā*) because people are produced by these [hindrances];
or, "people" refers to those for whom there are various and manifold hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); or, people are obstructed by various hindrances... [and so on] ... "overturned."

This shows the etymology. By the words "puthūnan" and so forth, it shows the meaning as: "one who is born among many base practices," or "a person included among the many," or "many people"; by this, it explains or establishes the third quarter [of the verse].
By "puthu vā" and so forth, however, it [explains] the fourth quarter. "Puthu" means simply "detached" (visaṃsaṭṭha).
The meaning of the word here is "an ordinary person" (*puthujjana*).
In order to show those specific qualities which serve as the basis for the designation "Tathāgata" being applied to the Blessed One, it was said:
"For eight reasons the Blessed One is a Tathāgata," and so forth. For even a single word may be used with reference to many different bases for its application.
The Blessed One’s names reveal his meaning in manifold ways, and all the verbal designations for the Blessed One are indeed indicative of his many qualities. As it is said:
“Countless are the names of the Great Seer according to his qualities;
even from a thousand names, one name may be selected on account of a quality.”
When there is the inquiry, "But what are those?", having first briefly indicated their essential nature, he explains them by means of the words beginning with "how.
Regarding the phrase "thus come" (*tathā-āgata*), the word *tathā* here serves to establish a comparison by way of determining the mode [of coming].
Because a general description is restricted to a particular instance, and because one who possesses a particular [attribute] applies even a general term to that very particular meaning.

The word *āgata* (come) should be understood here in the sense of "coming by way of the path," because it is not to be employed [in the ordinary sense], as in such passages as "the word *āgata* comes in the sense of coming by way of knowledge" or "it has come to the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*)," and not in the sense of physical movement, as in such passages as "The Great Ascetic has indeed arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans.
In that context, the word *tathā* (such/as) serves to provide a simile by way of determining a particular mode; that mode—

Because compassion is his primary foundation, he spoke the passage beginning with “Just as in the whole world” to show, by way of an illustration of the path traversed by previous Buddhas through the gateway of Great Compassion, that [path] in its general character.
Furthermore, because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are invariably connected, the meaning of the word *tathā* is elucidated here by means of the word *yathā*. He now elaborates upon that very point:

“Just as the Blessed One Vipassī,” and so forth: it should be understood that this path is shown by way of those six Perfectly Enlightened Ones beginning with Vipassī, because they are well-known through the detailed accounts of their great deeds in such texts as the Mahāpadāna Sutta, and because they are [historically] proximate.
The connection “as he came, so he came” applies everywhere. Furthermore, by the words “What is meant? and so forth...
He explains that very point. Therein, "by which resolution" refers to the Great Resolve (mahāpaṇidhāna) endowed with eight factors, by way of:

human birth, possession of male gender, perfection of causes, meeting the Teacher, going forth, perfection of virtues, the [right] object, and zeal. For the initial resolve of all Buddhas is accomplished precisely by this method.
And here, it should be understood that "resolution" (abhinīhāra) is a designation for the root resolve (mūlapaṇidhāna).
Having thus shown the meaning of the term "Tathāgata" by way of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*), he now says "Alternatively," and so forth,

in order to show it also by way of the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramī*). Regarding this, the detailed exposition on the perfections provided by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla— beginning with the words, "And here,
this detailed discussion of the perfections is for the purpose of generating skill in those following the Great Vehicle of Enlightenment (*mahābodhiyāna*) according to the Suttas"— is as follows:
Although what has been stated here might seem to result in an expansion of the text if it were all repeated by us now,
nevertheless, since this commentary proceeds by way of purifying errors from the subsequent manuscript and by way of completing the remaining meaning,
that discourse on the perfections (pāramī) must also be told here; therefore, [it is taken] from that very *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*.
And having brought [these matters] forth, it will adorn them with verses as appropriate and clarify their meaning and intention. How so?
What are these perfections (pāramīs), in what sense, and how many kinds are there?
What is their sequence, and what are their characteristics and so forth in every respect?
What is the condition? Defilement, purification, and the antidote;
the analysis of practice, as well as synthesis and accomplishment.
To what extent is it accomplished? What is the benefit, and what is the fruit?
Having answered this question, the exposition will follow.
Herein, this is the answer:
What, then, are these perfections?
That which, being embraced by skillful means and wisdom, is free from craving, conceit, and the like—
that perfection (pāramī) is fully manifested.

Indeed, these actions— generosity and the rest— which are reckoned as virtues, when they are not impaired by craving, conceit, and so forth, and are embraced by compassion and skill in means, are manifested as "perfections."
In what sense are they called "perfections" (pāramī)? "Parama" means supreme in the sense of being most excellent; this is their "pāramī" [derived from that].
They are considered threefold according to their benefit: as action, as cultivation, and as giving and so forth.
He fulfills, he exists, he transcends others, he transcends, he immerses himself, he moves;
he knows, he measures, or likewise, he measures the supreme—thus he is the Supreme (Parama).
He immerses himself in the beyond, he purifies, or he exists and he moves.
It is called *māyā* because it measures (*māneti*), or because it measures (*minoti*) and measures out (*mināti*).
Furthermore, according to the traditional explanation, the Great Being is called a *pāramī*;
by means of the three types of derivative (*taddhita*) meanings, this is considered to be a *pāramī*.
Indeed, by virtue of his possession of the specific qualities of generosity, morality, and so forth, the Great Bodhisatta is supreme among beings;

thus, "pāramī" refers to him as the Supreme One (*paramo*), or else it refers to his state or activity, namely the practice of giving and the other perfections. Alternatively, according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), he is called *paramo* because he "fills up" (*parati pūreti*);
the Bodhisatta is the fulfiller and protector of the qualities such as generosity, and "pāramī" is his state or activity as the Supreme One (*paramassa*). Furthermore, others...

It is called *muni* because it binds sentient beings to itself through its connection with distinguished qualities; or because it immerses others in excellence, cleansing them of the stains of defilement;
or because it especially rejoices in or goes toward the supreme *nibbāna*; or because it measures and delimits the other world by means of its supreme knowledge as if it were this world;
or because it possesses an exceedingly great multitude of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).

It measures and casts [the defilements] into its own continuum; or, it measures and harms—that is, destroys—the "other," which is distinct from the Dhamma-body that has become one's self, namely the opposing host of thieves that are the defilements which cause harm.
Thus, it is "paramo," the Great Being. By the method stated in the passage beginning with "This belongs to the supreme one" (*paramassa ayan*), it is called a *pāramī*.
Alternatively, it rejoices in and purifies itself in the "far shore" (*pāre*), which is Nibbāna, and it also purifies sentient beings.
It is called *pāramī* because it measures (*māyati*), binds, and yokes beings there; or because it goes (*mayati*) to that [perfection]; or because it causes beings to go (*māyeti*) there;
or because it wisely knows (*munāti*) and delimits that [reality] as it truly is; or because it measures and places beings there;

or because it measures and destroys (*mināti*) the enemy of the defilements (*kilesāri*) of beings there. Thus, for the Great Being, it refers to the very acts of giving and so forth, according to the phrase beginning with "this belongs to him."
“Pāramī. In this manner, the etymological meaning of the perfections (*pāramī*) should be understood.

How many kinds are there? Briefly, they are tenfold; these are indeed presented in their specific forms in the *Buddhavaṃsa* scripture. As it is said: “Searching, I then beheld the first perfection, that of giving,” and so forth.
And as it is also said: “How many, venerable sir, are the qualities that make one a Buddha? There are ten, Sāriputta, qualities that make one a Buddha.”

“What ten? Sāriputta, generosity is a quality that makes one a Buddha; virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity are qualities that make one a Buddha. These, Sāriputta, are the ten qualities that make one a Buddha.
This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“Generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom with energy as the fifth, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.
However, some say they are “sixfold”; that is stated by way of grouping them together. That grouping, moreover, will be made clear later on.
"And what is their sequence?"—here, "sequence" (*kama*) refers to the order of teaching. That [order] is based on the order of undertaking; the undertaking is based on the order of investigation.
Thus, they are taught exactly as they were investigated and undertaken at the beginning, at the time of the first resolution.
As it is said: "While investigating, I saw that the first was the perfection of giving," and so forth. Therefore, this is stated:
“This sequence was stated by way of the order in which they are undertaken;
or else, it is because each one is of great assistance to the next.
For in that regard, giving is of great assistance to virtue and is easy to perform; thus, it is mentioned first. Moreover, giving is embraced by virtue.
"Virtue is of great fruit and great benefit," thus it is said that virtue follows immediately after giving.
Virtue is embraced by renunciation... [and so on] ...renunciation is embraced by wisdom... [and so on] ...wisdom is embraced by energy... [and so on] ...energy is embraced by patience...
[and so on] ...patience is embraced by truthfulness... [and so on] ...truthfulness is embraced by determination... [and so on] ...determination is embraced by loving-kindness... [and so on].
Loving-kindness (*mettā*), when embraced by equanimity (*upekkhā*), yields great fruit and great benefit; thus, equanimity is mentioned immediately after loving-kindness.
Furthermore, it should be understood that equanimity is embraced by compassion (*karuṇā*), and compassion is in turn embraced by equanimity.
But how is it that the Bodhisattvas, who possess great compassion, can be equanimous toward sentient beings? Toward those who are appropriate objects for equanimity, [they remain so]—anyone...
Some say that they are equanimous toward time, but not toward everything and at all times.
Others, however, say that they are not equanimous toward sentient beings, but are equanimous toward the misfortunes caused by sentient beings; this alone is appropriate here.
Another method:
Generosity is said to be first [among the perfections] for reasons such as its universal commonality,
while the others depend upon it even at the outset.
For generosity is practiced even among the common folk because it is common to all beings, yields little fruit [in comparison], and is easy to perform.

This was stated at the beginning. Virtue (*sīla*) is mentioned immediately after giving (*dāna*) because it purifies both the giver and the recipient; because it speaks of benefiting others following the description of refraining from harming others;

because it describes the nature of non-action (*akiriyadhamma*) following the description of the nature of action (*kiriyadhamma*); and because it describes the cause for the attainment of existence (*bhava*) following the description of the cause for the attainment of wealth (*bhoga*).
Renunciation (*nekkhamma*) follows virtue because the perfection of virtue is established through it, and it consists of good conduct of body and speech.
Having spoken thus, because [the Buddha] spoke of mental good conduct; because for one of purified virtue, meditative absorption (jhāna) is achieved with ease;
because, having spoken of purity of application through the abandoning of faults in action, he spoke of purity of disposition through the abandoning of faults in defilement;

and because he spoke of the abandoning of active obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) for one established in the abandoning of transgressions—it is for these reasons that renunciation (nekkhamma) was stated immediately after virtue (sīla). [This is] by means of wisdom (paññā).
Because of the accomplishment and purification of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), and because of the statement that in the absence of meditation (*jhāna*) there is an absence of wisdom (*paññā*).

For wisdom has concentration (*samādhi*) as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), and concentration has wisdom as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*). Furthermore, after mentioning the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*), there is the mention of the sign of equanimity (*upekkhā-nimitta*);
and because of the mention of skill in means for accomplishing the welfare of others through meditation for the benefit of others, wisdom follows immediately after renunciation.
It is so stated because the function of wisdom is accomplished through the arousal of energy;

because, after speaking of the patient acceptance that contemplates the phenomena of the emptiness of beings, it speaks of the wonderful nature of the exertion undertaken for the benefit of beings; because, after speaking of the sign of equanimity, it speaks of the sign of exertion;
and because, after speaking of acting with circumspection, it speaks of initiative. For the initiative of one who acts with circumspection brings about a distinction in the fruit.
Viriya (energy) is mentioned immediately after paññā (wisdom).

This is because endurance (titikkhā) is accomplished through energy; for one who possesses energy, by virtue of having initiated energy, dwells having overcome the suffering brought about by beings and formations. This is because energy serves as the adornment of endurance; for indeed, one who possesses energy has endurance.

It is fitting. This is because, after stating the sign of exertion (*paggahanimitta*), it speaks of the sign of serenity (*samathanimitta*); and because, through excessive exertion, it speaks of the abandoning of the fault of restlessness (*uddhaccadosa*).

For it is by means of the acceptance that arises from reflecting on the Dhamma (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*) that the fault of restlessness is abandoned. This is because it speaks of the practice of persistence for one who possesses energy (*vīriya*);

for one who abounds in patience (*khanti*) is unperturbed and practices with persistence. And because it speaks of the absence of craving for reward in the undertaking of deeds for the welfare of others for one who possesses diligence (*appamāda*).
