For when there is contemplation of phenomena as they truly are, craving does not arise. Furthermore, patience is mentioned immediately after energy because of the statement that one must endure the suffering caused by others even while engaged in the supreme effort for the welfare of others.

Patience follows truth because it is established through long practice; and having spoken of enduring the harm done by those who cause injury, one speaks of performing a service for them, which expresses non-deceptiveness. Through the unshakability of speech regarding patience, there is the quality of speaking what is true.

Truth (*sacca*) is stated immediately after patience (*khanti*), because of the statement regarding the non-abandonment [of what has been accepted], and because of the statement regarding the truth of reality for one whose knowledge has been further developed by that reflective acceptance of the Dhamma of the emptiness of beings. This is because truth is established through resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

For when there is unshakable resolution, abstinence (*virati*) is accomplished. This is because, having spoken what is non-deceptive, one speaks of an unshakable state therein. One who is devoted to truth (*saccasandha*)...

One proceeds unshakably in generosity and the other perfections in accordance with one’s promise. This is because, having spoken of the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*), there is the statement regarding the completion of the practice within the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
For one who possesses knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*) resolves upon the requisites for enlightenment and brings them to completion.

Furthermore, determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is mentioned immediately after the truth because it is unshakable by opposing factors. This is due to the accomplishment of the determination that undertakes the performance of the welfare of others through loving-kindness (*mettā*).

After stating the resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), loving-kindness (*mettā*) is mentioned next because it consists of speech that brings about welfare. For one who resolves upon the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) becomes an abider in loving-kindness.
Furthermore, because the undertaking of a resolve is possible through not disturbing what has been undertaken, loving-kindness is stated immediately after the resolve.
Equanimity (*upekkhā*) follows because it is the purification of loving-kindness; having spoken of bringing welfare to beings, [it is taught] regarding their transgressions.

Equanimity is taught immediately after loving-kindness because of the statement regarding its state of neutrality; because, having spoken of the development of loving-kindness, it speaks of the development that is its natural outflow;
and because it describes its marvelous quality by saying, "He is equanimous even toward beings who desire his welfare. Thus should their sequence be understood.
As for the question, "What are their characteristics and so forth in every respect?", here they are stated without distinction:
Assisting others is called its characteristic;
its function is to help and to be unshakable, and its essence is also the desire for their welfare.
Buddhahood is its manifestation, and compassion is said to be its knowledge.
"Foundation" (*padaṭṭhāna*) means "support. These [perfections] should be understood individually according to their distinctions.
For all the perfections have the characteristic of promoting the welfare of others; their function is to provide assistance to others, or their function is to be unshakable;

they are manifested as the desire for the good of others, or they are manifested as Buddhahood; they have great compassion as their proximate cause, or they have compassion and skillful means as their proximate cause.
In particular, however, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*) is the volition of relinquishing oneself and one’s requisites when embraced by compassion and skillful means (*upāya-kosalla*).

The perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*) consists, in its essential meaning, of the abstention from what should not be done and the volition to perform what should be done, as well as good conduct of body and speech, when embraced by compassion and skillful means.
[The perfection of renunciation] is preceded by the vision of the dangers of sensual pleasures and existence, when embraced by compassion and skillful means.

The arising of the mind of renunciation is the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*). The realization of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena, supported by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*).
The undertaking of the welfare of others through body and mind, supported by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramī*).

That which consists in enduring the offenses of beings and conditioned formations, dominated by non-hatred and proceeding in that manner, [supported by compassion and skillful means,] is... [the perfection of patience].

The arising of the thought [of non-harming] is the perfection of patience (*khantipāramī*). The perfection of truth (*saccapāramī*) is non-deceitfulness, consisting of various types such as volition of abstinence, which is embraced by compassion (*karuṇā*), skillful means (*upāya*), and wisdom (*kosalla*).

The perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānapāramī*) is the arising of the thought proceeding in that mode, characterized by the firm determination to undertake [the practice], which is embraced by compassion, skillful means, and wisdom.
The perfection of generosity (*cāgapāramī*) is the bestowing of welfare and happiness upon the world, which is embraced by compassion, skillful means, and wisdom.

In terms of its essential meaning, non-ill will is the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*). The perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) is the even engagement toward desirable and undesirable beings and conditioned phenomena—characterized by the destruction of attachment and aversion—and is embraced by compassion and skillful means.
Therefore, giving has the characteristic of relinquishing; its function is the destruction of greed regarding the object to be given; and it is manifested as non-attachment.
Or, it has the manifestation of the attainment of existence and non-existence, and the objects to be relinquished as its proximate cause.

Virtue (sīla) has the characteristic of restraining; it is said to have the characteristic of composing or the characteristic of establishing. Its function is the destruction of misconduct, or its function is blamelessness;
it has purity as its manifestation, and moral shame and moral dread as its proximate cause. [It is the opposite] of sensual desire and of existence...
Renunciation has the characteristic of going forth; its function is the manifestation of the danger therein; it is manifested as turning away from that very thing;

and its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their true nature, or alternatively, the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer;
its function is the illumination of the object, like a lamp; and it is manifested as non-delusion.
Concentration has the forest as its proximate cause, or it has the four noble truths as its proximate cause.

Energy has the characteristic of exertion; its function is to support; its manifestation is non-collapse; its proximate cause is the basis for the arousal of energy, or it has spiritual urgency as its proximate cause.
Patience has the characteristic of enduring; its function is to bear with the desirable and the undesirable; it is manifested as forbearance, or alternatively, as non-opposition;
its proximate cause is seeing things as they really are. Truth has the characteristic of non-deceptiveness; its function is to reveal things as they are;
it is manifested as goodness; its proximate cause is gentleness. Resolve, among the requisites for enlightenment, has the characteristic of determination.
Their function is the overcoming of opposites; their manifestation is immovability therein; their proximate cause is the requisites for enlightenment.
Loving-kindness has the characteristic of proceeding in a mode of welfare; its function is the promotion of welfare, or its function is the removal of ill-will;

its manifestation is gentleness; its proximate cause is the perception of beings as endearing. Equanimity has the characteristic of proceeding in a mode of neutrality; its function is the perception of evenness.
It has the subsiding of aversion and attachment as its manifestation, and the reflection on one’s own karma as its proximate cause.

Furthermore, in this context, the fact that giving and the other perfections are embraced by compassion and skillful means must be stated as a qualification of their characteristic of relinquishment and so forth;

for it is only when they are embraced by compassion and skillful means, and not otherwise, that they receive the designation of "perfections" (pāramī) directed toward supreme enlightenment and the like.
"Generosity and the other virtues lead to cyclic existence (vaṭṭagāmīni); how then do they receive the designation of 'perfections' (pāramī)?
What is their condition?"—The resolve for them, compassion, and knowledge are their conditions.

The basis for the arising of high resolve (*ussāha*), as well as conduct for the welfare of others (*hitācāra*) and so forth—namely, the "aspiration" (*abhinīhāra*)—is the condition for all the perfections (*pāramī*) alike. For this aspiration, accomplished through the convergence of the eight factors beginning with "human birth" (*manussatta*) and "possession of male gender" (*liṅgasampatti*), [is expressed as]:
"Having crossed over, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being awakened, may I awaken others; being purified..."
The aspiration expressed in such passages as, "I shall purify myself; being tamed, I shall tame others; being at peace, I shall bring others to peace; being comforted, I shall comfort others;
having attained final Nibbāna, I shall lead others to final Nibbāna," is a condition for all the perfections (pāramīs) without distinction.

For it is through the occurrence of this aspiration that the subsequent investigation, establishment, undertaking, resolution, and accomplishment of the perfections arise in Great Beings (mahāpurisa). This is the aspiration.

And as for its meaning: it is a state of consciousness that arises through the convergence of the eight factors of the Great Being (bhesamaṭṭhaṅga), consisting of aspirations such as, "O, may I awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and bring about the welfare and happiness of all beings.
Because it proceeds by aiming toward the inconceivable plane of Buddhahood and immeasurable benefit for the world, it is the root of all the qualities that produce a Buddha.
It should be understood as the most excellent, the most beautiful, and a distinction of merit of immeasurable power.

Simultaneously with its arising, the Great Man is said to have "descended" into the practice of the Great Vehicle of Enlightenment, because he has attained the state of certainty and because his nature is such that he cannot turn back;
thus he receives the designation "Bodhisatta" (Bodhisattva) in respect to Perfect Enlightenment in every aspect.
Therein, his right mindfulness and mental composure, as well as his capacity for training in the requisites of enlightenment, become firmly established.

For, by the successful fulfillment of the aforementioned resolution—which is a precursor sign to the attainment of omniscient knowledge—Great Beings rightly discern all the perfections (*pāramī*) through their self-awakened wisdom (*sayambhuñāṇa*), undertake them, and fulfill them in due order, just as the wise Sumedha did after making his great resolution. As it is said:
“Now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make a Buddha—
upwards, downwards, and in the ten directions, as far as the element of Dhamma extends.
Searching then, I beheld first of all the perfection of giving.”

The detailed exposition follows. Furthermore, with respect to its characteristics and other aspects, this [resolve] has the characteristic of being correctly directed toward the aspiration for perfect enlightenment;
it has the function of the aspiration, such as: "O, may I awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and bring about the welfare and happiness of all beings";

it is manifested through the state of being a cause for the requisites of enlightenment; it has great compassion as its proximate cause, or alternatively, it has the perfection of the necessary supporting conditions as its proximate cause.
Furthermore, for that great aspiration (*abhinīhāra*), four conditions, four causes, and four powers are to be understood.
In this regard, what are the four conditions for the great aspiration?
Here, the Great Being sees the Tathāgata performing a marvelous and wonderful miracle through the great majesty of a Buddha; depending upon that [sight], he...
Making that the object, the mind becomes settled upon the Great Enlightenment, thinking:

"How truly of great power is this element of Dhamma (dhammadhātu), through the thorough penetration of which the Blessed One possesses such marvelous and wonderful qualities and inconceivable majesty!
Relying on that very vision of its great power and making it the condition, he resolves his mind upon full enlightenment.
Therein, one fixes the mind; this is the first condition for the Great Resolve.
Not only does one see the aforementioned great majesty of the Tathāgata, but one also hears:
"The Blessed One is such and such. Relying upon that and making that a condition, while being resolute toward full enlightenment—
Therein one fixes the mind; this is the second condition for the great resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*).
One does not indeed see the aforementioned great majesty of the Tathāgata, nor does one hear of it from another;
nevertheless, while the Tathāgata is teaching the Dhamma, [one hears] such words as: "Monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers," and so forth.
He hears the Dhamma connected with the majesty of the Buddhas; relying on that... [as before] ...this is the third condition for the Great Resolve.
Furthermore, he neither sees the aforementioned great majesty of the Tathāgata, nor hears of it from another, nor does he hear the Dhamma of the Tathāgata;
nevertheless, being of lofty aspiration and resolute in what is wholesome, he thinks: "I..."
“I shall preserve the lineage of the Buddhas, the succession of the Buddhas, the tradition of the Buddhas,
and the nature of the Buddhas”— to this end, honoring, revering, esteeming, worshipping, and paying homage to the Dhamma alone,
and relying upon it… [as before] …he establishes it; this is the fourth condition for the Great Resolve.

What are the four causes for the Great Resolve? Here, a Great Being is by nature endowed with the necessary support (*upanissaya*) and has performed services under previous Buddhas; this is the first cause for the Great Resolve.
Furthermore, a Great Being is by nature inclined toward compassion (*karuṇā*), devoted to compassion, and desirous of removing the suffering of sentient beings.
Furthermore, he sacrificed both his own body and his life; this is the second cause for the Great Resolve.

Moreover, the Great Being, for the sake of the welfare of beings, remained untiring and undaunted while striving and exerting himself for an exceedingly long time—even through the entire suffering of saṃsāra and difficult practices—until the accomplishment of his desired goal; this is...

This is the third cause for the Great Resolve. Furthermore, the Great Man relies upon spiritual friends who restrain him from what is harmful and establish him in what is beneficial; this is the fourth cause for the Great Resolve.
In this regard, the Great Man’s perfection of the necessary support is such that his aspiration is directed exclusively toward awakening.

He becomes inclined toward full enlightenment and leaning toward full enlightenment through his conduct for the welfare of beings, because he has previously made a resolution for full enlightenment in the presence of former Buddhas, both mentally and verbally, thinking:
"May I too, having become a perfectly enlightened Buddha such as this, properly bring about the welfare and happiness of beings. For one who has thus acquired the necessary supporting conditions...
These are the signs of the perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya*),
endowed with which a Great Man is distinguished from Disciple-Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddha-Bodhisattvas by a great distinction and a vast difference in terms of his faculties,
his practice, and his skillfulness. For here, a Great Man who is endowed with the decisive support possesses clear faculties and clear knowledge.
The others are not like him. He practices for the benefit of others, not for his own benefit.
For he practices for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans;
the others are not like him. And therein he brings forth skill through presence-of-mind and ready wit, and through proficiency in discerning what is possible and what is impossible.
Likewise, by nature the Great Man has a disposition toward giving and delights in generosity;
when there is something to be given, he gives indeed, and does not fall into hesitation regarding giving. He is constantly and continuously disposed to sharing;
he gives with joy and with reverence, not with an indifferent mind. Even after giving a great gift, he is not satisfied by that gift, much less so otherwise.

The signs of the Great Being’s perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), whose inclination is toward generosity, are as follows: he speaks in praise of giving while inspiring others; he delivers discourses on the Dhamma connected with giving;
he is delighted upon seeing others giving to others; and he grants fearlessness to others in situations of danger—and so forth. These are the characteristics of one whose heart is set on giving.
Likewise, he feels shame and dread of wrongdoing regarding evil states such as the destruction of life;

he is by nature non-violent toward living beings, gentle, of pleasant character, not fraudulent, not deceitful, upright by nature, and easy to speak to, being endowed with those qualities that make one easy to converse with;
he is mild-natured, not stubborn, and not conceited; and he does not take what belongs to others, even so much as a blade of grass or a stalk of straw.
Having received a debt placed in his own hand, he does not deceive another;
or when something belonging to himself has been lost or forgotten by another, he informs them of it and restores it so that it does not fall into the hands of others.
He is free from greed and does not give rise to even an evil thought regarding what is possessed by others. [He avoids] the ruin of women and other such vices.
He avoids [such a person] from afar; he is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, a reconciler of those who are divided, a promoter of harmony among those who are united,
one who speaks kindly, one who smiles first and speaks first, a speaker of what is beneficial, a speaker of the Dhamma, free from covetousness, with a mind devoid of ill will,
possessing unperverted vision through the knowledge that one's actions are one's own property, through knowledge in accordance with truth, grateful, thankful, and respectful toward the elders.
One whose livelihood is perfectly pure, who loves the Dhamma, who encourages others in the Dhamma,
who restrains beings from what is entirely improper and establishes them in their duties, and who himself applies himself to those duties—
or having personally done what should not be done, quickly desists from it— such are the qualities of a Great Man whose inclination is toward virtue.
These are the signs of the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*).
Likewise, he becomes one with dull defilements, dull hindrances, a disposition toward seclusion, and abundant non-distraction;
evil thoughts do not flow into his mind, and when he has attained seclusion, his mind enters concentration with ease.
Furthermore, he quickly establishes a mind of loving-kindness even toward those on the side of his enemies, let alone toward others;
he is mindful, being able to remember and recollect what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago; he is wise, endowed with the wisdom that has the Dhamma as its nourishment;
he is discerning regarding the various duties that ought to be performed; and he is energetic in acts of benefit for sentient beings.

One should understand that the marks of the Great Man’s perfections, such as the perfection of renunciation, are characterized by such qualities as: being endowed with the power of patience and thus overcoming all things;
having an unshakable resolve and being firm in his undertakings; and maintaining equanimity toward those phenomena that call for equanimity.
These and similar traits should be understood as the signs of the Great Man’s inclination toward renunciation and the rest.
Thus, for the Great Being who is endowed with these marks of the requisites for enlightenment, regarding that which was stated—
"reliance upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) is the cause for the Great Resolve"—

herein is the definition of a spiritual friend in brief: here, a spiritual friend is one who is perfected in faith, perfected in virtue, perfected in learning, and perfected in generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Therein, through the perfection of faith, he has faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment, in karma, and in the fruit of karma;
thus, he does not abandon his desire for the welfare of beings, which is the cause of perfect enlightenment.

Through the perfection of virtue, he becomes dear and pleasing to beings, respected and esteemed, one who reproves, censures evil, speaks with propriety, and is patient with what is said. Through the perfection of learning...
He is one who delivers profound discourses on the Dhamma that bring welfare and happiness to sentient beings.

Through the perfection of generosity, he is of few desires, concentrated, contented, secluded, and unattached. Through the perfection of energy, he is one who has aroused energy for the practice of what is beneficial to sentient beings.
Through the perfection of mindfulness, he is one whose mindfulness is established regarding blameless states.
Through the perfection of concentration, he is undistracted and possesses a concentrated mind. Through the perfection of wisdom, he understands things without error.

Seeking the courses of wholesome states by means of mindfulness, and having understood through wisdom the benefit and harm for beings as they truly are, he becomes one-pointed in mind toward that [benefit] by means of concentration;
then, having restrained beings from what is harmful by means of energy, he enjoins them to what is beneficial. Therefore it was said:
“Dear, venerable, and inspiring; one who speaks and is patient with what is said;

one who delivers profound discourse and does not urge one toward what is improper”—relying upon a spiritual friend endowed with such qualities, the Great Man [realized] his own excellence of supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*).
He purifies it correctly. Having become one whose intention and application are perfectly pure, and being endowed with the four powers,

he soon unites the eight factors and, making the Great Resolve, becomes established in the state of a Bodhisatta— one whose nature is irreversible, who is destined for enlightenment, and whose goal is supreme awakening.

In this regard, these are his four powers: first, the internal power, which is the delight based on self-reliance toward perfect enlightenment through reverence for the Dhamma and an exclusive inclination of the heart;

by means of this, the Great Being—relying on self-mastery and moral shame, and being endowed with the initial resolve—fulfills the perfections and attains perfect enlightenment. Second, the external power, which is [the reliance on] perfect enlightenment...

The power of decisive support (*upanissaya-bala*) is the inclination and one-pointedness of aspiration based on decisive support, by means of which the Great Being— possessing the support of moral dread (*ottappa*) and being endowed with the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*)—
fulfills the perfections (*pāramitā*) and attains perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
It is that inclination and one-pointedness of aspiration based on the perfection of decisive support for perfect enlightenment, by means of which the Great Being...
Having possessed sharp faculties, a clear constitution, reliance upon mindfulness, and being endowed with resolute determination, one fulfills the perfections and attains perfect enlightenment.

As for the power of application: it is that excellence of application appropriate for perfect enlightenment, characterized by conscientiousness and constancy, by means of which the Great Being becomes one of purified application, one who acts without interruption, and is endowed with resolute determination.
And having made offerings and fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he attains perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). Thus, this aspiration— endowed with four conditions,
four causes, and four powers, and accomplished through the convergence of eight factors—
is the condition for the perfections by virtue of being their fundamental cause.
Furthermore, through his activity, four wonderful and marvelous qualities become established in the Great Man:
he embraces the entire multitude of beings with a heart of love as if they were his own legitimate children; his mind is no longer defiled by the influence of further corruption;
his aspiration brings welfare and happiness to sentient beings; and he possesses the practical application [to fulfill that aspiration].
The qualities that constitute the factors for Buddhahood increase further and further and reach full maturity; thus, the Great Being,
endowed with an ever-increasing outflow of sublime merit, an outflow of the wholesome, and the condition for his progress—
the sustenance of happiness— becomes worthy of offerings from beings, the supreme object of veneration, and an incomparable field of merit.
Thus, the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra), possessing manifold qualities and manifold benefits, should be understood as a condition for the perfections (pāramīs).
And just as the Great Resolve is such, so too are Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) and Skill in Means (upāyakosalla).

In this context, "Skill in Means" refers to the wisdom that serves as the cause for the factors of giving and the rest becoming requisites for enlightenment; it is by means of these—Great Compassion and Skill in Means—that [the perfections are fulfilled].
For Great Beings (mahāpurisa), there arises an indifference toward their own happiness, a constant devotion to bringing about the happiness of others,

an absence of despondency regarding the extremely difficult deeds of a Mahābodhisattva, and the state of being a cause for sentient beings to obtain welfare and happiness even during the occasions of seeing,
hearing, or recollecting the increase of their serene confidence. For it is through his wisdom that the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished.
Through compassion, the work of a Buddha is accomplished. By means of wisdom one crosses over oneself; by means of compassion one causes others to cross over.
Through wisdom one fully understands the suffering of others; through compassion one undertakes the remedy for the suffering of others.

Through wisdom one becomes weary of suffering; through compassion one accepts suffering. Through wisdom one is oriented toward Nibbāna; through compassion one does not reach it [for the sake of others]. Likewise...
Through compassion he is oriented toward *saṃsāra*, but through wisdom he does not take delight therein. Through wisdom he is dispassionate toward everything;
yet because he is followed by compassion, his activity is not one that fails to assist all beings.

Through compassion he sympathizes with everyone, but because he is followed by wisdom, his mind is not one that lacks dispassion toward anything. Through wisdom there is an absence of the notions of "I" and "mine," and through compassion there is an absence of indolence and dejection.

Likewise, through wisdom and compassion, there arise respectively: being one's own protector and the protector of others; the state of being steadfast and heroic; not tormenting oneself nor tormenting others;
the accomplishment of one's own welfare and the welfare of others; being fearless and free from terror; being a master of the Dhamma and a master of the world;

gratitude and thankfulness; the removal of delusion and craving; the perfection of true knowledge and conduct; and the achievement of the powers and intrepidities—this constitutes the entire fruit of the perfections.

In particular, wisdom and compassion are conditions for the perfections (*pāramī*) by way of being their means. Moreover, these two are conditions not only for the perfections but also for the aspiration (*paṇidhāna*).
Likewise, it should be understood that effort, ingenuity, steadfastness, and conduct for the welfare of others are conditions for the perfections. And as for the state of Buddhahood...

Because they are the source of arising, they are called "the stages of a Buddha" (*buddhabhūmiyo*). In this context, "exertion" (*ussāho*) refers to the energy that strives toward the requisites for enlightenment.
"Ingenuity" (*ummango*) refers to the wisdom consisting of skillful means regarding those requisites for enlightenment.

"Steadfastness" (*avatthānaṃ*) refers to resolve, specifically the quality of unshakable resolve. "Conduct for the welfare [of others]" (*hitacariyā*) refers to the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*). As it has been said:
“But how many, Bhante, are the stages of a Buddha? “There are four stages of a Buddha, Sāriputta. Which four? There is exertion and energy;
there is penetration and the development of wisdom; there is steadfastness and resolution;
and there is beneficial conduct and the development of loving-kindness. These, Sāriputta, are the four stages of a Buddha.”
Likewise, there are six inclinations, distinguished as renunciation, seclusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, and escape. For this has been said:
"Bodhisattvas have an inclination toward renunciation and see the fault in sensual pleasures and in the household life;

Bodhisattvas have an inclination toward seclusion and see the fault in social company. [They have] an inclination toward non-greed... [and see the fault] in greed... [an inclination toward] non-hatred... [and see the fault] in hatred... [an inclination toward] non-delusion... and so forth.
“Non-delusion... [and so on] ... delusion... [and so on] ... the escape... [and so on] ... for those who see the defects in all states of existence.
Therefore, it should be understood that these six inclinations are also conditions for the perfections.

For indeed, without seeing the danger in greed and the rest, and without the predominance of non-greed and the rest, the perfections such as giving cannot come to be. This is because of the predominance of non-greed and the rest.

The state of a mind inclined toward renunciation and so forth, and the disposition of non-greed and so forth; and just as these exist, so too do the dispositions toward giving and the rest. As it is said:
"But, venerable sir, how many are the dispositions of Bodhisattvas practicing for enlightenment?
There are ten, Sāriputta, dispositions of Bodhisattvas practicing for enlightenment. Which ten? Dispositions toward giving, Sāriputta..."
Bodhisattas see stinginess as a fault. [They see] virtue... non-restraint... renunciation... sensual desires...
knowledge of things as they really are... doubt... energy... laziness... patience... impatience...
truthfulness... deception... determination... lack of determination... loving-kindness... ill-will... equanimity... as a fault.
“...seeing the danger in pleasure and pain. For, among these— namely, stinginess,
lack of restraint, sensual desire, doubt, laziness, impatience, deception, lack of resolve, ill will, and the perception of pleasure and pain— the inclination toward giving and so forth,
characterized by a mind leaning toward generosity and the rest, preceded by the vision of their dangers, constitutes the disposition toward the perfections of giving and the others.

It is a condition for rebirth. Likewise, among the virtues such as non-renunciation and renunciation, the contemplation of danger and benefit respectively is also a condition for the perfections of giving and so forth.

Herein, this is the method of contemplation: [for those whose minds are distracted by attachment to possessions] such as fields, lands, silver, gold, cattle, buffaloes, male and female slaves, sons, wives, and so on—
Because fields and the like are objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), they are highly sought after by living beings; because they are common property shared with kings, thieves, and others;

because they are the basis for disputes; because they cause enmity; because they are devoid of essence; because they serve as a cause for harming others during both their acquisition and preservation;

because they bring about various calamities such as sorrow when they perish; and because they are the source of attachment that leads to minds overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess (*macchariya-mala*).

Because they are the cause for rebirth in the states of misery—thus these objects of attachment are said to bring about various and vast misfortunes—and because their relinquishment alone is the one state of safety, one should practice diligence in relinquishing them.
Furthermore, [one should consider]: "A beggar who asks is trustworthy to me because he reveals his own secret," and "Having abandoned..."
He is my "instructor" because he points out: "Take what belongs to you and go to the next world";
he is my "companion who carries away" because, when the world is ablaze with the fire of death as if it were a burning house, he carries away from there whatever belongs to me;
he is the "place where that which has been carried away is deposited and burnt"; and [he is the field] consisting of giving...

One should reflect: "He is the supreme spiritual friend because he acts as a companion in wholesome deeds, and because he is the cause for attaining the state of Buddhahood—the most difficult to reach and the pinnacle of all perfections.
Likewise, one should reflect: "I have been esteemed by him for sublime tasks; therefore, that esteem must be made well-founded."
And: “Even if my life were to be cut short entirely, I would give even when asked, let alone when solicited”;
and: “Though sought by those with noble aspirations, it should be given; he has come of his own accord through my merit”; and:
“Under the pretext of giving to a petitioner, this is actually a favor to me”; and: “Just as I am, this entire world must be favored by me.”
"How can my perfection of generosity be fulfilled if there are no supplicants? "I must relinquish everything I possess for the sake of supplicants alone.
"When will supplicants take what belongs to me of their own accord, even without asking?
"How can I become dear and pleasing to supplicants? "Or how can they become dear and pleasing to me?"
"May it be pleasing," and "How might I be joyful, glad, and filled with rapture and happiness both while giving and after having given?
and "How might there be supplicants for me, and how might my inclination toward generosity be sublime?
and "How might I give to supplicants even without being asked, knowing their hearts by myself?"—when wealth exists and supplicants are present, not relinquishing [it] is a great failure.
One should establish an inclination toward generosity by thinking, "What deception is there for me? and "How could I fail to sacrifice my own limbs and even my very life?

Furthermore, one should arouse a mind characterized by disregard for material gain, thinking: "This so-called 'benefit' follows after the donor who gives without expectation, just as a chip of wood follows a thrower who casts it without regard.
Moreover, if the person making the request is a beloved individual...
If it is a dear person who asks, one should arouse joy, thinking, "He asks me.
If it is a neutral person, one should arouse joy, thinking, "Since he asks me, he will surely become a friend through this act of relinquishment;
for by giving to supplicants, one becomes dear to them. But if it is a hostile person who asks, [one should think], "An enemy asks me."
Thinking, “This person, by making this sacrifice while begging from me, will surely become dear even to an enemy,” one should especially arouse joy.
Thus, as with a beloved person, one should give only after establishing compassion preceded by loving-kindness (mettā) toward neutral and hostile persons as well.
But if, due to the long-standing cultivation of greed, thoughts of greed regarding objects to be given should arise in him, he who has made the vow of a Bodhisatta should reflect thus:
"O noble being, when you made the aspiration for supreme enlightenment, did you not relinquish this body for the benefit of all beings? And was it not born of that very sacrifice?"
This is merit; indeed, even regarding external objects, the occurrence of attachment for you would be like bathing an elephant.
Therefore, you should not give rise to attachment toward anything at all. It is just as when a great medicinal tree stands there, those who need its roots take the root;
those who need the bark, the rind, the trunk, the branches, the twigs, or the leaves, they take them.
When those seeking fruit take the flower or the fruit, that tree does not have the occurrence of a thought such as,
"They are taking what belongs to me. In the same way, while this body— which is for the benefit of the whole world, which is subject to great suffering, ungrateful, and eternally impure—
is being employed for the sake of helping others, even the slightest wrong thought [should not arise].
It should not be produced. What difference is there here between the internal and external great elements, all of which are by nature subject to breaking up, scattering, and destruction?
This insistence—“This is mine, this am I, this is my self”—is merely the manifestation of delusion;
therefore, [the same applies] to the internal great elements, such as the hands, feet, and eyes, just as it does to the external ones.
“Furthermore, one should be without regard for the flesh and other parts, and should possess a mind of relinquishment, thinking: ‘Let those who need them take them away.
For one who reflects in this way, who is intent upon enlightenment and indifferent toward body and life, the actions of body, speech, and mind become thoroughly purified without difficulty;
thus, with purified body, speech, and mind, he is one whose livelihood is pure.

Established in the practice of the method, through being endowed with skill in means regarding gain and loss, he is even more capable of assisting all beings by the relinquishment of things to be given, as well as by the gift of fearlessness and the gift of the true Dhamma;
this, first of all, is the method of reflection regarding the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Regarding the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramitā*), however, it should be reflected upon in this way: "This thing called virtue cannot be purified by the water of the Ganges or similar waters..."

It is the water for washing away the stain of hatred, which cannot be washed away by anything else; it is the remedy for the fever of passion and the like, which cannot be dispelled by yellow sandalwood and other such means;
it is the extraordinary ornament of the virtuous, distinct from the common ornaments of ordinary people such as pearl necklaces, crowns, and earrings;
and it is renowned in all directions, being beyond measure (or, because it flows in all directions, it is immeasurable).

It possesses a fragrant scent suitable for all times; it is the supreme incantation for subjugation, bringing about a state worthy of veneration by great wealthy kṣatriyas and others, as well as by deities;
it is a flight of stairs for ascending to the celestial realms of the Four Great Kings and beyond; it is the means for attaining the meditative absorptions (jhānas) and direct knowledges (abhiññās);

it is the path leading to the great city of Nibbāna; and [it is the cause] of the enlightenment of disciples (sāvakabodhi), the enlightenment of pacceka-buddhas, and the perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).
It is the ground of establishment; because it is the means for the accomplishment of whatever is desired or prayed for, it surpasses even the wish-fulfilling gem, the tree of plenty, and so forth.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.
Furthermore, it has been said: "Monks, if a monk should desire [for his companions in the holy life]..."
“May I be dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed,” [he thinks]; thus, he should fulfill his duties regarding virtue alone.

Likewise, the qualities of virtue should be reflected upon by means of such suttas as, “Virtuous conduct, Ānanda, has non-regret as its purpose,” and, “Householders, there are these five benefits for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue. Likewise, by means of the *Agniskandhopama-sutta* (The Fire-Mass Simile) and others.

Furthermore, by way of this [virtue], there are the dangers in the absence of moral conduct (*sīla*). Moreover, because it is the cause of rapture and joy; because it is free from the fear of self-reproach, reproach by others, punishment, and rebirth in miserable states;

because it is praised by the wise; because it is the cause of freedom from remorse; because it is the state of supreme security; and because it is the foundation for the prosperity of one's family, wealth, sovereignty, life, physical form, status, and the attainment of kinsmen and friends.
And virtue should be reviewed by way of its excellence. For one who possesses virtue, great joy and gladness arise because of his own perfection in virtue, thinking:
"Indeed, I have done what is wholesome; I have done what is beautiful; I have provided a refuge for those who are afraid.
Likewise, one who possesses virtue does not reproach himself, nor do wise others reproach him, and there is simply no possibility of punishment or fear of an unhappy rebirth.
Furthermore, a wise person praises one who is virtuous and of beautiful character, saying, "This person is virtuous and possesses a lovely nature.
Likewise, that remorse which arises in an immoral person—thinking, "Alas, I have done evil; I have done cruel deeds;

I have committed a foul act"—does not arise in one who is virtuous. Moreover, this virtue, by way of being grounded in heedfulness and through the prevention of the loss of wealth and other such misfortunes, [brings about great benefit].
Because it accomplishes great benefit and because it possesses the nature of a blessing, it is the supreme state of security.
Even one of low birth who is virtuous becomes worthy of honor by kshatriyas, great householders, and others; thus, the perfection of virtue surpasses the excellence of lineage.
This is also confirmed by the words of the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* which will be cited here: "What do you think, Great King, suppose you had here a slave or a laborer... and so forth.

Virtue surpasses external wealth and possessions because it is not shared with thieves and the like, because it follows one into the next world, because it yields great fruit, and because it is the foundation for qualities such as serenity (*samatha*).
Virtue surpasses the sovereignty of kshatriyas and others because it is the foundation for the supreme sovereignty of the mind;
for it is through virtue as the cause that beings attain sovereignty within their respective classes of sentient beings.
Virtue is more distinguished than life because it is said that even a single day of life for one possessing virtue is superior to a lifespan of long duration such as a hundred years;
and because it is said that even while living, the laying aside of the training is death.
Virtue brings pleasantness even to enemies and cannot be overcome by old age, disease, or misfortune; thus it is more distinguished than physical beauty.

Virtue excels [all else]. Because it is the basis for specific forms of happiness—ranging from palaces and pleasure-houses to the distinguished positions of kings, crown princes, and generals—virtue excels them all.

Even toward kinsmen who are naturally affectionate and live in one’s presence, and toward friends, virtue excels them because it brings about absolute welfare and follows one even into the next world. “Not that... [the verse continues:]
The statement beginning with "Mother and father might [protect]" is the proof for this point.

Likewise, compared to the fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, or even the employment of mantras, medicinal herbs, and charms, virtue alone is far more distinguished as a form of protection—because it is self-dependent, independent of others, and possesses a vast scope—even for those who are helpless and difficult to protect. Therefore it was said: "Dhamma indeed protects..."

“Walking in the Dhamma,” and so forth. Thus, for one who reflects upon virtue endowed with these many qualities, an incomplete perfection of virtue reaches completion, and that which is unpurified attains purity.
However, if through long-standing habituation, states opposed to virtue such as hatred and the like should arise from time to time, [one must apply the appropriate remedy].
That one who professes to be a bodhisattva should reflect thus: "Have you not made the vow for enlightenment?
For if even mundane success cannot be attained or easily achieved due to a deficiency in virtue, how much less so the supramundane?
By means of virtue—which is the foundation for right self-awakening and the foremost of all successes—one must reach the highest excellence.
Therefore, by guarding virtue perfectly according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "like a hen protecting her eggs," you must become truly well-behaved (*pesala*).
Furthermore, through your teaching of the Dhamma, you must bring beings into the three vehicles and bring them to maturity; for one who is deficient in virtue...
And his word is not to be accepted, just as the treatment of a physician who prescribes unsuitable food [is not accepted].

Therefore, thinking, "How may I become trustworthy so that I may perform the work of introducing and maturing sentient beings? one must possess a nature of moral virtue that is pure by its very essence.

Furthermore, through the possession of distinguished qualities such as the meditative absorptions (jhāna), one has the capacity to benefit sentient beings, as well as the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) and the others.
Since qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) do not arise without the purity of virtue (*sīla*), one must thoroughly purify virtue.
Likewise, one should reflect upon the household life through such passages as, "Household life is crowded and dusty," and so forth;

upon sensual pleasures through such passages as, "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton," and so forth; and upon [the faults of] mother and son disputing through such passages as, "Just as a man, having taken a loan, engages in his work... and so forth.
By means of the passage beginning with “one should apply oneself,” one should first see the danger in sensual desire and so forth;

then, by way of reflecting on the benefits of renunciation through the opposite of what was stated—such as “the life of renunciation is like the open air”—one should perform the reviewing of the perfection of renunciation.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood from such suttas as the *Dukkhakkhandha* and the *Āsivisa-upama*.
Likewise, one should attend to the virtues of wisdom, reflecting: "Without wisdom, the qualities such as giving are not purified, nor are they capable of performing their respective functions.
For just as the mere physical frame does not shine without life, nor is it capable of engaging in its own activities; and just as the faculties such as the eye [are useless without life].

Just as the sense faculties are unable to perform their respective functions toward their objects without consciousness, so too the faculties such as faith are incapable of accomplishing their own functions without wisdom;
thus, wisdom is the primary cause for the practice of relinquishment and the like.
For the Great Beings, the Bodhisattvas, who have opened the eye of wisdom, do not exalt themselves even when giving away their own limbs and members.
They do not disparage others; like medicinal trees, they are free from expectations and are filled with joy throughout the three periods of time.
For generosity, when conjoined with skillful means through the power of wisdom, attains the status of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) by way of promoting the welfare of others.
Indeed, generosity practiced for one's own sake is like a mere head (or like mere growth).
Likewise, in the absence of wisdom, because one cannot be separated from the defilements such as craving, even the purification of virtue itself is not possible;

how much less, then, can there be the state of being the foundation for the qualities of omniscience? Only one possessed of wisdom, clearly perceiving the danger in household life, in the strands of sensual pleasure, and in cyclic existence, as well as the benefit in renunciation, in meditative attainments, and in Nibbāna, would go forth into homelessness.
Having realized the meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*), one inclines toward Nibbāna and establishes others therein as well.
Energy devoid of wisdom does not accomplish the desired goal because it is difficult to undertake;
indeed, non-undertaking is better than a difficult undertaking. However, with energy accompanied by wisdom, nothing is difficult to achieve due to the employment of skillful means (*upāya*).
Likewise, it is only one possessed of wisdom who is by nature able to endure injuries and the like inflicted by others, not one lacking wisdom.
For one devoid of wisdom, the injuries brought upon him by others only serve to nourish the very opposite of patience.

But for one possessed of wisdom, those same injuries lead to the strengthening of his patience through their cultivation, thereby resulting in its firmness. It is only the wise person who [endures] even all three...
Having understood the truths, their causes, and their opposites as they truly are, he does not deceive others.

Likewise, having supported himself through the power of wisdom (*paññā*), he possesses an unwavering resolve and commitment to undertake all the perfections (*pāramīs*) by means of perfection in steadfastness (*dhiti*).
And being wise, he does not differentiate between those who are dear, neutral, or hostile, but is skilled in promoting the welfare of all.
Likewise, by way of wisdom, one remains neutral amidst the gathering of worldly conditions such as gain and loss through being free from agitation.
Thus, since wisdom alone is the cause for the complete purification of all the perfections, the qualities of wisdom should be reflected upon.
Furthermore, without wisdom there is no perfection of vision; and without the perfection of view, there is no perfection of virtue.
For one devoid of the perfection of virtue and right view, there is no perfection of concentration;
and for one who is not concentrated, it is impossible to accomplish even one's own welfare, let alone the supreme welfare of others.
"Indeed, by you who have set out for the welfare of others, a diligent application to the purification of wisdom must be made"—thus should the Bodhisatta admonish himself. By the power of wisdom...

For the Great Being, established in the four foundations and favoring the world through the four means of attraction (*saṅgahavatthu*), leads sentient beings onto the path of deliverance and brings their faculties to maturity.

Likewise, by the power of wisdom, being preoccupied with the investigation of the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth, he understands, as they truly are, both the process of existence and its cessation;
thus, he causes the specific virtues such as generosity to partake in the state conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
Having thus defined the manifold qualities of wisdom— such as "one who leads [others] becomes a fulfiller of the bodhisattva training"—
the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*) should be cultivated.
Likewise, even those worldly tasks that appear to have reached the further shore are impossible for one of inferior energy to achieve, but not for one who disregards weariness.
However, for one who has aroused energy, there is nothing that cannot be attained.

For one of inferior energy is not even able to begin with the thought, "I shall ferry all beings across the great flood of saṃsāra. One of middling energy, having begun, reaches a point of desistance midway.
But one of superior energy, having begun without regard for his own happiness, reaches the further shore; thus, the perfection of energy should be reflected upon.

Furthermore: "Even for one whose undertaking is solely for the sake of pulling themselves out from the mire of *saṃsāra*, it is impossible to expect that their aspirations will reach their ultimate fulfillment through a slackening of energy, let alone for one who has made the resolve to pull out the world together with its devas from the mass of defects such as lust, which are like intoxicated great elephants. And: "Of the host of faults such as lust..."
Because it is difficult to restrain; because the undertaking of kamma caused by it is like a murderer with a raised sword;
because the miserable destinies resulting from it always have their mouths wide open; because evil friends who incite one to it are always present;
and because, when the possibility of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) exists, there is the likelihood that one will act upon their advice.

One should reflect upon the virtues of energy in such ways as: "It is fitting for me myself to escape from the suffering of saṃsāra," "Wrong thoughts are driven far away by the power of energy," and "If enlightenment can be attained through energy that is under one's own control, what is difficult about this?
It is in this manner that the qualities of energy should be contemplated.
Likewise: "Patience is indeed the unimpeded weapon of the virtuous for the accomplishment of good qualities, owing to its dispelling of anger, which is the adversary of all virtues without exception;
it is the ornament of those capable of overcoming others; it is the perfection of strength for recluses and brahmins;
it is a stream of water for subduing the serpent of anger; it is the birthplace of the sound of one's own fair fame; [it is the destruction] of wicked persons..."
One should reflect: "It is the incantation that neutralizes the poison of speech; it is the supreme nature of the wise for those established in restraint;

it is an ocean by virtue of its profound depth; it is the shoreline for the great ocean of hatred; it is the closing door-leaf of the gates to the lower realms; it is the flight of stairs for ascending to the worlds of the devas and brahmās;
it is the dwelling place of all virtues; it is the highest purity of body, speech, and mind. Furthermore:
“‘These beings burn in this world because they lack the attainment of patience, and in the next world because they are devoted to things that lead to burning’;

and ‘Even though suffering arises caused by the harm done by others, it is my own personal existence that serves as the field for that suffering, and my own karma that serves as its seed, which was fully fashioned by me alone’; and ‘This is the way to bring about freedom from debt regarding that suffering.’”
And: "In the absence of one who does me harm, how could my perfection of patience arise? and:
"Even though this person is currently harmful to me, in the past he actually performed a service for me"; and: "Indeed, even harm is a service by virtue of being the occasion for patience";
and: "All these beings are like my own children; and who would be angry at the offenses committed by their own children?"
And: "By whatever possession of the spirit of anger this person wrongs me, that very possession of the spirit of anger must be subdued by me";
and: "Whatever harmful act caused this suffering to arise in me, I too am the cause of it"; and:
"All those phenomena by which the harm was done, and the place where it was done—all of them have ceased at that very moment; who is there now [to be harmed]?"
“By whom should anger be directed? and “Since all phenomena are non-self, who can offend whom?”—contemplating thus, he should cultivate the perfection of patience.
However, if through long-standing habituation anger toward the signs of others’ harm should persist, seizing hold of his mind, [he must apply the following].
He should reflect thus: "This patience is indeed the means of counteracting those who act with hostility toward others";
and "hostility, by producing suffering in me, is a condition for faith that has suffering as its proximate cause, and for the perception of non-delight in the entire world";
and "this is the natural disposition of the faculties, namely, the encounter with desirable and undesirable objects."
In this regard: "How could it be possible for me not to encounter undesirable objects?
and "A being under the sway of anger is maddened and distracted by it; what is the use of retaliating against that?
and "All these beings are protected by the Perfectly Enlightened One like his own biological sons; therefore, I must not give way to anger toward them."
And: "Even when there is an offense, I must not become angry toward one who possesses virtue";
and "When virtue is absent, because of the total lack of any quality, he should be treated with special compassion"; and "Through anger, my own virtues and fame are diminished";
and "By becoming angry, undesirable consequences such as ugliness and painful sleep come upon me, which are pleasing to my enemies"; and "Anger..."
And [he thought]: "This powerful adversary indeed brings about all suffering and harm, and destroys all happiness and welfare";

and "when there is patience, there is no adversary whatsoever"; and "whatever suffering an offender might receive in the future on account of his offense, in my case that would be absent if there were patience"; and "by one who reflects, by one who is angry..."

And [it was said]: "I have indeed followed after my very enemy"; and "When anger has been overcome by patience, my enemy, who was like a slave to it, has been properly overcome"; and "It is not fitting for me to abandon the quality of patience on account of anger";
and "If anger—a state opposed to and contrary to virtuous qualities—exists, how can my qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth [endure]?"
“If these [perfections] were not fulfilled, how could I, being of great benefit to beings, attain the supreme success in accordance with my promise?

And: “When there is patience, because there is no external distraction, for one who is concentrated, all conditioned phenomena are seen as impermanent and suffering, all phenomena as non-self, and Nibbāna as unconditioned, deathless, sublime, and so forth.”
They endure contemplation, thinking: "The qualities of a Buddha have an inconceivable and immeasurable origin. Furthermore, established in this conformable patience, they think:
"All these things are devoid of self or anything belonging to a self; they are mere phenomena that arise and perish according to their respective conditions;
they do not come from anywhere, they do not go anywhere, and they are not established anywhere."

"Furthermore, when one reflects that 'herein there is no agency of anyone toward anything,' and thus finds satisfaction in the contemplation of non-adherence to the notions of 'I' and 'mine'—by which the Bodhisatta becomes fixed for enlightenment and subject to non-retrogression"—it is in this way that the reflection on the perfection of patience (*khantipāramī*) is to be understood. Likewise, [one reflects]:

"Since virtue (*sīla*) and the other perfections are impossible without truth (*sacca*); since there is an absence of practice in accordance with one's promise; and because of the transgression of the true Dhamma..."
And because it is the point of convergence for all unwholesome states; because one who is untrue to his word is unreliable;
because it brings about the state of having speech that is not to be accepted in the future; because truthfulness is the foundation for all virtues;
because through the resolve of truth, all the requisites for full enlightenment are accompanied by purity and fulfillment; and because of non-deception regarding the nature of phenomena.

The perfections of the perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramī*) should be reflected upon in such ways as: "Because it performs the function of providing all the requisites for enlightenment, and because it brings to full completion the practice of a bodhisattva.
Likewise: "Firm undertaking in giving and the other perfections, and an unshakable resolve even when encountering their opposites..."

In that regard, one should reflect upon the qualities of the foundation (adhiṭṭhāna-guṇa) by such means as: "Without the state of being firm and heroic, the accumulations of giving and so forth cannot arise as causes for full enlightenment.
Likewise: "Even for one who abides merely for their own benefit, it is not possible to attain the prosperities of this world and the next without a mind of benevolence toward sentient beings."
“...how much more so for one who wishes to establish all beings in the attainment of Nibbāna”;
and “For one who desires the supramundane success of all beings in the future, it is now appropriate to desire mundane success”;
and “At present, being unable to provide for the welfare and happiness of others through mere intention alone, when will I [be able to do so] through actual application?”
"I shall accomplish [this]," and "Now, having been raised by me through the provision of welfare and happiness, they will later become my companions in the sharing of the Dhamma," and "Without these,
the requisites for enlightenment do not arise for me; therefore, because they are the cause for the production of the manifestation of all the qualities of a Buddha,
they are for me the supreme field of merit, the unsurpassed sphere of the wholesome, and the highest object of veneration."
And furthermore, "an inclination toward the welfare of all beings, without exception, should be established;
moreover, through the foundation of compassion, loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be cultivated toward all beings.

For when one delights in bestowing benefit and happiness upon beings with a mind made boundless, a powerful and firmly rooted desire arises to remove their harm and suffering; and [this] is compassion for all."

The qualities of loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be reflected upon in such ways as: "It is the beginning, the feet, the foundation, the root, the mouth, and the foremost of the qualities that make one a Buddha.
Likewise: "In the absence of equanimity (*upekkhā*), the various provocations caused by beings would produce agitation in the mind;
and if there is agitation of the mind, there can be no arising of the requisites for giving and the other perfections. And: "When [the heart] is moistened by the moisture of loving-kindness..."

“Without equanimity in the mind, there is no complete purity of the requisites,” and “One who lacks equanimity toward mental formations is unable to dedicate the accumulation of merit and its result for the welfare of beings,” and “In the absence of equanimity,
one is unable to relinquish things to be given without making distinctions between recipients,” and “By one devoid of equanimity...”
Furthermore, it is said: "Without disregarding obstacles to life, it is not possible to purify one's virtue.
Likewise: "Because the power of renunciation is established precisely through the endurance of both aversion and delight by means of equanimity;

because all the functions of the requisites are accomplished precisely through the act of looking on with equanimity; and because for one whose energy is overly exerted, the failure to look on with equanimity results in the non-performance of the function of striving."
Because equanimity alone gives rise to patience and the jhānas; because through equanimity one does not deceive the world of beings and their formations;
because by maintaining equanimity toward the worldly conditions (lokadhammā), one achieves an unshakable resolve regarding the qualities undertaken;

and because through the very absence of effort toward the injuries of others and so forth, one accomplishes the dwelling in loving-kindness—thus [equanimity] brings about the undertaking, the resolution, the fulfillment, and the accomplishment of all the requisites for full enlightenment.
The perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) should be reflected upon in such a manner as: “They succeed through the power of equanimity,” and so forth.

Thus, it should be understood that the reflection on the disadvantages and advantages, respectively, regarding non-renunciation and renunciation, serves as the condition for the perfections of giving (dāna) and the others.
Likewise, there are the fifteen factors of conduct (*caraṇadhamma*) together with their requisites, and the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Among these, the "factors of conduct" consist of:

restraint by virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven true qualities (*saddhamma*), and the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
Within those, the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) are included among the four beginning with virtue, as are fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so forth.
And the requisites: through faith in the true Dhamma, there are the recollections of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, the devas, and peace;
avoiding persons who are harsh, associating with persons who are gentle, reflecting on the states that inspire confidence, and being intent upon them—these are the requisites.
For shame and fear of wrongdoing, there is the reflection on the danger in unwholesome states and the reflection on the danger in the states of deprivation.
Reflecting on the state of being a pillar for wholesome states; avoiding persons devoid of moral shame and dread of blame; associating with persons endowed with moral shame and dread of blame;
being intent upon those [wholesome states]; prior application to great learning; being an inquirer; devotion to the true Dhamma; familiarity with blameless branches of knowledge and so forth;
ripeness of the faculties; remoteness from the defilements; avoiding persons of little learning; and associating with persons of great learning.

And being intent upon that. For energy: reflecting on the fear of the states of misery, reflecting on the path of progress, reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma, dispelling sloth and torpor, avoiding persons who are indolent, associating with persons who have aroused energy, reflecting on the right exertions, and being intent upon that.
For mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons who are forgetful, and associating with persons whose mindfulness is established.

And being intent upon that. [The factors for wisdom are: the state of being an inquirer regarding wisdom, making the basis pure, bringing about the evenness of the faculties, avoiding persons of poor wisdom, associating with persons possessed of wisdom, reflecting on discourses concerning the practice of profound knowledge, reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma, and being intent upon that.
[Furthermore,] there is the fourfold set beginning with virtue for the four jhānas.
The preliminary development regarding the thirty-eight objects and the mastery of the processes such as adverting are the requisites.

In this regard, the way in which the factors of conduct and so forth serve as conditions for the equipment of giving and the rest should be determined accordingly: for instance, through purity of practice by means of virtue and so on, one becomes capable of granting the gift of fearlessness to beings; through purity of disposition, the gift of material things; and through purity of both, the gift of the Dhamma.
However, for fear of excessive prolixity, we have not elaborated further. Likewise, the wheel of prosperity and so forth should also be understood as conditions for giving and the other perfections.
Regarding the question "What is defilement?"—here:
The state of being defiled by craving and the other [defilements] is their corruption;
this applies both generally and specifically, according to what is appropriate, through various conceptualizations.

For, in a general sense, the state of being defiled by craving and the others is the corruption of the perfections (*pāramī*). Specifically, however, there are conceptualizations regarding the object to be given and the recipient.

The conceptualization of defilement regarding the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). The conceptualizations of the seven time-periods regarding the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*). The conceptualizations of delight and non-delight in sensual pleasures, existence, and their pacification regarding the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramitā*).
The conceptualizations of "I" and "mine" regarding the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramitā*). The conceptualizations of lethargy and agitation regarding the perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramitā*).

The conceptualizations of self and other regarding the perfection of patience (*khantipāramitā*). The conceptualizations of "view" and so forth regarding what is not seen and so forth regarding the perfection of truth (*saccapāramitā*). [These occur] with respect to the requisites for enlightenment and their opposites.
Conceptualizing faults and virtues is the defilement of the perfection of resolve. Conceptualizing the beneficial and the harmful is the defilement of the perfection of loving-kindness.
Conceptualizing the agreeable and the disagreeable is the defilement of the perfection of equanimity; this is how it should be understood.
What is its purification?
One should understand that "purity" (*vodāna*) consists in being unharmed by craving and the rest, and in being free from conceptual constructions (*vikappa*); this applies to all of them alike.
For [purity] is indeed the state of being unassailed by craving, conceit, views, anger, hostility, denigration, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, and guile.

The perfections of giving and the rest become completely pure and radiant when they are free from the defilements such as rigidity, violence, intoxication, and negligence, as well as from conceptualizations regarding the giver,
the recipient, and the gift. What is the antidote?
The unwholesome states and the defilements are their opposites when considered without distinction;
however, when distinguished, stinginess and so forth were mentioned previously as well.
For, without distinction, all unwholesome phenomena and all defilements are the opposites of these [three roots]. Specifically:
However, it should be understood that the types of stinginess and so forth mentioned previously are also included.

Furthermore, because it is endowed with the qualities of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion regarding the object to be given, the recipient, and the fruit of giving, generosity (*dāna*) is the opposite of greed, hatred, and delusion. Because it is free from the three crookednesses of body and so forth, virtue (*sīla*) is the opposite of greed and the rest.
Because it avoids sensual pleasure, harming others, and self-mortification, renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is the opposite of the three types of hatred. [This applies to] greed and the rest...
Wisdom is the antidote to greed and the rest because it causes blindness [to the truth] to be removed and knowledge not to become blind;

energy is the antidote to greed and the rest by way of undertaking the method that is neither sluggish nor agitated; patience is the antidote to greed and the rest because of its endurance of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and emptiness;
and truth is the antidote to greed and the rest because it proceeds according to reality even when there is benefit or harm from others.

It should be understood that resolution is the antidote to greed and so forth because it remains unshakable regarding the requisites undertaken as they were vowed, having overcome the worldly conditions;

loving-kindness is the antidote to greed and so forth because it is secluded from the hindrances; and equanimity is the antidote to greed and so forth because it destroys attraction and aversion toward the desirable and the undesirable, and because it proceeds with evenness.
What is practice?
It should be understood that the very modes of giving and so forth, when generated in manifold ways,
constitute practice in the sequence of fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs).

Regarding the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the practice consists of manifold ways of assisting sentient beings: by relinquishing material requisites, body, and life; by removing fear; and by providing instruction in the Dhamma.

In this context, giving is threefold according to the objects to be given: the gift of material things (*āmisa-dāna*), the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*), and the gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāna*).
Among these, the object to be given by the Bodhisattva is his own internal self.
The external is twofold. Therein, the external consists of ten kinds: food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lighting.
Furthermore, it is manifold through the various divisions of food and so forth, such as hard food (*khādanīya*) and soft food (*bhojanīya*).

Likewise, from the perspective of its object, it is sixfold, ranging from the visible-form object (*rūpārammaṇa*) up to the mental-phenomena object (*dhammārammaṇa*). And of these, the visible-form objects and so forth—

It is of many kinds through the division of blue and so forth. Likewise, it is of many kinds by way of various objects and requisites, such as gems, gold, silver, pearls, coral, and so on; fields, lands, and groves; and female and male slaves, cattle, buffaloes, and the like.
In that regard, when the Great Man gives an external object, he gives whatever one needs to that very person. While giving...
Knowing for himself, “And he has need of it,” he gives even when unasked, let alone when asked.
He gives with a mind free from stinginess, not with a mind not free from stinginess. He gives what is sufficient, not what is insufficient.

When there is a gift to be given, he does not give out of dependence on a reciprocal favor; when there is no gift to be given, or when it is sufficient, he shares it with those worthy of sharing. And he does not give that which would bring harm to others.
He does not give intoxicants such as liquor and spirits, nor anything that is for mere play, nor anything that is unbeneficial and conducive to negligence;
nor does he give to a sick person food or drink that is unsuitable, or in excessive measure. Rather, he gives only what is suitable and in the proper measure.
Likewise, when requested, he gives householders what is appropriate for householders, and those who have gone forth what is appropriate for those who have gone forth.
He gives. He gives without causing affliction to anyone among his mother and father, kinsmen and blood relations, friends and colleagues, children, wife, slaves, or laborers;
he does not promise a magnificent gift and then give something coarse; he does not give while relying on gain, honor, or fame;
he does not give while relying on a return favor; and he does not give while longing for a fruit other than perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
Nor does he give when asked, nor does he give while loathing the object to be given; nor does he give a discarded gift even to uncontrolled beggars who revile and abuse him.
On the contrary, with a confident mind and feeling compassion, he gives with due care.
He does not give being superstitious about omens and auspicious signs, but rather gives having faith in the fruit of kamma. Nor does he give by means of attending upon beggars and so forth.
He gives after having become defiled, yet he gives while remaining undefiled;
he does not give with the intention of deceiving others or with the intention of causing division, but gives with an undefiled mind.

He does not give with harsh speech or a frowning face, but gives being pleasant-spoken, the first to speak, and with a smiling countenance. And regarding the gift-object, because of its excellence and agreeableness...
Whether due to long-standing habituation or because of a greedy nature, greed may become predominant;
yet the Bodhisatta, recognizing this, quickly dispels it and gives even after seeking out supplicants.
And when the object to be given is meager while the supplicant stands before him, he does not hesitate, but even by running to fetch himself what is needed, he honors the supplicant.
Just as the wise Akitti did not, when requested, give his own children, wife, servants, laborers, or dependents to those beggars while they were unacquainted with him,
dejected, or filled with grief; rather, he gave them only when they were properly acquainted with him and filled with joy—
and even then, knowing whether the recipients were yakkhas, rakkhasas, pisācas, and so forth, or humans of cruel deeds.

He does not give; likewise, he does not grant even a kingdom to those who act for the world’s harm, suffering, and misfortune, but he does grant the gift of a kingdom to those who are righteous and protect the world according to the Dhamma.
Thus, first of all, should the practice regarding external giving be understood.

Internal giving should also be understood in two ways. How so? Just as a certain person, for the sake of food and clothing, surrenders himself to another and enters into a state of servitude, becoming subject to their will;

even so, the Great Being, for the sake of enlightenment, with a mind free from worldly attachment and desiring the unsurpassed welfare and happiness of sentient beings, [offers] his own perfection of generosity.
Desiring to fulfill [the perfection], he surrenders himself to another; he enters into a state of being subject to their will, such that they may do with him as they please.
