He unhesitatingly and without shrinking bestows his hands, feet, eyes, and other limbs and members upon those who require them.
He does not cling to them, nor does he experience any contraction of mind, just as he would toward external objects. For such is the Great Being.
One renounces external objects in two ways: either for the recipients to enjoy as they please, fulfilling their desires, or for the sake of one’s own mastery over them.

In this regard, one who is completely liberated in giving says, "By means of this state of non-attachment, I shall attain full enlightenment"; this should be understood to apply to internal objects as well.
In that regard, he gives whatever internal object, when given to a supplicant, leads exclusively to their welfare, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, the Great Man does not give his own person or his limbs and members to Māra or to deities belonging to Māra’s host who intend him harm, even while knowing this, thinking, "May no harm come to them. Just as...
Nor does he give to those possessed by the hosts of Māra; likewise, he does not give even to those who are possessed by them, nor to the insane.
However, when requested by others, he gives immediately upon being asked, because such a request is rare and because giving in such a manner is difficult to perform.

The gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), however, should be given by way of protection when beings are confronted with danger from kings, thieves, fire, water, hostile persons, or wild animals such as lions and tigers, as well as from *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *rakkhasas*, and *pisācas*.
The gift of the Dhamma (*dhammadāna*), moreover, is the teaching of the Dhamma without distortion by one whose mind is undefiled;

for his instruction is skillful, pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*), by which means those who have not yet entered the Dispensation are made to enter it, and those who have already entered it are brought to maturity.

[This is] the ripening [of beings]. Herein, this is the method: briefly, first, there is talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven, the danger, corruption, and degradation of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation.

In detail, however, for those whose minds are inclined toward the enlightenment of a disciple (śrāvaka-bodhi), there is going for refuge, restraint in virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and devotion to wakefulness.
The seven true qualities (*saddhamma*); the application of serenity (*samatha*) by way of performing the function [of meditation] upon the thirty-eight objects;

the application of insight (*vipassanā*) by way of appropriate application to the points of entry for insight such as the door of form (*rūpamukha*); likewise, the grasping of correctness through the path of purification (*visuddhipaṭipadā*);
the three knowledges (*vijjā*); the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*); the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*); and the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*)—of these...
It is the establishment [of beings] in various states as appropriate through the proclamation of virtues, and their purification. Likewise,
for those whose minds are inclined toward *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) and *sammāsambodhi* (perfect universal enlightenment),

it is the manifestation of the great majesty of those Buddhas across the three distinct stages by means of proclaiming the essential nature, intrinsic flavor, and characteristics of the perfections such as giving (*dāna*), as appropriate.
Establishing [beings] in the two vehicles and purifying them—thus does the Great Man give the gift of the Dhamma to sentient beings.

Likewise, when the Great Man gives a material gift, he gives food with the thought: "By this gift may I bring about for sentient beings the excellence of longevity, beauty, happiness, strength, eloquence, and so forth, as well as the delightful excellence of the supreme fruit. In the same way, he gives for the sake of allaying the thirst of sensual defilements in sentient beings.
He gives drink for the sake of attaining a golden complexion; he gives garments for the sake of producing the ornaments of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*);
he gives vehicles for the sake of producing the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) as well as the bliss of *nibbāna*;

he gives perfumes for the sake of producing the fragrance of virtue (*sīla*); he gives garlands and ointments for the sake of producing the splendor of the Buddha-qualities; and [he gives] seats for the sake of producing the seat at the terrace of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
He gives a seat; he gives a bed for the purpose of producing the Tathāgata’s posture; he gives a dwelling for the purpose of producing a refuge;
he gives lighting for the sake of obtaining the five eyes.
He gives a gift of forms for the purpose of producing the fathom-wide radiance; he gives a gift of sounds for the purpose of producing the Brahmā-voice; [he gives for] the sake of the entire world...

One gives the gift of flavors for the sake of being beloved; one gives the gift of tactile objects for the sake of the Buddha’s delicate state; one gives the gift of medicine for the sake of the state of being free from aging and death;

one gives the gift of freedom to slaves for the purpose of liberating them from the servitude of the defilements; one gives the gift of blameless play and delight as a cause for delighting in the True Dhamma;
and [one gives] for the purpose of bringing all beings into the state of being one's own children through noble birth.

He gives away his children; he gives away his wife so that she may become the counterpart for the entire world; he gives away gold, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth for the sake of attaining the perfection of auspicious marks (*lakkhaṇa*);

he gives away various kinds of ornaments for the sake of attaining the perfection of secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*); he gives away his treasury of wealth for the sake of acquiring the treasury of the True Dharma (*saddhamma*);

he gives away his kingdom for the sake of becoming a King of Dharma (*dhammarāja*); and he gives away monasteries, parks, forests, and so forth for the sake of attaining the perfections of giving and the other virtues.
The gift of feet for approaching the seat of enlightenment with feet marked by wheels;

the gift of hands for the purpose of giving the hand of the True Dhamma to beings so they may cross over the four floods; the gift of ears, nose, and so forth for the attainment of the faculty of faith and the rest;
the gift of eyes for the attainment of the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*); and [the gift of] "at all times in seeing, hearing, recollecting, serving, and so forth..."
“May my body bring welfare and happiness to all beings and be a source of sustenance for the entire world”—thus he gives the gift of flesh, blood, and so forth.
“May I become the supreme one in the entire world”—thus he gives the gift of his most excellent limbs.
And giving in this way, he does not give through improper means, nor by harming others, nor out of fear, nor out of shame, nor out of anger toward those worthy of offerings.

When there is something excellent, he does not give what is coarse; he does not give out of self-exaltation, nor out of disparaging others, nor with a longing for the fruit [of the gift], nor with loathing for the beggar, nor with a lack of respect;

rather, he gives attentively, he gives with his own hand, he gives at the right time, he gives with honor, he gives without partiality, and he gives with a joyful mind in the three times—precisely because of that.
Having given, he does not feel regret afterwards; he does not act with pride or contempt toward the recipients;

he behaves kindly toward the recipients, being generous, devoted to giving, and a donor who provides for their needs. For when giving a gift of food, thinking, "I shall give this along with its accessories," he gives it together with clothing and other items;
likewise, when giving a gift of clothing, [he gives it] "along with its accessories."
Thinking, “I will give it after making [these preparations],” he gives it together with food and other requisites. This same method applies to the giving of drinks and so forth;
likewise, when giving a gift of form (*rūpadāna*), he gives it while making other objects of sense pleasure its accompaniment, and the same holds true for the remaining gifts.
In this context, a “gift of form” refers to any one among the colors such as blue, yellow, red, or white, found in flowers, garments, or precious gems.
Having obtained a form and having directed the mind toward it, one thinks, "I shall give a gift of form;
this gift of form is mine," and establishes the gift upon such a worthy recipient (dakkhiṇeyya); this is called a gift of form.
Furthermore, a gift of sound should be understood by way of the sound of drums and so forth. In that regard, one does not uproot the sound like a bulbous root.
Just as one cannot give by placing a blue lotus in the hand [if it has no base], so too,
one who gives while providing a physical basis is said to give a gift of sound. Therefore, when one intends,

"I shall give a gift of sound," and makes an offering to the Three Jewels with any musical instrument such as a kettledrum or a drum, or causes one to be made, thinking, "I shall give a gift of sound"—
When one has drums and other such instruments set up with the thought, "This is my gift of sound," or when one gives medicinal tonics for the voice,
oil, molasses, and so forth to those who preach the Dhamma; when one proclaims the hearing of the Dhamma, recites the *sara-bhañña*, delivers a discourse on the Dhamma,
or engages in informal conversation and expressions of appreciation— and likewise causes these things to be done— then that is called the "gift of sound."
Likewise, having obtained any fragrant substance among the root-fragrances and so forth that is pleasing, or even the scent of raw meat itself, and having relished it by way of its fragrance,
one performs and causes to be performed an offering to the Buddha-jewel and the others, thinking, "I shall give a gift of fragrance;
this gift of fragrance is mine," using fragrant substances such as agallochum and sandalwood for the purpose of fragrant worship.
He relinquishes this; this is the gift of fragrance.

Likewise, having obtained any kind of delightful substance for taste, such as roots, juices, and so forth, and having inclined toward it by way of its flavor, he gives it to those worthy of offerings, thinking, "I shall give a gift of flavor;
this gift of flavor is mine," or else [he gives] another substance for taste.
Giving away cows and so forth is the gift of flavor (*rasadāna*).
Likewise, the gift of the tangible (*phoṭṭhabbadāna*) should be understood by way of beds, chairs, and the like, as well as by way of coverlets, blankets, and so forth.
For when one gives beds, chairs, couches, pillows, and the like, or garments for wearing and wrapping that are pleasant to the touch and delightful—

Having obtained a blameless tactile object and having directed the mind toward it by way of that tactile object, one gives it to those worthy of offerings, thinking, "I shall give a gift of touch; this gift of touch is mine.
Having obtained the aforementioned tactile object, one relinquishes it; this is the gift of touch.

As for the gift of the Dhamma (*dhammadāna*), since it is intended here as having the Dhamma as its object, it should be understood by way of nutritive essence (*ojā*), drink (*pāna*), and life-force (*jīvita*).

For, having obtained some delightful basis of the Dhamma among these—namely, nutritive essence and so forth—and having directed the mind toward it as an object of the Dhamma, one gives a gift of nutritive essence such as ghee or fresh butter, thinking, "I shall give a gift of the Dhamma; this is my gift of the Dhamma," or [one gives] the eightfold drink such as mango juice and so on.
He gives the gift of drink; having resolved upon the "gift of life," he gives tickets for meals, fortnightly meals, and so forth.
For those afflicted by disease and overcome by discomfort, he summons a physician, causes nets to be torn down, causes fish-traps to be destroyed, and causes bird-cages to be demolished;
he effects the release from bonds for beings who have been bound in captivity.
He causes the "Māghāta-bherī" (the drum of non-execution) to be sounded, and performs or causes others to perform other such deeds for the purpose of protecting the lives of sentient beings;
this is called the gift of Dhamma.
All of this, along with the aforementioned perfection of giving, he dedicates for the welfare and happiness of the entire world and for his own unshakable [nibbāna].
He dedicates it toward the imperishability of liberation, the imperishability of desire, the imperishability of energy,
the imperishability of concentration, the imperishability of inspired eloquence, the imperishability of meditative absorption, and the imperishability of perfect enlightenment;
and by the Great Being practicing this perfection of giving, the perception of impermanence regarding life must be established.
Likewise, one should keep in mind that these enjoyments are shared by many, and one should constantly and continuously maintain great compassion toward sentient beings.
For in this way, taking what is essential from enjoyments—
just as one who carries out all one's property and oneself from a burning house leaves nothing behind and retains nothing anywhere— one does not cling to anything.
He makes a division; rather, being entirely without expectation, he simply relinquishes it. This, first of all, is the method of practice for the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

As for the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*), this is the method of practice: since a Great Being who desires to adorn sentient beings with the ornaments of the virtues of the Omniscient One must first purify his own virtue, therein virtue [should be understood] in four ways.
It is purified by way of purity of intention, by way of undertaking, by way of non-transgression, and by way of making it manifest again should there be a transgression.

For, due to the state of having a pure intention, a certain person—acting as his own master and being by nature loathing evil—establishes the quality of moral shame within himself and becomes one of perfectly pure conduct; likewise, when there is an undertaking from another.
A certain person, having become a leader of the world, fearing evil and establishing the quality of moral dread (*ottappa*), becomes one whose conduct is perfectly pure;
thus, in both ways, they are established in virtue (*sīla*) by way of non-transgression. Nevertheless, there may at times be a breach or other defect in virtue due to a lapse of mindfulness;
however, this occurs only through such a failure of the aforementioned perfection of moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread.
They restore it immediately through such means as rising [from a lapse] and so forth.

This virtue (sīla) is twofold: that consisting of abstention (vāritta) and that consisting of conduct (cāritta). Regarding these, this is the method of practice for the Bodhisatta in the virtue of abstention:
he must possess a mind so imbued with compassion toward all beings that not even in a dream does he harbor ill will.
If such a thought should arise, because he has abstained from using the belongings of others, he must not touch them, for they are like a venomous snake.
If he is a renunciant, he lives far removed even from unchastity, abstaining from the seven forms of sexual union, let alone from adultery.
Even when he is a householder, he never gives rise to an evil thought toward the wives of others.
He speaks at the proper time, discourse on the Dhamma that is true, beneficial, pleasant, and measured.
He is everywhere free from covetousness, of a mind without ill will, possessing unperverted vision, and endowed with the knowledge that one’s own actions are one’s own property.
He places his faith and affection in those who are harmonious and practicing rightly.
Thus, for the Great Being who has desisted from the unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome states— which are the paths to the suffering of the cycle of the four miserable destinies—
and who is established in the wholesome courses of action and wholesome states which are the paths to heaven and liberation,
there arises, through his pure intention and application, that which is associated with the welfare and happiness of beings according to their aspirations.
His aspirations are fulfilled very quickly, and he brings the perfections (pāramīs) to completion; for such is this person.

In that regard, by abstaining from harming, he gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings, accomplishes the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) with ease, and attains the eleven benefits of loving-kindness; he is free from illness and affliction, and possesses a long life.
Abounding in happiness, one attains specific marks and eradicates the latent tendency toward hatred.
Likewise, by refraining from taking what is not given, one acquires wealth that is not shared with thieves and the like; one becomes unsuspected by others, dear, pleasing, and trustworthy;
one’s mind does not cling to the perfections of existence, one is disposed toward renunciation, and one eradicates the latent tendency toward greed. By refraining from unchastity...
He becomes free from greed, with a peaceful body and mind; he is dear and pleasing to beings, beyond suspicion;
a fine reputation for him spreads abroad; his mind is unattached to women and his disposition is not covetous;
he abounds in renunciation, attains distinguished marks, and eradicates the latent tendency of greed.
By abstaining from false speech, one becomes an authority for beings, trustworthy, reliable, and one whose words are accepted;

one is dear and pleasing even to the deities, possesses a mouth with fragrant breath, and—having body and speech conduct protected from unwholesome states—attains distinguished marks and eradicates the latent tendencies of the defilements.
By abstaining from malicious speech, one’s body remains unbreakable by the attacks of others.
He comes to have an inseparable retinue; he possesses unshakable faith in the true Dhamma;
he becomes a firm friend, beloved even by beings known from previous lives; and he is largely free from defilement.
By refraining from harsh speech, he becomes dear and pleasing to beings, virtuous in character, sweet-spoken, and worthy of esteem; and his voice arises endowed with the eight qualities.
By abstaining from idle chatter, one becomes dear and pleasing to beings, worthy of respect and honor, one whose words are accepted,
moderate in speech, influential, and possessed of great power. One is skilled in answering questions through spontaneous eloquence,
and on the level of a Buddha, one is capable of answering the many questions of beings who speak many languages with a single utterance.
Through freedom from covetousness, one acquires things without difficulty, gains a taste for sublime wealth,
becomes esteemed by wealthy kṣatriyas and others, cannot be overcome by adversaries, does not suffer from deficiencies of the sense faculties,
and becomes a person beyond compare. Through non-ill will, one becomes pleasant to behold and respected by beings, owing to one’s delight in the welfare of others.
He gladdens beings with ease, possesses a nature free from harshness, and dwells in loving-kindness; he becomes one of great influence and great power.
By virtue of being free from wrong views, he obtains virtuous companions; even when facing execution, he does not commit an evil deed.
Because he perceives that one is the owner of one’s own karma, he is not a superstitious seeker of omens, and he abides in the True Dhamma.
His faith is firmly established and rooted; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgatas and does not delight in other systems, just as a royal swan does not delight in a dung heap.
He is skilled in discerning the three characteristics, and at the end, he attains unobstructed knowledge.
Until he reaches enlightenment, throughout his various existences among the classes of beings, [he remains steadfast].
One becomes increasingly superior and attains sublime and magnificent successes.
Thus, having generated great reverence for this thing called virtue— thinking, "Virtue is indeed the foundation of all success, the source-ground of all the qualities of a Buddha,
the beginning, the footstep, the cause, the entrance, and the foremost of all the factors that make a Buddha"— [one should practice it].

In the restraint of body and speech, in the taming of the sense faculties, in the purity of livelihood, and in the use of the requisites, he is heedful by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Having perceived gain, honor, and fame as an enemy with a raised sword, he should carefully fulfill virtue according to the method stated in the passage beginning, "Like a hen guarding her eggs.
This, first of all, is the procedure for the practice regarding the virtue of abstention.
Regarding the virtue of conduct, the practice should be understood as follows:
here, the Bodhisatta from time to time performs salutation, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful service toward his spiritual friends and those worthy of honor;
likewise, he from time to time attends upon them, and provides physical assistance and verbal inquiry for those who are ill.
He is one who offers praise upon hearing well-spoken words; he is one who extols the virtues of those possessing virtue; he is one who is patient toward the harm of others;
he is one who remembers the benefits received from others; he is one who rejoices in the merits of others; he is one who dedicates his own merits toward supreme perfect enlightenment;
he is one who dwells at all times in heedfulness regarding wholesome states; and having seen a transgression as a transgression, he acknowledges it.
He reveals as they truly are such fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, and he perfectly fulfills the higher practice of right conduct himself.
Likewise, being diligent and intent upon what ought to be done for the welfare of beings, he enters into a state of companionship with those suitable to him.
And when illnesses or other sufferings arise among beings, he provides the appropriate remedies.
He dispels the sorrow of those fallen into calamities such as loss of kinsmen or wealth;

established in a nature that rescues others, he restrains by means of the Dhamma alone those who deserve restraint, solely for the purpose of raising them up from unwholesome states and establishing them in the wholesome;
and he encourages by means of the Dhamma alone those who deserve encouragement. These were the most sublime and supremely difficult deeds performed by the previous Great Bodhisattvas.
The conduct of beings possesses inconceivable power and brings about their absolute welfare and happiness;
having heard of those deeds by which their accumulations for enlightenment reached complete maturity, one should be neither agitated nor terrified, thinking:
"Those Great Beings were also merely human beings, but through the gradual fulfillment of training and the cultivation of their selves, they attained such supreme excellence of power."
They had reached the highest perfection in the requisites for enlightenment; therefore,

thinking, "I too must practice correctly in the trainings of virtue and so forth, by which practice I too shall gradually fulfill the training and ultimately attain that state," he does not relinquish the energy preceded by faith and becomes one who perfectly fulfills the precepts.
Likewise, he is one who conceals his virtues and reveals his faults; he has few desires and is contented, secluded, unassociated, and patient with suffering;
he is possessed of a non-perverted view, is not restless, not haughty, not fickle, not talkative, and does not speak in a scattered manner;
he has restrained sense-faculties, a peaceful mind, is free from wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and the like, and is perfected in conduct and resort, even regarding the slightest matters.
Seeing danger in the things to be avoided, he trains himself by undertaking the precepts of training; with energy aroused and resolute, he is indifferent toward body and life.
He does not tolerate, abandons, and dispels even a slight regard for body or life, let alone an excessive one.
[He likewise abandons] all defilements and secondary corruptions, such as anger and resentment, which serve as causes for immorality.

He abandons and dispels [these thoughts]; being dissatisfied with a mere slight attainment of distinction, he does not fall into despondency, but strives for the successive attainment of further distinctions.
In such a way that the prosperity he has obtained does not become partaking of decline or merely partaking of stability, so does the Great Man...
He acts as a guide for the blind, pointing out the path; he provides signs by means of hand gestures for the deaf and explains their meaning;
and likewise for the mute. He gives a chair to those who are cripples, or carries them.
He exerts himself so that those lacking faith may acquire it, so that the lazy may generate enthusiasm, and so that those with muddled mindfulness may attain mindfulness.
He strives for the attainment of concentration for those who have become distracted; he strives for the acquisition of wisdom for those lacking wisdom.

He strives for the removal of sensual desire in those obsessed by sensual desire; he strives for the removal of doubt in those obsessed by ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt.
He strives for the removal of wrong thoughts—such as thoughts of sensual desire—in those who are dominated by such thoughts of sensual desire and the like.
He exerts himself. Relying on gratitude toward beings who have done him a favor, he is one who speaks first, speaks kindly, and is inclusive;
he honors them with a reciprocal service that is either equal or superior.
He performs the duty of a companion in times of misfortune, and having thoroughly understood the natural disposition and essential character of various beings...
He associates with those with whom he ought to associate in whatever manner is appropriate, and he behaves toward those toward whom he ought to behave in whatever manner is appropriate.
Moreover, this is done by causing them to emerge from unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome ones, and not otherwise;
for the protection of the minds of others by Bodhisattvas serves solely for the increase of what is wholesome. Thus...

Even with a well-intentioned motive, one should not act rashly toward another, nor revile them, nor cause them embarrassment, nor arouse remorse in them, nor accuse them of a fault when they are not blameworthy;
one should not place oneself on a higher level than one who has entered upon a lower practice;
and one should neither associate with others to the exclusion of all else, nor associate excessively.
One should not be one who associates at the wrong time.

However, when beings are fit [for association], one associates with them in accordance with the place and time; one does not criticize those who are dear in the presence of others, nor praise those who are disliked;
one does not act with misplaced confidence, and one does not refuse a righteous invitation.
He does not conform to worldly designations, nor does he accept anything in excess. He encourages those endowed with faith by discourse on the benefits of faith;
he encourages those endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom by discourse on the benefits of wisdom.

Furthermore, if the Bodhisatta has attained the power of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he uses that power of the higher knowledges to lead beings who have fallen into negligence back to their respective states, such as the hells and so forth.
By bestowing [these gifts], he inspires those lacking faith and others with a sense of spiritual urgency, establishes them in faith and the other virtues, causes them to enter the Teaching,

and brings to maturity those already endowed with the qualities of faith and the rest. Thus, it should be understood that for this Great Being, the immeasurable flood of merit and flood of skillfulness,
which constitutes his conduct, increases further and further.
Furthermore, that detailed exposition of virtue (sīla) in its various aspects—which was set forth in the *Visuddhimagga* after posing the questions, "What is virtue? and "In what sense is it virtue?

and answering, "The states such as volition (cetanā) of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or who fulfills the practice of duties, are virtue"—all of that should be brought here and explained. For only...
In that context, the discourse on virtue was presented from the perspective of the disciple-bodhisattvas;
here, however, it must be explained from the perspective of the great bodhisattvas, preceded by compassion and skillful means—this alone is the distinction.

Therefore, this virtue is not for the sake of liberation from the defilements of one's own miserable rebirths, nor even for the attainment of sovereignty in a happy realm, nor for being a wheel-turning monarch, nor a deva, nor Sakka.

He does not dedicate it to the attainment of Māra or Brahmā; likewise, he does not dedicate it to his own possession of the three knowledges (*tevijjā*), nor to the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), nor to the attainment of the four analytical insights (*catupaṭisambhidā*), nor to the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*), nor to the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha.
Rather, he dedicates it solely for the sake of establishing all beings in the supreme ornament of virtue through the state of omniscience (*sabbaññubhāva*).
This is the method of practice for the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī).
Likewise, because the arising of wholesome states of consciousness— which is accompanied by compassion and skillful means, preceded by the vision of the danger [in sense pleasures],

and proceeds by way of renunciation from both sensual desires and existence— is the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī), therefore, due to its being the locus for the dwelling of all defilements, [the following applies]:
Because of the great confinement caused by children, wife, and so forth, and because of the agitation caused by being occupied with various occupations such as agriculture and trade,

the household life offers no room for the happiness of renunciation and the like; and because sensual pleasures— like a drop of honey on the edge of a sword-blade, or like a plantain tree— are followed by vast misfortune while their gratification is unattainable and meager, [he saw this] by means of the flash of lightning.
Like a dance, it is to be grasped only for a brief moment; like the adornment of a madman, it is to be experienced through perverted perception;
like a face covered with excrement, it serves as a mere disguise; like drinking water infused with *nisā* grass from a finger dipped in water, it fails to satisfy;
like food eaten by one who is already full, it is attended by affliction; and like bait on a hook, it is a cause for falling into calamity.

(As stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* 1.7: "The cause for the convergence of calamities"): Like the heat of a fire, they are the cause for the arising of suffering throughout the three periods of time;
like monkey-glue, they are the cause for bondage; like a nest of mosquitoes concealing a killer, they conceal harm;
like living in a village of enemies, they are a place of fear; and like one who nourishes an adversary, they serve as the bait for the defilements, Māra, and so forth.

Having observed the danger [of sense pleasures] by way of such methods as: "They are subject to the suffering of change like festival splendors; they burn from within like a fire in the hollow of a tree;

they possess many disadvantages like honeycombs on the grass hanging over an old well; they are causes of thirst like drinking salt water; they are resorted to by base people like liquor and spirits; and they are like a skeleton because of their meager gratification," and by way of their opposites—
Seeing the benefits of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), with a mind inclined, leaning, and bent toward the bliss of renunciation, seclusion, and peace, one should practice the perfection of renunciation.
Since renunciation is rooted in going forth (*pabbajjā*), one must first undertake going forth. By one who undertakes going forth...
When no Buddha has appeared, a Great Being who maintains the doctrine of karma and the efficacy of action should undertake the going-forth among ascetics and wanderers.
However, when Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas have appeared, he should go forth specifically within their dispensation.
Having gone forth and being established in the aforementioned virtue, he should undertake the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇas) for the sake of purifying that very perfection of virtue.

For Great Beings who have undertaken the ascetic practices (*dhuta-dhamma*) and maintain them correctly, their defilements and impurities are washed away by the waters of such virtues as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, non-attachment, the arousal of energy, and easy maintenance.
Thus, with conduct purified by blameless virtues of morality and observance, they are established in the first three of the ancient Noble Lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*).

To proceed toward the fourth Noble Lineage, known as "delight in meditation" (*bhāvanārāmatā*), they [apply themselves] to the forty meditation subjects according to what is appropriate for each, through the distinctions of access and absorption concentration.
They enter and dwell in jhāna. In this way, his perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) is truly fulfilled.

At this point, however, there are forty subjects for the development of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā-kammaṭṭhāna*): the ten kasiṇas, the ten foulness meditations (*asubha*), the ten recollections (*anussati*), the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), the four formless attainments (*āruppa*), one perception (*saññā*), and one analysis (*vavatthāna*), together with the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhuta-dhamma*).

The methods for the development [of these qualities] should be explained in detail; however, since all of this has been set forth in every aspect and in full detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, it should be understood according to the method stated there.
For while that was taught with reference to the disciple-bodhisatta, here it must be explained with reference to the great bodhisatta, preceded by compassion and skillful means.
This alone is the distinction. In this way, the sequence of practice for the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī) is to be understood here.

Likewise, by one who desires to fulfill the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), since wisdom—like light—cannot coexist with the darkness of delusion (moha), the Bodhisatta must first avoid the causes of delusion. Among these, the causes of delusion are as follows: discontent (arati).
Laziness, yawning, indolence, delighting in social crowds, a habit of sleepiness, a habit of indecisiveness,
lack of interest in knowledge, false conceit, failure to inquire, lack of proper care for the body, an unconcentrated mind,
associating with persons of poor wisdom, not honoring those possessed of wisdom, self-deprecation, and wrong conceptualization.

Perverse adherence, physical rigidity, lack of a sense of urgency, and the five hindrances—in brief, when one indulges in such secondary mental states (*yevāpanaka-dhamma*), wisdom that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen declines. These are the causes of delusion;
therefore, while avoiding them, one should apply oneself to great learning and to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth.
In this regard, the following is the classification of the domain of great learning (bāhusacca): the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā), the twelve bases (dvādasāyatanāni),
the eighteen elements (aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo), the four truths (cattāri saccāni), the twenty-two faculties (dvāvīsati indriyāni), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in its twelvefold form,

as well as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānādayo) and the various classifications of wholesome and other phenomena (kusalādi-dhamma-pabhedā), those branches of knowledge (vijjāṭṭhānāni) which are blameless in the world, and that which pertains to beings...
The method for providing welfare and happiness is a specific form of exposition.

Thus, having thoroughly penetrated the entire range of the Sutta in this manner—by means of wisdom preceded by skill in means, mindfulness, and energy, through diligent grasping, hearing, retention, mastery, and interrogation—and having established others therein, one should develop the wisdom consisting in what has been heard (*sutamaya-paññā*); likewise, regarding the duties that must be performed for sentient beings.
Wisdom that is situational and inspired, as well as wisdom consisting in skill regarding the means for welfare and adversity,

should be exercised appropriately in various instances by relying on the desire for the good; likewise, wisdom born of reflection (cintāmaya-paññā) should be developed by means of examining the modes of the constituent phenomena (khandha) and other things that possess intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma),
both through the process of scrutinizing their forms and by seeking to gain patient acceptance through contemplation.

Furthermore, by means of comprehending both the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates and so forth, one must accomplish the wisdom of the preliminary stage of development (*pubbhāga-bhāvanā-paññā*) which produces mundane full understanding (*lokiya-pariññā*).

For in this way, one realizes: "This is merely name-and-form; it arises and ceases according to its respective conditions. Herein there is no agent or instigator, in the sense of being non-existent after having been."
“Impermanent; suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away;

non-self in the sense of being devoid of mastery”—thus, thoroughly understanding internal and external phenomena without distinction, abandoning attachment to them, and causing others to abandon that attachment as well, he proceeds solely through the power of compassion until the qualities of a Buddha come within the palm of his hand.

Thus, establishing beings in the three vehicles through their introduction and maturation, and attaining mastery over the mundane states of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, attainments, and direct knowledges (abhiññā), he reaches the pinnacle of wisdom.

In this regard, there are these [knowledges]: the knowledge of the various modes of psychic power, the knowledge of the divine ear-element, the knowledge of the penetration of others' minds, and the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

The knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their karma, and the knowledge of future states—these, together with their respective adjuncts, are the five mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) consisting of wisdom born of meditation (*bhāvanā-paññā*).

Furthermore, there is the wisdom consisting of the cultivation of knowledge through study and inquiry regarding the phenomena belonging to the four planes, categorized as aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, and so forth;
this includes both purification of virtue (*sīla-visuddhi*) and purification of mind (*citta-visuddhi*).

Having established oneself upon these two purifications which serve as the foundation, one should develop the wisdom of cultivation—which is divided into mundane and supramundane types—by accomplishing these five purifications that constitute its body: purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision. Of these...

Regarding the method of accomplishment: because it is stated there [in the *Visuddhimagga*], "In that regard, by a beginner yogin who desires to perform a transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbana*) such as 'having been one, he becomes many,'" and so forth;
and because it is stated, "The aggregates (*khandhā*) are the five aggregates:

the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness," and so forth, according to the distinction between object and subject (or the distinction of objects).
—The Conduct (cariyā). (Eight. [This] has been explained in detail in all its aspects in the *Visuddhimagga* within the miscellaneous discussion (*pakiṇṇakakathā*);
therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated there.

For while wisdom (*paññā*) is presented there from the perspective of a disciple-awakening being (*sāvakabodhisatta*), here it must be explained from the perspective of a Great Awakening Being (*mahābodhisatta*), preceded by compassion (*karuṇā*) and skillful means (*upāyakosalla*).

The specific distinction here is that, without yet reaching the purification of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*), insight (*vipassanā*) must be established within the purification of knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) alone.
In this manner, the sequence of practice for the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*) is to be understood.
Likewise, because a Great Being who has made the aspiration for perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*) must at all times— [...for the sake of fulfilling the perfections... (text truncated)

One must be appropriately engaged and ready for action; therefore, from time to time, one should reflect day by day, thinking, "What store of merit or store of knowledge have I accumulated today? Or what benefit for others have I performed?
Thus, for the sake of the welfare of beings, one should exert effort for the assistance of all sentient beings.
One should relinquish with a mind free from attachment one's possessions, one's body, and even one's life;
whatever action one performs by way of body or speech, all that should be done with a mind inclined toward full enlightenment alone,
dedicated to enlightenment, and with a mind turned away from both sublime and inferior sensual pleasures.
One must be so; and in all matters of duty, one should proceed by establishing skill in means (*upāyakosalla*).
In each instance of benefiting beings, one must be diligent in energy, enduring all things—whether desirable or undesirable—and free from deceit.
All beings, without exception, should be suffused with loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*). Whatever arising of suffering there may be for beings, [one should respond accordingly].
All that should be expected of oneself. One should rejoice in the merit of all sentient beings;

the greatness and great majesty of the Buddhas should be frequently reflected upon; and whatever action one performs, whether by body or speech, all of it should be preceded by the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
For by this means, for one who is diligently engaged in generosity and the other perfections, [the goal is attained].
For the Great Being, the Bodhisatta, who possesses steadfastness and firm exertion,
his immeasurable accumulation of merit and accumulation of knowledge increase day by day.
Moreover, having sacrificed his own body and life for the sake of the enjoyment and protection of sentient beings—
One must seek and produce the remedy for the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, sun, and so forth;
and one likewise personally obtains the happiness born from such remedies for those aforementioned sufferings,

as well as the happiness one personally obtains by being thoroughly calmed through the absence of physical and mental distress in delightful parks, gardens, palaces, ponds, and the like, as well as in forest retreats.
And whatever he hears— that "Buddhas, Buddhas who followed after [the first], and Paccekabuddhas, as well as Mahābodhisattvas,
abide in the practice of renunciation," and that "they experience such bliss of meditative attainment (jhānasamāpatti), which constitutes a happy dwelling in this very life"—
he applies all of that to all beings without exception. This, first of all, is the method for one established on the plane of non-concentration.
But when established in the plane of concentration (samāhitabhūmi), one who resolves upon and directs toward all beings the rapture,
tranquility, bliss, concentration, and knowledge of things as they truly are— which have arisen from the attainment of distinction experienced by oneself—
likewise [directs them] toward the great suffering of saṃsāra and toward the suffering of defilements and volitional formations that are its cause.
Having seen the multitude of beings submerged therein, one sees them in hell experiencing for a long time, without interruption, intense, harsh,
and bitter feelings of suffering produced by devouring, cutting, splitting, crushing, piercing, harming, and the heat of fire; and among the animals,
they experience great suffering through mutual anger, terror, slaughter, injury, and subjection to others.
When the bodies of hungry ghosts (*petas*)—whose forms are wreathed in flames—are being scorched by hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and so forth;
when their food, such as vomit and spittle, is drying up; when they cry out with arms raised, experiencing the great suffering of parching thirst and the like;
and when they encounter great ruin and disaster rooted in their constant searching, through the infliction of hand-cutting and other punishments, and by becoming ugly, unsightly, and destitute.
Because they are to be overcome by the powerful due to the affliction of hunger, thirst, and other ailments; because they carry others;

and because they are dependent on others—in hell, among the hungry ghosts (petas), and among animals—beings experience suffering that is indistinguishable from the extreme misery of the states of woe (apāya).

Likewise, among humans, whose minds are distracted by the enjoyment of sense objects and who are being consumed by the fever of lust and other passions, it is like a heap of dry wood where a mass of flames has arisen through the force of the wind.

Just as birds that have plunged far into the sky with great effort, or as arrows shot from a powerful hand to a distance, [they do not remain] even though they have persisted for a long time, because of their non-eternality—[this applies] to the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) who live with unappeased fever like a mass of fire, and who are unappeased, ruined, and dependent on others. (cf. *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* 1.7: *anihataparādhīne*)
"Ending in a fall and never transcending birth, aging, and death"— seeing even the gods of the fine-material and immaterial realms in this way,
one should arouse a profound sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and pervade all beings without exception with loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā).
Thus, by continuously accumulating the requisites for enlightenment through body, speech, and mind, [one fulfills] the perfections (pāramī) as follows:
In this way, one who acts with diligence, acts with persistence, and conducts oneself without despondency should exert effort;
thus the perfection of energy (vīriya-pāramī) is to be fulfilled.

Furthermore, [this is for the sake of] that which is the source of the accumulation of a multitude of qualities that are inconceivable, immeasurable, vast, sublime, stainless, incomparable, and free from defilement.
The energy that strives for and is capable of attaining the state of Buddhahood is indeed of inconceivable power,
which ordinary people cannot even hear of, let alone practice. For instance, there is the threefold arising of the mind of resolution (*abhinīhāra-cittuppatti*),

the four stages of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*), the single flavor of compassion (*karuṇaikarasatā*), and the realization of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadhamma*).
The specific conditions are: reflective acceptance after contemplation; being unstained by any phenomena; regarding all beings as one’s own beloved child;
lack of weariness with the sufferings of saṃsāra; relinquishing all things worthy of giving; and being free from pride because of that;

the undertaking of the higher training in virtue and so forth; being unwavering therein; joy and gladness in wholesome activities; a mind inclined toward seclusion; and devotion to meditative absorption (jhāna).
Insatiability regarding blameless qualities; firmness of undertaking in teaching the Dhamma as it has been heard with the intention of benefiting others;
the state of being steadfast and heroic; the absence of perturbation in the face of slander or harm from others; resolve upon truth; mastery over the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
the attainment of power in the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*); the realization of the three characteristics; and [mastery] in the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
The accumulation of the requisites for the supramundane path through diligent application, the entry into the nine supramundane stages, and so forth—
all such practice for the equipment of enlightenment is accomplished solely by the power of energy. Therefore, from the initial resolution until the attainment of Great Enlightenment,
one who does not relinquish it should apply energy with care and continuity, so that it may bring about ever-increasing excellence.

It must be accomplished. And when the aforementioned energy is accomplished, all the requisites for enlightenment—such as patience, truthfulness, and resolve, as well as generosity, virtue, and so forth—become perfected precisely because they are dependent upon it.
Thus, the practice regarding patience and the other [perfections] should be understood by this same method.
Thus, practice through giving consists in providing manifold assistance by relinquishing the requisites for the happiness of beings;
through virtue, it consists in protecting their lives, property, and spouses, as well as speaking words that are endearing and beneficial and practicing non-violence;

through renunciation, it consists in various kinds of conduct for their welfare, such as accepting material gifts and giving the Dhamma; and through wisdom, it consists in skill in the means for accomplishing their welfare.
Through energy, there is enthusiasm, undertaking, and steadfastness in that regard; through patience, the endurance of their offenses;

through truthfulness, non-deception, the undertaking of beneficial actions for them, and freedom from falsehood; through determination, remaining unshakable even when obstacles to those beneficial means arise;
through loving-kindness, the constant reflection on their welfare and happiness; and through equanimity, the absence of mental perturbation whether they provide help or cause harm.

Thus, it should be understood that "practice" here refers to the immeasurable accumulation of the equipment of merit and knowledge belonging to the Bodhisatta— who has compassion for all beings and is thus distinct from ordinary persons— with respect to immeasurable sentient beings;
and it also refers to the diligent accomplishment therein of whatever conditions for these have been mentioned.
What is the classification?
By way of their general division, these are tenfold;
when each is further divided into three, they are equally thirtyfold.
There are thirty perfections (pāramīs): namely, the ten perfections, the ten secondary perfections (upapāramīs), and the ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramīs).

In this context, for a Bodhisatta who has made the resolution and whose application is directed toward accomplishing the welfare of others, the bright qualities (sukka-dhammā) interspersed with dark qualities (kaṇha-dhammā) are the perfections;
those bright qualities not interspersed with them are the secondary perfections; and those qualities that are neither dark nor bright are the ultimate perfections.
Some say: "The *pāramīs* being fulfilled during the periods of their attainment are the *pāramīs*; those perfected on the level of a bodhisatta are the *upapāramīs*;
and those completely fulfilled in every aspect on the level of a Buddha are the *paramattha-pāramīs*.

Alternatively, on the level of a bodhisatta, they are called *pāramīs* because of accomplishing the welfare of others, *upapāramīs* because of accomplishing one's own welfare, and on the level of a Buddha, [they are so called] through the attainment of the powers and intrepidities."

"Others say: 'The classification of these [perfections] is according to their aspiration, undertaking, and completion—at the beginning, middle, and end—as the supreme perfections that fulfill the welfare of both [self and others].

"Still others say: 'Their classification is according to the different ways of accumulating merit by those whose nature is the pacification of hatred and compassion, and who have attained the bliss of existence, the bliss of liberation, and the supreme bliss.'"

"Some say: 'The aforementioned classification [of the requisites] is due to the attainment of the three types of enlightenment through the pāramīs, upapāramīs, and paramattha-pāramīs of those who have shame, mindfulness, and modesty as their refuge;

who take supramundane states as their sovereign; who revere virtue, concentration, and wisdom; and who are themselves crossed over, have caused others to cross over, and are crossing over others—namely, the Anubuddha-Paccekabuddhas and Sammāsambuddhas.
"Furthermore, the requisites that function from the mental aspiration up until the verbal aspiration..."
Others say: "The *pāramīs* are those that proceed from the aspiration of speech down to the aspiration of body; those that proceed from the aspiration of body onwards are the *upapāramīs*;

and those that proceed from the point of performing them oneself are the *paramatthapāramīs*. Still others, however, say: "The requisites (*sambhāra*) that proceed by way of rejoicing in the merit of others are the *pāramīs*;
those that proceed by way of causing others to perform [meritorious deeds] are the *upapāramīs*; and those that proceed by way of performing them oneself..."
They say, "The ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramiyo). Likewise, some say: "The equipment of merit and knowledge that brings about one's own happiness in existence is a *pāramī*;
that which brings about one's own happiness of *nibbāna* is an *upapāramī*; and that which brings about both kinds of happiness for others is an *paramattha-pāramī*.

Furthermore, the relinquishing of requisites such as children, wife, and wealth is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*); the relinquishing of one's own limbs is the near-perfection of giving (*dāna-upapāramī*).
The perfection of giving in its ultimate sense is the relinquishing of one’s own life.

Likewise, there are three perfections of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*) by way of not transgressing for the sake of the three types of things, beginning with children and wife; and there are three perfections of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) by way of departing after cutting off attachment to those same three types of objects;
and [there are three perfections of wisdom] by way of uprooting craving for requisites, limbs, and life for the sake of sentient beings...
There are three perfections of wisdom by way of making the determination of what is beneficial and what is harmful;

three perfections of energy by way of striving in the relinquishment and so forth of the types already mentioned; three perfections of patience by way of enduring those things that create obstacles to requisites, limbs, and life;
and three perfections of truth by way of not abandoning truth for the sake of requisites, limbs, or life.

The perfections of giving and the rest are accomplished only by way of an unshakable resolve; thus, there are three perfections of resolve by way of an unswerving resolve even when one's requisites and so forth are destroyed.
There are three perfections of loving-kindness by way of not abandoning loving-kindness toward beings who cause the destruction of one's requisites and so forth.
And [there are three perfections of equanimity] by way of attaining a state of neutrality toward beings and conditioned phenomena who perform benefit or harm toward the three aforementioned bases.
The classification of these should be understood through such passages as "the three perfections of equanimity" (*upekkhāpāramī*). As for their grouping:
"Just as they are thirtyfold by way of classification, they are tenfold by way of grouping."
In these [perfections], one should establish them through the sixfold aspects by means of the pairs and so forth.

For just as this [perfection] is thirtyfold when divided, it is tenfold by way of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*) and the others; likewise, it is sixfold by way of the nature of giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), patience (*khanti*), energy (*vīriya*), meditation (*jhāna*), and wisdom (*paññā*).

Among these, the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) is included within the perfection of virtue, because its state is that of going forth (*pabbajjā*), and because its state is seclusion from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-viveka*).

Furthermore, the perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramī*), being a wholesome state (*kusaladhamma*), is included within all six perfections; it constitutes a portion of the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*) on the side of verbal truth and the truth of abstinence.
On the side of the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*), however, it is included within the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*).

The perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) is included within the perfection of meditation (*jhāna-pāramī*) alone. The perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) is included within both the perfections of meditation and wisdom. The perfection of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*)...
"All are included by all" means that among these six qualities—generosity and the rest—which are mutually connected, there are fifteen pairs and so forth that accomplish fifteen pairs and so forth.
For example: through the pair of generosity and virtue, there is the accomplishment of the pair of performing what is beneficial for others and refraining from what is harmful.

Through the pair of generosity and patience, there is the accomplishment of the pair of non-greed and non-hatred; through the pair of generosity and energy, there is the accomplishment of the pair of relinquishment and wisdom;

through the pair of generosity and jhāna, there is the accomplishment of the pair of abandoning sensual desire and hatred; through the pair of generosity and wisdom, there is the accomplishment of the pair of the burdens of the Noble Vehicle;

through the pair of virtue and patience, there is the accomplishment of the pair of purity in practice and purity in intention; and through the pair of virtue and energy, there is the accomplishment of the two kinds of development.

By means of the pair consisting of virtue and jhāna, there is the accomplishment of the twofold abandonment of the obsession of immorality; by means of the pair consisting of virtue and wisdom, there is the accomplishment of the twofold giving;

by means of the pair consisting of patience and energy, there is the accomplishment of the twofold splendor of forbearance; by means of the dyad of patience and jhāna, there is the accomplishment of the dyad of abandoning opposition and compliance;

by means of the dyad of patience and wisdom, there is the accomplishment of the dyad of penetration into emptiness and patience; and by means of the dyad of energy and jhāna, there is the accomplishment of the dyad of exertion and non-distraction.
The accomplishment of the two pairs of refuges is through the dyad of energy and wisdom; the accomplishment of the two pairs of vehicles is through the dyad of meditation and wisdom.

The accomplishment of the triad of abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and patience; the accomplishment of the triad of acquiring wealth, life, and the essence of the body is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and energy;

the accomplishment of the triad of bases for meritorious action is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and meditation; and the accomplishment of the triad of giving material goods, fearlessness, and the Dhamma is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and wisdom.
In this same way, the triads and tetrad-groups, etc., should be combined with the other triads and tetrad-groups as far as possible.
Furthermore, the inclusion of these sixfold perfections (pāramīs) should be understood by means of the four foundations (adhiṭṭhānas).
For, from the perspective of grouping all the perfections together, there are four foundations. Namely: the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna),...
The foundation of relinquishment, the foundation of peace, and the foundation of wisdom.
In this context, it is called a "foundation" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) because one stands firm by means of it, or one stands firm in it, or simply because it is a foundation itself.

It is a "truth-foundation" (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) because it is both truth and a foundation, or because it is the foundation for truth, or because truth is its foundation. The same applies to the remaining [foundations].
Therein, without distinction, for the Great Being who has made his resolution and has compassion for all beings:

there is the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) from embracing all the perfections in accordance with his promise; the foundation of relinquishment (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*) from abandoning their opposites;

the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) from the pacification through the qualities of all the perfections; and the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*) from skill in means regarding the welfare of others by means of those very same qualities.
In particular, however, it is distinguished by: making a promise to people who come as supplicants with the thought, "I shall give without deceiving them";
giving without contradicting that promise; expressing appreciation without failing to acknowledge the gift; renouncing the opposites such as stinginess;
and pacifying greed, hatred, delusion, and fear regarding the recipient, the giver, the act of giving, and the depletion of the object to be given—each according to its appropriate case.
Generosity is the foundation for the four foundations of virtue through giving at the proper time and according to the prescribed method, and through being preceded by wisdom among wholesome states.

Likewise, virtue is the foundation for the four foundations of virtue through the non-transgression of undertaken restraints, the relinquishing of misconduct, the pacification of evil conduct, and being preceded by wisdom.
Patience is the foundation for the four foundations of virtue through enduring according to one's promise and through the relinquishing of resentment toward committed offenses.
Patience has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it pacifies the obsession of anger and because it culminates in wisdom.

Energy has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it accomplishes the welfare of others in accordance with one’s promise, because it relinquishes sense objects, because it pacifies unwholesome states, and because it culminates in wisdom.

Mindfulness has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it contemplates the welfare of the world in accordance with one’s promise, because it relinquishes the hindrances, and because it pacifies the mind.
And because it has wisdom as its supreme factor, jhāna has the four foundations as its proximate cause.

Because of skill in the means for the welfare of others according to one's promise, because of the relinquishing of unskillful action, because of the pacification of the fever born of delusion, and because of the attainment of omniscience, wisdom has the four foundations as its proximate cause.

Therein, the foundation of truth is established through conformity with what is known and what was promised; the foundation of relinquishment is established through the relinquishing of sensual objects as bases and sensual objects as defilements.
The foundation of tranquility through the subsiding of faults and suffering; the foundation of wisdom through awakening and penetration;

the foundation of truth, which embraces the threefold truth and opposes the threefold fault; the foundation of relinquishment, which embraces the threefold relinquishment and opposes the threefold fault;
the foundation of tranquility, which embraces the threefold tranquility and opposes the threefold fault; and that which is embraced by the threefold knowledge.

The foundation of wisdom is opposed to the threefold corruption. The foundations of renunciation, tranquility, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of truth because they do not deceive and because they conform to what has been promised.

The foundations of truth, tranquility, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of renunciation because of the relinquishing of opposites and because they have the relinquishing of everything as their fruit. The foundations of truth, renunciation, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of tranquility...
Because they pacify the fever of defilements and the fever of karma;
and because the foundations of truth, generosity, and peace—when embraced by the foundation of wisdom—are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
Thus, all the perfections are manifested through truth, embellished by generosity, nurtured by peace, and purified by wisdom. For truth indeed...
Of these, giving is the cause of their arising; receiving is the cause of their manifestation; tranquility is the cause of their increase; and wisdom is the cause of their purification.

Likewise, at the beginning there is the foundation of truth, because of the declaration of truth; in the middle there is the foundation of giving, because one who has made the vow relinquishes oneself for the welfare of others;
and at the end there is the foundation of tranquility, because all things culminate in tranquility. [This applies] to the beginning, middle, and end.
The foundation of wisdom exists because it arises when those [other foundations] are present, does not arise when they are absent, and arises in accordance with one's promise.

In that regard, when great beings are householders, they assist others through the giving of material goods by means of the foundations of truth and generosity, which constantly bring about their own welfare and the welfare of others, and which engender respect and affection.
Likewise, they do so by means of those things that bring about their own welfare and the welfare of others, and engender respect and affection.
Having become renunciants through the foundations of tranquility and wisdom, they assist others by means of the gift of the Dhamma.
In that regard, the Bodhisatta fulfills the four foundations in his final existence. For some say that the assumption of the final existence occurs for one whose four foundations are fulfilled;
for even in that case, through the realization of the foundation of wisdom during the descent into the womb and the great departure.
Mindful and clearly comprehending, born for the fulfillment of the foundation of truth, he walked seven steps facing north;

then, having surveyed all directions, with speech that followed the truth, he uttered the lion’s roar three times: "I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world," through the realization of the foundation of peace.

For one who has seen the aged, the sick, and those gone forth and is skilled in the specific meaning of the four truths, there is the tranquility that arises from the abandonment of pride regarding youth, health, and life; and through the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity,
there is the relinquishment, without regard, of a vast circle of kinsmen and of the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch already in his grasp.
Regarding the second stage, the full perfection of the four foundations at the time of supreme enlightenment:

some say that herein, through the realization of the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) in accordance with his promise, there is the clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths; thus, the foundation of truth is perfected.
Through the realization of the foundation of relinquishment (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*), there is the abandonment of all defilements and secondary stains; thus, the foundation of relinquishment [is perfected].
It is fulfilled. Through the realization of the foundation of tranquility, there is the attainment of supreme peace; therefore, the foundation of tranquility is fulfilled.
Through the realization of the foundation of wisdom, there is the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge; therefore, the foundation of wisdom is fulfilled.
This [fulfillment] is not yet established, because even in the case of full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), it exists only in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Others say that in the third stage, the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the four foundations are fulfilled.
For therein, the foundation of truth is fulfilled by the teaching of the Noble Truths in twelve aspects for one who has mastered the foundation of truth;
and the foundation of generosity is fulfilled by performing the great sacrifice of the True Dhamma for one who has mastered the foundation of generosity.
It is claimed that for one who has attained the foundation of tranquility and is himself tranquil, the foundation of tranquility is fulfilled by bringing others to tranquility;
and for one who has attained the foundation of wisdom, the foundation of wisdom is fulfilled by thoroughly understanding the dispositions and so forth of those to be trained.
However, this too is unproven, because the work of a Buddha remains incomplete.
Others say that in the fourth stage, at the moment of final Nibbāna, the four foundations are fulfilled.

For therein, through the attainment of the ultimate truth by virtue of having attained final Nibbāna, there is the fulfillment of the foundation of truth; through the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*upadhi*), there is the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity (*cāga*);

through the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), there is the fulfillment of the foundation of peace (*upasama*); and through the final Nibbāna which is the employment of wisdom, there is the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom (*paññā*).

In that regard, for the Great Being, the fulfillment of the foundation of truth is especially manifest at the birth-stage within the field of loving-kindness, having been brought forth by the foundation of truth;
the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom is especially manifest at the stage of perfect enlightenment within the field of compassion, having been brought forth by the foundation of wisdom;
and [the fulfillment of the foundation of resolve] is especially manifest at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma within the field of sympathetic joy.
It should be understood that for one who has accomplished the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*), the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity is clearly manifest;

and specifically, for one who has accomplished the foundation of tranquility (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) in the field of equanimity (*upekkhākhette*) at the moment of final Nibbāna, the fulfillment of the foundation of tranquility is clearly manifest.

Furthermore, in that regard, virtue (*sīla*) should be known through association with one who has accomplished the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*), and [virtue] through association with one who has accomplished the foundation of generosity.
Purity should be understood through one’s social dealings; fortitude in times of adversity should be understood in one who has attained the foundation of tranquility;
and wisdom should be understood through discussion in one who has attained the foundation of wisdom. In this way, the purifications of virtue, livelihood, mind, and view are to be understood.
Likewise, by the attainment of the foundation of truth, one does not go to a state of fault because of non-deception.
Through the accomplishment of the foundation of relinquishment, one does not follow a wrong course out of desire, because of non-attachment;

through the accomplishment of the foundation of peace, one does not follow a wrong course out of fear, because of non-oppression; through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom, one does not follow a wrong course out of delusion, because of awakening to things as they truly are.
Likewise, by the first [foundation of mindfulness], one who is not corrupted endures; by the second, one who is not greedy partakes; by the third, one who is not afraid avoids;
and by the fourth, one who is not deluded dispels [unwholesome states]. Through the first, there is the arising of the happiness of renunciation;

through the others, there is the arising of the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, and the happiness of enlightenment. Likewise, there is the happiness of rapture born of seclusion, the happiness of rapture born of concentration, and the happiness of the body born of the absence of rapture.
The arising of equanimity born of purity of mindfulness and of happiness occurs respectively through these four foundations.
Thus, the inclusion of the entire collection of all perfections (pāramīs) should be understood as being comprised by these four foundations, which are accompanied by manifold virtues.

And just as the inclusion of all perfections is achieved through the four foundations, it should likewise be seen that this is accomplished through compassion (karuṇā) and wisdom (paññā). For the entire equipment for enlightenment is contained within compassion and wisdom.
They are embraced. For the qualities such as giving, when embraced by compassion and wisdom, become the accumulations for great enlightenment, culminating in the attainment of Buddhahood.
In this way, their embrace is to be understood.
What, then, is the means of accomplishment?
Furthermore, for all of those [perfections], the means for their accomplishment are considered to be non-deficiency and so forth, as well as the surrendering of oneself and so forth. For indeed,
the complete accumulation of the entire equipment of merit and the rest, directed toward perfect enlightenment, occurs by way of practicing without deficiency.
In this context, "acting with care" means being endowed with reverence and great respect; "acting with constancy" means being engaged in uninterrupted application;
and "application over a long period of time" means not reaching a conclusion midway. Furthermore, the specific duration of that time will be made clear later on.
Thus, the practice of these four factors is the means for accomplishing these perfections (pāramīs).
Likewise, a Great Being practicing for enlightenment must surrender himself to the Buddhas even before his attainment of Perfect Enlightenment, thinking:

"I surrender this personal existence to the Buddhas. Furthermore, each and every object of possession must be relinquished through the gateway of giving even prior to its acquisition, thinking: "Whatever arises for me..."
“Whatever collection of requisites for life there may be, all that I shall give away when asked; however, I must use only what remains after giving to them.
When he has thus formed a mental volition for the sake of complete renunciation, whatever article of possession arises—

Whether it be inanimate or animate, there are four obstructions to giving: lack of prior practice in giving, the meagerness of the object to be given, the excellence and desirability of that object, and anxiety over its depletion.
Among these, when the Great Bodhisatta possesses things to be given and supplicants have presented themselves for the sake of giving...
If the mind does not leap forward and incline toward it, one should reach the conclusion: "Surely I have not practiced generosity in the past;
that is why my desire to give does not settle in my mind now. He [should think]:
"In this way, from now on, my mind will delight in giving. Come now, I shall give a gift starting from today. Is it not by me..."
"Having already relinquished the objects of possession to beggars," he gives gifts— liberal-handed, pure-handed,
delighting in renunciation, devoted to begging, and rejoicing in giving and sharing. In this way, the Great Being’s first bond of giving is struck down,
shattered, and utterly cut off.
Likewise, when the object to be given was meager and there was a deficiency of requisites, the Great Being reflected thus:
"Because of my lack of generosity and virtue in the past, I have now come to such a state of deficiency in requisites;
therefore, even if it causes me personal hardship, I must now give only gifts, using whatever object to be given I have obtained, whether it be small or inferior."
"By this means, I shall also reach the very pinnacle of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in the future.
Thus, with various kinds of gifts, he gives with a liberated hand, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to supplicants, and rejoicing in the sharing of gifts.
In this way, the Great Being’s second bond of giving is struck down, destroyed, and utterly severed.
Likewise, when a mind of reluctance to give arose due to the excellence and high value of the object to be given, the Great Being reflected thus:
"Is it not true, O good man, that you have aspired to the most sublime and most excellent Perfect Enlightenment?
Therefore, for the sake of that goal, it is only fitting for you to give objects of such great value. Thus he [gave] that which was sublime.
He gives agreeable gifts; he is liberal-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to prayer, and rejoicing in the distribution of charity.
Thus the Great Being’s third bond of giving is destroyed, shattered, and utterly cut off.
Likewise, when the Great Being, while giving a gift, perceives the exhaustion of the objects to be given, he reflects thus:
“This is indeed the inherent nature of wealth: that it is subject to exhaustion and subject to decline.
Moreover, because I did not practice such giving in the past, this depletion of my wealth is now seen.
Come now, with whatever gift I have obtained—whether small or great—I shall give only in charity, so that I may reach the pinnacle of the perfection of generosity in the future.”
‘I shall attain. Thus, with whatever he has obtained, he gives gifts—liberal-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to solicitation, and rejoicing in giving and sharing.
In this way, the Great Being’s fourth bond of giving is struck down, shattered, and utterly cut off.
