Thus, having reflected appropriately upon each and every disadvantage that constitutes a bond to the perfection of giving, [he abandons them].
The means for dispelling [the hindrances] is the method. And just as it is with the perfection of giving, so too should it be understood regarding the perfections of virtue and the rest.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s self-surrender to the Buddhas is the correct method for accomplishing all the perfections;
and having surrendered himself to the Buddhas, the Great Being remains therein for the sake of fulfilling the requisites of enlightenment in each respective instance.

While striving and exerting himself for the sake of his body and his requisites for comfort, even when faced with unbearable tasks that interrupt those comforts—tasks that are difficult to accomplish, brought about by the conditioned nature of beings, undesirable, intense, and life-threatening—he thinks:
"This personal existence has been surrendered by me to the Buddhas; whether it be this or that..."
Or let it be otherwise here,” he does not tremble or shake because of that, nor does he undergo even the slightest change;
rather, in undertaking what is wholesome, he possesses an entirely unshakable resolve. Thus, the surrendering of oneself is also a means for their accomplishment.
Furthermore, in brief, it is the exhaustion (or drying up) of attachment to oneself by one who has made the aspiration, [and] the complete consumption of that tendency.
Eight. (Miscellaneous Discussion: The means for accomplishing these [perfections] is the increase of affection (*sineha*) toward others.

For when a Great Being who has made the great aspiration for the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment understands all phenomena as they truly are, his attachment to himself—which is unstained by any phenomena—comes to exhaustion and total consummation through the cultivation of the union with Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Conduct. (The miscellaneous discourse on the eight [bases]: Furthermore, for one who regards all beings as if they were a beloved son, the moisture of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) increases toward them.

Consequently, at that stage, the Great Being—who has removed the obstacles to the requisites of enlightenment such as stinginess by means of the disappearance of greed, hatred, and delusion from his own and others' continuums—[practices] giving, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and... [conduct].

By means of the four bases of sympathy—known as impartiality—which follow upon the four foundations, he effects the gathering of people to the utmost degree, thereby introducing them to and bringing them to maturity in the three higher vehicles.
For the great compassion and great wisdom of the Great Beings are adorned by generosity; generosity, in turn, is adorned by pleasant speech; and pleasant speech...
Beneficial conduct is adorned by and comprised of impartiality toward all beings.

For those who practice the requisites of enlightenment having made all beings no different from themselves, the accomplishment of impartiality arises through the state of sharing the same pleasure and pain in all circumstances.
And even for those who have become Buddhas, it is by means of these same four bases of sympathy and the four foundations that [they act].
The thorough training of people is accomplished by means of the absolute gathering-in of beings through those who have fulfilled their awakening.
For the Perfectly Awakened Ones, generosity is fulfilled through the foundation of relinquishment; kind speech through the foundation of truth;
beneficial conduct through the foundation of wisdom; and impartiality through the foundation of peace—all these are fulfilled by those who have attained supreme awakening.
For the Tathāgatas, there is equality with all disciples and paccekabuddhas at the moment of final nibbāna.
For in that state, there is for them an undifferentiated unity. Therefore it is said: “There is no diversity in liberation. And on this point there are these verses:
“Truthful, generous, peaceful, wise, and compassionate;”
Having gathered all necessary provisions, what purpose would he not accomplish?
The Teacher is possessed of great compassion, yet seeks the welfare of others while remaining equanimous;
indifferent toward everything, oh, how marvelous is the Victor!
Detached from all phenomena and impartial toward all beings,
ever intent on the welfare of living creatures— oh, how marvelous is the Victor!
Always for the benefit and happiness of all beings.
“Exerted and untiring—oh, how marvelous is the Victor!
Regarding the duration required for attainment:
“By means of the divisions such as those predominant in wisdom, and those who know by a mere hint (ugghāṭitaññū), and so forth.”
The time for all three types of Bodhisattvas is considered to be threefold.
According to the lowest limit, it is four *asaṅkhyeyyas* and one hundred thousand *mahākappas*;

according to the middle limit, it is eight *asaṅkhyeyyas* and one hundred thousand *mahākappas*; and according to the highest limit, it is sixteen [asaṅkhyeyyas and one hundred thousand *mahākappas*].
[The periods are] incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) and one hundred thousand great aeons (*mahākappa*).

These divisions should be understood according to the sequence [of those] who are preeminent in wisdom (*paññā*), preeminent in faith (*saddhā*), and preeminent in energy (*vīriya*). For those preeminent in wisdom, faith is dull and wisdom is sharp;
for those preeminent in faith, wisdom is middling; for those preeminent in energy, wisdom is dull. And it is by the power of wisdom that perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*) is to be attained.
This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Others, however, say: "This division of time for Bodhisattvas is according to whether their energy is sharp, medium, or dull";
yet [it is] without distinction according to whether the factors conducive to the maturation of liberation are sharp, medium, or dull.
They also say that these three distinctions of time are appropriate because the accumulations for enlightenment reach their fulfillment through the aforementioned divisions of time.

For in this way, at the moment of the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), Bodhisattvas are of three types: one who understands by a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*), one who understands by detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*), and one who is to be guided (*neyya*).
Among them, he who is one who understands by a brief indication [is the one] in the presence of a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha...
One who hears a four-line verse becomes possessed of the necessary potential to attain arahantship together with the six direct knowledges and the analytical insights,
even before the third line of the verse has been finished, provided that one is intent upon the enlightenment of a disciple.
A second person, hearing a four-line verse in the presence of the Blessed One, [attains it] even before the fourth line of the verse has been finished.
There is the requisite capacity to attain Arahatship through the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) if one is intent upon the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi).

However, another person, having heard a four-line verse in the presence of the Blessed One, possesses the requisite capacity to attain Arahatship through the six higher knowledges once that verse is finished.
These three, having made their aspirations at different times and received their predictions from the Buddhas, [attained their goals] in due order.

Fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) in due order according to the aforementioned classification, they attain perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) in due time. However, when those respective periods of time have not yet been fulfilled,
even though those Great Beings (mahāsattas) give great gifts day after day like the Vessantara-giving,
and even while accumulating all the qualities of the perfections such as virtue (sīla) appropriate to that, [they still undergo] the five great renunciations (pañca mahāpariccāgā).

Even while practicing for the benefit of relatives, for the benefit of the world, and for the benefit of Buddhahood, and even while bringing these practices to their ultimate peak, it is impossible that they would become perfectly enlightened Buddhas in the interim.
Why? Because their knowledge has not yet matured and the qualities that constitute a Buddha have not yet reached completion.
For [the path] is like a crop that is produced only after a specific, delimited period of time.

It should be understood that since perfect enlightenment is accomplished only within the time-limit already specified, it cannot be attained even by one striving with all their effort during the interval; thus, the fulfillment of the perfections is achieved only through that specific duration of time.
What is the benefit?
To those Bodhisattas who have made their resolution:
"Thus, endowed with all factors, these persons destined for enlightenment will wander through the long course of saṃsāra for even hundreds of millions of eons."
They are not reborn in the Avīci hell, nor likewise in the Lokantara hells;
they are free from parching thirst and hunger, and they do not become Kālakañjaka spirits. (The conduct of the Kālakañjakas. Eight. Miscellaneous discourse);
There are no small creatures that are reborn in states of misery.
Being born among human beings, they do not become blind from birth.
They have no deficiency in hearing, nor are they born mute;
they do not enter into womanhood, nor are they hermaphrodites or eunuchs.
These people are not included within the realms of existence; they are destined for enlightenment.
Freed from the deeds of immediate retribution, their sphere of activity is pure in every respect.
Seeing the efficacy of kamma, they do not cultivate wrong view.
Even while dwelling in the heavens, they do not take rebirth among the non-percipient beings.
Among the gods of the Pure Abodes, no cause for such rebirth exists;
for these true men are inclined toward renunciation and are detached from existence after existence.
“They practice deeds for the welfare of the world and fulfill all the perfections.

Thus have the benefits been described; as well as the sixteen modes of marvelous and wonderful phenomena, beginning with: “Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta descends from the Tusita realm into his mother’s womb”; and [the phenomena] such as: “The cold has departed...”
By such passages as, "it becomes cool, and the heat is pacified," and, "Sāriputta, when the Bodhisatta is being born,
this ten-thousandfold world system quivers, trembles, and shakes," there are thirty-two kinds of prior signs; or else,
other [qualities] such as the fulfillment of the Bodhisattas' intentions and their mastery over karma and so forth.
The benefits demonstrated in various places in the Jātaka, Buddhavaṃsa, and other texts—all of these are the benefits of these [perfections].
Likewise, it should be understood that they consist of pairs of qualities such as non-greed and non-hatred, according to the classifications shown.
Furthermore, because from the moment of his initial resolve, the Bodhisatta is like a father to all beings through his desire for their welfare;
One who is worthy of offerings is venerable and worthy of cultivation; by virtue of possessing distinguished qualities, he becomes a supreme field of merit.
For the most part, he is dear to human beings and dear to non-human beings; he is protected by the deities.
Because his mental continuum is permeated with loving-kindness and compassion, he cannot be overcome by wild beasts and the like. And in whichever order of beings he is reborn, in that...
By means of his sublime beauty, sublime fame, sublime happiness, sublime strength, and sublime sovereignty, he surpasses other beings due to his possession of distinguished merit.
He is free from illness and free from affliction; his faith is perfectly purified and clear, and his energy is perfectly purified.
When mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are well-purified, one has dull defilements, dull distress, and dull fever;
precisely because of the dullness of the defilements, one is easy to speak to and accepts instruction respectfully; one is patient and gentle, kindly and skilled in encouraging others;
one is free from anger and resentment, free from slandering and disparaging, free from envy and avarice, and free from deceit.
He is free from deceit, without arrogance, and not conceited; he is not agitated and is heedful; he endures the provocations of others and does not provoke others;

and in whatever village or field he dwells, misfortunes such as fear generally do not arise among the beings there, and those that have arisen are pacified; and as for the states of woe in which he might be reborn—
In that state, one is not excessively oppressed by suffering like the common multitude; rather, one experiences an even greater sense of spiritual urgency and fear.

Therefore, these specific qualities—such as being equal to a father and being worthy of offerings—which are obtained by a Great Being according to his fitness in each respective birth, should be understood as his benefits.

Likewise, perfection of lifespan, perfection of form, perfection of lineage, perfection of sovereignty, authority in speech, and great majesty—these too should be understood as the benefits of the Great Being’s perfections (*pāramī*).
In this context, "perfection of lifespan" means having a long life and enduring for a long time in each respective rebirth; by means of that, the wholesome undertakings commenced [are maintained].
He brings it to completion and accumulates much merit. "Perfection of form" means being handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing;
through this, one inspires confidence and is held in high esteem by beings who judge by physical appearance.
"Perfection of family" means rebirth in noble families; through this, even those possessed by the intoxication of birth and so forth—[or those intoxicated by pride]—...
[Conduct. Eight. Miscellaneous Discussion: He is one who should be approached and waited upon; therefore, they perform services for him.
What is called "perfection of sovereignty" consists of great wealth, high status, and a large retinue.
By means of these, he should gather those who are to be gathered through the four bases of sympathy, and he should restrain those who are to be restrained in accordance with the Dhamma.
He is capable. "Worthiness of one's word" means being trustworthy and reliable;
by this, he becomes an authority for beings, and his command is not to be transgressed. "Great majesty" means the greatness of power;
by this, he is not overcome by others, but rather he himself overcomes others through the Dhamma, through justice, and through qualities as they truly are.
And thus, these perfections of a Great Being— beginning with the perfection of longevity— are to be understood as the benefits of the perfections,
which serve as the causes for the increase of one’s own immeasurable accumulation of merit, and as the means for introducing and maturing sentient beings within the Three Vehicles.
What is their fruit?
One should know that, in brief, their fruit is Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambuddhatā);
in detail, they are considered to be an infinite and immeasurable multitude of virtues.
In brief, the state of being a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha) is their fruit. In detail, however, it is the splendor of an infinite and immeasurable collection of qualities—

beginning with the ten powers (dasabala), the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja), the six unique knowledges (asādhāraṇañāṇa), and the eighteen exclusive qualities of a Buddha (aveṇikabuddhadhamma)—

which is adorned by the excellence of a physical body radiant with a multitude of virtues such as the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), the eighty minor characteristics (anubyañjana), and the fathom-wide halo (byāmappabhā).

The glory of the Dhamma-body—indeed, whatever qualities of a Buddha cannot be fully exhausted even by the Perfectly Enlightened One’s speech throughout many eons—this alone is their fruit. And this was said by the Blessed One:
“Even a Buddha might speak the praise of a Buddha...”
"Even if one were to speak of another for an entire eon,
and that eon were to be exhausted after a very long time,
the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted."
In this way, the miscellaneous discussion regarding the perfections (pāramīs) should be understood here.
Thus, with reference to the fulfillment of the perfections as divided according to the aforementioned method of practice, it is said:

"Having fulfilled the thirty perfections. Although the great renunciations are indeed instances of the perfection of giving (dānapāramī), they are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing them to be specific types of renunciation.
The separate mention of these [two] is for the purpose of showing their specific accumulation of merit (*sambhāra*) and for the purpose of showing their extreme difficulty.

For that very reason, even though there is a commonality in the nature of relinquishing what is cherished, the relinquishing of wife and children is mentioned separately from the relinquishing of wealth and kingdom; this is because the relinquishing of the eyes is more difficult than the relinquishing of limbs.
Thus it has been stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
In the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*, the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta also states that some count the renunciation of kingdom as one of the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*),
either by treating the renunciation of children and wife separately or by including the renunciation of eyes or the renunciation of life instead of the renunciation of kingdom.

The preliminary application (*pubbayoga*) consists of the accomplishment of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) together with the prior-stage practice known as the "going-and-returning" cycle (*gatapaccāgatika-vatta*).

The former conduct (*pubbacariyā*) consists of the accomplishment of an especially distinguished practice regarding giving and the other perfections; alternatively, that which is comprised in the *Cariyāpiṭaka* is the former conduct.
Some, however, say: "The preliminary resolution (*abhinīhāra*) is the preliminary application; or else, the practice of giving and so forth by way of physical seclusion [is it]."

They say it is either "wandering alone" or "the former way of life. "Teaching of the Dhamma" (dhammakkhāna) is discourse that proceeds by way of clarifying the giving of gifts and so forth, as well as fewness of desires and so forth, and the disadvantages and advantages of saṃsāra and nibbāna, and by way of establishing and maturing beings in the three types of enlightenment.
"Conduct for the welfare of relatives" (ñātatthacariyā) is conduct for the sake of kinsmen; that too occurs solely through the exercise of compassion.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), worldly conduct (*lokatthacariyā*) and so forth are included. The range of knowledge (*ñāṇacāra*)—consisting in the practice of wisdom (*buddhicariyā*) by way of the knowledge of one's own karma as one's own property (*kammassakatāñāṇa*), by way of proficiency in blameless spheres of action, spheres of craft, and branches of science (*vijjāṭṭhāna*), by way of proficiency in the aggregates, bases, and so forth, and by way of the investigation of the three characteristics—is in its actual meaning nothing other than the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*);
however, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*). "The limit" (*koṭi*)...
The limit is the peak. Likewise, in the phrase "our Blessed One has also come," the connection is also made with the words "having fulfilled the perfection of giving" and so forth.

Having thus shown the meaning of the phrase "has come in such a way" by way of the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramī*), he now says "the four foundations of mindfulness" (*cattāro satipaṭṭhāne*) and so forth, showing it also by way of the qualities conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).
Therein, by the mention of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, [he indicates] the path of arrival.
He shows [the goal] by reaching the summit, because only those factors belonging to the path and its fruits are to be grasped;

or alternatively, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth should be understood as being comprised within insight (vipassanā), since they are included in the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā).

"Having developed" means having produced. "Having cultivated" means having increased. And here, by the words "by which resolution," etc., he shows the beginning of the path of approach (āgamana-paṭipadā).
“Having fulfilled the perfection of giving,” and so forth, refers to the middle; “the four foundations of mindfulness,” and so forth, refers to the conclusion.

Therefore, it should be understood that the distinction of the three methods consists precisely in showing the specific path of practice that serves as the cause for the arrival mentioned by the word “arrived.
Now, regarding the first reason established by the threefold application of meaning as previously stated:
The passage beginning with “yatheva” was stated in order to show this by way of verse composition. Therein, the construction is as follows:

just as in this world the sages such as Vipassī and others attained omniscience through the three aforementioned causes, so too this Sakyan Sage, who possesses vision through the five eyes, has arrived by that same cause; for that reason, he is called “Tathāgata.”
"Just born" means having been released from the hands of humans and being newly born for a moment; it does not mean merely having emerged from the mother's womb.
For as soon as the Great Being had emerged from the mother's womb, first the Brahmās received him with a golden net;
from their hands, the Four Great Kings received him on a deerskin rug; and from their hands, humans received him on a cotton-wool mattress.
They accepted it, thinking, "Having escaped from the hands of men, he has landed upon the earth. The passage beginning with "And how?
is a detailed exposition, just as the Blessed One spoke in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*. "In a white parasol" means in a divine white parasol.
"While being carried" means while being held; "while being borne along" is also the reading now. And here, by the mention of the parasol alone...

It should be understood that the five insignia of royalty, beginning with the sword, were also taken. For at that time, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the *morahatthaka* fan, the *vāla* fan, the turban, and the head-band were present together with the parasol.
It was stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla that "only the parasol and the other items were seen at that time, not those who held the parasol and the rest";
and the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta has likewise stated in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*.
Even items such as palm-leaf fans receive the designation of "kakudhabhaṇḍa" (regalia).
Furthermore, it was stated thus with the intention that while swords and the like are regalia, other items such as palm-leaf fans were also present at that time.
"All directions" refers to the ten directions. "He gazes around" means that when the miracle of opening up the world occurred through the power of his merit.
The meaning is that he beheld the ten-thousandfold world system with his very eye of flesh (*maṃsacakkhu*).
This was not a survey of all directions performed after the seven strides; rather, it was the very first survey.
For as soon as the Great Being was released from the hands of men, he looked toward the eastern direction. There, gods and humans were making offerings of perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
“O Great Being, here there is not even anyone equal to you, much less one superior to you,” they said.
Thus, having surveyed all directions— the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above— and seeing no one anywhere who was his equal,
he took seven strides toward the northern direction, according to the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla and the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta.
And so it has been said. It is described in exactly the same way in the *Mahāpadāna-sutta-aṭṭhakathā*.
Therefore, it should be understood that after first surveying all directions with the seven steps, he proceeded by taking those seven steps and thereafter uttered the lion’s roar.
However, in this [work] and in other commentaries, because of his standing firm with level feet...
From the moment he set out until the utterance of his bull-like voice, [the commentator] explains the sequence of these events as being the successive portents, saying:
"Standing upon the seventh step, he surveyed all directions; this was the acquisition of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience," and so forth.
Thus, the meaning should be understood in such a way that there is no contradiction. Regarding the phrase, "standing upon the seventh step":
Furthermore, this reading [appears] due to a later error in transcription; it is not found in such a sequence of words in the *Mahāpadāna-aṭṭhakathā*.
"Āsabhi" means supreme, or unshakable, or fearless—this is the meaning. For that which belongs to a bull (*usabha*) is "bull-like" (*āsabha*);
because it is endowed with that quality of heroism (*sūrabhāva*), this speech is called "bull-like" (*āsabhī*). "The foremost" (*agga*) means the very first. "The eldest" (*jeṭṭha*),...
"Best" (*seṭṭha*) is a synonym for that very same term. From the perspective of the mere meaning of the words: "foremost" (*agga*) means preeminent among all things by virtue of its qualities;

"eldest" (*jeṭṭha*) means, by virtue of its qualities alone, the most senior among all, which is to say, the most venerable by virtue of its qualities; "best" (*seṭṭha*) means, by virtue of its qualities alone, the most praiseworthy among all.
Regarding the word "of the world" (*lokassa*), the genitive case is used in the sense of an ablative of separation, where the limit has been specified.

"This is the last birth; now there is no further becoming"—by means of this, he prophesied the attainment of Arahantship in this very existence, because through that very attainment there is no further becoming.
Now, praising his arrival in such a manner, he said, "And that for him," and so forth. Because it serves as a precursor, it is "tatha," meaning not false.
The connection [is as follows]. "Of the specific attainments" means of the attainments of specific qualities. He demonstrates that same meaning in detail with the words beginning "For that which...

and so forth. Therein, "that which" (yam) is a reference to an action; by it, he refers to the action of establishing (*patiṭṭhāna-kiriyā*) in its natural sense at the point where it says "he established himself.
"This is his" (*idam assa*) means this act of establishing belongs to this Blessed One. In the word *paṭilābha* ("attainment"), there is a designation of the possessor (*sāminiddesa*).

This is either a description of the agent or a description of the action. "A foretoken" (*pubbanimitta*) means the first occurrence and the cause for recognition of the welfare that will arise in the future, which is comprised of the attainment of that [state].

For when the Blessed One attains his extraordinary and marvelous special qualities, these signs of recognition appear, just as the five great dreams and so forth did upon his attainment [of Buddhahood], as is the case with those possessed of merit in the world.
Regarding "the attainment of the distinction of the fruit of merit":
"of the state transcending the entire world" means either the state that is supreme over all worlds, or the state of having gone beyond the entire world.
"Seven steps" (*sattapada*) refers to seven footprints; "the stride of seven steps" (*sattapadavītihāra*) is the specific, distinguished stepping forward, that is, the placing of the seven steps.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding its size when brought together, it is said to be the measure of a fist between two fingers.
"And the gods held in the sky a parasol with many branches and a thousand circles."
"Golden-handled yak-tail whisks are being waved about,
yet those who hold the whisks and the parasols are not seen"—
this refers to the introductory verse spoken by the Venerable Elder Ānanda in the Nāḷaka Sutta of the Suttanipāta.
"Chowries with golden handles are being waved about"—this is what is stated here. "Here" means in this verse-line.
However, since the waving of the chowries is not mentioned in the Mahāpadāna Sutta, that statement should be understood as referring to it [in the present context].
For, following what has been recorded there, he describes its nature as a precursor here; a *camara* is a specific kind of deer. Of which...
They make a chowrie (*vālabījani*) from the hair that constitutes the royal insignia;
its tail is called *cāmarī*. Its waving is likewise [described]; thus it is "the waving of the chowrie" (*vuttacāmarukkhepo*).

"Of the attainment of the supreme, stainless white parasol of the liberation of Arahantship" means: of the attainment of the supreme, stainless white parasol consisting of the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the fruit of Arahantship. "Beyond the seventh step" (*sattamapadūpari*).
Here, the word *pada* (foot) signifies the stepping of a foot; therefore, the meaning is "above the seventh step.
Because the knowledge of omniscience alone possesses unimpeded movement everywhere, it is called "unobstructed"; thus he says, "for the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience.

Likewise, regarding the passage "this Blessed One... [omitted] ...the cultivation of the preliminary signs," because of the governing context beginning with "for indeed" (*yañhi*) and because it is understood from the context.
And this was not stated; by this, he shows that the specific qualities arising by way of natural law (*dhammatā*) in the birth [of a Buddha] are common to all Bodhisattvas.
For these are the outflows (*nissanda*) of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"The ancient ones" refers to the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*). Gavampati is called *usabha* because he possesses wealth (*vasu*), meaning jewels, with his even feet.

"Just as he touched the earth known as Vasundharā," the meaning is that having been released from the hands of humans, Gotama, immediately upon birth, touched the Vasundharā (the earth) with his level feet.
"He strode" means he went. "Seven steps" refers to the seven places where the seven steps were taken.
This is the accusative case used to denote duration (accantasaṃyoga); [the sense is] "by way of seven strides of the steps."
Alternatively, the sense of the suffix *-ta* (in *samata*) should be understood through the elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*).
"Marus" refers to the gods, so called because they have the nature of dying according to their respective limits. "Equal" (*sama*) means equal or similar by virtue of the equality of his surveying;

for just as the Great Being surveyed one direction, so too did he survey the remaining directions—there was no obstruction whatsoever in his surveying. Alternatively, "equal" means that it was appropriate for him to survey [all directions] equally.
The meaning is as follows: for at that time, forms that were deformed, hideous, and repulsive did not appear before the Bodhisatta in the various directions;
rather, he uttered speech endowed with the eight factors—such as being distinct, sweet, and intelligible—and roared like a lion standing upon a mountain peak. This is the meaning.

Having thus explained the term *tathāgata* by means of the word *gata* in the sense of physical movement, he now says "Alternatively," etc., in order to explain it by means of the sense of the movement of knowledge.

In that context, in passages such as "Just as the Blessed One Vipassī [did]," it should be connected with the phrase "having abandoned sensual desire through renunciation," and so forth. "Through renunciation" (*nekkhammena*) means by way of an arising of wholesome consciousness dominated by non-greed (*alobha*).

For here, wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*) constitute renunciation (*nekkhamma*), because all of them are the opposites of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and not merely the going forth (*pabbajjā*) and so on.
Some say it refers to the "first jhāna," but that is indeed incorrect, because here what is intended is specifically the preliminary path (*pubbhāga-paṭipadā*) to the first jhāna.
"Having abandoned" means having relinquished. "Gone" means one who has set out by way of the progress of knowledge toward a further distinction.
*Pahāya* means either "by reason of abandoning" (*pahānahetu*) or "when there is abandoning" (*pahāne sati*).
For this particle *tvā* is used in the senses of cause and characteristic, as in such expressions as "having become Sakka, he was reborn.

Here, the "going" (*gata*) mentioned in the phrase "gone" refers to either awakening (*avabodha*) or practice (*paṭipatti*), both of which have the abandoning of sensual desire and the other hindrances as their cause; and by that very abandoning of sensual desire and so forth, it is characterized.
This same method applies to the terms “having split open,” and so forth. “By non-ill will” means by loving-kindness (*mettā*).
“By perception of light” means by the manifestation of the perception of light through mental attention that has made [the object] clear. “By non-distraction” means by concentration (*samādhi*).
“By the definition of phenomena” means by the determination of wholesome and other phenomena as they truly are; some also say it means the definition of name-and-form together with their conditions.

Having thus shown the state of a Tathāgata— distinguished by the progression of the Blessed One’s knowledge through the preliminary practice for the first jhāna described as “having abandoned covetousness for the world” and so forth by means of abandoning the hindrances such as sensual desire—
he now says “by knowledge,” etc., in order to show that same state together with the means, namely, the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights.

For when delusion—which acts as a fetter for one who has not yet mastered name-and-form and has not transcended doubt—is removed, the perception of impermanence and the other [perceptions] are accomplished for one established in full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).
Therefore, the shattering of ignorance is the means for insight (*vipassanā*).

Likewise, by means of gladness (*pāmojja*), which is the sign of delight in the meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*), and by the dispelling of lack of delight therein, the jhānas and so forth [are attained].
"Attainment" (samadhigama) refers to the means for dispelling dissatisfaction with meditative absorption (samāpatti).

Although it should be demonstrated according to the sequence of absorption and insight in the manner that will be explained below, this presentation in reverse order should be understood as intended to show the inclusion of ignorance—
which has the nature of an hindrance— within the hindrances previously shown under the headings of sensual desire and so forth.

Because they are the basis for entering the dwelling of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-vihāra*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are like door-panels; thus it is said, "having thrown open the door-panel of the hindrances.
As stated in the *Vammika Sutta* of the *Mūlapaññāsa* in the *Majjhima Āgama*:

"Having reflected and deliberated by night, one applies oneself to work by day," in that passage, the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*) is intended as the "smoking" (*dhūmāyanā*).
Having intended this, it is said: “having stilled the smoke of applied and sustained thought” (*vitakkavicāradhūmaṃ vūpasametvā*);
the meaning is, “having stilled the smoke known as applied and sustained thought. The reading “vitakkavicāram” is a recent one;
it is not ancient, because it was recorded exactly as stated by the teachers Dhammapāla Thera and Sāriputta Thera. “Virājetvā” means having felt disgust for [them].
Or, it means having "surpassed" them. This is because this term has both meanings, as in the expression “with the fading away of rapture” (*pītiyā ca virāgā*) and so forth.

Granted, suffering is abandoned precisely in the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna, and pleasure is abandoned precisely in the access concentration of the fourth jhāna; however, the statement “having abandoned pleasure and pain by means of the fourth jhāna” refers to their abandonment in an intensified sense.
"Perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) refers, by way of the term "perception," both the fine-material-sphere jhānas and their objects.
For the fine-material-sphere jhāna itself is called "form" through the elision of the latter member of the compound, as in such passages as "one possessing form sees forms.
Its object—the kasiṇa-form—is also called "form" through the elision of the former member, as in such passages as "he sees external forms, beautiful and ugly. Therefore...
Here, in the case of form and the jhāna of form, the perception associated with that is "perception of form"; thus the fine-material-sphere jhānas are spoken of by way of the term "perception.
"Perception of form" means that there is perception of form; what is meant is that it is possessed of the perception of form.
It should be understood that this is a designation for the object of those [jhānas], which is distinguished as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth. "Perceptions of resistance" (paṭighasaññā) ...

Perception accompanied by the two sets of fivefold consciousnesses that arises through the striking, the impinging, and the meeting of the sense bases— the eye and so forth— with their respective objects— the visible forms and so forth.
"Diverse perceptions" refers to the eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere,
the twelve unwholesome perceptions, the eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense sphere, and the two unwholesome-resultant perceptions.
“Eleven types of sense-sphere functional perception”: this is a designation for these forty-four types of perception.
They are called “perceptions of diversity” because they occur with respect to diverse objects—distinguished by form, sound, and so forth—which possess diverse intrinsic natures;
and because, being diverse and possessing diverse intrinsic natures, they are dissimilar from one another. Thus they are called “perceptions of diversity.”

Contemplation of impermanence as "impermanent" regarding what is impermanent is *aniccānupassanā*; this is the name for insight (*vipassanā*) that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
"Perception of permanence" refers to the false perception that occurs regarding conditioned phenomena, thinking, "They are permanent and eternal.
Here, by way of the term "perception," one should understand that views and consciousness are also included. This...

The method is the same for what follows as well. "By means of contemplation of disenchantment" means by means of contemplation occurring in the mode of becoming disenchanted with formations (*saṅkhāra*).
"Delight" (*nandi*) refers to craving accompanied by rapture. "By means of contemplation of fading away" means by means of contemplation occurring in the mode of fading away from formations.
"By means of contemplation of cessation" means by means of contemplating the cessation of formations: "Those formations..."
"Only they cease; they do not arise in the future by way of origination"—thus is the contemplation of cessation.

For this very reason it was said: "By means of the contemplation of cessation, one causes cessation, not origination. For this [contemplation] has attained strength as the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*).

Contemplation that proceeds in the manner of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*). It is the stabilizing through reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanā*).

Indeed, this is so. "Grasping" (*ādāna*) is the apprehension [of things] by way of their permanence and so forth. "The perception of density" (*ghanasaññā*) is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, collection, function, and object.

"Accumulation" (*āyūhana*) is formative activity (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*). "Transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) is the arrival at a particular state. "The perception of stability" (*dhuvasaññā*) is the perception that grasps at a state of firmness.
"The sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the delimitation of the specific functions of formations (*saṅkhārā*) by way of their density as a collection and so forth.
"Absorption" (*saviggahatam*). "Aspiration" (*paṇidhim*) refers to the aspiration for lust and so forth; in its actual meaning, it is the inclination toward mental formations by way of craving.

"Adherence" (*abhinivesam*) refers to the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*). "Higher wisdom as insight into phenomena" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) is the investigation of all phenomena by way of their impermanence and other characteristics.

"Adherence to grasping at the essential" (*sārādānābhiniveso*) is the perversion of perceiving the non-essential as essential. "The world has arisen through the creation of a Lord" (*issarakuttādivasena loko samuppanno*)... [and so on].

Adherence is what is called adherence through delusion (*sammohābhiniveso*). Some, however, say that adherence through delusion is the falling into doubt that occurs in such ways as, "Did I exist in the past?
and so forth. The grasping at formations as a shelter or protection is adherence through attachment (*ālayābhiniveso*).
Because of the statement, "Delighting in attachment, arisen from attachment," attachment is said to be craving; it is that very [craving]...
Some say that "adherence through settling" (*ālayābhinivesa*) refers to the occurrence [of consciousness] by way of adherence to the eye and so forth, as well as to visible forms and so forth.
"Contemplation of reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*) is the knowledge occurring in the form: "Such formations are to be relinquished.

Because it is free from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it is "the turning away" (*vivaṭṭa*), namely Nibbāna; "contemplation of turning away" (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*) is the occurrence by way of contemplation defined as taking that as its object.
*Gotrabhū*: "Adherence through conjunction" (*saṃyogābhinivesa*) means adherence to formations by way of conjoining.

"Associated with views" (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*) means associated with views both by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of abandonment (*pahāna*). "Coarse" (*oḷārika*) is said in relation to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths;
otherwise, since those [defilements] to be abandoned by the path of seeing are also coarser than those to be abandoned by the second path, they too would have to be designated as such.
It may be so. "Aṇusahagata" means "subtly experienced. Here, the word *sahagata* functions in the sense of "existing as that" (*tabbhāvavuttika*).
This, however, is stated with reference to what is to be abandoned by the lower paths. "All defilements" refers to all remaining defilements;

for defilements already abandoned by the first and subsequent paths are not abandoned again. Furthermore, the word "all" here has a partial scope (*sappadesavisaya*), as in such expressions as "all tremble at the rod."
Hardness is the state of being rigid. Fluidity is the state of being liquid.
Cohesion is that by which there is the swelling or the state of rigidity of this or that group [of atoms], like a bellows filled with worldly air.
As for those who maintain that space is the limit of form, defined as the distinctness of each respective element even when there is contact between elements belonging to different groups:

That which is the delimitation is not actually touched by those [great elements]; otherwise, there would be no state of delimitation for the elements, as they would fall into a state of pervasiveness.
The characteristic of non-contact is the state of being untouched therein within the aggregate (kalāpa) where the delimitation of the elements occurs;
therefore, the Blessed One said in the description of the space element: "It is untouched by the four great elements."
“Rūpaṇā” (being affected) is the arising of something dissimilar when opposing conditions come together.

Because volition is predominant among the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), this is stated by way of volition as: “the characteristic of volitional formation of formations.

For indeed, in the *Suttantabhājaniya* of the *Vibhaṅga* on the aggregate of formations, it is volition alone that is analyzed, beginning with: “volition born of eye-contact,” and so forth. Thus, they have the characteristic of volitional formation.
And volition (*cetanā*). As it is said: "In this context, what is the formation of merit? It is wholesome volition," and so forth.
The placing and directing of associated states toward an object is *abhiniropana*. Following after objects is *anumajjana*. Pervasive expansion is *pharaṇa*.
Resolute determination and conviction is *adhimokkha*. "Due to lack of faith" means because of lack of faith. [The suffix] *-ya* is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
This is the meaning of the locative case. This same method applies to indolence (*kosajja*) and the other [hindrances] as well.

The characteristic of tranquility (*vūpasama*) is the subsiding of the feverish distress of body and mind. When the higher mind (*adhicitta*) proceeds free from lethargy and agitation, equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanā*) consists in reflection (*paṭisaṅkhāna*), because it does not involve itself in exertion, suppression, or encouragement, thereby cutting off partiality.

Right speech has the characteristic of embracing because it embraces the associated states through its smoothness, and because it embraces the person who hears the well-spoken words conditioned by right speech.
This is due to its being the opposite of harsh and non-embracing states such as lying, which have the function of deceiving. Bodily action arouses whatever needs to be done.
Since there is a simultaneous arising and a joining together, it should be understood that the abstinence termed right action has the characteristic of being a simultaneous arising;
or rather, "simultaneous arising" (*samuṭṭhāna*) is the lifting up of associated states, like the lifting of a burden by bodily activity.
For a living being, or for the associated states, it is the purification and cleansing through the functioning of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), or simply the purity of livelihood itself.

“Volitional formations” (*saṅkhārā*) here refers specifically to volition (*cetanā*), and not to the fifty-three mental factors as in such passages as “volitional formations are the aggregate of volitional formations.
Thus it is said: “The characteristic of volitional formations is volition. For it is precisely volition—consisting of meritorious formations and so forth—that arises with ignorance as its condition.
Inclination toward an object is “bending” (*namana*). Proceeding is “arising” (*āyatana*). For it is by way of the six sense bases that mind and mental factors proceed.

Occurrence (*pavatti*). Regarding "the characteristic of craving as a cause": here, the state of being the productive cause of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is the characteristic of craving as a cause;
however, for the Path, which will be explained later, it is the quality of leading to Nibbāna—this is the distinction between them.

The characteristic of the object (*ārammaṇa*) is grasping. The characteristic of renewed arising is accumulation (*āyūhana*). The characteristic of emptiness (*suññatā*) is [to be understood] from the perspective of the absence of a sentient being or a life-principle (*satta-jīva*). Exertion (*padahana*)...

Ussāhana (exertion) is the act of inspiring. Ijjhana (success) is attainment. Nissaraṇa (emergence) is the going forth from the round of existence. Tathalakkhaṇa (the characteristic of suchness) is the state of being non-perverted.
Ekarasa (single function) is the mutual non-transcending of one another, which is simply the state of being neither deficient nor excessive.

Samatha and vipassanā are called "yuganaddha" (yoked together) because they must be bound together as a pair by virtue of their mutual assistance. It is also said: "Faith and wisdom, exertion and non-distraction."
They say: "Purification of mind" (cittavisuddhi) is concentration (samādhi). "Purification of view" (diṭṭhivisuddhi) is wisdom (paññā).
"Destruction" (khaya) is the destruction of the defilements, which is the Path; it has the characteristic of cutting off the knowledge termed right view that occurs therein.

"Non-arising" (anuppāda) is the Fruit, because it is the state of the non-arising of defilements. "Tranquility" (passaddhi) is the subsiding of the defilements. "Of desire" (chandassa) refers to the desire for agency (the wish to act). Its state is that of being a foundation (patiṭṭhābhāva).

The root characteristic (*mūlalakkhaṇa*). The characteristic of origination (*samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇa*) is the state of being a cause for the arising of associated phenomena by way of presenting an object.

Convergence (*samodhāna*) is the mode to be grasped through the meeting of the sense-object and so forth; it is that which is called "conjunction" (*saṅgati*) in such passages as, "the conjunction of the three is contact.
It is also [defined] as that by which associated phenomena are equally (*samaṃ*), or rightly (*sammā*), directed toward, or brought together (*sampiṇḍitā*).
Combination (*samodhāna*) is contact (*phassa*); its state is the characteristic of combination. It is a meeting place (*samosaraṇa*) because associated states meet and gather there;
this refers to feeling (*vedanā*). For it is said that without it, the associated states do not occur, and thus they appear as if gathered together for the purpose of experiencing feeling;
its state is the characteristic of meeting. [It is like] the rafters in a palace and so forth.
The characteristic of being pre-eminent (*pamukha-lakkhaṇa*) is the state of leadership among associated states, like a peak.
The characteristic of sovereignty (*ādhipateyya-lakkhaṇa*) is the state of predominance over associated states due to mindfulness being all-pervasive.

The characteristic of being superior (*tatuttariya-lakkhaṇa*) is the state of being further beyond, more excellent, or more pre-eminent than those associated states, or than that [state of predominance].
For wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme factor. "Liberation" (vimutti) is so called because the fruit is liberated from the defilements.

Furthermore, it is the "essence" (sāra) by virtue of being the ultimate excellence of the essence consisting of qualities such as virtue (sīla). It is the "conclusion" (pariyosāna) because there is no state beyond it.

And this analysis of characteristics is according to the method handed down in the ancient commentaries, following the respective words of the Suttas concerning the six elements, the five jhāna factors, and so forth.

It should be understood as "stated. For even though some phenomena have been stated previously, they are shown again for the purpose of explaining them through another method. And for this very reason, it is said:
"Phenomena are rooted in desire, originate from attention, converge in contact, and culminate in feeling";
"Wholesome phenomena have wisdom as their supreme"; and "This holy life has liberation as its essence."

Based on such scriptural passages as, “For the holy life, friends, has Nibbāna as its consummation, Nibbāna as its final goal,” it is said that zeal has the characteristic of being the root, and so forth. By the words “thus,” etc., he demonstrates the meaning:
that [the Dhamma] comes as the true and unerring characteristic of those various phenomena. Furthermore, that...
"Going" here means precisely the going of knowledge; thus it is said, "by the course of knowledge.

Although the word *gata* has the sense of "understanding," this specific usage is established solely in the sense of the "going of knowledge," and so it was not explicitly stated [as such]. Furthermore, the prefix *ā-* here merely follows the word *gata*.
Therefore, he said: "attained, fully attained."
Because their intrinsic nature is non-perverted, it is said: "The four noble truths are called 'such' (tathā) dhammas. They are "such" because their intrinsic nature is non-perverted;
they are "not otherwise" (avitathā) because their nature is not different from what it is; they are "not otherwise" (anaññathā) because they are devoid of any other mode of appearance.

By saying "thus is the detailed exposition," he refers to the discourse on the complete tetrad of truths as it appears in the *Saccasaṃyutta* and other collections. Having said "therefore," [he continues:]
By the phrase "because they have been fully awakened to them as such," he shows that those [truths] are indeed not to be misapprehended. This same method applies to similar cases.

Having thus shown the fourth reason by way of the truths, he now says "Furthermore" (*apica*) and so forth, showing it also by way of the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), which are "as they are" (*tathabhūtānaṃ*) because their intrinsic nature is non-perverted due to the relationship between condition and conditioned.
In that context, the meaning of "produced and arisen with birth as condition" (*jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho*) is as follows:

The meaning of "the state of having arisen" (*sambhūta*) is the nature of coming higher and higher, having come into being conditioned by birth (*jāti*), for one who is associated [with it] and conforms to its own conditions;

the sense is that of "continuous occurrence. Alternatively, the compound *sambhūtasamudāgata* means both the state of having arisen (*sambhūta*) and the state of having been fully acquired (*samudāgata*), by way of eliding the latter member of the first term (*pubbapada*).
For grammarians (*neruttika*) maintain that even in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), the masculine gender may be used.

In this context, aging-and-death does not exist apart from birth, nor does it arise from anything other than birth; thus, it has the sense of being produced with birth as its condition (*jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭha*).
Likewise, it arises precisely from birth; thus, birth has the sense of being the source from which it emerges (*paccayasamudāgataṭṭha*). This is what is meant:
whatever kind of birth serves as the condition in whatever manner, the nature [of aging-and-death] manifests accordingly. Regarding the side of conditions (*paccayapakkhe*):
Regarding the phrase "but ignorance is the condition for volitional formations" (*avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho*):
it is not that ignorance is not a condition for volitional formations, nor do volitional formations arise without ignorance.

In whatever way ignorance serves as a condition for whichever volitional formations, this is the meaning of "ignorance as the condition for volitional formations," which is to say, its nature as a condition. Likewise...

“Of phenomena” (dhammānaṃ) means of the phenomena consisting of the mode of conditions (paccayākāra). In phrases such as “the Sugata,” the word *gama* is intended to have the meaning of “awakening” (*buddhi*);
thus it is said “because of having fully awakened” (*abhisambuddhattā*), not in the sense of the movement of knowledge.

For words whose meanings are “going” (*gati*) and “awakening” (*buddhi*) are mutual synonyms. Therefore, the governing context here is that the word *gata* has the meaning of “fully awakened”; or alternatively, it is not applicable because [the object] is already understood.
The connection is: "Whatever object called 'form' exists, that the Blessed One knows and sees. Regarding the phrase "in the world with its devas...

and so forth, the word "exists" (*atthi*) serves as the locus; furthermore, it is stated with reference to the sentient beings dwelling in immeasurable world-systems, or with reference to [the form] coming into the range of perception.
That base of form (*rūpāyatana*), being analyzed by the Blessed One, is exactly as it is.
The word "occurs" (*hoti*) should be supplied [to complete the sentence]. He states the reason for its being thus and not otherwise: "by one who knows and sees in this way.
For these two phrases—“because of having known” and “because of having seen”—are included within the sense of the causal particle *hi* (for), meaning because of having known and seen in every aspect.

In the phrase "by way of the desirable, the undesirable, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the neutral. Likewise, it includes the distinctions of past, future, and present; limited, internal, external, and both; and so forth.

"By way of the terms as they are currently obtainable": because of the statement, "The visible base is seen; the audible base is heard; the olfactory base, the gustatory base, and the tangible base are sensed;
all material form is cognized by the mind," both the term 'seen' and the term 'cognized' are applicable to the objective field of material form.
This objective field of material form may be desirable, undesirable, or neutral; limited; past, or future.

“Present, internal or external, seen, cognized, visible form, the sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana), the element of visible form (rūpadhātu), appearance of color, with visibility, with resistance, blue, yellow,” and so forth by means of these and many other names.
By the phrase beginning with “by way of the desirable, the undesirable, etc.,” he demonstrates the state of having many names according to its own nature.
“By thirteen sections” refers to the Rūpakaṇḍa in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.

He says this with reference to the thirteen modes of exposition (*niddesa*) that follow. Furthermore, in each of these modes, because there are four methods of determining [the factors] in each case, it is said, "by fifty-two methods.

"Just as it is" means that it is truly so (*sacca*) because of the uncontradictable teaching through the aforementioned way of knowing, and because of the non-erroneous seeing through the aforementioned way of seeing. This meaning is found in the *Catur-aṅguttara*.
Establishing [the point] by means of the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, he said, “And this has been said,” and so forth. Here, the word *ca* (and) indicates strengthening;
thus, it illuminates the strengthening of the meaning as previously stated. Alternatively, it has the sense of conjunction (*sampiṇḍana*), used in the sense of inclusion (*aṭṭhāna*):
not only by me, but also by the Blessed One. *Anuvicaritam* means thoroughly investigated (*paricaritam*). *Jānāmi abbhaññāsim* means “I know, I have directly known.”
By demonstrating the occurrence of knowledge in the present and past times, the occurrence of knowledge in the future is also demonstrated by way of that same method.

Furthermore, the word *vidita* (known) does not specify a particular time because it is common to all three times—just as in expressions such as "seen, heard, sensed"—and thus its meaning is "made manifest and known. By this, he shows that [this knowledge] is different from others...
“They indeed know [this], but it has been made known and understood by me. For with these words, the Blessed One spoke of what is called the ground of omniscience (*sabbaññubhūmi*).
“It did not stand before him”: that object of the six sense-doors did not stand before, nor was it approached by the Tathāgata as a self or as belonging to a self, through craving or through views;
by this word, however, the ground of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsavabhūmi*) is spoken of.

Just as phenomena such as visible forms as objects (rūpārammaṇa) possess a certain intrinsic nature (sabhāva) and a certain mode (pakāra), so too he goes to, sees, and knows those phenomena in their respective natures and modes;
it is with reference to this meaning that it is said, “one who sees thus” (*tathadassī*) in the sense of [the term] *tathāgata*.
For verbal roots (*dhātu*) have many meanings. Some, however, [derive it] according to the rules of etymology (*nirukti*), by including it in the *pisodarādi* group.
Alternatively, some explain the derivation of the word *tathāgata* here by eliding the syllable *dassī* and adding the augment *ā* to the word *āgata*;
however, that is entirely incorrect, because it involves discarding an existing word and adopting one that does not exist.
And it is said in the *Buddhavamsa-aṭṭhakathā*:
“He who knows and contemplates phenomena in their true manner;
seeing thus, he is a Sambuddha, and therefore he is called a Tathāgata.

Here, having stated the meaning of the word as it occurs in the phrase “contemplates,” the word “knows” is used to show that this very contemplation is indeed knowledge. Furthermore, the phrase “seeing thus” is stated to clarify the meaning already conveyed by the word itself.

"Yaṃ rattim" means "on which night. This is the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) used in the sense of absolute connection (*accanta-saṃyoga*), because it denotes absolute connection with the moment of full awakening (*abhisambujjhana-khaṇa*), which is a part of that night.

Alternatively, it should be understood that this entire night is, by way of figurative usage (*pariyāyena*), characterized by absolute connection, since it is the time of striving for full enlightenment.
[This is said] because [the Buddha] has reached the summit of the earth, the unsurpassed ground, and the pinnacle of the world.
"Unconquered" (*aparājita*) means not defeated by others in this place; that very seat is the "unconquered throne" (*aparājitapallaṅka*), and [the Buddha sits] upon it.

"Of the three Māras" refers to the Māras of defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the son of a deva (*devaputta*). This is stated according to the direct method (*nippariyāya*);

however, according to the indirect method (*pariyāya*), the crushing of all five Māras should be understood in the manner explained below. "The summit" (*matthaka*) signifies what is characterized by supreme power (*sāmatthiya*).
The head. "In the interval between these two" means in the interval between the two watches of the night.

By the phrase "even during the first enlightenment," etc., he specifies [the period] by defining it as being included within the time span of forty-five years. However, regarding those [periods], it is stated in the *Vinaya-gaṇṭhipada* that the first enlightenment is delimited by twenty years;
and that very point is stated in its own commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) as follows: "Indeed, during the Blessed One’s first enlightenment..."
Because it was stated that "there was no one who served [the Buddha] continuously for twenty years," it is said here taking the first enlightenment (*paṭhamabodhi*) to be twenty years.
However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated: "Of the forty-five years, the first fifteen years from the beginning constitute the first enlightenment.
And this being the case, the middle fifteen years in between would be the intermediate enlightenment (*majjhimabodhi*).

It might be argued that the equality in measure of the three enlightenments could exist in the sense that the final enlightenment occurred fifteen years before [the Parinibbāna], for fifteen years added to forty-five years indeed complete fifty years.
However, since in the Commentary the first enlightenment is included within those very twenty years as being fifteen years in measure, it is said: "In the first enlightenment..."
It can also be understood thus: "It was spoken within twenty years. The connection is with the words beginning "That discourse" (*yaṃ suttaṃ*).
It is *anupavajja* because it is faultless and beyond reproach. It is *anūna* because there is nothing to be added. It is *anadhika* because there is nothing to be removed.
It is *sabbākāraparipuṇṇa* due to its perfection in meaning, phrasing, and so forth. It is *nimmadana* because it is the cause for subduing pride.
“Even as much as the tip of a hair” means even the measure of the end of a single hair on the tail. “Lapsed” means violated or spoken falsely. “By a single seal” means by a single royal insignia.
“By a single tube” means by a single *āḷhaka* measure, or by a single *tumba*. “By a single scale” means by a single measure (*māna*).
“It is exactly so” indicates by way of contrast that it is precisely the meaning stated and not otherwise; therefore, for whatever purpose—
“Spoken” (bhāsitaṃ) indicates that it is a teaching free from error, because it accomplishes its purpose absolutely exactly as it was spoken by the Blessed One.
By the term “one who speaks what is real” (gad-attha), he shows the etymological derivation: one who speaks—that is, utters—what is real (tathaṃ) is a Tathāgata;

here, the letter *da* is replaced by *ta*, and according to the rules of grammar (*niruttinaya*), the vowel *ā* is added, or alternatively, it is derived from the sense of the verbal root (*dhātu*) through its specific mode (*ākārena*).

Thus, having shown the etymology (*nirutti*) by means of a grammatical derivation (*dhātusaddanipphatti*)—as in the case of terms such as “Sugata”—the phrase beginning with “Moreover” (*apicā*) was stated in order to show it also by way of a compound with an external meaning (*bāhiratthasamāsa*).
“Āgadaṇaṃ” means an intense speaking or utterance because it accomplishes all that is beneficial;
or else, the prefix *ā-* denotes the mere state of being that.

“Tathāgata” means one whose going is thus (*tathā-gatam-assa*). Or, his bodily activity proceeds just as his speech proceeds, and his speech proceeds just as his bodily activity proceeds; therefore, the meaning is “one who has gone thus.
To show that very etymology, he said “of the Blessed One” (*bhagavato*), and so forth. For therein, by the words “gone, proceeded” and “gone, proceeded,” it is shown.
He shows that the term *gata* here refers to the occurrence of body and speech in mutual conformity with each other according to one’s verbal intention;
this is indicated by the external compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) in the phrase “of one who has become thus,” and so forth.
By the words “in whatever way,” because of the inseparable connection between the pronouns *yaṃ* and *taṃ*, when “in that way” is stated, the meaning “in whatever way” is already present.
“*Hoti*” signifies the meaning of the word *tathā* (thus). By the phrase “the speaker and the doer,” the nature of his activity is indicated;
by the phrase “of the Blessed One,” the cause—such as acting in accordance with what he says—is indicated.

“*Evaṃbhūtassā*” means of one who proceeds in the manner of acting according to what he says, or of one who has attained this state. “*Iti*” points back to the aforementioned manner. Furthermore, because here...

The word *gata* also indicates occurrence by way of speech; therefore, while the meaning "Thus-Gone" (*tathāgata*) is certainly established in the sense of having spoken thus, that has already been shown by a previous method of exposition.
Consequently, in order to show specifically the meaning of "acting thus" (*tathākāritā*) by means of the method of elimination (*pārisesanaya*), it is said:
"He is a Thus-Gone because of acting thus. And it has been said:
“As his speech has gone,
so has his body gone;
as his body is, so is his speech.”
“Then the Teacher, the Tathāgata”—
this is the connection [to the phrase] “having made the peak of existence (bhavagga) the limit. However,
it should be understood that this was said in order to refute those who claim, “Just as there are [worlds] across, so too above and below, there are immeasurable world-systems.”
"By liberation" means by the fruit (*phala*). "By the knowledge and vision of liberation" means by the vision consisting of the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa*).
"Equal" means similar. "Measure" means the instrument of measuring. One who overcomes others, surpasses them in virtue, and becomes superior to them is "the Overcomer" (*abhibhū*).
One who is not overcome or surpassed by others is "the Unconquered" (*anabhibhūta*). "Exclusively" (*aññadatthu*) is a term used for emphasis.
*Nipāta* is a particle. *Dasa* means "seeing," in the sense of seeing everything; thus the meaning is "he sees all. *Vasavattī* means "one who brings others under his own control.

Regarding the statement, "The Tathāgata is so called in the sense of overcoming," this is not derived from the literal word-meaning (*saddato*); rather, it was stated as "in that very same way" (*tattheva*) and so forth in order to show that [the term] is used in that sense according to the word-meaning.
In that context, *agada* refers to a divine medicine (*dibbāgada*); it is called *agada* because it cuts away (*dāti*, *avakhaṇḍati*) *aga*, which is disease. There is no...

Or, having considered that it is "a non-disease" (*agada*) because it removes disease (*gada*); since here, in the sense of being similar to that, the state of being "non-disease" is obtained for both the elegance of the teaching and the abundance of merit, he said, "like a non-disease.
That element of the Dhamma (*dhammadhātu*) which has reached the expansion of the teaching is the "elegance of the teaching.
And the "element of the Dhamma" is precisely the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). For by means of that, [it reveals] the differentiation of the modes of phenomena.

Having understood [the disciple's disposition], he establishes them in the teaching appropriate to that. The "splendor of the teaching" (*desanāvilāsa*) itself consists of the splendor of the teaching, as in the phrases “consisting of giving” (*dānamaya*) and “consisting of virtue” (*sīlamaya*);
however, nowadays the word *maya* is not seen in many manuscripts.

"Accumulation of merit" (*puññussaya*) means an abundance or an excess of merit consisting of the requisites such as knowledge. The passage beginning with "By that" (*tenā*) is the application of the simile. By that...
The connection is that the Blessed One surpasses [others] by means of both: the elegance of his teaching and his abundance of merit.

With the words “iti” and so forth, he demonstrates a bahir-attha compound (a compound whose meaning lies outside its constituent parts). It is said that he is “tathā” because he has surpassed the entire world, and not otherwise.

He is called “gata” in relation to the tathā because he has gone to it; this refers to the first three Truths. However, when it is said “gone to the tathā,” it refers to the final Truth. This is according to the sequence of the Four Noble Truths.
And here, a fourfold meaning for the word *gata* has been stated. Since prefixes and particles function by indicating that very meaning when they are in proximity to a denotative word (*vācaka*),
the author shows by the phrase "understood, past" (*avagato atīto*) that the word *gata* alone— even without a prefix— expresses the sense of being understood and the sense of having passed.

“*Tatthā*,” etc., is the explanation of that [verse]. “The world” (*loka*) refers to the world as the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). It should be construed with “for the sake of its thorough comprehension by way of such investigation” (*tathāya tīraṇapariññāya*).
“The path leading to the cessation of the world” (*lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*) refers to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), and not merely to the act of awakening itself.
To show that the duty to be performed therein has indeed been fulfilled, [the text] says: “The Tathāgata is detached from the world,” and so forth.
The second alternative is also stated in the Fourfold Truths; or rather, he shows the cause of his perfect enlightenment by means of these.

For it is precisely because of this that he is called "the Perfectly Enlightened One" (*abhisambuddho*). "Monks, whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after,"
"Whatever has been investigated by the mind, all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata;
therefore he is called the 'Tathāgata'"—this passage from the Catukka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya is presented here by way of a formulaic summary (peyyāla-mukhena).

And this is done solely for the sake of connecting the meaning, not for the purpose of proving this specific point. For that canonical text indicated by the formula demonstrates the meaning as it truly is.
“Sādhikāti. By the words “The meaning of this too should be understood in this way,” he effects a correlation between the probandum and the proof.
With the words “And this too,” etc., he shows the vast scope of the term *tathāgata* and provides a mere illustration of the eightfold reason already stated.
Therein, “this” refers to the eightfold reason stated in its fully expanded form.
The word *pi* or *api* is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvane*), as in: “Even this much is merely the face, let alone anything else.

Regarding the phrase “illuminating the state of a Tathāgata,” it means illuminating the name “Tathāgata. For the Blessed One is called “Tathāgata” by virtue of his qualities, and the term “Tathāgata” is applied to the Blessed One by way of that name.

Indeed, it has been said: “The names of the Great Seer are incalculable, according to his qualities. Just as the word for heedfulness (*appamāda*) serves as the basis for the practice of all wholesome states, [so too does the name serve as the basis for the realization of all qualities].
In order to show that the footprint of the Tathāgata encompasses all the qualities of a Buddha, he said, “in every way,” and so forth.
“Should describe” is a hypothetical expression, meaning “whether one should describe it or not.
And it has been said: “Even a Buddha might speak the praise of a Buddha...”
“Even if one were to speak of another for an eon,
and that eon were to be exhausted after a very long interval,
the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”
Some also say that this [term] refers to the state of being established, as in such passages as, "He shall unravel this tangle.

However, here is the method according to the *Aṭṭhakathā-muttaka*: from the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*) up until Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), because there is an absence of decline, defilement, or turning back in the practice of the Great Vehicle of Awakening (*mahābodhiyāna*), it is in accordance with his original aspiration (*yathāpaṇidhāna*).

The Tathāgata is so called because he has practiced in accordance with his original resolve (*abhinīhāra*). Alternatively, he is the Tathāgata because his movements, goings, and activities of body, speech, and mind proceed "thus" (*tathā*) according to his wish, due to his great supernormal power, his attainment of the excellence of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and the absence of any obstruction whatsoever in his unimpeded knowledge.
Furthermore, in the world, there are words such as *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*, and *pakāra*.

Similar meanings are seen; therefore, because he possesses the entirety of the qualities of omniscience just as the Blessed Ones such as Vipassī and others did, this Blessed One is likewise "Tathāgata.
Furthermore, because he is endowed with those [qualities] in the manner described, this Blessed One is likewise "Tathāgata.
Another method: because truth, reality, and suchness are "tatha," [he is Tathāgata].
This is a designation for knowledge; therefore, because he has come by means of such knowledge, he is called the Tathāgata.
“Just as Vipassī and the others have gone, having abandoned the stains of sense-desire and so forth by means of concentration and knowledge;”
The Sage of the Sakyas, Mahesī, who possesses radiance,
is thus called the Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) in that way (tathā). And likewise,
he is so called because he maintains (dhātā) the characteristics of the elements, the sense-bases, and so forth.
Through the distinction between individual essence and commonality,
the Victor, having attained [knowledge] by means of his own independent wisdom,
is called the Tathāgata, the Bull of the Śākyas.
The truths are thus by the universal eye,
and likewise is this specific conditionality in every respect;
since they have been fully disclosed by him who is not to be led by others.
Because he knows things as they truly are, he is the Conqueror, the Tathāgata.
Even within world-systems of manifold divisions,
regarding the range of the Conqueror’s sense-sphere of visible form and so forth—
In the diversity of various phenomena, his vision is exactly as it is;
therefore, the Tathāgata is one whose vision is all-pervading.
And because he speaks of the Dhamma exactly as it is, [he is called the Tathāgata].
He acts in accordance with his own speech;
he proceeds having surpassed the world by means of his virtues.
For that reason also, the Tathāgata is the Leader of the World.
According to his former aspiration, according to his inclination,
and through the manifestation of speech, body, and mind as they occurred,
in whatever manner and by whom the Great Seers were formerly [honored].
Such is the Victor, the Tathāgata.
And just as the Sugatas of old were endowed [with these qualities],
so too is he endowed with them, because of his knowledge of suchness.
“Because he has come together [with all beings], he is called the All-Seeing One; the Tathāgata, the Bull of the Sakyas.
— This is the summary verse.
“And what, monks, is that?”—to whom is this question addressed? He says, “By which,” and so forth.

Having thus shown that there is a general inquiry regarding the mere virtue already mentioned, he now demonstrates, by way of enumerating the meanings, all the inquiries as they appear in the *Mahāniddesa* for the purpose of making known their specific nature, beginning with the words, “In that context, ‘inquiry’ means... and so on. Therein:
* Tattha means: in this context, regarding the general statement of inquiry that was uttered as "What is that? * Pakatiyā means: by its own nature;
that is to say, spontaneously. * Lakkhaṇaṃ means: any intrinsic nature (sabhāva) that one wishes to know. * Aññātaṃ means:
unknown by any kind of knowledge whatsoever, whether it be that associated with specific modes such as seeing, or otherwise.
For these are specific stages consisting of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), vision (*dassana*), weighing (*tulanā*), and investigation (*tīraṇā*).

"Not seen" means not seen as if by direct perception through knowledge that has become vision. "Not weighed" means not weighed by means of knowledge that has become a process of weighing, such as thinking, "This is so much.

"Not investigated" means the completion of the cognitive act of knowing has not been achieved by means of knowledge that has become an investigation, such as thinking, "It is exactly thus. "Not manifested" means it has not become clear to knowledge. "Not made manifest" means...
"Made manifest by knowledge. "Of that" means of what has been described by the aforementioned characteristics. "Illumination of the unseen":
