The meaning is that the mind enters with ease by means of the two aforementioned causes; this is an aluttasamāsa compound, as in the expression "gone to the deathless" (amataṅgato).
"Pure" means completely full of qualities; hence he says, "by way of being full of qualities. "Grown up in the city" (pure saṃvaḍḍhā).
The word *porī* means "such a woman," and by the passage beginning with "in former times" (*pure*), it explains that even her speech is refined (*porī*). "Delicate" (*sukumārā*) means very young.
On the side of the object of comparison (*upameyya*), however, delicacy (*sukumāratā*) is simply the state of being soft due to its lack of harshness. Regarding the word *purassa*:
here the term *pura* denotes the inhabitants of that city through association, as in expressions such as "the village has arrived"; for this very reason, he says "of the city-dwellers."
*Esā*: this is speech indicating that which is related to it. *Evarūpī kathā*: speech manifested by way of three meanings [of the word *evarūpa*].
*Kantā*: desired or pleasing, just as in the word "pakkanta"; or it is a substitution for the final syllable of the word *māna*, meaning "that which is being desired.
Just as in the phrase "there is no offense for one who does not admonish," it is called *manāpā* because it applies or increases the mind (*manaṃ appeti vaḍḍheti*); thus it is said.
"Cittavuḍḍhikarā" means "acting in such a way. Therefore, in the phrase "of many people," the genitive case is used here in relation to the object, and not as an agent as in the previous instance.
Granted, the meaning intended to be expressed by them is possible; however, because it is fruitless, it is [treated] according to the figurative sense of the stated meaning.
He said, "meaningless" (*anatthaviññāpikā*), because there is indeed no meaning whatsoever.

Furthermore, it is also appropriate to say that speech is "meaningless" (*anatthā*) due to the absence of purpose, and that [idle chatter] makes such speech known. Idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*), so called because by means of it one prattles nonsense (*samphaṃ palapanti*).
"Cultivation" (*āsevanā*) means development (*bhāvanā*) and frequent practice (*bahulīkaraṇa*). When the person for whom it was intended to cause to grasp [the meaning] does not grasp it—
It is of slight offense when [the object] is not taken, but of great offense when it is taken.

Furthermore, the degree of slight or great offense should be applied according to the mildness or intensity of the defilements (*kilesa*). There is the account of the war between the two brothers named Bharata;
the account of the abduction of the queen named Sītā by the yakkha of Mount Daśagrīva; and the account of her recovery by King Rāma—just as these are [told] nowadays by outsiders.
“Idle chatter” (samphappalāpa) refers to such useless talk as familiarity with the Sanskrit language, knots [of rhetoric], and stories from the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, and other purāṇas;
thus it is said: “the *Mahābhārata*... [down to] ...prioritizing [them].

The passage beginning with “speaking at the right time” is a demonstration of the practice for one who abstains from idle chatter, just as [the following is] for one who abstains from the taking of life: “from the destruction of living beings...”

The passage beginning with “abstaining from” (*paṭivirato*) is a demonstration of the practice for the abandonment of the destruction of life. For when it is said, “He dwells having abandoned the destruction of life,” since a question may arise as to how that abandonment of the destruction of life occurs, it is stated: “He is abstaining from the destruction of life.
Furthermore, as to what that abstinence is, it is said: “one who has laid aside the rod, one who has laid aside the weapon. And that...

"How is the laying aside of the stick and weapons explained? This is stated by the passage beginning with "one who is conscientious" (*lajjī*). Thus, there is a demonstration of successive means for each preceding factor.
In the same way, this should be applied as appropriate to the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth. Therefore it was said:

"'One who speaks at the proper time,' etc., is a demonstration of the practice for one who abstains from idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*). For even speech that is beneficial may, through its application at an improper time, [fail to produce its intended result].

“May it not bring harm” accords with the state of indicating what is disadvantageous; therefore, in order to show that one who abandons idle chatter must avoid speaking at the wrong time, it is said, “one who speaks at the right time.
Even when speaking at the right time, because it does not accomplish the welfare of both [sides], one must avoid what is untrue;
thus he says, “one who speaks what is true. And for one who speaks what is true, that which brings about the attainment of welfare in this world and the next—
"That very thing should be spoken" is what is meant by "one who speaks of the goal" (*atthavādī*).

Even when speaking of the goal, one should not speak only that which is based on worldly phenomena (*lokīyadhamma*), but rather also that which is based on supramundane phenomena (*lokuttaradhamma*); thus he said "one who speaks of the Dhamma" (*dhammavādī*).
And in order to show how the goal is based on supramundane phenomena, it was said "one who speaks of the discipline" (*vinayavādī*).
When the meaning is explained by way of the fivefold discipline of restraint— namely, restraint by the Pātimokkha, and the restraints of mindfulness, knowledge, patience, and energy—
and by way of the fivefold discipline of abandonment— namely, abandonment as a factor, suppression, eradication, subsiding, and escape—
it is dependent on supramundane states because it serves as the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna.
To show that a subject endowed with such specific qualities shines when being taught, provided there is skill in teaching, and that it fulfills its function and not otherwise, it is said:
"He spoke words that were well-founded. Now, in order to clarify that very skill in teaching, he says "at the proper time," and so forth.
[This refers to] the scope of the teaching as it has been entered upon by way of the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*), the origin of the topic (*ṭhuppatti*), and the question (*pucchā*).

Having discerned the distinctions between categorical and other types of explanations, one who— through a teaching that is measured, well-defined, profound, sublime, abundant in meaning, extensive, and comprehensive—
clarifies the setting aside (*ṭhapanā*), the reasons (*hetu*), the examples (*dāharaṇa*), and the connections (*saṃsandanā*) according to the requirements of each occasion,
establishes others in the attainment of the ultimate goal (*paramattha-siddhi*) according to their respective inclinations, is called "skilled in teaching" (*desanā-kusala*).
In this case as well, the application of the meaning should be understood in this way.
"The time appropriate for what is to be said" means the time suitable for the words to be spoken, or the time when they ought to be employed therein.

He says "only the intrinsic nature" because it is real by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). One who speaks the meaning is an "expositor of the meaning" (*atthavādī*). And the speaking of the meaning...

It is stated with the intention that it refers precisely to speaking words based upon that [object], namely: "having made it dependent solely on benefits pertaining to the present life and the future life.
The same method applies to the phrases "one who speaks the Dhamma" (*dhammavādī*) and so forth.
It is called a "repository" (*nidhāna*) because one deposits or stores things therein; it is the place of placement. When the term "possessing a place" (*ṭhānavatī*) is used, in that...

The meaning "fit to be placed in its proper position" is also possible; thus he says, "in the heart," and so forth. Alternatively, even speech that is well-founded (*nidhānavatī*) brings benefit only when it is appropriate to the occasion;
therefore, by the words "of such a kind," etc., he shows that the phrase "by the right time" is a dependent statement referring back to the phrase "one who speaks well-founded speech.
It is that which should be referred to, or that which is referred to, for the purpose of producing the desired goal.

“Sāpadesā” (with a basis) means speech that exists together with a basis (*apadesa*)—that is, a desired object, a simile, or a cause such as a reason or an example. Therefore he said: “The meaning is ‘with a simile and with a cause.
“Having shown the delimitation” means having shown the boundary to the extent that a conclusion is possible; hence it was stated: “Just as... [etc. ...he speaks.”

For speech that has not reached its conclusion is not said to be "conducive to welfare. Regarding the phrase "connected with welfare" (*atthasaṃhita*), it is stated that the word *attha* here is a synonym for "the meaning expressed," as in the passage beginning with "even by many [words].

And what is called "the meaning expressed" includes everything attained by following the words—the meanings of roots, suffixes, nominal stems, case endings, and so forth; for this very reason, it is the word of the Blessed One.

"Even a single line of a verse, by virtue of its capacity for analysis through numerous methods—such as the concise and the detailed, unity and so forth, or the *nandiyāvatta* and other patterns—brings forth a meaning that cannot be exhausted.
Having thus commented upon it according to the commonality of its meaning, he says "Or rather...
and so forth, in order to comment upon it also according to the specific intended meaning. For here, only the meaning intended to be expressed by the speaker of the meaning is taken up.
He clears away the objection raised from within—that "surely the speech of everyone must be consistent with the meaning intended by themselves;

what is there to be said here?"—with the words beginning "not another," and so forth. The intention is this: having first set down one meaning, he does not later speak of another meaning without a logical connection (*ananusandhi*); rather, he concludes his discourse by following the very sequence established at the outset.
10. Having thus analyzed the seven root precepts in their proper order, and although the abandoning of covetousness and so forth is included within the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*),
the Blessed One set that aside and, in order to include the subsequent qualities, because they pertain to a sphere beyond that of ordinary worldly people,
and to analyze the morality of conduct (*ācāra-sīla*) which is well-known to common folk, he spoke the words beginning with, "From the destruction of seeds and plants."
The connection [of the terms] should be stated according to the Pāḷi. In this context, they are called *bījāni* (seeds) because things are born (*vijāyanti*) or grow (*viruhanti*) by means of them.

This is a designation for heartwood, fruit, and so forth, which are capable of growing because they serve as the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when combined with other conditions.

They are called *bhūtā* (beings) because they "come to be" (*bhavanti*) or "have been" (*ahuvuṃ*). The meaning is that they are born (*jāyanti*), increase (*vaḍḍhanti*), have been born (*jātā*), and have increased (*vaḍḍhitā*). [This refers to] those who are currently increasing.
"Having grown" (*vaḍḍhitvā*) and "standing" (*ṭhitānaṃ*) are, respectively, designations for trees, shrubs, and so forth.

For young trees and shrubs that have developed roots and attained a green state are said to be "born" (*jātā*) and "growing" (*vaḍḍhantī*); once they have grown and stand as large trees or shrubs, they are said to be "born" and "grown.
"Village" (*gāmo*) means a collection; and that is a heap of the eight pure factors, of seeds...
It is "thus" (*tathā*) because it is a village of eight types of beings who have received such designations, or because those very beings themselves constitute the village.
For since there is no whole apart from its parts, by either of these two meanings, those very same grasses, trees, creepers, and so forth are included.
Furthermore, trees, shrubs, and the like that have become green after being established upon the earth are understood to be possessed by deities.
Therefore, because it is a dwelling place for beings (*bhūta*), they also call it a "village of beings" (*bhūtagāma*). To show these [terms] according to their actual form, he says:
"Root-seed," and so forth. A root that is itself the seed is a "root-seed. This same method applies to the others as well. "Joint-seed" (*phaḷubīja*) means a node-seed (*pabbabīja*).
Because it is the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when other conditions come together, it is capable of growing.
The word *bīja* (seed), being established primarily in its literal sense, is applied to certain things such as roots and so forth for the sake of establishing that same meaning.

Therefore, in order to exclude [the application of] "seed" to roots and the like, it is specified by the term *bīja* itself as "*bījabīja*" (the seed of seeds), just as one says "*rūparūpa*" (form-form) or "*dukkhadukkha*" (suffering-suffering).
The phrase "of green grass, trees, etc. refers both to moist grass and to moist trees and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), medicinal herbs, shrubs, creepers, and so forth are to be understood. Here, "undertaking" (*samārambha*) means injuring;

and that consists specifically of cutting and so on, as stated in the phrase "by way of cutting, breaking, cooking, and so forth. But are not trees and the like not living beings (*jīva*) because they lack consciousness?
And their lack of consciousness is due to the absence of movement, because they grow back when cut, and because they belong to a different species [from sentient beings].

And they should be understood as not being included within the four modes of birth (*catuyoni*). Furthermore, since growth is found even in coral, stones, salt, and so forth, this is not a reason for them to possess the state of being living beings (*jīva*).
Moreover, their "grasping of objects" is merely a mental construction, like the sleep of *ciñcā* trees and the like;

likewise, their "longings" (*dohala*) due to bitter or sour tastes and so forth [are also mere constructions]. In that regard, why is it said: "from the destruction of seeds and the destruction of the community of beings" (*bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā*)?
Is abstinence desired? Yes, because it is befitting for a recluse and because it involves compassion for the sentient beings dependent upon those [trees].
For this very reason, regarding the instances of the Āḷavakas cutting down trees and so forth, it was said: "For people, O foolish men, perceive life in a tree," and so on.
*Ekabhatta* means a single meal; one who has that—eating only once in a single day—is an *ekabhattika*.
This was said with reference to when that single meal should be eaten, [as in] the phrase "the morning meal" (*pātarāsabhatta*) and so forth;
the intention is that he speaks with reference to the morning meal among the two meals. That which is to be eaten in the morning is *pātarāsa*;
that which is to be eaten in the evening is *sāyamāsa*, and that very meal is likewise [designated]. And here, the word "one" (*eka*) is used in the sense of delimiting the time to the midday period.
By the words beginning with “therefore,” he shows that [the meal] is not included within the scope of that [time].

The eating at night is expressed by the word *ratti* through the elision of the final member of the compound, or else by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), since such an intended meaning is possible;
therefore he says “at night,” and so forth. From the rising of the dawn until midday—this is [the time for the meal] of the Buddhas and others.
The time for eating is that which has been practiced as the habitual practice of the Noble Ones; any other time is "the wrong time" (*vikāla*).

In this context, since eating at night is prohibited by the second phrase, the third phrase is stated—"when midday has passed," etc.—to clarify the meaning of the third phrase by way of elimination (*pārisesanaya*), showing that here "the wrong time" refers specifically to the afternoon.
Furthermore, in this instance, the word *bhojana* (eating) functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).
By the phrase "as long as the sun has not set," he indicates that [the term] expresses the sense of "swallowing" (ajjhoharaṇa). But for what is there that swallowing?

Since the "time-for-a-watch" (yāmakālika) and other types of food are permitted, and because the word *vikālabhojana* (eating at the wrong time) is conventionally established only for the swallowing of "time-for-as-long-as-the-sun-has-not-set" (*yāvakālika*) food, it is understood to mean "of that which is for as long as the sun has not set.
This, however, is the remainder of the commentary according to the teachers.
The method is as follows: "Food" (*bhojana*) is so called in the sense of being something to be eaten;

it refers to all things that may be consumed during the proper time, such as rice gruel, boiled rice, and so forth. And just as in the expression "one who refrains from eating at night," the word "night" (*ratti*) denotes eating at night, so here the word "food" (*bhojana*) denotes the swallowing of food.

Eating at an improper time is "unseasonable eating" (*vikālabhojana*); [the term refers to] abstaining from that unseasonable eating. [It refers to] abstaining from consuming things that are proper for the proper time at an improper time.
"Consuming" is the meaning. To show that such an abundance of qualities does not exist only during the time of a Buddha, he says "on the bank of the Anomā River," and so forth.

Now, this is the sequence of the text: when it is said "eating one meal a day" because of eating only once in a single day, the term "refraining from food at night" is stated in order to exclude eating at night.
This being the case, [one might think] he is also a "sāyanhabhojī" (an evening eater).

The phrase "one should eat only one meal a day" was stated in order to prevent the misconception that [the rule] might apply at other times; thus, it is said "abstaining from eating at improper times.

In brief, because the Blessed One’s teaching—as set forth in the method beginning with "the non-doing of all evil"—is inconsistent with the viewing of dancing and so forth due to the occurrence of desire and lust, he says: "because it is not in conformity with the teaching. The teaching is purified.
It is called *visūka* because it pierces by way of being non-conformable; that is to say, it is "contrary.
He shows a simile for this with the phrase "become a *paṭāṇī*," the meaning of which is "become like a wedge known as a *paṭāṇī*.
Some also say that the meaning of the word *visūka* is "become a *paṭāṇī*. [This applies to] that which is set in motion by oneself and that which is caused to be set in motion by others.

In the Canon, dancing (*nacca*) is included by means of the single word *nacca* through the method of a general designation based on the commonality of the state of dancing, or else by the method of "one-remainder" (*ekasesa*).

Similarly, by the words *gīta* (song) and *vādita* (instrumental music), singing, causing to sing, playing instruments, and causing to play instruments are implied; thus he says, "by way of dancing, causing to dance, and so forth.

For these terms are intended in two ways, according to whether they indicate the pure cause or the associated factors. [The phrase refers to] dancing, song, instrumental music, and frivolous spectacles.

Regarding dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the viewing of spectacles, there is a unification here by way of their collective gathering. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the phrase "from dancing and...

(*naccā cā*) and so forth is stated in accordance with the reading of the text, for the purpose of demonstrating a copulative compound (*samuccaya-samāsa*) together with the word ending in the ablative case (*vākyāvatthika*).

This applies in all such instances. [This is because] by prohibiting the viewing of peacock dances and the like within the sphere of "seeing," it also prohibits the act of causing others to dance within that same sphere.
The rejection [of the objection] is to be understood as the substantiation of the meaning already stated by the phrase "dancing and so forth.
Furthermore, in this context, hearing is included within seeing by way of the grammatical principle of "residual inclusion of dissimilar items" (*virūpekasesa-naya*);

or rather, because the five types of consciousness have the nature of perceiving their respective objects, even the act of hearing can be subsumed under the term "seeing," hence the expression "by seeing" (*dassanā*).
Thus it was said. For this very reason he said: “By means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not acknowledge any state whatsoever, except for the mere occurrence [of the object].
By the phrase “and seeing that which has become a spectacle,” he shows that the hearing of song that is *not* a spectacle is sometimes permissible.
For it is likewise stated in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*: “Even that which is connected with the Dhamma...”
And here, singing is not permitted, but the Dhamma associated with song is permitted. In some places, however, a reading is seen with the inversion of the negative particle (*na*).
In both cases, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: if it is *gīta* (song), it is not permitted even if it is connected with the meaning that accords with the Dhamma;
but if it is *dhamma* (the Teaching), it is permitted even if it is connected with the word *gīta*. [As it is said: “Monks, one should not [recite] in a singing tone...”

"For the Dhamma is to be sung; whoever should sing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This is indeed a prohibition against teaching [the Dhamma] by way of singing, not against hearing it.
And because this training rule (sikkhāpada) is established separately, it is understood that "even the Dhamma taught with a melodic voice is not sung.
Furthermore, as for what was stated in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta while defining the terms "to be cultivated" and "not to be cultivated":

However, when it is said, "Even if one hears the songs of a slave-girl with a water-jar, if faith arises or disenchantment becomes established for one who listens to that which is based on the goal (attha) and based on the Dhamma,
such a sound should be cultivated," this was stated by way of the mere necessity of cultivating it for one who has not formally undertaken the training rule (asamādāna-sikkhāpada).
For regarding one who has formally undertaken the training rule (samādāna-sikkhāpada), even upon hearing such [sounds], there is the restraint of the training rule.
It should be understood that the nature of the sound of singing ceases [at the moment of contact]. For it is said in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathās: "As for 'song' (gīta):
whether it be the song of actors and the like; or the song of praise associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem sung at the time of the Noble Ones' Parinibbāna;
or the song of Dhamma-preachers by unrestrained bhikkhus; or even a tooth-song (dantagīta)—whatever [is intended] when one thinks, 'We shall sing'..."
"In the preliminary stage they produce the *okūjita* sound; all of this is called 'song' (*gīta*).
Although the word *mālā* in the world denotes bound flowers, in the Teaching it is used by convention for unbound flowers as well;
therefore, any flower whatsoever, whether bound or unbound, should be understood simply as "garland" (*mālā*).
He said: "Whatever flower. And here, "whatever fragrance" refers to any kind of fragrant substance other than ointments, such as perfumed powders, incense, and so forth.
For a word can express a specific meaning even when it is not mentioned alongside the meaning already stated.
"That which produces coloration of the skin" refers to any fragrant powder prepared by grinding for the purpose of coloring the skin with an ointment.

Adorning (*piḷandhana*) is wearing [ornaments]. Beautifying (*maṇḍana*) is filling out deficient parts. Embellishing (*vibhūsana*) is taking pleasure in them by means of perfumes and by means of the coloring of the skin.
He illustrates that very meaning by way of a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānena*), beginning with the words, "Therein, one who adorns," and so forth.
This is likewise stated in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*; however, in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*...
It is stated only thus: “In the case of garlands and so forth, wearing and so forth should be applied respectively.
Even there, by one who applies them, they must be applied according to the very method already stated. To the question, “What is the reason for this? he says: “By which,” and so forth.
That immoral volition by which one acts is the cause here. For the phrase “abstaining from that” must be connected to both instances; it is by this very [principle] that...
The phrase “the place for garlands... ornaments, or the garlands... ornaments themselves as the place” also demonstrates the state of equality.
For the mental factors such as volition (cetanā) that arise in that mode are themselves the act of wearing and so forth.

And therein, the cause of the factors associated with volition is by way of being co-nascent and supportive, and by way of being predominant. “Having willed, one performs an action by body or speech...”
For it is said, "by mind. And volition, being of the nature of retention and so forth, is the "basis" (*ṭhāna*).
The word *ṭhāna* should be construed with each [member] individually, because it is heard following a compound term (*dvandapada*).
As for "high," there is another word ending in *-ā* that has the same meaning as the word "high" (*ucca*) ending in *-a*, signifying something that has risen up very high.
He said, "Exceeding the measure. A *sayana* is that wherein one lies, such as a bed and so forth.

To show that what is intended here is an "unallowable great bed" (*mahāsayana*)—because it is devoid of suitability for a recluse and because it is esteemed as superior by householders—the term "unallowable covering" (*akappiyattharaṇa*) is used.
It should be understood, however, that the sitting mat (*nisīdana*) is included here by the very mention of the "bed."
Since, however, when the basis is prohibited, the action supported by that basis is also necessarily prohibited, it is therefore stated simply as "high and luxurious beds and seats.
In terms of meaning, it should be understood that the abstention from sitting and lying down—which constitute the enjoyment of those [beds and seats]—is thereby shown.
Alternatively, this designation "high and luxurious beds and seats" follows the method of single-remainder (ekasesanaya), just as in the expression "conditioned by name-and-form" (nāmarūpapaccayā).

Regarding this alternative interpretation, "the six sense bases" (*saḷāyatana*), it should be understood that because sitting precedes lying down, the act of lying down includes the act of sitting by the very mention of "lying down.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Vinaya-ṭīkā* that this is an instance of the elision of the latter member of a compound (*uttarapadalopaniddesa*) resulting from the elision of the words "sitting" (*āsana*) and "lying down" (*sayana*), which denote the actions themselves.
It is *jātarūpa* because its form, once born, does not change; it is gold-colored.
It is *rajata* because it is colored white, or because beings take delight (*rañjanti*) in it, as in the phrase "their circumambulation.
According to the definition stated—"four *vīhaya* make one *guñjā*, two *guñjā* make one *māsaka*"—it refers to a blue *kahāpaṇa* worth twenty *māsakas*, or a *dudradāmaka* coin, and so forth.
Or it is a coin (kahāpaṇa) made according to the conventional usage of various regions. That which is made from iron and so forth is an iron māsaka and the like.
"Those which enter into commerce" is an inclusive expression. And "commerce" refers to all forms of trade by way of buying and selling.
Since the sense of "accepting" is obtained in the cases of causing others to take [the goods] and consenting to what has been deposited as a pledge, he said: "he does not cause them to be taken up."
“Nor does one consent to what has been placed near. Alternatively, there are three kinds of acceptance:
by body, by speech, and by mind. Among these, acceptance by body is taking hold; acceptance by speech is causing to take hold; and acceptance by mind is consenting.
These three types of acceptance are understood either through a general designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*) or by the method of “taking one [from each]” (*ekasesanaya*).
Because it was stated [in the rule] as "acceptance," he said, "he does not accept it," and so forth. This same method applies to the phrases "acceptance of raw grain" and so on.

Since secondary grains such as *nīvāra* are included within the primary grains such as *sāli*, it is said, "even of the sevenfold [grain]. That which ripens in sixty days is a specific kind of excellent grain called *sāli*; it is so named because it is *salīyate*, meaning it is gathered or piled up. However, in the *Dabbaguṇapakāsa*:
"Now, grain is threefold, according to the division of *sāli*, *saṭṭhika*, and *vīhi*..."
"The *sāli* [rice] is harvested there in winter; the *saṭṭhika* [rice], even though born in summer;
while the *vīhi* [rice] is said to be harvested on the full moon of Āsāḷha, arising in the rainy season.
Thus it is said. It is called *vīhi* because it carries (*vahati*) or nourishes (*brūheti*) the life of beings; it is a crop. It is to be joined (*yuvitabbo*) or mixed (*missitabbo*).

*Yava*: This is indeed used by being mixed with other things because of its extreme dryness. *Godhuma*: It is called *godhūma* because it swallows (*gudhati*), consumes (*parivedhati*), and obstructs (*palibuddhati*);
it is also what they call "the food of the foreigners" (*milakkhabhojana*). *Kaṅgu*: It is called *kaṅgu* because it becomes desirable due to its beauty;
it is a specific type of very fine grain. *Varī*: It is called *varī* because it is excluded (*varīyati*) due to its extreme dryness, or because it wards off hunger (*khuddāpaṭivinayanato*).

It is called *varaka* because it is easily broken (*bhajīyati*). It is called *kudrūsaka* because it stains (*dūseti*) the blood; due to its change of color, it is also called "go-vaḍḍhana" (cow-increaser).
These seven types of grain, together with their varieties, are called "grains" (*dhaññāni*) because they are excellent for storage and nourishment.
By the phrase "not only this," etc., both the act of receiving and the act of touching are expressed here by the word "acceptance" (*paṭiggahaṇa*).
[The text] shows this. In such cases as these, because it was said: “Monks, I allow medicinal fats:
bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat,” these five kinds of medicine are called specifically permitted (*odissa-anuññāta*).
Furthermore, since it was stated that they must be “received at the proper time,” their acceptance is allowable.
He said, "Except for that which is specifically permitted. To show that by the word "meat" (maṃsa) the meat of fish is also included, it was stated as "raw meat and fish.

It should be understood that by this [statement], the method of "residual inclusion of dissimilar terms" (virūpekasesanaya) is demonstrated; for fish and meat that are pure in three respects—namely, not seen, not heard, and not suspected—are permitted, as shown by the description of the practice.
Granted that worldly people say:
"An eight-year-old is a *gorī*, a ten-year-old is a *kaññakā*;
when she has reached twelve years of age, she is designated as a *kumārī*."

They say this. However, here, because there is a distinction between women and girls based on whether or not they have gone to another man, he says: “A woman is one who has gone to another man,” and so forth.

“Only by way of female and male slaves” means only by way of the conventional designation (*vohāra*) of female and male slaves. “When spoken thus” means when spoken with such an allowable expression (*kappiya-vacana*).

The phrase “by way of the Vinaya” is stated with reference to the legal decisions (*vinicchaya*) found in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentaries on the Vinaya). That [decision] is to be found in the commentary on the training rule regarding the building of a hut (*kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada*), and elsewhere.
It is called a *khetta* (field) because seeds are sown therein, or because the seed sown therein is protected (*tāyati*). He says it is a "paddy field" (*kedāra*) because "in it the early crop grows.
"Early crop" (*pubbaṇṇaṃ*) refers to grain that was produced previously; by changing the letter *na* to *ṇa*, it means rice and so forth.

He shows the meaning of *vatthu* as "a site" (*vatthūti atthaṃ dasseti*) with the words "what is called a site," etc., in the sense that other crops dwell (*vasanti*) or are established (*patiṭṭhahanti*) therein.
“*Aparaṇṇa*” (other grain) refers to the subsequent crop of rice that grows after the first crop, according to the method already stated.

Having thus shown the meaning in accordance with the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he now says “*yattha vā*,” etc., showing the meaning also in accordance with the method of the Vinaya Piṭaka text which states:
“*Khettaṃ nāma yattha pubbaṇṇaṃ vā aparaṇṇaṃ vā jāyatī*. “*Tadatthāya*” means for the purpose of [obtaining] a field. “*Akatabhūmibhāgo*” means a portion of ground that has not been prepared.
The ground designated for that purpose is not measured out. By the phrase "with fields and lands as the foremost," he shows that this is merely an illustration;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), ponds, wells, and so forth are included.
It is called *dūteyya* because it belongs to a messenger, or because it is fit to be performed by a messenger. A *paṇṇa* is a written message. A *sāsana* is...
A "verbal instruction" (*mukhasāsana*) is when they go from one house to another house.

A "short journey" (*khuddakagamana*) means a journey shorter than going on an embassy; the meaning is a journey not on a long road, a brief journey. "Devotion" (*anuyoga*) is the application to both of these;
thus he says, "performing both. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because it is precisely the performance of both that constitutes devotion.
*Kayanaṃ* is *kāya*; it is the giving away of one’s own wealth by means of a succession [of transactions].
For they recite the word *kī-* in the sense of the exchange of goods: *vikkayanaṃ* is *vikko*. They say it is the very first giving away of one’s own wealth to others.
However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī* and other works, "purchase" (*kāya*) is defined as the taking of another's goods, while "sale" (*vikkāya*) is the [giving] of one's own goods.

It is said, "giving. This very [act] accords with the statement in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is 'bought' by one who brings another's goods into his own hand, and it is 'sold' by one who places his own goods into another's hand.
Deceit (*vañcanā*) is the practice of trickery; it is the taking of another's property through skill in means (*upāyakosalla*) by way of producing a semblance (*paṭibhāna*).
This has been stated. A "scale" (*tulā*) is that by which something is weighed or measured; cheating with that is called "cheating with the scale" (*tulākūṭa*).
Furthermore, when making such a scale, one does so by way of the shape concealed by the manner of grasping the material parts of the scale; thus its fourfold nature is stated. [The four ways are:
weighing by placing the goods to be taken by oneself at the rear end and those to be given to others at the front end.
He said: “While grasping at the rear,” and so forth. The connection is that it presses down and squeezes; it presses down at the front.
“At the root, a rope” means the rope attached to the root of the scale. Likewise at the tip. “That” refers to the copper powder.
It resounds (*kanati*) or shines (*dibbati*), thus it is *kaṃsa*; these are bowls for food and drink made of gold, silver, and so forth. But here, [it refers to] one made of gold.
Regarding "drinking bowl," he says "golden bowl. "Deception by means of that" refers to deception by way of trickery (*nikati*).
For "trickery" is the taking of another's property after showing something counterfeit; however, "deception" is the act of deceiving through the skillful use of means by way of producing a semblance.
Thus, the distinction between trickery and deception is stated in the *Kaṇha-jātaka-ṭīkā* and other commentaries; but here, both of these [are intended].
“Deception” (vañcanā) alone [is intended]. By the words “How? and so forth, he clarifies that it is precisely the taking of another’s property after displaying a semblance [of it].
“Of equal value” (samagghataraṃ) refers to the mutual difference in value among those bowls. Regarding “on a stone”: on a stone capable of discerning whether something is real gold or not.
Since the recognition of its being gold is established by the very act of rubbing, he says simply “having rubbed.”

*Hadaya-bheda*: The interior of vessels such as *nāḷi* measures; the breaking of that [interior], the making of a hole, is "breaking of the heart" (*hadaya-bheda*). *Sikhā-bheda*: At the time of measuring sesame seeds and so forth with *nāḷi* measures and the like, the very peak that has been raised up is the "peak";
the breaking of that, the diminishing of it, is "breaking of the peak" (*sikhā-bheda*). *Rajju-bheda*: The breaking of the rope, the making of it uneven, is "breaking of the rope" (*rajju-bheda*).

"Those" refers to the ghee, oil, and so forth. "In the vessel" means in the vessel where they were first placed. "Having raised up" means having caused to rise; it is said, "having made a heap above. "Cutting" means removing.
*Ukkoṭana* is the reopening or overturning of a legal act that has already been performed.

It refers to the taking of bribes by those who act untruthfully, and not merely the reopening of a case for further proceedings; thus he says, "the taking [of bribes] from those who are not owners... and so forth.

"By means" (*upāyehi*) refers to methods that appear to be legitimate reasons. "Therein" (*tatra*) means in that deception. By saying "one matter" instead of simply "matter," he indicates that there are others as well.
He shows that there are many [such instances]. For other examples, such as those concerning the hare and so forth, are also mentioned here and there.

"A deer" (*miga*) means a large deer. "Therefore" (*tena hi*) is an exhortation to catch the deer; or rather, the meaning is: "for the reason that he said, 'Give me a deer,' for that reason. The word *hi* is a mere particle.
"By way of application" (*yogavasena*) means by way of the practice of incantations, muttering spells, and so forth.

"By means of illusion" (*māyāvasena*) means by means of an eye-deluding illusion that causes even what is unreal to appear as if it were real, without the recitation of mantras—by means of which even things that are not jewels appear in the form of jewels and so forth.

A *pāmaṅga* is a particular kind of ornament appropriate to the customs of one's family, which is called "the sacrificial thread" (*yaññopavitta*) in the world. This is also stated in the *Therāpadāna* of the Elder Vakkali:
“Behold this young man, wearing a bright yellow robe, his limbs adorned with golden sacrificial ornaments, captivating the eyes of the people.
Regarding this, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) also states: “Wearing a bright yellow robe means he was clothed in garments of smooth, golden color.”
The meaning is as follows: *hemayaññopavittaṅgaṃ* means "one whose limbs are adorned with golden ornaments," such is the meaning. *Savanaṃ* is crookedness;
it is a lack of straightness, hence he says "crooked application" (*kuṭilayogo*), which means the application of curvature.

With the words "of these very [factors]," etc., he demonstrates the grammatical coreferentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇatā*). "Therefore," etc., shows the qualities thus acquired. As for those who [interpret] all four terms...
They state that there is a difference in the grammatical locus (*bhinnādhikaraṇatā*); he states their argument with the words beginning “some” (*keci*).

Therein, “some” refers to the teachers who composed the *Sārasamāsa* and those residing at Uttaravihāra; he shows by means of the passage beginning “that, however,” that this is not correct for them, because what was already included by way of deception is taken up again.
"Killing" (*māraṇa*) is spoken of with reference to harming and injuring by means of blows with the fist, slaps, and so forth; it does not, however, refer to the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
For the word "killing" (*vadha*) is seen even in the sense of injuring, as in such passages as, "Having killed oneself again and again, one might weep.
It should be understood that here too, the word "killing" (*māraṇa*) refers specifically to injury. Some, however, [claim] that previously... [the taking of life].

Regarding the statement, "In such passages as 'having abandoned,' it is one's own effort; here, it is the effort of another," it is not possible to say so, because it has been stated that "the volition which originates bodily and verbal application constitutes the six types of effort.

For just as, despite the commonality of being unaccepted, women, boys, female slaves, male slaves, and so forth, are specified individually in order to demonstrate the specific things that must not be accepted by those who have gone forth; [so too is this case].

It has been stated. And just as, although there is a commonality in the nature of taking what is not given due to the act of seizing another's property, the specific instances such as cheating with scales and so forth are stated separately for the purpose of demonstrating those particular types of *adinnādāna*, there is no purpose in mentioning again "killing" (*vadha*)—which is synonymous with "taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*)—because there is nothing further to be analyzed in that manner. Therefore, the meaning as it was already stated is indeed more excellent.
*Viparāmoso* means causing one to be thoroughly and completely deluded or bewildered on all sides, or it means stealing. For *theyya*, *corikā*, and *moso* are synonyms.
That [stealing] is of two kinds according to its cause; thus he said, "theft by way of concealment" (*himaviparāmoso*), and so forth.
"They steal" (*musanti*) means they rob, or they cause delusion (*mosenti*); that is to say, having caused delusion, they take what belongs to those [owners].
And they involve the grasping of that action. Even in the case of others, there is the qualification "people who have set out on the path.
*Ālopa* means plundering or seizing. *Sahasākāra* means acting with haste. That which proceeds with haste is *sāhasika*; such is the nature of that action.
By "to this extent" is meant the full measure beginning with "having abandoned the taking of life" and ending with "abstaining from acting with haste."

By way of recitation: without taking into account internal subdivisions, this virtue—which comprises twenty-six training rules (sikkhāpada) exactly as they appear in the text—is called "the minor virtue" (cūḷasīla) because, for the most part, the training rules have not been analyzed.

Indeed, here the status of being "minor," "intermediate," and so forth should be understood by way of the teaching (desanā), not by way of the actual phenomena (dhamma). For it is thus that those [rules] which were briefly indicated here...
The teaching on the middle morality was set forth by way of analyzing the training rules that had not yet been analyzed; for this very reason, it says: "expounding the middle morality in detail.
The commentary on the Minor Morality is finished.
The commentary on the Middle Morality.
11. With the words “Or just as some venerable ones,” and so forth, he states the connection to the teaching with the words “Now,” and so on.

Herein, this is the method not found in the commentaries: *yathā* is a particle used in the sense of a simile; *vā* is used in the sense of an alternative. By means of that, he presents this alternative meaning:
“Even though an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), having exerted effort, speaks in praise of me, he has abandoned the taking of life and abstains from the taking of life,” and so forth.
Or, according to the method of indirect indication (*parānuddeśika-naya*), one might say that in every respect he possesses only the morality of conduct (*ācāra-sīla*) and nothing beyond that.

"Unlike many other venerable recluses and brahmins who, while claiming the status of such and being so regarded by others, fail to achieve it because they neither know nor are capable of the corresponding practice—this one is not like them. Indeed, this recluse Gotama..."

"In every respect, he would surely fulfill the practice befitting a recluse"—thus, by way of a general indication (*aññuddesika-naya*), one might say that he possesses only the mere virtue of conduct (*ācāra-sīlamatta*) in every respect, and nothing beyond that.
The word *pana* is a poetic ornament (*vacanālaṅkāra*) used for the purpose of providing an alternative;
since the meaning of "introduction" and so forth is established by this very sense of optionality. *Eke* means "others. Some also say it means "some. *Bhonto* refers to the virtuous (*sādhūnaṃ*).
“Beloved of the gods” (*piyasamudāhāro*). For virtuous people address others as “sirs,” “beloved of the gods,” or “venerable ones.
Regarding “ascetics and brahmins”: anyone who has entered the life of renunciation is an ascetic (*samaṇa*); and by virtue of birth alone, one is a brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*).
As for “faith” (*saddhā*), he says “action and so forth” because faith here refers to the four bases [of confidence]. It is precisely through the connection between action and its result that...
Faith in this world and the world beyond should be understood as the conviction that "herein action ripens, and the fruit of action must be experienced.
To clarify this meaning through the method of contrast (byatireka), he says, "This [merit] is mine," and so forth. "He will repay" means he will perform a counter-favor.
To substantiate that very point, he says, "For gifts given in such a way," and so on; this is stated as an illustration, making the primary principle the general heading of the teaching.
Therefore, it is said, "But as to its meaning," and so forth, to point out the fourfold condition.
The word *seyyathidaṃ* is a single particle, or rather a collection of particles, used in the sense of "which is this?

And by means of that [word], in the phrase "the destruction of seeds, plants, and living beings," although the seeds, plants, and living beings are subordinate according to the sequence of the words, [they are nevertheless indicated].
It is pointed out as if it were the primary factor among those things that ought to be analyzed. For the sequence of words is one thing, while the sequence of meanings is another;
thus he said, "What is that seed-life and vegetation-life? For when that [life] is analyzed, the undertaking directed toward its objects is also analyzed.
Indeed, it was said, "They dwell devoted to the undertaking of which," in order to show this meaning. Therefore...

And it is indicated in the Pāli by the passage beginning with “root-seed” (*mūlabīja*) and so forth. “Root-seed” (*mūlabīja*) means either that the root itself is the seed, or that its root is the seed;
thus there are two meanings here. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Therefore, one should not raise the objection:
“Why is it that, having asked about both the ‘seed-group’ and the ‘being-group,’ only the seed-group is analyzed? For in that context...
By the first meaning, the category of seeds (*bījagāma*) is indicated; by the second, the category of beings (*bhūtagāma*).

This twofold division should be understood as being indicated either by a general designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*)—that is, "root-seed and root-seed" [repeated] as "root-seed"—or by the method of single-remainder (*ekasesanaya*).
For this very reason, he will say: "All this," and so forth. *Ativisa* means that which is exceedingly poisonous (*ativisa*), or that which consists of excessive poison (*ativisā*).
That which is called “Mahosadha,” also known as *kacchaka* or *kāḷakacchaka*, and what they call *pilakkha*. *Kapitthana* is a white tree with sour buds and fruit.
For it is called *kapitthana* because it shakes or moves (*kampati calati*)—the suffix *-thana* being added to the root *kamp*;
or else, *kapi* means a monkey, and since its fruit resembles the breast (*thana*) of a monkey, it is called *kapitthana*. [Some say] “*Kapitthana* is the *pippali* tree.”
For this is stated in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*: "Phaḷubīja" means a bamboo seed. "Ajjaka" means white basil. "Phaṇijjaka" means coriander. "Hirivera" means cucumber.

He shows that the word "seed" (*bīja*) is conventionally used for a substantial fruit capable of sprouting, because it serves as the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when combined with other conditions, by saying: "only that which is capable of sprouting."
By this [phrase]. For the other [kind of plant] has reached the status of being seedless, and that only when it has been separated from the tree.
However, if it is not separated, whether it exists in that state or otherwise, it is called a "community of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*) according to the second sense already mentioned.
By the words beginning with "therein," he shows their distinction in accordance with the Vinaya. What should be said regarding this has already been stated above.
12. *Sannidhānaṃ* means storing (*sannidhi*). That which is done by means of this is *sannidhikāra*, namely food, drink, and so forth.
Thus, with reference to the sense of the object (*kamma*) inherent in the word *kāra*, it is said: "consumption of what has been stored" (*sannidhikāraparibhoga*). This is another method:

just as when one ought to say "leading to accumulation" (*ācayaṃ gāmino*), the designation "leading to accumulation" (*ācayagāmino*) is made by eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*), so too here [the term *sannidhikāra* is used].
Where "paribhoga" (use) should have been said, it is stated as "sannidhikāraparibhoga" through the elision of the nasal vowel;
the meaning is "use after having made a store. "By way of the Vinaya" means by way of the conduct established in the Vinaya.

For the conduct established in the Vinaya is called "Vinaya" through the elision of the latter member [of the compound], or else "Vinaya" is the disciplining (*vinayana*) of body and speech. Regarding the practice according to the method of the Suttantas:

Because it is mentioned separately, only the conduct of the Vinaya (vinayācāra) is understood here. Because "effacement" (sallekha)—defined as "it correctly scrapes away the defilements"—is also mentioned separately, it refers specifically to the practice according to the method of the Suttas.
"Received" means received by means of the body or by means of something connected to the body. "On the following day" means on another day. "Having given" means by way of exchange.
"Having given. And "having had [it] set aside" means having had it set aside by making it one's own property.

It is permissible for them also to use that which belongs to them by way of receiving it on trust and so forth. According to the method of the Suttas, there is simply the refinement (*sallekha*) [of the mind].
And as for "those things which are suitable for them," herein [there are]: the juice of grain that is suitable, the juice of *madhuka* flowers, and the juice of ripe *ḍāka* vegetables.
Excluding those [specific items], it should be understood that all remaining fruits, flowers, leaves, and juices are "drinks in accordance with the rule" (*anulomapāna*);
the meaning is that they have not been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assigned (*vikappita*) at the time of their delimitation.

It is called *sannidhi* because it is stored; it refers to the substance itself. It is called *pariyāya* because it is made allowable (*kappīyati*); this is according to the formula for making things allowable (*kappiyavācā*).

"Practice" refers to his way of speaking; thus, it is "figurative discourse" (*pariyāyakathā*). Its opposite is "non-figurative" (*nippariyāya*): practice that consists in contentment without even resorting to what is permissible.
Alternatively, the word *pariyāya* means "cause"; therefore, discourse spoken by way of a permissible cause is "figurative discourse.
Without mentioning even that, discourse spoken by way of contentment is "non-figurative. "If," and so forth.
This is the demonstration of another mode of giving. *Uddesa* is the recitation of the text; *paripucchana* is the inquiry into its meaning.

By the phrase "it is not permissible not to give," he shows that non-giving causes the agitation of one's spiritual refinement (*sallekha*). "When there is insufficiency" means when it is insufficient for the purpose.
"In expectation" means in expectation of obtaining a robe. "At the permitted time" refers to, when the Kathina has not been spread, the single month of the latter Kattika.

When the *kathina* has been spread, the period permitted by the third *kathina-sikkhāpada* and other rules consists of the four winter months together with the last month of the Kattika season, and whichever single month occurs during the subsequent period (*piṭṭhisamaya*). "Sutta" refers to the thread for sewing robes.
"Having performed a formal act of the Vinaya" means having determined the basic robe as a requisite cloth, [and then] the expected robe itself.
Having made it the basic robe, it must be set aside; that [robe] again receives the one-month grace period.

By this method, as long as one wishes, one may continue to set aside successive robes as basic robes, according to the stated rule, or by performing a formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) through the process of assignment (*vikappanā*).
Why is it not permitted? He says: "Because there would be both storage (*sannidhi*) and the destruction of austerity (*sallekha*)."
A *vayha* is a vehicle made by covering [the frame] with planks like a pavilion above, or entirely enclosed on all sides.
A *sandamānikā* is one constructed in the manner of Garuḷa’s wings, with crossbeams (*gopānasi*) made of gold, silver, and so forth, provided on both sides.
A *sivikā* is a palanquin made of wooden boards and the like. A *pāṭaṅkī* is a small cloth bag known as an *antolikā*. "For a single bhikkhu... [and so forth].
“Hī” and so forth is the substantiation of that meaning. “For the sake of going to the forest” means for the purpose of traveling to the wilderness (*arañña*).
“For the sake of protecting washed feet” means for the purpose of preserving feet that have been washed. “*Saṅghāṭā*” means they should be joined or bound together;

thus, sandals themselves are *saṅghāṭā*. The meaning is: sandals that are joined in pairs. “They should be given to another”—here, the manner of giving should be understood according to the method already stated.

"Mañca" (bed) is merely an illustration; for all items such as stools, couches, and so forth, which are suitable for sitting or lying down, should be included, since one must behave in the same manner toward them as well.
By the phrase "when there is an affliction such as scabs, itch, or skin diseases," he shows that only those perfumes which are to be used by oneself for the sake of curing a disease are permissible.
Indeed, it was already stated above that "when a characteristic [of a cause] is present, the sense of 'cause' (hetu) can also apply in certain instances."
In this context, *kaṇḍū* means itch. *Kacchū* means scabies. *Chavidoso* refers to skin diseases such as leprosy (*kilāsa*).

"Having had it brought" means having it brought either from what has been set aside for relatives, or by way of the practice of alms-round, or by any other means whatsoever. It is also permissible to request medicinal requisites for one who is ill.
[The Buddha said: "Monks, I allow you, having taken perfume, to apply it as a five-finger mark on the door."
Because of the statement, "having taken a flower, one should place it to one side in the monastery," the words "at the door" and so forth were spoken.

Incense for the house is the perfuming of the monastery, or the perfuming of the shrine room (*cetiyaghara*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), offerings to the shrine (*cetiyapūjā*) and images (*paṭimāpūjā*) and so on are included.
It is called "fleshly" (*āmisa*) because it can be touched by defilements; it refers to any object worthy of enjoyment. Therefore, even for those things already mentioned...
In order to prevent an unwarranted extension [of the rule], he said, "the remainder of what has been stated should be understood.

The intention is that because it is grasped by way of the method of elimination (pārisesanaya), the remainder of what has been stated should be understood. As for the question "What, then, is this?", he said, "That is to say" (*seyyathidaṃ*), and so forth.

"At such a time" refers to a time when it is difficult to enter a village, and so on. "Dried meat" (*vallūra*) means dried flesh. The word "vessel" (*bhājana*) [is used] together with the words for ghee, oil, and molasses...
It should be applied because of its inseparable connection with that. "At the very time" means even before. "In water and mud" refers to both water and mud.

This locative case is used either in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*) or as a characteristic of a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇa*). "Stay" means sit down. "Even while eating" means while the bhikkhu is indeed eating;
this is a dative of the recipient (*sampadāna*), or it is a genitive used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*), due to its connection with the exclusion of other actions.
"Herein, there is disregard. *Gīvāyamakaṃ* is a term in the neuter abstract form;
the meaning is "having stretched out the neck, having made it extended," or alternatively, it is also permissible to take it as "just as the neck must be stretched due to overeating after a meal.
*Catumāsampi* means "even for four months of the year. *Kuṭumbaṃ* is said to mean wealth; one who possesses that is a *kuṭumbika*. *Muṇḍo*...
And he is a householder who has shaved his head—a "shaven-headed householder"—meaning he makes his living by doing that.
This should be understood as merely an illustration of the bases for storing up, which are shown here by the term "worldly gain" (*āmisa*).
Showing the practice of a recluse that is free from those [bases], he said, "But for a bhikkhu," and so forth. In that context, "a lump of sugar... [and so on].
"In the size of a ripe palm fruit," so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. "The measure of a fourth part" is said to be the measure of a *kuṭumba*.
However, because it is stated as "one stalk of rice," they say that a fourth part of that is one *pattha*. And it is said:
"One *kuḍuva* is a *pasata*; four of those would be a *pattha*."
"Four *pattha* make one *āḷhaka*, or four *āḷhaka* make one *doṇa*.
Why is it said, "For those," and so forth? It is permissible to set it aside even after having it brought; how much more so when it is obtained as it happens.
By the phrase "at a time of discomfort," etc., he shows that the consumption of what has been set aside with a pure mind does not disturb one's austerity (*sallekha*).

The four types of huts, beginning with the *sammutikuṭikā*, or the five huts including the Uposatha hall and others that serve as non-residential buildings—referring to these, it is said, “the kappiyakuṭī,” and so forth.
There is no “storing” (*sannidhi*) there, because it is permitted to have food grown or prepared inside.
By the words “of the Tathāgata,” and so forth, he applies the meaning according to the context. “A piece of rags” (*pilotikakhaṇḍa*) means a fragment of worn-out cloth.
13. By the phrase “having stretched out the neck,” he shows that there is no fault when [the object] comes into range on its own.

“Even this much” refers to both the investigation of the legal definition (*vinicchaya*) and the description of the subject matter (*vatthu*). “Merely the purpose” means merely the application of the word-meanings (*padattha*).
However, for those words whose meaning cannot be understood without an extensive commentary (*vitthārakathā*), an extensive commentary is also provided.
It falls under the category of the literal meaning (*padattha*).
It is called *pekkha* because it is to be watched out of curiosity; it is a performance according to the rules of the dramatic art (*naṭasattha*).

However, it is called "the assembly of actors" (*naṭasammajja*) because it is to be performed by a group of actors before a multitude of people. It is formed in the sense of a gathering (*sammada*) or assembly (*samūha*) of people.
Indeed, [it refers to] the sweeping. In the *Sārasamāsa*, however, they also say "we shall see" (*pekkhāma*);

in their opinion, the meaning is "the tradition of seeing the sweeping. It is a narrative (*akkhāna*) because the battles and other events of the two royal brothers named Bhārata and of King Rāma must be recounted by those devoted to them.
It is not even proper to go there, much less to listen to it. With the hand...

Regarding the phrase "the sound of striking with the hand" (*pāṇissara*), he says it is "the bronze cymbal" (*kaṃsatāḷa*). *Kaṃsa* is a specific type of musical instrument made of metal, or a metal bowl;
the meaning is "the sound of striking that. With reference to the meaning "the sound of striking with the hands," they also say "hand-striking" (*pāṇitāḷa*).
"Striking the specific musical instruments known as *ghana*" is called "solid-striking" (*ghanatāḷa*).
A drum made of wood or a slab of stone. "With a mantra" means with a mantra for exorcising spirits. "Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa* and the residents of the Uttaravihāra;
as it is here, so it is in all subsequent instances where "some" occurs. They, it is said, were proponents of a specific commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
A "square drum" (*caturassa-ambaṇaka*) is that which [is struck] upon the heartwood of a tree trunk or similar materials.
Someone makes a square vessel (*ambaṇa*), covers its four sides with leather in accordance with the rules, and beats it as a musical instrument.
Because it possesses a specific shape and measurement of eleven *doṇas*, it is called an "ambaṇaka"; *bimbisaka* is also a name for that same object.

Likewise, because of its jar-like shape, it is called a *kumbha* (jar), or simply a *ghaṭa* (pot); the reciters of the Minor Collection (*Khuddakabhāṇakas*) call it a "shaking" (*dhunana*) of that [vessel].

*Abbhokkiraṇaṃ* means the making of colored offerings (*raṅgabalikaraṇaṃ*). For they play in a dancing place after having made what is called an offering to the deities, which is also called "joy" (*nandī*).
*Paṭibhānacittaṃ* (pictorial art) is called *sobhanakaraṃ* because it makes things beautiful by producing images that give rise to defilements such as the union of men and women;
this is stated in the *Sārasamāsa* as "the beautiful house" (*sobhanagharakaṃ*). *Caṇḍāya*... [text fragment]
*Caṇḍālaṃ*: the game of the iron ball. *Caṇḍāla* refers to those of low birth who eat the flesh of dogs; their game is called *caṇḍālaṃ*.
*Sāṇadhovanakīḷā*: the game of washing hemp, which is a game of beating one another after soaking the hemp in water.
Regarding *vaṃsaṃ*, he says it is a game made with a bamboo pole, meaning "playing by raising up a bamboo."
"Having buried" means having dug it into the ground. "At the time of the constellations" means at the time of the festival for the conjunction of the constellations.
Confirming this meaning by means of the text of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Dasaka-nipāta*, he said, "And this has also been said," and so forth. "Therein" refers to that washing of the bones.
"With a magical net" (*indajālena*) means having recited the incantation for washing the bones, such that others [perceive] only bones.
They see [the forms], not the flesh and so forth; thus, it is by means of the illusion (*māyā*) that causes the disappearance of the flesh and so forth.
Because it is capable of concealing things like Indra’s net (*indajāla*), illusion is called "Indra’s net," just as in the case of Indra’s bow (the rainbow) and other such phenomena.
"Bathing the bones" refers to the game of bathing the bones. "To fight with elephants and so forth" means mounting upon elephants and so forth to engage in combat with others.
This is said with reference to fighting by oneself against elephants and so forth;

the meaning is: either to cause others to fight against elephants and so forth, or to fight by oneself. "Them" refers to the elephants and so forth. "Mallas" are those who wrestle, who strike and crush one another;
their combat is the *sampahāra*, which is battle (*saṅgāma*). It is the vanguard of the army.
*Balagga*: That in which they perform the calculation of units is *balagga*; it is a place for counting the forces, such as "there are so many elephants, so many horses," and so forth.
*Senābyūha*: It is where they arrange the army by dividing it and placing it; or, it is the arraying and deployment of the army.
Thus, *senābyūha* refers to the specific positions within the fourfold army for the purpose of battle, such as "let the elephants be here, let the horses be there," and so forth.

The place for deliberation; furthermore, by way of its divisions, it consists of the chariot-array (*sakaṭabyūha*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the wheel-array (*cakkabyūha*), the lotus-array (*padumabyūha*), and the arrays known as the staff (*daṇḍabyūha*), the coil (*bhogabyūha*), the circle (*maṇḍalabyūha*), and the compact (*asaṃhatabyūha*).
[As for the army: "Three elephants constitute the rear elephant-force (*hatthānīka*);
three horses constitute the rear horse-force (*assānīka*); three chariots constitute the rear chariot-force (*rathānīka*); four men with swords in hand..."

Regarding the phrase "the foot-soldiers as the rear army," he said, "stated in the manner beginning with 'three... with reference to the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) on the training rule concerning being pierced by an arrow.
Furthermore, this should be understood according to the enumeration of elephants and so forth based on the definition stated thus:
"a chariot consists of twelve men, a horse of three men, a carriage of four men, and a foot-soldier consists of four men equipped with spears."
By this, he rejects the army formation described in the commentary on the *Cammakkhandhaka* as "six female elephants and one male elephant—this is one [unit].
14. "Cause" (*kāraṇa*) is said to be the ground for a result, as stated: "negligence... is a cause. "Footprints" (*padāni*) refers to the footprints of Sārī and others.
"Eight-footed" (*aṭṭhapada*) is due to the length of the designation; they also read it as "aṭṭhapada. "Ten-footed" (*dasapada*).
"Played with twenty pieces" refers to the game played with twenty pieces (*jūta*). "On eight-padded or ten-padded [boards]" means on gaming boards consisting of eight or ten squares.

"Playing in the air alone" refers to playing the game in the air itself by those who say only with their mouths, "This piece has been moved by me to such-and-such a square; this one to such-and-such a square.
"Various paths and circles" refers to the winding of many different types of paths for the pieces.
“Pariharitabbaṃ” means that which is fit to be moved by the *sāris*. They are called *sāris* because they move about, being remembered (or kept in mind) here and there;
they are seeds for dice made of any material whatsoever. “Tattha” means in those *sāris*, or in that process of removing and placing them.
“Jūtakhalikā” means on the gambling board (*jūtamaṇḍala*). Nowadays, the reading is also “jūtaphalake. “Pāsakaṃ” refers to the six [dice].

Having shown one to six [squares] in the compartments, they play with what has been made; then, increasing that, they play by removing and placing back the pieces according to what they have obtained, starting from one and so on.
It is called *pāsaka* because it "binds" (*bādhati*) and "touches" (*phusati*) in the eight-square board and other such games;
it is a twenty-four-fold die (*akkha*). With reference to this, it was said:
“The Aṭṭhaka is said to be the Mālika, and the Sāvaṭṭa is considered the Chaka;
the Catukka should be known as the Bahula, and the Dvibindu as the Santibhadraka;
these twenty-four meters were proclaimed by the Lord of Sages.”
The game played with that here is the *pāsaka*-game (dice-game). Striking is the hitting; the play with that is the *ghaṭikā* (club-game), which is why he says, "with a long stick," and so forth.
Some say that the *ghaṭikā* is the game played with a *ghaṭa* (water-pot) or a *kumbha* (jar).

"With madder" (*mañjiṭṭhikāya vā*) refers to taking the heartwood of the *yojanavalli* tree known as madder, speaking with reference to its fermented decoction. "With rice-water" (*sitthodakena vā*)—[or with flour-water, according to the commentary].
And *pakkamadhusitthodakaṃ*. "With a handful of counting-sticks" (*salākahattha*) is a designation for a bundle of palm-leaf slips and so forth.

Some say that they play with a "handful of counting-sticks" by taking one counting-stick that is indistinguishable from many others, inserting it among them, and then drawing out that very same one again.
"Ball-play" (*guḷakīḷā*) is ball-and-board play, or [play] with anything whatsoever.
The game of clay balls (*kataguḷakīḷā*). A tube made from a leaf in the shape of a bamboo is a "leaf-tube" (*paṇṇanāḷikā*); for this reason, he says "blowing through it" (*taṃdhamantā*).
By the phrase "small plough" (*khuddakanaṅgala*), he shows that the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of "small.

It is called a "swinging-cradle" (*mokkhacikā*) because by means of its release—that is, the loosening of the hands and feet—one moves or turns about; therefore, he says "or in the air," and so forth. Precisely because of this whirling motion...
To show that it is called a "wheel" (cakkam), the term "revolving wheel" (paribbhamanacakkam) is used.
A tube made of leaves is a "leaf-tube" (paṇṇanāḷi); by this, he shows the respective synonyms for the two terms *patta* and *āḷhaka*.

Furthermore, the game played with that [tube] is called "leaf-tube" (*pattāḷhaka*); thus it is said, "by that," and so forth. A small chariot is a "chariotlet" (*rathaka*), due to the elision of the letter *k-a*.
Because it consists of speaking small things. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
*Akkharikā* is a game played by knowing that "it is thus" through writing a syllable either in the air, on the back of someone, or in some other manner;
they also say it is a game for knowing what has been lost or found, such as a pearl, by taking the syllable that comes to the mouth of the questioner. The word *vajja*...

The phrase "in the sense of an offense" is expressed by the words, "that which is called 'according to the fault' (*yathāvajjaṃ*)," and so forth. They also say that "according to the fault" refers to dancing or singing in accordance with the musical accompaniment.

One should understand that even activities such as the *parihārapatha* (the path of evasion) constitute grounds for negligence through gambling when performed with the aim of victory or defeat, thinking, "If it is done in this way, there will be victory;
if it is done in that way, there will be defeat. This applies to games involving pieces such as the *paṅgacīra* (the "limb-cloth").
The accomplishment or non-accomplishment of the task to be performed with bamboo and other materials is called a "game" (payoga) because it brings about victory or defeat;

and it is described as being "like dice" (yathāvajja) because, through the display of similar forms such as the "one-eyed" (kāṇa) and so forth, it functions as a game of dice by way of victory and defeat.
All these [terms] illuminate—that is, they make manifest—those things associated with that practice by way of victory and defeat, and they "move" (javanti), meaning they proceed.
Or, in the sense that "one wins or loses by means of these," they do not exceed the status of being denotable by the word *jūta* (gambling).
15. "A seat exceeding the proper measure" refers to a seat that exceeds the measure stated as: "It should be made with feet eight finger-breadths long according to the Sugata-finger.
Regarding the purpose of the action, it is said [they] "dwell devotedly," in consideration of this phrase.
It has been stated. "Forms of beasts" (*vāḷarūpāni*) refers to imported forms of beasts such as lions, tigers, and so forth. For it is said in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*:
"A couch (*pallaṅka*) is one made with imported beasts"; and in the *Sārasamāsa* it is said: "A couch (*pallaṅka*) is an improper bed (*akappiyamañca*) cluttered with improper forms.
A "great woolen rug with long hair" (*dīghalomako mahākojava*) is a black-colored great woolen rug whose hair exceeds four finger-breadths in length.
What is called *pathavī*? It is that upon which one moves (*javati*) by way of its being beautiful and spread out; thus it is a *kojava*.

Because of the statement, "It is said that its hairs are more than four finger-breadths long," they say it is permissible [to use] what is below four finger-breadths. The terms *uddalomī* (with hair pointing upward) and *ekantalomī* (with hair on one side) are for the purpose of showing a distinction;
therefore, if something does not fall under those two categories, it should be understood as permissible. *Vānavicittaṃ* (variegated by weaving).
It is variegated by means of this weaving in the form of wall-coverings and the like, or by means of stitching. An *uṇṇāmaya-attharaṇa* is a coverlet made from animal hair.
A *setattharaṇa* is a white coverlet; it is called a white coverlet because it should be used by those who require coolness, and they also say it is "made of very soft wool.
A *ghanapupphaka* is one that possesses the appearance of flowers in every respect. [The text repeats: "An *uṇṇāmaya-attharaṇa* is made of wool."
"It has a red covering"—this is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. Because it is mostly made with rows of flowers having the shape of *āmalaka* leaves, it is also called "the *āmalaka*-leaf [bed]".
"Of the three kinds of cotton" refers to the three types of cotton known as tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and silk-worm-cotton. "Appeared in two" [is explained as follows].
*Uddalomī*: "One whose hair and fringe (*lomaṃ dasā*) are upward" (*udda-lomī*). This is formed by changing the vowel *i* to *a*, eliding the letter *t*, and doubling the following consonant.
*Ekantalomī*: "One whose hair and fringe are on one side" (*ekasmiṃ ante lomaṃ dasā yassā*).

Regarding both terms, some—namely the masters of the *Sārasamāsa* and the residents of the Uttaravihāra—hold that they are so called because, according to the method already stated, "one whose flower made of hair has arisen (*uggata*) from one side" (*uditamekato*). Thus it is said *uddalomī*.
The etymological meaning of *ekantalomī* is: that which has a single tuft of woolen flowers at both ends.
However, in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “*Uddalomī* is a woolen rug with hair growing out from one side; *uddhalomī* is also a reading for this.
*Ekantalomī* is a woolen rug with hair growing out from both sides. This is merely a difference in name; as for the actual meaning, however—
It should be understood that the term *aggahitāvaseso* (the remainder not included) does not appear in either of the two commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Regarding *koseyyañ ca kaṭṭissañ ca*: the word *kaṭṭissāni* is formed by the grammatical rule of retaining only one member when the members are dissimilar (*virūpekasesa*).
A bedspread made of those [materials] is a *kaṭṭissa*. To demonstrate this very meaning, it is stated as "a bedspread consisting of silk and *kaṭṭissa*," where between the silk threads...
Having inserted golden threads, it is called a "woven coverlet" (*vītam-attharaṇa*). It is said that they call golden thread "kaṭṭissaṃ" or "kassaṭaṃ.
For this very reason, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated that it is "made of *koseyya* and *kassaṭa*.
Some also say that *kaṭṭissaṃ* is a specific kind of flax. "Woven with jewels" means interlaced with jewels.
"Gold-plated," some say. "Pure silk" means free from being sewn together with gems. This was stated with reference to the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* or the *Vinaya-pāḷi*;
for here, in the discourse of the Suttanta tradition, it is said:
"Except for the stuffed mattress (*tūlikā*), all [bedspreads] such as the *gonaka* are permissible provided they are sewn together with gems. However, according to the *Vinaya* tradition:
The determination should be understood as follows: since one must stand upon something heavy once having stepped upon it, only pure silk (*suddhakoseyya*) is permitted, not the others.
However, according to the Suttanta method, even a mattress (*tūlikā*) that is not sewn with jewels is not permitted, whereas the others are permitted;
even if those [others] are sewn with jewels, they are allowed when used as floor coverings or, as appropriate, on beds, chairs, and so forth.
"And it is permissible to bring [them]. Because this was stated with reference to householders as well in the teaching of the Suttantas, others say:
"It is said that, 'excepting... they are not permissible,' for the purpose of including them.
Regarding the reading "in the Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā," the meaning is "in the ancient Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā. "Suitable for dancing" means sufficient for dancing. They perform [it].
Here, they dance the *kuttaka* (courtly dance), which is specifically the *uddalomi*, *ekantalomi*, and *visesa*. And it is said:
“The *dvidasa*, *ekadasa*, *anyudda*, *lomi*, and *ekantalomi*;
that very same [dance] is the *soḷasī* for women, for it is the *kuttaka* suitable for dancing.”

“Elephant-back rug” (*hatthatthara*) refers to the rug spread upon the back of an elephant; the same applies to the remaining terms. “With antelope skins” (*ajinacammehi*) means with the skins of the *ajina* deer;
it is said that those skins are very fine, and therefore they are sewn together after being made into double or triple layers. Hence it is called an “antelope-skin quilt” (*ajinappaveṇī*);
for it is called a “quilt” (*paveṇī*) because it is made into a continuous whole by being sewn while placed one on top of the other.
The *kadalīmiga* is a deer shaped like a flower bud; a magnificent rug made from its hide is likewise [prohibited].
The phrase beginning with “*taṃ kira*” (it is said that) serves to demonstrate its appearance; therefore, they say that only the pure skin of the *kadalīmiga* deer is permitted.
It covers the upper part, thus it is called an *uttaracchada*, which is a canopy (*vitāna*). That too must be red in this context.
