He said: "By means of a dyed canopy. The remainder [of the phrase] is "whatever is appropriate is with an upper covering," meaning it proceeds together with the state of being sewn together. Among dyed canopies, the saffron-colored (kāṣāya) is permitted;
however, that which is dyed with safflower and the like is not permitted, and that must be entirely dyed. But as for that which is multicolored, or has woven patterns, or plastered patterns—
That is permissible. Because the spread itself is the primary object, it is stated that even a white canopy attached to it is not permissible.
"On both sides" means on both parts of the bed: the head end and the foot end. Here too, the determination is the same as for a bed with a canopy.
"Lotus-colored" is said with reference to what is not excessively red. "Or variegated," however, refers to all kinds.
It was stated [as such] because it is allowable, but not because it is unallowable in both types of pillows.

For the word *lohitaka* (red) is not applicable to a mind. Since the inclusion of the term *paṭalika* (patchwork) would entail that even a multicolored spread (*cittaka*) should be included, he said, "But a large pillow is prohibited," in order to support that very point through its opposite.
"Mahāupadhāna" refers to a pillow that exceeds the proper measure. For its measure is indeed the size of the head.
And it has been said: "I allow you, monks, to make a bolster the size of the head.
Now, what is called "the size of the head" is that which, when measured across the three corners from one corner to another, is one span (vidatthi) and four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula).
The middle part of the pillow is one cubit across and one and a half or two cubits in length.
However, it is prohibited solely because it is unallowable (*akappiya*), and not because it falls under the category of high or luxurious beds (*uccāsayana-mahāsayana*).
"Both" refers to the head-pillow and the foot-pillow. "Having spread a covering" means having made a bed-covering (*paccattharaṇa*).

"Having spread out" is the meaning; and this was said specifically with reference to one who is ill. Therefore, it is said in the commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka in the Vinaya, according to the method stated there:
"Even for one who is not ill, only two things are permitted: a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet.
For one who is ill, it is also permitted to lie down after spreading out bolsters and placing a coverlet over them. Thus it is in the Vinaya.
It is according to the method stated by the Blessed One. To explain how it was stated, he says: "For this has been said," and so forth.
Just as [the rule] applies when there is a foot [of a bed] eight finger-breadths long, so too should the cutting off of the feet of a *āsandi* (stool) be understood.
As for a *pallaṅka* (couch), however, even bringing in carved animal figures and then detaching them again constitutes breaking [the rule]. "Having disentangled" means having unraveled the tangles.
"To make a pillow" means to make a pillow by inserting those disheveled cotton fibers inside. 16.
By the phrase "of children who have emerged from the mother's womb," only those born from eggs or from a womb are included;

furthermore, this indicates the reason for their inclusion, namely, that they have emerged from the mother's womb. For this very reason, the following meaning is established: "Because of being within the bed for many days..."
"This is the fragrance. They rub and scrub [the body]. "For the sake of producing a good shape" means for the sake of achieving a well-proportioned form.
"They massage" means they rub all over.
"Of those very children" refers specifically to children who possess merit; for it is only for them that [this is done] in accordance with their specific circumstances.
“Taking up”: “Of the great wrestlers” means of those who engage in wrestling with their arms.

An “adāsa” (mirror) is a particular type of vessel made of bronze, brass, or similar materials for people whose nature is to adorn themselves, intended for them to behold the reflection of their own faces.
Referring to such [mirrors], it is said: “Whatever... is not permitted. This refers specifically to decorative ointment, not medicinal ointment.

For since the application of adornment (*maṇḍana*) is intended here, that [garland] is not what is intended. In common usage, the word *mālā* refers only to a bound garland, according to the statement:
"A *mālā*, a *mālya*, is a wreath of flowers. However, in the Teaching (*sāsana*), it is established as a term for loose flowers as well;
thus he says, "or an unbound garland. "Of black moles, etc. means of black-colored moles and so forth. "Clay paste" (*mattikakakka*) is that which is prepared with medicinal herbs.
*Yogamattikācuṇṇaṃ*: "They apply" means they smear it on. "Agitated" means having reached a state of movement by way of undergoing a change;
the meaning is "provoked. "By that" means by the mustard-paste. "Humors" (*dosa*) refers to the blood-humors that are the cause of black boils and the like.
"Consumed" means consumed by way of being removed. "Settled" means when such corrupted blood has been completely exhausted. "By facial powder" (*mukhacuṇṇakena*).

"By means of facial ointment. "Smearing" (*cuṇṇenti*) means they apply it as an ointment. "All that" refers to facial powder—consisting of clay, lime, *sappatiḷa*, turmeric, and *kakkadāna*—and facial ointment;
both are not permitted. This commentary on these two terms is given because their sequence follows the order of their occurrence in the text.
Alternatively, the clarification of the meaning of the two terms—"facial powder" and "facial ointment"—is presented here as having a common grammatical substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).
*Hatthabandha* refers to an ornament to be bound on the hand; however, that consists of conch shells, skull-cups, and so forth—thus he says "on the hand," and so on.
With the words "Others," etc., he explains the meaning of the terms *sikhābandha*, etc., in their respective order.
In this context, *sikhā* means the topknot (*cūḷā*). A *cīraka* is that by which the topknot is made firm and beautified.

It pierces. A pearl-string (*muttālatā*) is a string of pearls, or a row of pearls; it is like a garland of pearls (*muttāvaḷi*). Regarding the term "staff" (*daṇḍa*), it is said to be four cubits long, as in the phrase "or a staff of four cubits.
However, the term "decorated staff" (*alaṅkatadaṇḍaka*) refers to something shorter than that, such as a chariot-pole and so forth.
"Medicine-tube" (*bhesajjanāḷika*) means a vessel for medicine. Hanging [items] such as bowls from the left shoulder alone is the established custom.
It is said, "suspended on the left side. A *kaṇṇikā* is a pinnacle; its treasury (*kosa*) was thus surrounded by that [pinnacle] and by jewels.
"Sewn with threads of five colors" means the three types of parasols were sewn with threads of five colors, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and madder.
"The size of a jewel in length and four finger-breadths in width" refers to those...
It is stated [either] according to the measurement of the hairline, or by a measure sufficient to bind it upon the forehead.
By the phrase "having shown the limit of the hair," he indicates the manner of binding in such a way that it does not extend beyond that point. "In the mouth of the cloud" means inside [the cloud].
Regarding the word "jewel," he says "crest-jewel" (*cūḷāmaṇi*) because this refers to the crest-gem; the meaning is "a jewel on the crest."
This chowrie belongs to a yak; it is the hair itself, and the fan made from that hair is a "yak-hair fan" (*cāmaravālabījanī*).

However, since other types of fans—such as those made of mosquito-netting, reeds, *uśīra* grass, or peacock feathers—as well as handheld fans (*vidhūpana*) and palm-leaf fans (*tālavaṇṭa*), are allowable, the inclusion of this specific term should be understood as referring to them as well.
17. It is called *niyyāna* because by means of it one goes forth from misfortune and from *saṃsāra*; thus it is the path to heaven and the path to liberation.
It is *niyyānika* because it deserves that *niyyāna*, or because it is connected to that *niyyāna*, or because that *niyyāna*—as its fruit—is its [result].
Alternatively, it is *niyyānika* because it leads away (*niyyāti*) from the defilement of verbal misconduct; here the long vowel *ī* has been shortened, and the letter *ya* [has been elided].

And having formed the word *ka* [from *aniyyānikattā*]. For the term *anīya* frequently expresses the sense of the suffix *-tva*. Here, it is the abstention from frivolous chatter (*samphappalāpa*) together with volition (*cetanā*) that is intended.
Because it is the opposite of that [abstention], it is "not leading out" (*aniyyānika*); frivolous chatter is so called. Its state is "the quality of not leading out" (*aniyyānikatta*);
therefore, it is "because of the quality of not leading out. "Become like an animal" means become like something that obstructs, something that acts as a barrier. "Even he indeed... [etc.]

Here, the word *nāma* is used in the sense of reproach. "Developing it as a meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānabhāveti*) means developing it as a meditation subject on the Four Noble Truths because it is connected with impermanence.

"By way of the gratification of sensual pleasure" (*kāmassādavasena*) means by way of the gratification known as sensual pleasure. "Together with its meaning" (*saha atthena*) means "meaningful" (*sātthakaṃ*), which is to say, connected with welfare.
"Shoes" (*upāhanā*) is said with reference to the connection with the discourse on vehicles. "It should be well-fixed" (*suṭṭhu nivesitabbo*) means "well-settled" (*suniviṭṭho*).
Likewise, "ill-placed" (*dunniviṭṭho*). Since the word "village" (*gāma*) includes the people living in the village as well, he says, "of those living in such-and-such a village," and so forth.
Regarding the term "heroic talk" (*sūrakathā*), he shows that the word *sūra* here signifies a hero by means of the phrase "he was a hero. A "street" (*visikhā*) is a settlement on a road;
however, in this context, by the mention of the street, the inhabitants thereof are also included, as in expressions such as "the whole village has come."
For this very reason, it says: “with faith, confident,” and so forth.
The “place of the jar” (*kumbhaṭṭhāna*) is said to be the place of water; thus, it is called the “discourse on the place of water.
It is also called the “discourse on the ford of water” because they are both contained therein. Furthermore, the “place of making the jar” is the “jar-place. By way of that designation—
The phrase "or the talk of water-carrier slaves" is used to show that they were indeed called "water-carrier slaves. "Those who have passed away before" means *pubbapeta*;
for "peto," "pareto," and "kālaṅkato" are synonymous terms. The words beginning with "therein" (*tattha*) are stated in order to extend by reference the method already explained above.
"Released from former and latter discourses" means released from the discourses that have come down here, both those preceding and those following.
"Of various natures" refers to the sense of the word *ātman* as a synonym for "nature. "By such-and-such a name" means by Pajāpati Brahmā, or by Īśvara.
It is called "the exposition of the world" (*lokakkhāyikā*) because by it the world is explained in terms of its origin, its subsistence, its constituent parts, and so forth. This is [the meaning].
However, by the phrase "discourse on the Lokāyata sophistry" (*lokāyatavitaṇḍasallāpakathā*), he shows that it is a form of contentious discussion based on the science of Lokāyata.

It is called *lokāyata* because foolish people (*loka*) exert themselves (*āyatanti*) therein, taking pleasure in debate; or, it is called *lokāyata* because the world (*loka*) does not strive (*yatati*) or endeavor (*īhati*) for its welfare (*hita*) by means of it.
For, relying on that treatise, beings do not even direct their minds toward the performance of meritorious deeds.
They do not produce [them]. It is called *vitaṇḍa* because they stretch out (*tanonti*) here a discourse that is mutually contradictory, or one that is opposed to heaven and liberation;

or it is called *vitaṇḍa* because the disputants strike (*tāḷenti*) here with the staff of argumentation that is contradictory. In all cases, the derivation of the word is according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*).
Regarding the phrase "dug up by Sāgaradeva," some say it means "dug up by the sons of King Sāgara. It exists as the cause for making known.
“Samudda” (the ocean) is so called because its head [is at the shore]—having changed the letter *dha* to *da*.

Here, the word *saha* expresses the sense of existence (*vijjamāna*), as in such examples as “salomakosapakkhaka” (possessing hair and wings). “Bhava” means growth, based on the derivation that one “becomes” (*bhavati*) or increases.
“Vibhava” means decline, due to being devoid of that [growth]. Since the word *iti*, which is heard before the compound (*dvanda*), must be construed with each member individually, he says: “iti...”
"Existence" and "non-existence. "Whatever it may be" means anything whatsoever; thus, the meaning is that they are indeterminate.

For teachers explain that the word *yaṃ-taṃ* (whatever-it-may-be), together with the term *vikappa* (conceptualization), indicates the non-existent and the indeterminate. Furthermore, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to eternalism (*sassata*);
"non-existence" (*abhava*) refers to annihilationism (*uccheda*). Or, "existence" refers to sensual pleasure; "non-existence" refers to self-mortification.
Thus, together with these six kinds of talk concerning "it may be thus" and "it may be otherwise," there are thirty-two types of what are called "animal-talk.

Alternatively, even though talk concerning forests, mountains, rivers, and islands is not explicitly mentioned by name in the text, it is included under the word "thus" (iti), and so they are called the thirty-two types of animal-talk.
For in the text, the word "thus" (iti) in the phrase "or thus" (iti vā) [serves this inclusive function].
The word *vā* has the sense of "kind" or "alternative. This is what is meant: "They dwell devoted to such a kind of talk, or to another similar kind of useless talk.

Alternatively, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with," as in the expression "one who abstains from dancing, singing, music, and the sight of spectacles," etc.; thus, *iti* refers to that which begins with such [talk], namely, other similar kinds as well.
The meaning is: "How do they dwell engaged [in discussion]?

(18) *Viggāhikā* means those who possess *viggaho*—that is, the grasping of what is contradictory; thus it is *viggāhikā*. Alternatively, that by which one grasps what is contradictory is *viggāhikā*;
that very discourse is likewise [called *viggāhikā-kathā*]. *Sārambhakathā* is a discourse of reproach. *Sahitaṃ*...
It is not contradictory in its sequence (pubbāpara). For that very reason, it is "coherent" (siliṭṭha).
To show that this is because it is joined with purpose and reason, it is said: "the meaning is 'joined with purpose' and 'joined with reason'. "It" (taṃ) refers to the statement.

Having turned back and remained [there], like a warrior who has reached the enemy but is unable [to fight], you know nothing; rather, the intention is that you have defeated yourself. "The debate is a fault" (vādo doso).
It is a figurative expression (*pariyāyavacana*). "Act thus" means "wander. "In this and that" means in this or that teacher’s lineage (*ācariyakula*).
"Pierce through" means: relinquish the doctrine planted by me. 19.
*Dūteyya* is the business of a messenger; the discourse concerning it is likewise [called] *dūteyya*. In this context, "here" and "there" are used in the sense of the locative case.
This is the word for the ground; therefore, he says, "a certain place.
Since the detailed analysis has been stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, the phrase beginning with "In brief, however" was spoken here to show it concisely.
"The teaching for householders" refers to a teaching contrary to that which was previously described. "Of others" means of householders alone.

20. "In three ways" means by way of the three divisions: whispering in the presence of others (*sāmantajappana*), dependence on postures (*iriyāpathasannissita*), and the use of requisites (*paccayapaṭisevana*).
"Causing wonder" (*vimhāpayanti*) means they produce in others a sense of astonishment and admiration regarding themselves, thinking, "This person is marvelous.
For those learned in grammar say that the word *mhi* preceded by the prefix *vi-* denotes admiration. The manner of such admiration is as follows:
And it is wonderful. "They speak" means they speak by way of praising themselves or the donor, having raised them up;
that is, they explain by way of such praise, as if saying, "In such a way he gives something. "Those whose habit (*sīla*) is signs are sign-makers (*nemittika*).
This is a derivative formation (*taddhita*) expressing the sense of habit, just as in the term "one who wears rag-robes" (*paṃsukūlika*). Furthermore, they speak by means of signs; a sign—
They are called "hinters" (*nemittika*) because they act [in this way]. A "hint" (*nimitta*) is said to be bodily or verbal action that causes others to perceive it as the giving of requisites.
"Grinding" (*nippesa*) means the act of grinding, like making something into powder. Alternatively, they are "grinders" (*nippesa*) because they grind;

those who are grinders are themselves "grinders by profession" (*nippesika*). Or, "grinding" is the act of grinding itself; they are "grinders by profession" because they perform that act. Furthermore, a "grinder" is a hired man.
Like [the former], there is the state of reviling, censuring, mocking, and backbiting for the sake of gain and honor.
"From gain to gain" means from a gain here to a gain elsewhere. "They strive for" and "they seek" are synonymous terms.

As for the words *kuhaka* (deceiver) and so forth, they are applied to persons possessing those qualities by making deception (*kuhāna*) and the like their characteristic mark; thus he says: "Deceit... etc., is a designation."
"And the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathaṃ*) means the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) which constitute the exegesis of their respective scriptures.
The commentary on the medium-length precepts is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the long precepts.

21. Because it proceeds by taking the limbs as its object, the science associated with the limbs (*aṅgasahacarita-sattha*) is called "limbs" (*aṅga*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound.
The same principle applies here to the term "signs" (*nimitta*); therefore, he says, "in the hands, feet, and so forth," and so on.

Some, however, say: "Limb" (*aṅga*) refers to a modification of a limb; and by observing the modifications of others' limbs, one discerns gain, loss, and so forth. This is the "science of signs" (*nimitta-sattha*).
The text [beginning with] "by means of a sign" (*nimittena*) illustrates the manner of perceiving;
in order to clarify that by means of the subject matter (*vatthu*), he said, "King Paṇḍu," and so forth. Regarding "King Paṇḍu," it is stated that he was "the lord of Dakkhiṇārāma.
They say he was the builder of the Saṅghārāma named Dakkhiṇārāma on the island of Siṃhala. In some places, however, it is written as "the lord of Dakkhiṇamadhura."

The meaning is "the lord of the city of Dakkhiṇamadhura. *Muttāyo* means pearls. *Muṭṭhiyā* means by means of a hand-gesture (*hatthamuddā*). *Gharagolikāyā* means by means of a house-lizard (*sarabū*).
He spoke [of them] as "pearls" by way of a sign of perception (*saññānimitta*), but as "three" by way of a sign of number (*saṅkhyānimitta*).
By the word "large," he indicates that the sign itself is small, whereas the omen (*uppāda*) is large; thus, he distinguishes between the sign and the omen.
It shows a distinction. "Uppātitaṃ" means flying up. That which arises and goes forth, manifesting the fruit of the beautiful and the ugly, is "uppāda";
it is also the transformation of the primary elements (bhūtavikati) that indicates the beautiful and the ugly.
For that [transformation] merely makes the fruit of karma manifest, like smoke does for fire, but it does not produce it. "Idaṃ" means this specific fruit. "Evaṃ" means by this.
"By name" means by way of form. "They point out" means they describe. "In the morning time" is said by way of time. "This is the name" is said by way of the object (*vatthu*).

For one who sees himself in a dream as having just mounted a bull, an elephant, a palace, or a mountain, there is a description of the object in such terms as, "this is the fruit. "Dream" refers to the science of dreams.

Previously, it was called "limb" (*aṅga*) merely by way of showing the perfection or deficiency of the limbs; here, however, it is called "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) by way of showing the specific characteristics that produce such qualities as great majesty.
This is the distinction between them. Therefore, he said, "By this characteristic," and so forth.

For "characteristic" refers to the specific visible forms appearing on the major and minor limbs—such as the lion, the śrīvatsa, the mace, the palace, and so on—which are intended here, and by which each respective fruit is characterized.
Having taken "by this" as the cause, the "knife" (sattha) is the characteristic because it reveals that [cause]. "Worn" (āhata) refers to old [cloth]; "unworn" (anāhata) refers to new.
However, in the reading "new" (ahata), the meaning is the opposite of what was stated. "From this point on" means:

when a portion of various cloths—distinguished by gods, rākṣasas, humans, and so forth, and imagined according to their respective fruits—is torn here or there, such and such a fruit, beginning with wealth, [arises].
“By such wood” means by wood such as *palāsa*, *sirīsa*, or *phala* trees, and likewise by a ladle (*dabbi*).
If ladle-offerings (*dabbihoma*) and so forth are indeed fire-offerings (*aggihoma*), then why were they mentioned separately? To this he says, “by such [a ladle],” and so on.

Ladle-offerings and the like are mentioned by way of showing specific fruits resulting from specific offering implements and materials; however, the fire-offering is mentioned by way of the remaining means of accomplishment.
This is the intended meaning. Therefore, he said:

“The *dabbī-homa* and so forth. *Kuṇḍaka* means a broken grain of rice; *tela* (oil) is that which belongs to sesame (*tila*). Since these are compound and derivative words that have become common designations for well-known things, the term “sesame oil and so forth” (*tilatelādika*) was stated for the purpose of specifying them.
“Pouring in” (*pakkhipana*) means for the purpose of pouring in. It is also called the “science of pouring in” (*pakkhipanavijjā*).

The meaning of *pāṭho* is that there exists [a method] which serves as the cause for insertion. "By means of the blood of the right knee, the blood of the right shank, and so forth" means by means of the blood of the right knee, the blood of the right shank, and so on.
By the words "Previously," etc., he removes the charge of tautology through the demonstration of the specific distinctions among the various types of limb-divination (*aṅgavijjā*).
"Having seen a finger-bone" means having seen a bone that has become a finger, or a bone produced from a finger; it does not mean having seen merely the skin of a finger.
It is meant that they explain it precisely by way of insight into bones (*aṭṭhivipassanā*). However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has stated: "The 'bone-staff' (*aṅgalaṭṭhi*) is the body.
This being so, since the body resembles a staff (*laṭṭhi*) due to its nature as the growth of limbs and members, it is understood that the body itself is the "bone-staff.
The term *kulaputta* refers both to one who is a son of noble birth and to one who is a son of noble conduct.
Regarding the word *disvāpi*: here the particle *api* has the sense of inclusion, meaning "even without having seen" (*adisvāpi*). *Abbhinaṃ satthaṃ* means "the science of piercing.
A treatise composed by Māsurakkha is called the *Māsurakkha*. A science employed by kings is the *rājasattha*. All of these are treatises on the science of the Khattavijjā (royal science).
Since the word *siva* has the sense of "peace," he says "the science that brings about peace" (*santikaraṇavijjā*), which means the science for the pacification of calamities.
Having shortened the sound of *sivā* to *si*, they say "the science of jackal cries" (*siṅgālarutavijjā*), intending that it is thus;

the meaning is: the science for perceiving the auspicious and inauspicious in the cries of jackals. "The spell for subduing spirits" (*bhūtavejjamanta*) means a spell for bringing spirits under control.
"In a house with many rooms" (*bhūrighare*) means in a house built underground or a house made of clay. "The great science" (*bhūrivijjā*) means the science for causing an increase in crops.

In the *Sārasamāsa*: "The science of summoning snakes" (*sappāvhāyanavijjā*) means the science of making snakes come. "Or indeed the measure of poison" (*visavaṃtameva vā*) means "or indeed the extent of the poison.
For in the description of abstract nouns (*bhāvaniddesa*), there is a locative usage for the word *māna*. The construction is: "That by which they act is the science of poison" (*visavijjā*).

There is also a reading: "Or indeed the treatise on poison" (*visatantrameva vā*). This being so, it is a presentation of the same form [as the previous term], namely, that it is simply a book concerning the investigation of poison.
This is the meaning. For *tantra* is a common designation for a book (*gantha*). Regarding "those with wings, those without wings, and bipeds and quadrupeds":

this refers to winged creatures such as *piṅgala* flies; wingless creatures such as house-lizards (*gharagolikā*); bipeds such as gods and humans; and quadrupeds such as *caṅgora* deer, *kaṇṭasa* antelopes, and jackals. "Sound" means crying out. "Gone" means movement;
by this [term], the elision of the word "animal" (*miga*) from the compound "bird-science" (*sakuṇavijjā*) is indicated, which serves merely as an illustration.
Or it shows [this]. "Knowledge of birds" (sakuṇañāṇa) means knowing the results, whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of birds.

One might ask: "Is not the science of crows (vāyasavijjā) already included within the science of birds? To this he says: "That is a separate treatise. For here, one should understand that the words of each respective author are used in accordance with the specific treatise that elucidates them.

The phrase "the state of having reached maturity" is shown by the words beginning with "now" (*idāni*) to be understood by way of both the personal existence (*attabhāva*) and the duration of life (*jīvitakāla*).

"Knowledge of what is indicated" (*ādiṭṭhañāṇa*) means knowledge regarding that which is to be indicated. "Protection from arrows" (*sararakkhaṇa*) means protecting oneself from an arrow, or protecting an arrow from oneself.
By the term "comprehensive" (*sabbasaṅgāhika*), [the author] shows the application of the word *miga* (deer) to all birds and quadrupeds.
It shows [this], or rather, this is an *ekasesa* (single-remainder) designation because the word *miga* (deer/animal) is conventionally established only for the four types of beings.

The name *migacakkā* (deer-wheel) applies to the science that knows the cries of all birds and quadrupeds, just as the names *cakka* (wheel) and so forth apply to the various ways of knowing what is auspicious and inauspicious in every respect; thus he said: "All... is stated."
22. “*Sāmino*” and so forth is a statement regarding the causes of praise and blame. “*Lakkhaṇaṃ*” refers to the treatise that elucidates their characteristics.

By way of the method of exclusion (*pārisesanaya*), the remainder is the weapon. By the passage beginning with “*Yamhi kule*,” it shows that in this context, the remaining [factors] are characteristics precisely because they are the cause for knowing things as they are.
This is the distinction: from the characteristic mentioned below as “*lakkhaṇaṃ*,”...
This is the distinction. To clarify its meaning, it is said: "And herein, this is the basis," namely, "blowing on the fire," which means kindling the fire with the breath from the mouth.
"He destroyed" means he ruined. "Of the ear-ornament" refers to the ear-decoration. "Of the house-eaves" refers to the roof-peak;
by this, either the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*) or a general designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*) is intended. "The tortoise-sign" refers to...
The mark of the hump (*kumma-lakkhaṇaṃ*). Regarding "of all four-footed creatures" (*sabbacatuppadānaṃ*):

he states that the word *miga* (deer) denotes four-footed animals. 23. "On such-and-such a day": this is stated by way of the second, third, and so forth lunar dates (*tithi*). "Under such-and-such a constellation" (*asukanakkhattena*): by way of conjunction with constellations such as Assayuja, Bharaṇī, Kattikā, Ārohaṇī, and so forth.
"Of those who have gone abroad" (*vippavutthānaṃ*): of those who have departed from their own country. "Approaching" (*upasaṅkamanaṃ*) means going near; "departing" (*apayānaṃ*) means going away.
The retreat. "In the second statement also" means even when it is said in the second sentence: "There will be [victory] for the external kings... pe ...".
Victory and defeat stated by the two sentences beginning with "Victory for the internal kings" are indeed evident.
24. *Rāhu*: Rāhu is the name of the lord of the Asuras, the king of the Asuras. For thus it is said in the *Mahāsamaya Sutta* regarding the class of Asuras:
“Then the hundred Bali-sons, all named Veroca,
having arrayed the army of Bali, approached the auspicious Rāhu.
His seizing of the moon and sun is to be illustrated by the *Candimasutta* and *Sūriyasutta* in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (or "etcetera"), because it is stated as "eclipses of the moon and so forth.

By this, eclipses of the sun and eclipses of the constellations (*nakkhatta*) are included. Therefore, one should understand that the seizing of the constellations by Rāhu is just like the seizing of the moon and the sun.

For this very reason, a second method regarding the eclipse of the constellations is stated with the words "Moreover... and so on. [The phrase] "also the conjunction with the seizing by Aṅgāraka and others" refers to this.

By the inclusion of what has already been mentioned, even the conjunction of the planets known as Aṅgāraka (Mars), Sasi-putta (Mercury), Sūra (Venus), Guru (Jupiter), Sukka (Venus), Ravi (the Sun), Visuta (Saturn), and Ketu (the Comet) is indeed a planetary seizure (*nakkhatta-gāha*), because they are seized along with their functional application.

For even the functional application is called a "seizure" according to the Vedic tradition. "The falling of meteors" refers to the falling of meteoric lights; for when masses of wind collide with great force against one another...
A radiance arises like the light of a lamp when [objects] collide and falls from the sky; this is the conventional designation for a "falling meteor" (*ukkāpāta*).
It is also stated in the *Jotisattha*:
"And the great crest, with a white tip, blazing with a red wind-crest;..."
"By measure, it is like a man; the firebrands are considered to be of various kinds.

Regarding "confusion of the directions," this refers to agitation within the quarters; he shows its actual nature with the phrase, "like a state of being overwhelmed by crests of flame and crests of smoke," for the manifold manifestation of crests of flame, crests of smoke, and so forth, is indeed what is called the "burning of the directions."
That very thing is what worldly people call a "comet" (*dhūmaketu*). And it is said in the *Jotisattha*:
"A meteor has a crest like a banner; its appearance is that of a portentous light.

"The roaring of a dry cloud" refers to the thundering of a cloud driven by the force of the wind in the absence of rain, which worldly people call a "thunderclap" (*nighāta*). And it is said in the *Jotisattha*:
“When a powerful wind in the sky, driven by the winds,
falls downward as a downpour, that which arises from the wind is produced.
*Udayana* means clinging and accumulation.
“It is when it arises that there is clinging; it follows the sequence of the heaps. Thus it was said. Its setting should also be understood by way of the measure of the seventh heap.
Impurity is due to these four causes: clouds, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. Purity is being free from them. And it is said: “These four...”
“Monks, there are four defilements of the moon and the sun, by which defilements being defiled, the moon and the sun do not shine, do not glow, and do not radiate. What are the four?
Clouds, monks, are a defilement of the moon and the sun, by which... smoke... dust... Rāhu, monks... these, indeed... do not radiate.”
25. "Of the god" means of the cloud. "Bestowing showers" means raining. "A poor grasp" means a faulty grasp of the shower;
hence he says "obstructing the rain. "Hand-gesture" (hatthamuddā) means making known what is intended by the hand;
however, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has stated that this is indeed a form of counting by the contraction of the fingers. [This was also stated] by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta.

However, "hand-finger counting" (*hatthamuddā*) is defined as "counting by placing signs on the finger joints. Counting (*gaṇanā*) here refers to "unbroken counting" (*acchiddakagaṇanā*) according to the method of exhaustion;
it should be understood as a continuous counting from "one, two," and so forth, up to nine, like the *pādasika*, *milakkhaka*, and other such methods.
"Clearing away" (*samūhana*) means collecting together or producing separately.
*Apanayana* means removal; *paṭuppādana* means production. [In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is read as *saṭuppādana*;
some also read it as *saduppādana*, which means "producing rightly. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes the division into parts (*vokalanabhāgahāra*) and so forth.
Therein, *vokalanam* means making separate or forming a collection; the meaning is "mixing apart" (*vomissanam*). *Bhāgakaraṇam* is "division" (*bhāgo*). *Bhuñjanam* is "distribution" (*vibhajanam*).
“Hāro. As for the phrase “having seen,” which refers to the aforementioned counting of groups (*piṇḍagaṇanā*), the meaning to be understood here is “having counted by means of mere sight.
Regarding the term “*paṭibhānakavī*,” the words “stated in the *Aṅguttaranikāya*” are to be supplied; the connection is with “the poetic composition of poets. By this, he shows the meaning:
“that which was made by poets” or “this belongs to the poets (*kāveyya*). The passage beginning with “by way of his own reflection” and so forth...

This is the vision of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For in this way, a "thought-poet" (*cintākavi*) is to be understood by virtue of composing [works] after having personally reflected for a long time upon both the subject matter (*vatthu*) and the connection (*anusandhi*).
A "heard-poet" (*sutakavi*) is one who, having heard something, composes by connecting what was heard with what was not heard.
An "meaning-poet" (*atthakavi*) is one who, having considered some meaning, composes by means of abbreviating, expanding, and so forth that meaning. Whatever...
A *paṭibhānakavī* (an impromptu poet) is one who, having seen a poem or a drama composed by another, creates another work similar to it through his own spontaneous wit (*ṭhānuppattika-paṭibhāna*).
This is the meaning of "that. *Tappaṭibhāgaṃ* means "similar to what was seen by him. In the phrase "to be made" (*kattabbaṃ*), this is an adjective;
or in the phrase "I shall make," it is a gerundive (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*). *Ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānavasena* means "by way of spontaneous wit arising from the occasion."
By way of knowledge that functions in accordance with its cause. "For the sake of livelihood" is stated precisely according to what has been understood in this treatise.
That which belongs to poets is *kavya*, which is called "song. 26.
Marriage (*āvāhana*) is the taking of a girl by way of formal acceptance; likewise, giving [her away] is *vivāhana*. However, here—
The expression "tathākaraṇassa" (of one who acts accordingly) is a designation formed by the elision of the latter member of the compound, or alternatively, it contains the underlying cause;
thus he says, "of this boy," and so forth. "Iti" means "thus occurring" or "because of such a state. "Uṭṭhāna" refers to wealth arising from fields and other sources.
"Iṇa" is a loan given to another for the purpose of increasing one's capital. Even before the previously determined time has arrived, the repayment of the debt constitutes "uṭṭhāna."
Some say that when the time previously delimited has arrived, it is "debt" (*iṇa*); however, that is indeed incorrect, because it is established by the very act of taking on debt.

The connection is: "debt" or "wealth" given to others. "Immovable" (*thāvara*) means long-lasting. "Investment" (*payoga*) refers to the employment of goods by way of taking double, triple, or more in another region.
Therein, or elsewhere, it is by way of taking interest according to the delimited time.
The purpose (*payojana*) is the loan (*uddhāra*). Some say: "The lending of money with the instruction, 'Act as a merchant for those who are without capital;
give back the principal along with this much profit,' is the *payoga*; the temporary lending is the *uddhāra*.
If goods lent today become double or fourfold [in value], then if the goods lent today are such that they become double tomorrow, [and so on]. Today...
The meaning is that it possesses four qualities. *Subhaga* means the going forth or proceeding by way of beauty; the making of that is *subhagakaraṇa*.
However, since that is precisely the making of one who is dear and pleasing, or of one who is resplendent, he said "the making of one who is dear and pleasing," and so forth.
"The making of one who is resplendent" means the making of excellence in bodily splendor. "Of that which has melted away" means even after having been established, [it] has not reached full maturity.
Of the miscarriage. Likewise, of that which has not remained due to being fully ripened. This set of four terms is a figurative expression.
"The giving of medicine" means the giving of medicine for stabilizing the embryo. Regarding the phrase "by three causes":

here, when the embryo perishes due to wind or microorganisms, it is not because space was made by previous karma; rather, karma ripens precisely on account of those conditions, and [the embryo] ceases of its own accord.
However, it should be understood that the statement regarding karma as a distinct cause means that once space has been made by karma,
one need not necessarily depend upon wind or insects [to destroy the embryo]. In the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, however,
it is stated that "other than those two causes" with the intention that an embryo being destroyed by wind or by insects does not perish without karma.
*Nibbāpanīya* means that which brings about pacification. *Paṭikamma* means making amends so that they do not eat [the food].
*Bandhakaraṇa* means making it so that he cannot stir the heap, thus keeping it undisturbed.
*Parivattanattha* means for the purpose of turning those who have raised their hands with weapons and so forth elsewhere, to a place protected by oneself.

"Not having thrown [it] here" means for the purpose of throwing it elsewhere; "he throws" means he throws it to another place. "In the place of legal decision" means in the place where lawsuits are decided.
They also call "whispering in the ear" (*kaṇṇajappana*) the muttering directed toward a deity by way of whispering the desired matter into its ear.
Regarding the phrase "having caused the deity to descend," [it refers to] the deity [being summoned] by the muttering of mantras.
“Inducing. “For the sake of a livelihood”: this means for the purpose of establishing a way of life, such that one’s livelihood is maintained by performing service.
“Service to the sun” (*ādiccapāricariyā*): this refers to attending upon the sun by making offerings with *karamālā* garlands and standing facing the sun throughout the entire day.
By the phrase “just so,” the term “for the sake of a livelihood” is drawn back [as a parallel]. “Calling out ‘Siri’” (*sirivhāyanaṃ*).
This is an exposition of the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) by means of the elision of the vowel *a* after the vowel *ī*; therefore, he says, “the invocation by means of glory” (*siriyā avhāyana*).
By the phrase “by means of *sire*,” however, he shows the manner of invocation according to its location.

As for those who, having effected the elision of the vowel *a* after the vowel *a*, read it as “*siravhāyana*,” the meaning in their reading is: “the invocation of the desired object by means of the head (*sirasā*) after reciting the mantra.”
27. "Devasthāna" means a divine abode (*devāyatana*). "Upahāra" means an offering (*pūjā*). "At the time of success" (*samiddhikāla*) means the time when the requested purpose has been accomplished.
"The act of promising peace" (*santipaṭissavakamma*) means the making of a promise regarding that peace which is to be performed in response to the supplication to a deity.

Here, "peace" (*santi*) refers to the performance of worship through the recitation of mantras; the meaning is that it is the application of the supplication by means of that peace. Regarding the word "therein" (*tasmiṃ*):

Regarding that which was stated as, "If such-and-such for me should succeed," it refers to that very undertaking performed according to one's aspiration, which constitutes the fruit of the promise (*paṭissava*).

"Of that" means of that promise, which is also called "aspiration" (*paṇidhi*); for when an offering is made in accordance with the promise, the aspiration and the entreaty are fulfilled and delivered.
"Of one who has grasped the mantra" means of one who has mastered the mantra. "The performance of the ritual application" (*payogakaraṇa*)...
The performance of service. The word *iti* is a particle used in the sense of a reason (*kāraṇatthe*).

By it, he shows that the application of the terms *vassa* and *vossa* to male paṇḍakas is based on their causal status: one is called *vassa* because, being distinct from a paṇḍaka, he exists (*bhavati*) by means of [sexual] emission (*rasa*).

One is called *vossa* because, being devoid of the male sexual organ, he exists in a state of being reviled (*ava-asati*, *hīḷito hutvā*). Alternatively, *vassa* refers to one whose specific outflow (*assava*) of passion exists. [The prefix *vi-*] signifies "gone away" (*vigata*).

They also say that the word *vossa* is established according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*) as "one for whom there is an outflow of passion" (*rāgassavo yassa*). The making of a *vassa* (rain) is by means of medicine appropriate to that;

however, the making of a *vossa* (drought) occurs even through the state of having parched seeds and so forth—for this very reason, it is said in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*: "The *vossavara* are the guards of the irrigation embankments who have parched seeds.
The phrase "mere state of lack of desire" refers to the mere absence of sexual desire in a woman. "The sign" (*liṅga*) refers to the male characteristic (*purisanimitta*).

"Performing the house-site ritual" (*vatthubalikammakaraṇa*) means performing a ritual offering (*balikamma*) on the site of a house; they perform it for the purpose of warding off calamities and for the purpose of prosperity.
By means of the recitation of mantras, it effects the purification of the mouths of oneself and others. "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to others.
"Application" (*yoga*) means the application of medicinal substances. "Emetic" (*vamana*) means purging. "Purgative" (*uddhaṃvirecana*) is a specific type of emetic.
Because it is said, "the removal of humors from above," *virecana* refers specifically to natural purging.
*Adhovirecana* refers to the administration of suppositories, such as those made of pure *vatthika-sāva*, because it is said to be "the removal of humors from below.
Furthermore, *vamana* is simply vomiting; it is the removal of humors by purging from above. Likewise, *virecana* is simply purging; *adhovirecana* is...
The removal of humors (*doṣanīharaṇa*)—this is their manifest distinction. "Of humors" (*dosānaṃ*) means of bile and other such humors.

The removal of phlegm (*semhanīharaṇa*) and so forth refers to head-purgatives (*sirovirecana*). "For the purpose of joining the ears" (*kaṇṇabandhanatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of reconnecting severed ears.
"For the purpose of healing wounds" (*vaṇaharaṇatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of removing pus. "Oil for applying to the eyes" (*akkhitappanatelam*) is oil for removing heat from the eyes.
That by which heat and steam issue forth when the eye is anointed is *natthu*, which is what is taken up by the nose.

"Membranes" (*paṭalāni*) refers to the membranes of the eye. "Capable of removing" means capable of taking away. "Alkaline ointment" (*khārañjana*) means an ointment made of alkali. According to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), it is "cold" (*sīta*) alone that is true;
its cause is the ointment, which is "true-ointment" (*saccañjana*). Thus he said, "the ointment of cooling medicine" (*sītalabhesajjañjana*).

"Surgery with a probe" (*sālākavejjakamma*) means the medical treatment for eye diseases. It is called *sālākiya* because it is the medical treatment for the eye disease designated as "the probe" (*salāka*), owing to its similarity to a probe.
This term, however, is stated in order to include the remaining treatments for eye diseases;
for it is said: "Tapping [the eye] and so forth are also indeed *sālākiya*. [The following refers to] for the purpose of extracting a probe that has been inserted.

Some say that *vejjakammaṃ* (medical practice) refers to the practice of using a probe (*salākavejjakammaṃ*); however, it should be understood that this is already included by the term *sallakattiya* (surgery).
*Sallakattiya* means the extracting (*kattanaṃ*) or removal (*ubbāhanaṃ*) of an embedded arrow (*salla*); medical practice for that purpose is *sallakattiya-vejjakammaṃ*.
One who supports a prince is a *kumārabhaṭa*; the state of being such is *komārabhaccaṃ*. Alternatively, a prince himself is a *komāra*, and [the practice] is the supporting (*bhatanaṃ*) of him.
“Food” (bhaccaṃ): the meaning is that it is food for him, and likewise, medical treatment that produces that [health] is what is meant.
“Root-remedies” (mūlabhesajjāni) refers to primary medicines capable of pacifying diseases; or alternatively, they are the remedies for root-diseases (mūla-vyādhi).
For disease is of two kinds according to its connection with a root. In that regard, when the root-disease has been treated, for the most part...
It pacifies the other [the secondary affliction]; therefore, he says, "He demonstrates the healing of the body," and so forth.

Therein, "healing of the body" (*kāyatikicchatā*) refers to the state of being a healer through medicines that have become like the body itself, or by virtue of their being the very body, with respect to diseases that have become like the body.
"Alkali and so forth" (*khārādīni*) means alkaline water and the like. "In a wound corresponding to that" (*tadanurūpe vaṇe*) means in a wound suitable for the primary disease that has been pacified.
"In those": that is, of the medicinal roots. "Removal" means taking away; what is meant is that they are beyond the scope of those [other branches].
And this is stated by way of elimination (*pārisesa*), because the specific branches such as *Komārabhacca*, *Sallakatta*, and *Sālākiya* have already been mentioned previously.
Therefore, the inclusion here should be understood as referring to the remaining branch; all [of these]...
These [five] alone are intended here as being caused by wrong livelihood, because it is stated: "They make their living by wrong livelihood.
As for that which is expressed in various places in the Pāḷi as “*iti vā*”: therein, *iti* is a particle used in the sense of manner, and *vā* is used in the sense of an alternative.
This is what is meant: “either in this manner, or otherwise than this. Therefore, those...
It should be understood that outsiders who have gone forth into homelessness subsist by means of crafts, sciences, branches of knowledge, and so forth, which serve as their livelihood;
thus, their property is considered "taken.
The commentary on the Great Virtue is finished.
28. Now, explaining the meaning of the section on the elucidation of emptiness (*suññatāpakāsanavāra*), he says "Thus," etc., in order to reveal the connection (*anusandhi*).

Therein, the word "of the aforementioned description" (*vuttavaṇṇassa*) is a genitive case used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*), or in the sense of ownership (*sāmiatthe*), because the word "connection" (*anusandhi*) functions as both an abstract noun and an action noun.
Because it occurs within the teachings on functional phenomena (*kiriyā*).

"Of the praise spoken by the Saṅgha of monks" means of the praise spoken in such passages as, "To this extent indeed [is the power] of that Blessed One," and so forth. Therein, in the Pāḷi, the connection is as follows:
"Monks, these alone are not all the Buddha-qualities that are manifest to you; however, there are other qualities, monks"—this is the detailed explanation. "These..."
Because it demonstrates the emptiness of the modes in which the bases for views—such as eternalism and so forth—are grasped, by means of the passage beginning, "The bases for views are thus grasped";

and because it demonstrates the absence of any permanent essence by showing that the understanding [of those bases] does not cling to them, thereby illustrating that virtue and the other factors are not to be clung to;
and because these [bases] arise as obstacles to right view for outsiders due to their lack of dispassion toward those feelings...

And because this teaching has the elucidation of emptiness as its primary aim— by way of demonstrating that all phenomena are devoid of selfhood or anything belonging to a self through the demonstration that the conditions themselves,
such as delusion and so forth, lack the intrinsic nature of an experiencer or an agent, and by way of demonstrating final Nibbāna without clinging—
it is said: "He undertook the exposition of emptiness."
"Pariyatti" (the teaching) refers to the textual tradition (*tantrī*) differentiated by the divisions of the Vinaya and so forth, which has been determined by the mind.

"Desanā" (teaching) is the manifestation of that textual tradition once it has been determined by the mind; or it is the proclamation of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, or the exposition according to the sequence of the *anuloma* and so forth.
It was established previously that this distinction between *pariyatti* and *desanā* is intended here.

It is also said: “in the teaching (desanā), in the doctrine (pariyatti). Regarding the phrase “and so forth,” the word “etc. includes such categories as the truths (sacca), intrinsic nature (sabhāva), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), the formed (pakata), merit (puñña), attainment (āpatti), and the knowable (ñeyya).
For instance, this term *dhamma* occurs in the sense of “truth” in passages such as, “Bhikkhus, it is through not fully awakening to four things”;

it occurs in the sense of “intrinsic nature” in passages such as, “wholesome states (dhammā), unwholesome states (dhammā)”; and it occurs in the sense of “having such a nature” in passages such as, “those Blessed Ones were of such a nature (evaṃdhammā).”

In such passages as "they were," it refers to concentration (*samādhi*); in such passages as "Truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—he indeed does not grieve after passing away," it refers to wisdom (*paññā*);
in such passages as "Monks, for beings subject to birth, such a desire arises," it refers to nature (*pakati*);
in such passages as "Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness," it refers to merit (*puñña*); and in such passages as "the four *pārājika* offenses," it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).
In such passages as, “All phenomena (dhammā) in all their modes come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One,” it occurs with respect to the knowable.
“They are phenomena” means that they are mere phenomena, empty of a sentient being or a life-principle. To the question, “For what purpose does it occur with respect to qualities?
he says, “Therefore,” and so forth.
“By the needle of the *makasatuṇḍa* fly” means by the needle that is the mouth of the *sūcimukha* fly.
It is connected with the phrase “as if unobtainable as a foothold. “Except for a Tathāgata” means setting aside the Tathāgata.
Since the difficulty of plunging into those phenomena is already indicated by the word “hard to see,” it is stated simply as “unobtainable as a foothold. They are to be obtained...
*Labbhanīyā* means that which is obtainable; or *labbhanaṃ* is that which is being obtained, and one who is worthy of that is *labbhaneyyā*.
That which is not obtainable is *alabbhaneyyā*. A *patiṭṭhā* (foundation) is that wherein things are established, or it is the act of establishing itself.
That wherein an unobtainable foundation exists is *alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā*. This is what is meant: if anyone...

If one who does not know his own measure were to make an effort to plunge into those teachings with wisdom, that wisdom of his would find no footing at all, like the needle-point of a gnat’s snout in the great ocean.

Because they cannot be plunged into, it is said that "precisely because of their profundity, they are difficult to see," such that one is unable to perceive them by saying, "These are so many, or they are like this. However, those who...
"It is not even possible to see them; there is no talk of their being understood step by step after having plunged into them. Thus he said:

"Because they are difficult to see, they are difficult to awaken to. They are "with all fever of defilements extinguished" because they have arisen at the pinnacle of the supreme fruit, which is characterized by the subsiding of the fever of all defilements, and because they are permeated by the attainment in which all fever of defilements has been extinguished through the preceding and following [stages].

The meaning is that they are "peaceful" because of the absence of those [defilements]. The paths, fruits, and Nibbāna have peaceful objects because of the absence of defilements and formations, whose intrinsic nature is not peaceful.

Alternatively, it is because of the complete eradication of distraction, just as there is an infinite state in the consciousnesses whose objects are the space remaining after the removal of the kasiṇa.
The state of peace regarding those phenomena that serve as objects should be understood by way of constant, concentrated attention.
Just as archers who do not miss their mark penetrate the target, the awakening to the true nature of phenomena without missing it is of excellent flavor, like a great taste;
thus he said, "in the sense of being non-satiating," meaning by its nature of producing no satiety.

"Meaning" (*attha*): "Satisfying" (*sōhiccaṃ*) and "quenching" (*tappanaṃ*) are synonyms. They also explain the meaning as "in the sense of making one satisfied" (*atittikaraṇaṭṭhena*), which is to say, in the sense of making it delicious after having desired it.
Because these [truths] become objects in every aspect only for Buddhas who have attained penetration (*paṭivedha*), they are not the domain of speculative intellect (*takka-buddhi*);
thus he says, "Because they are the object of supreme knowledge," and so forth. "Subtle" (*nipuṇā*): because of their sharp occurrence regarding the knowable (*ñeyya*).

"Skilled" (cheka). However, because that state of skillfulness is made manifest by its unimpeded operation toward the object and its capacity to grasp what is subtle and difficult to know, it is therefore said: "because of its nature of being delicate and subtle.
He says "because it is not the domain of fools" in order to establish the restriction "only by the wise."
This is another method according to the tradition of the commentaries: it is profound because it reveals the profound and subtle meanings of the Vinaya-paññatti and other teachings.
It is difficult to see because its vision is rarely obtained even after the passing of incalculable great aeons.

And here, "vision" should be understood solely by way of the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu), since the awakening known as the "discernment of the sequence of the Dhamma" (dhammanvaya-saṅkhāta-anubodha) occurs only for some rare individuals.
It is difficult to realize. It is peaceful because its intrinsic nature is peaceful, and because it is the culmination of all the perfections of those to be trained.
It is sublime because it has been brought to a state of excellence through its own conditions.

It is beyond the sphere of reasoning because it is to be traversed by individuals who are free from conjecture, or by knowledge that is free from conjecture, due to its having attained the characteristics of truth. It is subtle, or it pertains to subtle meanings.

They are subtle because they are analyzed by way of the modes of conditionality such as truth (sacca-paccayākāra). They are "to be known by the wise" because they must be understood and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme sage in the world.
Indeed, through the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I am all-knowing; I am endowed with the ten powers."

By the words "the Tathāgata," etc., he manifested his own qualities such as omniscience; for this very reason, it is said: "having realized them by his own direct knowledge (abhiññā), he makes them known.
To show the meaning that must be excluded by the word "himself" (sayaṃ) or by the restrictive emphasis, it is stated:
"being not led by others" (anaññaneyyo hutvā); the sense is: "not having been awakened by others. In the term *abhiññā*, there is the elision of the letter *ya*.
By the phrase "by means of distinguished knowledge," he shows [the meaning] as in such passages as "one falls into ignorance.

Furthermore, the explanatory gloss for the term "having directly known" (*sayam abhiññā*) is "without being led by another," while the gloss for the term "having realized" (*sacchikatvā*) is "having done so by oneself...
The word *sayaṃ* (oneself) should also be construed with the word "having realized. By means of distinguished...
"By means of knowledge" (ñāṇena) is a statement of its cause or a statement of its instrument.

In this regard, although omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) does not have the nature of something to be realized like the fruit or Nibbāna, once the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) has been attained, it is indeed attained;
therefore, its making manifest through direct experience is "realization" (sacchikiriyā).

He said: "Having made it manifest through distinguished knowledge. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is: "by means of the cause which is the attainment of distinguished knowledge, namely, the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga-ñāṇa*). Alternatively, if "distinguished knowledge" is intended to refer to the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa*), then the instrumental case is also appropriate in the sense of an instrument.
And here, "proclamation" refers to the Truths and so forth, which are objects of further knowledge.
It should be understood from the accomplishment of the task of teaching and from the declaration, “I am the one, the perfectly enlightened Buddha,” and so forth.

“By means of qualities” (guṇadhammehi) means by means of those phenomena (dhammehi) designated as qualities. “According to reality” (yathābhūtaṃ) is the same as “according to truth” (yathābhuccaṃ), by virtue of the suffix -ṇya used in its own sense.
Regarding the word “vadamānā” (speaking): here the word *māna* has the sense of existence (sattiattha), as in the passage, “Bhikkhus, when one person arises in the world...”
"...arises," meaning that they make an effort to speak [in such a way]. For those who are thus disposed are indeed called "desirous of speaking";
therefore he said, "of the Tathāgata," and so forth. Even though they speak with omissions, they should not be said to speak correctly as if they were speaking erroneously;
thus, in order to show how they speak correctly, it was said, "without omitting," and so forth. By that, indeed—

This shows that speaking without remainder is indeed "speaking rightly. By the phrase "they would be able to speak," he indicates that the word "vadeyyuṃ" (they would speak) has the sense of capability (*samattha*), just as in the expression "he would unravel this tangle" (*so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ*).
The construction is: "Which are those qualities (*dhammā*) praised by the Blessed One in this way?
[The answer follows: "There are, monks, other qualities... and so forth, up to "the knowledge of omniscience" (*sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ*) according to the canonical text.
Challenging the contradiction with the statement already made, he says, “If it were so,” and so forth. Therein, “if it were so” means:

if the statement “all-knowing knowledge” were indeed thus [as previously stated]. The designation in the plural number is said with reference to such passages as “There are, monks,” for even the word *atthi* (is/there are) here is used in the plural, as in “there are curds, there are cows,” and so on.

Because it is intended as a particle (*nipāta*) itself. Although this knowledge is indeed one in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), nevertheless, because of its association and its object, it deserves to be expressed in the plural; thus he answers with the passage:
"By way of various minds... by way of objects. "By way of association with various minds" means by way of association with many different minds. "Various objects" [means...]
"Of this" means "of that which has a manifold object"; by virtue of its being such, it is said to have "all as its object.

Furthermore, in the sense of "that which has a manifold object as its object," the term *puthuārammaṇārammaṇa*—where one instance of the word *ārammaṇa* is elided, as in the cases of *oṭṭhamukha* (lip-mouth) or *kāmāvacara* (sense-sphere)—is rendered here as "from having a manifold object."
Thus it is said; by this, he demonstrates that this [wisdom] accomplishes the function of manifold knowledge (*puthuñāṇakicca*).

For indeed, this wisdom is unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth (*yoni*), the knowledge that delimits the five destinations (*gati*), the remaining among the six uncommon knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*), the knowledge that distinguishes the seven noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), and the unshakable knowledge in the eight assemblies (*parisā*).

It accomplishes, as appropriate, the function of the various hundreds of thousands of types of knowledge—such as the knowledge of the full comprehension of the nine abodes of beings and the knowledge of the ten powers—by way of being the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for those numerous phenomena that serve as its objects. The passage beginning with “For that... is an explanation of that [preceding point] in due order. The passage beginning with “As it is said... [is explained as follows]: *Pakiṇṇakakathā* (Miscellaneous Discussion) The Blessed One has taught the dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in many ways. Among these, the following is the most fundamental: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; from the cessation of this, that ceases. This is called the "dependent origination of the primary meaning" (*padatthāna-paṭiccasamuppāda*). Furthermore, there is the "dependent origination of the specific characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa-paṭiccasamuppāda*), which is the teaching on the causal relationship between the aggregates, bases, and elements. There is also the "dependent origination of the process" (*pavatti-paṭiccasamuppāda*), which is the teaching on the sequence of the twelve factors starting from ignorance. And there is the "dependent origination of the cessation" (*nirodha-paṭiccasamuppāda*), which is the teaching on the sequence of the cessation of those same factors. Regarding the first, the "dependent origination of the primary meaning," it is taught in the *Mahānidāna Sutta*: "Bhikkhus, when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; from the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be... with volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases come to be; with the six sense bases as condition, contact comes to be; with contact as condition, feeling comes to be; with feeling as condition, craving comes to be; with craving as condition, clinging comes to be; with clinging as condition, existence comes to be; with existence as condition, birth comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. "But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very birth, aging-and-death ceases... from the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; from the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; from the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; from the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; from the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; from the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; from the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; from the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; from the cessation of existence, birth ceases; from the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this context, "birth" (*jāti*) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in a new existence. "Aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇa*) refers to the state of the aggregates from the time they have manifested until the moment immediately preceding death.

"Volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*) refer to the wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral kamma performed during the course of existence (*pavatta*) in a previous life. "Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) itself. "Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the mental and physical aggregates from the moment after rebirth-linking until the end of the five aggregates in the womb. "The six sense bases" (*saḷāyatana*) refers to the six internal bases from the time the fetus emerges from the womb until the faculties mature. "Contact" (*phassa*) refers to the meeting of the three—the faculty, the object, and consciousness—at the stage of matured faculties. "Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the experience of the result of kamma at the stage of matured faculties. "Craving" (*taṇhā*) refers to the intense longing for sense pleasures at the stage of matured faculties. "Clinging" (*upādāna*) refers to the firm adherence to sense pleasures at the stage of matured faculties. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the wholesome or unwholesome kamma accumulated at the stage of matured faculties, which leads to future rebirth. "Birth" (*jāti*) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking in the future existence. Regarding the second, the "dependent origination of the specific characteristics," it is taught in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*: "And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering; association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one desires is suffering—in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. Regarding the third, the "dependent origination of the process," it is taught in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta*: "And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases come to be; with the six sense bases as condition, contact comes to be; with contact as condition, feeling comes to be; with feeling as condition, craving comes to be; with craving as condition, clinging comes to be; with clinging as condition, existence comes to be; with existence as condition, birth comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. Regarding the fourth, the "dependent origination of the cessation," it is taught in the same sutta: "But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, volitional formations cease; from the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases... such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Among these, the "dependent origination of the primary meaning" is the most fundamental. It is by means of this that the other types of dependent origination are established. Furthermore, the "dependent origination of the process" is included within the "dependent origination of the primary meaning," while the "dependent origination of the specific characteristics" and the "dependent origination of the cessation" are included within the "dependent origination of the process. Now, regarding the "dependent origination of the primary meaning," the phrase "when this exists, that comes to be" indicates the presence of the cause. The phrase "from the arising of this, that arises" indicates the arising of the effect. The phrase "when this does not exist, that does not come to be" indicates the absence of the cause. The phrase "from the cessation of this, that ceases" indicates the cessation of the effect. Thus, it should be understood that this dependent origination possesses four characteristics: the characteristic of presence, the characteristic of arising, the characteristic of absence, and the characteristic of cessation. Furthermore, this dependent origination is to be understood as having three periods: the past, the present, and the future. In the past, there was ignorance and volitional formations; in the present, there is consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling; in the future, there will be craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging-and-death. Moreover, it is to be understood as having two aspects: the aspect of defilement (*saṃkilesa*) and the aspect of purification (*vodāna*). The aspect of defilement consists of the sequence of ignorance through to existence. The aspect of purification consists of the sequence of the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering. Finally, it is to be understood as having three roots: the root of craving, the root of views, and the root of misconduct. The root of craving is the cause for the cycle of rebirth. The root of views is the cause for the cycle of wandering in saṃsāra. The root of misconduct is the cause for experiencing suffering in the realms of misery. By abandoning these three roots, one attains the cessation of suffering. Thus, the Blessed One has taught the dependent origination in these various ways for the purpose of making known the nature of reality, for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the Dhamma, and for the purpose of establishing the path to liberation.
He shows the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi* as the means of proof. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it refers to past phenomena.
Having set aside the state of having diverse objects by way of a single occurrence, the expression "by way of repeated arising" is stated in order to show that state through successive occurrences.
For even in succession, the knowledge of omniscience proceeds toward its objects; it does not do so in that [other] manner.
"Simultaneously. As the outsiders say: "The Omniscient One knows everything simultaneously, not gradually.

If that were so, how could there be a complete penetration of the knowable—which has inconceivable and immeasurable divisions—by means of a single cognition that possesses limits? Or who says that "the knowledge of omniscience has limits"? For it is without limits.
That knowledge is like the knowable. For this has been said: "As far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge.

Even so, when the knowable—which is divided into many distinctions by way of genus, plane, intrinsic nature, and so forth, and by way of direction, location, time, and so forth—is grasped successively, would it not be impossible to achieve a penetration that leaves nothing remaining? This is not so. For that which...
Whether it be something desired to be known by the Blessed One in its entirety or in part, regarding that, his knowledge proceeds through direct perception due to his unimpeded movement.
And because there is no distraction, the Blessed One is at all times in a state of meditative concentration;
thus, the direct perceptibility of whatever he desires to know cannot be prevented. For it is said: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, is dependent upon his own wish..."

“Knowledge,” etc. One might ask: "Is it not to be understood here that, like those looking at a cloth from a distance, or like those practicing insight (vipassanā) into 'all phenomena are non-self,' the Blessed One’s knowledge proceeds in an undetermined form at the time of awakening to many phenomena?
It is indeed to be so understood, because of the inconceivable power of a Buddha’s knowledge. For this very reason, he said: "The domain of a Buddha..."
“[He is] inconceivable”—this, however, is the definitive conclusion here:

by the attainment of unobstructed knowledge—which is capable of awakening to all phenomena in every aspect and functions according to his own wish—the Blessed One became capable of penetrating all phenomena through his mental continuum due to the abandonment of all obscurations to the knowable;
therefore, he is “all-knowing,” not merely because of a single simultaneous awakening to all phenomena.
Just as fire is called "all-consuming" because it has the capacity to burn all fuel according to its own continuity, so too is this meaning intended.

Although this matter has indeed been explained in detail previously, it is elucidated again here out of a desire to benefit those who hear it by way of a different method, and because this [work] proceeds by way of purifying the ancient commentary; thus, there is no fault of redundancy here.

...should be sought in such cases as these. And here, although the Blessed One’s ten powers and other forms of knowledge are indeed not shared by others, because those knowledges have all places as their object, the Buddha-qualities are not said to be fully grasped by them alone.
However, because the knowledge of omniscience has an unrestricted range of objects, when that is grasped, all the Buddha-qualities are grasped.
They are indeed so; therefore, it should be understood that by following the meaning of the text (*pāḷi*), that very same knowledge is what is intended.

For even in the text, in the passage stating, "Those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata’s true praise," it is precisely this [knowledge] that is revealed, because there is no other [knowledge] that encompasses the entire range [of objects], and it is only by means of that which encompasses the entire range that one speaks of the "true" (*yathābhūta*).
"Because it arises from correct speaking.

Regarding the phrase "it is quite another," the word *eva* (quite) is intended to show a definitive determination; thus it is said, "‘It is quite another’ is here a word of delimitation (*vavatthāpanavacana*).
The meaning of "a word of delimitation" is "a word of definitive determination (*sanniṭṭhāpanavacana*)," and definitive determination is indeed restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
To explain how this is so, he says, “It is another,” and so forth. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase “not the abstentions from taking life, etc.,” he shows what is excluded.
Furthermore, because its scope is not fixed, this word *eva*—just like the word *ca*—stands for something other than where it is actually uttered, according to the speaker’s intention;
thus he says, “They are profound,” and so forth. And by the word *iti*, used in the sense of “beginning with,” [it is implied that they are] difficult to see.
It shows that [the Dhamma] has turned away from being easy to understand—yet not difficult to understand; peaceful—yet not distressing; sublime—yet not inferior;
beyond the sphere of reasoning—yet not within the sphere of reasoning; subtle—yet not coarse; and to be realized by the wise—yet not to be realized by fools.
"By all the phrases" means by all the phrases up to the phrase "to be realized by the wise."
Thus, strengthening the necessity for this reversal by means of reasoning, he said: "The knowledge of the disciples' perfections," and so forth.

Therein, "the knowledge of the disciples' perfections" refers to the knowledge consisting of the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*), the six direct knowledges (*abhijñā*), and the four analytical insights (*pratisamvid*), which is accomplished through the fulfillment of the perfections such as giving by the disciples;
likewise, there is the knowledge of individual enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*) belonging to the Paccekabuddhas. "Than that" means than the knowledge of the disciples' perfections. "Therein" means...
Regarding the knowledge of the perfection of the disciples (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*). "Even than that" means even than the knowledge of private enlightenment (*paccekabodhiñāṇa*) which was just mentioned.

By the word *api* (or the particle *pi*), he implies: "What need is there to mention the knowledge of the perfection of the disciples? "There too" means even in the knowledge of private enlightenment.
"But from this," however, means from the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); therefore, it is in this knowledge of omniscience that a definitive distinction is found.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). They are "profoundly distinguished" (*gambhīresu visesā*) because they are distinguished among the profound, or because they are profoundly distinguished from others. Alternatively, "this one is profound and this one is profound;

these are more profound than those" means they are "more profound" (*gambhīratarā*). Here, the exclusion [of what is not profound] is established by the suffix *-tara* itself. The construction here is as follows:
