Because of the expression “for one who does not grasp,” it is shown by the phrase “of those defilements consisting of grasping” that the extinction (*nibbuti*) taught here refers specifically to the graspings (*parāmāsa*), since through that very teaching, the extinction of others as well is established.
The meaning is: “of the defilements known as graspings. Furthermore, although...
From the expression “of one who does not misapprehend,” it is understood that here the extinction (nibbuti) of the misapprehensions themselves is taught;
however, by that teaching, the extinction of the remaining defilements is also said to be taught, because they share the same function of being abandoned.
Therefore, their extinction must also be extracted and shown, which is why it is stated: “of those defilements consisting of misapprehension.”
The meaning is: of the misapprehensions (parāmāsa) known as craving, views, and conceit, as well as of the other defilements. This is according to the "cow-and-calf" method (gobalībaddanaya).

Furthermore, "extinction" (nibbuti) refers to the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), which consists in the state of being extinguished; and that the Blessed One attained right at the foot of the Bodhi tree, therefore it was known by him personally (paccattaṃyeva).
"By one who has practiced accordingly" means by one who has practiced in that manner. To show that practice, the connection is shown with the words:
"Of those very [feelings]... he stated the beginning. But why does he teach the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) specifically for feelings?

He says: "In which," and so forth; by this, he shows the elegance of his teaching. For the Blessed One, having attained mastery in teaching and being skilled in instruction, [teaches] by way of the aggregates, bases, and so on.

Although various teachings on the Four Noble Truths exist, [the Buddha] extracts feeling itself as the ground for full understanding—since it is the root of such plunging—in order to show that the thicket of views leaps into the dense forest of views through wrong practice.
"Here" (*idha*) means in this doctrine; it may also mean "in this way. "Meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) refers to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.
For here, the five aggregates of clinging, comprised by the mention of "feeling," are the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).

The origin of ignorance, comprised by the mention of the "origin of feelings," is the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*). The truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) is indicated by the terms "disappearance" and "escape.
And the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is indicated by the phrase "having known it as it really is. Thus, the four truths are to be understood. "As it really is..."

Regarding the phrase “having understood,” this is a term that requires an analytical explanation (*vibhajjabyākaraṇa*); therefore, in order to demonstrate its meaning through analysis, the passage beginning with “therein” (*tattha*) and so forth was stated.

For specifically, the meaning regarding the origin and other [truths] must be shown by analyzing them according to their respective characteristics, such as “with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling.
However, generally speaking, the origin and other [aspects] of feeling are [to be understood] by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanāpaññā*).
The meaning is: having known and penetrated by way of penetrating the object, and by way of penetrating without delusion through path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*).

"In the sense of the arising of conditions" means: by the arising of conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth—characterized by the statement, "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises"—and by the fact that [the defilements] have not been eradicated by the Path. As far as...
As long as something is not eradicated by the Path, it is called a "condition" (paccaya). "The characteristic of arising" means the characteristic of origination;

the sense is "birth. Regarding the phrase "of the five characteristics," here one must include the characteristic of conditionality (*paccayalakkhaṇa*) in addition to the characteristic of origination for all four types of conditions, because they act as supports for those [phenomena] accordingly, depending on their arising.
It is described in exactly that way as "by means of the path and by non-eradication.
"In the sense of the cessation of conditions" means by the cessation of conditions such as ignorance, according to the characteristic stated thus: "When this has ceased, that ceases;
with the cessation of this, that ceases," and by both the path and eradication. "The characteristic of transformation" is the characteristic of cessation.
"Bhaṅga" means destruction; "vaya" means cessation. "Yanti" [means they go] because of the cause known as the state of being a condition.
"Paṭicca vedanaṃ" means having obtained a previously arisen feeling that serves as a condition, such as an object.
"Sukhaṃ somanassaṃ" means both pleasure and mental joy. "Ayaṃ" refers to the subsequent pleasure and joy that arise accordingly from the preceding feeling.
The state of being a condition. "Taste" (*assāda*) is so called because it is something to be tasted.

Another method of explanation: *yaṃ* refers to pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*somanassa*). Furthermore, although pleasure and mental joy were previously indicated in the neuter gender, they are here indicated in the masculine gender in view of the word "taste" (*assāda*), which is in the masculine.
However, in this alternative interpretation, [the term refers to] pleasure and mental joy themselves.
The arising itself is demonstrated by those things that possess arising, because there is no difference between the power and the possessor of the power.

For their arising is not obtained apart from pleasure and joy. Thus, the arising of pleasure and joy dependent on a preceding feeling is called the "gratification" (assāda) of that preceding feeling, in the sense that it is what is gratified. This, then, is the summary meaning here: the previously arisen...

Regarding the arising of joy based on feeling: that aspect of the preceding feeling which is characterized as a condition to be relished, or the aspect of relishing characterized by the arising of joy—this is the "relishing of the preceding feeling.
But how does pleasure arise based on feeling? Is it not the case that [pleasure] has tangible objects as its object? It is indeed the mental pleasure alone [that arises].

This fault does not apply because what is intended here is the occurrence [of feeling] based on an object (*ārabbha-pavatti*). For in the case of occurrence based on an object, the mention of "joy" (*somanassa*) serves as a qualification;

thus, "joy" is taken as "pleasure" (*sukha*), just as one says "the tree is a *sīsapā*. However, in the case of its arising through the influence of other conditions (*añña-paccaya-vasena*), even bodily pleasure is indeed a gratification (*assāda*).
Alternatively, this should be understood as a statement regarding whatever is obtained.

By the passage beginning, “Whatever feeling is impermanent,” etc., the power of the possessor of power is demonstrated. Herein, this is the meaning: whatever feeling, having come to be, is impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been;

is suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away; and is subject to change in the sense of being transformed in two ways—by aging and by death. Of such a feeling, this state of impermanence, suffering, and liability to change [is thus shown].
"Disadvantage (*ādīnava*) refers to every kind of feeling (*vedanā*). For it is called *ādīnava* because from it there arises what is most miserable (*ādīnaṃ paramakāruññaṃ*).
Furthermore, in the sense of proceeding in an extremely wretched manner, a miserable person is an *ādīnava*;
since this [feeling] also has such a nature, it is likewise so called. For power (*satti*) is inseparable from one who possesses power (*sattimā*), due to their invariable concomitance."

And here, by the phrase "impermanent," he states the disadvantage of equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) by way of the suffering inherent in formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā), or else the disadvantage of all feelings;

by the phrase "painful," he states it of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) by way of the suffering of pain itself (dukkha-dukkhatā); and by the phrase "subject to change," he states it of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) by way of the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā).
Alternatively, all three terms may be applied without distinction to all three types of feeling.
“Chandarāgavinayo” means the disciplining, that is, the destruction, of passion (rāga) which is designated as desire (chanda).

According to the statement, “The change of gender and case-ending occurs for the sake of the sense,” one should connect this with the phrase “the abandoning of desire and passion. These two terms are merely synonymous expressions.

Regarding the phrase “having known it as it really is” (yathābhūtaṃ viditvā), since the Path has been mentioned, the application may also be made respectively according to the Path and Nibbāna. [The object is] “of feeling” (vedanāya).
This is the ablative case. "Escaping" (*nissaraṇa*) means renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
For as long as one does not abandon the desire and lust bound up with feeling, for that long this person remains attached to feeling.
But when one abandons that desire and lust, then this person has escaped from feeling and is detached from it; therefore, the abandoning of desire and lust is the escape from feeling.
It has been stated. Furthermore, by that very definition, material and immaterial phenomena—which serve as the co-nascent support and object for feeling—are indeed included;
thus, the statement regarding escape from the five aggregates of clinging is established.

For the teaching was delivered under the heading of "feeling," and the reason for this has already been explained above. This same meaning may also be understood by way of the "conveying of characteristics" (lakkhaṇahāra).
It is to be analyzed. For it was said by the venerable elder Mahākaccāna:
“When a single state has been stated, whatever states have the same characteristic as that which is stated—all those become stated;
this is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics.”

Because the remaining types of clinging are rooted in clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), and because when clinging to sense-pleasures has been abandoned there is no remainder of clinging, it is said: "through the disappearance of desire and lust, he is without clinging.
By this, the meaning of the phrase "liberated through non-clinging" (*anupādāvimutto*) is shown in brief. This is what is meant:
through the disappearance of desire and lust he is without clinging, and because of that absence of clinging, he is liberated through non-clinging. This is the meaning.

In order to elaborate upon or explain [the term], the passage beginning with "yasmiṃ" was stated. Therein, "yasmiṃ upādāne" refers to sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*), which serves as the root for the remaining types of clinging.
"Tassa" refers to that sense-desire clinging. "Anupādiyitvā" means not grasping by way of desire and lust;
by this, he demonstrates that the compound "anupādāvimutto" may be analyzed either as a contraction through the elision of the *ya*-sound or as a non-compound (analytic) expression.
37. “These indeed,” and so forth, is the concluding statement regarding the manner in which the Dhamma was answered as asked.

To show that the very understanding mentioned by the word “understands” (*pajānāti*) is indicated here by the word “these” (*ime*), he said “those which,” and so forth. Those Dhammas of omniscient knowledge... [as before] ...which I asked about;
those Dhammas of omniscient knowledge... [as before] ...by which they would speak; and that... [as before] ...he understands—thus they are indicated.
The construction is as follows: "It should be understood that these qualities of omniscient knowledge are profound... [and so on]... and are to be realized by the wise.

The phrase beginning with "Thus" (*evaṃ*) shows the summarized meaning. In that context, although by the statement "Monks, the Tathāgata is liberated through non-clinging" he demonstrates the arising of the fruit of the supreme path, and by "the origin of feelings," etc., he demonstrates the meditation subject of the Four Truths; nevertheless, for whichever...
Because the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) has been thoroughly penetrated, one is capable of analyzing this speculative view in its divisions, along with its causes and its destinations.

Desiring to make that very same [element] even more evident by means of its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), as well as the stage of its arising through the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā), the King of Dhamma shows it thus; hence it is said: "That very [element] is set forth."

"Concluded" (*nigamita*) means "brought to a conclusion. "In between" (*antara*) means that, in the interval between the statements posing questions and those providing answers which demonstrate the Dhamma, the various views have been analyzed by way of showing the manner in which he understands them.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) on the commentary to the first section of recitation.
Commentary on the Theory of Partial Eternity (Ekaccasassatavāda): 38. To clarify the derivative term “Ekaccasassatikā” by means of its corresponding compound, it is stated as “Ekaccasassatavādā.
One for whom a certain portion among beings and formations is eternal is an “ekaccasassata”; those who hold such a doctrine are the “Ekaccasassatavādā.”

The "Partial-Eternalists" (*ekaccasassatikā*) are so called because they hold the doctrine of partial eternity by means of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*); alternatively, they are "those for whom there is a doctrine of partial eternity" by means of compounds (*samāsa*).

This same method applies to the term "Partial-Non-Eternalists" (*ekaccaasassatikā*). Now, one might ask: "When 'Partial-Eternalists' is stated, does it not already follow as a matter of course that others are determined to be 'Partial-Non-Eternalists'?

True, this is established in terms of meaning (*attha*), but it is not established in terms of the word itself (*sadda*). Therefore, [the other term] is more clearly evident from the standpoint of the word.
It was stated in that way in order to show [this]. For here, the Master of Dhamma does not teach the Dhamma by leaving anything remaining.
Those who hold the doctrine that "the Lord is eternal, but other beings are impermanent" are partial-eternalists regarding beings, such as those who maintain the theory of a Creator (Issaravāda).
Likewise, those who hold the doctrine that "Brahmā is eternal, but others are impermanent" are also [partial-eternalists]. [So too are those who say] "atoms are eternal..."
"dyads and so forth are impermanent" (to be seen in the first section of the seventh chapter on the *Vaiśeṣika-darśana*).
Those who maintain such doctrines are the "partial-eternalists" (*ekaccasassatikā*) regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), such as the followers of Kaṇāda (*Kāṇāda*).

Likewise, those who maintain the doctrine that "the eye and so forth are impermanent, but consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is permanent" (to be seen in the *Nyāya-darśana* and the *Vaiśeṣika-darśana*) are also [partial-eternalists].

*Idha* means in this phrase, "certain eternalists," or in this teaching. *Gahitā* means stated, or accepted by the knowledge of the teaching through the mode of being what ought to be taught, because it was taught in that very way. For here, the first three doctrines were taught with reference to beings, while the fourth was taught with reference to formations (*saṅkhāra*). This was stated by way of showing the true nature of those phenomena that are grasped as being eternal, but not by way of showing the doctrine of certain eternalists.
For their view is that what is considered eternal is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: “Whether called ‘mind’... [etc. ...it will endure. For there is no intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) that has been conditioned by causes.

If one were to claim that it possesses the state of being eternal and stable, such a claim could not be made by anyone who is not insane; and by this, the irrationality of the doctrine of the sevenfold predication (sattabhaṅgavāda)—
which proceeds by asserting that "intrinsic natures associated with arising, passing away, and stability might be permanent, might be impermanent,
or might be indescribable," and so forth— is demonstrated.

In this regard, here is the analysis of the inconsistency: If it were said that "by the very same nature by which a phenomenon is said to exist, by that same nature that phenomenon does not exist," then there would be a doctrine of non-absolutism (anekantavāda).
If, however, it were said [they do not exist] by another nature, then there would be no doctrine of non-absolutism.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assert here a connection with another location and so forth, because such a thing is established for all the world and because there is no dispute regarding it.
Furthermore, those who say, "Just as when a golden jar is fashioned into a crown, the state of being a jar perishes, the state of being a crown arises, yet the state of being gold remains;
so too, among all intrinsic natures (sabhāva), some phenomena perish, some phenomena arise, while the intrinsic nature itself remains"—they should be asked: "What is that gold which was in the jar?"
If that which is situated on the crown [of the head] is form and so forth, then it is impermanent like sound.

Or, if it is merely a conventional designation for a collection of form and so forth, then neither its existence, nor its non-existence, nor its permanence can be established; therefore, the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekantavāda) would not hold.

Furthermore, the fault regarding the occurrence of the attributes (dhamma) and the possessor of attributes (dhammin) as being either different or not different has already been stated in the investigation of the eternalist view (sassatavāda).

Therefore, that [self] should be understood there according to the method already stated. Furthermore, neither the self nor the world exists in an ultimate sense as something of a nature that is permanent, impermanent, or indescribable—just as permanence and the other [terms] are each a specific nature, or like a lamp and so forth.
For it is impossible for form and the other aggregates, whose intrinsic nature is arising and passing away, to possess a nature that is permanent, impermanent, or indescribable.
One might think that the soul (*jīva*) could possess some form of permanence or other [quality] among the sevenfold propositions;

thus, just as with the first proposition, the impossibility of the remaining propositions must likewise be understood, and so the irrationality of the doctrine of the sevenfold propositions (*sattabhaṅgavāda*) should be known.
But is it not the case that in the doctrine stating, "some phenomena are eternal, some are non-eternal," there is a determination of the non-eternal nature of the eye and so forth?
It is simply the realization of things according to their true nature; therefore, how could there be wrong view for those who speak thus?
Or who says that "the determination of the non-eternal nature of the eye and so forth is wrong view"?
Rather, it should be understood here that wrong view is the determination of certain phenomena—which are actually non-eternal—as being eternal. By that [determination], however, in one position...
Furthermore, while it is active, its realization of the non-eternality of the eye and so forth is corrupted by association—
like a lump of ghee mixed with poison— and thus, because it is incapable of performing its own function, it does not deserve to be placed on the side of right view. Alternatively,
even though the eye and so forth are determined to be non-eternal, they are still regarded by those holding wrong views as having the very nature of a soul (jīva) superimposed upon them.
"Those who grasp [it]"—the state of wrong view regarding the realization of that [self] cannot be prevented. For this very reason, the Pāḷi says:

"The eye, too... the body, too—this is the self," and so forth. And having established it thus, according to the unconditioned and conditioned elements respectively, there occurs the following [view]: "Some phenomena are eternal; some are non-eternal."

The objection that even the doctrine of analysis (vibhajjavāda) would be nothing other than the doctrine of partial eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda) finds no ground, because it is a practice based on the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) as they are without error.
Indeed, this is precisely a practice according to the true nature of phenomena without error, because— as explained by the aforementioned method—
it is unmixed [with speculative views] and does not superimpose an intrinsic nature of a "life-principle" (jīva).
Here it is said: Even in the former doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavāda*), the apprehension of impermanent phenomena as "eternal" is specifically a wrong view (*micchādassana*).
However, the grasping of what is eternal as "eternal" is not a wrong view, because it is an apprehension according to their actual nature (*yathāsabhāvaggāha*).
This being so, one cannot say that this doctrine is merely another variety of the same doctrine; for just as here, so too in the former case, it refers to exactly the same things.
Regarding the phrase "because of the possibility of grasping at eternalism with respect to phenomena":

this must indeed be stated because this doctrine—namely, the conceptualization that "some phenomena are eternal and some are non-eternal"—is shown to function by way of a distinction among the phenomena to be grasped, even though they are all non-eternal.
But is this not a partial grasping at eternalism (*sappadesa-sassataggāha*), since a single part is included within the whole? [In response: It is so in the former case...

Would there be a convergence with the grasping at eternalism without remainder? Even so, it cannot be said [that they are identical], because the two doctrines proceed according to their respective specific objects.

For some proponents of views are intent upon the view that "all phenomena are eternal," while others hold that "some are eternal and some are non-eternal. This is because one group takes up all conditioned formations without exception, whereas the other takes them only partially.

And this is indeed well-known from both of these two positions. Moreover, it cannot be maintained in that way because of the nature of the adherence to the continuity of the aggregates (khandha-pabandha) in both the case of multiple bases and the case of a single base.

For even the fourfold eternalist adheres to the eternity of the mass of immaterial phenomena (arūpa-dhamma-puñja) only in dependence upon various types of material bodies (rūpa-kāya) according to the distinction of their births.
It is born from the grasping of the destruction of the material body through direct knowledge (*abhiññāṇa*), as well as through hearsay (*anussava*) and so forth. Thus it has been said:

"Having passed away from there, he arose there," and "They pass away and they are reborn," and so on. However, one who gains a specific [wrong] view, such as an eternalist (*ekaccasassatika*), produces a dogmatic adherence by grasping at the aspect of eternity within the continuity of phenomena (*dhammapabandha*), which is a composite whole whose divisions have not been properly investigated.
This is because that adherence has as its object the continuum of aggregates comprised within a single existence.
For indeed, in all three theories, it is stated only this much: "He recollects that past life, but does not recollect beyond that.

However, the distinction between the adherence to eternalism held by both types of rationalists—the eternalists and the partial-eternalists—is quite evident from their having as their objects both material and immaterial phenomena.

And here there is a substitution of the letter *ṭ* for *t*.
For it is said that the world contracts (*saṃvaṭṭati*) from the moment the great cloud that causes dissolution arises until not even a subtle formation remains.

In the Pāli, the term "world" (*loka*) is intended to mean the receptacle-world consisting of the earth and so forth, because the remainder [of the world] is predominant; he shows this by stating "for the most part" (*yebhuyyena*).
“By ‘ye’ and so forth. “In the higher Brahma-worlds” means in the planes above the Ābhassara plane. For it is the destruction of an eon by fire that is intended here;
therefore the text says, “they belong to the Ābhassara realm.
If one asks why only that is mentioned, it is because that [destruction] occurs most frequently. This is the restriction of the section.
“Seven times seven [fire] cycles, and water every eighth;
when sixty-four are complete, there shall be one wind-cycle. (This is also found in the commentary on the fifth chapter of the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*).

Regarding the phrase “or in the formless realms,” here the word “or” (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative, referring to other world-systems apart from those world-systems currently undergoing dissolution.
He explains it thus: It cannot be understood that all beings in the states of loss (apāya) arise at that time in the fine-material or immaterial realms;

for it is impossible for those with particularly long lifespans in the states of loss to be reborn in the human world, and without such rebirth in the human world, their arising in those [higher] realms at that time would be impossible.
For even one who holds fixed wrong view, when the world is contracting...
It is stated in the commentaries that for an eon he is not released from hell, but is reborn only on the back of the Cakkavāḷa.
Although all beings are produced by the mind through the volitional formations of merit and demerit,

those belonging to the fine-material sphere alone are called "mind-made" (manomaya) because they are produced by mind alone without external conditions, and not because they are prepared by external conditions.
To show that it is something other than those [previously mentioned], he said, "It is mind-made (manomaya) because it is produced by the mind.
If this is so, does it not follow that even spontaneously born beings (opapātika) in the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara) would possess the quality of being mind-made? It does not follow;

for he specified [the term] with the word "jhāna," saying "by means of jhāna-mind," to demonstrate that the designation "mind-made" applies only to those beings produced by an extraordinary mind consisting of higher consciousness (adhicitta).
It has been stated thus. But does this not imply that beings in the formless realm (arūpāvacara) possess a mind-made nature (manomaya)?
No; for in that case, since there is no possibility of restriction—because there is no suspicion that [the body] must be produced by external conditions—the term "mind-made" cannot be applied.

This conventional expression "mind-made" is established in the world with reference to beings in the fine-material realm (rūpāvacara). For it is said: "consisting of food, consisting of drink, consisting of mind, consisting of bliss."
Proponents of the Vedas conceive of the self in five ways as "consisting of consciousness. Regarding the doctrine of annihilationism as well, he will say, "divine, material, mind-made";
however, because of the power of their meditative absorptions (jhāna), they feed on rapture, possess their own radiance, and move through the sky—thus he says, "rapture for them," and so forth;
the meaning is that they possess the radiance of the self itself. Or, it means their beautiful abiding nature.
It is also appropriate to say that "these [beings] abide in beauty. The phrase "at the maximum" is said with reference to the Ābhassara (Streaming-Radiance) deities.

However, the Parittābha (Limited Radiance) and Appamāṇābha (Immeasurable Radiance) deities abide for two and four *kappas* respectively. "Eight *kappas*" refers to eight great *kappas*, which constitute a collection of four incalculable *kappas*.
40. The word *vaṭṭa* (wheel/round), though denoting destruction, indicates the sense of "staying" (*saṇṭhāna*) because it is joined with a prefix that expresses negation.
He said, "It consolidates" (*saṇṭhāti*); or, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the sense is that it "is produced" or "increases.

For, starting from the arising of the great clouds of prosperity, through the successive emergence of the waters that support the earth and the winds that support those waters, and so on, up until the manifestation of the moon and sun, the world is said to be "expanding" (*vivaṭṭati*).
"By nature" (*pakatiyā*) means by its own inherent character; of that [nature], it is "empty" (*suñña*).
This is the connection. He states the reason for its emptiness thus: "because of the non-existence of beings born there.

The meaning is that other beings have not yet arisen there beforehand; by this, he shows that it is not like certain celestial mansions (*vimāna*) which are empty because they have been abandoned by the beings born there.
Another method: "The first performance of one's own karma is the nature (pakati)," [and] the connection is "of the beings produced by that.
By this, he shows that just as this [world-system] arose first through the power of its own karma, so it is not for others;
there is no arising of them either earlier than that or at the same time. Thus, because of the non-existence of beings produced in such a way, it is "empty" (suññam).
The *Brahmapārisajja*, *Brahmapurohita*, and *Mahābrahma* deities are here [referred to as] the *Brahmakāyika* (those belonging to the Brahma-body).

Because they are the dwelling place of those [deities], the plane is also called "the *Brahmakāyika*. However, in the reading *brahmakāyikabhūmi*, the meaning is "the plane belonging to the *Brahmakāyikas*.

The agent (*kattā*) is one who acts himself; the causer (*kāretā*) is one who commands others. [This is stated] in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the discourse on the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇakathā*).
By this method, he demonstrates the order of production as well as the reason for its being produced by both kamma-condition and temperature (utu).
It is called "kamma-condition" (kammapaccayā) because kamma is its condition by way of being a decisive support (upanissaya).

Alternatively, it is called "kamma-condition" because it is the condition for kamma, insofar as it acts as a cooperative factor for the kamma that ripens for the beings born therein. It is called "temperature-originated" (utusamuṭṭhāna) because temperature is its source (samuṭṭhāna).

“Arising from temperature conditioned by kamma” (*kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānā*). Alternatively, according to the method of compound formation, the reading is “arising from temperature which has kamma as its concurrent condition” (*kammapaccaya-utusamuṭṭhānā*).

A “kamma-condition” (*kammapaccaya*) is a condition that is accompanied by kamma; or, in the manner already stated, it is a condition that has become a companion to kamma. That very [condition] is the temperature (*utu*), and that itself is its source (*samuṭṭhāna*); thus, it is “arising from temperature conditioned by kamma.
“A ground of jewels” (*ratanabhūmi*) is so called because of the power of meritorious kamma that has reached its highest excellence.
The ground is like a jewel; it is not merely the ground itself, but rather that which surrounds it as well—thus he said, "the natural state" (*pakati*), and so forth.
"In the place where they were naturally born" means in the birthplace of those who lived in previous eons. "Therein" refers to the plane of the Brahmakāyika devas mentioned as the "Brahmā-palace.
These two locative bases are given according to both the general and the specific. How is it superior?
"For those established on the plane of the second jhāna, there is rebirth on the inferior plane of the first jhāna"—thus he said, "Then, for beings," and so forth;
it is implied that they have developed the first jhāna through the influence of attachment (*nikanti*). The connection is:

"By its very nature (*pakati*), by its own characteristic (*sabhāva*), attachment—that is, craving—arises. "In the place where one has dwelt" means in a place previously inhabited. "Descending from there" means...
By way of rebirth, they descend from the plane of the second jhāna to the plane of the first jhāna; the meaning is that they go [down].
"Short-lived" means having a lifespan of limited measure due to the connection with the result arising from that sublime meritorious deed performed.
"Of that world of gods" means in that world of gods; or it is a designation of relation by way of support. "Precisely by the measure of their lifespan."

By the measure of the maximum lifespan. "Limited" means small. "They fall away in the interval" means that, like a measure of rice placed in a royal storehouse, they—having exhausted their merit—fall away from that divine world in the midst of its maximum lifespan, according to the measure of their own karma.
But what is this so-called "maximum lifespan," and how is its measure determined? It is said: that which belongs to them...

For those beings, in each specific state of existence (*bhava*), there is a fixed duration for the continuity of karmic fruition (*vipākappabandha*). This occurs by way of a decisive support (*upanissaya*) consisting of previously established aspirations for that particular state of existence;

thus, as with the specific differences in the limbs, color, shape, and size of the body, there is generally a fixed limit regarding their respective destinies (*gati*), classes (*nikāya*), and so forth.
This is supported by conditions arising from such factors as semen and blood, or seasonal food and climate, in the case of womb-born beings, sense-sphere deities, and fine-material-sphere beings.
And because it is the cause of life, it is called "life" (*āyu*) by way of metaphorical designation; and by way of its maximum limit, it is called "maximum life" (*paramāyu*).

For the material and immaterial life-faculties (*rūpa- and arūpa-jīvitindriya*), which cause the co-nascent material and immaterial phenomena—though these exist for only their own respective moments—to persist in their mode of being, act as causes not only for their momentary stability, but also for their continued occurrence.
Furthermore, they are "sustainers" because they serve as the cause for the non-interruption of the continuity [of existence] until the cessation of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Therefore, this [life-span] has the life-force itself as its cause; moreover, for most gods and denizens of hell, it has a fixed limit, whereas for those of Uttarakuru, it is exclusively of a fixed limit. As for the remaining humans, ghosts, and animals—
However, during a period when there is an abundance of karma conducive to long duration,

the lifespan is of indefinite limit due to its varying length— whether long or short— depending on the conditions of the semen and blood produced by a continuum accompanied by that karma, as well as the conditions of temperature, nutriment, and so forth,

generated by the regular or irregular revolutions of the moon and sun which are rooted in those [karmic factors]. And of that [lifespan], it is according to the aspiration for existence previously established...
The restriction regarding specific colors, shapes, and so forth within various destinies and classes is established,
because their initial apprehension occurs exactly in that manner through seeing, tradition, and the like; thus,

having received from seeing and tradition the generally uniform duration of the stay for beings born in those various rebirths, [the desire for existence] proceeds by way of clinging to that as the ultimate goal.
First, the determination of the limit [of lifespan] should be understood.
For while karma is capable of producing the physical form and other characteristics dependent on this or that particular rebirth,
it is likewise incapable of producing a result in rebirths where the limit of lifespan is fixed, by exceeding that fixed limit.
It is not capable [of sustaining itself]; therefore it is said, "they pass away precisely at the measure of their lifespan.

Furthermore, because the mode of occurrence of the acquired aggregates—assisted by supporting conditions and accompanied by maintaining conditions—is in its essential nature the ultimate lifespan, since it does not exceed the aforementioned limit, it is impossible for them to remain even if there is a residue of karma.
Therefore it was said: "They are unable to remain by the power of their own merit.

Furthermore, from the statement, "Having passed away from the Ābhassara realm due to the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit," one should understand that, just as with the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), the inhabitants of the Brahma-realm (brahmakāyika) also generally possess a fixed limit to their lifespan.
For instance, when sons of the gods depart from the celestial world due to the exhaustion of their lifespan...
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathās* that beings pass away due to four causes: the exhaustion of merit, the exhaustion of food, and anger.
Regarding the phrase "for an eon (*kappa*) or for half an eon," it is the incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*) that is intended;
and that is indeed such a period of time. The word "or" (*vā*), however, has the sense of an alternative, meaning "or a third part of an eon, or less than that, or more."
41. *Anabhirati* means the very desire to associate with others, characterized by a lack of delight in dwelling alone.
Regarding this, it is said in the Pāḷi, "Because of having lived alone for a long time," that [the phrase] beginning with "even for another" was stated.

Having thus shown the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the meaning, [the author now presents] the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by way of resolving the objection: "Could there not also be dissatisfaction (*ukkaṇṭhitā*)?"
He shows this with the words beginning, "But that which... Discontent (*ukkaṇṭhitā*) is the agitation of the mind caused by separation from a beloved object or by failure to obtain a beloved object;
in its essential nature, however, it is simply an arising of a state of mental distress (*domanassa-cittuppāda*). Therefore, he says, "associated with aversion" (*paṭigha-sampayuttā*).

That [discontent] does not exist in the Brahma-world because it has been abandoned through the power of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). It is a prior state of the mind characterized by craving and views.

Terror and trembling are themselves agitation (*paritassanā*) here. For that [agitation] arises for one who has long remained in the delight of *jhāna* as a cause for the aforementioned lack of delight, and it is the basis for the grasping of "I" and "mine.
Therefore, he will say: "Neither craving nor views suffice for one who is agitated.
But was it not stated in the *Atthuddhāra* that, having cited this very same passage from the *Pāḷi*, [the Buddha said]: "Oh, may other beings also..."?
‘May they come to this state’—this is called ‘craving for existence. [Objection: Is this true? [Reply: It is true;
however, by giving a separate illustration for “craving for views,” that very craving for existence was extracted from it and stated.
But there is no fault here, because craving for views is not absent in this context. Now follows the extraction of meanings expressed by synonymous terms.

Having established what is intended here, he said, “But this [fear], etc.,” in order to clarify it. The very terror of the mind, which is designated as “aversion” (*paṭigha*), is the state of being afraid.
The same applies elsewhere as appropriate. The passage beginning with “dependent on birth” (*jātiṃ paṭicca*) is from the *Vibhaṅga* text;

herein is the commentary on its meaning: “Dependent on birth, fear” means the fear arisen with birth as its condition. “Terrifying” (*bhayānaka*) is a description of its mode. “Trembling” (*chambhitatta*)...

Trembling of the limbs due to fear is, specifically, the quivering of the heart-flesh. "Horripilation" (*lomahaṃsa*) means the bristling of the body hairs, like the upward-pointing state of pegs on a wall.
Having shown fear by way of its function through these two terms, it is further shown by way of its essential nature as "the mind’s terror.
In the *Ṭīkā*, however, it says: "Terrifying" (*bhayānaka*) refers to the sign of a formidable object.
"Powerful fear" is said to be "the state of rigidity and trepidation of the body"; by this very term "fear," minor fear is shown here.
Thus, in all such applications, the meaning is "this is its function.
Regarding the phrase "mere agitation and vacillation": here, it refers to the agitation characterized by both views and craving.
The commentary will explain the meaning as: "merely quivering, merely moving, merely shaking.

By this it is understood that even when [the object] is being apprehended, it is apprehended solely by the craving for views (*diṭṭhitaṇhā*), and not by the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). Regarding the passage beginning with "Those too," etc., this is the canonical text of the *Sīhaparibbājaka-sutta*.

In that context, "those too" refers even to the long-lived deities. "Fear" refers to [the fear arising] from all conditioned phenomena once one has become proficient in the contemplation of their dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*).
Knowledge of fear is that which has arisen by way of fear. *Saṃvega* is knowledge accompanied by moral dread, or moral dread itself.

*Santāsa* is knowledge of the terror caused by conditioned phenomena through the contemplations of danger and disenchantment. "By way of rebirth" means precisely by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Regarding "companionship" (*sahabyatā*), the meaning derived from the word is simply the state of being a companion, since the word *sahabya* functions in the sense of a companion.
For it is called "companionship" (*sahabya*) because it expands together, proceeds together, or conceals a fault; the state of that is "companionship-ness" (*sahabyatā*).

However, the state of being a companion is simply the state of being together (*sahabhāva*); thus, in order to show the meaning according to this intention, it is stated as "the state of being together.
Alternatively, the word *saha* has the sense of a collection accompanied by its means, just like the prefix *adhi* in the word *adhikicca*; therefore, *saha*—

It is also stated by way of the future. For they have "been" (*ahesuṃ*), thus they are "beings" (*bhūtā*). They "are" (*bhavanti*) and they "will be" (*bhavissanti*), thus they are "those who are to be" (*bhavyā*);
for the *ṇya*-suffix, like the suffixes *tabba* and *anīya*, can also function in the sense of the agent.
Even after saying, "The Lord is the maker, the creator," what is the purpose of the further statement, "These beings were created by me"?

He said: “Now, by way of the cause,” and so forth. This means it was stated for the purpose of making a formal declaration out of a desire to establish [the point] by way of the cause—[as noted in the commentary under the heading] “by way of the cause.

But is it not the case that this Brahmā, because his vision is unstable, having abandoned even the knowledge of being the owner of one’s own karma (*kammassakatā*) familiar from previous births as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), [acts] by means of the power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*), dependent merely upon a momentary arising of consciousness?

Perverted by the conceit of self regarding beings, one who leaps into the view of a creator-god (*issarakutta*) such as "These beings were created by me," is established through the mode of misapprehension (*abhinivesa*), but not through the mode of establishing [others].

Now, why is it said that he makes a formal admission (*paṭiñña*) desiring to prove it by way of a reason? It should not be viewed in this way; for even they [the proponents of creation] say, "It happens thus," and so forth.

Since it will be explained later that those who arise subsequently also have such a fixed conviction (*abhinivesa*), it should be understood that this conviction arose for him specifically through the process of establishing others in it, and not merely by virtue of his own subjective conviction; therefore, it is stated thus.

In the Pāli, regarding the phrase "a certain being" (*aññataro satto*), the word *yaṃ* is a mere particle;
or else this particle is used in the sense of a cause, or it is a personal designation for the reason, meaning "by which state";
or it is a reference to the action itself. In the phrase "he comes to this state of being" (*itthattaṃ āgacchati*), that state which is called "coming to this state of being" exists.
The meaning is as follows: this person does not go forth (*pabbajati*), he attains concentration of mind (*cetosamādhi*), and he recollects his past lives (*pubbenivāsa*);

these phrases should also be applied individually with the words "he goes forth" and so on. For these words—"It is possible, monks, that some being"—should each be joined with the words "he goes forth" and the rest.
It is called *agāra* because one does not go (*na gacchati*) to it; [it refers to] the house, the home. Of the house...

"Later" (*para*) means subsequently, or excessively, or even another previous existence—this is the meaning. When it is said, "he does not remember," [the sense is already established].
He shows that this meaning follows by means of the words beginning with "to remember. "Not seeing" means because of not seeing by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives;

Yet, in order to demonstrate the meaning itself without regard for the grammatical form, it is said: "by play," and so forth. [The term is also used as] "those who corrupt through play" (*khiḍḍāpadosakā*).

For this commentary proceeded according to the recensional tradition (*vācanāmaggavaśa*) of those belonging to the Mahāvihāra-vāsin Nikāya. Furthermore:

By saying "and the nature of delight in laughter," etc., he shows that they have entered into those [states] through application. Of whom there is play...

"By means of glorious splendor" (*sirivibhavena*) refers to the glory of physical beauty and so forth, as well as the excellence of one's retinue and other such attainments. "Festival" (*nakkhatta*) means a celebration.

And what is their meal-time? For all the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), the food is ambrosia (sudhā).
Because it sustains happiness by warding off the twelve evil qualities, the food of the gods is called "ambrosia.

The strength of the body-heat born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*) is due to its being produced from sublime merit (*puñña*).
And it is due to the digestion of the nourishment of sublime, heavy, and oily ambrosia. Furthermore, the feebleness of the body born of karma (*karajakāya*) is due to its state of extreme delicacy.
For this very reason, when Sakka, the king of the gods, was unable to stand upon the natural ground in the Indasāla Cave, the Blessed One said to him, "Resolve upon a gross body.

And the state of being powerful is to be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. Regarding the term *karajakāya*: here, what is called "body" (*sarīra*) is that which occurs therein.

"Dust born of action" (*karaja-rajo*): what is that? It is semen and blood. For, because it is the fruit of the dust of passion (*rāga-raja*) spoken of in the passage, "Passion is dust, but it is not called 'dust' [in the sense of earth-dust]," it is distinguished by the word *ka*, which denotes the body, and is referred to by way of its cause.
It is called "karaja. The teachers say that the body produced from that which is reckoned as semen and blood—namely, *karaja*—is therefore the "body born of *karaja*" (*karajakāya*).
For it is said that the body is "born of mother and father" (*mātāpettikasambhava*). However, in the commentary on the Mahā-assapurasutta, it says:
"It is called *kara* because it is made (*karīyati*) or cast into the womb; it is *sambhava*. That which is born from *kara* is *karaja*, meaning 'born of mother and father.'"
"Meaning: Some say it is called *karaja* because it is born from the hand (*kara*) of one who performs the act of bringing about the formation of the mother and so forth.

In either case, they say that 'the body born of the hand' (*karajakāya*) refers to the material form of the fourfold continuity (*catusantatirūpa*). Others say: it is called *kara* because it produces children;

thus, semen and blood are the *kara*, and what is born from that is *karaja*. Likewise, even though the bodies of gods and others are not produced in this way, they are designated as 'the body born of the hand' (*karajakāya*) by way of that conventional usage."
It is called [a corpse], as in the expressions “a putrid body” or “an old jackal. “Of them” means of human beings. “Clear gruel” (acchayāgu) means unfermented, unsedimented gruel.

Having thus demonstrated [the point] through positive and negative concomitance, he spoke the passage beginning with “Just as if,” etc., in order to clarify that very matter by means of a simile.

“Without distinction” means without making a distinction such as “of the devas”; for the kamma-born heat of devas is powerful while their material (corporeal) heat is weak, or rather, it is by way of the commonality of the cause known as the strength and weakness of the kamma-born heat and the material body. For this is the reason.

As for the reading, "They are called 'corrupted by play' simply because they are corrupted by play," [it continues]: "they themselves pass away."
It should be recited immediately after the words "should be understood," because it follows that sequence. This is the connection here:

if all those who act in this way were to pass away as sense-sphere deities (*kāmāvacara-deva*), then why did the Blessed One state them by the specific name "those corrupted by play" (*khiḍḍāpadosika*)?

"Even those who are departing [from the world] are described in that way because of their specific names, referring merely to their nature of being prone to corruption by play.

If some were to say, "This reading is one established by someone's arbitrary opinion," that is indeed incorrect, because of the presence of the word *iti* within the phrase and because that word is absent at the end.
However, for those seeking the meaning, the word *iti* should be joined at the end to include that arbitrary opinion within the scope of the statement.
47–48. *Manopadosino* is established as a word by way of its agent; *manopadosikā* is likewise [established] by way of expressing its own meaning (*sakatthavutti*).
However, to show the mere sense, it is said, "by means of the mind," and so forth. Or rather, although one might say *manopadosakā*, it is stated thus by way of the addition of the vowel *i*.
"By means of the mind" means by a mind defiled through being possessed by envy. Another method: by way of the act of envying.

Based on the statement, “With minds corrupted toward one another, with bodies exhausted and minds exhausted, those devas fall away from that host,” it is said, “These are the Cātumahārājika [devas].

"Kirā" and so forth is the detailed explanation. "He sets out upon the road by means of a chariot" is merely an illustration, since it is possible to set out elsewhere by other means as well.
"This" refers to his own prosperity. "As if bloated" means as if elevated by joy acting as the cause.
"As if breaking apart" means as if being broken by that [joy], or as if shattered by joy acting as the agent.
...as it were. Those who are angry are easy to recognize; therefore, the meaning is "having known his state of anger.

"One who is not angry protects" means that when another person does not become angry in response to an angry person, that anger—being without fuel (anupādāna) and, having arisen only once, being unpracticed—cannot cause him to fall away;
it is extinguished like a fire reaching the edge of water.
Therefore, one who is not angry protects the other from falling away.

But when both are angry, anger—arising with an increasingly sharp manifestation through the process of mutual intensification, having the function of burning up its support—strikes down the heart-base and destroys the extremely delicate royal body;
thereafter, the entire personal existence (attabhāva) vanishes.
To demonstrate this point, he said, "But in both cases," and so forth. Thus it is said in the Pāḷi:
"With minds corrupted toward one another, their bodies exhausted and their minds exhausted, those devas fall away from that host.
Here, the anger of one becomes a condition for the other, and the anger of the latter also becomes a condition for the former; thus, there is a progressive intensification of the anger.

Thus should the state of being a condition be understood: not by means of the function of supporting the falling away, but because of the falling away of the extremely delicate "body born of karma" (karajakāya) due to one's own anger, which burns the heart-base (hadayavatthu).
The genitive case in the phrase "of the weeping women of the harem" (kandantānaṃyeva orodhānaṃ) is used in the sense of disregard.
"This is the natural law here" (ayamettha dhammatā) refers to this [fact] that, due to the weakness of their body born of karma, for those [women] who arise in such a manner...

And the meaning is that the state of falling away instantly due to the power of anger, as well as the natural law (*dhammaniyāma*) of material and immaterial phenomena among these devas, is their inherent nature (*sabhāva*). 49–52.

"He sees the dissolution of the eye and so forth" means that he sees their transformation upon the convergence of opposing conditions, and he sees their destruction because they eventually reach a state of non-appearance; this is because the dissolution of material phenomena is coarse. [He sees] the condition...
"Having given" means having provided the power of a condition by way of the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and so forth; "having become a condition" is what is meant.
Therefore, the connection is "it does not see. The intention is that even though it is more powerful, it does not see for this reason.
And "more powerful" is said with reference to a specific type of extreme lightness of consciousness. For indeed, while one form is still persisting—

Sixteen types of consciousness break up. Regarding the statement "he does not see the breaking up of consciousness": although consciousness breaks up moment by moment, it breaks up precisely through its status as a condition for the immediately succeeding consciousness of another.

Therefore, because the arising of the subsequent consciousness occurs as if concealing the absence of the preceding consciousness, the aspect of existence (bhāvapakkha) becomes more powerful and manifest, whereas the aspect of non-existence (abhāvapakkha) does not.
It should be understood that the passage beginning with “But as for consciousness” (*cittaṃ panā*) was stated in order to show this reason.

And this meaning can be illustrated by the demonstration of the wheel of non-attainment (*alābhacakkā*). For the proponent of logic (the *takkīvādī*), because the method of diversity (*nānattanaya*) is difficult to grasp and the method of unity (*ekattanaya*) has been wrongly apprehended, [he thinks]:
“Since this very consciousness always proceeds in such a manner, this is my self (*attā*), which is permanent,” and so forth.
He gave rise to a dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*); therefore, he clarifies that matter together with a simile by means of the passage beginning, "Not seeing that...

(so taṃ apassanto). 53. The doctrine associated with the finite and the infinite is called "finite-and-infinite" (*antānanta*), just as one says, "The spears are walking," [meaning those carrying the spears]. It is dependent upon the finite and the infinite.

Or, just as in the expression "the beds are shouting," the term "antānantikā" is used to show that these [views] belong to those [who hold such views]. To indicate the meaning, it is said "antānantavādā.

According to the method already stated, they are called "antānantavādā" because their doctrine is associated with or dependent upon the finite and the infinite, or because the doctrine operates regarding the finite and the infinite.
Now, the meaning is given in accordance with the text that will be spoken of later, beginning with "This world is finite."
Analyzing this, he says, “or an end,” and so forth. For “end” (*anta*) means that a state (*bhāva*) goes to or reaches its conclusion there; it is a limit.

By its negation, one has “the endless” (*ananta*). Both “end” and “endless” are referred to as “end-and-endless” (*antānanta*) by way of a general designation, or through the principle of “single remainder” (*ekasesa*), as in such expressions as “the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form. The same applies to “neither-end-nor-endless” (*nevantānanta*).

Since the fourth term here has the same meaning as the third, the meaning is understood in four ways through the terms "end" (anta) and "endless" (ananta) according to the two methods already stated. But of what is this "end" or "endless"?

It is that which is "looked upon" (lokiyati)—that is, scrutinized—by those holding views who seek escape from saṃsāra; or else, it is that in which they "cast their lot" (lokiyanti), namely, merit and demerit and their respective results.
“World” (*loka*) refers to one’s own self as it has come to be reckoned [by conventional designation]. Therefore, it is said in the text: “They proclaim the world to be finite or infinite.
But what is this “self”? It is the *kasiṇa-nimitta* (the sign of the meditation object) which has become the domain of jhāna.

For this proponent of a speculative view [regards] the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*), either as limited by the circle of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-pariyanta*) through the process of expansion, or as unlimited, and based on hearsay and so forth regarding that [sign], he [perceives it thus].
One dwells perceiving the world; and thus the Commentary will say: "Having grasped that as 'the world'.
However, some say: "In this context, the jhāna and the states associated with it are the self, and they are grasped as 'the world'";
but that does not accord with the Commentary.

Here it is asked: It is indeed appropriate that the first three proponents are "extremists" (*antānantika*), because their doctrines proceed by taking as their object both the finite (*anta*) and the infinite (*ananta*), as well as both the finite and the infinite;

but how can the last one, the rationalist, be an extremist, given that his doctrine proceeds by way of negating both of those? [The answer is: Because his doctrine proceeds by way of negating both of those.
It is exactly so. For even the doctrine that negates both the finite and the infinite has as its very object the finite and the infinite, because it proceeds by taking those as its basis.

It is with reference to this very point that it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Doctrines that proceed by taking as their basis either the finite, or the infinite, or both the finite and the infinite, or neither the finite nor the infinite.
Alternatively, just as in the third doctrine, due to the distinction of location, [it applies] to one and the same [thing].

The world may exist as having an end and as being infinite; thus, even in this case of the theorist’s doctrine, because both of these are possible for a single [world] through a distinction of time, both are stated by way of mutual negation, and both negations are of the nature of a *pariyudāsa* (implicatory negation). How so?
For by the negation of "having an end," "being infinite" is expressed, and by the negation of "being infinite," [the other is expressed].

And [it is] finite. For a double negation indicates the original affirmative meaning. Thus, because both the finite and the infinite have been stated by way of negation, it is indeed appropriate that the latter, which is their object, also possesses the nature of being "finite-infinite" (antānantika).
If this is so, would it not follow that, due to its being a doctrine of the finite-infinite, it must be included within the third position? No, because the intended distinction is based on time.
Indeed, by way of the distinction of time, the latter rationalist (takkin) is one who holds to the view of the finite and infinite, just like the third proponent.
How so? Because this self, known as the world, has at some time been seen to be infinite;
thus it is reported by great seers who have attained distinction that it is not finite. Yet, because it is at other times finite, [it is both].
"Seen by oneself" (sakkhidiṭṭha) means it is not heard from others; therefore, it is not "one who holds [the world] to be infinite.

This rationalist, because the state of increase of the counterpart-signs (paṭibhāganimitta) is preceded by a state of non-increase, and because he stands merely at the level of hearsay and so forth due to his own lack of direct perception regarding the two-fold possible conceptualized increase, rejects the position "one who holds [the world] to be finite" on account of the time of increase.
However, it is said "not one who holds [the world] to be infinite" by way of not having developed that [view] over time;

it is not, however, because of the absolute non-existence of finitude or infinity, as is the case with "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And just as for those who reason based on what has been heard, so too should this be applied, as appropriate, to those who reason from recollection of births and so forth.
Some, however, [argue]: "If this self were finite, then, that being the case, the performance of functions such as recollecting rebirth in distant places would not be possible.
If, on the other hand, it were infinite, then even while remaining right here, one would experience pleasure and pain in the heavenly realms, the hells, and so forth.
But if it were both finite and infinite, there would likewise be a combination of both those faults. Therefore..."
They describe the occurrence of the fourth position by way of such reasoning as: “The self is finite, or it is infinite—this is undeclared.
However, if this [self] were to be either finite or infinite in the manner already stated, then for what reason would there be a rejection of its three preceding positions in such passages as:
“Those recluses and brahmins who say, ‘This world is finite and bounded,’ they are lying”?
Why was it stated [that he is not an "eel-wriggler"]? Because the three preceding views lack the specific characteristics intended by that term.
For that very reason, such a denial was stated; it was not because of his absence of being an "endless-ist" (*antānantika*), nor because of a denial expressed through views that are devoid of limits.
This must certainly be understood in this way alone. Otherwise, he would simply fall into the category of the "eel-wriggler" (*amarāvikkhepa*).
One should side with the fourth position. For there is no mode of self-existence that is free from both finitude and infinity;

and the proponent of reasoning (takkīvādī) follows only the path of logic. Furthermore, even in a single world, those two [finitude and infinity] are not untenable when distinguished by difference in time.
Let it be granted, then, that the state of being finite or infinite is appropriate for the latter two positions regarding the finite and the infinite.

Because their doctrine has both as its object by virtue of that [classification]. But how is it appropriate for each of the first two proponents to be an "eternalist" (antānantika) individually, given that their respective doctrines have only one object each?
It is said: because a term that applies to a whole may also be used metaphorically for its parts.
For the term "eternalist" (antānantika), which applies to those who hold views regarding both the finite and the infinite in combination, [is applied here to each individual].

Therein, because it is conventionally established, the term applies to each of its constituent parts among those who hold views on finitude and infinity, just as one speaks of "the eight liberations" individually in the context of formless jhānas, or as one says "seven hundred beings in the world.
Alternatively, this conventional usage was applied there by way of the thoughts that occurred in previous times due to their dogmatic adherence. For those proponents of wrong views—

Prior to the attainment of such a state of mental concentration, the state of being an "annihilationist" (antānantika) was established by way of a thought that clings to both modes— namely, "Is this world finite,
or is it infinite? Subsequently, although through the acquisition of distinction there arises an inclusion of only one of those doctrines regarding finitude and infinity,
it is still designated by the conventional usage of the previously established linguistic convention.

Just as in such cases as “all beings are subject to death,” the term *satta* (being) is used [figuratively] for an Arahant; and just as the designation “frog” and so forth is applied even when one has passed into another existence.

54–60. To show that the state of being finite or infinite is determined by whether one goes or does not go to the ends of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) below, above, and across, it is said: “the counterpart sign,” and so forth. *Taṃ* refers to the counterpart sign.

Regarding the phrase "without extending upwards or downwards, but extending across," here too it should be connected by way of the governing context as "having made the limit of the world-system (cakkavāḷa).

"By the method stated" means by the method stated in the eternalist doctrine (sassatavāda), both from the perspective of the word—such as "one who reasons is a rationalist (takkin)"—and from the perspective of the meaning—such as "the rationalist is fourfold.
"In accordance with what was previously seen" means by means of consciousness (viññāṇa) which consists of seeing.

By means of recollecting what was previously perceived as having an end and so forth—and by doing so, the inclusion here of both those purified through hearsay and those purified through reasoning is established.

Alternatively, it should be understood that by the very mention of "view" (*diṭṭhi*), the inclusion of "hearing" (*suta*) and so on is also intended, just as in the expression "dancing, singing, music, and witnessing performances of the vulgar.
This is because [the view] consists precisely in the misapprehension of a self that exists at all times, as expressed by the term "having an end" (*antavā*) and so forth.
Because these doctrines are set forth, they should be understood as being included within the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). For it will be said:
"There are exactly six views of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*); the rest are eternalist views.
Commentary on the Evasive Doctrine (*amarāvikkhepavāda*).
61. "It does not die" (*na marati*): because there is an absence of a definitive conclusion such as "it is exactly thus," it is not cut off;

what is meant is that it remains merely indeterminate. "Without limit" (*pariyantarahitā*) means devoid of a final end; the meaning is that it has not reached its conclusion. "Diverse" (*vividho*) means manifold, in various ways such as "it is for me thus," and so forth.
"Thrusting aside" (*khepo*) is the casting away of the opposing doctrines by one's own doctrine. But what is this "eel-wriggling" (*amarāvikkhepa*)?
The very arising of consciousness that originates such speech, being dominated by views as it thus proceeds, is itself [the "eel-wriggler"].
They waver with indecisive views and speech, or they lead [others] away in various ways; thus they are "Amarāvikkhepino" (Eel-Wrigglers), and it is also appropriate to call them "Amarāvikkhepikā.
By saying "one kind" instead of simply "a species of fish," he shows that this is a specific variety of fish.

It wanders hither and thither because it does not abide in any single nature. Because it wanders in such a way that it does not admit to being grasped, it is called "the wandering of the immortal" (*amarāvikkhepa*);
this meaning is expressed by the phrase "by way of surfacing and submerging," etc., since it is compared to the meaning of the term "wandering" (*vikkhepa*). For this very [reason]...
The meaning has also been stated by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. Some say that "amarāvikkhepa" means "vacillation like an immortal" (*amarā viya vikkhepo*).
Alternatively, those who vacillate like immortals are "amarāvikkhepino," and they themselves are the "amarāvikkhepikā.

62. [They are so called] because they are proponents of vacillation regarding superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) and indeterminate states (*abyākatadhamma*)—[the commentary also mentions] unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*).

(Ṭī. 1.62) Since there is no knowledge capable of penetrating [the meaning] by way of a distinction in their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the meaning of the terms "wholesome" and "unwholesome" is stated solely by way of wholesome and unwholesome courses of action (*kamma-patha*).

"Affliction" (*vighāta*) and "torment" (*vihesā*) refer to bodily suffering; this is because [the term] is spoken as the cause for the arising of remorse (*vippaṭisāra*), which is a state of mental grief (*domanassa*).
Therefore, he said, "it would be suffering. In the phrase "in false speech" (*musāvāde*), the locative case is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*), or in the sense of an ablative (*nissakka*).
Or: by means of both shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) regarding false speech, or because of false speech—this is the meaning.

To the question, "What kind of 'eel-wriggling' does he resort to?", he says, "endless wriggling" (*apariyantavikkhepa*); by this, he excludes the second method, which is characterized as wriggling like an eel (*amarā*).
For while this meaning has been shown according to the first of the two aforementioned methods, by way of the second method, however—
In order to demonstrate a diversion (*vikkhepa*) similar to that of the immortals (*amarā-vikkhepa*), he will say:

“When asked, ‘Is this wholesome? and so forth. Regarding the phrase “‘It is thus’—this is not my [view],” the meaning is: “Regarding what you have asked, ‘Is it thus?’, such a tenet (*laddhi*) is not mine.

This should be applied in all instances as appropriate. An undetermined diversion (*aniyamita-vikkhepa*) is the act of diverting the question without settling upon any one of the modes, such as eternalism (*sassata*) and so on.
This means that when an opponent asks anything at all in any manner, there is a rejection and evasion of that question.
Alternatively, the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself demonstrates the "limitless evasion" (*apariyantavikkhepa*) through such passages as:

“‘It is not so for me’ is the indefinite evasion,” and “When asked whether this is wholesome or unwholesome,” and so forth. For by not specifying [an answer] with the words “It is not so for me,” and so on, [one evades].

Having thus restricted [the discussion], he rejects each respective doctrine by refuting the views of eternalism, partial-eternalism, annihilationism, and agnosticism, because they are doctrines of endless equivocation.
Having shown them to be "eel-wrigglers" (*amarāvikkhepino*), he says, "But as for himself...
he does not declare this," in order to show that, because his own doctrine is unsettled, he does not abide in any position whatsoever.
He said: Now, by not declaring [the dhamma] as wholesome and so forth, he clarifies that very same lack of a fixed position with the words, "When asked, 'Is this wholesome?
and so on. For this very reason he says, "It does not abide even in one side.
What is your position regarding "not"? Your position is "it is neither not," which means what? My position is "it is neither not," which means my position is "it is neither not."
63. In order to provide an application [of the verse] specifically to the lust and other defilements that pertain to one’s own state of being wise, he said, “Even though not knowing,” and so forth.
“Sahasā” means impulsively, without reflection. “Bhadramukha” is a customary form of address for the wise;

the meaning is “one with a beautiful face. “Tattha” refers to that grammatical exposition; here it is used in the locative sense as a marker. Although the terms *chanda* and *rāga* have the same meaning, [the distinction is as follows:]...
By the word *vā* used as a distributive particle, a difference in meaning is appropriate according to the principle of "the cow and the ox" (*gobalībadda*), which implies fitness;
thus he says: "Desire (*chanda*) is weak lust, while lust (*rāga*) is strong lust. The same method applies to hatred (*dosa*) and aversion (*paṭigha*).

Regarding the phrase "even this much," the word *api* functions here as a conjunction (*sampiṇḍana*), and the word *nāma* expresses censure (*garahā*). It is not only that which follows this [which is superior], but even this much.

The meaning is: "I do not even know this much, let alone know more than that. However, with reference to lust and the other [defilements] which have as their object the honors and respect performed by others, the application is as follows:

even though one does not understand wholesome and unwholesome states as they truly are, regarding those through whose combination I would declare what is wholesome as "wholesome" and what is unwholesome as "unwholesome," among them—
Likewise, regarding the cause of formal declaration: "May there be desire or lust in me when they show honor and respect, thinking, 'Oh, what a wise man!'";
and in the case of hatred and aversion, it should be applied by reversing the aforementioned [positive] formulation. "That would be my clinging;
that would be my vexation"—this statement, which follows the method of the Abhidhamma, should be applied according to what is obtained and as far as possible.
He says, “The pair of desire and lust,” and so forth. For it is craving and views alone that are called “clinging” (*upādāna*) in the Abhidhamma;
now, he shows the application [of the term] without distinction according to the method of the Suttas with the words, “Or both as well,” and so on.

For in the Suttas even hatred (*dosa*) is called “clinging,” as in such passages as, “Bound by the clinging of anger, they fall into affliction. And as for the phrase “both as well,” in terms of its meaning—
It is stated [thus], not because of the word itself, since all four words denote two meanings. "Firm grasping" means grasping without releasing.
For even aversion (*paṭigha*) does not release its object, as it proceeds by way of resentment (*upanāha*) and so forth;

however, because greed alone is manifest in the state of clinging (*upādāna*), this was said to show that hatred (*dosa*) also possesses the nature of clinging. "Striking," "injuring," and "oppressing" are synonyms.
For passion (*rāga*), too, by its state of being agitated through the nature of its feverish burning, destroys its own support.

The passage beginning with “Passion, indeed,” establishes that meaning by way of showing the distinction between passion and hatred (*dosa*) in their status as forms of clinging (*upādāna*). The connection is: “It grasps the object because of the desire to destroy it.
“Thus” (*iti*) means therefore, because of both grasping and destroying.
64. *Paṇḍā* is so called because it knows the true nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena, or because it goes toward their true nature;
those who possess this are "wise" (*paṇḍita*). This meaning is shown by the passage beginning with "by wisdom" (*paṇḍiccenā*). The state of being wise is "wisdom" (*paṇḍicca*), which is *paññā*.

For that very quality (*dhamma*)—which serves as the cause for the occurrence [of the designation] and by virtue of which one is called "wise"—is itself "wisdom. By means of that, there is the wisdom consisting of what is heard and what is reflected upon (*sutacintāmayapaññā*).

They are so called because they constitute the objective domain for those very [knowledges]. For the wisdom consisting of development belongs to those who have attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). By the term "subtle" (*nipuṇa*), however, he refers to the innate knowledge known as the wisdom of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-paññā*) produced by kamma; thus he says, "of subtle and delicate intellect. "Another meaning" means a diversity of meanings, or simply the meaning itself. By the phrase "those who have understood the doctrines of others," the word *kata*— [...]* ...is indicated. This is the meaning.
