Moreover, it is said that the Blessed One is the foremost among those who possess the power of knowledge regarding the past, the future, and the present because he possesses the power of knowledge regarding the past, the future, and the present. Furthermore, it is said that the Blessed One is the foremost among those who possess the power of knowledge
He shows that because it expresses the commonality of action, as in the case of "one who has done what is to be done" (*katavijjo*) and so forth, the word *kata* denotes being devoted to knowledge.

By the phrase "familiar with the doctrine he has mastered" (*katavādaparicayā*), however, it denotes a doctrine that has been thoroughly practiced, as in the case of "one who has mastered a craft" (*katasippo*) and so forth.
Between these two, one should understand either a general designation through a double conjunction or a single remainder (*ekasesa*). [This refers to] the hair-piercers (*vālavedhīnaṃ*).
Because form has these [qualities] as its inherent nature (sabhāva), they are called "hair-piercing forms" (*vālavedhirūpa*);
thus it is said, "like an archer who pierces a hair. The meaning is: "like an archer capable of piercing the tip of a hair split into a hundred parts.
For it is precisely such a person who is intended by the term "hair-piercer" (*vālavedhī*). It is stated that the word *maññe* indicates a simile; hence it says, "as if piercing."
“By means of wisdom” (*paññāgata*) means by way of the distinctions of wisdom, or simply by wisdom itself. “Interrogation” (*samanuyuñjanā*) is a question regarding a tenet.

He shows that “thorough investigation” (*samanugāhanā*) refers to the cause of that [tenet] by means of the passage beginning with “What is wholesome? (*kiṃ kusalaṃ*). Since “admonition” (*samanubhāsanā*) is also a form of interrogation by way of instruction, he says “they should interrogate” (*samanuyuñjeyyuṃ*).
In the phrase “he would not be able to explain” (*na sampāyeyya*), there is a substitution of the letter *y* for the letter *d*, and [this applies to] the word *eyya*.
And in order to show the sense of capability (*sāmatthiya*), it was said: "he would not accomplish [it]," and so forth. 65–66.
One whose wisdom (*paññā*) is dull (*manda*) and not sharp is "one of dull wisdom" (*mandapañño*); therefore he said: "This is indeed the name for one who lacks wisdom.
In what should have been "deluded by delusion" (*mohamūho*), the word *momūho* is used by eliding the letter *ha*; and that indicates the sense of excess through two synonymous terms.
Regarding the phrase "because of the state of having an additional meaning": it is as when "proximate cause" (*padatthāna*) is stated [in the sense of] "one who is utterly deluded.

For when something is already established, a restatement is made either for the sake of restriction or for the sake of indicating a different meaning. Thus, "Tathāgata" means a being who has come here in the same way as he came previously by way of karma.
And here, although it is true that even the previous three [terms] do not understand the intrinsic nature of wholesome and other phenomena...

There is indeed dullness; however, there is a distinction because, for those [former ones], it consists in the non-comprehension of their own wholesome and other states, whereas for the latter alone, due to the absence of that [non-comprehension], it is described as dullness and delusion (*momūha*).
But is it not the case that even for the latter there is indeed comprehension of the non-comprehension of his own states? [As it is said: "If it were my thought: 'There is another world'..."
Is it because of such statements as, "If one were to declare to you, 'There is another world,' I would not say, 'It is so' for me," and so forth?
Although [another world] does exist, he is not like those who previously [made declarations] out of fear of lying or loathing the proclamation of phenomena they had not fully understood;
rather, he is described thus because he is indeed greatly deluded. Or else, [it is said] by way of the passage beginning, "I would not say, 'It is so' for me," and so forth.
In order to cause confusion regarding the question, the mere posing of the question—“If you ask me, ‘Is there a world beyond?’”—is what is shown by him;
it does not indicate his own realization or non-realization of the Dhamma. It is for this very reason that he is specifically called “dull and utterly deluded.
Indeed, it was with reference to Belaṭṭhaputta, who was among the assembly of those who spoke thus, that [the Buddha said]: “And this one, of these recluses and brahmins...”
It is said: "He is entirely foolish, entirely deluded. In this context, the question "Is there another world?
is asked either from the standpoint of the view of eternalism (*sassatadassana*) or from the standpoint of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).

For whether it be one who holds to a speculative view asking from the standpoint of the view of eternalism, or one with right view asking from the standpoint of right vision—both meanings are applicable. [The question] "Is there no other world?"...
Whether by way of the view of non-existence or by way of right view, or by way of the annihilationist view that "the other world both exists and does not exist" or by way of right view,
when there is a negation of the three aforementioned modes— namely, "the other world neither exists nor does not exist"— since no other mode is possible,
the other world is of an inexpressible nature in terms of existence and non-existence; this is indeed "wavering" (vikkhepa).
The question is asked by way of precedence or by way of right view. The meaning in the remaining three tetrads should also be understood according to the method already stated.

For just as with the triad of meritorious formations (*puññasaṅkhāra*), the meaning included in the first tetrad by means of the triad of bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) is likewise [to be understood] by means of the remaining three tetrads, according to the method of challenging [the opponent] regarding the fruitfulness of the seven types of adherence (*sattaparāmāsa*)—such as the adherence to a self (*attaparāmāsa*)—and of merit and so forth.
(Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā 1.65, 66) It should be understood that here, by means of the third tetrad,

the method of exhortation is stated regarding the fruitfulness of meritorious and other kamma, and by means of the remaining three tetrads, regarding the seven types of dogmatic adherence (*sattaparāmāsa*).
As for the Eel-wriggler (*amarāvikkhepika*), because he does not approve of eternalism and the other views, he says in every case, "It is not thus for me," and so forth.

He merely creates evasion. In this context, the passage beginning with “‘It is not so for me’” demonstrates the manner of evasion by way of negating the various modes of questioning posed here and there.
But why is it that only a refutation is stated everywhere for one who propounds evasion?
Is it not appropriate for the side of evasion to also admit, “It is exactly so,” since such an admission would likewise remain within the scope of the position of evasion?
"Could it be? No; because even there he was confused, and because the doctrine of evasion proceeds precisely by way of negation.

For instance, when Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta was questioned by King Ajātasattu regarding the visible fruits of the ascetic life, he evaded the answer by means of denying the existence of the afterlife and so forth.

Here it may be asked: Surely this Eel-Wriggler, not understanding as they truly are the states such as the wholesome and so forth, nor the existence of the next world and so on, merely resorts to evasive wriggling whenever he is questioned on various points;
how then can he be considered a holder of a speculative view? For one who does not know the meaning of what is asked—unlike one who simply does not wish to speak—[cannot be said to hold a view].
Is it appropriate to say that one who resorts to evasion is a holder of a wrong view? It is said:
No, indeed; it is not by the mere act of evading that such a person is a holder of a wrong view, but rather by way of a false adherence.

For it is precisely because a person has falsely adhered through the adherence to eternalism that—due to dullness of intellect—they fail to understand, as they truly are, wholesome states and so forth, as well as the existence of the next world and other such matters.
He falls into equivocation because he is unable to make another understand a matter that he himself does not understand, and out of fear of telling a lie.
For it will be said: "Of those views, seven are annihilationist views, and the rest are eternalist views.

Alternatively, due to a lack of comprehension and a lack of conviction regarding merit and demerit, as well as their respective results, he merely practices equivocation when questioned on those subjects.

It should be understood that this view, which arises in one who conceives and adheres to [the idea] "it is beautiful" after having generated patience and approval, is indeed a distinct single view, like the "sevenfold negation view" (*sattabhaṅgadiṭṭhi*).
And so it has been said: "The view and speech of one who follows a course of views are without limit. Furthermore, as for what was stated:
"These four [views] also, by following the very same principles as those doctrines previously discussed..."

"Because they are seized by [wrong] views, they have entered among those who speculate about the past"—this was said with reference to the inclusion of this doctrine of endless equivocation (amarāvikkhepa) within the category of the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). But how is it included in the eternalist view?
Because there is no adherence to annihilationism. For there is no one who knows things as they truly are, owing to the world's abundance of dispute.
With the words “In the same way,” however, the contemplation of phenomena (dhammanijjhānana) has been occurring in the world since beginningless time;
therefore, because the doctrine of eternalism (sassatavāda) is found here, this [view] should be understood as being included within the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi).
Commentary on the Doctrine of Fortuitous Origination (Adhiccasamuppannavāda):
67. "Adhicca" means by chance or arbitrarily; it refers to whatever cause arises for anyone without being preceded by intelligence.
Thus, "adhiccasamuppanna" (fortuitous origination) is the viewing of the aggregates—known as the self and the world—as having the mode and object of arising by chance.
Because it proceeds based on that very mode and because it is associated with that mode, it is like saying, "The beds are crying out."

Regarding the phrase "spears are moving about," the view of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppanna-dassana*) is expressed by dropping the final member of the compound, just as "form-existence" (*rūpabhava*) is shortened to "form" (*rūpa*).
It is with reference to this meaning that the passage beginning with "fortuitously arisen" was spoken.
"Arisen without cause" means arisen at will, independent of any cause.

68–73. Regarding the term *asaññasatta*: here the meaning is that this is a designation for those without perception (*asaññāvacana*). It is called the "head of the teaching" (*desanāsīsa*) because it is taken as the primary or principal element within the teaching;
thus, it shows that this teaching was delivered by the Blessed One with perception as its focal point, and not because other immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) are absent there.
For this very reason, he says, "without the arising of consciousness," and so forth.

For just as the Blessed One, when teaching supramundane dhamma, teaches making either concentration or wisdom the primary focus, so too, when teaching mundane dhamma, he makes either consciousness or perception the primary focus. In that context:
"At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna—right concentration with five factors, right concentration with five knowledges—and having seen with wisdom, his taints..."
"...are completely exhausted. Likewise, such suttas as "At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen," "What is your mind, monk?

"Phenomena are preceded by the mind," "There are, monks, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception," and "The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—these and others are the proofs for this meaning.
"Tittha" refers to wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*), because fools "cross over" (*taranti*) there by wandering about mostly within it; thus, it is called *tittha*.
That very thing is a "basis" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being the birthplace or dwelling place of numerous misfortunes and of the sectarians (*titthiya*);
hence, it is "the basis of the sectarians" (*titthāyatana*). The meaning is: "in that [basis], namely, in the doctrine of other sectarians. For the sectarians, in regard to a particular rebirth...

Perceiving [this state] as liberation, and having seen both the danger and the benefit in the fading away and non-fading away of perception, they attain the attainment of non-perception and are reborn in a plane of no opportunity;
they are not followers of the Dispensation. Therefore it is said: "A certain person, having gone forth in a sectarian order...
Having performed the preliminary work on the air-kasina means: on the fourth, the earth-element kasina, the first three [preliminary stages].

Having produced the jhānas and become proficient in the third jhāna, he emerges from it and performs the preliminary work for the attainment of the fourth jhāna; therefore, it is said: "having produced the fourth jhāna.
But why is the preliminary work mentioned here specifically with the air-kasiṇa? It is said: just as in those [kasiṇas] that are counterparts to form...

By the contemplation of form (*rūpa-vibhāvana*) upon specific *kasiṇas*, the specific attainment of the formless (*arūpa-samāpatti*), which is termed the cultivation of dispassion toward form, is realized.

Likewise, by the contemplation of the formless (*arūpa-vibhāvana*) upon specific *kasiṇas* that serve as counterparts to the formless due to their lack of distinct configuration, the specific attainment of the fine-material (*rūpa-samāpatti*), which is termed the cultivation of dispassion toward the formless, is reached.
Therefore, in this context, it is said: "Perception is a disease, perception is a boil," and so forth; "Alas..."
And by way of such passages as, "The mind is called *citta*," one sees the disadvantage in the occurrence of the formless;
and by determining the state of peace and excellence in the absence of that [form], there is the volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*) for the attainment of the formless.

However, the cultivation of dispassion toward form, together with its access, refers specifically to the first formless jhāna among the formless attainments. If this is so, then even in the case of the "limited space kasiṇa" (paricchinnākāsakasiṇa) ...
It should be said. For is it not the case that even for that [consciousness], a resemblance to the formless (*arūpa*) is obtained? This indeed must be said of some;
however, it was not mentioned by the ancient masters because it had not been included [by them].

Just as the cultivation of dispassion toward the material (*rūpavirāgabhāvanā*)—which is fully accomplished simply by means of the state of being objects of dispassion (*virajjanīyadhammabhāvamattena*)—[applies] to that which has become a counterpart to those objects of dispassion...
And just as [the mind] manifests with respect to a specific object, so too there is no contradiction in saying that the cultivation of dispassion toward the formless is likewise.
However, because that attainment must be practiced by the non-Buddhist sectarians (tīrthikas) themselves,

and because those teachers— seeing that very reason for it— practiced that jhāna only upon the sign of a location or a specific object, the former masters [placed it] only in the fourth [jhāna] among the kasiṇas of the primary elements.
It should be understood that the preliminary work for the development of dispassion toward the formless has been stated.

Furthermore, just as in the case of the color-kasinas, even in the first three elemental kasinas, it is only the concealment of the color that serves as the conceptual object of the jhāna; this occurs solely in conformity with worldly convention.
And having done so, the comparison of the earth-kasina to the disk of the moon in a mirror in the *Visuddhimagga* becomes appropriate.
It is established. However, in the case of the fourth, the kasiṇa of the primary elements (*bhūtakaṣina*), it is the shadow of the primary element itself that becomes the object of jhāna;

therefore, it is appropriate that this alone has the appearance of a formless state (*arūpa*). Consequently, it should be understood that the preliminary work (*parikamma*) is taught specifically for the kasiṇa of air.
To the question "How does he see?", he says: "When the mind exists," and so forth. "Peaceful" means extinguished (*nibbuta*); this is Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*).

This is what is meant. "Having passed away" means having undergone death; or alternatively, it means having completed that period of life in the human world which is sustained by supporting conditions.

"He is reborn among the non-percipient beings" means he arises by way of a material rebirth-linking (*rūpa-paṭisandhi*) within the category of beings known as non-percipient beings, or in other world-systems where that plane exists.
It should also be understood that the designation in the plural number is made with reference to the manifold nature [of the aggregates].
"In this very [existence]" means in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) itself. "Therein" means in the non-percipient existence (*asaññībhava*).

If only the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) alone manifests in the non-percipient existence, how does form proceed there without dependence on the immaterial? Would it not be the case that the aggregate of form depends precisely upon the immaterial?
Is it because its arising is not seen here in this very five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*)? This inquiry is not restricted to this case alone;
for how is it that the formless (*arūpa*) proceeds in the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*) without dependence on material form? For this too is of the same nature as that.
Why? Because it is not seen here either. And how [is it] without edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*)?
"Form proceeds in the form-element. This too is of that very same nature; for what reason? Precisely because it is not seen here.
Thus, since such proceeding is observed elsewhere as well, what is the use of this demonstration of something else through an inquiry restricted to this case alone?
Furthermore, just as for whatever mental continuum the cause of its production is craving that has not ceased regarding form, for that [continuum] simultaneously—
Because the cause depends on form for its occurrence, there is occurrence by way of form; that is, due to the dependence of the cause upon form.
However, for one whose cause for the production [of existence] is free from craving for form, there is occurrence without form, due to the independence of the cause from form.
Likewise, for one whose cause for the production of a continuity of form is free from craving for the formless, there is occurrence without the formless, due to the independence from the formless.
Because of the absence of the power of development (bhāvanābala) for such a cause, just as there is the arising of both form and formless [phenomena] in the five-aggregate existence,

and just as there is the arising of only the formless through the power of development in the four-aggregate existence, so too in the non-percipient existence, it should be understood that there is the arising of form alone through the power of development.
But how is it to be understood that there, a mere continuity of form proceeds for a long time devoid of present conditions?
Or for how long does it proceed? Having taken such an objection to mind, he said, "Just as if," and so forth.
By this, it is shown that not only is scripture (āgama) stated here and elsewhere to make this meaning known, but furthermore, this...
Here he demonstrates the logical reasoning (*yutti*). "Hurled by the force of the bowstring" means shot by the power of the bowstring.
"The force of jhāna" refers to the majesty of jhāna, its capacity to yield its fruit. "For exactly that long" means at most five hundred great eons (*mahākappa*).
"They remain" means they remain in the very posture in which they were produced, like figures created by a painter. "By the force of jhāna."
In the karmic momentum of the fourth jhāna or the karmic momentum of the fifth jhāna, which is surrounded by the attainment of non-perception (*asaññasamāpatti*), [the consciousness] "disappears.
This means it ceases through the cessation of its conditions and does not proceed. "Here" means in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmāvacarabhava*), because those [attainments] do not arise elsewhere.
"Rebirth-perception" (*paṭisandhisaññā*) is said by way of the term "perception" for the very arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). How?
But consciousness arises here from a consciousness that has ceased long ago, having passed through many hundreds of eons.
Is it not seen that visual consciousness arises when the sensitivity of the eye has already ceased? This should not be regarded as an absolute rule.
For even though a state of mind has ceased, because another of the same class does not arise in the interval, it remains merely an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*).
It exists, but it is not the seed. The seed, however, is precisely karma;

therefore, for those who have passed away from the non-percipient existence (*asaññībhava*) due to conditions such as the object (*ārammaṇa*) based on that seed-like karma, there certainly arises the rebirth-consciousness (*upapatti-viññāṇa*) in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Thus he said: "Here, the perception of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-saññā*) arises. And here, just as, for example, by the law of the seasons, flowers are gathered at fixed times—
Just as when a slit is made in trees— known as "vekhā"— there is no restriction on the gathering of flowers by the power of that slit,

even so, when the "vekhā" known as the cultivation of dispassion toward the material and immaterial is made in the material and immaterial phenomena existing in inseparable association within the five-aggregate existence,
then, by the power of that attainment-vekhā, [beings are reborn] respectively in the immaterial realm and the non-percipient realm.
It should be understood that the occurrence of the aggregates takes place both devoid of form and not devoid of form.

But why, in this context, is the arising of perception stated as the cause for their passing away from that plane with the words, "And with the arising of perception, those devas pass away from that body"?
Or, what is the purpose of the expression "with the arising of perception"?

In response to the objection, he says, "But because... and so forth. Here, it is stated as an indicative cause (*ñāpakahetu*) because their passing away is made known by the arising of the rebirth-linking perception (*paṭisandhisaññuppāda*).
Alternatively, the expression "from the arising of perception" (*saññuppādā*) is intended to show the state of making their passing away known.
For [the phrase] "from the arising of perception" means that they pass away by means of the arising of perception acting as the cause; thus, "from the arising of perception."
The connection is: "or the perception of arising, O gods. "For the sake of peace" means for the sake of Nibbāna. One might ask:

"Is it not the case that here, by way of rebirth in the non-percipient realm—which occurs either at the end of a hundred thousand births and ten aeons of dissolution, or within them—the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannavāda*) would also be possible in many varieties, just like the doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavāda*), due to the attainment of such a state?
This is indeed true; however, because it is immediate, it is proximate [to the present context].

It should be understood that, by way of rebirth in the non-percipient realm (*asaññūpapatti*), the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannikavāda*) is shown as only one, by way of a general illustration.

Alternatively, because the doctrine of fortuitous origination is included within the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), the entire method of teaching presented under the eternalist view should be understood, as far as applicable, to apply to the doctrine of fortuitous origination as well. This...
For the purpose of showing the distinction, the Blessed One presented the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhicca-samuppannika-vāda*) without analysis;

yet it must necessarily be included within the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*), because the inclinations of beings on the side of defilement are twofold—consisting precisely of the eternalist and annihilationist tendencies—and because among those two, [the former] lacks the consequence of annihilationism. For thus it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
The phrase "eternalism and annihilationism" is stated by way of extracting the meaning of the word *āsaya* (inclination). And so he will say:
"Of these, only seven are views of annihilation; the rest are views of eternalism.

But is it not the case that the inclusion of the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannikavāda*) within the category of eternalism is inappropriate, given that it proceeds from such [views] as "I did not exist previously"?

Because it proceeds by making manifest beings who have never existed before. But as for the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), which grasps at the perpetual existence of both oneself and the world, does it not proceed by the thought, "I shall indeed exist eternally"?
No, that is not correct, because it is subsumed under the grasping at eternity through its failure to see the limit of the future.
For even if this doctrine says, "Having not been, I have now become transformed into a state of permanence," [it still fails to see the future limit].
It proceeds by grasping at the past limits of oneself and the world; nevertheless, from the present time onward, it does not see any limit for them in the future.

Specifically, the eternalist doctrine (sassatavāda) is characterized by a vision of the absence of limits regarding the present and future times, as it is said: "It will remain exactly thus for eternity."

If this were so, would it not follow that the inclusion of this doctrine and the eternalist views (*sassatavāda*) among those who speculate about the past (*pubbantakappika*) is indeed inappropriate, since they proceed by way of misapprehending the future time?
It is indeed appropriate, because their origin (*samudāgama*) belongs to the past portion.
For their origin is through the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*) extending back into the past, as well as through recollections and traditions propagated in imitation thereof.

And it is likewise described as being comprised by reasoning. Alternatively, these views were proclaimed by the Lord of Dhamma—who, through the unimpeded range of his knowledge, has personally realized without exception both the non-path and the path as they truly are—having directly known them through higher knowledge;
therefore, insofar as views were taught by the Blessed One, and in whatever manner they were taught...
It should be accepted exactly as it is established by that much, and no further logical analysis should be made here, because this is the domain of the Buddhas.
For the domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable; and thus he will say:
"In this matter, one should not exclusively seek for a cause."
The commentary on the second recitation section is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the doctrine of those who speculate about the future:

in such passages as “knowledge of the future limit (aparante ñāṇaṃ), those with views regarding the future limit (aparantānudiṭṭhino),” the words *aparanta* [and its derivatives] follow their respective order.
He says, "reckoned as the future portion," with reference to its being a designation for the section of the future time.

The meaning in "having speculated about the prior end" and so forth should be understood in the same manner as in "having speculated about the subsequent end" and so forth. We shall state here only the specific difference. [End of] the commentary on the doctrine of conscious existence (*saññīvāda*).

75. *Āghātanā* means they dig up; *uddhamāghātanaṃ* means that which proceeds after death, the meaning being "the self" (*attā*). Alternatively, the doctrine that proceeds [with the claim] "after death" is *uddhamāghātana*;
this is due to association (*sahacaraṇa*) and due to secondary derivation (*taddhita*), or it is an elision of the middle term (*antalopa-niddesa*).
Those who hold such [a view] are *uddhamāghātanikā*. Thus, having established the word-form, he now demonstrates the meaning:
Regarding the statement, “They declare themselves [to exist] above the place of execution,” the meaning is that the self (attabhāva) exists above, that is, beyond the place of execution.
For those proponents of false views say, “The self remains unchanging after death.

By the phrase “He has these,” etc., [the author] demonstrates the sense of possession (*assatthiya*), just as one is called a “Buddha” because he possesses awakening (*buddha*). This is another [explanation] from the commentary.

The method (*naya*): the term "proponent of a conscious self" (*saññīvāda*) refers to one who speaks as a proponent of a conscious self by way of association and so forth; or, by way of a compound (*samāsa*), they are "proponents of a conscious self" because they possess a doctrine of a conscious self.
The meaning is that their doctrine is precisely the doctrine of a conscious self.
76–77. Regarding the phrase "the self possesses form" (*rūpī attā*): why is the *kasiṇa*-form called "self" here? Is it not [the case that the self] is distinct from form?
One must understand [the self] by means of oneself; for when it is said, "form belongs to this [self]," form is likewise a property of the self, just as perception is.
Indeed, in the phrase "the self is percipient," it is not perception itself that is the self; rather, it is a property of the self in the sense that "perception belongs to it.
And so it has been said: "Having taken the perception occurring therein as 'perception' for him... Is this not so? No.

This should be understood in this way: one is "possessed of form" (*rūpī*) because "form exists for him," but rather, one is "possessed of form" because "one has the nature of being affected by change" (*ruppanasīla*).
And here, "being affected by change" refers to the attainment of specific qualities in the kasiṇa-form through its increase or non-increase over time, due to its similarity to [material] form.
For it cannot be said that such change does not exist, since distinctions such as limitedness or vastness are present. If this were so, it might be argued:

If it is argued that the inclusion of this doctrine within the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) is untenable because one whose nature is to be affected by change (*ruppanasīla*) must possess disintegration, [we reply:
it is indeed tenable, because what is intended by him is a self conceived to be changeless after the dissolution of the body.
For it has been said: "He is free from disease after death. Alternatively, [the term] "possessing form" (*rūpī*) means "he has form."

Even when it is stated as "possessing form" (*rūpī*), there is no fault whatsoever, because it is shown that non-difference can be described by means of a distinction established through conceptual construction (*kappanā*),
just as in the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*silāputtakassa sarīraṃ*).
Furthermore, it is because the whole (*avayavin*) is described in such a way by way of its parts (*avayava*), just as in the expression "contemplating the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*).
Or, *rūpa* is that which is subject to transformation (*ruppana*), its intrinsic nature being such; because he possesses that, he is "possessed of form" (*rūpī*).

This is like [the usage] in such passages as "the self is possessed of form" (*rūpino dhammā*). Having established it thus, the statement "the self is possessed of form" is entirely consistent with reason because the self has the intrinsic nature of form;
thus it was said, "The kasiṇa-form is the self. This connects with the word "having taken" (*gahetvā*). "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the kasiṇa-form. "His" (*assa*)...
The meaning is that the Ājīvakas and others proclaim their own imagined self by means of mere reasoning (*takkamatta*).
For the Ājīvakas are indeed mere reasoners, not attainers [of meditative states]. Because they are proponents of determinism (*niyatavāda*), they reject the fruit of karma;

thus, for them, there is no attainment of the jhānas or meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). Indeed, some Ājīvakas regard the black and other colors in the "black birth" (*kaṇhābhijāti*) and so forth as the "self."
They claim this. Here, by the former method he shows those who possess [the realization], but by the latter method he shows the rationalist. It is the same with such cases as these.

The word *roga* (disease) is a synonym for dissolution (*bhaṅga*), because even dissolution has the nature of being afflicted (*rujjanabhāva*). And having established it thus, the status of the word *aroga* (healthy) as a synonym for permanence (*nicca*) becomes logical;
therefore he says, "permanent. Alternatively, the word *roga* is a synonym for illness (*byādhi*). Thus, "healthy" (*aroga*)...

However, it is said to be "permanent" (*nicca*) to show that the one who holds to a wrong view (*diṭṭhigatika*) professes permanence by way of being free from disease—that is, by way of being changeless.

The kasiṇa, the space resulting from the removal [of the kasiṇa], the first formless attainment (*āruppa*), consciousness, non-existence, and the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) are, as appropriate, called the signs for the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*).
Like the bitter taste limited to the size of a neem leaf, [the self] is limited to the size of the body.
"The Nigaṇṭhas proclaim that 'the formless self remains in the body' based on mere reasoning;
thus it is said, 'like the Nigaṇṭhas and others.

As for "but the third," this is the view: "the self is both material and formless. "By way of grasping a mixture" refers to the meditative attainments (samāpatti) of both the material and the formless.

By taking the aforementioned signs together as a single unit and grasping them as "self," as well as the perception occurring therein as "perception"—for this proponent of a view, having attained the form and formless attainments, grasps their signs as "self" both by way of their formal nature and their formless nature, and thus generates the dogmatic adherence:
"He is both possessed of form and formless. This is the view of the eternalist.
Or, by means of mere reasoning alone, through the apprehension of material and immaterial phenomena as a mixture, he persisted in the dogmatic adherence: "The self is both material and immaterial.
"Fourth" refers to the tenet: "The self is neither immaterial nor non-immaterial.

"By means of reasoning alone" [is said] because, like phenomena that have reached a state of subtle essence through the refinement of conditioned factors (*saṅkhāra*), these [views] have reached an ultimate subtlety such that they are incapable of accomplishing their own function.

Like a collection of hands, feet, and so forth within a pillar-shaped belly (or pillar-base), it is neither material (*rūpī*), because it does not transcend the nature of matter, nor is it immaterial (*arūpī*);
thus it proceeds by means of a conceptual grasp.
This is the method found in the *Aṭṭhakathā-muttaka*: for in this context of the fourth doctrine among the views concerning the finite and infinite, it is "neither material nor immaterial."
The meaning should be understood by way of their mutual exclusion, as if they were distinct.

And although this [third statement] has the same meaning as the third statement [in the previous context], the distinction between the third and fourth statements here should be seen as being due to a difference in time and basis (*vatthu*), just as in that case it was due to a difference in place and time.
For here, the occurrence of the third statement is due to a difference in time, pertaining to the signs of the material and immaterial.

Because they arise together. As for the fourth position, its occurrence is by way of a distinction in its objective basis (*vatthu*), as it consists of a collection of both material and immaterial phenomena.

The second tetrad should be understood according to the method explained in the discussion on the views of the Finitists and Infinitists (*antānantika-vāda*), because the meaning of the words is identical in every respect.
Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated by us in such passages as: "The state moves and goes; the end is right here."

However, the distinction here is indeed evident: that [the previous passage] proceeded by way of conceiving the past (*pubbantakappanā*), whereas this [passage] proceeds by way of conceiving the future (*aparantakappanā*).
Granted, the claim "one who perceives diversity as self" (*nānattasaññī attā*) can also be found in reference to those who have attained meditative absorption (*samāpannaka*);

for such a variety of perceptions is possible in the case of a proponent of wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*) who has attained the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*). Nevertheless, regarding the attainment itself...

Because perception presents itself through a single form, it is especially appropriate to speak of "perceiving unity" by way of attainment; thus he says, "perceiving unity by way of one who has attained.
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as referring specifically to one who has attained a single meditative absorption (samāpatti).

And although a differentiation of perception might occur due to the differentiation of absorptions, since a coarse diversity of perceptions occurs only with respect to external, manifold objects, [the state of concentration] is described in this way.
In order to show that there is diversity by way of mere reasoning, it is said: "one who perceives diversity by way of one not attained [to jhāna].
"By way of a limited kasiṇa" means by way of a small kasiṇa because it has not been expanded; and here, the mention of "kasiṇa" is for the purpose of showing the object of perception.
For the limitation of perception is by way of its object, and by this [statement], even though there are phenomena dissociated from perception...
He shows that [the proponent] says, "Perception itself is the self. This same method applies here as well regarding the "vast kasiṇa" (vipulakasiṇa).

And by doing so, although the first and second positions in both the doctrine of the finitist-infiniteist (antānantika) and this present tetrad on the finite and infinite are identical in their mere verbal meaning, a distinction between these two sets of positions is established by way of their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) from those two doctrines.

Otherwise, even though there are differences among the aforementioned doctrines merely in terms of their conceptualization of the past and future limits, some would remain without distinction from others.
This, however, is the method not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), based on views such as "the self is the size of a thumb" or "the self is the size of an atom": [it is as follows].
"Having limited perception" means one who perceives what is limited, such as the followers of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others.
"Having immeasurable perception" means one who perceives what is immeasurable by virtue of professing for oneself a state of being all-pervading.
Because it is an adjunct to the divine eye, the knowledge of rebirths according to karma is produced by the power of the divine eye; thus, by means of that knowledge of rebirths according to karma...
"Even though beings are endowed with happiness and so forth, this is seen only by the divine eye (dibbacakkhu)"; thus he said, "by the divine eye," and so on.
With reference to the fourfold method and the fivefold method, it is stated, "in the plane of the threefold and fourfold jhānas.
For, among the planes of five-aggregate jhāna that are the domain of those who hold wrong views, excluding the plane of the Vehapphala [deities]—

The remaining [realms] are called the planes of the threefold and fourfold jhānas because they are the fruit-places (*vipākaṭṭhāna*) of the threefold jhāna in the fourfold system and of the fourfold jhāna in the fivefold system, respectively, according to their suitability.
However, the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) are not within their domain. "Nibbattamānaṃ" means arising.

But is it not the case that since doctrines such as "the self is exclusively happy" constitute views regarding the future limit (*aparantadiṭṭhi*), [they do not apply to those realms]? "Nibbattamānaṃ... [is used here].
“Having seen” would indeed be an inappropriate expression for the present; for these theories have the future as their object. [Reply:
It is indeed appropriate, because by showing the production in the present, what is intended is the conceptualizing (*pakappanā*) of the future state of being exclusively happy and so forth.
For this very reason it was said: “Having seen it being produced, one grasps it as ‘exclusively happy. And here, in each of those...

It should be understood that because the manifestation of phenomena accompanied by pleasure and so forth occurs predominantly on that plane, the description of them as "exclusively happy" (*ekantasukhī*) and so on refers to that very plane accordingly.

For a specific meaning can be obtained not only through connection with other words, but also by way of context and so forth. And in such cases as "exclusively happy," the state of being "exclusive" (*ekanta*) refers primarily to the predominant occurrence.
It is appropriate, because they grasp those [phenomena] by seeing only their occurrence in such a manner.
Alternatively, like blind men who have seen an elephant, those of wrong view adhere to whatever they see and describe only that.
For this was said by the Blessed One in the Udāna: "Bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects are blind and sightless," and so forth; therefore...
“There is no need here to seek further reasoning. To support the meaning already stated—that [the Buddha] saw with the divine eye—the phrase beginning with “especially” (*visesato hi*) was spoken.
[Commentary on the views of non-perception, neither-perception-nor-non-perception, §§ 78–83.
Then, in order to clear away the objection that there is no distinction [between these states], he says “only” (*kevalañhi*), etc. [The term] “non-percipient” (*asaññī*)...

The connection is that these are the views of those who grasp [the state] as "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. "Reason" means a specific reason, or rather, the cause for the arising of the view.

Although there may be some possibility of searching for a reason, it is said, "One should not search for a reason in an absolute sense," in order to show the disregard for the doctrines of those who follow wrong views. He asks, "Why? and says:
“Of one who holds a wrong view,” and so forth; by this, he shows the reason why it should not be sought, namely, because it is incapable of being investigated.
This is what is meant: the first position proceeds by way of a being born into the non-percipient realm (asaññī-bhava) according to the doctrine of non-perception;
[the second] takes that very perception as “self” in the manner stated in the passage, “one regards perception as self,” and then...
The second thesis proceeds from the notion that one is "non-percipient" due to the absence of any other perception existing in a state of having nothing whatsoever;
likewise, the third thesis proceeds by grasping material phenomena together with perception—or indeed all material and immaterial phenomena—as the "self";
and the fourth thesis proceeds solely by way of speculative grasping.
In the second tetrad as well, because the kasiṇa-form lacks the nature of being perceived, it is termed "non-percipient" (asaññī);
thus, four alternatives proceed according to the method stated in the discussion on the proponents of finitude and infinity (antānantikavāda).

However, in the case of the proponents of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda), [the alternatives apply] to a being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception during the moments of death and rebirth-linking, or everywhere, because of the inability to perform the function of clear perception.

The first position arises by way of professing the existence of a subtle perception; the second position and those following it proceed by way of subtle perception—as described in the method for the doctrine of non-perception—and by way of professing the nature of cognizing.
Thus, even if some manner of seeking a cause were possible, because the doctrines of those who hold to views are incapable of withstanding such investigation, [they are not to be accepted].

"One should not seek the reasons for their views with excessive zeal or great effort. Furthermore, the inclusion of these proponents of the views of "percipient," "non-percipient," and "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" within the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*) is evident from the statement:
"He is healthy after death. *Commentary on the Annihilationist View* (*Ucchedavāda-vaṇṇanā*)

84. To show that annihilation (uccheda) is caused by the state of existence because destruction is impossible for that which does not exist, he says "of what exists" (*vijjamānassa*), since the word "existent" (*santa*)—which denotes that which exists—is used as "of one who exists" (*sato*) in the Pāḷi.

Furthermore, in order to show that here it is specifically the "being" (*satta*)—the object of the doctrines of those who hold wrong views—that is intended by this term associated with existence, the Pāḷi says "of a being" (*sattassa*).
It has been said; by this he shows the following meaning:

although phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) proceed as cause and fruit and are included within a single continuum, nevertheless—because those existing as cause and fruit possess distinct intrinsic natures in the ultimate sense (paramattha)—there is a determination of absolute difference through the method of diversity (nānattanaya), just as in the case of things belonging to different continua, despite the distinction from those fallen into separate continua due to their being comprised within one and the same continuum.

A false grasp is the cause of the dogmatic adherence to annihilationism; likewise, even though there exists a difference in intrinsic nature between those things that stand in the relation of cause and fruit, the grasping of them as absolutely non-different by way of the "principle of unity"—due to their being included within a single continuum—is also a cause [of such adherence].
For, among the aggregates (khandhas) occurring by way of a continuum, the grasp of them here as a "being" arises because of the absence of a clear discernment of their distinctness. Of the being...

Furthermore, the doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) is based on grasping at the existence [of a self]; however, what is intended here by "annihilation" (uccheda) is uninterrupted destruction by way of successive cessation.
He says "cutting off" (upaccheda) because it refers to the grasping that as long as this self is being cut off, it continues to exist.
For the word *u-* is a synonym for the word *upa-*, and that has the sense of approaching; and in this context, approaching is—
It is continuity by way of cessation as one [moment] arises after another in succession.

Furthermore, it is called "annihilation" (uccheda) because there is only the destruction of what has arisen without further arising, according to the method already stated; thus he says "cutting off" (upaccheda).

For here, both the prefix *u-* and the prefix *upa-* have the sense of "subsequent part" (*uparibhāga*). And in this context, the subsequent part following that which has ceased is called the "subsequent part."
"Disappearance" (*vināsa*) means destruction by way of non-interruption or by way of non-arising.
However, because it transcends the range of vision of both the fleshly eye and the eye of wisdom, it is "non-perception"; thus he says "non-perception.

For the word "disappearance" (*nāsa*) is established in common usage in the sense of non-perception, as in such phrases as "the two other [types of] disappearance through change of color" (*vaṇṇavikāranāsa*) (see Kaccāyana 6-3-109).

"Disappearance of existence" (*bhāvavigama*) means the departure from intrinsic nature (*sabhāvāpagama*). For here, the word "existence" (*bhāva*), in the sense of "becoming according to its own nature" (*yathādhammaṃ bhavanaṃ bhāvo*), denotes intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
However, that which is cut off by way of constant non-arising and non-destruction is called the "departure from existence" because it is incapable of persisting through its own intrinsic nature.
With the words "In that regard," etc., [the text] addresses the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
He shows the attainment according to the reading by way of mere illustration; therefore he will say: "having conceptualized it both thus and otherwise. Therein:
in the statement, "they proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.

"An obtainer" means an obtainer of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*). Here, one who has obtained the remainder of that [knowledge] as well as one who has not obtained it at all is meant.
In the context of those who speculate about the future limit (*aparantakappika*), he is called simply "one who does not obtain [the vision].
"Death" (*cuti*) refers specifically to the death of both trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*). This same method applies here as well in the phrase "merely death.
"Not seeing rebirth" means not seeing it by way of non-observation, even though one is capable of seeing. "No falling away" (*na upapāta*) is due to the absence of prior application (*pubbayoga*).
Or, by not performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*), one is unable to see rebirth; and by doing so, the distinction between the two methods becomes manifest.

The connection with the elliptical remainder of the text is as follows: "Who knows the other world? One certainly does not know"—thus, by way of the doctrine of non-existence (*natthikavāda*), one adopts annihilationism (*uccheda*).
Precisely through the state of being a great deluded person by way of the doctrine of non-existence, [one thinks]: "Other than this, there is no other world."
The intention is that one adopts this view because of a failure to understand that [the world] exists.

One also adopts it out of a craving for sensual pleasure—like a king who takes his daughter by the hand, thinking, "This alone is the extent of the domain, namely the range of the senses"—as expressed by the phrase "or through greed for sensual pleasure.
[He states this] regarding the lack of reconnection of leaves fallen from their stalks with that stalk.

Having intended this, it is said: "They do not grow again. In the same way, "all beings"—just as a withered leaf that has fallen from its bond is not reattached, even so all beings, having death as their end, are without re-linking;
they do not come to further existence, but undergo death itself without re-linking. For they are like bubbles on the water.

Furthermore, his tenet is that "existence does not arise again. "In that way" means by the manner described through the illustration of the Arahant in the passage beginning with "recalling his acquisitions," and so forth.
"In another way" means by a different mode as well, since reasoning can occur in many ways.
Even for one who has attained [the goal], it is merely by means of reasoning regarding the non-perception of rebirth after death.
"These views arise" is stated as "having conceptualized [them]. And thus, the connection is: "having conceptualized them in one way they arise, and having conceptualized them otherwise they arise.
Therein, by showing the various distinctions of those who hold to annihilationism through the passage beginning with "two persons," he demonstrates this point:
just as the doctrines of the Amarāvikkhepikas were taught solely on the basis of being entirely unsuccessful, so too...

Furthermore, in the fourth tetrad of the "Doctrine of Those Who Exist After Death" (*uddhamāghātanika-saññīvāda*), the doctrines of those who maintain that beings exist after death were taught solely by way of those who obtain [a specific rebirth] exclusively; these [doctrines here] are not such.
Rather, like the doctrines of eternalism (*sassata*) and partial-eternalism (*ekacca-sassata*), these are taught by way of both those who obtain [the rebirth] and those who do not.

If this is so, why has there been no separate teaching for each [doctrine] by way of those who obtain [the rebirth] and by way of those who rely on reasoning (*takkī*), as was done in the case of the doctrines of eternalism and the rest? [It is because they are included] within the teachings on eternalism and the others.
"Is it otherwise that the teaching was given here? It is said: because they have attained the elegance of teaching.
For the Blessed Buddhas have attained the elegance of teaching; they teach the Dhamma in various ways according to the inclinations of those to be trained, and not otherwise.
For if, even in this case, there were an inclination on the part of those to be trained as the basis for such a teaching, [then it would be so].

The Blessed One might indeed speak in such a manner; how so? “In this case, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor … [as before] … when his mind is concentrated, directs his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees the death-moment consciousness of an Arahant, and that of ordinary persons.”
Or [he speaks] regarding other beings, but certainly not regarding rebirth beyond that. He says thus:

“Sirs, when this self—which possesses form, consists of the four great elements, and is born of mother and father—is destroyed and perishes at the breaking up of the body, it does not exist after death,” and so forth;
having thus distinguished those who have attained specific distinctions and those who rely on reasoning. For, by such a teaching...
The disposition of those to be trained (*vineyyajjhāsaya*), which serves as the basis [for the teaching], does not exist here;

therefore, it should be understood that this teaching was delivered by means of a skillful method of instruction (*desanāvilāsa*) in a manner entirely different from the teachings on eternalism (*sassatavāda*) and so forth, in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained.

Alternatively, unlike in the cases of eternalism, partial-eternalism, and so forth, the doctrine of attaining distinction (*visesalābhīvāda*) here is not a distinct form [of view] separate from the doctrine of rationalists (*takkīvāda*).

Now, in order to clarify this distinction—that because they are of a similar nature, they are indeed of a similar form—this doctrine of annihilationism was taught by the Blessed One as having a mode distinct from the preceding doctrines.

For here, even one who reasons may have a dogmatic adherence based on hearsay and so forth, just like one who possesses realization. Furthermore, these views were not [taught] by the Blessed One merely with reference to what will happen in the future.
They were not taught by way of mere supposition that "these might not be so," but rather, exactly as these views have been conceived by those holding to wrong views—
thinking "this alone is truth, all else is vain"— so too have these views been disclosed by the All-Knowing One after delimiting them according to their true nature,
through which they are profound and of various kinds, being the domain of those who are not worldlings.
The Buddha-qualities are revealed, and by means of their praise, the Tathāgatas are rightly extolled.

Another method: just as those holding views of annihilationism, who see only successive future existences, established their respective doctrines by way of refuting those who see subsequent existences, so too was this teaching delivered in contrast to the previous teachings.

The diversity of occurrences within this teaching should not be questioned; and having established it thus, just as the doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) is divided fourfold according to the divisions of the formless existence (arūpabhava), it should likewise be stated as being manifoldly divided according to the divisions of the sense-sphere and fine-material existences (kāmarūpabhava).
If that were so, the doctrine of annihilationism would result in having more divisions than the sevenfold [classification] spoken of by the Blessed One. Alternatively:

Just as it is not stated by dividing [the existence] individually according to the distinctions of sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*), so too it should not be stated by way of immaterial existence (*arūpa-bhava*).

Even if this were the case, such an objection—that the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) would result in having fewer divisions than the sevenfold classification taught by the Blessed One—is likewise without foundation.
For the teaching proceeds according to what is intended by those who hold to speculative views (*diṭṭhigatika*).
85. "Of the mother and father" (*mātāpitūnaṃ*): because it is connected to them, the meaning is that this belongs to the mother and father.
"Semen and blood" (*sukkasoṇitaṃ*): the semen of the father and the blood of the mother; or, the blood reckoned as the semen of both. "Born of mother and father" (*mātāpettika*):

here the locative case is used in the sense of the cause. "By these three terms": rather than saying "by way of the material body" (*rūpakāyavasena*), he says "by way of the material body as the primary factor" (*rūpakāyasīsena*).
By saying that even the formless is their "self," he makes known their grasping [at it]. In this manner, he said "thus" (ittham) with the words "so say some" (evameke).
Here, the word *evaṃ* has the sense of "this" (*idam*), meaning "in this manner. "Some" (*eke*) means certain individuals or others. 86.

Since humans have already been included and because it is impossible for others [to be meant here], the term "belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) means, in this context, being comprised within the six classes of sense-sphere devas. And here, "edible food" (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) refers to the aforementioned food of ambrosia (*sudhā*).
87. Regarding the phrase "born by means of jhāna," that which ought to be said has already been stated above.
A "limb" (*aṅga*) is a major part; a "minor limb" (*paccaṅga*) is that which functions separately therein. Thus, it is "endowed with all limbs and minor limbs.
"Of those" refers to the faculties of the eye and the ear. "Of the others" refers to the faculties of the nose, tongue, and body. The shape of these faculties as well—
This should be understood by way of the power of the beings themselves. For it is said in the commentaries:
"Even though both genders are absent there, the Brahmās there have the form of males, not the form of females.
(88–92) He says, "the existence of the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanabhava*), because the term "base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) occurs here as well. Here it is asked:

It is indeed appropriate to say "with the breakup of the body" in the case of the first three doctrines, because those doctrines proceed by taking as their basis a personal existence (attabhāva) included within the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava).

But why is it said "with the breakup of the body" in the four doctrines beginning with the fourth, which proceed by depending on a personal existence included within the four-aggregate existence (catuvokāra-bhava)? For [in that case], it is not...
“Does a body exist for those who are formless, such that it could be called ‘disintegration’? “Yes, that is true.

“But the holder of wrong views speaks thus by superimposing the conventional term ‘body’ onto the formless state, using the very same terminology that is current for the physical form-body. For in the world, a convention seen to apply to one thing is sometimes superimposed upon another;
as, for example, when one speaks of a ‘hare’s horn’ or a ‘sky-flower. And so it is with the holders of wrong views.”

They propound various views, and the Blessed One teaches in exactly that same way. Furthermore, the designation "body" (kāya) should be understood as referring to the immaterial nature of existence, which consists of a collection of phenomena such as contact and so forth, because it is a composite of mental factors (nāmakāya).
For the word "body" is used in the sense of a collection, as in expressions such as "a herd of elephants" (hatthikāya) or "a troop of horses" (assakāya).
And herein, [it refers to] those who establish themselves in the complete dissolution of the immaterial state of existence, such as the bodies of gods in the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara).
It may be appropriate for the second and subsequent views to be classified as speculators about the future (*aparantakappika*), since those views have the future time period as their object;

but how could the first view be appropriately classified as a speculation about the future, given that it has the present time period as its object and establishes the departure from the human state—which is directly perceived by the holder of the view? For, as for the second view and the others...

The view of speculating about the future (aparantakappika) is appropriate because it recognizes the total cessation of one’s own self—which was included within each preceding state of existence—once it has been reborn in a subsequent state in the future.
It is for this very reason that it is stated: "But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by this much," and so forth.
As for what is further stated there, "There is indeed another self, sir," that refers to the self in relation to specific lower states of existence, such as the human form and so on.

It was stated [as such], but not because it is entirely different in nature. However, as for the first view, since there is no realization of one's own annihilation when one is reborn in a higher existence in the future, and because it does not apprehend [the self] as being different in the statement, "There is indeed, sir, another self," it would not be tenable for it to be a "speculator about the future" (*aparantakappika*).
[Response: It is not untenable; for even though the object of the first view is included within this world (*idhaloka*), [it still pertains to the future].

But since this is simply a state of lack of confidence in the mind, he said, "characterized by despondency" (*visāda-lakkhaṇa*).

*Sādana* means clearing away (*pasādana*), which is clarity (*sāda*), the state of being confident. For even a word without a prefix can convey the aforementioned meaning as if it had one, just as in the case of the term "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*).
This applies everywhere. Despondency (*visāda*) is the departure from that [clarity]; it is the state of being unconfident.

By this, he illuminates this meaning: "Because vitakka and vicāra have the nature of causing agitation..."
“Even when accompanied by those [factors], that jhāna is as if it were under pressure”; therefore he said, “it appears as if with thorns.
For its grossness consists in its proceeding together with the “thorn” known as applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
And this state of being accompanied by thorns is precisely the state of being under pressure; for in the world, people say that what is “with thorns” is harsh and gross.

For this is the custom of commentators: namely, providing an explanation of the meaning while setting aside words that are meaningless or words that share the same grammatical base (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).

And so forth. That very joy which, having become a cause (*nimitta*), when it has arisen, makes the mind "exhilarated" (*ubbilāvita*)—that itself is called "the state of being exhilarated" (*ubbilāvitatta*), because it functions as the signifier (*nimitta*) for the state (*bhāva*).
Thus, since the mind becomes exhilarated precisely through the arising of joy, the state of being exhilarated is produced by joy;
therefore, he says "that which produces the state of exhilaration."

However, this is the method stated in the commentary: the state of being directed toward (*ābhuggabhāva*) by the mind, the state of being bent toward the object (*abhinatabhāva*), is application (*ābhoga*).
For by means of pleasure the mind is bent toward the object, not—as with pain—repelled away, nor...
It is neither leaning toward nor leaning away from the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling].

And here, for one who is being secluded from sensual pleasures—as if one overcome by hunger and thirst when faced with pleasant food and such—the craving for the object of clinging increases due to a particular longing;
however, for one who has eaten their fill of excellent sensual flavors, like one who has already eaten a delicious meal, there is no desire to eat more.

“There is no state of being drunk upon sensual pleasures; because of the absence of greed for sense objects, one is released from those sense objects that are difficult to escape from, just as a leech releases itself.
Thus, having emerged from improper reflection, the first proponent declared the subsiding of the suffering of saṃsāra through the satisfaction of the strands of sensual pleasure.
[This was said] because of his vision of the danger in sensual desires and so forth, and because of his vision of the peaceful nature of the bliss of the first jhāna.
And those who maintain the doctrine of the second and subsequent jhānas declared that the bliss of the first jhāna and so forth results in the cutting off of the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
Here too, the aforementioned analysis regarding the annihilationist view (*ucchedavāda*) should be applied as far as possible. However, there is this distinction here:

all five doctrines can be found even within a single individual existence (*attabhāva*). In the first doctrine, if the self (*attā*) is fully immersed in the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), [it is annihilated].
Thus he has attained Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatta*). Regarding the second and subsequent views:
if that very same self (*attā*) included in the first view is the one possessing the first jhāna and so forth, then it follows that he has attained Nibbāna in this very life.

For this very reason, as in the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), the word "another" (*añña*) was not used here in the text to denote "another self. But how [is it] for one who demonstrates ultimate Nibbāna?
Is his own doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life included within the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*) rather than the annihilationist view (*ucchedaditthi*)?

Because it demonstrates that the self, being purified by the liberation from the bonds [of karma] obtained through the possession of various specific pleasures, remains established in its own essential nature.
For, having become pure through such liberation from the bonds of karma as thus obtained, they [the proponents of this doctrine] have attained Nibbāna in this very life.

The tenet is that the self persists in its own form. For thus, in the Pāḷi, their doctrine is presented under the very guise of indicating eternalism: “In this way, sir, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this very life.
The phrase beginning with “In this way” summarizes the meaning of the Pāḷi. Therein, the word *yāsām* is an indefinite demonstrative referring to the views already mentioned.

The statement "these sixty-two views have been explained" is a definitive restriction, or it is a statement that does not require further qualification, as in the passage where it says, "with reference to which it was said. The remaining fifty-five views are those other than these.

Among them, the fact that the doctrines of the speculators on the finite and infinite (antānantikavāda) and so forth are included within eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) has already been demonstrated in various places. But what is the reason for this [classification], regarding the past and the future?
Is it not the case that these two are shown as objects for one who is intent upon such views, but not as a single unified whole?
The reason here is simply impossibility. For a conceptualization of views regarding a "middle" period, distinct from both the past and the future, is impossible;
this is because that which exists merely between those two is of a limited duration. Furthermore, the present personal existence (*attabhāva*) is the interval between those two.

This being so, since that nature which is capable of conceptualizing views regarding both [the past and the future] is itself included within the very limits of the prior and subsequent ends, how could those two not be shown together as one?
Alternatively, because it possesses the prior and subsequent ends, the middle is called "the prior and subsequent ends";
and that [middle] is also [referred to as] "those who theorize about the prior end and those who theorize about the subsequent end" (pubbantakappikā ca aparantakappikā ca pubbantāparantakappikā).
It should be understood that by saying "and" (cā), the Blessed One spoke [of them] as being distinct from those who speculate about the past and the future.

It should also be known that in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), they are included by the general designation "all those speculators about the past and the future," either through this inclusive description or by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*).
Otherwise, because the statement made by summarizing [them] would lack a summary that is exhaustive (*niravasesa*).
"May they fall into misfortune": who, then, are those speculators on the past and the future?
They are to be understood as those who, having been proponents of finitude or infinity, hold views such as "Nirvana in this very life," and thus are attached to both ends.
(100–104) By the words beginning with "Now," he shows the distinction between the two types of absorption statements. Therein, "in one place" (*ekajjhaṃ*) means in the sense of making into a heap.
*Nipāta* is a particle. The grammarians (*neruttika*) say that *ekajjhaṃ* means "he makes into one"; this is a neuter locative singular. The word *iti* has the sense of "this" (*idam*);
the meaning is: "having asked in this manner, he answered. *Ajjhāsayaṃ* refers to the inclination toward views based on eternalism or annihilationism.
For, according to those two [views], the inclination of beings on the side of defilement is twofold. Thus it has been said:
“Eternalism and annihilationism views, as well as conformable patience,
and that knowledge which is according to reality— this is what is designated as ‘disposition.
And the Blessed One [knows] this in regard to the immeasurable diversity of the knowable among immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems.

Although [the views] are divided into many different types by way of their arising, he says, "as if weighing them with a balance," because he demonstrates—having delimited them with his omniscient knowledge by way of grouping them into sixty-two varieties starting with "four persons who are eternalists"—that he is like one holding them up with a balance that has become a standard of measure. For he will say later: "They are included within the net," and so forth.

Furthermore, by the phrase “like one removing sand from the foot of Mount Sineru,” he shows that no knowledge other than omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is capable of delivering this teaching, because it is described as being supremely profound. And here, [the Buddha says]:
“All those [wrong views] are included within these sixty-two bases, or by one or another of them; there is nothing beyond this.”
Because of the statement "externally," and because there is no proponent of views whatsoever who is not included within the three types of speculators regarding the past,

those various forms of doctrines such as non-actionism, non-causality, and nihilism mentioned in other discourses like the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, as well as those various types of views distinguished as the doctrines of God (*issara*), primordial nature (*pakati*), the Lord of Creatures (*pajāpati*), the person (*purisa*), time (*kāla*), inherent nature (*sabhāva*), destiny (*niyati*), and chance (*yadicchā*), [are all subsumed].
Even those views appearing externally should be understood as being included within these very categories because they are subsumed therein. How so?

First, the doctrine of non-action (*akiriyavāda*) is included within eternalism (*sassatavāda*), because it demonstrates the absence of action through such statements as "barren" and "fixed like a peak.

Likewise, the doctrine of Pakudha, which proceeds according to the method beginning with "these seven bodies," and the view beginning with "there is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings," [are also included].

The doctrine of causelessness (*ahetukavāda*) proceeds by way of the same method as the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannavāda*). The nihilistic doctrine (*natthikavāda*), which proceeds by way of the method beginning with “there is no other world,” belongs to the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*);
for it is therein stated that “with the breakup of the body, one is annihilated,” and so forth.
By the first word “etc. (*ādi*), the doctrines of the Nigaṇṭhas and others are included.

Although the fourfold restraint (*cātuyāmasaṃvara*) is presented in the Canon as the doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, nevertheless, because it involves a denial of the seven points and is characterized by equivocation,
the doctrine of Nātaputta is included among the doctrines of "infinite equivocation" (*amarāvikkhepa*), just like the doctrine of "accumulation" (*sañcaya*). However,
doctrines such as "the soul is the same as the body" and "the soul is one thing, the body another," which take the form of "the self possesses form" (*rūpī attā*)...
[These views] are included among such statements as: “One exists healthy after death. Statements of this kind—such as “The Tathāgata exists after death;
there are beings of spontaneous birth”—belong to the doctrine of eternalism (sassatavāda). Statements of this kind—such as “The Tathāgata does not exist after death;

there are no beings of spontaneous birth”—belong to the doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda). [Statements such as] “The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death... [are included in the doctrine of neither-eternalism-nor-annihilationism].
“After death, beings of spontaneous birth both exist and do not exist”—such views belong to the doctrine of partial eternalism.
“After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; beings of spontaneous birth neither exist nor do not exist”—such views belong to the doctrine of the Eel-Wriggler (amarāvikkhepa).
The doctrines of God (issara), Primordial Matter (pakati), Pajāpati, the Person (purisa), and Time (kāla) belong to the doctrine of partial eternalism. The doctrine of Kaṇāda—
The doctrines of inherent nature (*sabhāva*), necessity (*niyati*), and chance (*yadicchā*) are included within the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannavāda*).

By this method, it should be understood that the various speculative views found in other Suttantas and in the systems of external non-Buddhist teachers are all contained within these sixty-two views.
When those [views] are explained according to the method [of classification] applied here and there, they are subsumed under these categories.
We have not expanded [the text] because it would result in excessive bulk, like leaping across where there is no ford;
for our burden here consists only of investigating the meaning of the Pāḷi and clarifying the points not explicitly stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
Following the mention of the words, “Thus this teaching has come down by way of its internal connections,” we shall now set forth the sequence of the Sutta.
In order to analyze [this], he said, "For three," and so forth. For the purpose of excluding other meanings, there is the specific determination (*visesaniddhāraṇa*).
In that context, *anusandhi* means connection; it is merely the relationship, which is also called the "source" (*samuṭṭhāna*) in the sense of being the cause for the teaching.
For questions and so forth are the external causes for the teaching, since the teaching proceeds in accordance with them. That connection also...
Because it is dependent upon that, it is indeed the cause. The internal causes, however, are the knowledge of the teaching of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and so forth.

This meaning will be made clear further on. "The connection made by way of a question" means the connection of the discourse (*sutta*), because it is taught having established a question as the connection; thus, the connection is said to be made by way of the question. It is the connection designated as the question.

The term *pucchānusandhi* (connection by way of question) is also appropriate. For, by means of a connection (*anusandhi*) supported by a question, the question which serves as its basis is also included.

Alternatively, it is called *anusandhi* because it connects (*anusandahati*). That which has a connection consisting of a question is *pucchānusandhi*, referring to each respective passage of the Sutta.
Or, it is called *pucchānusandhi* because it is connected (*anusandhīyati*) by means of a question; that is, the connection of speech through questioning.
Having done so, that very passage of the Sutta which originates from it is taught. This same method applies to the connection of intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*) as well.
It is called "connection" (*anusandhi*) because it is connected; whatever is the connection, or that which is in accordance with the connection, is "according to the connection" (*yathānusandhi*).
By way of the question and the intention, there is a connection at the beginning through a dharma that is appropriate to the dharma already taught.
The subsequent passage of the Sutta proceeds either by way of that [topic] itself or by way of its opposite.
