For it is stated in the Commentary: “By which teaching... [etc. ...the simile of the saw has come down,” and so forth;
thus, with the words “Therein,” etc., he shows the analysis according to the text. Therein: “When this was said, Nanda the cowherd said this to the Blessed One.”
They recite [the passage], but that is not correct because it does not exist so in the Sutta.
Instead, it should be read as: “When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One,” for such is the meaning established in that Sutta, the Nandagopālaka Sutta.
Indeed, this is the Saṅgīta Sutta in the Saḷāyatana Vagga of the Saṃyutta Āgama. Regarding the Gaṅgā...
Having used the simile of a log being carried away by the current to teach noble sons who had gone forth out of faith, the Blessed One instructed them;
Nanda the cowherd, thinking, "I shall fulfill this practice," received the going-forth and full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One.
Practicing accordingly, he attained arahantship before long. Therefore, it became known as the "Nandagopālaka Sutta."
“‘What then, venerable sir? and so forth was said by a certain bhikkhu. For it is stated there:
‘When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “What then, venerable sir, is the near shore?
and so forth. In this context, the meaning is as follows: ‘When this was said’ refers to [the passage] beginning with, ‘If, bhikkhus, the log does not approach the near shore,’ and so on.”
Having used the simile of a log of wood being carried away by the Ganges, this was taught to the sons of good family who had gone forth out of faith.
[The monk] said this to the Blessed One because of his skill in discerning the underlying connection, saying, “But why, venerable sir? and so forth.

For the Tathāgata thought, “There is someone sitting in this assembly who is skilled in discerning the underlying connection; he will ask me a question,” and it was for that very reason [that he spoke].
He brought the teaching to its conclusion. "The near shore" (*orimatīra*) means the shore that is near; likewise for "the far shore" (*pārimatīra*).

"Sinking in the middle" (*majjhe saṃsīdo*) means sinking or submerging in the midst. "Rising on the dry land" (*thale ussādo*) means having emerged from the midst of the water and risen or ascended onto the dry land.
"Seizing of men" (*manussaggāho*) means belonging to those who are men, or the seizing by men.
"Seized by non-humans" means seized by a whirlpool; that is, being caught in a swirl of water.
"Rotten within" means that even if the kidneys, heart, and so forth are not putrid, they are "rotten within" because of the putrefaction of their qualities (*guṇa*).
The passage beginning with "Then, to a certain bhikkhu... is found in the *Mahāpuṇṇama-sutta* of the *Upari-paṇṇāsa* in the *Majjhima Āgama*.
In this context, the meaning is as follows: *iti kira*—here the particle *kira* expresses disapproval;

by it, he indicates his own lack of approval regarding the self-emptiness (*attasuññatā*) as taught by the Blessed One. *Bho* is an address to the Dhamma, meaning "O, you phenomena whose nature is such!

[The passage continues: "If form is not-self... up to ...if consciousness is not-self. The construction includes a supplementary portion of the text: "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*). [And finally: "done by what is not-self" (*anattakatāni*).
"Not performed by oneself" means not performed by the aggregates (khandhas) that have become non-self.

"Whom will those kamma-actions touch? means: what kind of personal existence (attabhāva) will they touch? Since there is no self and because the aggregates are momentary, those kamma-actions will touch what self with their own fruit?
What is meant is: who will experience the fruit of kamma? To that bhikkhu...

The connection is: "having known" (*aññāya*)—that is, having understood through his own mind the reflection in the other's mind by means of knowledge consisting in the penetration of minds (*ceto-pariya-ñāṇa*), or by means of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
"Unwise" (*avidū*) means one who is not clever due to a lack of skill in the noble Dhamma because of being devoid of learning and so forth. For "wise" (*vidū*) is a designation for a clever person.

"Vidati" means "he knows. "Enveloped in ignorance" (*avijjāgata*) means "approached by ignorance"; the meaning is that one has not abandoned ignorance due to a lack of discipline regarding the noble Dhamma.
"With a mind dominated by craving" refers to the predominance of craving [with the thought]:

"If there were no such thing as 'I,' then who would experience the fruit of the action performed by me? But if that [self] exists, there could be the enjoyment of the fruit of action. Thus it is from the predominance of craving.
"With a mind that has arrived, accompanied by the clinging to a self. "It should be run beyond" means it should be run past.

This is what is meant: although formations are momentary, because the fruit arises right there in the same continuum where the karma was performed, the connection between karma and its fruit is established merely as a heap of phenomena;
therefore, to hold to the principle of identity (ekattanaya) is wrong.
Having grasped this, one must necessarily exist as either the agent or the experiencer;

otherwise, there would be no connection between the action and its fruit, and one might think that the Teacher’s instruction—which clarifies the emptiness of self and what belongs to self—has been transgressed.
Now, in order to clarify that one must not overstep [this principle], he said, "What do you think? and so forth.
"Subsequent teaching" (*upari desanā*) refers to a teaching that occurs subsequent to a preceding teaching within the *Desanāsamuṭṭhānadhammadīpikā*.

This "demonstration of the sequence of the discourse" (*yathānusandhidassana*)—in the sense of revealing the appropriate counter-factors for the factors that constitute the origin of the teaching—is stated as:
"The six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) follow [the preceding teaching] above. This is done by way of revealing the appropriate factors corresponding to the two types of sequences of the discourse.
Furthermore, all that remains is by way of elucidating the opposing states (*paṭipakkhadhamma*). These very suttas are found in the *Mūlapaññāsa* of the *Majjhima Āgama*.
"By defilement" means by way of the defilements (*kilesa*), according to such passages as "Greed is a corruption of the mind.
"By quarreling" means by dispute. "By impatience" means by anger. "The simile of the saw" is a simile for a harsh rowing. In the phrase "in this too," the word "too" (*pi*)...
In this context, it functions either as a reference—as in such passages as "this too is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense"—or as a conjunction.

Thus, just as in the *Vatthasutta* and other discourses there is a sequential connection by way of elucidating opposing doctrines, so too in this *Brahmajāla Sutta* there is either a reference or a conjunction.
For this [discourse] has arisen by way of those speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) which proclaim eternal substance and so forth.

The teaching is concluded by the exposition of emptiness regarding the permanent, the substantial, and so forth. With the words "Therefore," etc., he demonstrates the excellence of the commentary as it has been stated.
[This concludes] the commentary on the section concerning agitation and vacillation (verses 105–117).
"For the purpose of showing the delimitation" means that for the followers of wrong views, [the Blessed One spoke] of the adherence to craving and views [regarding] the Tathāgatas...

This is for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of confusion and the distinction between them by means of knowing-and-seeing, and by means of right seeing as opposed to wrong views such as eternalism.
For them, there is only the misapprehension of craving and views; it is not, as it is for the Tathāgatas, knowing-and-seeing according to reality.
This is merely the agitation of craving and views, the experience of wrong seeing, and not the experience of right seeing as it is for a stream-enterer.
And by the word "immovable" (*niccala*) in this teaching, he shows the demarcation of the boundary. Therefore, he will say:

"That feeling which [arises] from the gratification of views...," and "He shows it as being designated by 'view' and so forth. Because of the expression "that too," the sense that "by which they designate the state of joy" is obtained;
to show this, the passage beginning with "by which" was stated. This follows from the force of the context.

For here, by the word *ta* (that), there is a reference precisely to that which has already been understood. "By the gratification of views" means by the gratification that serves as the condition for views.
"By the pleasure of views," and so forth, are synonyms for that very same thing.
The connection is: for those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, even that feeling is a feeling belonging to those who are immersed in craving (*taṇhāgata*).
And it is stated without qualification as "the individual essence of phenomena as they really are.
For it is not merely by failing to know the individual essence of conditioned phenomena that people adhere wrongly. Furthermore, a general definition must be restricted to its specific application.
Therefore, this specific application should be made here: "The self and the world are eternal"—this is the very basis of view thus grasped.
"Thus afflicted, thus fated, and thus in the future"—this refers to those who do not know and do not see according to reality;

or rather, it refers to those who, due to unextinguished craving for whatever is felt, cling to such a course of views, and who do not know and do not see that feeling according to reality from the perspectives of its origin and its passing away.
For by means of this specific application, [the teaching is] as if [seen] with the unobstructed knowledge and the universal eye.

It becomes clear that by this teaching he shows this meaning: "In this matter, there is for the Tathāgatas knowledge and vision according to reality as it is, whereas for those who follow speculative views there is none; rather, they possess only the adherence to craving and views.
Furthermore, this teaching was given for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between boundaries.
“Feeling” (*vedayita*) refers to that which proceeds by way of establishing views such as “the self and the world are eternal”;

it is spoken of by way of the pleasure of the relish of views, and it too is an experience (*anubhavana*). “Of those gone to craving” (*taṇhāgatānaṃ*) means of those who have approached craving, or of those who proceed [with it].
He explains that very same point according to the method already stated: “Only... feeling. And furthermore, “that indeed” (*tañca kho pana etad*) refers to what has been stated above.

One understands it precisely as feeling; by this it is shown: having severed the phrase, “Even that feeling is indeed feeling for those who have fallen into craving,” one must again connect it with, “Even that feeling is indeed agitation and vacillation.
To show the demarcation of the lower limit, [the text says], “Even that does not reach it... not for the stream-enterer.”
It is said, “like vision, it is motionless. And by “vision,” the bliss of right vision—the bliss of the path and the fruit—is meant.
From where is this meaning obtained? It is obtained from the force of the word *eva* (just/only).
For by the phrase “only trembling and writhing,” it is implied that [the mind] does not remain in a single state without writhing like the bliss of the path and fruit; rather, [it remains so].

The meaning is that because it consists of the bait of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāmiṣa*) and is pierced by the thorn of views and craving (*diṭṭhitaṇhā*), it is subject to oppression and thus necessarily involves agitation;
for this very reason, he said, "by one who is agitated," and so forth. This is the method of connecting the commentary not found [explicitly] in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Having thus analyzed the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) by way of their specific causes, [the author now treats them] by way of their non-specific causes.

To demonstrate this, the teaching beginning with “In this regard, monks,” and so forth, was undertaken. For feeling, ignorance, and craving are the undifferentiated causes of all speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*).

In that context, the phrase “that too” refers to the threefold variety of pleasure and so on, which serves as the cause for their proclaiming, “The self and the world are eternal,” as found in the passage: “Monks, those recluses and brahmins who proclaim the self and the world to be eternal.”

That which is felt— whether it be suffering, a dart, or impermanence— arises for those who do not know and do not see it as it truly is, either in its specific aspects or generally in terms of its origin,
passing away, gratification, danger, and escape. Precisely because of that, and because the longing for pleasure and so forth becomes possible,
there occurs for those who have entered into craving, through the agitation of craving, the very flickering of views, the very movement of views.
The thought, “When there is no self, who experiences feeling? is merely an instance of the view being applied to the doors of body and speech;
it does not mean that there is some eternal phenomenon to be described by means of that view. This same method applies to the views of partial-eternalism and so forth.
Commentary on the Section on Conditionality through Contact (Phassa-paccaya-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

118. "For the purpose of showing the succession of conditions": this means for the purpose of showing the succession of conditions, such that there is a root cause for the view, a cause for that [cause] as well, and again a cause for that [cause] too.
For whatever agitation of craving by which these speculative views proceed, its condition is feeling (*vedayita*), and the condition for feeling is contact (*phassa*).
Thus, this teaching is one that analyzes the succession of conditions.
If it is asked, "For what purpose is the demonstration of the succession of conditions? it is for the purpose of making another point known.

For by that, just as the phenomenon of designation—which consists of views—and the phenomena that are its conditions arise solely through their respective conditions and not without conditions, so too do the phenomena to be designated.
"Form, feeling, and so forth— herein there is no eternal self or world"— thus a different meaning is made known.
The sense is that even that feeling which is agitated by craving and views arises with contact as its condition, being the condition for the craving that serves as the cause for those views.

131. "Of that condition" means of that condition designated as contact (*phassa*). "In feeling associated with views" means in feeling that has become a condition for views, which is to be produced by its own conditions dominated by contact; this locative case (*bhummavacana*) is used in the sense of "that which is to be accomplished.
"For the purpose of showing its state of being a powerful [cause]" means for the purpose of showing its state of being a potent cause. For it is thus:
Feeling arises even without the bases such as the eye and without certain associated mental states; however, it never arises without contact.
Therefore, contact is the powerful cause of feeling. This applies not only to feeling alone, but also to all other associated states.
For even if an object is present, if the arising of consciousness is devoid of the mode of contacting, [feeling does not arise].
Contact is not merely a condition for itself; rather, it is a specific condition for all associated mental states.
For this reason, when the Blessed One analyzed the arising of consciousness in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* treatise, he first extracted "contact" alone, saying "there is contact.
However, feeling is its preeminent objective condition (*adhiṭṭhānapaccaya*).
Because it was stated, “they will experience,” the term “that too” (tadapi) is understood here as a reference to the subject; thus he says, “that feeling.

Furthermore, this [particle *vā*] is not employed because the particle *vā*—which has an implied sense—is used optionally, and because it is either elided or remains as a residual element. This applies to similar cases. And there is a verse on this point:
“From an implied sense, from a governing context, From elision, and from what remains;”
“By all four causes as well, a sound is not possible anywhere.

With the words beginning “For just as,” he supports that point by demonstrating that contact (*phassa*) is the powerful cause. Therein, *patato* means “of one who is falling. *Thūṇā* is a designation for a supporting pillar of wood.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion concerning the adherence to the views of those who hold to wrong views.

144. Although feeling (*vedayita*) does not appear in the text at this point, because it has been mentioned in the three preceding sections and because it will be stated later on that they "experience it again and again" (*phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedenti*), feeling alone is the primary factor here;
thus he says, "he combines all views and feelings. Regarding the word *api* (also/even) in the phrase "those who... which occurs in various places:
It is with reference to this meaning that it is said, "he synthesizes. For those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists...
[and so forth] ...all of them experience by repeatedly contacting through the six bases of contact;

thus, because those various proponents of views are synthesized by way of the activity of feeling, there occurs precisely a synthesis of what is felt. For every statement has action as its primary focus.
“For the purpose of including contact above”: this means for the purpose of including contact when it is stated, “by way of the six bases of contact.

And here, “including” is simply the demonstration that feeling has contact as its condition. For by the phrase, “experiencing repeatedly through the six bases of contact,” the experiencing of the six objects by way of the six internal bases is shown.
It is thus shown that [the body] is exclusively caused by the six types of contact; therefore, it is said, “all those,” and so forth.

*Kamboja* is a kingdom with that name. Likewise is *Dakkhiṇāpatha*. By the term “place of birth” (*sañjātiṭṭhāna*), he shows that the word *sañjāti* has the sense of a locus (an *adhikaraṇa*), meaning “that wherein they are born.
The same applies to the word *samosaraṇa*. The word *āyatana* is also [to be understood in this way].
In both cases, "āyatana" means a place of convergence, like a crossroads. "Naṃ" refers to the great banyan tree.
This is indeed a passage from the *Saddhānisaṃsa-sutta* in the fifth chapter (*pañcanipāta*) of the *Aṅguttara-nikāya*. And therein it is explained:
"Just as, monks, at a crossroads on level ground, a great banyan tree becomes a refuge for birds from all sides. This is the description of that [tree].

It is said: "In the presence of mindfulness as a base" (*sati-āyatane*). The meaning is that when the cause known as mindfulness is present, one attains the state of being a witness in each respective instance.

It is called a "base" (*āyatana*) because fruits proceed therein, depending on it for their existence; or because it extends (*tanoti*) and brings forth its own fruit, which has become its source (*āya*), thus it is a cause. "They settle" (*sammanti*) means they become tranquil and find relief.
They produce [them]. Since the word *āyatana* does not here signify a different meaning as it does in other contexts, he says "merely a designation" (*paṇṇattimatte*);

the meaning is "merely designated in such and such a way. For the conventional expression "forest" (*arañña*) applies to a mere designation for a collection of trees and shrubs, and that very forest is the "base of the forest" (*araññāyatana*).
Regarding the phrase "in all three meanings," the particle *pi* (also/even) includes the meanings of source (*ākara*), dwelling (*nivāsa*), and foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
It means "to collect" (*sampiṇḍeti*). For in such cases as "the mine of gold, the mine of silver," it occurs in the sense of a *ākara* (a source or mine);

in "the abode of Īśvara, the abode of Vāsudeva," it occurs in the sense of a *nivāsa* (an abode or dwelling); and in "the sphere of action, the sphere of craft," it occurs in the sense of an *adhiṭṭhāna* (a basis or foundation), meaning a support (*nissaya*).

The etymological definition (*vacanattha*) is, respectively: they "mine" (*ākaronti*) here, they "dwell" (*nivasanti*) here, they "establish themselves" (*adhiṭṭhahanti*) here. [This applies] to the eye and so forth.

Furthermore, contact and the other [mental factors] are crowded together there, and those [bases] are their "abode" because they serve as the condition of support (*nissaya-paccaya*) and the basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Therefore, these three meanings are indeed applicable here. To explain how they are applicable, he says: "For among the eye and so forth," and so on.
Contact, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—these five factors, with contact as the fifth, are mentioned by way of illustration.
They are so called because they serve as the bases for other associated states, or else because of their predominance.
For when the Blessed One analyzed the arising of consciousness, he first analyzed those very factors, saying: "There is contact, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness.
They are said to "arise" because they originate right there, by virtue of having that [consciousness] as their support and object.

They "converge" (*samosaranti*) because they converge there in the capacity of being the basis, the door, and the object. And these [three] are their cause, because in their absence, those [mental states] do not exist.
However, this aforementioned meaning of "place of origin" and so forth occurs only by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), since it functions precisely through being established in various contexts;
thus it was stated by the Elder Ācariya Ānanda. This, moreover, is by way of explaining the meaning of the words...

The meaning as it occurs is: *āyatana* is so called because of extending (*āya-tana*), because of the stretching out (*tana*) of what has come (*āya*), and because of leading (*nayana*) what has come (*āyata*).

For, in the case of the eye and the other [senses], the states of consciousness and mental factors extend, arise, strive, and exert themselves toward their respective doors and objects by means of their respective functions such as experiencing;
and these [bases] stretch out—that is, expand—the states that have become the source (*āya*), and they lead what has come.

"They lead to and cause the occurrence of the suffering of *saṃsāra*. Regarding the phrase "by this method" (*iminā nayenā*), the word *iti* here has the sense of "beginning with," and thus includes the Pāli passage beginning with "dependent on the ear" (*sotaṃ paṭicca*).

In that context, "of the three" refers to the triad of object, faculty, and consciousness—namely, the eye-consciousness and so forth, which have the sensitive eye-faculty and visible form as their objects.
Because it is to be grasped through the state of their coming together, contact (*phassa*) is called "conjunction" (*saṅgati*). For it is said to be "manifested as a meeting.
By this method, the connection is made with the phrase "having brought [it] forward. By this, he shows the following meaning:

just as in the sutta, "Dependent upon the eye... [etc.]... contact," although mental factors such as perception (*saññā*) and others are present, it is for the purpose of showing that feeling (*vedanā*) is the primary cause.

The teaching was given under the heading of contact (*phassa*). Likewise here, beginning with contact in the sequence “with contact as condition, feeling,” and so forth, the teaching is given under the heading of contact—both by saying “through the six bases of contact” and “having contacted, having contacted”—in order to show the succession of conditions by linking them to the subsequent [life].
By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “the bases of contact, etcetera,” the expression “having contacted, having contacted” is included.

By the phrase beginning with “Kiñcāpi,” he shows the mere appearance of a challenge based on the literal sound of the words; then, by the phrase beginning with “Tathāpi,” he resolves that [challenge] according to the actual meaning.
The sense bases do not touch [their objects] because visible forms lack the status of being an object (ārammaṇa).

Contact (phassa), being a non-material phenomenon (arūpadhamma), does not adhere to its object even in part; nevertheless, because it proceeds in the mode of touching, it is said to be “touching. Thus he says: “Contact itself...”
"It touches each respective object. For that very reason, it is said to have "touching as its characteristic" and "striking as its function.

In the phrase "having touched through the six bases of contact," even those [faculties] whose function is not touching are treated as having the function of touching by way of a metaphorical designation based on their dependence [on the mind].
Thus, seeing itself is what is meant by "placing it within contact," just as one says, "The beds are crying out. "Having placed it within" means...

The meaning is: "having introduced [them] into contact by way of assigning the function of touching. What is meant is: "having made them conform to the nature of contact and having attributed the designation of contact [to them].
A "designation" (upacāra) is merely a conventional expression; no purpose is accomplished by it, because it does not possess that intrinsic nature.
To show that only that which accomplishes the purpose—the thing possessing that intrinsic nature—is to be understood as the actual meaning, he said "Therefore," and so forth. As they have said:
“For the Protector spoke of the goal as refuge, not of the mere letter, O Great Seer who benefits the world.

With reference to the six kinds of contact in brief—ranging from eye-contact to mind-contact—which serve as conditions for oneself, it is said: “Feeling arises from the six bases of contact. In detail, however:
“Sixfold by way of contact, divided by way of mental exploration;

threefold by way of the three bases, twofold by way of two, and increased threefold by way of time”—thus, according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhasata-pariyāya*, there are eight hundred divisions. And here, the residents of the Mahāvihāra [explain] consciousness as follows:

They maintain that name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—even though they are both conditions and conditionally arisen—are included within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpanna*) only when they are kamma-result (*vipāka*).
Others, however, maintain that everything [is included], for there is no way to exclude the state of being a condition, regardless of how it occurs.
"That" refers to feeling as previously classified. "Of the kinds such as craving for form" means...

Just as one might refer to someone by their father’s name, such as “the merchant’s son” or “the brahmin’s son,” craving for form (*rūpa-taṇhā*) is spoken of here by way of the names of its objects, ranging up to craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma-taṇhā*).
Thus, in brief, it is sixfold. But in detail:
“Craving for form and so forth is further divided threefold by way of sensual craving (*kāma-taṇhā*) and the rest.”
"From the perspective of the mental continuum, they would be doubled by the distinction of time.

Thus, regarding that which has been stated as having eight hundred divisions: "By way of decisive support" (*upanissaya-koṭiyā*) means by way of the heading of decisive support (*upanissaya-sīsenā*). But why is only the condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*) mentioned here?

Is it not the case that pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling serve as objects for craving by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇa*), predominance-condition (*adhipati*), object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*), and natural decisive-support (*pakatūpanissaya*)?
Is it the case that there are four kinds of conditions, and that [the object-condition] is twofold by way of being a mere object and a natural decisive support? This is true;
however, all of that is included within the decisive support (upanissaya) alone—thus it has been extracted.

While it is indeed appropriate for the object-decisive support to be included within the decisive support due to its commonality with the general term "decisive support," how then [are] the mere-object and the object-predominance [included]?

In that case, could it be said that they are included within it? Since even those [other types of support] are comprised within the decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) by virtue of the commonality of their object, their inclusion occurs precisely within the decisive support itself, which constitutes the convergence of the decisive support.

It is with this very purpose in mind that, instead of saying "by way of the decisive support," it is stated "by way of the limit of the decisive support" (upanissayakoṭiyā). For an undertaking is made only when something is already established.
"It is either for the sake of a restriction or for the purpose of making another meaning known"—thus it is in such cases.
"Of the fourfold" means of the fourfold [clinging], from sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*) up to self-theory clinging (*attavādupādāna*). But is not craving itself (*taṇhā*) sense-desire clinging;
how then can that very same thing be its own condition? True, but by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) of prior craving...
Because of the firmness of subsequent craving (*taṇhā*), the preceding craving itself becomes the condition for the subsequent one.
For the prefix *upa-* occurs in the sense of firmness in such passages as "craving-firmness is sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*) and despair (*upāyāsa*)," and so forth.
Moreover, weak craving is simply craving, whereas powerful craving is sensual clinging. Alternatively, it is the longing for an object not yet attained.

Craving is like the stretching out of hands by thieves in the darkness; the grasping for objects already attained, which is sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*), is like the seizing of goods already in the hands of those thieves.
Craving is the opposite of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*); sensual clinging is the opposite of contentment (*santuṭṭhitā*).
Craving is the root of the suffering of seeking; sensual clinging is the root of the suffering of guarding. This too...

The distinction between these two has been shown by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla according to the views of certain teachers; for it was stated in the *Visuddhimagga* according to the former method as being the "own-doctrine" (*sakavāda*).

The meaning, as far as applicable, is that for non-conascent clinging there is [a condition] by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), whereas for conascent [clinging] it is by way of conascence (*sahajāta*).

It should be understood thus: therein, those [states] that are not co-nascent but have ceased immediately prior act as conditions in six ways—by way of the immediate, the contiguous, the proximate-immediate, the proximity-object, the absence, and the disappearance conditions.
However, when they function as objects, they act as conditions in three ways—by way of the object, the object-predominance, and the object-strong-dependence.
All of these, moreover, are subsumed under strong-dependence alone according to the method already explained, and are therefore described as being "within the scope of strong-dependence."

And because one, having relished forms and so forth through craving, falls into a state of being drunk with sensual pleasures, craving is therefore a condition for the clinging to sense-pleasures by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Likewise, there is the wrong view such as "there is no giving" arising from delusion regarding the distinctions of form and so forth;
the adherence to a path of purification where there is no pure path, by one desiring liberation from saṃsāra; and the grasping at a self or what belongs to a self within the aggregates.

And it grasps at the view of a self-identity (*sakkāya-dassana*). Therefore, it should be understood that for the other three [aggregates] as well, craving is a condition by way of the extreme of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
As for co-nascence, however, it is a condition for co-nascent states in seven ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root-cause.
Having subsumed all of that under the single category of co-nascence condition, it is stated as "by way of the extreme of co-nascence."
"Becoming" (*bhava*) refers to both *kamma-bhava* (the becoming of action) and *upapatti-bhava* (the becoming of rebirth).
Therein, all action leading to becoming—comprising volition and so forth—is *kamma-bhava*. The ninefold rebirth-becoming, beginning with the sense-sphere becoming (*kāma-bhava*), is *upapatti-bhava*.
Among these, the fourfold clinging (*upādāna*) pertains to *upapatti-bhava* because it serves as the causal condition for *kamma-bhava*, which is the cause of *upapatti-bhava*. Regarding that...
And by way of becoming an associate, it is a condition through the mode of natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
At the time of performing an action as its object, however, the clinging co-arising with that action is a condition for the existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*) by way of being its object.

For the existence of the kamma-process (*kammabhava*), however, the clinging co-arising with it is [a condition] by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

Furthermore, the condition is manifold by way of both cause and path. However, for that which is not co-nascent (*asahajāta*) but immediate (*anantara*), the non-co-nascent fuel (*upādāna*) is a condition by way of the immediate, the contiguous, the immediate-strong-dependence (*anantarūpanissaya*), the presence, the absence, and the repetition conditions;

and for that which is other than the immediate, it is a condition by way of the natural strong-dependence (*pakatūpanissaya*). Moreover, at times such as during comprehension (*sammasana*), it is a condition by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*) and so forth. In this context, regarding the immediate and the rest...
Having included the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) and the co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*) such as the co-nascent and others, it is stated "likewise.

This [term] has the sense of bringing forward (*rūpūpahāra*) or the sense of drawing along (*anukaḍḍhana*). By this, he shows the meaning as "by way of the limit of decisive support and by way of the limit of co-nascence.

Regarding the phrase "existence [is a condition] for birth," here "existence" (*bhava*) refers to kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*), for that is the condition for birth, not rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).
For birth itself is the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), and that consists of the aggregates first produced. Therefore it was said:
“In this context, ‘birth’ should be understood as the five aggregates together with their modifications. By this, the following objection is refuted:
“Is not birth itself an existence? How then can it be a condition for birth? But how is it to be known that “kamma-existence is the condition for birth”?

If it is asked, "Is it not a condition?"—[the answer is no], because even when external conditions are equal, the distinctions such as inferiority and superiority are seen solely through the power of karma.
As the Blessed One said: "Karma divides beings, namely, according to their inferiority and superiority.

They are "with modification" (savikārā) by virtue of the modification of their arising, and not by other [factors]; and these, in actual meaning, are simply the state of rebirth-existence (upapattibhava), and that alone is unfit to be its cause.
Because, just as in the case of craving being the condition for the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*),

no distinction such as "prior" or "subsequent" is possible [between them], it follows that kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) alone is the condition for birth— which is termed rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*)— by way of both the kamma-condition (*kammapaccaya*) and the natural decisive-support condition (*pakatūpanissayapaccaya*).
Therefore, in order to show this meaning, [the text] groups the kamma-condition under the decisive-support [condition] and [explains it] by way of the limit of decisive support (*upanissayakoṭiyā*).

"...is a condition," it is said. However, since aging-and-death occurs when there is birth, and for a fool touched by aging-and-death and so forth, sorrow and the rest come into being, whereas they do not when [birth] is absent, therefore it is said that birth is a condition for aging-and-death and so forth by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Because a detailed analysis of the meaning has not been made, [it is stated] solely under the heading of co-nascent and decisive support conditions (*sahajāta-upanissaya*).

Because the investigation of conditions has already been shown, and because the detailed exposition of the factors and so forth has not yet been touched upon, it is said, "This is the summary here," and so on.

To dispel the objection—"Since the investigation of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) has such a vast scope, how can this [summary] be obtained in its entirety?"—he says, "In detail," and so forth.
Furthermore, the discussion of dependent origination is found even in the Pāḷi itself in the passage beginning, "But here... and so on.
This shows that it was taught only by way of a single portion. In this context, "here" means in this *Brahmajāla Sutta*. "Of this" refers to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
"Merely the purpose" means merely a portion of the purpose, by way of the feeling that serves as the cause for the [wrong] view.
Indeed, the word "merely" (*mattam eva*) is a synonymous expression used in the sense of restriction, as in: "The lifespan is but a mere hundred years; now, at this present time..."
Because it has a purpose by way of making known the mutual meaning—as in the passage beginning with “vijjati”—the word *matta* means “measure.
The sense is that it is precisely the measure known as the purpose, and nothing beyond that. Some also say: “The word *matta* is used for restriction;
the word *eva* is used for determination. This applies everywhere. And there is this verse on the matter:

“*Mattaṃ* has the same meaning as *ekaṃ*; the word *matta* [is used] in the sense of measure (*pamāṇa*), or in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), or else in the sense of certainty (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
Because it is stated here in the Pāḷi even by way of a partial [explanation], when dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is explained in that manner, it is accompanied by an illustration.
Showing the reason, he said, "The Blessed One," and so forth. By this, he shows the following intention:

"When the Blessed One speaks on the discourse of the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), he speaks by way of one of the heads [of the defilements], namely ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), or views (*diṭṭhi*).
Among these, speaking here specifically by way of the head of views, because views are a powerful cause for feeling (*vedanā*), he teaches only a portion of dependent origination rooted in feeling."
...so he spoke. And regarding these suttas in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Dasanipāta* (Book of Tens), the prior limit is not known;

that is to say, it is not known—even by my unimpeded omniscience—whether ignorance arose during the time of a certain Sammasambuddha or a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*), or whether it arose before that.
Thus, the first boundary of ignorance is not discerned.
The meaning is: "because no limit exists. By the phrase "even so" (*evaṃ cetan-ti*), it is acknowledged that this ignorance is indeed called such by way of its lack of a limit.

However, even though it is spoken of as having a limit through the restriction of time—by the phrase "from this condition" (*idappaccayā*)—ignorance arises from this condition known as the five hindrances;
thus, by way of the fixed law of phenomena (*dhammaniyāma*), [ignorance is defined].
The meaning is that "a limit is discerned. For it is stated in that very same [text]: "And what is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: 'The five hindrances.
However, in the *Ṭīkā*, he says "conditioned by the taints" (*āsavapaccayā*); that does not agree with the illustrative sutta.
This is "this-condition" (*idappaccaya*), by way of the substitution of the letter *d* for the letter *m*. But those learned in grammar [say] regarding such a usage...

Some say that the word *ida* itself is the base form (*pakati*) because it is seen [in usage]; however, this is entirely incorrect, as various applications are observed through vowel modification (*vaṇṇavikāra*) and other changes.
For instance, when "these" (*amū*) is stated, it appears as "asū" due to vowel modification; and when "in these" (*imesu*) is stated, it appears as "esu.
Likewise here, vowel modification occurs not only in a sentence but also in a compound (*samāsa*), just as in the example "husband of a wife" (*jānipati*).

"Thus spoke the couple. What more need be said here? It should be understood that what was spoken by the Venerable Elder Mahākaccāyana, who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), is itself the authority.
"Of craving for existence" means of craving which constitutes the fetter of existence. "From this condition" means from this condition of ignorance (*avijjā*).
“For what is the nutriment of craving for existence? ‘Ignorance,’ it should be said,” so it has been stated. “Craving for existence” means the view of eternalism (*sassataditthi*).
“Conditioned by this” (*idappaccaya*) here, however, has the meaning of being conditioned specifically by feeling (*vedanā*). To the objection, “Should not only the views be explained;
what is the purpose of explaining dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)? he says, beginning with “Therefore,” etc. This is what is meant: [he explains] in forward order (*anuloma*).
The discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is called the discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

By means of that very discourse, the Blessed One showed that as long as these proponents of views do not relinquish this wrong view, they will continue to sink into the cycle of existence through this succession of conditions.

"From this becoming" (*ito bhavā*); "from this" (*ito*) refers to among those [three] states of becoming (*bhava*). This same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well. By this, [it is shown to be] without end.
It shows successive arising. "Vipannaṭṭhā" means destroyed in various ways.
145. "The basis for those who hold wrong views" means that which serves as a basis by way of showing the false graspings of those who hold wrong views.
It is said that this is a teaching addressed to persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) by way of those who hold views (*diṭṭhigatika*).

For this is a teaching of Dhamma addressed to persons. "Addressed to monks engaged in yoga" means it is the basis for monks engaged in yoga; it is said to be a teaching addressed to persons by way of monks.
"Turning away" (*vivaṭṭa*) means departed from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). By the words "by whom," etc., [it refers to] those who hold views.

The Blessed One, skilled in teaching, has included here the sphere of contact (phassāyatana) mentioned previously as the condition for feeling, which itself serves as the cause for wrong view; this is what is shown. Regarding the phrase "in the meditation subject of feeling," this is said with reference to the Pāli passage beginning, "the origin of feelings.
He says "but there is only a slight difference" and so forth, meaning: "As, however... [and] "that" refers to "from the origin of contact."
The reason stated is “from the cessation of contact. In the phrases beginning with “from the arising of nutriment,” physical (edible) nutriment is to be understood.

For, according to the *Paṭṭhāna* statement, “Physical nutriment is a condition for this body by way of the nutriment condition,” it is indeed a supporting condition even for the eye and other faculties that are produced by kamma. In the phrases beginning with “from the arising of name-and-form,”...

The triad of aggregates beginning with feeling alone is "name. Now, since it is stated that "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [arise]," should it not be said that for all six bases of contact, "[they arise] from the arising of name-and-form and cease through the cessation of name-and-form"?
Why, then, is it said of the eye-base and so forth that "[they arise] from the arising of nutriment and cease through the cessation of nutriment"? This is true without distinction.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this was stated in such a way specifically to show that [this knowledge] also occurs in the case of the eye and so forth.
Since the knowledge of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) is established by means of knowing the higher [truths], although it is not mentioned in the Pāḷi, it is said: "and he knows views.
Virtue, concentration, and wisdom are a mixture of mundane and supramundane; however, liberation here is the lower [type].
The attainment of the fruits [is mentioned] up to “arahantship,” because the supreme fruit (agga-phala) is mentioned separately.

Here, understanding occurs through both direct perception and inference; for this very reason it is said, “a learned bhikkhu who has mastered the texts knows,” and so forth, or it should be applied according to what is available.
As for the phrase “but the teaching,” here the word *pana* expresses a lack of approval; by this he indicates that even though...

Although non-returners and others understand things as they truly are, nevertheless, because the teaching is given by way of discerning the ultimate attainment (ukkamsagati) of the Arahant, it is brought to its conclusion with the Arahantship as its pinnacle.
The meaning is that, just as a golden house might be finished with a jewel-encrusted pediment, this teaching is brought to its conclusion with the pediment of Arahantship.
And here, by the words "From which... [he] understands," the fact that the Dhamma is a vehicle for deliverance is shown.

This demonstrates the excellent practice (*suppaṭipatti*) of the Saṅgha; for that very reason, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is presented in its full extent by completing the passage:
"Who knows this? One whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) knows it, down to one who has begun insight (*āraddhavipassaka*)".
Therefore, that which was stated above—"it should also be illustrated by way of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha"—is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*) alone.
It should be understood that it is "illuminated.

146. The statement, "There is no one who holds a speculative view (diṭṭhigatika) that is outside the net of the teaching," should be understood as intended to make known the absolute completeness of the teaching.
"Within the net" means inside the net; even those not caught within the net by way of entering its substance [are included].
"Antojālīkatā" means made into an inner net by way of entering into speech dependent upon that; or, "antojālā" means those standing within a net.
Even though they are not an inner net by way of their substance (*dabba*), they are made into an inner net by way of speech dependent upon that, hence "antojālīkatā.

Grammarians state that the suffix *ī* occurs after a word expressing a modification when used with the suffixes *ka*, *ra*, and *sa* to denote the state of becoming what it was not, or that there is a substitution of the vowel *ī* for the final *a* of "anta."
The phrase beginning with “of this” was stated in order to show the meaning of “the maker white” and “the maker into a morsel.
The sense is that they are emerging while remaining dependent and settled; thus, they are “emerging.

Here, the word *māna* has the sense of a characteristic (*bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa*), because the state of emerging again is characterized by the state of emerging [previously] which has not been abandoned. The same applies to the expressions “sinking,” and so forth.
The word *anta* (end). By the phrase beginning with "sinking down" (*osīdantā*), it is shown that by the very act of emerging, the act of submerging—though not explicitly stated—is also included.

In this context, "sinking down" refers to falling downward through rebirth in the states of deprivation (*apāya*), while "rising upward" refers to ascending through the existence of success (*sampattibhava*). Likewise, it refers to the limited plane and the sublime plane;
to the sluggishness and the over-exertion of views; and to the view of the past limit and the view of the future limit.
And these should be applied in their proper order. "Included" (*pariyāpannā*) means contained within; its state [of being included] is by virtue of being bound to that, as it is said: "bound by this.
With the words "Not here," etc., he shows the meaning arrived at through the aforementioned canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Now he states the correlation with the simile, beginning with "like a fisherman" (*kevaṭṭo viya*), etc. One who moves (*vaṭṭati*) or frequents the water (*udake*) is a fisherman (*kevaṭṭo*).
The fisherman: Although the disciple of the fisherman is also mentioned in the text, he was described in that way because he follows after him.

"The ten-thousandfold world-system" is said with reference to the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*), because it is there alone that full penetration (*paṭivedha*) is possible, and because others are included by the inclusion of that very field.
For even those who hold other views are included here, as they are caught within the net.
“Coarse” (*oḷārika*) means gross due to its manifest nature. “Of that” refers to the limited water.
(147) By the phrase “because all views are included,” he shows that through this inclusion of doctrines, there is an inclusion of persons.
“Showing to himself…” [and so forth]—due to his skill in teaching, among those aforementioned proponents of views who serve as the points for emerging and submerging, he demonstrates...
Showing that he himself is not restricted to any particular state of existence such as *bhava* (existence) and so forth. "They lead" means they bring sentient beings to their desired destination;

and since that occurs by way of drawing them along, he says "by the neck," and so on. By the phrase "because of its similarity to a nettle," he indicates either a metaphorical expression (*sadisavohāra*) or a derivative formed from a comparison (*upamātaddhita*).
The passage beginning with "For that... is an exposition of that similarity. Regarding the word "by the neck," [it refers to] "of the great multitude."

In the phrase "the exposition of the connection is *neti*," here too it should be connected by way of the object (*kamma*), because the word *nī-* takes two objects, and because in the employment of a verb, the genitive case frequently indicates the sense of the agent or the object. "By him" means by this Blessed One;

the connection is: "that conduit to existence (*bhava-netti*) has been cut off. Furthermore, he states "the state of being without rebirth-connection" for the sake of the implied meaning (*sāmatthiya*).
For when the exhaustion of life has been stated, the state of being without rebirth-linking is likewise stated, because that very non-appearance is the primary cause [of such a state].
In the phrase "they will not see," the formation of the word is by way of a future tense, as shown in such passages as:
"In that a disciple would know, or see, or bear witness to such a thing."
By the phrase "they will not see," what is meant? He says: "They will go to a state of non-designation (*apaṇṇattika*).
And by "state of non-designation," he means the state of non-designation of the very designation that is currently existing;

however, as for past designations, the designation of the Tathāgata persists until the disappearance of the Dispensation, and even beyond that, it continues to function during the arising of other Buddhas.
It is just as it is now for Vipassī and the others. For he will say: "It will be merely a matter of conventional usage.
And here, according to the etymologists (*neruttika*), the term *paññā* is a substitute for *paññatti*.

"Body" (*kāya*) means the personal existence (*attabhāva*), which is the aggregate of material and immaterial phenomena. In this way, its similarity to a mango tree (*ambarukkha*) [is established], as well as that of its constituent parts.
The resemblance of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), the eye-element (cakkhudhātu), and so forth, to the mango fruit is appropriate. "That" refers to the body.

"Measuring five fruits, twelve fruits, and eighteen fruits" means there are three types, like a cluster of mango fruits: one measuring five fruits, one measuring twelve fruits, and one measuring eighteen fruits. "That which has a cluster (piṇḍa) as its essence" is [the meaning of *piṇḍa*].
A cluster, a stalk. "Following that" means following the stalk; therefore he said, "following that very stalk.

"Contact with the poison of a frog-thorn" refers to contact with the thorn of a particular poisonous frog, or with other poisons, or contact with the poison existing in the frog-thorn itself. A thorny aquatic creature.
The creature here is called a frog (*maṇḍūka*), which people refer to as a "stone-tortoise" (*pāsāṇakacchapa*);
they say there is also a thorn situated at the very tip of its tail. Some say it is a single uneven fish-thorn.
The word *kira* is a particle used in the sense of hearsay or tradition. And in this context, when the stalk is severed, the mango fruits attached to that stalk are separated from the mango tree.
Just as when the eye of existence is severed, there is a severance of the continuity of the aggregates and so forth that are bound to it—this much is the simile found in the Pāḷi;
however, it should be understood that the remainder is obtained by implication from the meaning.
148. "The power of the Buddhas" means the power of the knowledge of the Buddhas. Regarding the phrase "of the sutta thus spoken," the word *nāma* here is used in the sense of esteem (*sambhāvane*).

*Nipāta* is a particle; by it, one esteems the excellence of the Sutta according to the method stated as: “Even though this sutta has been spoken thus. *Handa* is used in the sense of relinquishment (*vossagga*).
By that, one makes a relinquishment, thinking: “Indeed, I shall have it committed to memory right now; I will not make a delay.
*Dhammapariyāye* means in the textual discourse known as the teaching of the Dhamma. *Idhattha* means benefit in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammahita*). *Parattha* means...

It is for the benefit of the future life, or for the welfare of both. The meaning of the expression as it was spoken is also appropriate here, because in the phrase "the net of Dhamma" (*dhammajāla*), the Dhamma of the threads is intended.
"Here" (*iha*) means in this dispensation. "Na" is a mere particle, as in such expressions as "The ascetic Gotama has not heard that...
"Dhamma" refers to the textual Dhamma (*pāḷidhamma*). Because it encompasses everything in its entirety, the "net" (*jāla*) is that which consists of the meaning (*attha*) within it.

The "net of meaning" (*atthajāla*). Likewise, there is also the "net of Dhamma," the "net of Brahma," and the "net of views. It is called "victory in battle" (*saṅgāmavijaya*) because one conquers the battle by means of this;
and here, "battle" refers to the encounter with and the engagement against the five Māras. Thus he said, "even against the Devaputta Māra," and so forth.
For it is a "net of meaning" due to the perfection of its meaning, and due to the perfection of its phrasing, since it is an exposition of blameless phenomena such as virtue (*sīla*).
And it is a "net of Dhamma" (*dhammajāla*). It is a "Brahma-net" (*brahmajāla*) because it analyzes the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, which have become "Brahma" in the sense of being supreme.
It is a "net of views" (*diṭṭhijāla*) because it analyzes right view by means of the discernment of views and the exposition of emptiness.
It is the "supreme victory in battle" because it is the means for crushing the doctrines of the sectarians; such is the application of the meaning here that should be understood.
"From the conclusion of the introduction" means from the end of the introduction, which consists of the words "Then the Blessed One arrived. For this is a term denoting a limit.
Furthermore, "from the conclusion of the introduction" means because it was spoken at the end of the introduction, being the conclusion of the introduction, as in the passage beginning:
"Or, monks, others might speak dispraise of me. For this is a term denoting an inclusive limit. And this [refers to] "he said."

This was stated by way of connection with the *kiriyā* (action). However, because of the statement, "It is good in the beginning by way of its introduction (*nidāna*"), the introduction itself is indeed included within the discourse (*sutta*), just like the conclusion. "Unobtainable... profound" is an epithet for the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). 149.

Just as those who are displeased are called "enemies" (*verimanā*) because they act for their own disadvantage and for the disadvantage of others—as the Dhamma King has said in the *Dhammapada* and the *Udāna*—
“Whatever a foe might do to a foe, or an enemy to an enemy, a mind wrongly directed would do him even worse than that. It is not that these [beings] are thus displeased;

rather, they are called “pleased” because they are pleased by their own welfare. Therefore, he said “pleased with themselves” (*sakamanā*). And he shows that this state of being pleased with themselves arises from the mind being seized by joy through the phrase beginning with “directed toward the Buddha” (*buddhagatāya*), and so forth.

Furthermore, this is another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “With uplifted minds” (*attamanā*) means with fully satisfied minds; the meaning is that their mental intentions were fulfilled by this teaching.
“The splendor of the teaching” (*desanāvilāsa*) is the unfolding of the teaching, and that is precisely the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) which accomplishes the function of the teaching.

“By him whose voice is as lovely and sweet as the song of the *karavīka* bird” means by him who possesses a voice as charming and sweet as the cry of the *karavīka*. “Like the consecration with the nectar of immortality” (*amatābhisekasadisa*).
The water, which pacifies the distress of body and mind and is produced from all constituent parts, is called "the deathless" (*amata*) because it leads to long life;

[he approaches] by means of that [water], which is like a consecration. He whose voice possesses the eight qualities like the voice of Brahmā is "one with a voice surpassing that of Brahmā" (*atibrahmassara*);
by him [it is said]. "He rejoices" (*abhinandati*) means he craves (*taṇhāyati*); therefore he said, "he has come even to craving. This is because verbal roots have multiple meanings.
“Abhinandanti” means they approach or serve; thus he says, “also in approaching.

Likewise, “abhinandanti” means they accept; thus he says, “also in accepting. Since the very same meaning expressed by “abhinanditvā” is made clear by the word “anumoditvā,” he says, “also in rejoicing.
To show this same meaning through the structure of a verse, he says, “well-spoken,” and so forth. Therein, it is well-spoken in terms of its sound.
It is well-spoken in terms of its meaning; it is well-uttered by way of revealing virtue (*sīla*), and it is well-spoken by way of revealing emptiness (*suññatā*).
Alternatively, it is well-uttered by way of analyzing views (*diṭṭhi*), and it is well-spoken by way of analyzing the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) that penetrates them.

In this manner, it should also be applied here through the types of explanations shown, such as the refutation of dispraise and praise. "Such a one" (*tādino*) refers to [the Buddha] by way of the five qualities, beginning with equanimity toward the desirable and the undesirable.
[This refers to] the reasons for one who has become such (tādibhūta). The detailed explanation of this term—“He is ‘such’ because he is indifferent to the desirable and undesirable;
he is ‘such’ because he has abandoned [them]; he is ‘such’ because he has vomited them out,” and so forth—is stated in the *Mahāniddesa*, and it will also appear later in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, although there are inquiries expressing a desire to speak, occurring here and there in such passages as, “And what is that, monks? and so on, [the answer follows].
Because it is spoken by way of answering questions, this discourse is called *veyyākaraṇa*. For *vyākaraṇa* (explanation) itself is indeed *veyyākaraṇa* (analytical exposition);
nevertheless, a discourse that proceeds by way of question and answer is called *geyya* if it contains verses (*sagāthaka*).
If it is without verses (*niggāthaka*) and lacks the causes for being another *aṅga*, it is called *veyyākaraṇa*. Thus, by way of question and answer...

Because the *pavatta* is shared with the *geyya*, and because the state of being without verses (*niggāthaka*)— which lacks the causes for other [nine] factors— is unique to it and not shared with anything else, he stated,
"For this is a *veyyākaraṇa* because it is without verses," thereby showing that the very state of being without verses,
regardless of whether it takes the form of a question or an answer, constitutes the cause for its being a *veyyākaraṇa*.

The objection "Why? is resolved by the phrase "for it is said: 'while being recited,'" because this is a word connected to both [the preceding and the following], as it links back below and forward above. This is what is meant:
since it is stated in the present tense by the words "while being recited," it was not only at the conclusion of the Sutta that [the earth] shook, but rather it shook on sixty-two occasions.
"It should be understood" means: even when this entire sutta is being recited in this manner, does it not follow that the meaning is simply that [the earth] did not shake?
Or rather, is the meaning not that [it shook] at the conclusion of each respective speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*) as they were presented one after another?
This inquiry is not irrelevant in any context, for it is pursued merely on the basis of its possibility; however, this particular meaning is not established by mere possibility alone.
Rather, it was spoken at the time of the teaching precisely in the manner of its recitation, as handed down through the succession of teachers.
It must be understood that this meaning was included in the Council (saṅgīti) in that very same form, and that the compiler spoke it according to the method in which it had been thus recorded;
otherwise, for this matter—which lies beyond the reach of mere reasoning—it would be inappropriate to speak by means of speculative reasoning.
In such cases as these, the meaning of phrases like “by the disturbance of the elements” and so forth should be understood from the commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.
Regarding the phrase “and in others,” the word “and” (pi) here includes the analysis of the perfections (pāramī). For it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa:
“For one who comprehends these phenomena, Which possess the characteristics of their own intrinsic nature and essence...”
“By the power of the Dhamma, the earth, with its ten thousand worlds, trembled.

Likewise, there were also the establishment of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), its disappearance, and so forth. Regarding those, first, as for the establishment of the Dispensation: at the time of the Blessed One’s acceptance of the Veḷuvana Grove;
at the time of the Elder Mahā-Mahinda’s acceptance of the Mahāmeghavana Grove; and at the time of the Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha’s recitation of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
In such instances as these, because the roots of the Dispensation had sunk deep, this great earth shook as if dancing under the influence of joy.

But upon the disappearance of the Dispensation, it was as if overcome by grief, thinking, "Alas, the disappearance of such a True Dhamma!"—just as it was at the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s Dispensation. For this is stated in the Apadāna:
“Then this entire earth, though immovable, shook and trembled;
and the ocean, as if filled with grief, uttered a piteous cry.
This refers to the first approach to the seat of enlightenment on the full moon day of Visākha. Regarding the taking of the rag-robe:

Regarding the taking up [of robes]: having shaken off a quantity of living beings the size of a gourd from a hempen rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) discarded in a raw charnel ground—which he had covered with a female slave named Puṇṇā—he stood in the Great Noble Lineage (*mahāariyavaṃsa*). Regarding the washing of the rag-robe: it refers to the washing of that very same rag-robe.
The *Kāḷakārāmasutta* is in the *Catukkanipāta* of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*. The *Gotamakasutta* is also in that same place.
In the Tikanipāta: "By the power of energy" means by the radiance of the energy that served as the cause for renouncing the glory of a wheel-turning monarch during the Great Renunciation.
Regarding his approach to the seat of enlightenment:
"Let skin, sinew, and bone remain; [let only my flesh and blood dry up]."
"Let the flesh and blood in my body dry up entirely.

Regarding the phrase "by the power of the energy endowed with the four factors as described," the meaning should be understood according to the context. "Struck by the force of wonder" means impelled by the impact of the majesty of a marvelous deed.
Some say this refers to the splendor of the Blessed One’s merit resulting from his washing of the rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*).
Regarding the taking of rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*), it appears as if it were appropriate to say that [the earth] was struck by the force of a marvel;
however, because that occurred only occasionally, it is described as "an untimely shaking.

In the *Vessantara Jātaka*, however, because the earth shook many times due to the power of the merit from fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*), it is called an "untimely shaking. Regarding the demonstration of witnesses, what is to be told...
It is said, "by way of being a witness," because it acts like a witness in accordance with the matter, as occurred at the time of the victory over Māra.
It is said, "by the giving of applause," according to the requirements of the context, as occurred at the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, during the recitations (*saṅgīti*), and so forth.
By the words beginning with "not only," through the demonstration of the shaking of the earth for many purposes, the great majesty of this very Sutta is shown.

It has been shown. Therein, "Jotivana" means Nandavana; for it is stated in the *Vinaya-saṃvaṇṇanā* that it is called Jotivana because it is the place where the light—consisting of the illumination of knowledge (*ñāṇāloka*)—of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) has appeared. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma such as the *Anamatagga-sutta*.
"The site of Pācīna-ambaḷṭṭhika" is the location characterized by a young mango tree situated in the eastern direction.
In this way, the earthquake is extended [to other instances] such as the times taught by the Blessed One. “Anekasoti” means in many ways (*anekadhā*). The construction is:
“of that best of suttas, the *Brahmajāla*, taught by the Self-Existent One (*sayambhu*)”; thus it should be joined. “Idha” means in this dispensation (*sāsana*).

“Yoniso” means so that they may practice by means of the proper method or skillful means (*upāya*), namely through the abandoning of wrong view and the undertaking of right view; this is the meaning. This...
Thus ends here the *Līnatthavibhāvanā* commentary on the *Aṭṭhakathā*. As for the commentary on the method of this treatise (*pakaraṇa*),
that which was composed by the teacher Dhammapāla from this point onward—
The detailed exposition of various meanings, such as origination and the modes of conveying meaning,
should not be regarded by us with indifference, for this [work] is their purification.
Therefore, we shall explain that as well, for the increase of the wisdom of those who listen.

This is indeed a commentary on the meaning of the Pāḷi according to the method of the *pakaraṇa* (treatise); for "the method of the *pakaraṇa*" is, in the Tambapaṇṇi language, the method of commentary (*vaṇṇanā-naya*).
It is stated in the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā*: "They say it is also the method of arrangement for preachers of the Dhamma in the *Netti*, *Peṭaka*, and *Pakaraṇa*.
Furthermore, because this [commentary] first [deals with] the origin, purpose, and receptacles of the teaching, as well as the summarized meanings.
When these have been extracted, it becomes easy and well understood. Therefore— the wise person,
having extracted the origin, the purpose, and the receptacle as the summarized meaning,
should thereafter elaborate upon the modes of inclusion and so forth.
In this context, "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) refers to the source of the teaching. That is twofold:
common and uncommon; likewise, the common type is further divided into internal and external. Therein, the internal common origin is the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Blessed One.
For it is by being impelled by that [Compassion] that the Lord of the World directs his mind toward the teaching of the Dhamma for those who are to be trained.
It arose; with reference to this it was said: "Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye," and so forth.

And here, the inclusion of the threefold state of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) should be understood as its arising for the purpose of ferrying beings across the great flood of *saṃsāra* by means of the gift of the hand of the True Dharma's teaching.
And just as with Great Compassion, so too with the knowledge of omniscience, the knowledge of the ten powers, and the rest.

The internal common origin of the teaching is as follows: knowing all knowable phenomena—the manner in which they should be taught to them, as well as the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings—exactly as they are, the Blessed One, through his skill regarding what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*), set forth a teaching of diverse methods in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained.
As for the external common origin, it was [the assembly] of the Great Brahmā together with his retinue of ten thousand.

The entreaty of Sahampati Brahmā. Indeed, upon that entreaty, the Master of Dhamma—having allayed his indolence born from reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma—became inspired to teach the Dhamma.
Furthermore, [this inspiration] is twofold: internal and external. Of these, the internal is that great compassion by which...

And that knowledge of teaching by which this sutta was set forth—both of these [are the bases]. For although it is common to the state of being an ascetic (sāmañña), it becomes uncommon in respect to specific states such as great compassion;
however, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that external praise or blame, which arise from what is uncommon, is an offense because it causes beings who are to be trained to feel resentment or joy.
Furthermore, in cases of censure or praise, there is the fault of causing beings who are to be trained to experience resentment or joy.
And therein, the vision of the disadvantage [of sensual pleasures] is the specific origin for the external [perfections]; likewise for the sequence of conduct regarding blame and praise;
for the manifold kinds of virtue, such as the minor precepts and so forth, which are the object of praise;
for omniscient knowledge regarding the ground of views such as eternalism and so forth; and for the Tathāgata’s unimpeded range of activity beyond that.
And because it is not included within any of the realms of existence (bhava) and so forth, the lack of understanding by sentient beings is also an external, uncommon origin.

Purpose (payojana) is likewise twofold: common and uncommon. Therein, the common purpose is the attainment of final nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna), which is the flavor of liberation for all of the Blessed One’s teaching;
for this very reason he said: "This is the purpose of discourse, this is the purpose..."
The passage beginning with “reflection,” etc., should be understood as the uncommon [factor], by way of the opposite of external origination.

For in this teaching, the occurrence of states such as resentment or joy in beings toward blame or praise—which is the fruit of this teaching—is employed as the cause for the presentation of this teaching.
Indeed, a fruit is said to employ its cause through the power that produces it, only when the fruit exists.
Because that power has attained the state of being the cause. Alternatively, as stated by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta: "The aforementioned fruit applies the Blessed One to this teaching.
For whatever fruit is to be accomplished by a teaching, because it is desired, one says that the teaching "applies" the teacher to that fruit.
Furthermore, [it serves] to destroy various forms of wrong livelihood, such as hypocrisy and flattery.

The purpose [of this treatise] is indeed the unraveling of the sixty-two-fold net of views, the elucidation of the structure of conditions by way of the head of views, the presentation of the four truths as a meditation subject by way of the six bases of contact, the exhaustive elimination of all types of views without exception, and the demonstration of one’s own parinibbāna through non-clinging.
The vessel, however, is the basis for the teaching. For those whose minds possess praise and blame, signs, attachment and aversion—

Those who are intent on various forms of livelihood based on hypocrisy and the like, who are mired in the mud of views such as eternalism, who fail to fulfill the aggregate of virtue and the other perfections,
and who lack knowledge of the specific qualities of a Buddha— such persons are the vessels for this teaching. Furthermore,
the summary meaning (*piṇḍattha*) here is comprised, as far as possible, by the words of the sutta both individually and collectively.
The purpose [is as follows]: By the statement that malice and so forth are not to be committed, there is shown the application of the perception of being a recluse in accordance with one's promise;

likewise, the practice of patience and gentleness, devotion to the cultivation of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), the conjunction of faith and wisdom, the foundation of mindfulness and clear comprehension, the accomplishment of the power of reflection and cultivation, the abandonment of obsessions and underlying tendencies, the practice for the welfare of both [self and others], and freedom from defilement by worldly conditions.

The purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) is shown by the statement of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth; and through that, there is the perfection of moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa),
the possession of loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā), the abandoning of transgression, the abandoning by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅgappahāna),

the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct, the accomplishment of the three types of abstinence, the achievement of being dear, pleasing, and venerable, and the attainment of gain, honor, and renown.
The state of being the foundation for serenity and insight; the thinning of the roots of unwholesomeness; the planting of the roots of wholesomeness; the removal of both kinds of harm;
confidence in assemblies; dwelling in heedfulness; being difficult for others to overcome;

and possessing such qualities as freedom from remorse—this is the elucidation of the profound Dhamma shown by the words beginning with "profound," as well as the state of having no foothold [for adversaries].
The state of being difficult to manifest even in an incalculable number of eons; the impossibility of penetrating through direct personal experience even with subtle knowledge;
the difficulty of attainment even by inferential knowledge known as "dhammanvaya"; the subsiding of all disturbances; the manifestation of the peaceful Dhamma;
the state of having a beautiful conclusion; the quality of never bringing satisfaction; and the attainment of the state of supreme striving.
It is the domain of knowledge as it truly is, its subtle intrinsic nature, and the manifestation of great wisdom.
Briefly shown by the words that illuminate views, it is the manifestation of the views of eternalism and annihilationism,
the description of the two fetters, the proclamation of false adherence, the exposition of following the wrong path, the making known of inverted grasping, and the encompassing of misapprehension.
The establishment of views regarding the past and the future; the differentiation of views concerning existence and non-existence;
the manifestation of craving and ignorance; the exposition of the views that the world is finite or infinite; the entry into the two extremes;

and the detailed classification of the outflows, floods, yokes, defilements, ties, fetters, and graspings—likewise, the accomplishment of the awakening and the full realization of the Four Noble Truths as shown by such statements as "the arising of feelings," and so forth.
The abandoning by suppression and the abandoning by eradication; the removal of craving and ignorance; the grasping of the sign of the persistence of the true Dhamma;
the attainment of scriptural mastery and realization; the practice for the welfare of both; the embracing of the threefold wisdom;
the application of mindfulness and clear comprehension; the conjunction of faith and wisdom; the cultivation of evenness in energy; and the accomplishment of serenity and insight.

The establishment of ignorance (*avijjā*) is shown by the phrases "of those who do not know and do not see"; likewise, the establishment of craving (*taṇhā*) is shown by the phrases "the agitation and vacillation of those possessed by craving.

By both of these, the establishment of the two—hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and fetters (*saññojana*)—is shown, as well as the non-interruption of the cycle of saṃsāra which has no discoverable beginning, the drawing back from the past and the linking on to the future, and the analysis of causes according to the past and present times of ignorance and craving.

The non-transgression of one another, mutual assistance, and the demonstration of the opposites of wisdom-liberation and mind-liberation—these are shown by the phrase "that too is conditioned by contact.
