This demonstrates that the manifestation of eternalism and so forth is dependent upon conditions;
thereby, the permanence of phenomena is denied, their impermanence is established, and from the perspective of ultimate truth, the existence of a creator and so forth is rejected.
This is the exposition of the nature of things (*dhammatā*), the illumination of emptiness (*suññatā*), and the manifestation of the characteristics of conditions as being even and effortless.
Through the passage beginning with "He whose conduit to existence is cut off," it is shown: the Blessed One’s perfection in abandonment;

his mastery over clear knowledge and liberation; the accomplishment of the three trainings; the distinction between the two elements of Nibbāna; the fulfillment of the four foundations; and his non-inclusion within the realms of existence, modes of birth, and so forth.
By the entire sutta passage, however, is shown the Blessed One’s state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) toward the desirable and undesirable, as well as his establishing others therein;

the description of the two factors that are the beginning of wholesome states, which is the instruction on the three trainings (*sikkhattaya*); the establishment of the fourfold group of persons beginning with those who torment themselves (*attantapa*); the classification of the fourfold group of kamma beginning with the black-with-black-ripening;
the description of the fourfold sphere of the immeasurables (*appamaññā*); and [the description] of the pentad beginning with origin and passing away.

The summary meaning (*piṇḍattha*) should be shown by grouping together, as appropriate, such points as "understanding things as they really are," "the manifestation of the qualities that inspire confidence," and "establishing the Dhamma that provides protection. This concludes the commentary on the sixteen modes of exposition (*soḷasahāra*).
Commentary on the Modes of Conveying (Desanāhāra):
Now follows the determination of the modes (hāra) and so forth according to the method set forth in the *Netti* and the *Peṭakopadesa*.
In that context, regarding the five [aggregates] grasped through the standpoint of the views "self" and "world," and by way of feeling, contact, the sense bases, and so forth:

Among the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), the five aggregates of clinging excluding craving (*taṇhā*) are the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). Craving is the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*).

Furthermore, that [craving] is explicitly included in the Canon by way of its own form through the phrases “of those who have entered into craving by means of grasping at agitation” and “craving with feeling as condition,” as well as by the inclusion of the origin itself.
This, first of all, is the method of the Suttas.
In the Abhidhamma, however, according to the method presented in the Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa, [the term "suffering" is indicated] by such words as "ill-will" (āghāta) and "delight" (ānanda);

by phrases such as "exerting oneself with ardor" (ātappa-manvāya); by the expression "corruption of mind" (cittapadosa); by all terms referring to those who hold wrong views (diṭṭhigatika); by the inclusion of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; by the inclusion of existence (bhava);
by the inclusion of sorrow and so forth; by the inclusion of views; and by the inclusion of the origin (samudaya) in various places—in brief, it is thus.
The defilements of phenomena comprised by the terms that distinguish all mundane wholesome and unwholesome states constitute the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).

The non-occurrence of both of these constitutes the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*). Furthermore, its inclusion in the Canon should be understood through the expressions "the subsiding and escape from feelings" in various contexts, as well as by the terms "personal extinction" (*nibbuti*) and "liberation through non-clinging" (*anupādāvimutti*).

The path-truth is the practice that leads to the full understanding of cessation. It should be understood that this too is included therein by way of the penetration of the origin and so forth of feelings as they really are in various instances;
by way of the method of fully understanding the origin and so forth of the six bases of contact;
and by the statement regarding the cutting off of the conduit to existence (*bhavanetti*).

In this context, gratification (*assāda*) is by way of the origin (*samudaya*), danger (*ādīnava*) is by way of suffering (*dukkha*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*) is by way of the path (*magga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). Thus, according to the four truths, the gratification, danger, and escape should be understood here by way of those very same gratification, danger, and escape that have been presented in their specific forms within the Canon.
The fruit for those to be trained is the attainment of the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) and so forth. For that which is to be accomplished through the teaching was [already] explained below.
The purpose has been stated. That very thing is called the fruit; this is the meaning already expressed. For it was for that purpose that this discourse was taught by the Blessed One.

The non-performance of malice and so forth, the fact that the fruit of malice and so forth is not produced in another’s continuum, and the unraveling through acknowledging things as they truly are in both blame and praise—thus, these are the means for attaining their respective purposes. [Regarding] malice and so forth...

"By means of such pretexts as the prohibition of [wrong] instruments, those who desire one's welfare must carefully guard the mind from that"—this is the command of the Dhamma-King, the possessor of authority.
This is called the "Provision of Teaching," characterized by the demonstration of the sixfold Dhamma by way of its gratification, disadvantage, escape, fruit, and means. And it is said:
“The gratification, the danger, and the escape, as well as the fruit and the means;
and the command of the Blessed One—these are the nutriment of the teaching for yogis. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Investigation.
Even in the absence of a specific [grammatical] construction, it is said "mine" by way of conventional usage and by way of censure.

The inclusion of the word "speech" (vācaṃ) is for the purpose of providing an alternative, since there is no fixed restriction. The address "O monks" (bhikkhave) is used for the sake of making them attentive through their possession of those qualities.
It is said "others" (pare) because they are different and because they are opposed; it is said "dispraise" (avaṇṇaṃ) because it is the opposite of praise and because it is not to be praised.
They say "they might speak" by way of proficiency and by way of detail; "of the Dhamma" because its nature is to be remembered and because it is the opposite of non-Dhamma;
"of the Saṅgha" because it is bound together by right view and virtue and because it effects the breaking up of the defilements;
"therein" (tatra) by way of the aforementioned reference and by way of the introduction of the statement; and [the plural] because of their presence and because of their multiplicity.

“By you”: because it strikes the mind and strikes the object, it is called “resentment” (*āghāta*). Because of its contraction in its engagement with the object, its lack of orientation toward it, and its state of dissatisfaction, it is called “discontent” (*appaccaya*).
Because it thinks about the object and because it is dependent upon it, it is called “mental” (*cetasa*).

Because it does not accomplish what is beneficial and because it repeatedly accomplishes what is harmful, it is called “dissatisfaction” (*anabhiraddhi*). [It is so called] because it is unworthy of the cause [of peace], within the Teacher’s dispensation.

And because it is impossible for those who are already established [in the path] to perform [these tasks], it is said: "they are not to be done. Thus, by demonstrating how [each term] functions according to its intended meaning, and according to its sense:
*mamam* is a pronoun (*sabbānāmapada*) indicated as a possessor (*sāminiddiṭṭha*). *Vā* is a particle (*nipātapada*) indicated as an alternative (*vikappana*).

*Bhikkhave* is a noun (*nāmapada*) indicated as an address (*ālapananiddiṭṭha*). *Pare* is a noun (*nāmapada*) indicated as an agent (*kattuniddiṭṭha*). *Avaṇṇam* is indicated as the object (*kammaniddiṭṭha*).
*Nāmapada* (noun): *Bhāseyyuṃ* (they should speak) is a verb indicated as an action (*kiriyā*). *Dhammassa* (of the Dhamma) and *saṅghassa* (of the Saṅgha) are nouns indicated as possessors (*sāmī*).
*Tattha* (therein) is a pronoun indicated as a locus (*ādhāra*). *Tumhehi* (by you) is a pronoun indicated as an agent (*kattā*). *Na* (not) is a particle indicated as a negation (*paṭisedha*).
*Āghāto*, *appaccayo*, and *anabhiraddhī* (resentment, displeasure, and dissatisfaction) are indicated as objects (*kamma*).
"Name-word": *cetaso* is a name-word indicated as the agent (the possessor). "To be done": this is a name-word indicated as the action.
Thus, the investigation of words (*padavicaya*) is the analysis according to the phrasing (*byañjanaso*) by way of demonstrating the specific distinctions of each respective word.
However, for fear of excessive prolixity, one should follow only the Aṭṭhakathā itself and its *Līnatthavibhāvanī*.
This meaning has been clarified by the wise, so we have not elaborated upon it.
“If you were there, angry or displeased, would you be able to discern what others have spoken well and what they have spoken ill?”—this is a question seeking consent (*anumatipucchā*).
It is based on sentient beings (*sattādhiṭṭhānā*), based on the manifold (*anekādhiṭṭhānā*), and concerns the ultimate sense (*paramatthavisayā*).
"Having present objects"—thus, the investigation of questions according to their occurrence in all cases is the "investigation of questions.
"No, indeed, Bhante"—this answer is a categorical response (*ekamsavyākaraṇa*); it is exhaustive, it is surpassed, and it is mundane.
Thus, the investigation of every answer as appropriate is the "investigation of answers."
“Monks, others may speak dispraise of me... [as before] ...one should not allow dissatisfaction to arise in the mind.
By means of this first teaching, the second teaching—“Whether it be of me... [as before] ...that would only be an obstacle for you”—is brought into harmony.
Why? Because the first teaching prevents malice of mind, while the second demonstrates the danger inherent therein.
Likewise, this third teaching—“Would you be able to recognize the well-spoken and the ill-spoken of others?”—is consistent with this second teaching.

Why? Because while the second [teaching] demonstrates the danger therein, the third demonstrates the state of being incapable even of discerning the meaning of words. Likewise, by means of this third teaching...
“Or [the thought] ‘In me... [and so on], yet this is not found among us”—this fourth teaching accords with that.
Why? Because, having completely prevented mental corruption by means of the third [teaching], the fourth demonstrates the manner in which one should proceed regarding the grounds for dispraise.

By this method, the investigation that links what follows with what precedes is the "investigation of the preceding and following" (*pubbāparavicaya*). The "investigation of gratification" (*assādavicaya*) and the others follow.
It is exactly as previously stated; here, the distinction lies merely in the demonstration of their characteristics.
Regarding the question, "Would you be able to recognize the well-spoken and the ill-spoken words of others?
the answer, "Certainly not, Bhante," is consistent with this. For one who is angry cannot [recognize them], whether they be Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or noble disciples.
One does not understand the meaning of what is well-spoken or ill-spoken by one’s parents, nor by one’s enemies.

To the question, "And what, monks, is that trifling thing... [as far as] ...one who speaks in praise of the Tathāgata should speak?"—this answer, beginning with "Having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from the taking of life," is consistent with it. The Blessed One...

For he is endowed with the unsurpassed quality of abstaining from taking life and so forth, yet this is merely a small, limited, and inferior matter of mere virtue when compared to concentration and wisdom.

This is shown by the answer to the question, "And what, monks, are those things that are deep and hard to see? which begins: "There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past... and so on.
The answer accords with the question. Since the qualities of the knowledge of omniscience cannot find a footing through the knowledge of others except for the Tathāgatas—
being profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise—

it is in this manner that the investigation of the correspondence between the answer and the question constitutes here the "investigation of the subsequent verses" (*anugītivicaya*), as there is no summary verse (*saṅgahagāthā*) present.

This method of investigation, characterized by the examination of eleven factors beginning with the question-and-answer format, is called the Mode of Investigation (*vicayahāra*). And it has been said:
"That which is both asked and answered," and so forth. This concludes the commentary on the Mode of Logical Reasoning (*yuttihāra*).
The designation *mamaṃ* as a term of ownership is appropriate, because such usage is seen in the natural language (*sabhāvanirutti*) and because the negative particle (*avaṇṇa*) is dependent upon it.
The designation *vā* as a particle of option (*vikappana*) is appropriate, because indeclinables (*nepātika*) have multiple meanings and because there is no restrictive rule here.
The designation *bhikkhave* as a form of address (*āmantana*) is appropriate, because this usage of it is seen only in that specific sense, [referring] to the speaker.

And by way of the phrasing, such as "and because of the expectation of recipients," it is logical that the complete non-performance of malice and so forth leads to the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*),
because of the presence of even-handedness toward the desirable and the undesirable. For whatever continuum in which malice and so forth have arisen, there are obstacles caused by those very factors.
It is logical that these [defilements] lead to the obstruction of success for that very person, because karma does not transfer into other continuums (*santāna*).

It is logical that malice and the like, having arisen by overwhelming the mind, lead to an incapacity even for discerning what is well-spoken or ill-spoken, because anger and greed are of the nature of blinding darkness.
[This refers to] abstaining from unvirtuous conduct such as the destruction of living beings.
It is appropriate that this leads to the praise of joy for all beings, because through the perfection of virtue a great sound of fame has arisen.

It is appropriate that even a partial description of the Tathāgata’s qualities—though endowed with distinctions such as profundity—leads to the grasping of the entirety of the Omniscient One’s qualities, because these are not shared by anyone else.
These [qualities] are encompassed by the corresponding appropriate and thorough attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
It is logical that speculative reasonings lead to dogmatic adherence to eternalism and other views, because the net of conceptual construction has not been eradicated.
It is logical that craving increases with feeling as its condition due to a lack of clear understanding of feelings and so forth, because of the presence of the contemplation of gratification;
and when there is the state of being felt, there arises therein the grasping for a self or what belongs to a self in the one who feels.
And it is logical that the grasping at eternalism and so forth wavers, because its cause is present;
for clinging arises with craving as its condition. For those who propound views such as eternalism and those who experience the feeling corresponding thereto, contact is the cause;
this is logical, because without the conjunction of object, faculty, and consciousness, that [contact] cannot exist. It has the six bases of contact as its sign.
The phrase "the non-interruption of the cycle" is appropriate because ignorance and craving have not been abandoned therein.

The phrase "understanding the arising and passing away of the six bases of contact stands transcending all perceptions of speculative views" is appropriate because of the realization of the Four Noble Truths.
It is appropriate that all sixty-two types of speculative views, including the doctrine of non-action and so forth, are encompassed within the net by these very [truths].
And because theories such as the doctrine of a creator god (issaravāda) are included therein, it has been explained accordingly below.

It is fitting to say that "the Tathāgata’s body has cut off the conduit to existence" because, through the perfection of his original resolve, the Blessed One stood in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) as they truly are. "With the breakup of the body, he has attained final Nibbāna."

"It is not fitting [to say] 'they will not be seen,' because in the attainment of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*), there is no remainder whatsoever of form and so forth"—by this method, the "Mode of Conveying Reason" (*yuttihāra*) is characterized by the elucidation of the logical consistency between the phrasing and the meaning in the Sutta.
As it is said: "The ground of all the Modes... and so forth.

Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Footings (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra): The footings for failures—such as being undeserving of praise, having an unattractive complexion, and having speech that is not trustworthy—are [unwholesome states] like malice.

The footings for successes—such as being deserving of praise, having a beautiful complexion, and having speech that is trustworthy—are [wholesome states] such as the non-performance of malice and so forth. Likewise, malice and the like are the footings for the suffering of hell and other realms; the non-performance of malice and the like are the footings for the opposite.
It is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for all attainments, such as the attainment of heaven. Abstinence from killing and so forth is the proximate cause for the Noble Aggregate of Virtue;
the Noble Aggregate of Virtue is the proximate cause for the Noble Aggregate of Concentration; the Noble Aggregate of Concentration is the proximate cause for the Noble Aggregate of Wisdom.
It is the Blessed One’s knowledge of the mode of penetration, endowed with distinctions such as profundity.

The proximate cause for the knowledge of teaching is the knowledge of teaching itself. The knowledge of teaching is the proximate cause for the escape from the entire round of suffering for those to be trained.
Since all views constitute the clinging to views, they are, accordingly, the proximate cause for the ninefold existence (*bhava*).
Existence is the proximate cause for birth. Birth is the proximate cause for aging-and-death and for sorrow and the rest. [This leads to] the feelings as they truly are...
The penetration of the arising, passing away, and so forth of the four noble truths constitutes the awakening and penetration of them.
In this context, awakening is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for penetration; penetration is the proximate cause for the fourfold fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

The phrase "for those who do not know and do not see" refers to the grasping of ignorance (*avijjā*). In that regard, ignorance is the proximate cause for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), and volitional formations...

Regarding consciousness: having traced it back as far as feeling being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for craving, it should be connected with those [factors] according to the method found in the Canon, beginning with "with feeling as condition, craving arises.

In the phrase "the agitation and vacillation of those possessed by craving," craving is the proximate cause for clinging (*upādāna*). In the phrase "that too is conditioned by contact," there is the manifestation of eternalism and so forth.

It is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for others’ wrong adherence. Wrong adherence is the proximate cause for not hearing the true Dhamma, for not relying upon noble persons, for improper attention, and for practicing contrary to the Dhamma;
it is also the proximate cause for hearing what is not the true Dhamma and so forth. In such passages as “apart from contact,” contact is the proximate cause for feeling.
The six bases of contact are the proximate cause for contact, and for the entire suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
The knowledge of the six bases of contact as they really are—regarding their origin and so forth—is the proximate cause for disenchantment (*nibbidā*).
Following the sequence beginning with "Disenchantment leads to dispassion (*virāga*)," this should be traced all the way to final Nibbāna through non-clinging.

The severing of the conduit to existence by the Blessed One is the proximate cause for omniscience, and likewise for final Nibbāna through non-clinging. This is [the explanation] of the teachings as they appear in the Sutta.

The "Mode of Conveying Footings" (padaṭṭhānahāra) is defined as having the characteristic of determining the footing-factors (padaṭṭhānadhamma) and the factors that are their footings, according to how they occur.
For it is said: "The Victor teaches the Dhamma, and [he teaches] what the footing for that Dhamma is," and so forth. [End of] the Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇahāra).
By the inclusion of "ill-will" (*āghāta*) and so forth, there is a grouping of anger, enmity, denigration, spite, envy, avarice, aggression, and disparagement of others;

for these share a single characteristic by virtue of being comprised within the category of hostile mental states (*paṭigha-cittuppāda*). By the inclusion of "delight" (*ānanda*) and so forth, there is a grouping of covetousness, improper greed, pride, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence;

for these share a single characteristic by virtue of being comprised within the category of greedy mental states (*lobha-cittuppāda*). Likewise, by the inclusion of "ill-will," the remaining fetters (*gantha*) and hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are included.
“Comprehension” (*saṅgaha*) is due to their having a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of bodily fetters and hindrances.

By the inclusion of “joy” (*ānanda*), there is the inclusion of contact and the rest, because they have a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).

By the inclusion of “virtue” (*sīla*), there is the inclusion of the trainings in higher mind and higher wisdom, because they have a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of training (*sikkhā*). By the inclusion of “view” (*diṭṭhi*), there is the inclusion of the remaining types of clinging (*upādāna*).

Because they share the single characteristic of being aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhaṇa*). In the phrase "of feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*), by the mention of "feelings," there is an inclusion of the remaining aggregates of clinging because they share the single characteristic of being aggregates of clinging.

Likewise, by the mention of the feeling included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), there is an inclusion of all bases and elements that come under investigation, by way of the characteristic of a base (*āyatanalakkhaṇa*) and the characteristic of an element (*dhātulakkhaṇa*).

And because they share a single characteristic. In the phrase "of those who do not know and do not see," by the mention of ignorance (*avijjā*), there is an inclusion of the taints (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and so forth, because they share a single characteristic through their nature as causes and the like;
likewise, in the phrase "the agitation and vacillation of those gone under the sway of craving," there is an inclusion by the mention of craving (*taṇhā*) itself.
And in the phrase "that too is conditioned by contact (*phassa*)," by the mention of contact, there is an inclusion of perception (*saññā*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
The inclusion [of all phenomena] is due to their having a single characteristic by way of being causes for perversion and by way of the characteristics of the aggregates (*khandha*).

By the mention of the six bases of contact (*phassāyatana*), there is the inclusion of the remaining aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, and so forth, because they have a single characteristic by way of being the objective conditions for the arising of contact and by way of being objects of comprehension.

By the mention of the "fetter of existence" (*bhavanetti*), there is the inclusion of the defiled states beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), because they have a single characteristic by way of being the causes of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

"By way of a single characteristic": this is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra*), which has the characteristic of determining [a specific meaning] by means of the single characteristic shared by phenomena that have not been explicitly mentioned in the Sutta, as if they were mentioned there.
For it is said: "When one phenomenon has been stated, those phenomena which share its single characteristic," and so forth.
The Explanation of the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array (*catubyūhahāravaṇṇanā*).
*Mamanti* is a non-etymological term (*aneruttapada*), and it is likewise *vāti*. Those whose nature is to beg are *bhikkhus*.

They approach a state opposed to others, thus they are *parā*; however, in other contexts this is a non-etymological term—such is the etymology (*nerutta*) according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the introductory phrases such as “Thus” (*evaṃ*) and so forth, and on the canonical phrases (*pāḷipada*) such as “my” (*mama*) and so forth, because it is easily understood through that [commentary] which elucidates the hidden meaning (*līnatthavibhāvanī*).
We have not elaborated further for fear of excessive prolixity. As for those disciples whose minds are shaken by blame and praise,

who do not refrain from wrong livelihood, who are attached to false views such as eternalism and so forth, who are not established in the aggregates of virtue and other qualities, and who are averse to the flavor of the virtues of the Perfectly Enlightened One—
how indeed might they be freed from the aforementioned faults and become intent on the welfare of both worlds through right practice?

"May they become"—this is the Blessed One’s intended meaning here. Thus, the persons intended [by the teaching], as well as their place as the recipients of the teaching, constitute the introduction (*nidāna*) to this discourse.

Furthermore, the connection between what precedes and what follows (*pubbāparānusandhi*) is sixfold, by way of: connection of words (*padasandhi*), meaning of words (*padatthāna*), demonstration (*niddesa*), placement (*nikkhepa*), sutta, and connection of the teaching (*desanāsandhi*).
In this context, the connection between one word and another word—such as the connection of the word “*mama*” (of me) with the word “*avaṇṇaṃ*” (dispraise)—is *padasandhi* (word-connection).

The connection between the meaning of one word and the meaning of another word—such as the connection of the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One as “*mamaṃ*” with the meaning of what was said by others as “*avaṇṇaṃ*,” namely, the fault (non-virtue) consisting in their censure—is *padatthasandhi* (meaning-connection). [As it is said:
“*Mamaṃ vā, bhikkhave, pare avaṇṇaṃ...*” (Or, monks, others may speak dispraise of me...)
The teaching beginning with “They would speak praise” was delivered by way of a connection to the praise uttered by the wanderer Suppiya.
The teaching beginning with “Monks, others might speak praise of me” was delivered by way of a connection to the praise uttered by the young Brahmin Brahmadatta.
The teaching beginning with “There are, monks, other phenomena that are deep, difficult to see, and hard to understand”...

The *niddesasandhi* (connection of exposition) is the connection of a sutta with multiple sections through the various sections as they proceed according to the sequence of topics stated by the bhikkhus, and the connection of a sutta with a single section through its preceding and succeeding parts.
The *nikkhepasandhi* (connection of presentation), however, is by way of the fourfold presentation of a sutta.
And the *suttasandhi* (connection of the sutta) is by way of the threefold sequence of the sutta, as explained in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Thus it has been investigated and previously expounded by us. The "connection of teaching" (*desanā-sandhi*) is the correlation of one teaching with other teachings;
that should be understood as follows: “Monks, regarding me... [as stated] ...no dissatisfaction of mind should be made,” this teaching [is correlated with]:
“Monks, even if bandits with saws having teeth on both sides were to saw away at your limbs and members...”
This accords with the teaching: "If they should go to the edge of the ocean, yet therein one should corrupt his mind, he is not thereby a follower of my Dispensation.
And this [accords with]: "It is for you alone, young man, that there would be no obstacle;
for beings are the owners of their karma, heirs to their karma, born of their karma, bound by their karma, and have karma as their refuge. It is karma that divides beings, namely..."
Regarding the phrase "inferiority and superiority," this [question], "Would you... pe ... understand? refers to the verse:
"An angry person does not know his own welfare; an angry person does not see the Dhamma.
Blind darkness then prevails for the man whom anger overcomes."
By this [passage]: "Monks, when others praise me... you should not allow the mind to become elated," and by this [passage]:
"Monks, even wholesome states (dhammas) must be abandoned, how much more so unwholesome ones (adhammas)," and by this [passage]:
"Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma as a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping," and [by the passage]: "In that case, if you... etc.
“By that very act, the obstacle will be yours alone”—this refers to the verse:
“The greedy one does not know his welfare; the greedy one does not see the Dhamma.
Blind darkness then arises for the man whom greed overcomes.”
“Blinded and shrouded in a net, covered by the veil of craving,
bound by their kinsman the heedless one— like fish in the mouth of a net,
they follow after aging and death, like a suckling calf following its mother. And:
By means of this [statement], namely: “But this is merely trifling, a mere matter of virtue,” and by means of this [statement] regarding the first jhāna:

“Quite secluded from sensual pleasures… one enters and dwells in the first jhāna; this sacrifice too, brahmin, is more excellent and less troublesome than the previous sacrifices, and it is of greater fruit and greater benefit. Thus, [it refers] to the first jhāna.

Because by stating that [virtue] has great fruit and great benefit in terms of its moral quality (*sīla*), it is shown that compared to meditative absorption (*jhāna*), virtue possesses lesser fruit and lesser benefit.
The teaching beginning with "Having abandoned the taking of life" and so forth corresponds to the teaching beginning with "The ascetic Gotama is indeed virtuous,
endowed with noble virtue," while the teaching beginning with "Other phenomena are profound" corresponds to the teaching beginning with "This Dhamma realized by me is profound, difficult to see..."

Through the teaching beginning with “difficult to awaken to,” the profound nature and other qualities of knowledge are understood by means of penetrating those Dhammas endowed with distinctions such as profundity.
The teaching beginning with “There are, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins who speculate about the past...
[and so on]... they assert that both the self and the world are eternal, this alone... [is an example].

“‘This alone is the truth, all else is vain’—thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are eternal,’ ‘they are non-eternal,’ ‘they are both eternal and non-eternal,’ ‘they are neither eternal nor non-eternal,’ ‘they are finite,’ ‘they are infinite,’ ‘they are both finite and infinite,’ or ‘they are neither finite nor infinite’—thus some assert.
This alone is the truth, all else is vain. Such is the teaching.
Likewise, the teaching beginning with, “Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the future,” and so forth:
“Bhikkhus, ... they assert: ‘The self is percipient and healthy after death. In this way some assert:
‘The self is non-percipient,’ or ‘both percipient and non-percipient,’ or ‘neither percipient nor non-percipient, and it is healthy after death. In this way some...”

"By means of such teachings as, 'They assert the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being, or some declare Nibbāna in this very life,' and by the teaching, 'The Tathāgata [fully understands] the arising of feelings... and so forth, [the Buddha taught] having understood:
"This is conditioned and gross; however, there is indeed a cessation of formations, and it exists. Thus it was known.
By means of such teachings as, "The Tathāgata, seeing the escape from that, has transcended it," [the Buddha said], "That too is merely their... writhing.

This refers to the passage: "Alas, for them there will be no personal knowledge that is purified—apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it—" [but rather] "this very thing shall be known by them personally."

"‘It is purified’—this is not possible. But, monks, when there is no personal knowledge that is pure and purified, even that mere state of having knowledge which those venerable recluses and brahmins purify therein is declared to be clinging on the part of those venerable recluses and brahmins. Thus, by such a teaching, "even that..."
“With contact as condition”: this refers to [the passage], “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving;
with craving as condition, clinging,” and [also], “Friends, these states have desire as their root, are produced by attention, converge upon contact, and meet in feeling.”
And [it is] to be sought through the initial teaching; for the teaching beginning with, "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu [does not regard] the six bases of contact," and the teaching beginning with,
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu does not regard feeling as self, nor perception, nor volitional formations, nor consciousness as self— regarding them thus, he does not cling to anything in the world."
By such teachings as, "Not grasping, one does not tremble;

not trembling, one attains nibbāna within oneself," and by such teachings as, "All these are encompassed within this very net of sixty-two bases," and by such teachings as, "Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, hold views...
all these hold views regarding these five aggregates or one or another of them."
“With the breakup of the body... [and] gods and humans”—this refers to:
“As a flame cast by the force of the wind, O Upasīva, goes out and can no longer be reckoned as such; (said the Blessed One).
"Thus the Sage, liberated from the group of names, reaches his goal and does not enter into reckoning. This [verse] accords with the introductory teaching.

This is called the Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra), characterized by the elucidation of the four factors: etymology (nirutta), intention (adhippāya), teaching (desanā), and the sequence of the introduction and the subsequent connection. And this has also been stated: "Etymology, intention," and so forth.

The commentary on the removal of the cycle (*āvattahāra*): By the statement that malice and so forth are not to be practiced, there is the non-undertaking of impatience and lack of gentleness. In this context, patience includes faith, wisdom, and the endurance of harm inflicted by others and suffering;

likewise, gentleness includes virtue (*sīla*). And by the inclusion of faith and the rest, all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), beginning with the faculty of faith, are encompassed.
They are included. By the mention of "virtue" (*sīla*), all the qualities that are benefits of virtue, such as freedom from remorse (*avippaṭisāra*) and so forth, are included.

By the expression "abstaining from killing living beings and so forth," the dwelling in heedfulness (*appamādavihāra*) is implied, and through that, the entire holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*) is included. By the mention of the Dhamma endowed with distinctions such as profundity, the Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is indicated;

for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*) has unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa*) as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints has [the knowledge of the path] as its proximate cause.
Unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) is called "Great Enlightenment" (*mahābodhi*); by means of that, all the qualities of a Buddha, such as the Ten Powers (*dasabala*), are brought back.
By the inclusion of views such as eternalism (*sassata*), craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*vijjā*) are comprised; through these, the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāravaṭṭa*) is turned back.
Through the penetration of the arising and so forth of feelings as they really are, there is for the Blessed One the purification of the threefold full understanding (*pariññāttaya*); by that—

All the perfections (pāramīs) converge through the gateway of the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī). In the phrase "of those who do not know, who do not see," by the mention of ignorance (avijjā), unwise attention (ayonisomanasikāra) is included;
and through that, the nine states rooted in unwise attention are brought together.
In the phrase "the agitation and vacillation of those gone with craving," by the mention of craving (taṇhā), the nine states rooted in craving [are included].

“They turn back. The passage beginning with “That too is conditioned by contact” shows that existence is dependent on conditions for the purpose of establishing [the truths] such as eternalism; through this, the three characteristics such as impermanence are turned back.
The description of the perfection of liberation through the thorough knowledge of the six bases of contact indicates the seven stages of purification;
through this, all seven purifications are turned back. “The Tathāgata has cut off the cord of becoming...”
"Body" refers here to the abandoning of craving; by this, the Blessed One’s abandonment of all defilements is encompassed.
This is called the Mode of Conveying the Conversion (āvattahāra), characterized by the conversion of the factors taken up in the teaching according to their similar and dissimilar qualities.
As it is said: "When one footing has been found, he seeks the remaining footings," and so forth.
Commentary on the Analysis:
Unwholesome states such as malice and delight have improper attention and so forth as their proximate cause.
Those wholesome states such as non-malice and so forth, by means of which there is the non-doing and non-arising of malice, delight, and the rest—of these [the following is said]:

Appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and so forth are the proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*). Among those, malice (*āghāta*) and the like belong only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), whereas non-malice (*abyāpāda*) and the like pertain to all four planes.
Likewise, the abstinence from killing and so forth is either wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*);

for its proximate causes are the factors such as moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*). Among these, the wholesome ones may be either sense-sphere or supramundane (*lokuttara*), while the indeterminate ones are exclusively supramundane.
“Monks, there are other states that are profound”—the states thus spoken of may be either wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*).

Among them, for the wholesome states, insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). For the indeterminate states, the path-states (*maggadhamma*), insight, or adverting consciousness (*āvajjanā*) are the proximate causes.
Of these, the wholesome ones are exclusively supramundane (*lokuttara*); the indeterminate ones may be either sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) or [fine-material or immaterial sphere].
All supramundane views are unwholesome and belong exclusively to the sense-sphere; their proximate cause, without distinction, is improper attention through wrong adherence.

Specifically, however, the wrong grasp of the principle of unity—due to the absence of the analytical resolution of the compactness of continuity—accompanied by the recollection of past births and speculative reasoning, is the proximate cause for the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*). [This occurs] by way of the relationship between cause and fruit...

Because the absence of a [permanent] relationship is not grasped, there is a false apprehension of diversity; this, accompanied by the corresponding attention, is the proximate cause for the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*).

In the same way, this should be stated for the remaining views as well, according to their respective possibilities. Regarding the phrase "of feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*): here, feeling may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; it may belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and so forth.
They may belong to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*); contact (*phassa*) is their proximate cause (*padatthāna*).

Regarding feelings, the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*) is the penetration of the origin and so forth of feelings as they really are, while the knowledge of the fruit (*phalañāṇa*) is liberation through non-clinging (*anupādāvimutti*).

The classification of these factors, such as "other profound phenomena" (*aññe dhammā gambhīrā*), should be understood here according to the method stated previously. This applies to passages such as "for those who do not know, who do not see," and so forth.

Ignorance and craving are unwholesome states belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Among these, the underlying tendencies (*āsava*) of ignorance have their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) in improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*).

For craving, the proximate cause is the perception of gratification in things that are conducive to fettering (*saṃyojaniya-dhamma*). Regarding the statement, "That too has contact as its condition," the classification of factors such as mental objects (*dhamma*) and so forth should be understood here for contact just as it was for feeling.
By this same method, [the classification] for the bases of contact (*phassāyatana*) and so forth should also be understood.

The classification of phenomena (dhammas) and so forth should be applied as appropriate. This is called the Mode of Conveying Analysis (*vibhattihāra*), which has the characteristic of analyzing phenomena—both those subject to defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*) and those subject to purification (*vodānadhamma*)—in terms of their common and uncommon [features], their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), and their plane (*bhūmi*). As it is said:
"This mode conveys by analyzing the phenomenon, the proximate cause, and the plane," and so forth.
Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Reversal:

By cultivating patience and gentleness through the non-occurrence of malice and the like, one brings about the practice for the welfare of both [self and others] by means of achieving the power of reflective contemplation and meditative development.
However, when malice and the like arise, they lead to ugliness, an uncomfortable sleep, the loss of wealth, ill-repute, and [contempt] by others.

By producing the quality of being difficult to approach, they bring about great suffering in the hells and other realms. The abstention from killing living beings and so forth brings about, in succession, the excellence of freedom from remorse and the like.
Killing living beings and so forth, however, brings about, in succession, the unwholesome states such as remorse and the like.

Knowledge endowed with distinctions such as profundity brings about, for those to be trained according to their capacity, specific qualities such as the types of higher knowledge (*vidyā-abhijñā*) and the superknowledges.

Because it awakens to the true nature of all that is to be known, [the Buddha's knowledge] possesses such distinctions as profundity. However, knowledge devoid of these distinctions—being common to all objects of knowledge—does not bring about the aforementioned specific qualities.
Furthermore, all these views, according to their respective natures, fall into the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism;
they do not transcend the shore of the personality-belief (sakkāya), because their intrinsic nature is non-leading to liberation.

Right view, however, when accompanied by its requisites and having become the Middle Way, crosses over to the further shore beyond the realm of personality (sakkāya), because its intrinsic nature is that of leading to liberation.
The penetration, as it truly is, of the origin and other characteristics of feelings brings about liberation through non-clinging, owing to its being the state of the Path.
Conversely, the failure to penetrate the origin and other characteristics of feelings as they truly are brings about confinement within the prison of saṃsāra.
Because it is the condition for the formations (*saṅkhārā*). Delusion, which conceals the nature of what is felt, brings about delight in that [feeling];
however, the realization of things as they truly are brings about penetration and dispassion toward it.

Craving, accompanied by improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), spreads out the manifold web of views (*diṭṭhi*) regarding wrong adherence. The first path is the complete cutting off of the aforementioned craving; it...
It contracts the net of views. Contact (*phassa*) is the condition for the proclamation of eternalism and other such views, because in the absence of contact, those views do not exist.

For those bound by the fetters of views, the non-cessation of contact, the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, results in the non-cessation of contact and the rest, which is nothing other than the non-turning back from the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
The thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) of the sense-bases and so forth, exactly as they are, transcends all views and perceptions; of these...
However, such lack of full understanding does not transcend the manifestation of views. The severing of the conduit to existence leads to the non-production of a future personal identity;
whereas when the conduit to existence is not severed, the continuity of existence simply revolves on into the future.
This is the "Method of Reversal," characterized by the reversal of the factors taught in the Sutta from their opposites.
What does he say? “When wholesome and unwholesome states have been pointed out, cultivated, and abandoned,” and so forth.
This is the commentary on the method of synonyms (*vevacana-hāra*): “Mine, my, for me” is a synonymous expression; “or, if” is a synonymous expression. “O monks, [the] recluses...”
“Ascetics” is a figurative expression. “Others, different [people], who are hostile” … [and so on] … “Dispraise, ill-repute,
and blame” … [and so on] … “They would speak, utter, or discourse” … [and so on] … “Of the Dhamma, the Vinaya,
and the Teacher’s instruction” … [and so on] … “Of the Saṅgha, the assembly, the community” … [and so on] … “In this or that [instance].”
“Among those... [and so on]... “By you, sirs... [and so on]... “Resentment, hatred, ill will... [and so on]...
“Displeasure, dejection, mental suffering... [and so on]... “Of the mind, of consciousness, of the intellect... [and so on]...
“Dissatisfaction, hostility, corruption of the mind... [and so on]... “Not ours, not me... [and so on]... “To be done.”
“...should be generated and maintained”—this is a statement of synonyms (*pariyāyavacana*). According to this method, synonyms should be stated for all terms;
this is called the Mode of Synonyms (*vevacanahāra*), characterized by the application of various synonymous terms to their respective meanings. For it has been said:
“Indeed, many synonyms for a single state of phenomena are spoken in the Sutta,” and so forth.
The explanation of the presentation [of the terms]:

*Āghāta* (enmity) is presented as tenfold or nineteenfold according to its objective basis (*vatthu*). *Appaccaya* (gratification) is presented in six ways according to the modes of mental application (*upavicāra*).
*Ānanda* (joy) is presented ninefold by way of synonyms such as *pīti* (rapture), and so forth. *Pīti* is [further] presented generally...
Furthermore, it is classified in five ways by way of the minor [factors] and so forth; joy is classified in six ways by way of the mental applications (upavicāra);

virtue is classified in many ways by way of the practice of restraint and observance and so forth; knowledge associated with distinctions such as profundity is classified in four ways or twelve ways by way of the arising of consciousness, and in many ways according to the differentiation of its objects;
and [wrong view] is classified in sixty-two ways by way of eternalism and so forth.
By way of its divisions, and by way of its internal classifications, feeling is manifold; it is sixfold, one hundred and eightfold, and manifold.
Its origin is fivefold, and likewise its passing away. Its gratification is twofold, its danger is threefold, and its escape is both singlefold and fourfold.
Non-clinging liberation is twofold, as stated in the passage beginning, "for those who do not know and do not see."

Ignorance (*avijjā*) is fourfold according to the distinction of its objects, and eightfold; craving (*taṇhā*), as stated in the passage beginning with "of those who have gone to craving," is sixfold, one hundred and eightfold, and manifold;
contact (*phassa*) is sixfold by way of its basis; clinging (*upādāna*) is fourfold; becoming (*bhava*) is twofold and manifold;
birth (*jāti*) is sixfold by way of its synonyms; likewise, aging (*jarā*) is sevenfold; and death (*maraṇa*) is eightfold and ninefold.
Furthermore, sorrow is fivefold, lamentation sixfold, pain fourfold, likewise mental grief, and despair is designated as fourfold;
this is a designation of classification (*pabhedapaññatti*) and a designation of a collection (*samūhapaññatti*).
"There is an origin" is a designation of source (*pabhavapaññatti*); "he understands it as it really is" is a designation of the full comprehension of suffering (*dukkhapariññāpaññatti*).
The designation of the abandoning of origination (*samudaya*), the designation of the realization of cessation (*nirodha*), and the designation of the cultivation of the path (*magga*).

The phrase “entangled within the net,” etc., is the designation of the inclusion of all views. The phrase “one whose cord of existence is severed,” etc., is the twofold designation of final nibbāna (*parinibbāna*).
Thus, [these are explained] by way of the designation of the source of malice and so forth, and the designation of full understanding, and so on. Likewise...

“‘Āghāta’ (malice) is a designation as a synonym for ill-will (*byāpāda*); ‘appaccaya’ (lack of confidence) is a designation as a synonym for mental distress (*domanassa*)”—in this manner, the classification of designations should be analyzed.

This is called the Mode of Conveying Designations (*paññatti-hāra*), which has the characteristic of elucidating the ways in which each individual phenomenon is to be designated by means of multiple designations.
Thus it was said: “The Blessed One teaches a single phenomenon through various designations,” and so forth.
The commentary on the Mode of Conveying Descent:
By the inclusion of resentment (*āghāta*), there is the inclusion of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); likewise by the inclusion of dissatisfaction (*anabhiraddhi*).

By the inclusion of lack of confidence (*appaccaya*), there is the inclusion of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*)—this is the descent by way of the aggregates. Likewise, by the inclusion of resentment and so forth, there is the inclusion of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*).

When the *dhammadhātu* (mental-object element) is taken as either the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) or the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), this constitutes an entry by way of the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the truths (*sacca*).

Likewise, ignorance (*avijjā*) co-arising with resentment (*āghāta*) and so forth is a condition by way of the conditions of root, co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, and non-disappearance;

whereas that which does not co-arise, having ceased immediately prior, is a condition by way of the conditions of proximity, contiguity, immediate-proximity, decisive-support, absence, disappearance, and repetition.
[Craving] is a condition by way of proximity. However, subsequent [states] are conditions only by way of decisive support (upanissaya).

The manner in which craving, clinging, and so forth serve as conditions for contact and the rest—both those that arise simultaneously with them and those that do not—should be stated according to the case.

Furthermore, in some instances here, it is by way of predominance (adhipati); in some, by way of kamma; in some, by way of nutriment (āhāra); in some, by way of faculty (indriya); and in some, by way of jhāna.
That "some [condition] is also a condition by way of the path"—this distinction too should be understood;
this is the entry by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). By this same method, the entry of Ānanda and others by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth should also be clarified.
Likewise, virtue (*sīla*) is the volition of abstaining from killing and so forth, as well as mental factors such as non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*), while killing and so forth are [the opposites].

Because volition and those states that assist it—such as shame and fear of wrongdoing—are included within the aggregates, the bases, and so forth, their entry by way of the aggregates and other categories should be clarified in the same manner as before. This same method applies to the inclusion of knowledge, views, feeling, ignorance, craving, and the rest.
However, in the cases of the inclusion of escape, non-clinging, and liberation, there is also entry by way of the elements, specifically by way of the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

It should be analyzed; likewise, by the statement “...of feelings... liberated through non-clinging,” the Blessed One’s five aggregates of dhamma beginning with virtue (sīla), as well as the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), are revealed—thus entry should be understood by way of that as well.
By the phrase “That too is conditioned by contact,” the fact that the proclamation of eternalism and so forth depends upon conditions is indicated; thus, entry is by way of impermanence (aniccatā).
The entry [into the meaning of the Sutta] is likewise by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) through such a nature of phenomena (*evamdhammatā*).

Because that which is impermanent is suffering and non-self, there is entry by way of the signless (*appaṇihita*) and by way of emptiness (*suññatā*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

This is called the Mode of Conveying Entry (*otaraṇahāra*), characterized by the entry into the meaning of the Sutta by way of dependent origination and so forth. For it has been said: "And that which is dependent origination..."
“The aggregates of the faculties, as well as the elements and bases,” and so forth.
The commentary on the “Harvesting of Purification” begins with: “Monks, others might speak dispraise of me,” or “they might speak dispraise of the Dhamma.”
“‘They might speak dispraise of the Saṅgha’—this is purity of the words (*padasuddhi*), not purity of the undertaking (*ārambhasuddhi*).
‘In this matter, you should harbor no resentment, no ill-will, and no dissatisfaction of mind’—this is both purity of the words and purity of the undertaking.
The same method applies to the second method and those that follow; likewise, ‘But this is indeed a trifling matter,’ etc., refers to the undertaking. ‘Which [is it],’ etc., refers to...”

The question: “Having abandoned the taking of life,” and so forth, is purity of phrasing (*padasuddhi*), not purity of undertaking (*ārambhasuddhi*), nor is it purity of the question (*pucchāsuddhi*).
“This indeed,” and so forth, is both purity of the question and purity of phrasing, as well as purity of undertaking.
Likewise, “There are, monks,” and so forth, is the undertaking; “And which are those,” and so forth, is the question; “There are, monks,” and so forth—[is purity of phrasing].

The introduction: “By what means? and so forth is an introductory inquiry (*ārambhapucchā*). “As when concentrated” and so forth is a purification of the words (*padasuddhi*), but not a purification of the introduction (*ārambhasuddhi*) nor a purification of the inquiry (*pucchāsuddhi*).
“These indeed” and so forth is both a purification of the words, a purification of the inquiry, and a purification of the introduction.

In this manner, the introductions and so forth are to be understood in all instances. This is characterized by an investigation into the state of being purified or unpurified regarding the words and the introductions.
The method of analysis (sodhanahāra) is as follows; for it is said: "When the question has been answered, beginning from the verse that was asked," and so forth.

Regarding the commentary on the method of determination (adhiṭṭhānahāra): "Dispraise" (avaṇṇa) is the general determination. Without qualifying that, the specific expression is "or mine" (mamaṃ vā). Of the Dhamma...
The same method applies to the phrase "or to the Saṅgha" as well. Likewise, "virtue" (*sīla*) is a general determination;

without specifying that, the particular statement follows, such as "abstaining from the destruction of life," and so forth. "Other phenomena" (*aññe dhammā*) and so on constitute a general determination;
without specifying that, the particular statement follows, such as "This, monks, the Tathāgata understands," and so forth; likewise, [the same applies].
“Those who speculate about the past,” and so forth, is the general designation (*sāmañña-adhiṭṭhāna*). Without altering that, the specific statement is “those who hold to eternalism,” and so forth.
Following this method, in all instances, the general and specific [terms] should be determined exactly as they have been taught.

This is the Mode of Conveying Designation (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*), characterized by the determination of the general and specific [terms] exactly as they were taught, by way of not altering the phenomena (*dhamma*) contained in the Sutta.
Namely, as it is said: “The phenomena [are taught] by way of unity, and those which are demonstrated by way of diversity,” and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the requisites:
for Ānanda and others, the nineteen grounds for resentment—such as “He has done me harm”—are the cause. For Ānanda and others...
The cause for the moisture of the object is the root-cause (*hetu*). For virtue (*sīla*), the cause is moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), and so forth.
For the dhamma described by the words "profound" (*gambhīra*) and so on, all the perfections (*pāramitā*) are the cause; specifically, the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*).

For views, the causes without distinction are reliance upon unworthy persons (*asappurisūpanissaya*), listening to what is not the true Dhamma (*asaddhammassavana*), and improper attention through wrong adherence (*micchābhinivesena ayonisomanasikāro*). Specifically:

Furthermore, the cause for the eternalist view (*sassatavāda*) and so forth is the recollection of past births. For feelings (*vedanā*), the causes are ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), and contact (*phassa*) such as that of karma.
For liberation through non-clinging (*anupādāvimutti*), the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is the cause. For lack of knowledge (*aññāṇa*), improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) is the cause.

For craving, the cause is the contemplation of gratification in things conducive to fetters (*saṃyojaniya*). For contact, the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) are the cause. For the six sense bases, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the cause.

The cause (*hetu*). The phrase "the development of purification is the cause for the eradication of the conduit to existence" is called the Mode of Conveying Requisites (*parikkhāra-hāra*), which has the characteristic of explaining by determining the causal condition (*hetu-paccaya*) known as a requisite. Therefore it was said:
"Those states which, as conditions, produce another state in succession," and so forth.
Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Synthesis:

By the statement regarding the non-performance of malice and so forth, the perfection of patience (*khantisampadā*) is shown. By the passage beginning with “But this is a trifle,” the perfection of gentleness (*soraccasampadā*) is shown.
By the passage beginning with “There is, monks,” the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*) is shown. And for one who does not grasp [at things], by means of personal direct knowledge...
By the statements, “Nibbāna has been realized,” and “Having understood feelings as they really are...
being liberated through non-clinging,” the perfection of knowledge and liberation along with mastery are shown together with the perfection of concentration.

In this context, the perfection of patience is the proximate cause for the perfection of gentleness, because it is established by the power of reflective contemplation; as for the perfection of gentleness, its meaning is as follows:
"Virtue itself is the footing for the perfection of concentration; concentration is the footing for the perfection of knowledge"—this is the application of the footing (*padaṭṭhāna-samāropanā*).

"The statement regarding abstinence from killing and so forth is a demonstration of the synonyms of virtue; the demonstration of the divisions such as the doctrine of eternalism, however, is a synonymic expression for view"—this is the application of synonyms (*vevacana-samāropanā*).
Through virtue, the abandoning of transgression, abandoning by way of its constituent parts, and the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct are accomplished.
Through concentration, the abandoning of obsessions, abandoning by suppression, and the abandoning of the defilement of craving are accomplished.
Through wisdom, the abandoning of the defilement of views, abandoning by eradication, and the abandoning of underlying tendencies are accomplished.
This is the application of abandoning (*pahānasamāropanā*).

Because the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) reaches fulfillment through the aggregates of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth by means of the accomplishment of the three types of abandoning, this is the application of cultivation (*bhāvanāsamāropanā*).

This [section] has the characteristic of investigating the application of the proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*), synonyms (*vevacana*), abandoning, and cultivation of the teachings as they appear in the Suttas.

This is called the Mode of Conveying the Coordination (samāropana-hāra). For it has been said: "Those phenomena which have a certain root, and those which are explained by the Sage as having a single meaning," and so forth;
this is the application of the sixteen modes.
The commentary on the sixteen modes is finished.
Commentary on the Fivefold Method;
Commentary on the Method of the Conversion of Relishing.

By the statement regarding the non-committal of malice and so forth, the contraction of craving and ignorance is shown. For when there is mindfulness toward the bases of self and what belongs to self...
In the presence of affection (*sineha*) and delusion (*sammohe*), resentment (*āghāta*) arises through such thoughts as "He has done me harm," and so forth; it does not arise in their absence.

Likewise, by means of statements such as "abstaining from the destruction of life," and by statements such as "Nibbāna is personally realized, he is liberated through non-clinging, and he understands as it really is the six bases of contact...
[and so on]," the absolute abandonment of craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) is demonstrated.

Furthermore, for those [cravings and ignorance] shown by way of terms such as "speculators on the past" (*pubbantakappika*) and by phrases such as "not knowing, not seeing," their respective bases are material phenomena and immaterial phenomena. Their respective remedies are serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Their fruits, in turn, are liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) and liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*). Therein:
Craving is the truth of the origin; or else, craving and ignorance, along with the material and immaterial phenomena that serve as their basis, are the truth of suffering.
Their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation; and the understanding of that cessation through serenity and insight is the truth of the path.
In this way, the application of the four truths should be understood.

And here, by the mention of craving (*taṇhā*), the entire unwholesome side should be understood through such factors as deceit (*māyā*), fraud (*sāṭheyya*), conceit (*māna*), arrogance (*atimāna*), intoxication (*mada*), negligence (*pamāda*), evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), association with evil friends (*pāpamittatā*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*).

Likewise, by the mention of ignorance (*avijjā*), it should be understood through such factors as distorted attention (*viparītamanasikāra*), anger (*kodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), denigration (*makkha*), spite (*paḷāsa*), envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), hostility (*sārambha*), difficult-to-counselness (*dovacassatā*), the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*), the view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*), and so forth.
By the reverse of what has been stated, however, it should be understood through such factors as lack of deceit (*amāyā*), lack of fraud (*asāṭheyya*), and so on.
Furthermore, the entire side of the wholesome (*kusala-pakkha*) should be understood by way of non-erroneous attention (*aviparīta-manasikāra*) and so forth;

likewise, by way of the factors on the side of serenity (*samatha*), such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), and those on the side of insight (*vipassanā*), such as the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).

Thus, the meaning of the Sutta concerning the side of defilement (*saṃkilesa-pakkha*) through craving and ignorance, and the side of purification (*vodāna-pakkha*) through serenity and insight, is presented by way of the application of the Four Noble Truths.

This is the ground for the method of the "Swinging of the Palanquin" (Nandiyāvaṭṭa), which is characterized by the eye. For it has been said: "He who leads both craving and ignorance by means of serenity and insight," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the method of the "Threefold Basket" (Tipukkhalanaya).

By the statement regarding the non-committing of malice and so forth, the absence of hatred (*adveṣa*) is established; likewise by the statement regarding abstention from killing living beings and harsh speech.
By the statement regarding the non-committing of joy and so forth, however, the absence of greed (*alobha*) is established; likewise by the statement regarding abstention from unchaste conduct.
By the statement regarding abstention from taking what is not given and so forth, both [the absence of greed and hatred] are established. "For this, monks, the Tathāgata..."

Through the passage beginning with “he understands,” the establishment of non-delusion (*amoha*) is shown. Thus, when the three unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*) have been grasped, the three wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*) are necessarily established by their very opposition and by the statement regarding the non-performance of malice (*āghāta*) and so forth.

In this context, the entire side of the unwholesome should be elaborated upon by way of the three types of misconduct (*duccarita*), the stains of defilement (*saṃkilesa-mala*), and the five factors consisting of unwholesome perception (*saññā*), thought (*vitakka*), and so on, based on the three unwholesome roots.

Likewise, based on the three wholesome roots, [the side of the wholesome] should be elaborated by way of the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*), purification (*vodāna*), equanimity (*sama*), wholesome perception, thought, wisdom (*paññā*), the true Dhamma (*saddhamma*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
The entire side of the wholesome should be analyzed by way of the doors of liberation, the liberations, and so forth.
Herein, this is the application of the Truths: greed is the truth of origination, or alternatively, all wholesome and unwholesome roots [are the truth of origination].
The aggregates of clinging produced by those [roots], which constitute their basis and objective field, are the truth of suffering; the non-occurrence of these [aggregates] is...
The truth of cessation, the understanding of cessation, and the truth of the path beginning with liberation— this is the ground for the Tipukkhalanaya,

which has the characteristic of leading by way of the application of the Four Truths to the side of defilement through the unwholesome roots and to the side of purification through the wholesome roots.
For it has been said:
“He who leads away from the unwholesome together with its roots,
and towards the wholesome together with its wholesome roots,” and so forth.
This is the commentary on the method of the Lion’s Play (*Sīhavikkīḷita*).

The existence of mindfulness (*sati*) is established by the statement regarding the non-committal of anger, ill-will, and so forth. The existence of energy (*vīriya*) is established by the statement regarding abstention from wrong livelihood;
for it is by means of energy that one dispels thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty, and the morality of purity of livelihood is accomplished through energy.

The existence of mindfulness is established by the statement regarding abstention from killing living beings and so forth; for it is through mindfulness that what is blameworthy and what is blameless is clearly seen.
In that regard, having observed the dangers and benefits, one practices by abandoning what is blameworthy and undertaking what is blameless.

For this reason, it is said that [concentration] has "deliverance as its manifestation. Through the passage beginning, "This, monks, the Tathāgata understands," the accomplishment of concentration and wisdom is shown;
for one who possesses wisdom understands things as they truly are, and one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
Likewise, by such expressions as “permanent” and “eternal,” there is the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent.
By such expressions as “the self is healthy after death, exclusively happy, and has attained Nibbāna in this very life,” there is the perversion of perceiving what is not pleasant as pleasant.
By such expressions as “endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure,” there is the perversion of perceiving the foul as beautiful. This applies to all phrases that manifest [wrong] views.
The perversion that takes what is non-self to be “self”—thus, in this context, the four perversions are established;

and as their opposites, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are likewise established. Therein, the four types of persons are to be demonstrated by means of the four aforementioned faculties.
For craving-characterized persons are of two kinds: those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties; and the same applies to view-characterized persons.
Among them, the first, who possesses the distorted view of perceiving the foul as beautiful,

enters the fixed course of rightness after discerning the true nature of the body through the power of mindfulness. The second, who possesses the distorted view of perceiving the unpleasant as pleasant,
does so by means of the power of energy— known as the restraint of energy— as described in the passage beginning, "He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire."

He dispels that perversion. The third [type of person], whose view is perverted by regarding the impermanent as "permanent," penetrates, through the power of concentration and by virtue of being concentrated, the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as it truly is.

The fourth [type of person], whose view is perverted by regarding what is non-self as "self" within the mere heap of phenomena such as contact—which, due to the density and variety of the continuity, collection, function, and object, appears as a solid mass—[penetrates this] by means of mental attention to the emptiness of the fourfold analysis.

He shatters that false adherence. Furthermore, in this context, the entire unwholesome side should be understood by way of the four perversions, the four taints, the floods, the yokes, the ties, the destinations, the arising of craving, the kinds of clinging, the seven stations of consciousness, and the lack of full understanding.

Likewise, the entire side of purification should be understood by way of the four foundations of mindfulness, the fourfold abiding in jhāna, the states conducive to happiness, the immeasurables, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and so forth.
And here is the application of the Truths: through the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure—or indeed through all four perversions—the Truth of Origination is established;
the five aggregates of clinging, which serve as their basis and object, are the Truth of Suffering; the non-occurrence of these is the Truth of Cessation;
and the realization of that cessation, consisting of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, is the Truth of the Path. This is the side of defilement in relation to the perversions.

It is the ground for the method of the Lion’s Play (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*), which has the characteristic of leading [the mind] by way of the application to the Four Truths through the purification-side of the faculties beginning with faith (*saddhindriya*).
As it is said: “He who leads away from the perversions by means of the faculties, [establishing] the defilements in the True Dhamma,” and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the two methods of the Direction-Scanning Hook (*disālocana-aṅkusanaya*).

Thus, with the establishment of these three methods of meaning (*atthanaya*), the two methods of conventional expression (*vohāranaya*) are also necessarily established. For indeed, the method of "surveying the directions" (*disālocananaya*) is simply the examination of those phenomena that constitute the directions of the three methods of meaning.

The method of "the goad" (*aṅkusanaya*) is simply the bringing together of those [phenomena]. Therefore, according to the aforementioned method, those two methods should also be applied by way of the method of surveying the phenomena that constitute the directions of the methods of meaning.
Therefore it was said: "In the grammatical treatises, those [terms] that are wholesome or unwholesome," and so forth. This is the application of the five methods.
The commentary on the fivefold method is concluded.
The commentary on the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*.

Furthermore, this discourse belongs to the section on defilement, purification, and the state of one beyond training (*saṃkilesa-vāsanā-sekkha-bhāgiya*) among the sixteenfold *sāsana-paṭṭhāna*, because it analyzes the defilements such as craving and views, the meritorious deeds of virtue and so forth, and the aggregates of virtue and so forth of one beyond training.

Alternatively, it belongs specifically to the section on defilement, purification, penetration, and the state of one beyond training, because it analyzes the aforementioned meanings, such as the aggregate of virtue of one in training (*sekha*). However, within the twenty-eightfold [classification]...

In the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*, there is the mundane and supramundane, the seven categories of phenomena as the basis, knowledge and the knowable, seeing and development, our own words and the words of others, what is to be answered and what is not to be answered, karma and its result, the wholesome and the unwholesome, what is permitted and what is prohibited, and existence;
for the meanings of the mundane, supramundane, and so forth, are analyzed here. This is the exposition of the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*.
The commentary on the method of the *Pakaraṇa* is concluded.

Thus ends the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which elucidates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend; which generates a vast and stainless clarity of wisdom;
and which was composed by one endowed with the qualities of integrity, gentleness, modesty, faith, mindfulness, fortitude, intelligence, patience, energy, and other such virtues.
This is the *Līnatthavibhāvanā*, an exposition of the hidden meanings of the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, composed by the Elder Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati—
a great preceptor and eminent grammarian who possessed unimpeded, unshakeable, and confident wisdom, who plunged into the dense thickets of his own and other systems in their many varieties,
and who was the venerable teacher of the Great Dhammarājādhirāja— within his work titled *Sādhuvilāsini*, which elucidates the meaning of the Three Baskets together with their commentaries.
The commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta is finished.
The first part is finished.
